I first played PERISH in 2023, and I instantly hated it. At the time, I just couldn't get over the constantly respawning enemies, unclear objectives, and floaty movement. However, when I heard about their new game, DEFICIT, I decided to give PERISH another shot.
This time, I managed to play through it and, while I didn't get the "good" ending, I'd say I experienced everything the game has to offer. And this time, I actually had fun. I don't know what changed, perhaps I did. I was more patient and wanted to give PERISH a fair shake since I'd always loved its art style and setting.
Once you become familiar with PERISH's mechanics and objectives, it turns into a pretty fun, if flawed, roguelike. The most important thing is to keep moving, minimize the damage you take, and avoid exploring too much. Just focus on the objectives, or the enemies will wear you down, since they never stop spawning.
Your success depends heavily on the luck of the draw, as it should in a roguelike. Some upgrades become incredibly powerful and can carry you through the game, but I feel some hitboxes are simply unfair. Learning through failure is very much the name of the game here.
As I mentioned, I love the art style, and the locations are gorgeous. I just wish there were more opportunities to explore them. With the constant enemy spawns and the overall chaos of the battlefield, that's rarely possible. The worst offender is the Forges of Hephaestus, which is absolutely relentless.
I'm giving PERISH a thumbs up, but it's more of a "middle thumb." It's a very flawed roguelike, but what it lacks in gameplay it makes up for with stunning visuals and atmosphere. If you can put up with the problems this game has, or get a buddy to play in co-op, it can be a pretty fun game.
I think these are some extremely talented devs, which is why I'm excited for DEFICIT. I want to see what they learned from the development of PERISH, and I'm kind of hoping they go back to the world and art style of PERISH to make a better game.

PERISH, developed by ITEM42 and published by HandyGames, presents itself as a grim and stylized first-person shooter that merges roguelite design with a heavy dose of Greek mythological influence. From the moment the game begins, it establishes a stark and unforgiving tone, placing players in a desolate purgatorial realm where the only path forward is through relentless combat and calculated risk-taking. Rather than offering a traditional narrative-driven experience, PERISH focuses on a cyclical journey of struggle and progression, reinforcing the idea that advancement must be earned through repeated trials.

The central gameplay loop revolves around venturing into hostile territories, battling waves of enemies, and collecting a currency known as danake. This resource is crucial, as it allows players to acquire stronger weapons and upgrades that improve their chances in future runs. However, the game’s defining mechanic lies in how fragile that progress is. If a player falls in battle before securing their earnings, everything accumulated during that run is lost. This creates a constant tension between greed and caution, encouraging players to weigh their decisions carefully. The result is a gameplay rhythm that feels intense and deliberate, where every encounter carries meaningful consequences.

Combat in PERISH is designed to be fast, aggressive, and demanding. Players are expected to stay mobile, manage their positioning, and make effective use of a varied arsenal that includes both melee and ranged options. Weapons can be enhanced to suit different playstyles, offering some flexibility in how encounters are approached. The enemies, drawn from distorted mythological inspirations, are numerous and often overwhelming, forcing players to stay alert and adapt quickly. While the shooting mechanics themselves are solid and responsive, the game leans more on encounter design and pressure rather than innovation in core gunplay to maintain engagement.

One of the game’s strongest aspects is its cooperative multiplayer. Supporting up to four players, PERISH becomes significantly more dynamic when experienced with others. Team-based play introduces new strategic layers, such as coordinating attacks, managing shared threats, and reviving fallen allies in the middle of chaotic battles. The difficulty scaling encourages cooperation without completely sidelining solo players, but the overall design clearly benefits from group play. The shared tension of risking collected resources and the satisfaction of surviving a difficult encounter together make co-op sessions particularly rewarding.

Visually, PERISH stands out through its distinctive interpretation of a mythological afterlife. The environments are bleak and oppressive, featuring crumbling ruins, scorched landscapes, and surreal architecture that reinforces the sense of being trapped in a realm between worlds. The art direction prioritizes atmosphere over technical complexity, using bold contrasts and stylized elements to create a memorable identity. While the graphics are not cutting-edge, they effectively support the game’s tone and contribute to its immersive quality.

Despite its strengths, the game is not without flaws. The roguelite structure can lead to repetition, especially during longer play sessions or for those tackling the experience alone. Enemy variety and environmental changes, while present, may not always feel substantial enough to keep the experience consistently fresh. Additionally, the unforgiving progression system can become frustrating, as repeated failures may leave players feeling like they are not making meaningful progress. These elements can limit the game’s appeal, particularly for those who prefer a more forgiving or steadily rewarding system.

Ultimately, PERISH is a focused and atmospheric shooter that thrives on tension, risk, and persistence. It does not attempt to cater to everyone, instead committing to a design philosophy that emphasizes challenge and deliberate progression. Its combination of mythological themes, cooperative gameplay, and high-stakes mechanics gives it a unique place within the genre, even if its execution is not always perfectly balanced.

In the end, PERISH offers a compelling experience for players who enjoy demanding gameplay and cooperative challenges, though its repetitive elements and punishing systems may deter a broader audience. It is a game that rewards patience and teamwork, delivering moments of intensity and satisfaction for those willing to embrace its design.

PERISH is a first-person roguelike shooter that is, sadly, so mediocre in so many aspects that it's hard to recommend to anyone. There are good ideas here and there, but unfortunately, none of them are implemented in a particularly good or fun way.

Let me explain:

1. The Gameplay

The core gameplay becomes stale disappointingly fast. Each run follows the same level layout and room order, with only minor objective variations that fail to make different attempts feel significantly different. The perk system doesn’t help with this issue. The perks don’t offer major changes and the variety is quite low, meaning you'll have seen more or less everything the perk system has to offer within 3-4 runs. The lack of variety quickly leads to boredom.

The boredom is also paired with janky combat and significant quality-of-life pitfalls. The game is a FPS so you’d expect the weapons to feel good, but their handling feels meh. There's no ammo counter or any HUD info for ranged weapons, and melee combat feels like a last minute addition, with encounters clearly designed for ranged attacks. While the weapon variety is okay (from guns to special gimmick weapons) none of them feel cool to use. They range from being bland to being unrewarding to play with.

The enemies themselves are quite braindead and there is very little variety. You're going to see the common footsoldier from the first room to the last, with other enemy types only appearing here and there. The worst part is that the enemies aren't really smart, so you're never challenged when dealing with them.

2. The Artsy Stuff

The one area where PERISH undeniably succeeds is in its graphics. The game is visually stunning, with distinct and interesting areas that made me eager to see what came next. The enemy designs are also excellent.

However, this visual polish is superficial. The areas feel like disconnected concept art pieces rather than parts of a cohesive world. They don't flow together and lack a unifying spirit. Similarly, the enemy designs, while cool to look at, feel generic and forgettable. This is the perfect case study for why a strong, consistent and personalized art style is more important than high-fidelity graphics alone.

TL;DR:
PERISH might look visually great, but it's ultimately too generic, janky, and undercooked to be worth recommending. The repetitive gameplay, clunky combat, and lack of interesting visual make it a missed opportunity.
It's flawed, but really fun. Looks awesome and the weapons are great.

This game might be fun in co-op, but as a single-player experience it isn't very satisfying. I can't go into the story because to be honest it bored me after about an hour, and cracks in the game-play were already pretty apparent by this point.

Essentially it's a rogue-like mixture of first-person shooting and melee  set in the Greek underworld. Though calling it a shooter isn't quite true, as you only begin the game with a limited amount of throwing daggers for ranged attacks. You can get a gun but it requires progressing through the stages and finding the weapon, then purchasing it from a shop..

So you begin the game with a melee attack, a block, a kick and throwing knives. You then find a modest selection of buffs that add status effects to your attacks, as well as earn money to buy upgrades. Upon death you lose your money and these buffs, which is great if you like being stuck with basic things over and over again, but not so great if, you know, you don't. I don't.

You keep repeating the same basic areas over and over again with the same basic weapons, albeit with occasionally interesting things like the ability to cast lightning strikes upon enemies or boot them into spikes. Initially it is fun but you then notice how simple it is and that there's very little progression in the environments. Or things like killing the enemies gives very little reward due to them respawning so you may as well just run past them. 

If you like repeating the same three environments over and over and over again (even though they are reasonably designed, albeit very short), with the same enemy types over and over and over again, then you'll think this great. I don't. If you like enemies that teleport in every 5 seconds and don't mind the fact they can do it right in front of you, or right behind you, then you'll think this is great. I don't.

This stuff might work in co-op when you have someone watching your back, but in single-player it makes the game really irritating. One of the stages had me escorting a ballista that I had to stay in contact with to complete the mission, and it was impossible as enemies simultaneously teleported in front of me and from behind and then killed me in seconds. 

Even if you ignore how pathetic the design is in general, it doesn't seem at all considered for one person to play. Maybe they expect you to grind and grind the "levels" (such as they are and how limited they are) to gets buff and upgrades, and then approach certain "levels".  To me that kind of emphasis is boring, not to mention cheap design.

Having experienced this aspect of the game I thought I'd check out the "campaign". This campaign is something they advise you not to start until you're beefed up a bit, but I jumped in anyway and my advice is just don't play it at all. The "campaign" is even more simplistic dog-sh*t: the first area I started in was a bunch of bland corridors with exactly the same game-play but worse level design.

A constant stream of enemies teleporting into cramped locations with very little effort put into how it was arranged. How exciting! I flicked three switches and then got to the end, at which point I had to fend off a wave of enemies. Exactly like all the other elements that weren't in the "campaign", but this time it was topped off by having to battle three re-used "bosses" in an area with barely the room to swing a dead mouse, never-mind a dead cat. 

That's not my idea of a campaign. it's my idea of a poorly put-together load of old crap in a naff attempt at giving this title some content. Even the non-campaign stuff was a wee bit more inspired than this with environmental traps and actual space to move around in. After an hour to make an impression it had failed miserably.

There's a nice feel to the action, it runs quite well and has passable voice-acting. Yet for all that it has a reasonable foundation to build upon, the end result is repetitive and bland. Playing it with other people might mitigate the flaws in balancing that become apparent in single-player, but repeating three tiny maps over and over again would still be boring regardless of having someone accompanying me.

And you lose all connected cards and resurrected with 1 health bar. I see most people complaining about it and I was too. But then I sort of got used to it and it works for us. This is the death penalty, and it actually motivates you to move forward because you don't have much money to "bank" in the hub, so there is no reason interrupt the journey to go back to hub as you don't have much money to "bank". And absence of revival adds additional tension to the game loop as it's actually painful :). Well, as I said, once we got used to the rules of this game, I did not have any problems with it and was enjoying our intense run-throughs. Lastly, the weapons, enemies, and fight mechanics are actually quite good and very satisfying. I love the veriaty of weapons available to you as you progress though the game. Each of the weapons is unique and requires its own still set and loadout of rings, crowns, and consumables. And I loved practically each of them. Ok, there were few that I liked the most of course :). So, what we have at the end - the game mechanics are great, game loop takes some time to get used to, bugs are still there and devs seem to abandon the game and dont' plan to fix them. I'd give it 6 out of 10. If they fix the bugs, it will be 8 out of 10. And by the way, while the game is supposed to be cross play between Steam, Epic and GOG, GOG version is very outdated and is not compatible with Steam and Epic in multiplayer. And the devs do not care to update GOG version for more than a year, which tells you a lot about support for this game. Decide for yourself, I'm still playing it :).

I'm not doing my usual format for Perish, because there is so much to talk about in greater detail, I feel simple bullet points would not get across what kind of game this is. Because Perish is really cool, and I feel a lot of people don't understand what it is and what it's going for.

Perish is a very weird and interesting game, and honestly it's quite hard to nail down what it really is, but I'll do my best to explain what I think it is. Perish is basically what you get if you take Elderborn, Painkiller and a small dash of Hades and put it in a blender. But it also comes with a surprising dose of NES-inspired approach to difficulty design; with constantly respawning enemies, limited health points based on number of hits you can take, having a true ending in a fashion similar to games like Ghosts 'n Goblins, but it's all wrapped up in really shiny modern visuals with a pretty excellent Greek mythology-inspired underworld aesthetic, with lots of gold.

However, I feel Perish is not really a roguelite, as it lacks a lot of the elements like random levels, crazy synergies and such to warrant being called one. It does have upgrades between runs and has some random elements, like enemy spawns, the objectives you need to complete in said levels and the upgrades and powerups you get per run, but you are still running through the same levels in the same order.

The combat loop is a bit strange, but very satisfying. A lot of the time you can run through a lot of the levels and can even ignore enemies, but there will be certain objectives that force you to engage in the game's combat system and it is a lot of fun. You start out finding basic melee weapons, which have a slash and a block, pretty straight forward. However you're given other tools; a dash to evade enemy attacks, a kick to knock enemies down or off ledges and into traps, a consumable item of your choice, but also throwing daggers to deal with enemies from afar and can be powered up to be extremely formidable.

The game also has firearms and other magical and ancient ranged weaponry to find, which are incredibly powerful, dishing out way more damage way faster than even the strongest melee weapons in the game, and can make problematic enemies a breeze from afar. However, you can only carry one weapon, and by choosing to use ranged weapons you complete forgo your ability to block, meaning you lose a great deal of defensive capabilities, and enemies are more than happy to sneak up behind you. While melee weapons aren't as powerful damage-wise, that block makes them an invaluable option for skilled players who want to stay in the fight, as a block will protect you from literally every source of damage all around you, not just in front of you, plus granting you a couple of seconds of invincibility after a successful block thus making them just as viable in the grand scheme of the game's combat.

So depending on the situation, the enemy types and the objective; choosing the correct weapons that you unlocked can be the difference between life and death, as certain enemies are weak to ranged or melee and some objectives are easier with certain weapon types. So the combat seems very simple on the surface, but with multiple playthroughs, it's easy to see the game has more depth than it originally lets on.

However the right tools for the job, being your upgrades and acquired weapons and trinkets, will not apply if you're going for the true ending. To obtain the true ending, the game forces you to use the starting weapon, the starting consumable and deliberately forgoing all your crowns and rings and other upgrades you've accumulated over your playthrough. This is where the real NES-inspired mastery of the game comes into play, you need the know the game inside and out, know how to deal with every enemy, how to accomplish every objective on each level as fast as possible, how to properly manage your health and to plan your powerups in the run for the long term in order to achieve victory. The game becomes truly relentless and being stuck with such harsh limitations and having your character back to square one can be incredibly daunting.

Luckily all is not lost, as you have likely found all the orphic fragments in previous runs using upgrades and powerful weaponry, if you're the exploratory type of player. If given to the right NPC, your starting weapon becomes a powerhouse of a sword and also increases the power of your throwing daggers. making it a tool that's more than capable of achieving a win, so long as you're using every tool that you are allowed to use as best as you possibly can.

Getting that win on my orphic run was absolutely exhilarating, my heart pounding and hands even shaking a little when I finally beat the final boss, which is a real bugger of a fight. Getting to finally step into Elysium and getting that true ending definitely hit me harder than I expected.

I also have to give a ton of praise to the soundtrack and sound design. The music is genuinely fantastic, taking a lot of those ancient Greek motifs you often hear in a lot of other games and movies sharing similar themes and then mixing those together with some really crunchy heavy metal tunes. It's a weird and interesting mix and it absolutely rocks.

As for the sound design, it's also great; guns feel so punchy and powerful, slashing enemies with your melee weapons feels visceral as heck, and the sound you hear when you get a confirmed kill is always so satisfying the hear. The sound is also great for telling you what's happening around you and picking out sounds in the heat of a fight can be the difference between life and death. It is pretty great the game does that so well, even with hard tunes blasting in your ear.

All that gushing aside, I do have some gripes with Perish. My biggest issue by far is the second chapter of the game, I feel it should have been the final chapter, because it has by far the most dangerous enemies in the game by a really significant margin, along with huge levels filled to the brim with hazards. The most common enemy in said chapter is one that's insanely fast in running speed and attack animations, is nearly invincible when attacked in the body, is immune to fire damage and can only reliably be killed with headshots. They are very much overtuned. Other than that gripe, my second biggest issue is being unable to pause in a singleplayer session, which is really quite naff.

The others I have is mainly just some lack of visual polish in certain areas; things like a crusty texture here and there, the occasional small hole in level geometry where you can peak out of bounds, as well as some animations looking a bit rough and juddery at times. I do notice some areas can drop frames here and there, but it otherwise runs really well most of the time. I feel like the issues that a lot of other people seem to have with Perish don't really apply to me and is either a case of personal taste, or I just simply accepted Perish for what it is and met it halfway, in doing so I've come to love the game and really enjoy its eccentricities.

After completing Perish 100% last night I wanted to give this game a glowing review, because I feel it deserves a lot more love that it sadly never really got. It's a weird and strange game but is a huge load of fun and is really rewarding and punishing in equal measure. The game demands a lot from the player, and I was really happy to give my all for it, it was very much worth it in the end. It's also perfectly doable in solo, as almost all of my play sessions were singleplayer, with the rare session with randos in my earlier hours in the game, and it's great fun in both modes.

If you like Greek mythology stuff, horde shooters/slashers, banger soundtracks and games with really weird and eccentric game design, give Perish a go. It might take a bit of time and getting used to, but it's well worth the asking price once it clicks with you.

The last few levels are a highlight but this isn't a game where you can say "yeah but it gets better" because the rest of the game still falls short.

In the levels there is a random objective but for most levels it's one of three things, by far the worst type is where you collect a thing such as a log or torch and that's now your weapon: a slow moving stick that you have to maneuver with around enemies. It could be engaging if the movement system wasn't bog standard but it's just a drag that stops you from killing enemies effectively. Other objectives are to collect components and survive an oncoming hoard which is expected from this kind of game.

Combat is standard to bad, melee is hack and slash with fun looking weapons locked behind challenges and secrets but there are guns in the game that enemies don't know how to react to, you can have a shotgun and they will run in a straight line to you running slower than you are so you can basically walk around them and not take damage while mowing them down. A pistol is the third weapon unlock, once you get this, the game might as well be over. It's not as good as the revolver from something like Overwatch as it's quite slow and has a delay after you've reloaded but it's a one shot on most enemies in it's non upgraded form. Upgrades as unlocked via challenges which are mostly 'get x number of kills'. The sniper has 'get x number of kills with one bullet' but they all follow that pattern. No damage buffs but they get a new function or attachment. 

There's a card perk system which feels a bit tacked on, some are faster animations, more move speed etc, some are neat like throwing daggers may spawn spears that spawn from beneath the enemy or daggers may explode but there are some which are "Stare at enemy for chance of fatal poisoning" or "Chance to spawn puddle which may lead to a fatal fall" which are powerful but don't quite make sense or give a good visual effect that indicate it's the perk taking effect, just the enemy falling over which is comical yet sad.

Respawning in co-op is another area that leaves much to be desired. Respawning comes with a steep penalty of losing half your money which again, is expected in a Roguelike/lite but in co-op, if one person dies they then lose all of their perks and will continuously lose money upon each respawn. I had a run where we were onto the second act and at the boss, on one health point, the fall breaks and I immediately fall into the bosses flamethrower dying before I get a chance to react. Very unfair, my mate beats this boss and I'm now behind in movement speed and killing effectiveness and 2/3rds of my money was lost. The game isn't necessarily hard once you have a shotgun so we still won without fast reload, instant poison kills via looking in the general direction and dropping insta kill puddles but it was very frustrating. This punitive system feels overly harsh and can sour the multiplayer experience, which is a core reason of why we bought Perish.

Boss fights are lame. Big enemy that's slow. The design of the boss from the end of act one was ok, there was the boss at the end of act 3 which was a big crab and one which was a large stone wall with a bell. Overall, 4/10. It's so uninspired that I don't feel the need to talk about it, it feels like a non feature.

Cosmetically, the music is very short and on a loop, I began to notice it within the first hour and turned it off. Graphics are ugly, it's another game in Unreal Engine. I liked the Forge and port locations but I don't have any positives regarding the looks of the other levels. UI is lackluster. The main menu has video and audio in the same tab for some reason. The tips (As are many in these types of game) pointless. 

The game in rogue lite mode took 3 hours to beat, we then we played the other mode which was horrendous, it's small sets of rooms (maybe templates?) that just throw enemies at you, there's an NPC that talks to you but we quit the game as this was so boring.

Perish is a game with great potential, it fuses roguelite genre with FPS zombie/zed shooter, along with ancient Greek Mythology, 3 of my favorite things.
With that being said, the game is very early stage, in order to be an enjoyable experience for everyone, they need to patch a lot of stuff.

[u] Positives [/u]
-Weapon Design
-Enemy Design
-Level design
-Audio design
-Voice acting
-Soundtrack
-Boss design

There isn't much I could say in detail about the positive stuff, but I think I need to point out some of the bad stuff.
[h3] RogueLite/Like Experience [/h3]
The game is supposed to be roguelite/like, but the only element that reminds me of that is the card selection when you finish an objective, and even then, there are only a few cards so you end up seeing the same thing after a while. Everything else is set up and the same thing, variety isn't coming from levels and different rooms but from items and upgrades.
Oh, there are also 2-3 different objectives for each level which are random in every run, but still..After 2-3 replays you've seen everything. 
I could see past that, it's not like this game is meant to be played for the eternity, but the problem is, to justify the lack of replay value they added a HUGE difficulty spike after the second boss. Enemies will spawn nonstop, they are bulky and fast as all hell, and of course after a certain level, ranged enemies are introduced (I know acolytes spawn in the 2nd level of the game, but they are really low on numbers and not dangerous at all, and they also die in 1 hit). The game needs to rely on actual creativity instead of artificial difficulty, throwing me 20 enemies at once that need 2 hits from the strongest weapon to die, will make my run not enjoyable to say the least.

[h3] Ranged Weapons [/h3]
They are completely useless after the second boss encounter (some even before it). So, melee weapons provide you with close range combat and a block option. Perfectly balanced right? Maybe, you can block even ranged attacks but you need to engage in close quarter fights, seems fair to me.
What ranged weapons provide you with though? You cannot block, so someone would guess they deal massive damage? Well, no. Super Shotgun cannot kill anything after the second boss, yes you heard right, one of the strongest weapons in gaming can't do much against some robots and crabs. 

There are a few other problems, like bugs and bad optimization here and there, but nothing too important to point out, my 2 biggest complains are the ones mentioned.
All in all the game has great potential, they really need to invest more in that roguelite/like idea, make rooms randomly generated, add more cards, more levels etc.
Worth the price? No, buy it on sale.

[b] Overall [/b]
6/10

The only aspect I prefer Terraria over Starbound on is having a functional map, which counts for something because losing your stuff in an underground labyrinth sucks.

[h1]Exploration[/h1]
Starbound has more interesting pre-designed locations (probably from those volunteers) than Terraria. You can wander into interesting looking NPC cities/villages which differ by race, prisons, laboratories, temples, etc, which are actually pretty cool to explore compared to Terraria’s lifeless wasteland and few “Treasure Rooms”. These locations really inspire creativity, right before I make another rectangular wooden box as base. Starbound NPCs maintain a better illusion of living in their location over Terraria’s cavalcade of dipsh!ts who show up out of nowhere demanding you build a house for them, or at least they’re constantly stealing my bedroom without permission. 

Starbound Biomes are more varied and visually interesting, whereas Terraria’s world generation is rather predictable: start in grasslands, deserts and jungles somewhere left or right, oceans at left and rightmost borders that doesn’t loop around, red/purple jam corrupted area somewhere. Starbound has more varied planet types to explore at increasing tiers of difficulty based on what kind of star the system is around.

Travelling through space to different planets is more diagetic than creating a new world on the main menu, having to check on fuel, having different star types being part of progression.

Matter Manipulator beats having to carry the axe, pickaxe, and hammer separately; upgrading MM with modules beats making a new tool out of a higher tier metal that I might be hoarding for something else.

[h1]Combat[/h1]
Terraria has a lot of uninteresting hitboxes moving towards you (walk, fly or hop). Starbound also have those, but also has enemies that turtle or phase out of existence after a single hit, incentivizing slow but big hitting weapons like rocket launchers sometimes. Starbound also have humanoid enemies using similar weaponry to those you have access to, which aren’t that interesting or complex to fight, but it is variety. 

Starbound tends to give you an interesting variety of weapon faster and more frequently than Terraria, where you may be stuck with limited arsenal for extended periods of time.

In Terraria, you don’t need to pay that much attention to health or mana after you’ve hoarded a bunch of the max hp/mp boosts. In Starbound, health is only augmented by equipment defense, and your mana/energy also functions as your ammunition capacity, so you go through a period of firing before a recharge period.

Bosses in Starbound comes in an unmodifiable premade arena in quests that you choose to take part in; whereas in Terraria bosses may pop out of nowhere regardless of whether you want to engage with it or not, and people commonly build a makeshift arena in the sky because combat mobility without it kind of sucks. 

Erchius Horror is a slightly more interesting as a first boss compared to the Eye of Cthulu – a floating bulletsponge hitbox that summons smaller eyeballs that are also floating hitboxes, before the second phase where the boss itself charges at you with its own hitbox. Ironically a boring big bulletsponge eyeball that summon minions is Starbound’s last boss. I also found the Nymph somewhere underground in Terraria, and it’s disappointingly just another zombie with a bigger health pool.

This game has soooooo much potential. It’s gotten to the point where I leave it running on my PC during the day and connect through Steam Link from work. I love it...I’m addicted. For what it does well, it’s a 5/5 game for me.

I’ve played 237 hours at the time of this review. Obviously, a lot of that is background idling while sleeping or working, but that also means the game has essentially been running nonstop on my PC since release.

The problem is that it doesn’t yet do some of the things it really needs to do. I’m still giving it a thumbs up because I want people to play it and I want the game to succeed, but as of right now I think it is simultaneously one of the best games in its genre and one of the most painful.

I want to min-max the absolute crap out of this game. I genuinely think there are hundreds, maybe thousands, of hours of potential here. The systems are deep enough that I find myself experimenting with builds, comparing damage, changing priorities, testing breakpoints, and trying to squeeze every little bit of performance out of a character. That part is fantastic.

And I’ve had to learn most of it the hard way.

I’ve hit wall after wall throughout the game, and every time I hit one I’ve had to figure out what I misunderstood, what part of the build stopped scaling, what I should have invested in differently, and sometimes completely respec just to keep progressing. That process is actually one of the things I enjoy about the game. I like figuring out why something worked for 20 levels and suddenly doesn’t anymore.

At the time of this review, I’ve cleared level 235. The current record is 250 by Haqua. So I’m already pretty deep into the game, but I’m still finding new things I misunderstood about the systems and still changing the build as I learn how everything interacts.

The problem is that experimentation becomes physically and mechanically painful.

Respec costs need some attention...honestly, almost all of them. At higher levels, changing things becomes incredibly expensive, which discourages experimentation in a game that practically begs you to experiment. I’m now at the point where fully respeccing requires 500+ clicks.

Then your hand slips on the mouse, or you’re playing remotely on your phone, and you accidentally click something you didn’t want. Now the build is screwed up and you get to start fixing it all over again.

At some point I realized I’m not even competing against the game anymore. I’m competing against myself and my ability to never accidentally click something I’m not supposed to click.

I would love to see some kind of lock system where you can lock individual skills, talents, symbols, rings, or upgrades so they cannot be accidentally selected. This would be especially helpful on the first tab where you are buying skills with gold, but honestly I would like to be able to lock almost anything.

After thinking about it more, though, the easiest solution may simply be allowing individual respecs instead of forcing a full reset. If I made one bad choice, let me undo that one choice instead of having to redo every single choice since the beginning.

This is especially true in the Skills tab, where there are more than 150 nodes, and some of those nodes need to be clicked three, four, or even a dozen times each. One accidental click shouldn’t mean rebuilding the entire thing from scratch.

And BTW...this is even more true in the Ring system than anywhere else. If I decide I want to move away from Ring of Fury and try something completely different, I can be looking at 1,000+ clicks just to redistribute those points. That makes experimenting with another ring build something I almost don’t want to try, even though experimenting and figuring out what works is one of the best parts of the game.

That becomes especially frustrating because respeccing isn’t something I’ve done once or twice because I was bored. I’ve had to do it repeatedly as I’ve pushed higher, hit another wall, learned something new about how the game works, and realized that a decision I made 50 or 100 levels ago was holding the build back. That kind of learning and rebuilding should be encouraged, because it is where a huge amount of the game’s depth comes from.

And yes...I’m going to play the disabled veteran card here. 😉 My hands only have so many clicks in them each day. Requiring hundreds, or in some cases more than a thousand, repetitive clicks just to rebuild a character is legitimately uncomfortable after a while. Accessibility aside, though, I think almost everyone would benefit from fewer repetitive clicks and more precise control over respeccing.

I’d also love to see a prestige system that is on par with the rest of the game. There is already so much depth in building and optimizing a character that starting over could actually be something I look forward to if there were a meaningful long-term progression system attached to it. Give me a reason to push as far as I possibly can, reset, come back stronger, make different choices, and then see how much farther I can get the next time. This game feels almost built for that kind of loop, and a deep prestige system could add hundreds or thousands of hours to it.

There are a few other quality-of-life things I’d love to see too. The game generates a lot of files while you play, including what appear to be per-level files, and after multiple runs they can really clutter the same folder as the combat logs. Giving those their own subfolder, or automatically cleaning up anything that is no longer needed, would help a lot.

Despite all of that, I have continued playing this since launch. BTW...Valheim just launched too, and I’m playing that and this simultaneously, but Monday through Friday this is basically the only thing I play.

That probably says more than anything else I could write. I’ve already put 237 hours into it, I’m still thinking about builds when I’m not playing, I’ve pushed to 235 when the current record is 250, and I’ve literally been remotely connecting to my PC from work to check on it.

There is an insanely good game in here. A few changes around respeccing, accidental clicks, experimentation costs, prestige, and general quality of life would take it from “I love this game even though it hurts me” to something I could recommend without hesitation.

As someone who uses Sketchup to create houses etc from scratch for fun, this game seemed very intriguing. I really love the idea of this game, and the prompts, but the execution of functions during building creation need some tweaks. I have spent 16 hours on this game already, and I have completed 2 projects and maybe 25% of another due to functional issues during the creative process.

There are a couple things I hope that are fixed ASAP within the game that create a LOT of frustration when trying to create homes: 

1. If I choose to move an existing wall or draw a new wall and they happen to be near another wall, it will not allow me to move that wall where I want to for no reason (for example, if an East to West wall has a wall joining its north face at 10', and I want to draw a wall starting from the 11-12' mark on the south face, it will not let me even if nothing is in the way. It will turn red, and refuse to let me create a wall within 3'3"~ 4' of the wall that is adjoined on the opposite side. It also randomly refuses to let me divide rooms at certain points, again saying there is an error with distances. It also will decide to not allow walls partially in the room unless they are at really odd angles for no reason, which I will get into more later). There is no logical reason why I would not be able to put a wall within less than 4' of a wall on the opposite side of the adjoining wall. That needs to be fixed asap because it creates a lot of redoing/ frustration for no reason and doubles/triples the time it takes to get the base of the house drawn.

2. If I turn snap off, it will not actually turn off EXCEPT for objects. When snap is turned "off" while attempting to create walls/ structures, it will not turn off even if it says it is off.

2b. Speaking on that, if I turn snap onto angles, it will sometimes decide to snap to 90 degrees. However, most of the time it randomly decides to snap to 89 degrees, 64 degrees, 140 degrees, etc, and will refuse at all costs to do a 90 degree angle on a wall. When I turn snap off, it will again not turn off and continue to snap to random angles no matter what. It is beyond frustrating, because again it will turn red and tell me for no logical reason that I cannot put a 90 degree wall there. Again, nothing in its way, just deciding that other walls across the structure in different rooms somehow dictate that this wall must be a weird random angle for no reason.

3. I cannot draw a wall across an existing object, but objects are allowed to have their edges slightly phase through walls when they are placed..... makes no sense. In my opinion, to avoid a lot of those errors, all objects should be allowed to phase through objects to optimize creativity options (ESPECIALLY when it comes to cabinets in the kitchen, shelving, etc. No corner cabinets for floor or walls creates a lot of issues visually and functionally).

4. No corner kitchen cabinets for walls or floors. There is a "corner" shelf that has no 90 degree angles, so it never actually fits anywhere

5. TIp: Allow objects to be shrunk and enlarged by certain percentages to allow more creative freedom.

6. Tip: Appliances, toilets, showers, baths, tvs, and "extra"s in general should still cost money. That is apart of the challenge of meeting budgets. I recommend increasing the budget to more "real" amounts that people are paying for the houses and provide a more realistic experience in regards to budgeting for kitchen, bathroom, and otherwise items (cheap shower vs nice shower, cheap toilet vs nice toilet). It is confusing that that is done for some things but not others.

Architect Life: A House Design Simulator is a creative building and management simulation developed by Shine Research and published by Nacon. The game places players in the role of a professional architect responsible for designing, planning, and supervising the construction of modern residential homes. Unlike many design-focused simulation titles that concentrate mainly on interior decoration, this game attempts to simulate the entire architectural process from the initial concept phase all the way to the final completed building. Through a combination of creative building tools, project management mechanics, and client-driven objectives, the game provides a comprehensive look at the work involved in designing and constructing houses while still maintaining a gameplay structure accessible to players without architectural training.

The central component of the experience is its career mode, where players establish and manage their own architectural firm. Starting with relatively small projects and modest budgets, players gradually build their reputation by completing residential commissions for various clients. Each project begins with a set of requirements provided by the client, including preferences for room types, aesthetic styles, available budget, and sometimes specific environmental constraints tied to the building site. These conditions influence how players approach each design, requiring them to balance creativity with practicality. As projects are successfully completed, the architectural firm gains recognition and unlocks larger and more complex construction opportunities, allowing players to gradually tackle increasingly ambitious designs.

The design system itself forms the backbone of the gameplay. Players begin by shaping the structural layout of the house, creating floor plans by placing walls and defining rooms in a flexible 3D construction interface. The system allows for detailed control over building dimensions, including wall placement, ceiling height, roof structure, and window positioning. Roofs can be customized with different slopes and shapes, while doors, staircases, and architectural features can be carefully integrated into the layout. This planning stage requires players to consider not only visual appeal but also the functionality of the living space, ensuring that rooms connect logically and that the overall design remains comfortable and practical.

Once the structural layout has been finalized, the focus shifts toward interior design and customization. Players can select from a wide range of materials and furnishings to give each room its own character. Flooring options, wall textures, lighting fixtures, furniture arrangements, and decorative objects allow players to create homes that reflect a variety of architectural styles, from modern minimalist houses to cozy family residences. The system encourages attention to detail, allowing players to fine-tune color palettes and spatial arrangements in order to craft cohesive interiors that match the client’s expectations.

Beyond the interior, exterior design and landscaping also play an important role in shaping each project. Players can develop outdoor spaces that complement the architecture of the house by adding gardens, patios, terraces, swimming pools, garages, and other amenities. The game includes different environments and terrain types, meaning that houses may be built in diverse settings such as suburban neighborhoods, rural countryside landscapes, or mountainous regions. Designing homes that integrate well with their surroundings becomes an important creative challenge, especially when terrain features influence how the structure must be positioned.

Another significant aspect of the simulation involves overseeing the construction phase of the project. Once the design is approved, players must manage the building process by hiring subcontractors and allocating the available budget carefully. Construction does not always proceed perfectly, and unexpected issues can arise that require adjustments to the project plan. Managing these situations effectively becomes part of the challenge, as players must ensure that the project remains within budget while still meeting the client’s expectations. This layer of management adds depth to the gameplay, preventing the experience from being purely a creative sandbox and instead introducing elements of strategic decision-making.

Progression within the career mode unlocks additional building tools, materials, and architectural technologies. As players gain experience and reputation, they gain access to new construction options such as eco-friendly building systems, advanced materials, and more complex design features. These additions expand the range of possibilities available to players, allowing them to create increasingly sophisticated homes as their architectural firm grows.

For players who prefer unrestricted creativity, the game also offers a free build mode. In this mode, the constraints of client requests and budgets are removed, allowing players to design homes entirely according to their own imagination. Various terrain types and environmental settings can be selected, providing a sandbox environment where architectural experimentation becomes the primary focus. This mode is particularly appealing for players who enjoy construction and design tools without the pressure of completing structured objectives.

A particularly immersive feature of the game is the ability to explore completed houses from a first-person perspective. After finishing a project, players can walk through the interior and exterior spaces they created, experiencing the house as if they were physically visiting it. The lighting system allows players to adjust the position of the sun and observe how natural light interacts with different rooms throughout the day. This viewing mode enhances the sense of accomplishment by allowing players to appreciate the results of their design choices in a realistic spatial environment.

Visually, the game presents its environments with a clean and modern aesthetic that emphasizes architectural clarity. Buildings are rendered with realistic proportions and materials, allowing players to clearly see how their design decisions affect the final structure. Landscapes surrounding the houses add atmosphere and variety, with different environmental settings providing distinct backdrops for each project. While the graphics prioritize functionality rather than highly stylized visuals, they effectively support the creative focus of the gameplay.

The sound design is relatively subtle, providing a calm and relaxed atmosphere that complements the slow and thoughtful pace of architectural design. Background music remains unobtrusive, allowing players to concentrate on their projects without distraction. Sound effects associated with construction tools and environmental ambience add a sense of realism without overwhelming the player.

Overall, Architect Life: A House Design Simulator stands as an enjoyable entry in the construction simulation genre. Its blend of architectural design, project management, and creative freedom creates a gameplay experience that appeals to players who enjoy building and planning spaces. While it may not replicate every technical detail of real-world architecture, it captures the satisfaction of turning an empty plot of land into a thoughtfully designed home. For fans of creative simulation games and construction-focused gameplay, it offers a relaxing yet rewarding opportunity to step into the role of an architect and bring imaginative housing projects to life.

[i]……..why does this game even exist?[/i] [b]why did I spend actual money on it??[/b] and for the most baffling question [i]of them all, [b]why is it actually pretty good???[/b] [/i] Don’t get me wrong, I’m not trying to say that this is a [i]must play[/i] or a [i]hidden gem[/i] or [b]anything[/b] like that; all I’m trying to say is that [i]for what the game set out to be[/i], that being an [b]Exit 8[/b] parody with roughly a morbillion poop jokes, [b]Toilet 8[/b] ended up being an honest to goodness [i]spot the difference[/i] title that not only [i]runs properly[/i], but has plenty of content and is [i]kinda fun![/i] like, this obvious joke game somehow plays better than half its competition. [b]very stinky.[/b]


So, [i]yes[/i], [b]Toilet 8[/b] is [i]of course[/i] yet another [b]Exit 8[/b]-style “horror” game, following the exact formula as the other hundred or so nearly identical copycats (that’s not much of an exaggeration by the way; in fact, if anything, I’m [i]underexaggerating[/i]). Here we go again. (*ahem*) [b]YOU ARE TRAPPED IN.. TOILET! IF YOU DON’T SEE ANOMALY, GO FORWARD. BUT IF YOU [i]DO[/i] SEE ANOMALY, TURN BACK!!! AAAAA!! VERY SCARY!!! AAAA-ERGTFJLNE[/b]—[i]crap,[/i] the plot generator is glitching out again. [i]well[/i], I think you got the point. Same stuff, but just replace the train station with [i]a school or a hospital or a cemetery or [b]any place that isn’t a train station[/b] [/i]; and this time, [i]we’re in the bathroom.[/i] [spoiler]At this point, it’s less of reheating some leftovers and more of picking out the expired tootsie rolls from the candy bowl.[/spoiler] But what if I told you [b]the game is actually pretty good?[/b] [spoiler]…..I already told you that.[/spoiler] [b]Let me elaborate![/b] The thing that surprised me the most was just how well executed the anomalies were, [i]for a game called Toilet 8, [b]mind you.[/b] [/i] There are nearly FIFTY different anomalies to find, which is almost DOUBLE what was in the original [b]Exit 8[/b] [spoiler](I think they added a few more in correlation with the Exit 8 movie when that released a few months ago. ...they should make a Toilet 8 movie now).[/spoiler] The anomalies themselves are surprisingly varied, and taking full advantage of the environment. The big problem I usually have with games of this genre is that I’m always a little miffed when there’s some object that [i]never changes[/i] throughout the entire game. [spoiler]Half the posters in Exit 8 never do anything, for example.[/spoiler] But, like, [b]that never happened in Toilet 8![/b] Every time I started to think that, like [i]“bleah they really are underutilizing the sinks”[/i] or [i]“when are they gonna use the trashcans”[/i], lo and behold, [b]the next scare would use one of those things!! [i]It’s like the poop is reading my mind!!![/i] [/b] Final thing that might be a shocker, [b]this game isn’t completely toilet humor.[/b] [i]Yes, [b]it’s mostly just pee pee poo poo mighty big toots[/b] [/i], but there are some legit differences that made me think “huh. [i]that’s actually kinda clever[/i]”. PLUS, the game is really funny!….[b]if you like poop jokes!….[i]which I apparently do![/i] [/b] I really thought my humor level was higher than that of a five year old, but [i]here I am[/i], snickering when [spoiler]a man walks out of a stall, trips, and rips out a massive toot.[/spoiler] I don’t know what that says about me, but it can’t be good.


Let’s talk about the production values of [b]Toilet 8[/b], where [i]not only[/i] is it an [b]Exit 8[/b] style of game so it’s basically [i]the same thing over and over[/i], but this one focuses mostly on poopies! Yeah, I have [i]no idea[/i] where I went wrong in my life either. [spoiler]My parents always said I had so much potential.[/spoiler] ANYWAY, the game is [i]obviously[/i] made in Unreal Engine, giving it that [i]very sharp yet somehow [b]very generic[/b] [/i] look that’s very common with games nowadays (heck, aside from the setting change, it looks near identical to [b]Exit 8[/b], [i]right down to the tile floors[/i]). Still, even if it’s used for potty humor, there’s clearly a lot of talent on screen. Some of the posters are absolutely [i]hilarious[/i], like the [b]Pooper of the Month[/b] certificate that [i]actually uses your Steam profile picture[/i] for an anomaly [spoiler](it’s a Giga Chad looking dude any other run)[/spoiler] or the cheesy looking horror movie poster for [b]The Bathrooms[/b], [i]with critics calling it [b]“The worst movie I’ve ever seen”[/b] [/i] [spoiler](if THAT’S the review quote you’re putting right on the poster, you probably don’t have a lot of good reviews to choose from)[/spoiler] or [i]my personal favorite[/i], a poorly edited picture with a bunch of stock photos of things like the beach and a sports car on top of each other, with the caption “[i]The Developer After Release[/i]”. I especially like how it says [b]no Al was used to make this picture[/b] at the bottom. [i]Good to know, man.[/i] [b]It looks like you spammed the free-form button on the snipping tool.[/b] oh, before I forget, [b]I want you to meet a very special friend of mine.[/b] Meet [b]Ploppers[/b]; a sentient turd with a big toothy grin, who [i]pops up in the most unlikely of places.[/i] Sometimes he’s in the urinal! Other times he’s in the trashcan! Other times he’s swimming in the sink! And every time you find him, he laughs like a maniac and teases you! [b]This is the game’s mascot, obviously.[/b] [spoiler]He already shows more personality and screen presence than any character in Garten of BanBan. (...sheesh. how depressing is that?).[/spoiler] Now, to all of those who aren’t a fan of toilet humor, [b]why the actual frick did you buy this game.[/b] ...also, we got a few gags you guys might like! There’s a legitimately really good setup for a scare in one of the anomalies, where [i]both doors suddenly close[/i] and [b]you’re trapped in the bathroom. [i]The lights go blood red, bathing the room in this sinister demonic glow.[/i] …..one of the stall doors slowly opens.[/b] [b] [i]...you hear a baby crying.[/i] You have to go and look. You just HAVE to see what is in that stall. ...It’s….IT’S… IT’S AAAAAAA---[/b] [spoiler]It’s the words “Place Jump Scare Here” in Comic Sans, appearing unceremoniously on screen with a fart cloud. [/spoiler]….see, if this guy wanted to, he could probably make an effective horror game. The sound effects are exactly what you’d expect: [b]toots, farts, big toots, big farts, [i]ppbbhbtgtrghhh[/i] before the release, and the final p l o p and sigh of relief.[/b] Most of them just sound like meme noises you’ve [i]definitely[/i] heard before, but there are a few that sound… [i]homemade.[/i] … it’s good to enjoy your work, I suppose. Overall, it’s definitely a parody game, but still a decent amount of effort for an obvious parody game. [spoiler]Now where can I get a Funko Pop of Ploppers. I demand it.[/spoiler]

Toilet 8 is a minimalist psychological observation game developed by Benoît Freslon and published by OKASHI GAMES on Steam. The game belongs to the growing genre of anomaly-detection horror titles where players must carefully examine their surroundings to identify subtle changes within a looping environment. Despite the unusual premise and simple mechanics, the game succeeds in turning an everyday location into an unsettling puzzle space where attention to detail and memory become essential for survival.

The entire experience takes place within a seemingly ordinary public restroom corridor. At first glance the environment appears mundane: rows of sinks, mirrors, stall doors, and fluorescent lighting form a sterile and repetitive space that feels familiar and unremarkable. However, as the player progresses through the corridor again and again, small differences begin to emerge. Objects may disappear or move slightly, lighting may behave differently, or completely unexpected elements may appear where none existed before. The player’s task is to determine whether the current iteration of the corridor contains an anomaly or remains unchanged.

The core gameplay loop revolves around this process of careful observation. Players move forward through the restroom environment and must decide whether something is wrong. If they correctly identify the presence or absence of anomalies, they progress further into the sequence. A mistake, however, resets the player’s progress and forces them to begin again. Because of this structure, the game relies heavily on the player’s memory and ability to notice small details. Even a minor oversight can break the sequence, which makes each new pass through the corridor feel tense and uncertain.

One of the most compelling aspects of Toilet 8 is how it gradually escalates the nature of the anomalies themselves. Early changes may be relatively subtle, such as a misplaced object or a missing item that the player previously saw. These small alterations train the player to observe their surroundings carefully. As the game continues, however, the anomalies grow more unusual and surreal. Some distort the environment in strange ways, while others introduce unsettling visual elements that challenge the player’s expectations about what should exist in such a mundane location.

The decision to place the entire game inside a restroom might initially sound humorous or absurd, but the setting actually works surprisingly well for building atmosphere. The narrow corridors, identical stall doors, and reflective surfaces create an environment where repetition and subtle changes are easy to notice. At the same time, the sterile design and artificial lighting contribute to an unsettling sense of isolation. The player becomes hyperaware of the smallest details within the environment, which makes even minor anomalies feel disturbing.

Visually, the game uses a relatively realistic style that emphasizes clarity and environmental detail. The restroom is rendered with simple but believable textures and lighting that replicate the look of an everyday public facility. This grounded visual approach makes the appearance of strange anomalies even more effective because they stand out sharply against an otherwise ordinary environment. The realism also reinforces the psychological tension by making the setting feel plausible rather than fantastical.

Sound design plays a subtle yet effective role in enhancing the atmosphere. The environment is mostly quiet, filled with faint ambient noises such as distant ventilation systems or subtle echoes within the tiled corridor. These sounds create a sense of emptiness that heightens the player’s awareness of their surroundings. Occasionally, unexpected audio cues accompany certain anomalies, introducing moments of unease without relying on loud jump scares.

Another strength of the game lies in its psychological design. Because players repeatedly travel through the same environment, their minds begin to anticipate patterns and memorize details. This familiarity becomes part of the tension, as players constantly question whether a perceived change is real or simply a trick of memory. The uncertainty between what the player remembers and what actually appears in the corridor creates a unique form of suspense.

However, the minimalist structure of Toilet 8 also means that the experience is relatively limited in scope. The game revolves around a single environment and a single gameplay mechanic, which may lead to repetition during longer sessions. Players who prefer narrative-driven horror experiences or action-based gameplay may find the design somewhat restrictive. The game is best approached as a short, focused experiment in observation rather than a lengthy adventure.

Even with its simple concept, Toilet 8 manages to stand out within the anomaly-detection genre thanks to its creative use of a mundane setting and its carefully designed progression of environmental changes. The experience demonstrates how tension can be built through subtle details rather than dramatic scares. By encouraging players to pay attention to every object and corner of the environment, the game transforms ordinary surroundings into a source of constant suspicion.

Overall, Toilet 8 is a small but memorable psychological puzzle experience that successfully turns observation into a core gameplay mechanic. Its strange premise, unsettling anomalies, and tense repetition create an experience that rewards patience and attention to detail. While it may not offer the depth of larger horror titles, it provides a clever and atmospheric challenge for players who enjoy anomaly-hunting games and minimalist horror design.

These are my thoughts about the game:

First, I'll discuss the gameplay. It has massive improvements on everything. Puzzle variety, less trial-and-error, stealth mechanics, refined horror, and smoother progression. You progress in each chapter and these chapters reveal the story and connect the threads from the first game.

The visuals have also improved. I don't think I'll say much other than the fact that the art style and visual effects are slightly more fascinating to see compared to what the first game has offered. It truly is a stunning improvement as well.

The music evokes our emotions. It's not just there for us to hear, but feeling the music in specific moments connects us with the character. Sound effects are stellar with their ability to evoke emotions in us as players, giving you dread, fear, and any other emotions to feel.

(Warning ⚠️ : It may or may not be a spoiler to you so be warned reading this part. I will be diving into the narrative and themes based on how I interpreted it, but I think the review remains safe for new players.)

Lastly, the story. Our discovery of Price's history and his life has showed how trauma can affect us in the long run, and ignoring it can bring us stagnation. In this game, there are things I have come to realize.

Our fears, insecurities, and unworthiness would hold us back from our potential of who we can become. With reason to live, we can face our losses and regrets. Our ambitions, inspirations, and desire for comfort and love can help us confront our fears and agony.

Also, by forgiving ourselves, a spark of courage surges to pursue the things we hope for. This is how impactful the sequel is. It's an eye-opening game for all of us. This game absolutely deserves the overwhelmingly positive reviews and I highly recommend playing this game.

Recommended. A short, clever psychological journey through a surreal mindscape where emotions appear as characters, and a closing twist that places the entire story inside a single second, winning the trade of puzzle depth for narrative payoff.

The screen and music visibly tear apart in darkness because the protagonist is scared of the dark, working early and reframing every shadow as characterisation. Therapy-session chapters (Agony, Loss, Forgiveness, Realisation) build to a confronting childhood nightmare, the Hope's Domain domestic sequence is an unexpected mood lift, and the note-frequency machine puzzle is the strongest mechanical beat. Running, new to the series, speeds traversal. Roughly two hours in one sitting.

Puzzles are noticeably simpler than the first game, the console mapping shows PC keybinds with no equivalents, and the item-found fanfare startles more than any intended scare. Hiding rarely matters with no real fail state. Both entries together come recommended as a pair.

Kin and Quarry is a very cute incremental game where you dig in the ground at the request of a Magical Yet Vaguely Sinister Talking Tree in your forest and it lasts about 5-7 hours depending on how well you manage your little foxes, moles, exploding ferrets, necromancer cats, and rabbits. There's an addictive gameplay loop and I managed to make 3 hours magically disappear in one game sitting. The art style is also very cute, with 2D sprites sitting on top of a 3D environment with nice, autumn-flavored lighting. The game certainly looks very cozy and, for a while, it is! 

However, I will agree with most of the reviews and say the pacing is a problem after you get past the ninth layer. I get it; I've played incremental games before. I've played incremental games where you dig in a giant hole with pickaxes and a giant drill before. I know that after a certain point, the grind is going to increase and you're going to need to gather more points for the skill tree. The problem is the endgame in Kin and Quarry feels weirdly buggy and unfinished where most of the endgame upgrades cause the framerate to chug to a standstill (with the game helpfully warning you ahead of time and saying that no, it's the game's fault, not your computer) and, weirdly enough, make your damage output [i]decrease[/i] instead of increase. If you go over 75 units, you will ironically get [b]worse[/b] at digging, with various sources of damage just completely disappearing if you go over this limit. That's weird! I've honestly never seen an incremental game do that!

Skill tree progression also has a weird bottleneck where the 3rd and 4th rarest orbs are the ones that are used the most to level up your miners, with the rarest orbs often taking up space in my inventory. Those green orbs and beige orbs quickly became another chore for me to grind while my epic purple orbs were barely used for anything.

I did like the ending though. Sure, there isn't a boss battle or anything, but I appreciate that you get to watch your entire mining village gets gaslighted by God. 

Giving Kin and Quarry the thumb's up for now but it's a thumb's up with room for improvement. [b]TL;DR:[/b] Kin and Quarry is an above-average short incremental game that understands the systems that make a short incremental game good and presents them well.

In Kin and Quarry, you aim to dig deeper, more effectively, and efficiently with the digging team you assemble and the strategy you deploy through a skill tree. I finished the game and fully completed it in about five hours.

The game starts quite nicely in the beginning, where [b]you need to proceed with a strategy at each attempt to maximize your earnings within the digging sessions[/b]. This quickly gives way to auto-mining hordes, but only after a bit of playtime.

[b]The game offers a wide range of optimization options to suit different playstyles[/b]. The skill tree is huge, and you can choose from many workers to build a digging team. One thing to note is that there aren't really wrong answers when it comes to progression, which is expected from a short incremental game.

[b]One clear problem with the game is its optimization[/b]. Somehow, this game makes my PC's fans run crazier than a few recent AAA titles. It is a short game, so obviously not a huge problem, but it could definitely be better.

Finally, the story is there, and [b]there is a lot of text to enjoy if you are into it[/b], but it wasn't for me. If you are into gameplay rather than the story or discovering the world, the game does not force you to, so you'd be fine.

In short, I wouldn't put Kin and Quarry on the list of the best short incremental games I have played so far, but it's definitely not on the list I regret playing. The runs were short due to the time limit, and mostly consisted of clicking on rocks while controlling one mining unit(holding down an arrow key), else the progress would have been slower. After each run, you go to the progression tree, buy what you want/can, unlock new units/change the amount of each, then repeat, meaning it is no idler. You must pay attention, you must keep controlling things (until maybe at the end once everything is upgraded). If this had wanted to be an idler as its tag claims, there should have been the option to just keep looping runs without player input, allowing for passive progression alongside the option to directly engage and speed things up. Think of it like Cookie Clicker in a way but your clicks are limited, and, after every minute of automated and player clicks, the player must pause to chose upgrades and start everything to clicking again.

 It was a bit tedious, a good time waster if you're on the phone or something, but otherwise lacking in engaging gameplay beyond numbers go up and animals go down. If the intention was something less idler, I would have hoped for something to do besides mindlessly click and hold a key down, maybe some kind of basic enemy or option to go up and reposition or hazards. The drill, the sprites, and the 'events' did help shake things up a little, but the former tended to just go on it's own, the sprites often spawned off screen where I would never see them, and the events boiled down to 'good time to grind' and 'good time to progress'.

What did I like? The respec option was neat, though I never really took advantage of it besides the Ascension menu, and allowed me to pick upgrades with confidence. The story actually surprised me with how it ended, and I liked it. Art was cute, game ran smooth despite me having quite a few bomb-tossing ferrets, and the menus were easy to navigate and understand. I also liked that the achievements happened naturally over playing the game for the most part, rather than a 'grind to complete every progression tree'.

If the game made any claim of being an idler, I'd give it a negative review. But that's a faulty user tag. So have a positive review instead. The lack of painful grinding for achievements, the story, the art, the basic game loop combined with it being a fairly short game, and the generally chill experience gets it a positive review from me. I regret buying this game. There is clear, verifiable direct evidence that generative AI was used for art and content production; images created in Google Gemini were packaged directly into the Steam release build.

1. Raw Gemini filenames remain inside built-in presets
Three paint preset TextAssets shipped with the build: `engine`, `aero_engine`, `preset_abrams`. They contain decal layers with these exact layer names:
`картинка Gemini_Generated_Image_1sbiyv1sbiyv1sbi`
`картинка Gemini_Generated_Image_qscuahqscuahqscu`
`двигатель: картинка Gemini_Generated_Image_1sbiyv1sbiyv1sbi`

`Gemini_Generated_Image_<random string>` is Gemini’s default download naming scheme. The duplicated random suffix matches this pattern perfectly. The image data was not stripped: it is embedded base64 inside the JSON `image` field. Headers `F2DI1:185:77:` and `F2DI1:246:124:` correspond to 185×77 and 246×124 textures. After Deflate decompression, the data is raw RGBA bytes (width × height × 4).

The devs dropped Gemini-generated decals straight into the retail build, leaving the original auto-generated names intact.

2. The main logo shows classic AI generation geometric errors
`logo_armour_simulator.png` (1034×765, non-standard canvas size, appears cropped post-generation): uneven stroke thickness and double-line artifacts on the shield’s right edge; broken, disconnected floating lines where the missile overlaps the shield; inconsistent size and spacing for the three small left-side dots; highlight facets geometrically misaligned with the shield silhouette. These mistakes do not occur in hand-done vector logos.

Below are circumstantial signs consistent with widespread AI-assisted production (these are supporting indicators, not standalone proof):

- **Codebase**: `Assembly-CSharp` has 785 classes with heavily templated prefixes: 122 `Super*`, 112 `Mp*`, 75 `Flat2D*`, 38 `Ultra*`.
- **Test code in release**: 83 `*Tests` classes remain in the retail build; assembly stripping was disabled, which is unusual for a commercial release.
- **Metadata placeholders**: The 11 MB `global-metadata.dat` contains 12 `WARNING`, 62 `ASSUMED`, 4 `NO SOURCE` entries plus placeholder text such as *Technical detail (not translated)*.
- **Multilingual text**: Identical descriptions appear in English, German, Polish and Russian. The developer is a native Russian speaker (seen in preset names like `танк гипер - башня`), typical of bulk AI translation.
- **Broken asset assembly**: Crew body meshes include `Part_3_Large_Plumage` and `Part_4_Small_Plumage` — feather objects attached to human meshes. The asset pool mixes Russian primitive names (`Куб.001`, `Цилиндр`), generic `Cube.012`, and imported external assets such as `9M14_Malyutka_AT-3__FINAL_3D_STL`.

honestly, my opinions are kind of mixed, so i'll organize it by pros and cons.

there's a lot of negative and positive reviews on this, most aren't very clear, so i'll try to be as clear as possible on this one, including a lot of details!

the "->" is for additional details related to the main pro/con above.

starting with the pros:
1. it's very realistic, especially the Super Simulation mode. i was able to fool one of my friends into believing this was ANSYS.
-> what gives it away the most is the particles created from impacts and the lack of vibration simulation across a whole armor plate from an impact. the game simulates bulging extremely well, though.

2. lots of variety in ammunition
-> you're able to choose from American, German, and Russian rounds, including basic & standard rounds. includes APFSDS (Armor Piercing Fin-Stabilized Discarding Sabot) and HEAT (High-Explosive Anti Tank) shaped-charge shells, including the Javelin ATGM for infantry. this game also allows you to customize properties of the shell (Caliber, Velocity, Length (length only applicable on rod penetrators only)) [b] all rounds in the game at this moment are listed at the bottom of this review! [/b]

3. TONS of armor materials to select from
-> the game provides you with a large handful of materials and pre-modeled armor modules (NERA and ERA), on top of property customization (Thickness, Angle X, Angle Y, Width, Height).

4. you're able to pick from speed views (how fast a particle/projectile is moving in m/s), to the Von Mises Stress view in GPa, to plastic strain, as long as you're in the Super Simulation mode. genuinely impressive and lives up to its claim "ANSYS-class simulation"!

---

now the cons:
1. in Super Simulation, it's very limited on what you can do.
-> some shells aren't available by default and it's very picky on spacing, including whether or not the center of the armor is aligned with the direction of travel of the projectile. you also can't really change the playback length and the amount of frames you want generated (default is 150 frames, i can't find anything to actually change this setting as of right now) by much for a full, complete simulation.

2. VERY performance-intensive in Super Simulation.
-> while it's fine in Normal and Advanced (with lots of spalling only causing noticeable lag), Super Simulation is not your friend if you don't have a high-end computer. [b] Super Simulation's playback files are as large as 20GB-26GB each. this can be higher if you're running a simulation with multiple objects, and often fails to load and crashes if you've got a rather large ERA (Explosive Reactive Armor) object, or too many objects that experience damage. [/b] Ultra mode is just balanced between Super Simulation and Advanced, I haven't experienced the same issues so far on Ultra.
-> (Super-Simulation also [b] sometimes [/b] fails to fully render detailed simulations, but it'll tell you and let you decide if it should try again from where it failed, or if you want to discard it/do it later.)

3. UI design
-> some parts of the UI aren't fully translated from Russian to English, and the UI can be awkward, but it's pretty fast to get used to. no huge complaints. there's an option to save a video of simulations created in Super Simulation, but it throws a confusing error and doesn't work.



overall, [b] on top of this being early-access, [/b] it's a great close alternative to ANSYS (unless you're using this for actual engineering solutions, then no! and also if you have the patience to learn and troubleshoot some things), but it might not fit everyone. it really depends on what you're looking for, that's why I included all this detail.
