Honestly... I really DON'T want to recommend this game, like, at all. lol. Because the thing is...

I'm weird.

And I really don't think most people will like this game. I ended up spending so much time on this because I turned the games poor performance into a game within itself, but also against myself, it was weird. But oddly satisfying.

For whatever reason, I got really into Food Processing Simulator, and I don't even really know why. I've ended up going through and doing absolutely everything you can, with 100% achievements as well. I have no idea why I did that lol.

If you've combed through the negative reviews, everything they have to say is right lol. 

Every single recipe is basically the same. You do finally get more complex salad recipes but those basically just mean run three of those exact same production lines and combine them all. You unlock the different types of "end game" foods, and again, it's the exact same production line set ups. they just use different looking machines. There is no depth to literally anything, like AT ALL.

The in game economy/money is absolutely just slapped together. You can be like me, and spend over 50 hours grinding to level 55+ and it doesn't matter AT ALL how you do it. With the exception of one or two items, the end game food items you produce sell for basically the same amounts as the ones you first start the game with. But even still it doesn't matter because the money system is mostly forgiving.

You're telling me a box of plain, all lettuce, salads sell for 35 bucks but a box of complex multi-ingredient salads costs 36? Like Imagine going to KFC and they're like... "Well we can peel a head of lettuce for you and throw it in a box for 5 bucks, or you can try this fresh romaine chicken salad for 5.15" Like.. what? lol

It doesn't make logical sense at all, and this also makes progression boring. I didn't even bother with many of the end game fruit based items because I was already grinding for the ultra rare salad achievements anyways, and with how bad the game runs you can't go hog wild and that ironically ended up being part of why I enjoyed the game....

Because... The game runs like crap, and you'll realize quickly this is all due to the boxes. The more boxes you have in game, the crappier the game will run. I don't care how amazing your rig is, there is no way you could use every square inch of factory space, every square inch of cold storage, running 8 food trucks, and be able to get over 10 frames. 

As I said, this is ironically also what ended up being one of the reasons I spent so much time playing.

Unlike satisfactory where you completely start over multiple times because the rules start to change, and the needs keep growing, I ended up starting over multiple times, completely changing and deleting huge chunks of my production lines so I can change what I'm offering, and find ways to minimize my total on screen box counts so performance remained at a fair spot.

So I created a game with myself, how well could I optimize my outputs, still get rich, and still keep the performance at least half way decent. So I went BANANAS with that, min maxing walk times for employees so boxes are quickly dispensed into machines and improve the frame rates drastically.

This included building a "menu" where I can make as many finished products as possible using as few ingredients and supplies as humanly possible. Again, all towards the goal of limiting the amount of on screen boxes as low as humanly possible while still running high enough production numbers to get rich and get all the achievements. 

Honestly if the game didn't start running so poorly, it probably wouldn't have been any fun for me at all. hahaha

 I was able to design direct transfer lines so boxes could almost immediately feed into machines from their spawn points and drastically lower my storage needs. By the end of the game here I'm grinding out the last four rare Salad achievements and I've maximized my builds so much that there are probably never more then 40-50 boxes on screen at any given time, which has also bought me 60 FPS for a good while now too.

It's just... an odd thing...to enjoy and recommend a game when I've enjoyed it based solely on how bad it is lol. And that's why this recommend is a soft one. There isn't much depth here and it's only going to appeal to someone that finds a way to make their own fun. If you can't do that, you aren't going to enjoy this. ESPECIALLY for most hardcore fans of Satisfactory and the like. If you want automation depth and complexity, you won't get that here.

Value for Money:
The game is currently listed for $12.99 on the Steam store. It is definitely worth the full price for the hours of "zen" automation it provides, but it’s an absolute steal if you catch it on sale. It has previously dropped as low as $10.39 during Steam sales, so keep an eye on your wishlist.

A solid 9/10 for simulation fans. It’s still in Early Access, so there's plenty of room to grow, but the foundation is already excellent.

1. Please fix the frame drops....

A problem caused by materials accumulating inside the machine.


2. It would be great if bundle purchasing and installation were available.

It’s such a hassle every time I change the line. If I ever have to replace an entire set of equipment... oh my god.

3. The conveyor belt... its placement is inconvenient, and using things like mergers causes the speed to lag. It falls far short of being called a factory game. I also played the Automated Ranch Simulator demo, and I get the feeling that they don't understand the fundamental issues.

(Of course, the indicator showing connections was a very, very good idea.)

In factory-style games, organization and logistics are extremely, extremely important aspects.

In Food Processing Simulator, there is only one conveyor belt for logistics. However, you have to use one line for each ingredient to avoid blockages. (Even though three types of beans have been added as ingredients!)

However, installing multiple lines from the inserter to the packaging machine inevitably leads to areas where excessive input occurs. (This is related to employee movement patterns. Since one employee is assigned to each inserter and visits occur more frequently the closer the machine is, under the current logic, placing multiple identical inserters naturally results in more material piling up at the front.)

In fact, it is this situation of excessive input that causes logistics problems. Yet, if we try to distribute the materials using a single inserter, the speed slows down, causing production output to drop by half. (If we even use added a raw material distributor, it drops to one-fourth!)

If logistics cannot be resolved, the next factory-style game will likely have many shortcomings. This is an area that needs to be improved before moving on.

4. Once you've built a process, there's really nowhere to spend the money. It feels like the meaning of why you're saving it disappears.

Lastly, I think the game itself is very fun. It has improved a lot since I first bought it, and I really enjoyed it. If the game becomes a bit more polished, I think I'll play it again from the beginning.

I also think the sequel, Automated Ranch Simulator, will be very fun.

A lot of the shortcomings mentioned in the earlier reviews, and by earlier I mean as recently as December 2025, have already been addressed by the developers.  They are constantly working on the game, and it has been improved greatly even during the time I have been playing it.  They are responsive on the Steam forum, in spurts.

I can't speak to their dev log because it is on X.  Much as I like Elon Musk, I refuse to get another social media account.  I am on Discord because so many of the games I play are there.  I hated it at first but have gotten accustomed to it.  I dropped Facebook years ago.  Enough is enough.

Anyway, the game is about setting up assembly lines for food products and fulfilling contracts in a timely manner.  At first you are doing all the work yourself, but soon you can hire employees to feed the hungry maws of the food processing lines, and fill the trucks with boxes of your finished goods.  Your equipment needs maintenance and your finished goods will spoil outside the cold room.  There are three sizes of boxes, holding 6, 24, and 48 containers each.  Obviously it is more efficient to fill larger boxes in terms of moving them to the trucks, but the orders are for odd amounts so you have to make some of the smaller boxes as well.  This leads to some interesting logistics in terms of splitters and mergers.  There are several types of products, coming in bowls, bottles, jars, and pouches.  There are at this time 8 vegetables, packaged either alone or in combination with each other.  You get access to the more complicated recipes as you advance in level, which you increase by fulfilling contracts.

The devs are talking about adding more raw foods and more recipes, but they are a small team so things do not appear instantly.  They do appear in a regular basis, however.

PS: Some of the recipes are a little strange.  For instance, you slice your tomatoes before you wash them.  Then, having washed off all the good juice and flavor from the slices, you air-dry them.  Then you miraculously make tomato sauce from the dried tomato slices.  Well, no one said you have to personally cook according to the game's recipes.  :D

I'm surprised to see negative reviews about the physics.  This is a very fun ping pong game.  There are primarily two modes (besides multiplayer), they are Arcade and Simulation.  I don't personally see a huge difference between them but arcade mode will show you the path that the ball is going to follow.  

Outside of those two differences the heart of the game is the championship mode.  There are cup like circuits (think 50cc, 100cc, 150cc in Mario Kart) with AI to challenge.  Each AI has a slightly different personality and even in the second circuit they can be quite difficult to defeat.  

Adding to it there are different backgrounds you can play in (they don't change gameplay though) and it seems as you can customize your avatar (used really only in multiplayer).  Physics and control wise, I think this is spot on and is comparable to Eleven Table Tennis.  

Speaking of which, I actually prefer this game to Eleven.  There are less players online, but I feel as though there is more content for a single player.  The ambience of the crowd noise also is preferred over Eleven, however I will say it does seem a little too loud.

Considering the low price and the accurate  table tennis physics, I highly recommend this.  I also know it doesn't state it on the Steam Page but this game works fine with WMR.  You will see a Vive controller but that isn't a big deal.

[h1]PARTY HARD 2 — FOR PEOPLE WHO THINK MASS MURDER NEEDS A CRAFTING MENU[/h1]

Party Hard 2 somehow takes a simple joke of a game and stuffs it with enough systems to make it feel like somebody accidentally installed an RPG expansion into a drunken house party. You sneak around parties, set traps, craft items, manipulate NPCs, and kill everyone while pretending this has somehow become sophisticated strategy.

[b]It has 14 levels, 4 playable characters, crafting, traps, objectives, bosses, and co-op, yet somehow the core loop still boils down to “wait for idiot to stand near dangerous object.”[/b]

[strike]Truly, Sun Tzu would be proud.[/strike]

The game constantly wants you to feel clever for electrocuting a puddle, poisoning somebody, or causing a chain reaction, but after a while it starts feeling less like tactical genius and more like Home Alone for people on a watchlist.

[u]Having more ways to kill the same clueless NPCs does not automatically make the game deeper.[/u]

The funniest part is that the AI can be so braindead that half your “master plans” work because everyone at the party apparently shares one functioning brain cell. These people will watch three bodies appear next to a suspicious man covered in blood and still decide the real problem is somebody dancing too close to the stereo.

The Steam reception is Mixed in English, which honestly feels appropriate. Even the playerbase seems split between people who think this is underrated brilliance and people who realized they have been walking around pixel parties waiting for NPC pathfinding to cooperate.

[spoiler]The hardest boss is waiting for somebody to finally walk into your trap.[/spoiler]

I will give it credit for having more variety than the first game, but sometimes “more” just means more junk orbiting the same basic idea. Crafting, objectives, character abilities, and extra mechanics do not magically turn repetitive murder puzzles into chess.

[b][u]4/10 — NOT RECOMMENDED[/u][/b]

Irritating story, tedious gameplay.

The idea of having a clear storyline through levels is nice, but I wasn't a fan of the story itself. I actually like playing messed up games as messed up protagonists, but the story presents the guy as this suffering anti-hero battling an evil drug company and the psychiatrist who manipulated him. I much preferred the minimal justification from the first game where the guy's homicidal hatred of all things party-related is influenced by noise pollution, insomnia -- it was a straightforward motive, tapping into a common frustration with urban living and offering a colourful pixelated revenge fantasy. The guy wasn't a victim of some big conspiracy MKUltra-ing him into a murderer. Despite having an apparent split-personality, he was instead shown to be responsible for his own actions. It's a major tone shift, and it did not work at all for me and I've not even mentioned the most edgelord line in the whole game about how violence smells of melon bubblegum.
 
Despite my dislike of the story the gameplay is the main reason I'm marking this game 'not recommended'. Levels are often huge, with multiple patrolling hazards, and they take ages to clear. Most of my failed attempts were ten to twenty minutes of time lost to a split second mistake that I had no way to rectify. You can't outrun goons, you can't outrun cops. Your best hope is to lead them into traps, or use shortcuts, but if you're caught out in the open without anything close by it's pretty much game over unless you can get a direct hit with a molotov. A few failures like that and the joy of messily taking out party-goers in a burst of pixel gore starts to fade. It faded completely for me by the time I got to the third level. So many of the levels are just open space, making getting caught rather easy...especially when a character's AI just breaks and leaves them standing frozen in place, which makes it that much harder to isolate people and makes getting the last couple of kills a major pain in the arse. This was particularly noticeable on the Amusement Park level.
With the expanded item system, most of the time you'll have a bunch of unusable junk on hand which needs to be combined with something else to be potentially useful...good luck trying to get what you need in the limited randomised loot. More inventory slots would've been helpful here.
I'm undecided whether I liked the boss fights or not. I had to look up the last one because there was no indication how you're even supposed to do damage to her.
Some of the hidden objectives are just a joke (no 911 calls/no alerts), making already tedious, long-winded levels a fresh nightmare. You can't use the multi-kill on groups for these objectives, since it almost always results in an alert. Again the Amusement Park was the bane of my existence between the stealth objective and the 'shoot down a helicopter' objective.

All in all, I strongly disliked it.

Party Hard 2 is a unique blend of stealth, strategy, and dark humor that takes the frantic and chaotic premise of its predecessor and expands it with new mechanics, environments, and challenges. Developed by Pinokl Games, this sequel plunges players into a series of wild, out-of-control parties where the objective is disturbingly simple yet twisted: stop the noise by any means necessary. The game thrives on its ability to combine tense stealth gameplay with inventive kill methods and a satirical tone, offering an experience that’s as thrilling as it is morbidly amusing.

The core gameplay loop of Party Hard 2 revolves around sneaking through crowded party environments, avoiding detection, and strategically eliminating partygoers without drawing too much attention. Each level is designed with multiple layers of complexity, filled with NPCs going about their revelry, security personnel, and various interactive objects. The stealth mechanics encourage players to think creatively and plan their moves carefully. Unlike typical stealth games that often emphasize avoidance, Party Hard 2 demands a balance between aggression and subtlety. Timing, positioning, and understanding enemy patrol patterns become crucial as one wrong move can lead to chaotic chases and rapid escalation.

What sets Party Hard 2 apart is its wide array of inventive kill methods and environmental interactions. Players can utilize anything from hidden traps to improvised weapons or even manipulate the environment to create deadly accidents. The game rewards experimentation, allowing for a variety of approaches in each scenario. Whether you prefer silent takedowns or more theatrical methods of dispatching your targets, the game accommodates diverse playstyles. The dark humor embedded in these kill methods adds a layer of twisted charm that softens the macabre subject matter and keeps the tone engaging and often hilariously irreverent.

Visually, Party Hard 2 retains a stylized pixel art aesthetic that complements its chaotic gameplay perfectly. The environments are colorful and vibrant, filled with lively partygoers who bring each scene to life through their animations and behaviors. Despite the grim objective, the art style manages to keep the mood light and accessible. The level designs are cleverly crafted, with plenty of nooks, crannies, and interactive elements that encourage exploration and tactical planning. The user interface is clean and intuitive, ensuring players can focus on the action without unnecessary distractions.

The sound design and music play a significant role in building the game’s atmosphere. The soundtrack features energetic, party-themed tunes that contrast amusingly with the player’s violent agenda. Sound cues are crucial for gameplay, as listening for footsteps, conversations, or security alerts helps in planning moves and avoiding detection. This audio feedback enriches the immersion and heightens the tension during stealth segments, making every narrow escape or successful kill feel earned and satisfying.

Party Hard 2 also expands its narrative and character development compared to the original. The story is told through brief cutscenes and dialogue that maintain the series’ sardonic humor while providing context for the increasingly bizarre and dangerous party scenarios. Players get to experience the perspective of different characters, each with unique skills and backstories, adding variety to gameplay and encouraging replayability. These narrative touches deepen the game’s world and provide motivation beyond the core mechanics, enhancing player investment.

The game’s difficulty curve is well-balanced, starting with more straightforward scenarios and gradually introducing tougher security measures, more complex level layouts, and unpredictable AI behaviors. This progression keeps the challenge fresh and engaging, ensuring that players must continuously adapt their strategies. The AI is reasonably intelligent, responding to disturbances and investigating suspicious activities in a way that keeps players on their toes. However, the occasional unpredictability of NPCs can sometimes lead to frustrating moments, especially during tight stealth sequences.

Multiplayer modes and additional challenges add further depth and replayability to Party Hard 2. Cooperative play allows friends to team up and coordinate their silent takedowns, adding a social layer to the tension and strategy. Leaderboards, achievements, and time-based challenges incentivize mastery and provide goals for competitive players.

If there’s a drawback, it might be the game’s niche appeal; the dark humor and violent premise won’t resonate with everyone, and the stealth mechanics, while rewarding, can sometimes feel repetitive or punishing for those unfamiliar with such gameplay. Additionally, some may find the controls a bit finicky at times, requiring precision that can be challenging under pressure.

Overall, Party Hard 2 is a thrilling and darkly comedic stealth game that builds on its predecessor’s foundation with greater depth, variety, and polish. Its unique mix of tension, strategy, and humor creates a compelling experience for players who enjoy thinking on their feet and embracing chaotic scenarios with a mischievous grin. Whether you’re a fan of stealth games or just looking for an unconventional and entertaining title, Party Hard 2 offers a wickedly fun ride through the wildest parties you’ll ever want to crash.

Beat the first 6-7 levels at review time.

Recommended w/ cautions/complaints (of course):

1) this game gives a bit too much "Kingdom Rush" for my tastes.  feel free to read my review of *that* mess to see exactly what I'm on about but, in short: high difficulty levels turn it into a puzzle game where there's essentially only one correct method to win. + no checkpoints or saves. + it can be rather difficult anyway, so = a lot of un-fun, grindy, wasted time.

*so far*, Cursed Treasure seems less difficult and doesn't seem to quite reach that point of "literally only one way to win", but I reserve the right to change this review to "not recommended", if I find out later that it does. :P

2) if I didn't pay literally USD$.074 for this, I'd call it buggy. lots of crashes. as it is, I'll call it "quirky" instead. :P

3) did I mention it reminds me of Kingdom Rush, which I hate?

4) music is pretty generic and terrible. and that's probably exactly what the producers ordered. 🤦
4a) sound-design-direction-wise, I find some of the death SFX kinda misaligned w/ the game's cartoony/cutesy vibe. e.g. harsh death screams that literally sound like a person on fire. SFX need a little more Daffy Duck and a little less Ari Aster. (have some alliteration, no charge. 💁)

5) A bit generic and uninspired -- i.e. copycat -- in general. like... some towers are practically cloned from KR.

6) I don't like micro in my TD games. Maybe you do. I don't.
6a) having to click to pick up items on the trail is annoying. it's especially annoying when they stack and you have to pick up/wasted one-shot items unintentionally. e.g. gold coins "trapped" under a freeze scroll.
6b) there seem to be hotkeys for most things. unfortunately does not include placing/upgrading towers.

--------------

On the positive side...

it's that proven-fun combo of TD and RPG elements.

it does introduce some fresh mechanics -- at least ones I have not seen before, and I've played a lot of TD. The interplay between them can be mildly empowering and entertaining. To look at it another way, though, I can see them being part of the "TD as a puzzle" vibe which I hate so much.

it also recycles some mechanics from the wealth of TD games in existence, and it's fun to see those again. (e.g. Defense Grid's "enemies steal the cores, but they travel back to the vault" mechanic.)

yeah, there's a fine line between "recycling" and complaint #5 above, but I do happen to be of the opinion that combining known techniques in fresh, entertaining ways, *is* viable creativity. it would be pretty difficult to make a 100% original TD game at this point, in any case. (or any genre...)

Before you buy this, do yourself a favor and go to Armor Games (it's a site with 100s of HTML games - Free!) and look for [b]Cursed Treasure 1[/b] and [b]Cursed Treasure 1.5[/b].  If you're a fan of Tower Defense, you'll be playing for hours upon hours, with that awesome rush that these kind of games provide.  In my opinion, this series is in the top 6 of all TD franchises.  

(while you're there, also checkout the [b]GemCraft[/b] series - another in the top 6 of all time - which also has a game here on Steam)

So, yeah - all the great features you want:  very little grinding to move up the skill tree, plenty of choices on how to approach each level, and you get XP regardless if you can't finish a given level.  Lot's of endorphins kicking in.  It's funny, when you're in the midst of battling your butt off, the level often finishes before you thought it would - ha!

Yet, there are 3 MAJOR issues with the Steam version (which applies to many other TD games):

1. At higher levels, the designer(s) change the premise from a strategic placement and advancement of towers, to the same, BUT with [b]fast-twitch-response arcade crap[/b] added.  The screen gets filled with icons all over the screen that you have to click rapidly in order to keep your towers working.  It's very lazy game design.

2.  To beat the higher levels, you're gonna have to grind a TON in order to collect enough skulls to be able to cast the expensive spells necessary to win . Dull and repetitive...ughh.

3.  At the higher levels, there aren't enough squares to adequately defend your gems.  You'll find yourself with 2,000+ dollars, and nothing to spend it on.  That's also lazy game design.

Regardless, for the price, I HIGHLY recommend this game.  5 stars out 5.

Cursed Treasure 2 is a simple tower-defense strategy game where you play the bad guys. The closest comparison would be the Kingdom Rush series, although there are significant differences. From the intro, you see the character graphics are poor with those minimally drawn "googly-eye" enemies, but the pretty and colorful environments made up for it. The gameplay was very solid also. I liked levelling up and the upgrade chart between stages. Even when you lost, you gained experience so an unsuccessful run was not completely useless. However, I sometimes had infrequent crashes when failing a map (or elsewhere). Not enough to be a big issue, though. I liked the extraneous buildings on the maps, different from offensive towers, that could be upgraded and exploited, such as mines and taverns. This is something rarely seen in the genre.

 I liked very much being able to decide when the next wave would come because I could then better prepare. Later on, there were too many waves of enemies and this got tiresome. Half that number would have better. Only three towers but upgradable. Twice that would been better. Being stuck to one type of tower per terrain type limited placement choice, but it was also an original strategic consideration I learned to appreciate. Way too few musics, but at least they were good. From reviews I read, this PC version based on the original Flash version is better than the "Ultimate" edition that is a mobile port. Both are sold on Steam. At the reasonable price and length, with 24 stages, this little-known title in the genre deserves to be better known.

Why it's appreciated (PROS):
Inverted concept: It's fun to be the "bad guy" defending your treasures from "good" heroes.
Pure strategy: You can't just randomly place towers. You have to match the tower type (Orc, Demon, Undead) to the available terrain.
Gem system: Enemies have to steal gems and escape the map with them. If you kill them along the way, the gems stay there, giving you a chance to get them back.
Addictive: The experience and skill system makes you want to play "one more level".
What's not so good (CONS):
Grind: Sometimes you have to replay old levels to collect points for upgrades, otherwise the game becomes too hard.
Technical Issues: Some users have reported bugs related to saving progress.
Speed: Some players would have liked better acceleration options or more control during pausing.
Conclusion:
It's a classic game, easy to understand, but difficult to complete 100%. If you want something relaxing but that will challenge your mind, it's worth buying.

Cursed Treasure 2 is a polished and highly engaging tower defense game that stands out by flipping the genre’s usual moral perspective on its head. Developed by IriySoft and published by Armor Games Studios, the game casts you not as a noble defender of kingdoms, but as a dark overlord tasked with protecting cursed gems from waves of self-righteous heroes. This role reversal gives the experience a playful edge and immediately sets it apart from more conventional tower defense titles, reinforcing its identity through humor, theme, and mechanics.

At its core, the gameplay revolves around defending a set number of magical gems placed on the map. Instead of enemies simply reaching an endpoint, their goal is to steal your gems and carry them back along the path. If too many are taken, the level is lost. This mechanic creates constant tension, as players must think not only about stopping enemies early but also about intercepting retreating thieves. Even a single slip-up can cascade into disaster, making placement, timing, and upgrades feel meaningful throughout every wave.

The game offers three main tower factions: orcs, undead, and demons. Each tower type has a distinct attack style and upgrade tree, allowing for specialization and synergy. Orc towers excel at raw physical damage, undead towers focus on slowing and crowd control, and demonic towers emphasize magic damage and area effects. Towers gain experience as they defeat enemies, unlocking stronger evolutions and encouraging players to invest in fewer, more powerful towers rather than spamming weak ones. Deciding which towers to nurture and which paths to upgrade adds a layer of long-term planning to each level.

Spellcasting further deepens the strategy. Players can unlock and use spells such as meteors, curses, and time manipulation to control the battlefield during critical moments. These spells are powerful but limited by mana, requiring careful judgment about when to deploy them. On higher difficulties, spells often become essential tools rather than optional bonuses, especially when dealing with elite enemies or recovering from mistakes when gems are stolen.

Enemy variety is another of the game’s strengths. Adventurers come in many forms, including knights, archers, ninjas, angels, and other specialized units, each with resistances or abilities that counter specific tower types. Some enemies can fly, others resist magic or armor, and some actively target towers or use stealth mechanics. This diversity forces players to adapt their strategies from level to level rather than relying on a single dominant setup.

Progression is structured in a way that respects both success and failure. Even if a level is lost, players still earn experience points that can be spent on permanent upgrades, such as increased starting gold, stronger spells, or improved tower stats. This system reduces frustration and encourages experimentation, as setbacks still contribute to overall growth. For players seeking additional challenge, completed levels can be replayed in Night Mode, which restricts tower placement to illuminated areas and significantly increases difficulty, offering substantial replay value.

Visually, Cursed Treasure 2 uses a colorful, cartoon-inspired art style that reinforces its tongue-in-cheek tone. Enemy designs are expressive and easy to read at a glance, while tower animations clearly communicate their function and power. The environments are varied enough to keep levels visually distinct without distracting from gameplay clarity. Sound design and music support the action without overwhelming it, providing satisfying feedback for attacks and spell effects.

While the game is widely praised, it is not without limitations. Terrain restrictions, which dictate where specific tower types can be placed, sometimes reduce creative freedom and make certain strategies feel forced. Difficulty can also spike sharply in later levels or Night Mode, where perfect execution and heavy spell usage are often required. For some players, this pushes the game closer to trial-and-error than pure strategy.

Despite these issues, Cursed Treasure 2 remains a standout example of classic tower defense done right. Its clever premise, layered mechanics, strong progression system, and high replayability make it easy to recommend to fans of the genre. It doesn’t reinvent tower defense, but it refines it with confidence and personality, delivering a satisfying experience that rewards planning, adaptability, and a willingness to embrace the role of the villain guarding their ill-gotten treasure.

Cursed Treasure 2 is a simple tower defense game with 3 towers, few upgrades and skills. There are 24 levels in total with 2 modes to choose from. The game is fun with the huge variety of enemies and map mechanics. My only gripe with this game is that some levels are impossible to complete without the use of spells or simply having high skill levels, so grinding is necessary. Other than that, I enjoyed the game well.

Most tower defense games are made by little dinky indies like me. In contrast, this one, like Bloons or Plants vs Zombies, looks professional and polished. And cartoony.

Map Type: Predefined (you can't build your own walls). They tell you where you can build towers. On many maps there are few choices. Unusually, they tell you which tower you must use for each spot. Many maps have multiple goals you have to defend, sometimes on opposite ends of the map, which means if you pay attention to one you don't see what's happening to the other. You can't slow or pause the game so you end up spastically bouncing between them like an old RTS. It's not enjoyable. At all. 

Towers: There are only 3. But they level up with experience and you get 2 choices each time you level up. There is no slowing tower (although ghost towers can sometimes slow creeps) or sniper (but the orc catapult has decent range, although poor damage). The only area of effect tower is a fire tower choice at level 3 (some catapults has splash damage though). There is no damage over time tower.

Creeps: Normal, strong, fast, fliers, etc. An odd assortment of others - invisible, untargetable (can only hit with AOE or splash), healers, ones who makes others fast, spawners and a boss who stays at the start and makes the gems walk to her. One throws smoke bombs, stopping your towers from shooting and preventing you from seeing what's going on. One of the enemies loses her clothes when you attack her, causing you to whistle at her and all nearby towers stop shooting so that they can stare at her. That unit was childish and stupid. Enemies randomly drop coins and mana (mana is used for user spells and for cutting down trees, which you need to unlock spots to put towers on). 

Story and RPG: There is a minimal story, enough to say that maps must be played in a certain order, tower upgrades are unlocked at certain maps and you can't use them on earlier maps. Each map you beat gives the player experience which is used to unlock user spells, map conditions (start with more money) and tower perks (faster, add DOT effects, etc.). 

UI: This needs work. The UI is cute (although the text is way too small) but you can't see tower properties (speed, damage, type, etc.) and you can't see creep properties (although you can look them up in a dictionary). It's also not entirely clear whether a tower will hit anybody - with so few places to build, i built towers in second tier locations and while their hit circle touched the edge of the path i never knew if it was going to hit anything. 

Strategy: i'm conflicted on this. Many maps have few options and, i suspect, a single solution. Several seem like they can only be won by luck (early creeps drop gold and mana). i got perfect scores on most maps but the second to last set (pirates) took me 50 tries each, none of which were fun. i didn't even bother on the last maps (dwarves) - i'd rather uninstall the game then try to get perfect scores on them. 

One thing i dislike is that it's often hard to tell what's going on. Creeps drop things on top of each other making it difficult to see what's there (i frequently click on something i want to stay there in an attempt to get something i want). Some of the effects also make it hard to see. And then the awful smoke grenade monsters. i often had no idea what was happening even when i was staring closely at it. 

Additional: i hate, hate, hate games that switch or add genres. Who puts quick time events in tower defense? 

Overall Cursed Treasures is cute and it's a tower defense game. It's more arcadey than strategic. There are often very few places to put a tower, you can't choose the (initial) tower type, many maps only have a single solution, luck sometimes plays a critical role, you can't slow or pause the game, you sometimes have to rapidly alternate attention between sites and the game has god awful quick time whack-a-mole events. The game wants to look cute and tell a story (and maybe add novelty for novelty's sake?) and it sacrifices traditional "i want to sit and think" strategy to get it.
Still my favourite tower defence game of all time, was delighted to find it on Steam all these years after I played it.

They say it's a "thematic successor" to Planescape: Torment, but the similarities are merely cosmetic. Narratively, this is to Planescape: Torment what Esoteric Ebb is to Disco Elysium. Planescape carried real weight: its themes of regret, identity and mortality were woven into every character and every conversation, so the philosophy felt lived rather than recited. Tides of Numenera mostly gestures at big ideas without the rigour or conviction to follow them anywhere, and its musings on legacy and meaning rarely rise above what you'd find in a well-read fantasy novel. Where Planescape pulled you forward because you needed to know who you were and what you had done, Numenera's story unfolds at a polite distance, full of imaginative set dressing but short on stakes that feel personal. You finish it having seen a lot of strange things, but without having been changed by any of them.

A lot of people hate on this game, but I have to say I enjoyed it a lot. Yes, it's not Planescape: Torment 2, but I still found the story interesting as well as characters you meet (although a lot/most of them are kind of shallow). And what I especially liked is the world, which is such a novel and full of unseen and crazy stuff. This novelty and crazyness was what kept me playing even when there were some not-so-exciting parts of the game gameplay wise. 

Would I recommend it to everyone? No. Would I recommend it to general party based RPG fans? Yes. Would I recommend it to bookworms? Hell yeah. Would I recommend it to hardcore Planescape Torment fans? Still yes, but don't expect direct sequel and take it as a "game inspired by our beloved".

This is a semi-sequel to 'planescape torment', so there's two ways to approach it. Making a comparison against the first game for those who are familiar with it, and then a basic review for those who aren't.

Either way I think this sequel is quite wanting in many areas. It's a CRPG that has hardly any combat and is bland in the action when it does. In 13 hours of playing it there has been maybe 5 enemy encounters, and the rest of the time it was tons of dialogue.

Said dialogue really, really, reaaaaaally wants to be mysterious, enigmatic and trippy, but just ends up being bewildering 50% of the time and slightly tedious for the rest. 

Now, it takes place in a universe that is meant to be bizarre and unknowable, but still...the first game was far more accessible whilst being just as weird. If you've played 'planescape torment' then this can feel like it's a reskinned version of that without the charm or wit. 

You're an amnesiac who can't die, and even though there's a different explanation as to why that is, it to me feels like the story of the nameless one all over again.

If you're new to the world of Torment: it can be simultaneously the strangest world for an RPG to take place in, and yet the driest and dullest until they eventually start sprinkling in some droll humour and characters with some personality as the game goes on. 

This is a place where mad science, fantasy, the supernatural and the superliminal all merge; with robots, demons, monsters, gods and mortals all converging into one realm. It can cover anything it wants to, yet somehow manages to make it all rather boring for long stretches. 

The first game was kooky right from the start; with a compelling premise, oddball characters, amusing humour and a subversive approach to tropes. Whereas here it's pompous, verbose and has it's head up it's own behind for way too long to be particularly engaging. 

Eventually it does get intriguing, but if you don't have the patience (oodles and oodles of it) to get to that point, then there isn't much else here of interest.

Basically it goes like this: a brief bit of bog-standard combat, lots of dialogue, some more dialogue, even more dialogue, a brief bit of bog-standard combat, several hours of dialogue, some combat that is still dull, dialogue, dialogue, dialogue etc etc etc. 

The combat fails because you either (a) fight and it's dull due to a lack of tactical depth and synergies between your parties abilities. 

Or (b) it's been designed as a "stealth" sequence and consequently nothing happens of interest as you simply distract the enemy and walk past them. 

Or (c) use an "exciting" feature in the environment to do some damage, only it's just as underwhelming as every other option on offer. 

Every now and again there's a quest or character that is entertaining, but the mechanics behind it all are super basic and generally fall quite flat. I haven't played baldurs gate 3, but from what I've heard this is like a puddle to that games ocean when it comes to the depth, and even something like 'divinity original sin' makes this feel like it's simplistic pap from a bygone era.

Truthfully the game is kind of awful. Depending on your tastes (as someone who has persevered with it) it's boring and the "walking simulator" of RPGs, with far more story than action and the action is pretty basic when you do get some.

If (IF!!!!) you can get into it, then there is some modest spark here that can pass the time and occasionally deliver something rewarding, but otherwise it feels like it can't even beat an almost 30 year old title for the writing, story and game-play.

I almost gave this a thumbs-up, albeit with the massive caveat of it being marmite-y and only just scraping by into "meh" territory. But thinking about my time with it, it's not something I can recommend when even I (who will most likely finish it out of a mixture of masochism and some very mild appeal) have at times found it only marginally more appealing than watching paint dry.

It's interesting to talk to every character, explore every level, and finish every quest because you never know what you'll witness or find out—there are so many interesting ideas in this game it'll make your head spin.

The gameplay loop isn't that extraordinary but still pretty good due to the well-made leveling system with useful stats and skills. You'll constantly use them during journeys, dialogues and battles and find lots of different items you can utilize or sell. But keep in mind that as a true spiritual successor to Planescape, this game focuses on dialogues and storytelling rather than on combat and long travel sequences, so be prepared for A LOT of reading.

If you're tired of samey RPGs that don't offer anything new to the player and keep feeding you old concepts like orcs, elves, castles, brave knights, or sci-fi robots and spaceships, Tides of Numenera will become that very breath of fresh air you so desperately need.

Like so many others, I played Planescape: Torment back in the day and loved every minute of it. So I was one of the original backers for this game's Kickstarter, but I never did get around to playing it for one reason or another. I was in grad school when it finally came out and, though I tried to play it, I was just too busy with school, work and personal life, so I just played it for a couple of hours and set it aside for "later" and now it's been 15 years and I'm only just now getting around to finally sitting down and playing it for real. 

As expected, it's a very unique game with its own weird game mechanics and ruleset, that attempts to retain the spirit of the original Torment by touching upon similarly crazy ideas about identity, mortality and morality by telling the story of one of the discarded-and-now-sentient former bodies of  a being known as The Changing God, and set in a world easily as weird as Sigil the City of Doors from Planescape. And, as expected from PS:T's spiritual sequel, not everything can or needs to be fixed through combat.

I've seen a fair amount of criticism about how the game fails to live up to expectations as a spiritual sequel to Planescape: Torment, and though I certainly agree that the writing is not on the same level as PS:T and the gameplay has somewhat weird systems that take some time to start making real sense, I don't agree that it's as bad as people argue. 

I had a lot of fun with the game and, much to my surprise, I got invested in the companions' stories, and I was genuinely torn about having to make choices that would dictate their respective endings. 

For instance, I had Rhin in my active party for most of the game despite the fact that she's a child and her stats mostly suck and she's fairly useless. Why? Because I chose to have her tag along with me after convincing the slave trader to leave her in my care and, when I tried to bench her to bring someone else along in my active party, she reacted by getting really scared and begging me not to leave her and telling me I promised to take care of her. So I kept my promise and dealt with the fact that one of my companion spots was occupied by a character I liked but was mostly a liability until I got her to a level where she could be a fairly competent ranged fighter, even though she remained really squishy in comparison to the rest of my party, having about half their HP despite being the same level. She also kept me heroic, because I didn't want to do stuff that would disappoint her or maker her sad.

And then in the latter part of the game when you find a way to send her home through a portal and she started telling me all about how she wanted to go home but she also wanted to stay with me because she loved me, I honestly struggled to decide what to suggest she did until I ultimately opted to send her home for her own good, but I was genuinely sad about it and when I noticed that my new companion I could bring along in Rhin's spot was severely under-leveled I was certain I had made the wrong call and shot myself in the foot but I ultimately made my peace with it. But then at the final sequence in the Labyrinth a new portal opens and a grown woman steps in and it's Rhin, who came back in time to help me beat the final boss and now her stats don't suck and she says she grew up to be a hero following my example, I couldn't help but smile at my little girl who could now go toe-to-toe with me.

All in all, a solid CRPG with a high weirdness quotient but interesting ideas. Having said that, if you don't like reading, you'll probably hate this one. It's very text-heavy.

Torment: Tides of Numenera is a spiritual successor to Planescape: Torment. I loved Planescape and it became one of my favorite games. When I heard that there technically existed a second instalment I was hooked; but inXile didn't actually get permission from Wizards of the Coast who owns the Planescape IP to make an official sequel so it's not actually Planescape 2. But it spiritually follows the universe and if you've played Planescape you can easily connect the universes. There's a lot of similarities and references and they succeeded creating a similar vibe to the Planescape setting albeit the sci-fi element. 

There was A LOT I didn't get to experience in this single playthrough I've completed at the time of writing this review. Entire sections I've missed, multiple endings, characters I never met or fought alongside etc. and with the percentage dice roll mechanic and pool drains it's even more challenging to experience everything (unless you're a petty save scummer... well I'm that too...) but I actually like the system a lot. It creates variations in your playthroughs albeit subtle at times. 

The combat was great imo. Now, I know that better systems exist out there but I wasn't bothered by the fighting. Tides of Numenera is primarily a story based game just like Planescape and I felt like the combat served its purpose. You're essentially not super strong and need to be smart and efficient with your pools not to drain them too fast.

The story was amazing, the exploration felt just like Planescape along with the option trees… and the loading screen art was well made too! But I also have some criticism. 

Sometimes when interacting with NPC's with dialogue trees or just the NPC’s with single comment boxes you'd walk straight into them, noclipping into them, instead of engaging  conversation; this was a frustrating bug that I felt they should have fixed by now. I was also a little frustrated by how easily you could part with a party member by mistake by miss clicking. It can ruin the immersion. There should absolutely be another dialogue box in between to correct a miss click. I don't particularly like the character artwork. Some of them are decent but it doesn't fit the aesthetic of the game in my opinion. I also didn't like when the narrator took over a conversation, the names of the NPC's I was speaking with were regarded as the ones speaking as the narrator. It's a weird way of formatting the dialogue in my opinion. I also wasn't a fan of the merecaster UI; especially when one or more of your pools were drained and it abruptly cut the light effect of the pools. When I'm used to pause the game by hitting space it often frustrated me that in combat the space button was mapped to skip character rounds by default. Whether you disable or enable v-sync if you're having a long conversation with someone at some point the dialogue box starts to slow down and becomes unbearably slow; it's way worse with v-sync disabled but that was frustrating. Sometimes the single dialogue comments get stuck in the game and the only way to remove them is to find where they're located and click on them again which is tedious.

But other than that, it was an amazing game! The 95 hours I took to complete the first playthrough was well worth the hype. Since I bought the Immortal Edition I also got 5 e-books (among other cool things) which I will be reading so the universe definitely isn’t wrapped up for me yet.

Torment: Tides of Numenera — a spiritual successor to Planescape: Torment. Because the developers didn’t have the license, the setting was changed, but the core philosophy remained: combat is secondary, while dialogue, choices and consequences are the real heart of the game.

Just like its predecessor, the gameplay focuses much more on diplomacy, decision-making and exploring the protagonist’s identity than on fighting. The narrative is genuinely interesting, companions are well written, and the main character concept works very well. The early portion of the game especially shines — the atmosphere is fantastic and the primary antagonist creates real tension and mystery.

Unfortunately, about halfway through the game it feels as if development was rushed. The structure becomes repetitive, the story loses some of its intrigue, and encounters with the antagonists feel less like meaningful confrontations and more like recurring annoyances. The ending in particular feels abrupt and leaves many unanswered questions — almost like reading a novel that suddenly skips a few chapters near the conclusion.

Despite its flaws, it’s still worth playing, especially for players who value narrative RPGs. However, it’s definitely a title better picked up on sale rather than at full price.

+ strong narrative focus and meaningful choices
+ excellent atmosphere in the first half
+ well-written companions and protagonist
+ combat is optional and mechanically solid

− pacing issues in the later chapters
− story loses momentum halfway through
− underwhelming and abrupt ending
− not worth full price

Torment: Tides of Numenera is a dense, cerebral role-playing game that places narrative, philosophy, and consequence at the very center of its design. Developed and published by inXile Entertainment, it positions itself as a spiritual successor to classic story-driven CRPGs, most notably Planescape: Torment, and largely succeeds by committing to ideas that many modern RPGs only gesture toward. Set in the Ninth World—a far-future Earth shaped by the rise and collapse of countless advanced civilizations—the game presents a setting where science and magic are indistinguishable, and where meaning is discovered through interpretation rather than explanation.

You play as the Last Castoff, a being created and discarded by the godlike Changing God, whose past lives have left scars on the world and on the people who inhabit it. This premise immediately frames the story around identity, responsibility, and legacy rather than heroism or conquest. Instead of asking the player to save the world, the game consistently asks quieter but more unsettling questions: what remains after you are gone, how others are shaped by your actions, and whether intent matters more than outcome. These themes are not confined to cutscenes or exposition; they are embedded into nearly every quest, dialogue choice, and character interaction.

Dialogue is the backbone of the experience. Conversations are extensive, nuanced, and often layered with hidden meanings that only become clear later. Choices are rarely labeled as good or evil, and the consequences are often indirect or delayed. The game replaces traditional morality systems with the “Tides,” abstract forces that represent different philosophical approaches such as empathy, ambition, reason, or passion. Your actions subtly shift these tides, influencing character reactions, quest outcomes, and even mechanical bonuses. This system reinforces the idea that morality is contextual and interpretive rather than absolute, encouraging players to think carefully about why they make decisions, not just what those decisions are.

Exploration in Torment: Tides of Numenera is slow, deliberate, and richly textured. Locations feel alien yet lived-in, filled with strange technologies, unusual cultures, and characters whose motivations are rarely simple. Quests often unfold through conversation, investigation, and problem-solving rather than combat, and many situations can be resolved in multiple ways depending on your skills, background, or willingness to engage deeply with the narrative. The game rewards curiosity and attentiveness, frequently offering unique outcomes to players who read closely, ask the right questions, or approach problems creatively.

Combat exists, but it is intentionally de-emphasized. Turn-based encounters are relatively infrequent and can often be avoided entirely through dialogue or clever use of abilities. When combat does occur, it serves more as a narrative punctuation mark than a primary challenge system. Character builds influence how encounters play out, but the mechanics are clearly secondary to the story being told. For some players, this makes combat feel underdeveloped or lacking impact, while for others it reinforces the game’s identity as a narrative RPG rather than a tactical one.

Character progression supports this philosophy-driven design. The three core classes—Glaive, Nano, and Jack—act more as starting frameworks than rigid archetypes. Skills and attributes influence dialogue options as much as combat effectiveness, meaning that investing in intellect, empathy, or esoteric knowledge can open entirely new paths through the game. Companions are similarly complex, each bringing their own philosophical conflicts and personal histories. Their reactions to your choices add emotional weight and often challenge the player’s assumptions, making them feel like genuine participants in the world rather than simple party members.

The presentation reinforces the game’s contemplative tone. Visually, the environments are colorful, strange, and often surreal, conveying a sense of ancient wonder and quiet decay. The art direction favors mood and symbolism over realism, while the soundtrack complements the experience with subtle, atmospheric compositions that enhance immersion without drawing attention away from the text. Voice acting is used selectively but effectively, lending gravity to key moments without undermining the dominance of written dialogue.

That said, Torment: Tides of Numenera demands patience. The game is text-heavy, philosophically dense, and often slow to reveal its larger narrative threads. Players expecting fast-paced action or clear-cut objectives may struggle with its deliberate pacing and abstract themes. Some systems can feel opaque, and the sheer volume of reading can be intimidating. However, for players willing to engage on its terms, these same qualities become its greatest strengths.

In the end, Torment: Tides of Numenera is less about winning battles or collecting loot and more about understanding a world shaped by forgotten histories and unresolved consequences. It is a game that respects the player’s intelligence, trusting them to interpret meaning, wrestle with ambiguity, and reflect on the impact of their choices. While it may not appeal to everyone, it stands as one of the most thoughtful and ambitious narrative RPGs of its generation, offering an experience that lingers in the mind long after the final decision is made.

I'm leaving a positive review because ultimately it is a Good Game. Not a great one, however. And I'm going to use this text box to complain about some of the things that bug me about it.

The writing is... "good". Competent. Workmanlike. Blessedly, mostly free of typos and stylistic solecisms. But it is *absolutely* missing that spark that makes Planescape: Torment such an evergreen classic. And there is SO MUCH of it, it really throws off the game's overall pacing, *as* a game. It's a cliché to say this about this game at this point, but it really is more like reading a doorstopper novel than playing a CRPG, in terms of what the vast majority of your time is spent on. I read doorstopper fantasy/SF novels all the time, and I found myself skimming dialogue because it's incredibly wordy and starts to blur together into sludge. It's a shame, because if you take any one dialogue in isolation, it'll have 3 or 4 incredibly cool ideas packed into it. But when you have to read 10, 20, 50 of those dialogues to get through a 2-hour gaming session, the brain fatigues.

It also doesn't help that you quickly notice a certain writerly rhythm from which the narrative voice never really deviates.

> "One sentence of dialogue. A second sentence of dialogue." [b]She drags her hand through her hair.[/b] "Another sentence of dialogue." [b]She spreads her hands.[/b] "Another sentence of dialogue. A wry quip." [b]She grins.[/b]



This is how 95% of dialogues with NPCs are constructed. This basic pattern, over and over and over and over. It starts to feel very rote, very formulaic, like the vast amount of text in this game was assembled in a giant industrial Mad-Libs factory. It's "good writing" if you take any one of these dialogue snippets in isolation, but quickly becomes repetitive and grating.

The things about games with minimal combat and maximum story, is that they somehow have to remain engaging with minimal gameplay. It's no easy task. And, despite T:ToN having some great moments and interesting parts, overall the quality engagement just isn't consistent enough to keep me hooked. 

It feels like you're often just going from random to random and having forced conversations with them along the way. Yes, this does paint a picture of events and ties in together sometimes, but quite often it can take a while to cut to the chase and, because there's so much of this occurring throughout the game, it just grows tedious. 

I also played to engage as much combat as possible, picking every fight I could get into, and the first 3 hours only saw me have 1 fight. So that wasn't for me either. 

To top that all off, exploration feels very limited too. You're not discovering these people spread out amongst interesting areas, no - they're all bunched together in very tight predictable areas. So the dialogue isn't even broken up much with exploration. 

T:ToN throws all it's egg into one dialogue filled basket and, whilst the dialogue and writing is often great and the world + story interesting, because there's little else of interest even the great stuff starts to become tiresome. The game desperately needed more variety.

You know how they say that every person has a book in them? For the devs of Torment: Tides of Numenera (TToN) that was Planescape: Torment.

TToN is an extremely similar game, to a point that if you played P:T, then you'll know most of the twists and turns of TToN's main plot. Sadly, P:T was a superior game in its themes, and had better written companions, making TToN pale in comparison. 

That, however, isn't a fair metric. On its own, TToN is still an amazing game, set in a unique world. In fact, the best parts of TToN are all about exploring that bizarre setting. The world of Numenera is set in a far future, combing elements of both fantasy and sci-fi, very much in accordance with the phrase "any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic".
The game shows it well, as it combines the off-the-wall oddities, with the mundane reality of people living in their shadows.

The game uses the Numenera TTRPG ruleset, which uses the same simple rules for both combat and non-combat encounters, making it one of the best systems I've seen for story-heavy RPGs.

The game does have some problems. Chiefly, it's designed to be played several times (at least two, if not three), but the scripted nature of the game doesn't suit more than one playthrough. At least a quarter of the game can be missed if you're not playing with a walkthrough or are psychic: Some quests need to be completed in a certain order for the best outcome, resting can cause irreversible (and often bad) changes to the locations if done too early, and you need a very specific set of skills if you want to get the most out of dialogues.

That said, the game is still highly recommended for lovers of story-rich cRPGs.

The authors build a world that is really bizarre (mild spoilers ahead).  Time manipulation, parallel worlds, magic, tech, living artifacts that will just as likely grant you experience as consume your soul.  A living door that consumes a victim’s ability to feel some particular emotion as a key.

The problem the crowd that loves this genre seems to have is that the world is not especially cohesive - it’s weird for weirds sake and the surreality doesn’t seem to serve a purpose or connect to anything.  I was clicking through a lot of that dialogue without chewing on it anyway, so I just enjoyed the weird.

I found myself feeling like i was playing a pretty well-designed TTRPG.  The way skills and effort are designed was clever.  For example, you have a bank of strength points you can spend to augment your “smashing” skill - spend zero to have a 50% chance of success, 1 to have 65%, 5 to guarantee.  That system worked really well IMO, and incentivized a balanced party.  I had a couple of duds in battle but damn were they good at persuading out of battle and thus worth it.

The combat was pretty standard DND, but they had some really clever encounters (“crises”, so named because you weren’t always fighting).  A mild spoiler as an example: One crisis involved one person breaking into a thing while the group distracted a tour guide with lots of action-consuming dialogue options.  I thought this was really well done.

The morality/whatever system asked how well your dialogue aligned you with one of five axes.  Theoretically this changes how people treat you, but I was never aware of a “I’m doing this because you’ve been nice” or anything.  Then again, I never really did anything out of character - if the game uses it to auto-fail those choices then I wouldn’t know.
Interesting teammates, interesting encounters, interesting lore, interesting flawed villains with clear motivations.  I would totally believe that all falls apart upon closer inspection than I gave it, but I thought it was pretty good for a genre I typically bounce off of.  Not sad I played it, there are elements I’ll remember, I probably won’t ever touch it again.

Tides of Numenera is primarily of interest to freaks like me who enjoy experiencing everything the cRPG genre has to offer. In this respect, it is on the good end of the scale, but nothing exceptional. The ways it tries to emulate Planescape Torment are annoying and cause the game to handicap its potential in ways that are heartbreaking to witness. Two examples out of many I can point out are Aadiriis and Sagus Cliffs. These are respectively mirrors to Ravel and Sigil. And while Sagus manages to come off quite well in this comparison, Aadiriis does not. She is a far less charismatic and engaging character. 

It might seem unfair to compare Torment to Torment. But in addition to taking on the name itself, the game also constantly calls attention to it, from similarities in plot to constant irritating references found throughout. Bronze spheres and Adahn namedrops are found throughout the game. In fact, I bet the game would be much more enjoyable to someone who hasn't played Planescape simply because they wouldn't spot all the references. The game willingly takes on the challenge of being a spiritual successor and falls short in this regard. The antagonists aren't as interesting. The player-character is created in a way that mirrors The Nameless One from Planescape, but in a way that makes it completely uninteresting to play as them. And lastly, the game isn't as funny or cohesive as Planescape. A minor point, I know, but everything counts. It is at least a lot less gross than Planescape.

The reason I still recommend the game is that when it isn't trying to be Planescape, it's great. Fantastic most of the time. The game is wonderful when it focuses on this new world of Numenera. The setting is wondrous, with an almost infinite amount of strange things to uncover. You walk into a portal and suddenly find yourself in the middle of a battlefield where every person on every side is you. You find a blob creature of psychic matter that can manifest into the real world through your skull. A machine is using probability to turn a group of women into copies of its maker's dead daughter. This and so, so, so much more can be found in Numenera. 

The way the game engages with themes of agency and identity is mostly mediocre. But when the game gives me a box and lets me experience another person's life, and then promises that I get to do it again, I love it. I do. This theme of yearning to be different people, to experience different lives, to wear others' skin and watch wonders through their eyes, rings true to me. How wonderful it is to find a game that empathizes with me and my daydreaming. Unfortunately, the game is this good only a couple of times. 

The mechanics are essentially meaningless and superfluous, but that is doubly true for the other Torment. So that is at least consistent. The combat encounters found in this game are, for the most part, bland, and the crisis mechanic, where you talk and perform skill checks mid-combat, is underutilized. In short, this game is good, but not as good as what it compares itself to.

As obviously hinted by the name of this game, it is a spiritual successor to Planescape Torment, the 1999 classic developped by Black Isle. Basically, a CRPG where combat takes a seat back and where most situations can be solved through dialogue.

Disclaimer: I have played Planescape Torment only once, around 2007, and I don't have vivid memories of it (unlike some other CRPGs like Baldur's Gate 1 and 2). I thus won't comment on whether or not Tides of Numenera is a good spiritual successor. I'll just say that the basic premise of the game seems maybe a bit too inspired by Planescape Torment: you start out as a close to divine-being who has no memory of what he's doing here. 

That being said, is Torment: Tides of Numenera a good game in itself? Yes, I thought so too. The world is pretty cool (our Earth a few billions years in the future, after countless civilizations, human or not, have appeared and disappeared). The story is pretty good IMO, the companions are well-written... Basically, everything we can ask from a dialogue-based CRPG is here. 

My only beef is that, after BG3, CRPGs without voice acting and the same amount of veneer kinda feel... cheap. But I know the two games are on two different levels, cost-wise. The french translation was also full of typos and weird formatting. There again, I know the devs probably didn't have the budget to get a top quality french version, so heh, it will do.  

So, if you liked Planescape Torment or Disco Elyseum, I guess trying this one out won't hurt.

I'll be honest - there's a lot of on-the-fencery about this game.  Looking from the outside, deciding whether to play it or not, I took a chance - I was also nervous about what people said. 

I'll say this - this game is great.  It's very insightful, has a lot of charm, and is well-written.  Go into it with some patience.  Let the world wash over you.  All the dialogue and descriptions.  Talk to all the people.  The world has a very fleshed out feeling to it. There's some very insightful writing in this gem.

For example, you ask one of your companions (a homeless 10-year-old girl) what she thinks of another companion (a curmudgeonly old man), and the dialogue goes:

R- "He's sweet," she says. "And sad. Like an uncle no one goes to visit."

A - "I'm not sad, kid.  Just tired."

R- "It probably is tiring being sad all the time."

I mean, let's be real, that's something a 10-year-old would say to an adult.  Just the right amount of honest observation, and just the right amount of blunt logic.

-------

The bar quest with all the old veterans and their tales is wonderful.
-------

The companions (I'll just do the first letter of their names, 'cause spoilers are lame), O, R, E, and M, all have good chemistry.  The companions A and C were a bit dickish for my taste - they seemed more like you're on their adventure, and less like they would ever be your real companions/friends (which seems to be the point of their characters).
-------

To me, the writing, the atmosphere, the world, and the story are the key components that make this game.

Combat is solid - it's CRPG-esque.  There isn't a great deal of it - you can fight pretty often, but it isn't the focus.   Not as complex as Pathfinder, but not so simple as to be boring.  I would definitely focus on Speed and Intelligence in a character build - there aren't a lot of Might-based skill checks or weapons.  

Edge is massively important for not wasting your resource points. Put edge in speed or intelligence (if you do might, only one point is necessary, but it really is a waste.) 
--------

I think it's absolutely worth playing this game.  It does take time to get settled into it.  It is for the more story-oriented player.  But if you want to play something that attempts to reach a part of your soul, that tries to touch a bit on the human experience, that has depth - then play Tides of Numenera.  Worth it.

Viticulture, developed and published digitally by DIGIDICED, is a thoughtful and beautifully realized adaptation of the acclaimed vineyard-management board game. It brings the tactile, strategic experience of running a Tuscan winery into a polished digital format while preserving the charm, pacing, and depth of the original tabletop design. At its core, Viticulture revolves around building a thriving wine business from humble beginnings: planting grape vines, harvesting crops, aging wine, fulfilling customer orders, expanding facilities, and recruiting seasonal workers who each contribute in their own way. The digital version maintains the thematic elegance that has long defined the physical game—there’s a rhythm to the seasons, a steady forward momentum that mirrors the real-world patience required in winemaking, and a satisfying sense of turning raw potential into refined product.

The gameplay structure follows a worker-placement format, where each season offers limited actions and competition for shared spaces. Spring determines turn order, summer opens opportunities to plant vines and attract visitors, autumn introduces new visitor cards with unique effects, and winter focuses on harvesting, crushing, and fulfilling wine orders. This multi-season approach creates an intricate tapestry of decision-making: committing a worker too early might cost you a key opportunity later, while waiting too long might allow opponents to block a crucial space. The digital version translates these nuances smoothly, presenting each choice clearly and reinforcing the careful balancing act between short-term gains and long-term strategy. As your winery grows—through building cellars, acquiring trellises and irrigation, planting better vines, and recruiting more workers—the sense of progression feels rewarding and grounded.

DIGIDICED’s adaptation respects the atmosphere of the source material. The interface is warm, pastoral, and inviting, using artwork faithful to the tabletop game and layering gentle animations to evoke the serenity of Tuscan landscapes. The calming soundtrack and minimalist sound effects add to the sense of relaxation, making it easy to settle into long, contemplative sessions. Importantly, the digital edition supports multiple modes of play: solo games against AI, local pass-and-play, online multiplayer, and asynchronous matches that allow players to take turns at their own pace. These options bring Viticulture to life in a way that replicates the social experience of a board game night while removing the lengthy setup time and physical organization required of its tabletop counterpart.

However, the digital format also reveals some of the design’s intricacies in ways that may feel overwhelming for newcomers. Viticulture has quite a few interlocking systems—card management, seasonal planning, vineyard growth, wine aging, visitor effects, and order fulfillment—and learning how they overlap can initially feel dense. While the tutorial walks players through the basics, the wealth of icons, action descriptions, and clickable elements can make the interface feel cluttered. At times, key information may hide behind small buttons or submenus, requiring extra clicks to view card details or confirm production values. This is one area where the physical version’s tactile clarity—seeing everything laid out on a table—can sometimes feel more intuitive.

The digital edition also exposes certain weaknesses inherent to the original board game. The reliance on visitor cards and wine orders introduces a measure of luck that can significantly influence a match. Drawing a series of synergistic cards can create powerful engine-building opportunities, while an unlucky sequence may leave you struggling to find direction. Similarly, the limited number of action spaces each season can lead to frustration when opponents consistently block the actions you need. These aren’t flaws exclusive to the digital port—they reflect the personality of the board game’s design—but players who prefer more deterministic strategy games may find these elements less satisfying.

Despite these drawbacks, Viticulture remains a remarkably rewarding experience for those who enjoy measured, thoughtful gameplay. The joy of optimizing your vineyard over multiple years, predicting opponents’ choices, and finding clever card combinations gives the game significant depth without ever feeling overly punitive. The digital version’s ability to streamline tasks—automating wine aging, scoring, and order processing—also allows players to focus purely on strategy rather than bookkeeping. For fans of Euro-style strategy games, it offers a satisfying blend of resource management, planning, and thematic immersion.

Ultimately, Viticulture in digital form succeeds because it stays true to what made the board game beloved: the sense of calm, the satisfaction of building something meaningful, and the pleasure of making well-timed decisions that carry resonance over the course of a match. DIGIDICED’s adaptation offers a convenient, polished way to experience one of the most thematic and elegant worker-placement games on the market. While it carries a bit of a learning curve and inherits some of the tabletop version’s luck-driven quirks, it remains an excellent choice for players who enjoy deep yet peaceful strategy, whether played solo or with friends across the world.
