20XX is actually a pretty good roguelike, and honestly, if it wasn't one, it would probably be one of the BEST spiritual successors to Mega Man based on movement and gameplay alone. (And before everyone starts raising their pitchforks, I LOVE Azure Striker Gunvolt, but that series is its own unique thing with inspiration from Mega Man, whereas this IS basically Mega Man reskinned with modern controls.) As a roguelike, it's obviously a bit dated by today's standards since it was one of the earlier games in the genre, but it's still a pretty faithful Mega Man-esque experience. I know a lot of people would have preferred this game not to be a roguelike, and that's totally understandable, but if you enjoy roguelikes or don't mind that aspect, it's INCREDIBLY worth playing.

[h1][b]Gameplay[/b][/h1]

One of its biggest upsides is the movement. It's INCREDIBLY smooth and honestly feels just as good as the X games, if not better. You have two characters in the base game, Nina and Ace, who essentially fill the same roles as X and Zero in terms of playstyle. Nina focuses on ranged combat, while Ace specializes in melee.

There are also two DLC characters with relatively unique playstyles.

Hawk is my favorite and imo the best one to use if you want an easier time with achievements, particularly those requiring different modifiers in Defiant Mode. Her whip-gun restores 1 energy with each hit, making her particularly good at using weapons. The downside is that she cannot obtain other weapons, unlike the other three characters, who each have access to at least four different primary weapons. Instead, she gets unique powers from Diamond Chests, which are also pretty good, especially the flamethrower. Having essentially infinite energy can lead to some EXTREMELY busted synergies with just a handful of powers, namely Flame Shield.

Draco is pretty much the exact opposite. He can carry multiple weapons and even obtain Nina and Ace's weapons from chests, except for their starting ones. His downside is that he can only carry one power, which is hardly a downside imo since you'll usually only carry one or two powers with Nina and Ace anyway, unless you're playing Hawk or get a particularly power-heavy run.

He also has some pretty busted weapon and power synergies, but his playstyle can feel strange, especially when it comes to his charge attack. Like in the Mega Man games, you normally charge your buster by holding the attack button. Draco, on the other hand, has charges floating around him that you activate with Up + Attack. Having a free, instant charge attack sounds busted, and it definitely is, but its behavior with each weapon is a bit strange, so it takes some getting used to.

There are also Defiant versions of each character, unlocked by completing a Revenant run with 3 skulls. They're essentially prototype versions of the characters, each with their own unique name. They play exactly the same as their regular counterparts but have significantly lower stats across the board. Their main advantage is that prototype augments found in Very Safe Labs, which normally come with downsides, provide double the benefits when equipped by them. This can lead to some INCREDIBLY strong builds if you manage to get multiple prototypes in a run, but overall, they're essentially a hard mode for each character.

[h1][b]Progression[/b][/h1]

Progression is similar to your usual roguelikes. Bosses are always the same, while stages have different variants depending on how far you are into a run.

After beating a boss, you get three portals to choose where to go next. Each boss is tied to a specific stage. For example, Kur will always be a Skytemple stage, but its layout and difficulty depend on when you fight him. Pick him early, around stage 2 or 3, and the layout will be relatively easy. Pick him later, and you'll get a harder, longer stage. Bosses themselves also become harder and rely more on their gimmicks the later you fight them.

This means you can choose to fight the bosses you find hardest early to avoid their harder versions later. Personally, I HATE Twin Astrals and Rollster Beta in later stages because of their revive and divide mechanics, respectively, so I always choose them early. Plus, when playing as Hawk, you want to take on Twin Astrals as soon as possible anyway.

[spoiler]After defeating all 8 bosses, you have to fight the two doctors responsible for creating Nina and Ace. Their stages are very similar and always follow the same order, with Brighton coming first and Arlan afterwards.

Brighton is the usual kind of boss that incorporates abilities from all the other bosses, but honestly, he's VERY easy. He might hit you here and there, mostly because multiple attacks happen on screen at the same time rather than because his patterns are particularly difficult.

Arlan, on the other hand, is a somewhat interesting boss fight. You don't get an actual boss HP bar, so you basically have to guess how much health he has, which is around 3000. The fight consists of going from one edge of the room to the other, dodging stage hazards and broken versions of Nina and Ace, before hitting the top of the spider robot where the doctor is located. He then pushes you back, creates a new layout, and you rinse and repeat.

The whole design is very Wily-like, and having a boss fight that's essentially an entire stage is a somewhat unique concept. That said, it gets old pretty fast since he's the only boss in the entire game you can't immediately delete. I'm almost positive he has a damage threshold for each cycle, because if you deal too much damage in a single attack, he'll immediately push you back and trigger the next cycle instead.[/spoiler]

[h1][b]Upgrades & Items[/b][/h1]

When it comes to items, it's your usual run-of-the-mill roguelike progression. You do runs, collect chips, and use them to buy new items. The vast majority are stat boosters. The game isn't particularly "unique" with its upgrades, but they complement its already fun gameplay.

There's also Core Augments, which are basically armor pieces. Completing an entire set gives you a big bonus, but almost every individual piece is strong on its own too. Most should be familiar to Mega Man X players, taking inspiration from Parts in Mega Man X5 or features from other armors, like the Fourth Armor's hover, the Blade Armor's 8-directional air dash, or the Gaia Armor's anti-knockback mechanic.

Personally, I always tunnel vision on Draconpent because it's the most fun to use imo, especially with the enhanced buster, but any of the sets are solid. Owlhawk is what you'd want for Hawk, for example.

Once you buy all the unlocks, the shop turns into an undevelopment shop, letting you spend chips to temporarily remove items from the pool for your next run. This helps reduce RNG or target a specific build. It also applies to Core Augments, so you can prevent pieces from an unwanted set appearing in your next normal run (not Daily Challenges or the other portals at the top).

You also have another shop where you can buy items for your next run. Its selection is randomized every time, and purchases cost Soul Chips, so you can potentially get an early lead depending on the rotation.

Finally, if you have chips to spare and don't want to buy or remove anything, you can trade them for Shiny Tokens. Their price increases exponentially with each one you buy until your next run. They're basically just tokens for the slot machines that occasionally appear in stages, making them a chip sink since they don't guarantee you anything.

Gonna throw my hat in the ring and say this game is still worth playing, even after its sequel's release. If you're only gonna buy one, then yes, get 30XX. 30XX is a bigger game, with more in-depth mechanics, more features, a level editor, beautiful art style, even a non-roguelike campaign if you're interested in that sort of thing.

So with all those points in 30XX's favor, it's easy to see why that game has mostly replaced its predecessor for so many. However, I would also say that all of these mechanics turn 30XX into a slightly different type of roguelike. There's much more material management and decision-making, more currencies, optional challenges to be enabled at the start of a level, Nina can fuse her weapon now, overall more of a character-building element with more chances to choose between multiple distinct upgrades (some of which having drawbacks), and with all that: sometimes I do prefer the more simple experience 20XX offers

20XX is a simpler game, but never to the point of "shut your brain off and have fun", I don't tend to like that kind of game as much. Rather, 20XX feels much more like a traditional Mega Man X game with a roguelike twist. Almost every item and upgrade only makes you more powerful without drawback, additional mobility (without speed upgrades) is rarely more powerful than the strongest mobility upgrade in your average MMX game, and you can still get to a point of having a pretty strong power trip without having to put a ton of thought into long-term planning. I will never argue 20XX is better than it's successor. 30XX breaks into much more of its own identity, and the further planning elements objectively add more depth to the gameplay. Yet sometimes, I like focusing more on the Mega Man X elements than the roguelike elements.

30XX strikes a better balance between its roguelike and Mega Man-like elements, while forging its own identity. 20XX instead feels like a Mega Man X game with procedurally generated levels, and a lack of strength cap. This distinction makes 30XX a better roguelike, but I think it also makes both games worth playing if you're someone like me, who enjoy the average Mega Man game more than the average roguelike

Last thing, supposing you can only get one, note 30XX has a non-roguelike mode which makes it play like a traditional Mega Man game. This does forfeit any roguelike elements at all (i think), but if you're also someone like me here, that could balance the score out a bit for you.

LAST NOTE: Both games have full local and online co-op, either with someone who owns a copy of the game, or with someone who doesn't own it with remote play together (though do expect lightly worse connection if you use that last option). Both games are just more fun with a friend. Whichever one you decide to purchase, try and share the joy with someone, if you can

[code] IN THE YEAR 199X, A SUPER ROBOT NAMED MEGA MAN WAS CREATED. 

CAPCOM CREATED MEGA MAN TO FULFILL THE ACTION DESIRES OF CHILDREN EVERYWHERE.

 [/code]

okay so that's 20XX

It's a Mega Man X styled roguelike; and I already know that's not saying everything so here goes some more stuff.

It's a game where although your level progression choices are relatively limited versus classic Mega Man and Mega Man X, it's a game that nevertheless takes the most cues and inspiration from those games... and it's not cheap about it either... okay, art style aside; but it grows on you easily, I feel.

Like any good roguelike, the real meat and potatoes are the items and character progression. Nina, Ace, Hawk and Draco (the last two being DLC but pretty much worth it TBH) start small but grow much stronger as the game goes on; snowballing hard by the end game.

Nina's basically Mega Man X; with a classic buster and big boom blasty attack for her charge attack, Ace is basically Zero (albeit without techniques ala Mega Man X4-8), Hawk is a Belmont with a heavy focus on boss and special weapons and... I forgot what Draco's like, but he's a slight hybrid of Nina and Ace kinda. All four have a specific "shtick" they want to play to; and they all get unique options, even if they share a great deal of things beteen each other; especially boss weapons.

Of course, besides the boss weapons, 20XX being a roguelike means you get a number of powerful upgrades; or Augments as the game puts it. Whether it be new weapons for your character (like Nina getting a Metroid Wave Beam or Ace getting a blender), special Core augments that resemble the armor mechanics of Mega Man X (especially the first 4 where each part provided its own benefit), and the predictable risky Safe Lab Prototype augments (think Isaac Devil Deals; but instead of neccessarily being health costed, they come with extreme downsides), you won't be disappointed with the kinds of ways the game can be played...

Of course, being a Mega Man successor, it's gotta have good music. It just has to. Why shouldn't it? Thankfully, it does have good music that fits the mood quite nicely.

The bosses are also great too; there are several of them that are just flat out huge (Visage being a standout) and really feel like a spectacle. The last two bosses are definitely a surprise kinda, but it makes sense if you do your reading of the datalores (I promise, they're great, especially if you're the mood for the strangely, casually, and humorously cynical nature of the world surrounding the contractors).

That said... I wonder what a potential sequel, a "30XX" if you will, would be like.

...and why that game has 68 of my hours (at time of writing) versus this game's 29 (as of writing).

20XX, developed by Batterystaple Games in collaboration with Fire Hose Games and published by Batterystaple Games, is a fast-paced action platformer that successfully fuses the timeless appeal of retro side-scrolling shooters with modern roguelike mechanics. Clearly inspired by Capcom’s iconic Mega Man X series, the game builds upon that foundation by introducing procedural level generation, randomized power-ups, and a structure that rewards repeated playthroughs rather than linear progression. It manages to capture the speed, precision, and intensity of the classics while giving players a reason to keep returning for “just one more run.” The result is a game that feels both nostalgic and fresh, blending the rhythm of old-school design with the unpredictability of modern roguelite systems.

At its core, 20XX revolves around the idea of endless replayability. Each run consists of a series of procedurally generated stages, each filled with enemies, traps, and bosses that test your reflexes and pattern recognition. Players can choose between two main characters—Nina, a ranged blaster user reminiscent of Mega Man, and Ace, a melee-focused warrior who emphasizes close combat and precision timing. The choice between the two fundamentally changes how the game feels, encouraging experimentation and replaying levels to master each character’s strengths. Defeating bosses rewards players with new weapons or powers, while collecting “Soul Chips” during a run allows permanent upgrades to be unlocked between sessions. This creates a satisfying feedback loop that ensures each failure contributes to future success, striking a balance between the punishing difficulty of roguelikes and the sense of progression found in traditional action titles.

The gameplay is fluid and responsive, perhaps its greatest strength. Movement feels effortless, allowing for dashes, wall jumps, and mid-air maneuvers that make navigating the randomly assembled levels a joy. Combat, too, benefits from tight controls, giving each hit impact and clarity. What sets 20XX apart is its procedural level design, which draws from a variety of pre-made segments that are stitched together differently each run. This system keeps the experience unpredictable without losing coherence—stages still feel hand-crafted, even though no two playthroughs are exactly the same. Boss encounters are equally varied, presenting players with challenging patterns that encourage adaptability rather than memorization. The game’s fast pacing and rhythmic combat recall the best moments of classic action games, but its roguelike unpredictability ensures that mastery comes not from rote repetition, but from quick thinking and flexibility.

In addition to its solo mode, 20XX also offers cooperative multiplayer, both local and online, which significantly enhances its replay value. Running through the game with a partner adds a dynamic layer of strategy, as players can coordinate attacks, share power-ups, and compensate for each other’s weaknesses. Co-op play also helps offset some of the difficulty spikes, allowing the game to appeal to both newcomers and veterans of the genre. For those looking for additional variety, the game includes daily and weekly challenge modes with pre-set conditions, encouraging players to test their skills against others through leaderboards. These challenges highlight the game’s robust mechanics and give it an ongoing competitive edge that extends well beyond a single playthrough.

Aesthetically, 20XX takes a minimalist yet effective approach. The colorful, high-resolution pixel art evokes the style of its inspirations without feeling derivative. Character animations are smooth, and enemy designs—while clearly inspired by 1990s action games—retain a distinct, modern flair. The backgrounds, while simple, are clean and readable, ensuring that the focus remains on the action. The soundtrack complements the gameplay perfectly, featuring energetic electronic tracks and synth-driven melodies that echo the retro era while maintaining a modern punch. The audiovisual presentation may not be extravagant, but it’s cohesive and purposeful, reflecting the game’s dedication to clarity and momentum over spectacle.

Where 20XX occasionally stumbles is in the repetition inherent to its procedural nature. While the randomized stages ensure that no two runs are identical, the limited number of room templates means that players will begin to notice recurring structures and patterns after extended play. Some critics have noted that the level variety, while serviceable, doesn’t quite match the handcrafted charm of the games that inspired it. Likewise, the story is minimal to the point of being almost nonexistent—a deliberate design choice, but one that may leave players craving a stronger narrative hook or world-building. These shortcomings are easily forgiven, however, because the core gameplay loop remains engaging, and the thrill of overcoming a particularly brutal boss or discovering a new power-up keeps the experience fresh.

One of the game’s defining achievements is how well it bridges the gap between accessibility and challenge. It caters to players who crave fast, precision-based platforming while still offering enough progression systems and customization to keep things approachable. The inclusion of multiple difficulty modifiers, optional permanent upgrades, and different character loadouts allows players to tailor their experience to their comfort level. This flexibility, combined with responsive controls and smooth performance, makes 20XX one of the most welcoming yet rewarding roguelike platformers on Steam. It demonstrates a clear understanding of why players love both retro action games and modern roguelikes—and finds a near-perfect middle ground between the two.

Ultimately, 20XX stands as one of the most successful reinterpretations of the classic action-platformer formula in the indie scene. It honors the legacy of Mega Man and its contemporaries not by copying them outright, but by reimagining their mechanics through a modern, replay-driven design philosophy. Its snappy controls, fast-paced combat, and emphasis on procedural variety ensure that every run feels meaningful, even when failure strikes. While it lacks the handcrafted artistry of older platformers, its innovation and mechanical polish make it a standout in its genre. For players seeking a game that combines the spirit of the 16-bit era with the unpredictability of roguelikes, 20XX offers an exhilarating and endlessly replayable experience that captures the best of both worlds.

[h2]Very Cool Concept, Some Very Questionable Decisions[/h2]
It has some stuff going for it, but it unfortunately also has a bit more going against it.

In other words: changing this review from a [b]NEGATIVE[/b] to a [b]POSITIVE[/b].


Anyhoo...
I read a lot.
I mostly read sci-fi.
Alastair Reynolds, Greg Egan, Adrian Tchaikovsky, Asimov, Clement; you get the gist.

The story here feels like it's a split between Terminal World and House of Suns. And this is a good thing. The environments feel like they'd belong in those worlds. The multiverse twist is very Greg Egan/James Hogan, while the enemies are very Tchaikovsky/Orson Card.

It's nailed the space opera-ish, big picture, sci-fi vibe. In spades. I thought the voice acting was decent enough, and the characters have quirky personalities to them (more than everyone did in Revelation Space, at least).


So, what's the problem then?
The [b]GAMEPLAY[/b].

That's the AT-AT Walker in the room.

It's not exactly clunky, but it's not exactly as precise as you'd want this kind of game to be. You have some platforming, you have your combat, and they [i]do[/i] do something interesting with these things.. but it ends up somewhere between "almost clunk, and almost there".

Instead of writing a thesis here, I'll just list some gripes I have so far;

- Meta-progression: yes, it's there. But it is SLOW. Meta-progression is very very slow, because almost everything uses the SAME currency. It takes a while to unlock some considerably vital perks. Like, "Oh, damn... that thing would be really nice to have early game. Wait, it's HOW MUCH??"

- In-game currency: WHY does EVERYTHING cost coin? Hades had a good balance between "this requires coin" and "this requires other things". In this game, almost EVERYTHING requires the same currency; opening certain chests, fusing with your [i]others[/i] (which is one of the game's main selling points, by the way..). The economy is significantly worse than Pharloom, and that's saying a lot.

- Main/sub weapons are random starting out: this wouldn't be too big a deal, IF certain weapons/sub weapons just didn't suck. Things aren't balanced very well, and it shows, painfully.

- Bugs: Almost 3 years since release and I've encountered a few bugs. Random crashes on save slot load, spawning into a map [i]WITHOUT ANY WEAPONS[/i]... would have refunded right there, if my game time had been <2 hours.

- Random in-game pitch? I exited the hub once, expecting to see the menu, only to be greeted by a dev message going something like "We spent so-and-so many years developing this game... etc etc", and my jaw just dropped. Like "huh... [b]WHY[/b] are you trying to pitch the game to me!? [i]I already bought the f**king thing![/i]". Dunno, that was weird...

- Balance. Like I said earlier, it's not balanced very well. Runs depend entirely on if you get lucky with good drops or not (more on that below).

- The "curses" are NOT worth it. I had a curse once "lift 10 enemies into the sky"; I did not get a single "golf-swing" type weapon or sub weapon during the entire run. So yeah, running around the area taking 30% extra damage with ZERO benefits was fun.

- Even some of the "boons" come with a negative, which are poorly balanced. "Deal +100% damage, but take +100% damage", "50% extra health, but heal 50% less", and there are a lot more... like, can I just get a regular boon please? The take 100% damage for example is terribly balanced, your HP will [b]HALVE[/b] from one mistake.

- Weapon combos: weapons have different combos. X X (hold) X, X X ^ X, etc. The problem is, most of those don't even work. I don't know if it's the timing being finicky, or they weren't programmed properly... but you'll see this mentioned in Discussions, too. I guess the devs were trying to be fancy. Like "well, it'll get boring if it's just one light attack"

No, the only thing we needed was: X = light attack, (hold) X = strong/charged attack. That's it. That's all we needed, because we still have TWO sub-weapons, a slam attack and a dash attack. Combos just weren't necessary.

- The "fusion" thing... as mentioned earlier, it costs money. I do not find it worth while to fuse. It doesn't seem to add anything meaningful to a run or my power level.

- Speaking of power level, I don't get weapon/sub weapon power level at all. Everything during a run has a power level: you, your weapons, spells, etc. But if this [b]level 1[/b] weapon is clearly stronger and has better stats than that [b]level 4[/b] weapon, where's my incentive to swap? You get a main that does acid or weak, the "frost blast" sub, and you're set. That's it, no need to ever swap. What's even the point of having power levels?

- The late-game shielder enemies are [b]severely[/b] unbalanced. You can have a group of 3 VERY tanky and VERY agile enemies ALL being shielded by this shielder... and the shielder will TELEPORT away THREE SCREENS. Yeah, f**k that.

- Which also brings me to another point: you are not equipped to deal with hordes, but the game loves throwing groups at you. The later stages can get real messy, and not in a good, challenging, fun way.


And now, the MAGNUM OPUS!
- Weapon attributes vs elements: WHY? [i]"Why are you the way that you are?"[/i]
Weapon attributes and elements are randomly appointed to weapons, without any synergy. I know this, because it doesn't make a SHRED of sense. Take this: I picked up a [b]WEAK[/b]-affinity weapon. The attribute appointed to that weapon was "Inflict crits on enemies afflicted with [b]POISON[/b]. No random crits", meaning; you do crits ONLY on enemies affected with POISON, with no other way of doing crits. They are effectively disabled for anything else (even physical damage).

So, [b]why in the ever-loving F**K is the weapon element WEAK then??[/b]

I swear, Pee Wee Herman must have been in charge of weapon balancing or something... [i]"Oh, a fire weapon! I should make it crit with just frost damage... tee hee, it'll be kooky![/i]


F**king geniuses, I tell ya.



HOWEVER, even considering those considerable negatives, I really love multiverse/space opera stuff, so I'm giving it a barely passing grade. Plus, I got it for like $4.00.


If you're interested, get it on a DEEP sale.

A  decent met-rogue-vani-like with a couple of little quirks, but which delivers a fun experience overall.

The interesting, varied enemy designs have really clean animations, enabling a clarity in telegramming attacks which I find to be extremely rare in the genre (or at least, it’s rare that they click with me so well). It immediately rang alarm bells that the UX is unmistakably designed with consoles in mind – and navigating menus is often really clunky and unpleasant without a pad – but I was pleased to discover that gameplay itself actually feels really good on keyboard and mouse.

The combat is enjoyably fluid, and you can dodge almost continuously, meaning that at the standard difficulty level I could dash and slash my way through many encounters while barely taking a scratch. That said, it’s also pretty unpredictable, and sometimes very unforgiving; I was occasionally caught out by a room of enemies which didn’t look particularly impressive, but ended up giving me a damn good kicking.

One element which I have to question is the balancing of the RNG, especially when it comes to weapons and abilities. On one run you might exclusively be given a scant selection of options with mediocre stats and zero synergy, and on the next be handed on a silver platter a devastating combination that obliterates the opposition. Of course, some measure of that is to be expected in a roguelike, but entering a boss fight with a poor setup through no fault of your own just sucks, and feeling like you'd be better off abandoning a pretty lengthy run purely because of RNG is hugely discouraging.

Another unfortunate aspect is that the “fusion” of two characters, which you’d expect to have some pretty substantial impact on gameplay, seems almost entirely inconsequential, almost like an afterthought. It really feels like a wasted opportunity. A related disappointment is that the 3 different playable characters have such minimal sense of personality to them, and the runs are long enough that you are very rarely switching between them, so you don’t build any familiarity with which model correlates with which combat specialisation. They feel totally indistinct, and considering how nifty so many of the enemy designs are, that really seems a shame.

I'd also have to say that the story is really poor, and the voice acting, to be brutally honest, is just awful – I almost immediately felt I had to silence the vocals. Probably my biggest annoyance with the game, though, is how it doesn’t respect your time, and holds you hostage with the threat of losing your progress if you want to quit. I find that totally unacceptable; I should be able to quit whenever I want, and there’s just no excuse for forcing me to keep playing simply because you couldn’t be bothered coding in a save state for when I need to exit.

These issues are obviously frustrating, but all that being said, the core mechanics are what matter most, and on the whole they are really solid. I had a satisfying time with it, so if you’re a fan of the genre and spot the game on sale, I don’t think you’ll be disappointed.

[h2]## Trinity Fusion (2023) – one run… one more run… okay, *one* more[/h2]

[i]**Developer:** Angry Mob Games
**Genre:** action-platformer roguelite (“roguevania”)
**Playtime (my experience):** 5.7 hours
**My take in one sentence:** super fun fights and effortless-feeling combos wrapped in an addictive “one more run” loop—though I’d mainly recommend grabbing it on sale.[/i]

[b]### What is it?[/b]

*Trinity Fusion* is built around what a roguelite is all about: **start a run, die, start again**, and get just strong enough along the way to believe you’ll “definitely make it this time.” Spoiler: you usually die again. And you still hit *Start Run*.

[b]## Gameplay – great combat, combos like it’s nothing[/b]

Combat is where the game really shines. Fights feel **fast and smooth**, and the system encourages you to chain **combos** without it feeling like hard work. You flow through encounters, pick up upgrades, grow stronger, and before you know it you’re stuck in that satisfying cycle:

> destroy enemies → build combos → get stronger → destroy harder → “okay, one more run”

It’s tuned so well that you can easily jump back in whenever you feel like it. No fuss—just another run.

[b]## Progression & replay value – the core of the addiction[/b]

Repetition is the point, but in a good way: every run feels like a fresh chance to play a bit cleaner and push a bit farther. You die a lot, but it rarely feels like wasted time—more like you’ve warmed up for the next attempt.

I **didn’t finish** the game, but **5.7 hours** was already enough for me to feel satisfied.

[b]Story – present, but not memorable[/b]

Honestly, I don’t remember much of the story. That doesn’t mean it’s bad—it just means the game is mostly carried by **action and momentum**. If you’re here for narrative, it probably won’t be the reason you keep coming back.

[b]## Audiovisuals – everything clicks[/b]

Visually, it looks **really good**: sharp, stylish, and readable even when things get hectic. The music deserves a shout-out too—it **pushes you forward constantly**, like the soundtrack itself wants you to do “one more run.” Overall, the audio and visuals fit together nicely.

[b]## Price – buy it on sale[/b]

I got it in a bundle and definitely feel like I got my money’s worth. But price-wise, this is how I’d put it:

[i]* **€5.85 on sale:** absolutely worth it
* **~€19.50 full price:** I’d personally wait for a discount[/i]

[b]## Extras – Achievements yes, Trading Cards no[/b]

Nice for completionists: it has **Achievements**, but **(still) no Steam Trading Cards**.

[b]## Final verdict[/b]

*Trinity Fusion* is the kind of game you don’t necessarily need to “finish” to enjoy. If you like **snappy combat**, **chaining combos**, and that classic roguelite “I can do better next run” feeling, you’ll have a great time—especially if you pick it up for cheap during a sale.

If you want, I can also rewrite this in a more **Steam-review style** (shorter, with pros/cons and a clear “Recommended / Not Recommended” ending).

This is a typical “roguelike” game, where we have to climb through several game levels via a single run, and each failure pulls us back to the very beginning. During each attempt we accumulate some “persistent” currency, which can be used to upgrade our character, increasing chances of success for the next run. The cycle continues over and over again until the player's experience and purchased upgrades finally beat the odds and make it through the final boss.

There are 3 playable characters:
- Naira - uses various ranged weapons, like rifles, pistols, rocket launchers and bows
- Keira - specializes in close combat, using heavy melee weapons, like sledgehammers, two-handed swords and so on.
- Altara - uses projectiles with various elemental or debilitating effects (e.g. magic) like ice bolt, fire pillar and so on.

The game levels vary depending on the selected character. Each heroine is bound to the specific world and traverses through its landscape in order to reach a special machine - “harmonizer”, which is necessary for the universe's salvation. Altara has to deal with barren plains infested with mutants, Keira - with the factory world ruled by sapient machines, Naira - with the sky city inhabited with cyborgs, who pursue godhood.

Each world is unique with its own appearance, hazards and enemies. In order to win the game we have to reach a “harmonizer” from each world and then beat the final boss.

While traversing the levels we can stumble upon a special device, which allows us to fuse 2 different characters into one, making the 2 different side-arms available for the run. Ultimately we can fuse all 3 characters together. Hence the name - “Trinity fusion”.

Obviously the game designers considered this to be a core feature, but in reality it is kinda disappointing. First of all, many fusion combinations are pointless. Most likely you will end with merging Keira with either Naira or Altara, depending on which your starting character is. Such a combination allows you to use heavy melee strikes and some ranged attacks, being prepared for anything. Fusing Naira with Altara simply gives you 2 types of distant attacks, which make little practical sense.

Perhaps if Altara’s magic was somehow different, like creating a shield for brief invincibility, buff for the attack, healing or something - the choice for the fusion would not be so obvious.

The fusion with the 3rd character becomes available only at the very end before the fight with the final boss, which is a pity. It would be much more logical if we fuse all characters as soon as possible maximizing the odds for the victory.

The main gameplay is presented as a 2D platformer, where we have to fight our way through the enemies and occasional obstacles like lava pools and chasms. 

The combat is difficult but fair. Each enemy requires its own approach and tactics. Some use ranged attacks, some charges into you, some use projectiles with sophisticated trajectories. The key to the victory is using dodge and sidearms.

The bosses have been created nicely. They provide a fair challenge without making it absurd. All you have to do is pick the correct tactics. Overcoming the enemy is more of a mind challenge, instead of a “gym for the fingers”. Although you may still need both.

There are no puzzles and no “metroidvania” aspect. Each level has some secret rooms with chests with special prizes, but they are easy to get. The main problem is spotting them. 

Each character has a special “traverse” ability, which allows her to reach some closed points. For example: Altara can use a teleportation drone, Keira  - a grappler. But in reality they barely change anything.

The levels remain almost the same for each run. There are some slight changes, but mostly the layout always stays the same. It is clear that developers attempted to make the word to be “generated” instead of being static, but they were not very successful in that. The exit and fusion devices are always located at the same places of the map. This is not what you expect from a game in the “roguelike” genre.

The story and dialogues are quite shallow. Still the game describes a multiverse of several different worlds, its inhabitants and the crisis we have to solve. But way too many things remain unclear. For example: how does the character “fusion” work? Who and why built the “harmonizes”? And so on.

Some extra dialogue between runs would also come in handy, making the process more lively and confirming that running circles attempting to reach the final goal is a normal process. But alas…

The finale looks quite absurd. There are 2 ways to locate and deal with a final threat, but they make no difference as we have to fight the same boss in the end. What was the point in branching the main quest then?

The graphics are good. The 2D platformer is rendered with a modern 3D engine. The visual is more cartoon like, but all the elements: the environment, the characters and so on - were created thoroughly. The main disappointment is the character's running animation, which looks like a sidestepping, appearing quite weird.

The optimization is good. Even with many moving objects on the screen everything runs smoothly. Still if you use dash to quickly traverse through the scenery, you may encounter some lags. 

Music is unremarkable, but decent enough. SFX exactly as it should be. The dialogues are fully voiced, which makes the game more lively.

Total rating: 6/10.

English review:

After many hours of gameplay, having finished the game on Hard mode and also completed all achievements, I can say that this game is definitely worth it. I really enjoyed it.

It is a difficult game, especially on Hard, but the difficulty does not feel unfair. The game allows you to improve, get used to its mechanics, and become stronger through the permanent upgrades made in the Citadel.

What I liked the most about the game is the feeling that every run is unique because of the randomness of the amplifiers. When you manage to create a good build, combining weapons and amplifiers, you can become very strong.

An important tip: I recommend finishing the game first on Normal or Veteran and upgrading the Citadel, such as increasing your health and other useful improvements. After that, you can change the difficulty with the NPC Renan and try Hard mode already having those upgrades, which helps a lot.

To truly finish the game and reach the final boss, called Fusion, you need to complete the three main paths. Each path starts with a different character, and the character you choose defines the starting map and the route you will follow. So my recommendation is: first complete the three routes, one with each character, on an easier difficulty. After that, try the final run on Hard.

For this final run, I highly recommend starting with Naira and then fusing with Altara. On Hard, starting with Naira helps you get the right sequence of maps, and fusing with Altara makes the run much easier.

For anyone trying to finish the game on Hard, I recommend resetting the first map until you get the coin amplifier that gives 500% coins based on damage taken. In my opinion, it is almost mandatory on Hard, because it allows you to collect a lot of money early. However, to really take advantage of this, you also need the Citadel upgrade that lets you refresh the amplifier list, so you can spend that money rerolling and choosing better amplifiers during the run.

About the build, my main recommendation is to use the green retaliation amplifier, the double amplifier called Vital Surge, and the purple amplifier that increases skill damage, especially to combine with Faulty Dash. I also recommend red amplifiers such as Glass Cannon, boss damage, and Aerial Attacker. For blue amplifiers, Explosive Dodge is very strong, and completing a blue class that gives a temporary damage increase can also help a lot.

I also posted an image on Steam showing the build I used, which may help anyone who wants a better idea of the setup.

In the final boss fight, there is one very important detail: the tentacles that come out of the ground count as normal enemies. If you destroy them, you recover one point of the sync link for each tentacle. This helps a lot to keep the run alive during the fight.

I also recommend clearing 100% of the maps to increase your power level and get better weapons. This makes the final boss fight much shorter.

Overall, I highly recommend the game. The difficulty is challenging, but fair, and the gameplay becomes very fun once you understand the builds and start creating good combinations.

Trinity Fusion, developed and published by Angry Mob Games, is a sci-fi action roguelite that blends fast-paced platforming, methodical combat, and a multiverse-hopping storyline into a tightly executed, yet occasionally uneven experience. At its core, the game sets out to offer a polished mix of Metroidvania exploration and roguelite unpredictability, with each run offering new weapons, enemies, and environments to overcome. The gameplay foundation is solid, and while it doesn’t revolutionize the genre, it successfully distinguishes itself with a unique premise and fluid combat mechanics.

The narrative centers on Maya, a character psychically linked to three alternate versions of herself, each from a separate, collapsing universe. This concept of parallel selves is more than a plot device—it’s fully integrated into the gameplay. As players progress, they swap between these counterparts, each with distinct combat styles, traversal abilities, and starting universes. One character may specialize in swift melee strikes and aerial mobility, while another emphasizes heavy weaponry and ranged attacks. These differences encourage adaptability and give each run a different feel, especially when the game begins fusing their abilities together, creating a sense of progression that feels both narrative and mechanical.

Combat in Trinity Fusion is one of its standout strengths. Every strike, dash, dodge, and special attack feels snappy and precise, which is crucial in a game where positioning and timing matter as much as your loadout. Weapons range from traditional blades and axes to futuristic cannons and energy rifles, each with their own rhythm and risk-reward mechanics. There’s also a fusion system that allows you to merge stats and abilities between characters as you unlock more of the multiverse, which adds complexity and customization to each run. Boss fights punctuate the experience with memorable encounters that often require pattern recognition and skillful movement rather than just brute force.

Visually, Trinity Fusion embraces a clean sci-fi aesthetic with sleek character models, minimalist UI, and biome designs that range from neon-lit ruins to sterile industrial complexes. While the environments are distinctive, they do sometimes lack depth or variation, and after multiple runs the procedural generation begins to reveal its limitations. Certain enemy types and room layouts reappear frequently, which can undercut the sense of discovery that roguelites often thrive on. Still, the visual clarity during combat is commendable, with clear animations and well-defined enemy telegraphs that help players navigate the chaos.

The game’s structure mixes procedural level design with handcrafted elements, striking a balance between unpredictability and intentionality. Each universe has its own biome set, environmental hazards, and traversal challenges, and players can choose different starting points as they progress, which keeps things fresh. However, the randomness of item and weapon drops can sometimes lead to frustratingly uneven runs. Some weapons clearly outperform others, and it’s possible to be stuck with underwhelming gear during crucial segments, making certain encounters more punishing than they need to be. The permanent upgrade system attempts to offset this by offering meta-progression between runs, but grinding for resources to unlock those upgrades can begin to feel repetitive.

The story, while not heavily emphasized, adds context and stakes to the journey. The collapsing multiverse concept is simple yet effective, and the writing does a decent job of giving each version of Maya a distinct personality. However, the cutscenes and dialogue are minimal, and players looking for a deep, character-driven narrative may find the story elements undercooked. The game opts for a more gameplay-focused experience, which works in its favor for pacing but leaves the world-building feeling slightly underutilized.

Sound design complements the sci-fi tone nicely. Combat effects are punchy and satisfying, while the electronic soundtrack shifts between ambient and energetic tracks depending on the situation. Voice acting is sparse but effective where used, and environmental audio cues help guide players through enemy-heavy sections and alert them to hazards.

Despite a few shortcomings—such as occasional difficulty spikes, some repetitive design elements, and a relatively shallow narrative—Trinity Fusion delivers a strong, engaging roguelite experience. It finds its strength in responsive combat, varied character mechanics, and a multiverse concept that influences both story and gameplay. It doesn’t reinvent the wheel, but it polishes what it sets out to do with care and attention to detail. For fans of action roguelites and sci-fi settings, it offers a satisfying, replayable adventure filled with challenge, progression, and style.

The mechanics are not always as simple as click and drag. Sometimes you have to do other things like hold something in place or rotate it. I did find a couple of people in the discussions talking about the same suspected bugs, and the community was recommending exiting the level and coming back. I tried that and it actually worked, making the mechanic much easier to do so I could collect the cat. The hint option is kinda buggy though. I also found it annoying that when I launched the game I was thrown directly into the tutorial instead of the main menu, where I would rather check my settings before starting. Oh, I also have to mention that the levels are extremely easy to complete, but not necessarily in a bad way because the game moves between simple puzzle problems and finding collectibles. The postcard images on the back that you have to use to unlock the secret level were very clever. That one threw me off because it was a step more advanced than the normal puzzles in the game. Cats in Time is a charming "hidden cats" puzzler that excels as a shared experience. While it serves as a wonderful bonding tool for a parent and child, the core loop eventually struggles to maintain momentum, leading to a bit of fatigue by the time the final clock is wound.

It has exceptional tactile puzzles. The interaction with the dioramas is satisfyingly "clicky." Perfect for Steam Deck - the tactile puzzles feel right at home on the Deck’s screen.

It is also an incredible entry-point for younger players; played this with my daughter over 1.5 year period and it created lasting memories, becoming a nostalgic milestone in our gaming journey together.

It does, however stagnate mechanically - by the end, the puzzles felt increasingly similar. This lack of variety meant that both me and my daughter were losing steam toward the finish line. This in effect diluted our momentum, and because the game was played over such a long period, the repetitive nature of the puzzles became more apparent, making the final stretch feel like a bit of a crawl. By the end of the game, the puzzles lack new "hooks," leading to a little fatigue.

While the mechanical repetition makes this feel closer to a 3.5/5 by the end, the high nostalgic value for me and the quality of the favorite levels keep it at a solid 4 stars. It is a perfect example of a game being more than the sum of its parts when shared with the right person.

Cats in Time, developed and published by Pine Studio, is a delightful and visually engaging puzzle adventure that combines whimsical charm with accessible gameplay. At its heart lies a simple yet imaginative premise: a quirky professor’s time machine malfunctions, scattering his beloved cats across various points in history. As the player, your mission is to travel through time and retrieve every missing feline hidden in intricately designed dioramas. The concept alone sets the tone for what the experience aims to be—a relaxing, exploration-based puzzle game that favors atmosphere, discovery, and gentle problem-solving over intensity or difficulty. From the moment you enter the first time period, it’s clear that Cats in Time prioritizes player comfort, curiosity, and joy.

The gameplay structure is built around a series of beautifully rendered three-dimensional scenes, each representing a different historical or futuristic era. The player can rotate, zoom, and inspect these miniature worlds from every angle, searching for hidden cats and interacting with puzzles cleverly embedded within the environment. Each level features a unique thematic setting, such as ancient Egypt, medieval castles, industrial London, or even futuristic cityscapes, and within these spaces are interactive mechanisms like levers, codes, and switches. The design philosophy encourages observation and experimentation rather than trial and error, with puzzles that are intuitive enough for newcomers yet satisfying for seasoned casual gamers. There’s no time limit, no pressure, and no failure states—only the quiet pleasure of finding cats tucked away behind objects, inside boxes, and in all manner of playful hiding spots.

One of the game’s greatest strengths is its presentation. Every scene in Cats in Time feels like a handcrafted diorama filled with life and detail, and the art direction exudes warmth and humor. The pastel color palette, soft lighting, and smooth animations make the game feel like a living toy set rather than a digital puzzle. The soundtrack complements the visuals perfectly, with relaxing melodies and gentle ambient sounds that invite players to slow down and explore at their own pace. The overall tone is whimsical and calming, making the game ideal for those looking to unwind after a long day or simply enjoy a peaceful gaming session without stress. The tactile feeling of manipulating the world, zooming in to spot tiny details, and uncovering hidden mechanisms gives every discovery a quiet sense of reward.

While the gameplay loop is simple, it’s also consistent and polished. Cats in Time does not aim to frustrate or challenge players with overly complex riddles; instead, it focuses on maintaining a flow that keeps curiosity alive. Each time period introduces new visual themes and environmental puzzles that prevent the experience from feeling monotonous, even if the core mechanics remain largely the same. The satisfaction comes not from solving intricate logic puzzles, but from noticing details and methodically uncovering every cat in each scene. For players who prefer a more casual approach, the inclusion of a hint system and a “Kid Mode” ensures that the game remains accessible to all ages. This accessibility, combined with the delightful theme, makes it appealing not only to puzzle fans but also to families or players who appreciate cozy, low-stress experiences.

That said, the game’s relaxed design can also be seen as its primary limitation. Those seeking a deeply challenging puzzle experience may find Cats in Time too easy or repetitive over long play sessions. Its puzzles tend to prioritize simplicity over complexity, and while the changing time periods add visual variety, the underlying gameplay formula doesn’t evolve significantly as the game progresses. Still, these design choices align with the developer’s intentions: Pine Studio clearly crafted this game to be meditative rather than mentally demanding. The goal is not to test your intelligence but to create a joyful and tranquil escape from reality, where each found cat feels like a small victory in an otherwise soothing journey.

As a complete package, Cats in Time is an undeniably charming entry in the puzzle genre that successfully blends aesthetic appeal, user-friendly design, and stress-free gameplay. The combination of detailed diorama worlds, light environmental interaction, and adorable cat-themed objectives creates a sense of warmth that few games manage to achieve. It’s a testament to how simple concepts, when executed with care and artistry, can deliver experiences that are both relaxing and satisfying. Pine Studio’s work here captures the spirit of discovery and nostalgia, providing players with a comforting space to explore at their own pace. Whether you’re a puzzle enthusiast, a cat lover, or someone looking for a soothing and wholesome digital getaway, Cats in Time offers an enchanting and rewarding adventure through time—one cat at a time.

Someone decided that a roguelite should be fun instead of grindy. Finally.

Roboquest is a roguelite FPS that focuses on movement, rewards accurate shooting, and has a wealth of different archetypes and builds to make replaying fun. A run consists of: picking a class, picking a route through the world, selecting weapons that synergize with your class, creating a powerful build, shooting everything that moves, and dodging, skating, and bouncing around levels like your life depends on it (because it does).

Early runs will be largely low-power and simple, thanks to meta-progression taking time to unlock, which provides you with more character power and the ability to filter out weapons you don't want to see, but once you've unlocked a decent percentage of the upgrades available you'll start to feel builds coming together and real power in your character. And the meta-progression system is well tuned: it never feels like you're grinding a long time just to see an increase in power; more like you're learning the game, and by the time that you do, you've unlocked enough options to customize your runs the way you'd like.

General combat difficulty is also well balanced, with progression through the difficulty levels feeling natural. Your skill and knowledge increase with the difficulty in perfect tandem, and you never feel like the game is giving you a bigger challenge than you're capable of. [b]I don't want to breeze by that: a good-feeling difficulty curve in a roguelite is a very rare thing, and Roboquest does it very well.[/b]

There's also a cute little story about robots protecting the remains of humanity from a hostile AI that's presented in little vignettes, and that story is just enough to add a little spice to the gameplay without getting in the way or overstaying its welcome.

All told, Roboquest is an excellent game that absolutely shines with polish and care. It's a fun shooter, there's satisfying movement, builds are varied and interesting, and the difficulty curve is beautifully designed. It's absolutely worth your time.

Edna & Harvey: The Breakout - Anniversary Edition is a lovingly restored version of one of Daedalic Entertainment’s most distinctive and influential adventure games, offering a surreal, darkly comedic journey that remains as memorable today as it was at its original release. This Anniversary Edition doesn’t attempt to modernize the game beyond recognition; instead, it carefully enhances the presentation and usability while preserving the offbeat tone, unconventional humor, and narrative eccentricity that earned the title its cult status. The result is a game that feels timeless in spirit, even as it benefits from technical refinements that make it more approachable for contemporary players.

The story begins with a deliberately unsettling premise. Edna awakens in a psychiatric institution with no memory of how she ended up there, accompanied only by her talking stuffed rabbit, Harvey, whose sarcastic commentary and questionable advice quickly establish the game’s warped sense of reality. From this starting point, the narrative unfolds as a strange and often hilarious escape tale that blurs the line between sanity and delusion. The asylum is populated with a cast of bizarre and exaggerated characters, each with their own quirks, routines, and secrets, and interacting with them gradually reveals both the mechanics of the escape and fragments of Edna’s past. The writing thrives on absurdity, dark humor, and unexpected emotional beats, making the story far more engaging than its premise might initially suggest.

Gameplay follows classic point-and-click adventure traditions, emphasizing exploration, dialogue, inventory management, and puzzle-solving. Players move Edna through hand-drawn environments, collecting items and combining them in creative—and often illogical—ways to progress. Puzzles range widely in complexity, from straightforward interactions to solutions that require lateral thinking and a willingness to experiment. At times, the game deliberately leans into old-school adventure logic, which can feel obtuse or demanding, but this design choice also reinforces its identity as a genre throwback that rewards patience, curiosity, and persistence rather than hand-holding.

One of the most notable strengths of the Anniversary Edition is its visual overhaul. The game features fully redrawn high-resolution artwork that preserves the original’s expressive, cartoon-like style while significantly improving clarity and detail. Character animations are more fluid, environments are richer, and the overall presentation feels more polished without losing its eccentric charm. Importantly, players can switch between the updated visuals and the classic version at any time, offering a fascinating comparison and allowing long-time fans to revisit the game in its original form if they choose.

Audio design plays a crucial role in bringing the world to life. Voice acting adds personality and timing to the dialogue, enhancing the humor and making the characters feel more vivid and memorable. Harvey, in particular, benefits from strong vocal delivery that reinforces his role as both comedic relief and unsettling companion. The soundtrack and ambient sound effects subtly support the game’s atmosphere, shifting between playful, eerie, and whimsical tones depending on the situation, and helping to maintain immersion throughout the lengthy adventure.

Despite its many strengths, the game does retain some design elements that may feel dated to modern audiences. Backtracking can be frequent, puzzle solutions occasionally hinge on obscure logic, and the pacing can slow down during more complex sequences. These aspects are part of the classic adventure game DNA and may frustrate players unfamiliar with or resistant to the genre’s traditional conventions. However, for those who appreciate narrative-driven experiences and puzzle-heavy gameplay, these elements often feel like challenges to be unraveled rather than obstacles to enjoyment.

What truly sets Edna & Harvey: The Breakout – Anniversary Edition apart is its tone. Few games balance dark subject matter and humor as confidently, using absurdity to explore themes of identity, authority, and personal freedom without becoming heavy-handed. The asylum setting, while exaggerated, serves as a clever backdrop for questioning who defines normality and how easily control can be mistaken for care. Beneath the jokes and bizarre situations lies a surprisingly thoughtful narrative that lingers after the final puzzle is solved.

In the end, Edna & Harvey: The Breakout – Anniversary Edition stands as both a celebration of classic adventure game design and a testament to Daedalic Entertainment’s storytelling creativity. It offers a lengthy, character-rich experience filled with memorable moments, challenging puzzles, and a unique narrative voice that remains rare even within the genre. For fans of point-and-click adventures, dark humor, and unconventional storytelling, this Anniversary Edition provides a rewarding journey that respects its roots while ensuring the game remains accessible and enjoyable for a new generation of players.

I don't enjoy giving negative reviews, especially to point-and-click adventure games, a genre that is very close to my heart. I've heard a lot of praise for Edna & Harvey over the years, so I went in with certain expectations that sadly weren't met.

There's a lot of good here: the world and its characters are charming, it is pretty upbeat most of the time, and it sports a ridiculous amount of interactions and voiced lines. You can seemingly combine anything with anything and get a unique line from the characters; I've never experienced anything like that. It definitely shows that the game was made with love for the genre and wanted to innovate on this often-overlooked aspect of its gameplay.

I dislike two things in adventure games, and Edna & Harvey sadly does both of them. Firstly, it is very overwhelming with its number of rooms, hotspots, and items. It is not rare to be in a situation where you have more than 20 items in your inventory and can theoretically combine them with probably more than 200 things spread across... like 20–30 rooms? This gets incredibly annoying if you happen to get stuck because if you want to brute-force this, you're up for at least 1-2 hours of trying everything on everything, and you might still miss that one interaction that you're supposed to do. It sadly doesn't help that there are so many voiced lines because at times it's difficult to assess what is helpful info and what is just random blabbering. Especially since the game is set in an asylum.

The second thing is connected to the first and it's the moon logic of the puzzles. I consider myself fairly good at puzzles and have finished the last 5 or so adventure games without ever looking anything up. I don't know if I'm operating on a completely different wavelength than Poki (the designer), but I just don't understand his puzzles and find them pretty annoying most of the time. In my 4 hours or so of gameplay, I was already forced about 4 times to consult a walkthrough, and every single time my reaction wasn't "that was so obvious" but "how the hell was I ever supposed to figure that out". One example in recent memory, very mild puzzle spoiler: [spoiler] In order to get to a laundry room, you need a blanket on the floor (don't even ask). To get the blanket, you need to use scissors on a person who wears a sweater and sits on the blanket, then you need to repeat the steps to get in their room (you can't just leave the room and get back, nothing happens), and after you're there, you can't just take the blanket; you need to put a cookie on it so it gets dirty. Then you need to leave the room again, and it will appear in the laundry room the next time you get there. [/spoiler] The whole game is like this.

Another bad thing is the controls. I don't understand why anyone would use anything else than simple look/interact unless it's innovative or somehow beneficial to the gameplay. Edna & Harvey uses this annoying wheel that you need to use every time unless you want to use the "default action," which you have no idea what actually is. There are both pick-up and interact actions, and you never quite know which one to use, and it's always the second one you try. I've heard some obnoxious variant of "this is too big to carry around" about a million times, but you still can't count on it because there's a lot of pretty big items that you CAN carry around. It's just so annoying that you can't just have right-click to look at and left-click to interact with like 90% of well-designed adventure games.

I appreciate the mood of the game, and I recognize that there's a certain quality under all these issues (and I didn't even mention bugs...), but I simply can't recommend it. And frankly, I'm a little shocked it has 92% positive reviews on Steam.

If you filter by negative reviews, you’ll see people throwing around the words "scam" or "grift." They point to the game's chaotic past, the name changes (Dino Beatdown, Dino Horde), and old controversies. But after spending time with this game, calling it a scam is just completely inaccurate.

[list]

[/list]

[/list]

[list]
[*]The New Era Updates are FREE: The absolute death blow to the "cash grab" argument is what the developers are doing right now. They are pushing major new updates, optimizations, and content overhauls—and if you already own the game, you get all of it for $0.00. They aren't forcing a paid sequel or locking content behind a battle pass.
[/list]

Is Orion: Prelude a flawless AAA masterpiece? No. Its history is wild and messy, just like its gameplay. But it is an incredibly fun, ultra-budget indie survivor that refuses to die. If you want a chaotic, dinosaur-hunting good time with your friends, ignore the old drama and buy it.

ORION: Prelude stands as one of the most remarkable turnaround stories in indie gaming, evolving from a rocky launch into a highly entertaining, action-packed cooperative shooter. The gameplay centers on frantic, arcade-style survival where teams of players fend off waves of aggressive dinosaurs using an extensive arsenal of futuristic weaponry, jetpacks, and military vehicles. By prioritizing chaotic, fast-paced fun over strict realism, the game delivers an immensely satisfying and high-energy cooperative experience. The sheer variety of dinosaur types—ranging from agile raptors to towering Tyrannosaurs—keeps every encounter unpredictable, frantic, and structurally engaging.

The game's greatest strength lies in its incredible value and unapologetic focus on pure entertainment. Featuring a massive selection of maps, diverse game modes like dinosaur survival and PvPvE, and an incredibly robust progression system, the package offers a surprising amount of content. The responsive gunplay, smooth vehicular movement, and over-the-top sci-fi action create a highly addictive loop that is perfect for groups of friends looking for straightforward, cooperative combat. Ultimately, with its accessible mechanics and relentless pacing, the title remains a beloved, wildly entertaining classic within the budget-friendly indie shooter space.

*Space Hulk (Classic)*, developed by Full Control Studios and published by SNEG, is a digital adaptation that stays remarkably loyal to its tabletop origins, for better and for worse. Set within the oppressive, war-scarred universe of Warhammer 40,000, the game places players in command of elite Space Marine Terminators as they cautiously advance through derelict space hulks—vast, drifting wrecks filled with lurking Genestealers. It is a game built on tension and restraint, where every decision carries weight and survival depends on patience more than aggression.

The core gameplay revolves around turn-based tactical movement governed by strict action points, forcing players to think several steps ahead before committing to even the smallest maneuver. Terminators are powerful but slow, requiring careful positioning and coordinated overwatch to hold narrow corridors against fast-moving enemies. The Genestealers, by contrast, are fragile at a distance but devastating in close quarters, creating a constant sense of imbalance that drives the game’s tension. This asymmetrical design ensures that every encounter feels like a high-risk calculation, where a single mistake—turning the wrong way, mismanaging a reload, or leaving a blind spot—can lead to immediate and irreversible consequences.

What stands out most is the deliberate pacing. Missions unfold slowly, often feeling like a careful crawl through hostile territory rather than a traditional strategy experience. Players spend a significant amount of time setting up defensive lines, managing limited resources, and anticipating enemy approaches rather than engaging in frequent firefights. This measured approach captures the essence of the original board game, translating its suspense into a digital format. The inclusion of random command points adds a subtle layer of unpredictability, occasionally allowing players to extend their turn, but never enough to rely on as a consistent advantage.

However, this strict adherence to its source material also exposes the game’s limitations. Compared to modern tactical titles, the range of strategic options can feel narrow, and mission objectives rarely evolve beyond established patterns. While the core loop remains engaging for a time, the lack of variety can lead to repetition, especially during longer sessions. The game does not attempt to expand or reinterpret its foundation in meaningful ways, instead choosing to preserve the original experience almost intact. For longtime fans, this faithfulness is a strength; for others, it may feel like a missed opportunity for innovation.

The presentation reinforces the grim atmosphere effectively, with dark, industrial environments that evoke a sense of isolation and constant threat. The visual design aligns well with the Warhammer 40K aesthetic, emphasizing heavy armor, dimly lit corridors, and oppressive architecture. At the same time, the technical execution is uneven. Animations can feel stiff, environments occasionally lack detail, and the overall polish does not quite meet modern standards. These shortcomings do not completely break immersion, but they do remind players that the game is more focused on recreating a classic experience than delivering a cutting-edge one.

Artificial intelligence and overall gameplay flow further highlight this duality. Enemy behavior can become predictable after extended play, reducing the sense of unpredictability that initially defines the experience. Meanwhile, controlling the Terminators can feel cumbersome, as the slow, methodical pace sometimes crosses into tedium. Multiplayer options help alleviate this by introducing human unpredictability, which aligns more closely with the spirit of the original board game and adds a layer of replayability that the single-player mode alone struggles to sustain.

In the end, *Space Hulk (Classic)* is a very specific kind of game—one that prioritizes authenticity over accessibility. It delivers a tense and atmospheric tactical experience that rewards careful planning and disciplined execution, but it also demands patience and a willingness to accept its rigid structure. For fans of the original board game or those deeply invested in the Warhammer 40K setting, it offers a faithful and immersive recreation that captures the essence of its source material. For players looking for a more flexible or modern strategy experience, its limitations may prove difficult to overlook.

Operencia: The Stolen Sun takes the foundations of classic first-person dungeon crawlers and rebuilds them with modern visuals, extensive voice acting, tactical turn-based combat, and a fantasy world influenced by Central European mythology. Developed and published by Zen Studios, it feels deliberately old-fashioned in its exploration mechanics while remaining approachable for players who may have little experience with traditional grid-based RPGs. Instead of merely imitating classics of the genre, it establishes its own personality through folklore, historical inspiration, colorful environments, and a surprisingly character-driven adventure.

The story begins with the disappearance of the Sun King Napkiraly, an event that leaves the realm without sunlight and threatens its inhabitants with permanent darkness. The player's journey gradually expands into a larger quest involving legendary figures, mysterious kingdoms, supernatural creatures, and locations inspired by Central European history and folklore. Hungarian mythology plays an especially important role, giving the setting a flavor rarely encountered in fantasy RPGs. Historical locations such as Deva Fortress are transformed into fantastical destinations, while legendary personalities and traditional stories are incorporated into the wider narrative. Even without prior knowledge of these influences, the world remains understandable and enjoyable.

Exploration is presented from a first-person perspective with movement taking place across a grid. There are 13 major maps to investigate, ranging from underground complexes and castles to forests and increasingly supernatural locations. Each area combines navigation with environmental puzzles, hidden passages, treasures, traps, and combat encounters. The level design encourages careful observation rather than rushing toward the next objective. Finding a concealed route or finally understanding the mechanism behind a puzzle can be as satisfying as defeating a difficult enemy. Players seeking a more traditional experience can even disable automatic mapping and create their own maps through the optional Cartographer mode.

Combat uses a turn-based party system in which positioning your strategy around character abilities, enemy weaknesses, healing, buffs, and resource management becomes increasingly important. Seven upgradeable characters can eventually join the adventure, providing enough flexibility to experiment with different party combinations. Individual companions fulfill distinct combat roles, so assembling a balanced group matters considerably during tougher encounters. With more than 50 enemy types appearing throughout the campaign, battles regularly encourage players to reconsider which skills and tactics are most effective instead of depending entirely on basic attacks.

Character progression complements the combat well. Developing abilities and improving party members provides a satisfying sense of advancement, while companions contribute personalities and dialogue rather than functioning merely as collections of statistics. More than 30 characters feature full voice acting, helping conversations feel livelier than those in many traditional dungeon crawlers. Hand-drawn cutscenes and illustrated character portraits reinforce the storybook quality of the setting. The narrative may not have the enormous cinematic scope of a blockbuster RPG, but its mythology and personable adventuring party give the journey considerable charm.

Presentation is one of the game's most noticeable improvements over the genre's old-school roots. Built using Unreal Engine 4, the environments feature detailed scenery, atmospheric lighting, colorful landscapes, and distinctive fantasy architecture. Outdoor areas provide welcome relief from the enclosed stone corridors normally associated with dungeon crawlers. The orchestral soundtrack composed by Arthur Grosz complements the fairy-tale atmosphere, while environmental effects and voice performances give the world a stronger sense of place. Optional SteamVR support also allows the adventure to be experienced from a more immersive perspective without making virtual reality mandatory.

Difficulty options deserve particular praise because they allow players to determine how traditional they want the experience to become. Someone primarily interested in the world, puzzles, and story can select forgiving settings, while experienced dungeon-crawling enthusiasts can introduce harsher restrictions. Options involving limited saves, permadeath, and manual mapping can transform the campaign into a significantly more demanding undertaking. This flexibility makes the game welcoming without stripping away the possibility of a genuinely challenging old-school adventure.

The deliberate design will not appeal equally to everyone. Grid-based movement can initially seem stiff compared with unrestricted modern first-person exploration, and the methodical combination of puzzles, navigation, and turn-based battles produces a slower rhythm than an action RPG. Certain puzzles may also stall progress until their underlying logic becomes clear. Players who prefer constant action could therefore find the experience overly restrained, whereas those who enjoy carefully examining environments and planning encounters are much more likely to appreciate its pace.

Steam Deck compatibility is officially categorized as Playable rather than fully Verified. Performance with the default graphics configuration is considered suitable, and the game can run successfully on SteamOS. However, handheld players should expect compromises. Some functionality is not fully accessible through the default controller configuration, touchscreen interaction or a community controller layout may occasionally be useful, and text entry can require manually opening the virtual keyboard. Some interface text may also appear small, while certain prompts can display keyboard, mouse, or non-Steam Deck controller icons. It is therefore functional on the Deck, but the experience is less seamless than a fully optimized handheld release.

Operencia: The Stolen Sun is ultimately an impressive blend of traditional dungeon-crawling design and contemporary presentation. Its distinctive mythology, handcrafted environments, enjoyable party development, tactical battles, substantial puzzle content, flexible difficulty settings, and strong atmosphere give it an identity beyond simple nostalgia. It understands the appeal of classic dungeon RPGs while removing enough barriers to make the format accessible to a wider audience. Anyone who enjoys methodical exploration and turn-based party management should find a substantial fantasy adventure here.

I also wasn't a fan of the level cap or the fact that every enemy encounter is predetermined. Instead of feeling like I'm adventuring through a dangerous world (Wizardry, Eye of the Beholder, Legend of Grimmrock), it often felt like I was simply progressing through someone else's script.

My biggest disappointment was the reward for exploration. The game constantly encourages you to hunt down hidden secrets but the loot is usually mediocre or straight up trash. The perfect example is the optional secret boss with over 10,000 HP. By the time you can realistically reach it, you're already at about 99% completion, and the reward is an above average piece of gear you'll barely get to use before the game ends.

I still recommend Operencia because its world, story, atmosphere, and presentation are genuinely excellent. But with deeper combat, more meaningful exploration rewards, and a little more player freedom, it could have been something truly special.
