Some real plusses I want to mention:  The ability to respec at will makes playing with different skillsets fun and easy.  Combat is (reasonably) varied and never felt like a chore.  The puzzles were interesting but never frustrating.  The graphics are fine, but the art style used for the characters and the cutscenes is gorgeous and unique.  If you are looking for something with huge tactical depth or enjoy complex build-crafting, this may not be for you, but I thoroughly enjoyed my playtime, and I recommend the game highly.

I hate to be a single issue voter, but multiple things for the game's critical path are hidden in secret areas?

Nope!

That's not where that goes.

Secrets, and I get that this can be tricky, are for secret things. Core progression is the stuff that everyone is supposed to hit.

If you put your core progression in your secrets, what you are doing is wasting half your audience's time and making the other half's secret hunting meaningless.

Also the guide situation for this game is pretty dire. Thankfully there's a sketch website that has proper written documentation, as figuring out how to unstick yourself from a youtube video is like pulling rusted nails out of your foot with a chihuahua.

So, what is Operencia like outside of bungling a weird fundamental?

Well, it's pretty. There's some pop-up book aesthetic cutscenes that look really nice, and the environments are doing their best to be engrossing despite the eastern european fairytale look reading as stock fantasy some fifty years after Tolkein. There's a lot of voice acting, and the quality ranges from porn (the actors are trying) to porn (the actors are not trying.) The first dungeon is a castle in a lake and it's really good, actually. There's submerged sections with a hold your breath mechanic, and you'll look out the windows in the dry sections and see fish swimming past.

Combat is... not great. It's Star Crawlers, but Star Crawlers immediately clocks that if you have only two buttons to press it's not very interesting and Operencia... does not figure this out. Also you spend every fourth turn defending to recover mana and this is mandatory. You are 100% whiffing 25% of your turns on a cadence because mana expenditure is high and casting is limited.

The character classes are not super balanced. Ranged just isn't good, and casters are starved for hp but don't really have damage output to make up for it. Progression is slow as butts, and upgrades are small, and there appear to be some very wrong choices you can make (poison upgrading is an option, also everything and its father is immune to poison.)

The writing is okay. The characters are yappy, but unless you have an outright allergic reaction to that kinda bouncy quippy marvel dialog you should be fine. I think the game would have less personality if they talked less, so they haven't really gotten on my nerves (although the knight sounds like he popped a valium and did *not* want to show up to work today.)

I think for folks who like old school point and click adventure games, this might be a bit of a hidden gem. It really does feel like it fits in that genre more than anything else, even if the visual presentation is pure blobber. And a lot of the stuff that's annoying when you consider the game as a blobber is just genre hallmarks when you take it as a point and click.

For me, though, I wanted another Grimrock. And this looked like it might be another Grimrock. But it is not another Grimrock.

Grimrock II's really just going to be a commercially unsuccessful best in the genre forever, I suppose.

And enemy dodge chance keeps increasing across the course of the game, so you need to be leveling your to hit stats, but also enemy damage is constantly increasing and you do not have much hp, so the correct build is in fact to moderately invest in your hit stat and then roll well to dodge and hit, with the emphasis on rolling well being the important part of the build. No thank you. I ain't finishing that. I'll sweat out a hard combat system if it's interesting or rewarding to do so, but this is just "3.5e GM who suddenly got really interested in realism yesterday."

Operencia is certainly something.

There's a lot going on here and most of it ranges from middling to bad, but before going into that I'll say that the game looks not bad, and the some of the gameplay ideas they're working with could work to help make a fun video game if they were used properly. Part of what makes dungeon crawlers like this work is secret hunting and while a good chunk of them are just "hey here's a chest with some cash and gear you might've already surpassed" there's a some that are REALLY good. There's a potion system that's pretty fun to mess with, you find recipes and you need to solve a logic puzzle to unlock the potion for use, which is way more fun that just getting the potion as its a little departure from the regular gameplay.

Combat takes place with the enemies arranged in rows of set distances, and skills do more or less damage depending on how far away the enemy is positioned. Cool potential, but enemies never move from one distance to another and you have no skills to force enemies to move into a better position to fight them in so the game never really dives into the potential here. There's no way to predict what position an enemy group is going to take up, so there's not much point in trying to organize a teams skills with that in mind, and instead you end up sticking with other metrics like damage or cool down. There's a specific point in the game where it really feels the devs gave up on trying to make different enemy encounters and just start giving you groups of five of the same guy. It doesn't end up being EVERY enemy group, but it's certainly a lot of them.

You end up drowning in inconsequential gear. You get stuff for free after fights, in chests, and can buy stuff in the store you eventually unlock. There's so much that's just trash, that if you keep up with checking what you get, you'll end up being disappointed most of the time. There's also some sort of gear scoring system that means that instead of looking at what you got and comparing the stats and thinking about what works best, you just look for the green numbers. For some this would probably be seen as a convenience thing, which is fair, but it does feel like it really simplifies the gear system in a way that makes it more brain dead and less interesting.

Most of the puzzles are alright, but there's a standout that really strikes me as not great, where you need to have a specific character in your party to get an item, and the game is not clear at all that THAT is the solution, or what character you need. The clue dialog I heard initially made me think that I needed to get an item instead of swapping my team, and I only learned what I needed to do after getting frustrated and looking it up. Could just be a combination of bad luck and me being dumb, but it feels like bad puzzle design regardless.

The plot is kind of just there. There's cool stuff going on, but it never feels like it takes the forefront like it should. It feels like they going for a stageplay/opera retelling of myths for a culture that's similar to real life but not completely, and that's a cool idea, but it kind of doesn't follow through with the execution. Voice acting is inconsistent in quality and delivery, one guy REALLY goes into talking like someone would in a play when the others don't go as far, and one actor sounds like something is wrong with their microphone set up. Some of the dialog strikes me as out of place for how dumb it is when the rest of the game at least tries to play it legit.

Operencia is an example of untapped potential, which sucks but it is what it is. There are other dungeon crawler RPGs out there, so I would suggest giving this one a skip.

[h2]First Impressions and Early Gameplay[/h2]
Operencia: The Stolen Sun makes a strong initial impression, presenting itself as a classic dungeon crawler with polished visuals and a turn-based combat system. The game's interface allows for camera rotation with the mouse, enhancing the sense of exploration. Early on, the game introduces a story that unfolds gradually, and the battles are balanced with an appropriate level of difficulty.
In the beginning, you control a party of two characters, encountering a variety of enemies and discovering your first set of items. This stage also encourages experimentation with different skill combinations, resulting in an enjoyable and engaging gameplay flow.

[h2]Expanding the Party[/h2]
After completing the first area, you advance to a new location and quickly recruit additional allies, eventually assembling a group of four. However, the party size is limited to four members, so any extra characters must be kept in reserve. This introduces a minor issue: having to decide which characters to include in your active party. While some players might enjoy this aspect, it can be frustrating for those who prefer to use all available characters without restriction.

[h2]Item Management and Rest Points[/h2]
Throughout the game, item drops are frequent after battles. Each new item requires you to check whether it benefits your current party members or should be saved for those not presently in the party. However, you cannot equip or swap gear for reserve characters until you reach a campfire, where you can rest, trade items, and adjust your party composition. This system can feel cumbersome, especially when you wish to optimize your gear across all characters.

[h2]Reasons for Disengagement[/h2]
Despite these minor inconveniences, they were not the main reason for abandoning the game. The core issue was a growing sense of boredom after around 26 hours of play. The movement feels jerky, and exploration seems to serve little purpose beyond earning experience points through encounters. Puzzles fail to provide meaningful challenges, and the gameplay loop becomes repetitive, even by dungeon crawler standards. The story does little to maintain interest, as it mainly acts as a vehicle for moving from one area to another, lacking depth or engagement.
For comparison, it took 38 hours to complete Legend of Grimrock 2, indicating that the problem was not with the dungeon crawler genre itself, but rather with the monotony and lack of excitement in Operencia: The Stolen Sun.

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]
If there were a neutral rating option on Steam, it would be the most fitting choice for this game. However, since I did not play the game to the end, my usual approach is to leave a negative review (exceptions might happen, but not this time). This is not to discourage others from purchasing the game, but rather to caution that, unless you are a dedicated fan of this genre, you may find yourself abandoning it before reaching the end.

A surprisingly good entry into the DRPG subgenre. This game feels like a really well-made B movie: it’s not groundbreaking, but it’s genuine, and it kept me entertained from start to finish. It’s especially impressive considering it was developed by a Hungarian company best known for making physical pinball machines. As a debut in this style, it’s a surprisingly strong effort. I’d recommend it to anyone looking for a first-person dungeon crawler with turn-based combat.

The positives:
- Pretty faithful use of Hungarian folklore
- Beautiful environments
- Great music
- Fully voiced 
- Serviceable characters
- Really well-balanced puzzles (they are mostly on the easier side but solidly designed)
- Excellent choice for trying a forgiving DRPG (free respecs anytime at save points)

The negatives:
- The VA quality is a bit of a mixed bag
- The combat is a bit too simple and slow
- Some characters are a bit one-dimensional
- Small amount of backtracking (pet peeve of mine, I just don't enjoy doing it, too much mental load, but for a 20-25 hour game it's fine)
- Very derivative of the genre (if you played 10+ DRPGs this won't offer any new mechanics)

All in all great effort, give it a try if you are interested.

Operencia is a pretty neat little dungeon crawler that's well worth the price if you're into these types of games. The exploration aspect is not complex by any stretch of the word, but there's a lot of nice items that add some variety to the areas and have you returning to old dungeons to open new areas and secrets. Crafting your own potions through the various recipes discovered in the world is also a nice puzzle addition.

The graphics are arguably the greatest aspect of this. The world is quite frankly stunning, with each area having it's own theme and a decent, if not mind-blowing, fairytale story running along in the background. The game is fully voiced, and while the acting isn't the greatest out there, it's clear that those doing it were having a lot of fun.

Where the game falls down slightly is probably going to be in the combat. The encounters have been designed to test the player in each area, but many of them are extremely punishing if you don't have the right characters/stat/ability attributes assigned to deal with them. The game does, refreshingly, allow you to respec/reorganise your group at any point, but that's of little consequence if you're not fully understanding how the stats interact with abilities. In short, half of the talent trees are worthless, and the other half are heavily reliant on stat allocation that isn't always obvious, such as Int on the Rogue character for their poisons, Str for their backstab, while Agi affects one crossbow shot you probably won't even take. There are some secondary abilities that come over time, many of which interact with specific spell types that are not clear because the games hint system doesn't explain them. And the loot is just as confusing, with much of it in the middle and endgame being completely worthless and often downgrades to more powerful items that came before. These issues are then compounded in the later game with encounters that seem like they are designed for chance on instant kill abilities/mass party AoE attacks, with enemies that, if left up, are either locking down your entire party with ridiculous long stuns/sleeps/charms, or doing crazy AoE damage because all of them share the same cooldowns and it's being spammed by 2-3 of them all in a row right at the start of the encounter. That said, when you understand the abilities and equip the group appropriately, the fights become extremely fun as you start blowing everything out of existence, but that's something you have to work for and will likely suffer a huge amount of frustration in the journey getting to it. In short, the combat is guaranteed to be universally hated at the start, and will either grow to be loved as it's understood or else the player will just quit. You decide which type you're likely to fall into based on your own patience levels.

All in all a solid 4/5 from me. If you go full achievements it'll be a good 50-60 hours of gameplay. It's nothing you'll likely remember once it's done, but if you can come to grips with the combat then you'll have a fun journey while you're there.

"Operencia: The Stolen Sun" isn't just a game, it's a journey into a vibrant and captivating world that immediately charms you from the moment you step into its mystical realms. From its utterly delightful presentation to its engaging gameplay, this title truly shines.  One of the first things that grabs you is the sheer visual appeal.  Operencia boasts a unique and stylized look, full of rich colors and fantastical architecture that feels plucked straight from the pages of a beloved fairytale.  The environments are detailed and imaginative, constantly inviting you to explore every nook and cranny.

But the visual charm is only half the story.  Adding incredible depth to this world is the stellar voice acting. Each character, from your own companions to the intriguing NPCs you encounter, is brought to life with genuine personality and emotion. The voice performances are consistently strong, delivering lines with nuance and conviction that elevates the narrative and makes every conversation feel meaningful.  However, the true magic lies in the banter between your party members. This isn't just generic dialogue filler; the characters genuinely interact with each other, reacting to situations and offering their unique perspectives.  This witty and often heartwarming banter isn't just entertaining, it's crucial for building immersion. You feel like you're part of a real adventuring party, travelling alongside individuals with their own quirks and motivations. This constant stream of character interaction truly breathes life into the world of Operencia, making it feel lived-in and dynamic.

For those familiar with dungeon crawlers like "Legend of Grimrock", Operencia will feel both comfortably familiar and refreshingly different.  Like Grimrock, Operencia embraces the first-person perspective, navigating labyrinthine environments filled with puzzles and monsters.  The core gameplay of grid-based movement, tactical combat, and environmental interaction echoes Grimrock's strengths.  However, where they diverge is in their approach to story and character.  "Legend of Grimrock" favors a more atmospheric and isolated experience, often leaving the narrative to be pieced together through environmental clues. Operencia, on the other hand, is brimming with narrative and character interaction.  While Grimrock focuses on the thrill of survival and puzzle solving within a bleak dungeon, Operencia places a greater emphasis on its enchanting world, its engaging storyline rooted in Hungarian folklore, and the personalities of your companions.  Operencia offers a more guided and narratively rich experience, with voice acting and character banter providing a constant stream of engagement that Grimrock intentionally omits.

In conclusion, "Operencia: The Stolen Sun" is a truly wonderful game.  Its charming presentation, coupled with excellent voice acting and the genuinely delightful banter between characters, creates an immersive and captivating experience.  While drawing inspiration from classics like "Legend of Grimrock" in its core gameplay, Operencia carves its own unique path by prioritizing story, character interaction, and a vibrant, fairytale-inspired world.  If you're looking for a dungeon crawler that is not only challenging and engaging but also brimming with charm and personality, then look no further – "Operencia: The Stolen Sun" is an adventure you won't want to miss!

Steam only gives the option of "yes or no", so when one has a game that can easily sway to both sides of the fence, I can't just pick a neutral option.  But I will go "yes" here, an just say that it falls on the "better than average" side of the equation.

What does that mean?  When something is "above average", it could either be because it does everything slightly better than normal, or it does some things amazingly, and others... less so.  This game is the latter.

First off, this is a Blobber game.  Unlike Grimrock et. al,, the battles take place not in-grid, but on a separate battle screen, so... Grimrock meets Etrian Oddessey.  There's nothing wrong with that; but you do have to be a fan of these genres to enjoy this game.  I was, so I got it.

But preamble aside, how is it both good and... perhaps not, at once?

[hr][/hr]

 [h2] Graphics [/h2] 

For starters, the graphics.  The graphics are very nice; art is smooth, animations are mostly reactive and crisp, and it looks for all the world like it could be a triple-A title.  

And then... the cutscenes.  the backgrounds are single, often still-image shots, and conversations are done via the "show the character portraits talking, and light up whichever is currently saying something" approach.  Granted, this is the same thing that, say, Fire Emblem likes to do, and by itself isn't bad... but we aren't even talking, say, Ace Attorney here, where everyone has 6 images (neutral, happy, mad, dejected) that are used to express the situation.  It's literally a single image that lights up occasionally.

This is a STARK contrast to the rest of the game's (awesome!) graphics, to the point that, at least for me, I cannot look past it.  I'm not saying it's not allowed, but... pretend you are playing a final fantasy game, with a typically bombastic boss music theme.  Now imagine that theme playing as you rest for the night at an Inn.  Even if the theme is amazing, that just isn't fitting with everything else, is it?

Not everything has to be ABSOLUTELY SPECTACULAR at all times, but parts do have to fit together.  At least with the Fire Emblem example, the art of the images matches the art of the rest of the game.  Putting these still-frame different-artstyle single images on the screen as there is currently a fully-beautiful-boss-battle going on in the background is a major blow to the Suspension of Disbelief that a fictional visual-based medium needs.

Ok, enough graphics-conversation nitpicking.  what else?

[hr][/hr]

 [h2] Story-to-Sound [/h2] 

How about the character audio vis-a-vis the storyline?  This game is the utmost in "quaint fantasy".  Kingdom under attack, only your hero can save it, find the magic sword, slay the dragon, and 
[spoiler] inherit the kingdom [/spoiler].  Stock, but serviceable, so long as it's done well.  (as TvTropes says, "tropes aren't bad")

The issue is that the writers seem to have decided that any form of originality is unnecessary.  The game's twists are minimally surprising, and the very start of the game has two guys run into each other, and within 10 seconds of conversation, appear to be the best of longtime friends?

Which is a shame, because, while the story is too bland to describe in a review with any justice, the voice actors they got for it are high-talent.  One of the most effective ways I got through the visual-dichotomy of the conversations I whine about above, was to just turn my head, and listen to the conversations instead.  

It came across like hiring Hollywood talent to play in a highschool-written play.  The same issue as the visuals; the game designers obviously COULD do better, but the quality of different parts of the same scene clash to unignorable degrees.

Still reading?  No?  Fair enough.  But if you are... how about the most important part of a game.  The gameplay?

[hr][/hr]

 [h2] Is the Gameplay right for you? [/h2] 

Grid based world movement, world-based fast travel to any save point, turn-based battles in the old Final Fantasy/Dragon Quest style, full restoration at any camp if you choose to use one of the game's limited "firewood" resources (for reference, I finished the game with 9 to spare.  Enough to have a buffer, not enough to rest after every fight).

And...

This game uses the Might&Magic style of monsters:  a finite number of spawns in the world.  You will have a hard cap to the amount of experience you can earn, and therefore, the level you can achieve.

The good news is, the game is lenient with gaining that exp.  Someone not in your active party for the fight?  They get it too.  Someone dead before you win?  They get credit.  The only "loss" you can have to a character is if you fight a battle before they join (later) in the story, but they come with comparable levels anyway.

AND, you can respec your characters outside of combat.  All of them.  Skills AND statistics.  Any time, no cost.  So if you want to try out a totally different combination of skills to overcome a challenge, then go for it.  Just save before trying ;p.

Long story short, it's nigh-impossible to screw up your characters; you can always just rebuild them.  (I suppose you could try and break the game by selling and rebuying all of the game's limited gear until you ran out of money to pay the repurchase fees, but... don't do that ;p)

For anyone who wants a challenge in the form of *fixed* variables, this is right up your alley.

However, to anyone who prefers a "grind it out" style of gameplay, you can't.  You get the achievement for "hitting the highest level" at 24 (apparently, in some versions, 25 is possible, but I didn't see it).

I'm not making value judgements here.  But if your desired way of handling a fight you *just barely* can't beat, is to go out and grind a couple more levels, you are going to be heavily turned off by this game.

[hr][/hr]

So, there ya have it.  A game with a number of things that bring down the enjoyment; some things that I will personally call "flaws", and other things I will call "personal preferences that I may not share".  But through it all, I'll still give the thumbs up.  It does beat a number of other Blobbers out there.

A mostly, old school party based, dungeon crawler in the vein of Bard’s Tale, Wizardry, Might and Magic, etc.  For those who aren’t super old, the most similar game that is somewhat newer would be The Legend of Grimrock, though this has turn based combat.  This is a more modern take on the genre though, with the ability to look any direction, smooth movement and a much more story and character focused game.  Your character and party will often interject, commenting on dungeon features, story beats and just small talk.  The story and characters are all fully voiced, and the voice acting can be quite good (with some exceptions).  The gameplay itself is the usual for this type of game with exploring, fighting creatures in your way and a handful of puzzles per area.  The puzzles are mostly well done and intuitive, but there are some where the objective or clues are just too obscure.  One near the end was also a way too long / hard slide puzzle that killed the pacing.  Many puzzles also require artifacts you will find later in the game.  Once you unlock it though, getting back to those points is pretty painless.  The combat is turned based, with each party member and monster acting based off their initiative.  Unlike the old games, each character gets skills with cooldowns they can use in addition to their basic melee and ranged attack.  Beyond that, there are a few original things like a potion creation mini-game (you just have to figure out recipes you find, no experimentation) and an unusual fantasy setting based on non-D&D / non-western fantasy.

The positives are the characters, dungeon design, atmosphere and mostly the puzzles.  A lot of life is breathed into the game via the voice acting and storytelling with some very excellent voice acting from some characters (unfortunately this also makes the bad ones stick out more).  The characters are all unique, gameplay wise as well.  The first companion you find is a rogue, but if you start as a rogue your skill trees are pretty different.  The same goes for all others, making each character unique.  The puzzles are usually pretty short, and easy enough to figure out the concept and solution that you won’t get annoyed or frustrated.  Of course, there are some exceptions as I noted elsewhere, but there is the internet to help if needed.

For negatives, the game has a weird combat system where abilities use energy, but you don’t regenerate energy at all unless you camp (which uses limited wood) or defend during battle.  Defending has a cooldown and can only be done once every three turns.  Abilities tend to use a lot of EP’s, so you will find yourself defending a lot, which gives combat a weird feeling and is not particularly fun.  Not a fan of that system.  Also, the fact that camping uses wood and you have no clue how much wood you will find or how long the game is, can make you too conservative.  I ended the game with a lot of wood, but I also used the defend mechanism way more than I would have liked.  The game balance is a bit all over the place as well.  There are a few, very annoying enemies with abilities like energy drain or unlimited summoning that can be hard… but more so, they are just annoying and not fun.  Some of the abilities available to you, also feel off.  Your rogue will be your only source of healing for almost half the game for instance.  And if you don’t’ play as a mage, you will be lacking area of effect spells for a long time as well.  For the story, while well delivered, it was not my cup of tea.  You will be talking to gods, and hearing tales of tears making lakes and other over the top types of story beats.  While original, I prefer a more grounded setting.

So, is this worth a buy.  For me it was, but I think it will be hit or miss with many people, even those who like dungeon crawlers.  If you like, over the top and well delivered stories, exploration and puzzles and aren’t as interested in character building and combat, you will probably like it.  If you are used to this genre being very combat heavy, with well balanced and fun combat and that is mainly what you are looking for, this game might not be for you.

Everybody's favorite Soviet Simulator is BACK! (Yes, I know it's not LITERALLY set in the Soviet Union, but it perfectly nails THE VIBE of that way of living.)

I clocked it, each 2 seconds of REAL TIME passes 5 minutes of in-game time, meaning 24 real seconds equal 1 in-game hour, and 576 seconds of real time equals 1 in-game day. That explains why I can hardly get my bearings when there's 5 things to do at the same time. So when you see tasks due in 100 hours, you might think that's a comforting amount to plan for, until you realize that it's 24 real seconds per hour times 100, or due in 40 minutes of real time. 

The gameplay is an evolution of point-and-click where you go around, interacting with objects, and the game's primary selling point are 2 details: THE VIBE, and the WRITING. It really wants to drive home the characters, personalities, aspirations, all those things that real humans tend to lack with a sobering regularity. In terms of plot, there's a theme of "You can either save a life, or obey the law." With that in mind, the difference between this game world and Real Life is that you get put into a position of sufficient power where you CAN, in fact, make that sort of choice - Real Life generally leaves people with no choice whatsoever, no means of steering the course of events. 

Graphics, I like the monochromatic aesthetic, though as a matter of taste, I wish it were even MORE dark and bleak, to make what little details of white and red pop out far more boldly. It has the means to get expressive and really accentuate the feelings of fear and crushing dictatorship, but I find it only passable rather than outstanding. (Still cute though, would love to make a reference to it at some point in my creative processes.)

Lore, I have so many hyper-nerdy questions. 
1) It's set in 1989, but since this is a fictional world, what defines "Year 0"? I don't think it's "In the Year of Our Lord" like in Real Life, and if it's meant to have any realistic-ish parallel, then considering they establish in the tutorial that a TV is a privilege, that means either they're 30 years lagging (since TVs were a privilege as of USA 1959)
2) Carl, our main character...are they going to ever point to, uh...let's just say, "spoilers for Beholder 2"?
3) Every breath from the supervisor keeps threatening to "SEND YOU TO THE MINES" for every little misstep, but what was the thought process behind the many rules and regulations? (Some are big like forbidding sex services and citizen firearms, others are silly like not allowing jeans or dancing...even though I think the Regulation got overturned with Regulation 6032, so you have to keep track of that sort of stuff, to see what's currently on the books.) One good example is literally: "Regulation 6018 Sep 4, 1984 - Soda makes children sick and adults crazy, so it is banned with immediate effect." They allow alcohol consumption but don't allow books, soda, or even spare lightbulbs. All of this creates a very Spartan way of living, which makes me think it's trying to contrast the "Fat American" stereotype, meaning if you like Spartan living or are a rigid "rules to the letter" type, this world is your idea of paradise.

Overall, first impression, I like what's on offer, though maybe that'll change as I get deeper into it. The biggest challenge isn't that it's derived from point-and-click, the biggest challenge is how fast time moves...and how time-sensitive most tasks are. It really makes you feel like a land owner, having the weight of a whole house on your shoulders. Cute art style though.

Obligatory Forewore:  I bought all 4 Beholder Titles as Part of a Bundle, I played all 4.  I took some time to digest and here we are to list a review.

I liked Beholder 3.  I know there's a lot of negativity surrounding it and that's maybe because people were playing them in isolation of eachother, however as I tackled 1-3 back-to-back I can see what happened here.   The original Beholder was a short game, it had a lot of promise, it was a wonderfully interesting concept we hadn't seen before and I think that it was brought out and achieved such unexpected success that the second game was ultimately rushed and so whilst larger in scope failed to hit the same level of success and became linear and uninspired.

With 3 though it's a Return to Form.  It's not as grand as 2's ideals, it's much much much closer to the first title. 
Is it a perfect entry? No.  Unfortunately there are some truly horrible bugs but I had read up about this before going into this and so I backed up my saves multiple times as I progressed.

The fact I needed a break after this one before Conductor is not a disparaging comment to 3, it's just man can only take so much Beholder before you just give up the ghost.

I am going to get the obvious question out of the way first: is this game still bugged? Yes, it is. But--as you can see from my 100% completion--they aren't game-breaking. Primarily, issues sometimes occur when loading a game where you won't be able to interact with anything and the game clock breaks. While very frustrating, this was easily solved by quitting to desktop and relaunching the game. This didn't really impact anything during normal course of play for me, as I was rarely reloading in the middle of a session. However, when trying to load late game saves to explore alternate endings, this problem kept reoccurring.

Bugs aside, this is a decent entry into the Beholder series. Admittedly, I do think it is the weakest entry but it still had all the basic charm of a Beholder game: spying on people, deciding how moral to be in a fundamentally immoral world, juggling said morals against a ticking clock of bills and quest timers. It draws from both of its predecessors, although more from the first game than the second. You start off as the property manager of an apartment building just like in the first game, but you will earn an office job part way through the game. The office portion works much the same as the apartment portion, rather than how it played in Beholder 2. 

Overall, I would tentatively recommend it to anyone who enjoys the series. The bugs are annoying but it was still an overall enjoyable experience. To everyone else: start with one of the other games in the series. If you don't like those then the rough edges on this one are going to drive you insane.

I played Beholder 3 after playing Behold 1, Blissful Sleep (DLC), & 2 respectively, and I was nervous to play Beholder 3 because of the steam reviews complaining about issues with the game having several bugs, but I think most of them have been fixed because I only had issues twice which were fixed by reloading the save or rebooting the game.

As for the gameplay, Beholder 3 goes back to its landlord roots from 1 while retaining the workplace levelling mechanism from 2, so you play as both landlord/property manager and ministry employee. However, unlike Beholder 2, this game doesn't have mini-games, and you only have to do quests, side quests, and reporting and profiling to get enough reputation and authority to advance in your career. 

Beholder 3 is largely played like the first game, except with few upgrades and changes that I am not sure are bad, but definitely make the game a bit more challenging. 
1. You can now sneak into apartments when tenants are sleeping 
2. It has a surveillance mode where you can easily switch between cameras or fully zoom out and see the entire building. Only downside for me was that you couldn't put any cameras in the break rooms of the ministry, so they were blind spots unless the player character (Frank) was physically there in one of the breakrooms
3. Cameras placed notifies you when someone is doing an illegal activity even when you aren't focused on the particular camera or when you aren't on surveillance mode
4. Profiling, reporting, and blackmailing is much easier, as the game now autofills the tenants or colleagues basic info
5. Quests have more generous deadlines (something I struggled in 1)
6. You can now skip time forward (not the same as fast forwarding)
7. You can't fully exploit the blackmail mechanism anymore. Sometimes, you can get fined for blackmailing as it is now illegal. Moreover, blackmailing a character for the possession of an illegal item removes said item from the character's room/apartment. Also, repeatedly blackmailing a character can reduce the amount of money yielded until they completely ignore the blackmail
8. You can't exchange authority/reputation for items and sell them for money, and you don't use the reputation for anything (i.e. dialogue options) except for advancing at the ministry
9. However, I think the game balances out the lack of blackmail and reputation exploit, by making certain quests that need money to have a more reasonable amount or by offering alternatives other than making payment for quests that need an insanely high payment
These were the notable differences I can remember that made the gameplay smoother, but also challenging.

As for the story, I hoped it had more concrete ties or referrals to 1 and 2, like how Beholder 2 was a direct sequel to 1, but the connection with 3 is more inferred or speculative. At least, that is how I perceived it. Beholder 3, still has multiple endings, and some leeway on how you can do quests and handle tenants and colleagues, but it still a bit more linear than Beholder 1. Regardless, I really enjoyed the story, and enjoyed replaying the game to see the different endings.

Overall, I think Beholder 3 is a great game, and a good installment to the series. I also think the devs have fixed most of the bug issues, so the gameplay is much smoother. So, if you're, a fan of the Beholder series or want to roleplay as a normal family man trying to survive  in a surveillance state much like in George Orwell's 1984, definitely give this game a try!

Definitely the weakest of all three games in basically all aspects. There's a lot of lag, even on the lowest settings, the storyline is not very engaging and the tasks are... certainly something. 

To (try to) make it short: Beholder 3 throws all kinds of different tasks at you. So it's not like in Beholder 1 where your job is primarily to spy on your tenants as a landlord or like in Beholder 2 where you need to do beaurocratic work as a worker of the ministry, but it basically mixes the two and makes you both a landlord and a ministry worker which ends up being overwhelming/confusing. On top of that you're thrown into some tasks with insufficient information on how the game works. So you actually sometimes have to memorize things the NPC's say to be able to do your job (Which seems hella random because you don't need to always pay attention and you never know when it's important) and you can't ask them twice. There is also a task where you have to break into someone's apartment to place something there, but there's a person inside at all times and you're supposed to just somehow know that you can break in while they're sleeping and that's something that's expected to be logical to the player (if you played Beholder 1 you understand my confusion).

The storyline: I got fairly excited when I noticed that Beholder 3 has more mature themes in terms of how the regulations are more realistic but then I quickly noticed that it's just not making a difference. The only thing that actually made the new regulations matter at all, was the daughter, but I don't think her behaviour made a whole lot of sense, but maybe that's subjective. Other than that there were little quests here and there regarding prostitution etc. etc. but none of it made me feel any type of way. I would almost say it felt hollow? I mean in comparison to Beholder 1 where I was truly attached to many characters and wanted to help/be better, but here it didn't make me feel almost any empathy, which was certainly a missed opportunity. The short plotline with the son was too similar to Beholder 1 (which already made me desensitized) and executed poorly because there was not enough time to even get attached to any of the family members (in my opinion) since you have to leave the apartment complex so much. I did like the idea of these two sides and one of them wants to reform and the other doesn't but that also wasn't executed well, in my opinion. Overall I just didn't find the story engaging and would just briefly look over the dialogue at times (again a stark contrast to Beholder 1 where I was incredibly invested and wanted to discover more).

Wouldn't really recommend at a full price - or even not at all since the lag gets very frustrating (literally makes my laptop sound like it's about to take off and that's sad since the good graphics are actually probably one of, if not the best part) and I don't think I will be playing it a second time even just for that reason. Beholder 3 continues the dystopian narrative established by its predecessors, delivering a gripping and morally complex experience that challenges players to navigate the shadowy corridors of an authoritarian surveillance state. Developed by Alawar Premium, this installment refines the formula of spying, decision-making, and resource management while expanding the narrative scope to include deeper political intrigue and a more immersive world. It strikes a compelling balance between strategy, role-playing, and narrative-driven gameplay, immersing players in a grim, oppressive environment where every choice carries significant consequences.

Set in a totalitarian regime rife with paranoia and strict control over its citizens, Beholder 3 places you in the role of a secret agent tasked with rooting out dissent and maintaining order through surveillance and manipulation. Unlike traditional stealth games, the tension here comes less from avoiding detection and more from the psychological and ethical weight of your decisions. The game pushes players to weigh loyalty to the regime against personal morality, with branching storylines that respond dynamically to your choices. This moral ambiguity is at the core of Beholder 3, making every mission feel tense and impactful.

Gameplay involves a mix of investigative tasks, such as bugging rooms, tailing suspects, and analyzing collected intelligence, combined with managing relationships and resources to maintain your cover and influence. The game’s interface is intuitive, with various tools and gadgets available to gather information discreetly. The addition of a more open-ended structure compared to previous titles encourages exploration and experimentation. Players can approach missions with different strategies, whether through careful observation, direct confrontation, or manipulation of NPCs, which adds variety and replayability.

One of the most striking aspects of Beholder 3 is its narrative depth. The story is layered with political machinations, personal betrayals, and unexpected alliances, making the world feel lived-in and unpredictable. Characters are complex, often caught in their own struggles under the oppressive regime, and interactions with them can influence the story's direction dramatically. Dialogue options and choices often carry ambiguous outcomes, enhancing the sense of uncertainty and tension. The voice acting and writing quality contribute significantly to the immersion, delivering a mature and compelling story that keeps players invested.

Visually, Beholder 3 adopts a dark, moody art style that perfectly captures the oppressive atmosphere of the dystopian setting. The environments are detailed with subtle visual storytelling elements—graffiti, propaganda posters, and worn-down buildings—that enrich the world-building. Animations are smooth, and character designs emphasize the bleakness of life under constant surveillance. The sound design is equally effective, with ambient noises, distant sirens, and subdued music heightening the feeling of paranoia and unease.

Despite its strengths, the game does present some challenges. The pacing can feel slow at times, particularly during investigative phases that require patience and careful note-taking. Some players might find the controls and interface slightly clunky when managing multiple tasks or switching between locations. Additionally, while the branching storylines add replay value, certain narrative threads feel underdeveloped or abruptly resolved, which might leave players wanting more closure in some areas.

Overall, Beholder 3 is a thought-provoking and immersive experience that excels in delivering a nuanced look at surveillance, power, and personal ethics within a totalitarian regime. Its blend of strategic gameplay, rich storytelling, and atmospheric presentation makes it a standout title for fans of narrative-driven strategy games. Though it requires patience and careful attention to detail, the game rewards players with a deeply engaging world where every decision matters and moral ambiguity reigns. For those intrigued by stories of dystopia and human complexity, Beholder 3 offers a compelling journey through the shadows of control and resistance.

As I have written a review for Beholder 2, I feel compelled to write one for Beholder 3.

Beholder 3 is shallow, boring, without substance. It is a video game worth buying on the lowest price possible. It has nothing to say, it has nothing to add. It is nothing, but a capitalist victim, made to capitalize on the success of the previous video game. It is sad that only the first game in this series is good. Beholder 2 was, however, much better than this. Even though Beholder 2 had a nonsensical narrative, the gameplay was at least fun and it tried to be its own thing. This game takes Beholder 2 and Beholder 1, merges their gameplay together, tells you "dont worry about it, it makes sense" and proceeds with a boring narrative which does not even pretend to try and be inovative.

I really, really loved Beholder and Blissful Sleep and I'm cautiously optimistic for Beholder Conductor. This game, unfortunately, really let me down. 

The gameplay loop remains pretty fun, but the writing and bugs sink this game. The first Beholder and Blissful Sleep are masterclasses in efficient, environmental storytelling. The characters are unexpectedly complex, even the tutorial character who became one of my favorites of the series (Jacob) gains shocking depth in the prequel. None of the characters tell you who they are, though. You discover who they are through the objects in their house, their habits and routines, and how they discuss the events of the game. You build an idea of not only who they are but who they are becoming, naturally.

Beholder 3 goes the opposite extreme. Every character has a lengthy monologue if not several. Dialogue on dialogue that does not lead to deeper characterization, because the characters are unfortunately stereotypes. The sexy teacher is a sex worker, the playboy has an STD, the fat lady loves to eat and is greedy, the beaten wife is loyal to her husband, etc etc. None of these are people (with a few notable exceptions), they're just shallow sketches. 

Even the main character's family feels shallow. In the first game, I did genuinely want to help to keep the family alive and together. This time, when I got hit with a giant bill for my son it was like, "eh. I don't really know him." All I know is he's bad at grammar and likes the trumpet. That's it. 

The gameplay is also less tense than the first game due to the split locations. With the extra complication that poses, deadlines are much longer and there are very few hair-splitting tense moments that the first game provided. 

Finally: the bugs. It is easy to fail a quest that you have actually completed, leading to a frustrating loop of trying to get your save back on track. And because most of these quests are more tedious than exciting, failing and redoing it becomes tiresome. 

I really hope Beholder Conductor is as good as the demo appears, because this was a let down. Download the first game and its DLC, and skip this one.

Tap Tap Loot is a simple but surprisingly satisfying idle game where the main idea is all about collecting, upgrading, and watching your progress grow. It’s the kind of game you can open for a few minutes, make some upgrades, then come back later to see how far everything has gone.

The gameplay is pretty straightforward. You tap, collect rewards, unlock upgrades, and slowly build up your progress. There’s nothing complicated about it, but that’s also the appeal. It’s easy to understand and has that “just one more upgrade” feeling that makes idle games addictive.

The best part is the progression. Seeing numbers increase, unlocking new things, and improving your setup gives a nice sense of growth. It’s a good game to relax with because it doesn’t demand too much attention.

The downside is that the simplicity can also become its biggest weakness. After a while, the loop can start feeling repetitive if you’re looking for deeper mechanics or more variety. It’s more about the satisfaction of progression than having a lot of different things to do.

Overall, Tap Tap Loot is a small and casual game that knows exactly what it wants to be. It’s not trying to be a huge adventure, it’s just something fun to check on and slowly build up.

I enjoyed the fact that it was a task bar game, it doesn't take much space on your screen, so whether you have one screen or multiple, this game is made to be played while you do something else.

The game felt pretty complete regarding the builds you can make, you get a melee weapon (2-H or 1-H and an offhand), armor slots, and 3 accessories. Your build can be full melee, ranged, magic, crit, or dodge, you can focus on one aspect or mix a bit of everything. All in all I'd recommend this game to those that generally type or click a lot, as I don't think I'd have progressed much if it wasn't for my series. Alternatively, autoclickers also work. I view Sairento as a futuristic cyberpunk Japan with the ability to accelerate through time (aka bullet time). With an impressive amount of weapons, and the ability to upgrade your weapons and armor with varying traits, there are tons of ways to fight your opponents. There are also multiple skill trees to enhance your agent.

The campaign/story is very light. Stop the bad guy and his henchmen from taking over the city. That doesn't take long, so the real gameplay here is different missions you can undertake in the city, such as Assassinate a crime boss or Eliminate a gang from a city block. You'll play a lot of missions, but they're quick. Usually less than 5 minutes each.

The game itself it definitely a blast. My only complaint is, once you get good (around level 100), you will be able to destroy anything the game throws at you. Although that is always satisfying, the challenge part of the game disappears. I played levels 100-1000 at the highest difficulty (one hit kills you) and rarely died, while clearing out a room of 40+ guys in less than a minute. It's crazy fun, but eventually I moved on.

Sairento VR, developed by Mixed Realms Pte Ltd in collaboration with Swag Soft Holdings Pte Ltd and published by Mixed Realms Pte Ltd, is a high-intensity virtual reality action experience that fully embraces the fantasy of becoming an acrobatic cyber ninja. Rather than taking a cautious or grounded approach to VR combat, the game pushes mobility and spectacle to the forefront, giving players the ability to leap across rooftops, run along walls, perform mid-air flips, and slow time while unloading a barrage of bullets or slicing through enemies with a katana. It is a power fantasy distilled into kinetic motion, designed to make players feel unstoppable within a futuristic, neon-infused reimagining of Japan.

The core appeal of Sairento VR lies in its movement system. Triple jumps, sliding dodges, and aerial maneuvers are not just stylistic flourishes—they are integral to survival. The locomotion mechanics are surprisingly comfortable despite their speed and intensity, a notable achievement in VR where aggressive movement often leads to discomfort. By combining dash-based mobility with smooth traversal and customizable comfort options, the game allows players to tailor their experience to their tolerance level. Once mastered, movement becomes a form of expression. You are not simply navigating arenas; you are choreographing a ballet of destruction, stringing together jumps, wall runs, and slow-motion takedowns in a way that feels almost cinematic.

Combat is equally dynamic and flexible. Sairento VR offers an impressive arsenal of weapons ranging from traditional katanas and throwing stars to bows, pistols, shotguns, and futuristic firearms. Players can dual-wield weapons or mix melee and ranged combat seamlessly, encouraging experimentation with different playstyles. The ability to trigger slow-motion during aerial maneuvers adds a dramatic edge, allowing for precise shots or stylish finishing blows. Enemies come in various forms, from gun-wielding cyber soldiers to agile opponents that demand constant movement and awareness. While enemy AI can sometimes feel straightforward, the sheer intensity of encounters compensates for any lack of complexity.

Progression is handled through skill trees, relic upgrades, and weapon customization. Completing missions earns rewards that enhance movement abilities, increase damage output, or unlock new equipment. This layered upgrade system encourages repeated runs through missions, as players gradually refine their builds to match preferred combat strategies. Some may focus on stealthy blade combat, while others lean into dual firearms and ranged precision. Although mission objectives can occasionally feel repetitive—often revolving around eliminating waves of enemies or securing areas—the evolving character builds help maintain engagement over extended sessions.

Narratively, Sairento VR provides a framework rather than a deeply intricate storyline. The player assumes the role of a Silent One, a cyber-enhanced operative navigating a fractured futuristic society. The plot exists primarily to contextualize the action, with lore delivered through brief dialogues and mission descriptions. While the narrative may not be its strongest component, it succeeds in establishing an aesthetic and thematic foundation that complements the high-energy gameplay. The stylized cyberpunk environments, glowing cityscapes, and industrial interiors contribute to a cohesive atmosphere that supports the ninja fantasy.

Visually, the game adopts a stylized approach rather than aiming for hyperrealism. Character models and environments emphasize clarity and performance, ensuring smooth frame rates critical for VR immersion. The art direction blends neon accents with traditional Japanese architectural influences, creating a world that feels both futuristic and culturally grounded. Though it may not match the graphical fidelity of more recent VR titles, the design choices prioritize fluid gameplay and readability during intense combat sequences.

One of the most compelling aspects of Sairento VR is its ability to deliver adrenaline-fueled action in short, satisfying bursts. Missions can be completed relatively quickly, making the game well-suited for sessions that focus on mastering mechanics or testing new builds. Multiplayer options, including cooperative modes, add further replayability, allowing players to experience chaotic battles alongside friends. The learning curve can be steep initially, especially for newcomers to VR, but once the movement and combat systems click, the experience becomes deeply rewarding.

Despite its strengths, Sairento VR is not without shortcomings. Mission variety can feel limited over time, and players seeking a robust narrative campaign may find the story underdeveloped. Some menus and upgrade systems may initially appear dense or complex. However, these limitations rarely overshadow the core thrill of movement and combat that defines the game.

Ultimately, Sairento VR stands as one of the more distinctive action titles in the VR space. It demonstrates how virtual reality can elevate combat beyond traditional mechanics by making movement itself exhilarating. By combining acrobatic traversal, versatile weaponry, and customizable progression systems, it delivers a visceral experience that captures the essence of being a cybernetic ninja in a high-tech world. For players seeking intensity, mobility, and stylish combat in VR, Sairento VR remains a standout experience that continues to showcase the kinetic potential of immersive gaming.

Sairento feels like something out of an alternate timeline where devs weren't too scared of making their players vomit and VR games were made with PC in mind. Triple jumps, near-instant dashes, wallrunning, and backflips all in first person are still exhilarating in 2024; Even several years after getting my "VR legs", my brain still tries to escape my skull while doing slow-mo backflips and I love it every time. This is the only game I've played that appropriately utilizes teleport movement: depending on your physical stance IRL and how you aim the movement arc, you will either dash, dash slide, jump, jump and slide, etc., with either an arrow or circle at the end to predict your end position. Traditional locomotion is also available and works fine early on, but late game focuses on abusing time dilation and redirecting jumps mid-air to dodge projectiles. This also makes melee difficult to focus on late game since you spend so much time trying to be mobile and you're generally not on the ground. That's not a huge issue though because there's a good sized arsenal here and you can have two pistols/throwing weapons on your hips, two weapons on your back, and one weapon on your lower back that are all very easy and intuitive to grab, swap, or swap hands. 

I highly recommend this as long as you're okay with the grind being the gameplay. There's only 10 story missions and even then there's some padding with them but they provide a decent backdrop for the rest of the game. After that you have access to plenty of grinding for prestiges, new weapon and armor relics (mods), cranking up the difficulty scaling, and adding modifiers to levels. The only issue with the grind is that even though there are loadouts, the relics equipped are per weapon, per loadout, and it can be difficult to just swap them between weapons with how bloated your inventory gets (and with how poor the inventory UI is). Overall though the weapons feel fantastic to use, there's a good variety of melee, guns, and throwing weapons, and legendary relics can provide really game-changing unique buffs (like exploding kunai, homing throwing stars, or bouncing rifle rounds). Regardless of your weapon preferences, it rides like a bike with excellent controls and tons of options for controls, accessibility, movement preferences, and integrations. 

This game sits right at the mid price point that makes up the meat of any healthy game platform's library. I love Sairento because it just focuses on good gameplay; this isn't a $10, 20 minute "VR experience" or a full price desktop game ported to VR that has you clicking on 2D menus (you know what you did, Todd), but it's not flawless either. This is one of the few games that I felt didn't have a VR Tax on it, but your mileage may vary if you don't like the grind. As long as you can accept some jank and early VR awkwardness, this is a really unique experience that stands above the horde of bland wave shooters that crowded out the market of early VR games.

This game is awesome. Simply put, it's one of the best VR games I've played. I was initially hesitant due to the games' slightly older age it might not feel as good as some other releases but I needn't have worried. The game is incredibly responsive and intuitive. The gameplay is highly enjoyable and there's a very compelling 'just one more mission' feel to the game. 

Let's start with some positives:
+The game is HIGHLY customizable. You can tweak settings to your hearts content, including locomotion style (snapping or free move) choose automatic or manual reloads, 'sticky' weapons or manually gripped weapons, and  oh yeah, the ability to backflip.
+Good variety of weapons including SMGs, swords, rifles, bows, and grenade launchers
+Level up/Relic System let's you increase weapon ability/general survivability as well as customize each weapon with a unique colored emission. There are perks and you can craft your own relics with resources gathered from missions.
+Missions are largely the same in terms moment to moment gameplay, mostly involving killing a certain amount of enemies, but have modifiers, different environments and reframings (wave survival, vs room clearing vs endless enemies +boss) that keep them fresh.
+Movement feels really good. There's jumping, teleporting, sliding, wall running and backflipping and everything feels responsive. Combined with bullet time, you just feel so, so cool while playing this game.
+Environments are pretty and enemies are distinct. There's a good number of maps.
+The team is still offering technical support for the game and responds quickly.

There are a few small negatives:
-Sometimes a hand (usually right for me) will get briefly stuck, either unable to grip a weapon or let go. It happens rarely and always fixes itself pretty fast (though quickly turning the controller on and off fixes the issue as well). However, this might be a personal controller issue.
-Character model height is a little bit off even after calibration.  It's not by much and is a very minor issue that doesn't affect gameplay at all. Again, might be personal hardware issue.
-I got too into it during a session and smashed my finger against my closet door :(

Not negatives, but would have been awesome to have
+Environment climbing in a similar fashion as games like Blade and Sorcery. With all the traversal options, it would have been neat to grab ledges or swing off of things...but few games have such mechanics and with all the movement options in the game is basically not needed.
+Weight to melee. Not an issue for many enemies, but if an enemy takes multiple hits, melee loses a bit of wow factor.
+Cosmetic options (clothing colors) for player avatar, though the avatar model is nice as is. Def not essential, I just like customization :)

To conclude, some of the awesome I've done and you can do in this game
+Flip over a charging enemy, kill them in slow motion, land, slide, and gun down another enemy
+No look headshot an enemy with a bow
+Dash and slice an enemy akin to Overwatch's Genji
+Deflect bullets back at enemies
+Jump over an enemies attack and kill them.
+Hot swap weapons to get an opportune
+Many more to discover!

All in all, the game is currently a strong 9 to 9.5/10. With some more time with it. I can definitely see it becoming a full 10. If you've got VR hardware, this is one of the must plays.

I have found myself instantly charmed by this unusual title. I've dumped thousands of hours into VR titles like Boneworks, Bonelabs, and shooters like Gunclub, I would say I certainly am comfortable with VR and rarely see some minor issues so I may not highlight something that others see right away and for that I apologize - but this title takes an elegant approach to the golfbag of weapons most VR shooters are often associated with by having a reload system not unlike older arcade blaster cabinets like house of the dead, where in this case leaving the weapon near a holster begins a reload cycle without further input.
Movement feels strangely smooth, in a way that I almost didn't expect for a game that gives an appearance of kill, level, repeat. The main method is walking with the thumbstick as you may expect, but traditional teleporting is tweaked and inserted with slow-motion leaps, slides, and dashes as contextually appropriate - even allowing wall jumps and wall runs which are never a surprised as your trajectory indicator shows an arrow that either goes perpendicular to the wall for a bounce or parallel for a run.
The campaign so far, admittedly only being a little over an hour in I find myself only three missions in, feels somewhat strange but gives enough of a story to feel engaged at a satisfactory level for most any player - though being in the main area, the Dojo, for any length of time lent the feeling that the main meat of this game is the challenges and missions, rather than the campaign. Missions seemed to pop up Payday2 Crimenet style, appearing and fading out, though they meant nothing to me at this point in time as I simply haven't gotten too deep into the game beyond enjoying the mechanics.
Another deeply enjoyable part of the game is that the mission-end screen shows a detailed breakdown of your score across a plethora of categories, starting with time and ranging to some unexpected things such as how little damage you took for instance. It is genuinely engaging seeing such a layout with so many categories given and a full pie for each one showing how well I performed in the mission, and it leaves me wanting to try again when I was so clearly close to a perfect completion for another category. 

My only major complaint so far has been a small one, pertaining to a specific mission of the campaign sequence. It appears you can in fact aggro the enemy before you even have player control in any situation that enemies are nearby and you have access to weapons, something I learned and certainly did ditch my headset in a ragequit  because I was just trying to fuck around while the characters were doing way too much exposition.

Tooth and Tail immediately attracted attention with it’s WW1-WW2 poster style art, strategy tag and animals being put in place of humans according to their features

Pixel graphics you’d see during gameplay is ofc a lot less outstanding, it’s about average in that category, though in very few maps it could use some improvement for sure. There isn’t much else to talk about, cause it pretty much covers everything there is that regard, only other a bit more interesting aspect are hub zones for each faction - those have lots of neat details, despite having same pixel art.

Audio is mostly just average - sounds do their job well, nothing exceptionally good or bad there, osts on the other hand are a bit more divisive - piano does a lot of heavy lifting there and while most tracks just fit well enough, some are quite a bit above that level. Voice acting on the other hand all felt quite nice.

Story is pretty brutal - Tooth and Tail world is one of big social divide, where lower casts of society have to resort to cannibalism to survive, while upper classes might do the same, meaning they’d eat those beneath them. So you eat your friend\family, while I eat some plebeians - we are not the same. Obviously such situation could not continue indefinitely, so conflict arises where victor will feed on defeated. Each faction has campaign and you’d see their point of view on what’s happening, reasons it ended like that and what’ll it come to in the end. Also units, meaning animal species are not shared between them, each type belonging to their respective side and has unique function.

Game is leaning more towards tactics compared to full-on strategy, it’s still rts, but there are some limits on what and where you can build. There is very limited pool of buildings in general and even though unit variety is not that big per faction either, considering that each faction features their own completely separate roster remedies that point. Most of the time will be spent in combat encounters big and small, not build-up of economy or bases, since there are only so many nodes to capture, you’d have to be fast and have task force ready to repel enemy or deal with already established defences. Campaign will sometimes provide enough time to get your bearings, but half of the time it’d be very time sensitive, so unless you decent force fast, surprise early enemy raid might end you right at the start. Once again - since every side has their own army, there are plenty of combinations and styles to check, so everyone should find themselves something fitting their playstyle.

All the design decisions made in this game to shake up the RTS formula only serves to make fighting against the AI a deeply frustrating experience. Because the AI does not obey any of the limitations placed on you.

Biggest and most blatant issue : you cannot issue precise orders to your army. The only thing you can do, is call your entire army to your commander, or call all units of a specific type to your commander. That's it. Even if you wanted to split your army to attack on two fronts, you would need to go to your first attack spot, call the units you want there, then move to the other point and call the rest (being careful not to accidentally call the whole army and ruin the plan). The AI, for its part, can do whatever it pleases in that regard. It absolutely can, and will (all the time), split its forces, even amongt a single unit type, and attack you from multiple angles at once, while its commander is running around on the other side of the map entirely.
This results in you constantly needing to split your attention to multiple fronts - in a game where, BY DESIGN, you cannot split your attention.

The game also emphasizes short, ~5-10 minutes match. All well and good for multiplayer where you start at the same point, I'm sure. But a serious problem for the typical RTS campaign setup of you needing to build up your forces to take on an already established enemy. Enemy which, again due to the fast match focus, are only a short jaunt away since the maps are minuscule.
Still to push the fast match angle, you also run out of food rather quick. After which, units you can't afford will stop fighting, and if you stay stuck that way for 60 seconds, you lose. Well, as far as I can tell, the AI completely ignores that, too.

There's also the fact that maps can be difficult to parse sometimes, it can be hard to see the roads, everything slows you down, and some paths are only a tile wide and partially hidden by vegetation. But again, the AI isn't bothered by that, it'll always know the fastest route to anywhere it wants to go.

There are also multiple missions where enemy camps just... pop up. Typically those where your objective is to survive. No enemy hero on the map, but camps will just spontaneously start building here and there at regular intervals. Great concept, isn't it? Typically the game will try to keep it to the fog of war but if you have good map control, it'll just straight up spawn camps right in your base, next to your mill. Just because it can.

All in all, judging by the achievement rates, very few people have pushed to the end of the campaign, and I think it's rather telling.

Tooth and Tail, developed and published by Pocketwatch Games, is a real-time strategy game that rethinks the genre by stripping it down to its essentials and rebuilding it around speed, clarity, and immediacy. Instead of sprawling tech trees and heavy micromanagement, it delivers a condensed experience where every action matters and every second carries weight. The result is a game that feels both approachable and intense, offering a different kind of strategic depth—one rooted in decision-making under pressure rather than mechanical complexity.

The most defining feature is how you interact with the battlefield. Rather than commanding from an overhead perspective, you directly control a single leader unit who moves across the map, constructs buildings, gathers resources, and rallies troops. This design grounds the experience in a physical presence, forcing you to be in the right place at the right time. You can’t do everything at once, and that limitation creates constant tension. Choosing to expand your economy might leave your base vulnerable, while focusing on defense could slow your growth. This trade-off becomes the core of the gameplay, turning even simple decisions into meaningful ones.

Resource management is streamlined but impactful. Food acts as the primary currency, used to build structures and produce units, and it must be gathered from specific points on the map. Expansion is essential, but it comes with risk, as overextending can expose you to attacks. Before each match, players select a fixed set of units, which defines their strategy from the outset. There is no mid-game tech progression, so success depends on how well you use what you’ve chosen. This approach shifts the focus from long-term buildup to immediate tactical execution, rewarding players who can adapt their plans on the fly.

Matches are fast-paced and rarely overstay their welcome, often concluding within minutes. This brevity gives the game a sense of urgency that keeps engagement high, with little room for passive play. Every moment feels active, whether you’re scouting enemy positions, reinforcing defenses, or launching an attack. The use of procedurally generated maps adds variety, ensuring that each match presents new challenges and preventing the gameplay from becoming predictable. This combination of speed and unpredictability makes it easy to play multiple matches in succession without losing momentum.

Despite its simplicity, the game offers a surprising level of strategic depth. Unit interactions, positioning, and timing all play crucial roles, and small mistakes can quickly escalate into larger problems. The balance between offense and defense is constantly shifting, and understanding when to commit to a push or pull back can determine the outcome of a match. The streamlined mechanics make it easy to understand what is happening, but mastering the system requires careful observation and quick decision-making.

The setting adds another layer of identity, presenting a dark, allegorical world where anthropomorphic animals are locked in a brutal conflict driven by scarcity and ideology. The narrative is delivered through a series of short campaign missions that shift perspectives between different factions, offering glimpses into the motivations behind the war. While the story is not the main focus, it provides context and atmosphere, giving the battles a sense of purpose beyond simple competition.

Visually, the game uses a stylized pixel art approach that is both functional and distinctive. Units are clearly readable even during chaotic moments, and animations convey personality despite their simplicity. The art direction, combined with a strong and memorable soundtrack, creates a cohesive aesthetic that supports the game’s tone. The music, in particular, enhances the sense of urgency and tension, reinforcing the pace of the gameplay.

There are, however, some limitations to this design. The simplified mechanics, while elegant, may feel restrictive to players who prefer the complexity of traditional RTS games. The lack of direct control over individual units removes a layer of precision that some may find essential, and relying on the leader unit for all actions can occasionally feel limiting. The single-player campaign, while effective as an introduction, does not fully explore the depth of the systems, leaving multiplayer as the primary space where the game truly shines.

Ultimately, Tooth and Tail succeeds by committing to a clear and focused vision. It doesn’t try to replicate the scale or complexity of other strategy games, instead offering a faster, more immediate alternative that emphasizes meaningful choices and constant engagement. It captures the essence of strategy without the excess, delivering an experience that is both accessible and challenging.

In the end, it stands out as a bold reinterpretation of the RTS genre, offering a unique blend of simplicity and depth that rewards both quick thinking and long-term understanding. For players willing to embrace its approach, it provides a consistently engaging and highly replayable experience.
