Slotbound delivers an imaginative combination of roguelite progression, slot machine mechanics, and strategic auto-battler combat, creating an experience where calculated decisions and unpredictable outcomes constantly influence one another. Developed and published by Optima Arch, the game introduces a distinctive approach to army management by transforming slot machine spins into opportunities for recruiting warriors, strengthening existing units, and developing powerful defensive formations. Its central appeal comes from turning seemingly random results into meaningful strategic opportunities, making it particularly interesting for players who enjoy experimentation, character progression, and discovering powerful combinations.

The gameplay centers on a 3x3 slot machine that determines which units become available for recruitment. Matching symbols produces warriors, while particularly fortunate combinations can trigger jackpots and summon powerful Prism units. This system creates an entertaining sense of anticipation because every spin potentially changes the direction of a battle. However, the randomness also introduces uncertainty, requiring players to adjust their strategies according to the resources and characters they receive. Rather than following a completely predictable progression path, successful players must learn to maximize favorable outcomes while minimizing the consequences of unfortunate spins.

An important feature is the ability to absorb weaker units to strengthen more valuable warriors. This progression system encourages thoughtful resource management because sacrificing several ordinary fighters may produce a considerably stronger character capable of surviving increasingly difficult encounters. Branching class advancements further expand customization, allowing players to develop specialized units suited to different tactical situations. These mechanics give the army-building process greater depth than simply collecting the strongest available characters, rewarding players who understand when to consolidate their forces and when to maintain a broader defensive formation.

Character customization becomes even more interesting through randomized attributes, Imprints, Items, and Cores. These interconnected systems create opportunities to experiment with different combinations of abilities and enhancements. A seemingly ordinary unit can become exceptionally effective when supported by compatible bonuses, while powerful characters may underperform without appropriate development. The Core system adds another strategic layer by allowing players to influence slot machine probabilities and improve their chances of obtaining advantageous results. This helps balance the game's reliance on luck by giving players additional control over their progression.

Combat emphasizes preparation and strategic composition rather than constant manual intervention. Players assemble their armies and watch them confront successive enemy waves, including challenging judgement encounters and powerful bosses. The automated battles provide a satisfying opportunity to observe how different combinations perform under pressure. However, players who prefer direct combat controls may find this approach less immediately engaging. The enjoyment largely comes from constructing effective formations, optimizing character development, and discovering combinations capable of overcoming difficult encounters.

The roguelite structure supports replayability through unpredictable recruitment outcomes and varied character attributes. Different attempts can encourage alternative strategies, particularly when certain units or enhancements become available earlier than expected. This unpredictability helps maintain excitement, although excessive dependence on favorable combinations could occasionally become frustrating. The game's long-term appeal ultimately depends on whether its available builds remain sufficiently balanced and varied to reward experimentation rather than encouraging players to repeatedly pursue a small selection of dominant strategies.

Visually, Slotbound uses colorful pixel-art graphics that complement its fantasy-inspired atmosphere and mechanically focused presentation. The animated characters, slot machine effects, and increasingly crowded battles contribute to the excitement of watching an army develop. Its visual style emphasizes readability and energetic combat rather than elaborate cinematic presentation. Nevertheless, larger encounters may potentially become visually busy, making clear battlefield information particularly important when evaluating the effectiveness of individual units and abilities.

The game's accessibility benefits from its relatively modest system requirements, making it approachable for players without high-end gaming computers. Its single-player focus also suits those who prefer developing strategies at their own pace. The availability of multiple supported languages makes the experience accessible to a wider audience. Another consideration is the disclosed use of generative AI assistance in certain visual and promotional assets, which may influence how some players evaluate its artistic presentation.

Steam Deck compatibility is a notable advantage. The game is officially Steam Deck Verified, with its core functionality working through the handheld's controls and its interface remaining usable on the smaller display. Controller prompts and general navigation are appropriately supported, while the game can run using settings suitable for the device. Its viewpoint and methodical pacing also translate naturally to portable play, although demanding visual settings can still make sensible performance adjustments worthwhile for players prioritizing battery life or consistent performance.

Overall, Slotbound offers an appealing interpretation of roguelite strategy by combining the excitement of randomized recruitment with meaningful character development and tactical customization. Its strongest qualities are the satisfying progression mechanics, extensive synergy possibilities, and constant tension between calculated planning and unpredictable rewards. Although occasional unfavorable outcomes and the indirect nature of combat may discourage certain players, its inventive design provides an engaging foundation for strategy enthusiasts.

It's an incredibly fun game, though it skirts the line of balancing and fun quite narrowly. 

You spin the slot machine to get units and dopamine hits whenever you manage to grab something more special than a common unit. It's an addicting and good loop and one run doesn't take up too much time (5-30 minutes depending on difficulty and decision-making).

I like the variety of units and skills they come with a lot. However I feel like this is where the game is a bit too careful with its balancing. Getting specific units for actual team-building is just a bit too rng-dependant, as well as specific skills to make some units really shine that are otherwise lackluster (like debuffs on fast-hitting units). 
This is furthermore exacerbated by the fact that with the permanent skill tree you have to buy certain skills for the slot-machine or units in order to grab the following skills. This linearity kills some of the decision making, because some skills feel counter-productive, while some are useless (for example, there are two skills that scale with using the slot-machine or a unit killing enemies, which is fine, but they scale so slowly that any native buff doing the same thing is almost always better and better from the get go especially). Either some skills need serious buffs, they need to be re-rollable OR let the player de-activate some from appearing at all.
The same goes for skills that you get by sacrificing units. When sacrificing a unit to level up another unit you have to transfer a unit-specific skill as well. Often times I would like to put other skills on the leveled unit, which results in lost levels. I would like to not be forced to do that in order to have more control. On the other hand, getting some specific fun skills with debuffs or gameplay-changing mechanics is really rng-dependant. I feel like a shop mechanic for such skills could be a fun addition.

All of this doesn't really matter in the first 4 stages of the game, where you can play with almost any unit. However in the latter two stages, you really feel the power-difference between certain units of different families but the same rarity. For example, the units that are summoned by the spear symbol feel almost always worse than the shield symbol in both defensive and offensive capabilites, when most of their skills have the intention of making them more defense-oriented. In reality, the blue rarity defensive warrior branch will always outperform either blue rarity spearman branch. This is where I would like to see some buffs to the spearmen for example. Same goes for early-game healing, where it's just extremely sub-optimal compared to late-game where it sometimes becomes the superior strategy.

As always, writing about the negatives/problems takes up a lot more space than talking about the positives. But there is a reason why I'm recommending the game regardless. I'm having a lot of fun with the full game, trying out unit combos, seeing what works and what doesn't. The stone-quest mechanic is a lot of fun and changes up how you interact with certain elements of the gameplay. From what I am seeing, the developer is also extremely invested in making the game perfect and I really appreciate that dedication. It may need a bit of time to get there but it's far from impossible to do so. That is why I would recommend SlotBound if you like any quick game with some rng-dopamine and a lot of build-crafting.

The issue with this game is a complete lack of agency for the player. The game effectively plays itself.
Usually, with a roguelite, you are given random units/cards/etc, and must make the most of what you have by finding a build in the randomness. Here, your options are so limited and meaningless that you might as well not be making any choices yourself.

Each roll costs more than the last, so there is absolutely no reason to save your money from one round to the next. There is no planning or strategy, just spent it all every time. Sometimes you will save one roll to line up with an item and thats it. 
If the dev wanted to give the player agency in their choices, they would have given us a reason to save money round-to-round. For example, a trade-off where you are weaker due to having less units, but your money gains interest each round or you get a buff after not rolling the slot machine last round.
At the very least, why is rolling the slot machine, where I am most likely to get piss all, the only way to spend money?

The item shop is a disappointment, with the vast majority of items being placebo buffs for your units. There is no variety whatsoever and you never make enough cash to reroll enough to see anything interesting. Why can I find a legendary item round 1 but have no way to lock it so it doesn't get auto-rerolled?

The units are not significantly different from one another, save for a couple super OP ones (cough cavalry cough) and a couple weak ones, and the one guy who summons a bear. Traits and stat bonuses are extremely difficult to notice, might as well not even show the stats.

Unit placement might as well be random too. With how little it matters, why even let the player choose. Sure, I put the damage dealer two pixels further back than the tank so he doesn't draw aggro, or I sent everybody to the back so they stand in the healing fountain while they fight. Ultimately these decisions get lost in the moshpit of poor visibility.
You never get to see the enemy units before the fight anyways, not that there is enough enemy variety or space on the map to warrant deliberate unit placement.

Harder difficulties are not actually more difficult, they just make the runs longer. Since this is a roguelite, the early-midpoint of the run is the hardest, not the end.

And lastly, why are we not allowed to continue a run in endless mode after beating the boss?

I actually played this game once a long time ago, before it even appeared on Steam. I didn't like it back then, but I was still a kid, so I thought I might understand it better now that I'm much older. Well, no. I dislike it even more after replaying it.

--- Controls / gameplay

It's not all bad, but the gameplay mechanics can be annoying, especially in the graveyard maze. All the objects (graves in this case) are evenly spaced and separated by one grid, but the character moves freely and isn't restricted by the grid. He's also quite fast, so you'll often run into things, and sometimes it takes several tries to get between two objects. I'm playing on Steam Deck and have to use the D-pad, so it's especially annoying.

The good thing is that you don't have to be standing exactly in front of an object to interact with it. I'd probably lose my mind if that were the case.

The whole game is mostly "go there, interact with something, go somewhere else, interact with another thing, and backtrack." Overall, the controls and mechanics are simple and basic, so there's not much else to say about them.

--- Music

Honestly, it's nothing special, but it's quite okay. There are some classical pieces, and most of the tracks sound like music-box tunes, which is nice.

--- Graphics / level design

The sprites are pretty nice, it's all hand-drawn, but the level design is simply awful. 

I went the wrong way once (you really have no idea where you're supposed to go first - there are no signs or hints, either in this location or anywhere before it). There are 3 directions you can go, with just a plain fountain in the middle, but you can't even interact with it. It soft-locked me, so I couldn't go back and try the other paths - I had to load a previous save that I made at the very beginning of the level.

Every level is huge and empty, with barely anything to look at. It's really uninteresting - most rooms have a bed, a bookshelf, a desk... and that's pretty much it. Everything else is just floor.

There are long, empty corridors with not even a single object to interact with (or maybe one). One world is basically just graves everywhere with a few trees here and there, plus a fountain in one location, and pretty much nothing else.

--- Puzzles

The worst part.

Some of them are obvious, some are quite fun, but others expect you to give an answer (yes, you have to type it in yourself) without even asking you a question. You'll read a bunch of cryptic nonsense and then have to figure out both the question and the answer yourself.

At that point, it's better to just read a guide than try to make sense of it.

--- Characters / world

The world is really boring. When you interact with objects, they all say the same basic things. You interact with a bookshelf and it'll tell you it's full of books... oh, right, with the occasional variation of "strange" or "hard to understand" books. Amazing.

It's a plant. It's a bucket. It's a mug. Thanks, I wouldn't have known otherwise.

There's no lore, nothing interesting, nothing funny, just... nothing.

The characters are cryptic and unnatural. Some of them are based on characters from fairy tales (like Little Red Riding Hood), but they have pretty much no personality of their own, and the things they say are often confusing. They barely have any role in the story - they just follow you around and comment on one or two things.

By the end, they all start sounding the same and ask you similar questions, for which the answer doesn't really matter anyway.

The Cheshire Cat has more personality, but he mostly sounds like an edgy kid trying way too hard to be cool, "crazy" and mysterious.

--- Plot

Well, I didn't get it. Like, at all.

I don't know why, where, or what was happening. Why are we in an orphanage? How did we enter the "dream" world? Why are we entering other people's hearts? What does it actually do?

Nothing is explained. The characters talk in a very ambiguous and "mysterious" way, the world offers no lore, and your character doesn't have any dialogue boxes. So when he supposedly "says" something and another character responds to it, you have no idea what was actually said.

--- Conclusion

I bought it on sale for about the price of a big bread roll from my local bakery, and I'd still rather eat the bread roll.

There's nothing particularly interesting about this game. It had potential, but the attempt to be mysterious and "deep once you figure it out" ends up ruining it. Some actual lore, explanations, proper conversations instead of cryptic monologues, and better level design could have turned it into a surprisingly good game.

You can finish it in around 3 hours if you go for all the endings (using a guide for the ambiguous riddles), but it still took me days to reach all of the regular endings. I have yet to finish the hidden route and get the secret and true endings, but I still remember some of the things that happen, and they don’t make much more sense.

There are many better and more worthwhile games in similar style out there, so I just can't recommend this one to anyone.

Alicemare is a strange game where we're put in what appears to be a kindergarten for children with special needs. It's a standard RPGmaker-style game.

First of all, I must talk about the terrible movement system. The environment, like in a typical RPGmaker game, is divided into a grid, with one object per square. But, for some reason, the movement system in game is split into a half-grid, making movement, turns and interacting with environment painfully annoying, specially considering that no object in the game is placed on a half-tile. There is no sprint button either, and the character walks too quickly by default - it makes interacting with objects next to each other pointlessly difficult.

The graphics are hand-drawn, unique and pretty. However, the screenshots on the Steam page do not represent just how hollow and empty most locations in the game are. A lot of them are just floor, walls and one singular sprite repeated a hundred times. Whole rooms of nothing displayed on screen but floor. This is especially showing at the beginning of a game - for example, why is the entire front hallway of the beginning location totally empty, other than having a telephone? Have you ever seen a giant room in real life which has nothing but a telephone? The game features plenty of sprites in different rooms, so even copy-pasting them here and there would make the place feel a lot more natural. In the game's current state, many rooms look like placeholders.

The puzzles are fairly fun and tricky, however some form of a hint system is missing. There are a lot of puzzles, and alt-tabbing every 5 minutes to look up a solution is no fun. Some are straight up unfair however, and require nothing but luck.

The gameplay is fine, but it screams lack of originality. It's just "interact with this, then with that and with this again" - allowing you to predict what you'll have to do and what the outcome will be. The most egregious example is the game forcing you to interact with a hundred graves to find missing objects. There is no indication of which graves are correct - you are meant to try every single one.

I left the worst for last - the story. I'm sorry but I do not understand anything. I have no idea why we start where we start, what is happening, why are we in different worlds, why are we teleported into different worlds. I feel like the game makes an attempt at explaining some of it with the final few diary entries, but they had no impact of my understanding of the lore. When I saw a true ending achievement pop up, I was simply confused by what I've just witnessed. Perhaps I approached the game from a wrong standpoint, or I missed some obvious clues, nonetheless I'm totally lost with zero clue what was going on during my 6 hours of gameplay.

It pains me to say it, but I consider the game to be a clueless walking simulator with a bunch of puzzles in between for an additional bit of annoyance. It has a lot of potential - by removing the half-grid movement, filling up empty rooms with objects and explaining the story earlier, in simpler, more detailed way, the game would turn into a masterpiece.

I would not recommend it for any reason other than a handful of creative puzzles, which are not the primary focus of Alicemare anyway.

I really didn't like this game. The puzzles were either too easy or totally unclear; I wouldn't have minded if I enjoyed the rest of the game. But for a narrative-driven game, the story wasn't great. The premise is really interesting: travelling to different fairytale worlds. each distorted by the trauma of its originator. Brothers Grimm meets Kingdom Hearts? Sounds dope. 

Unfortunately, we don't spend enough time in each world. The characters are really interesting, but they're not fleshed out. And there are just too many unanswered questions. Did Ricky ever exist? We see both Letty and Ricky in the end credits, so was he ever a real person? Why was Chelsy obsessed with bears? Who was Cliff? Are the boy and teacher the same person? What's their history? What's up with the murder mystery? What's the deal with the cheshire cat and white rabbit? Why was Allen called Alice, and why was Alice treated as some sort of omnipotent being? 

As a total nitpick, the fairytale theming was a bit confused. I got Hansel and Gretel and Red Riding Hood immediately, but I had no idea about Stella or Joshua until I checked the other endings. Like I said, total nitpick. But I'm a sucker for a good theme, so I appreciate it when they're properly conveyed. 

The dream worlds weren't particularly interesting visually, and the puzzles didn't relate to the story being told, so they felt out of place. A character's telling me about their dying mother, then I'm confronted with a puzzle straight from an educational CD-ROM. Time spent there was super abrupt, with very little effort required to get each world key. So it didn't feel like much of an achievement when each world was cleared. There was no difficulty levelling either, so it never feels like you're progressing or getting better. 

The latter half of the game feels really out of place, as it shifts focus away from the main four kids to focus on the teacher and the institute's past. But it felt like unnecessary padding that caused the ending to be rushed and exposition-heavy. It was also filled with pointless busiwork to help solve a riddle that seemingly had no bearing on the main plot.  

This game had real promise, and I'd love to see it revisited with a higher budget behind it. It could honestly be on par with Little Goody Two Shoes or Goldenertraum in terms of storytelling and aesthetics. And if a remake is ever in the works, please scrap Stella's world entirely. Clicking around on a grey screen to find buried piano keys with no hint as to where they are doesn't make for engaging gameplay. Nor does navigating identical, all-grey mazes.

I am recommending the game because I like Miwashiba and the potential of the story Alicemare tells, but I don't think I could recommend the game in good faith because it quite frankly isn't a very good one.

I was really trying my hardest to enjoy this game, but I found the cryptic puzzles/riddles kind of annoying and the instantaneous deaths at most turns felt too punishing. I'm not gonna act like I couldn't save, but there are times when I over-saved and under-saved alike. There's no balance since there is no kind of autosave or return to a point before the death. If you played without saving the whole way through and died due to a single, seemingly insignificant choice, you lost potentially 30 minutes of progress in an instant. It's punishing in a way I didn't like that much. But the game itself is quite short if you're really skipping everything, so there's that I suppose.

Music was whatever, not much of an impact. I wasn't a fan of the super simplistic visuals too much, and I wish Miwashiba's art was shown to me at a higher quality. The game's visuals kinda lent itself to being difficult to look at sometimes and I know there might be some segments (like Stella's) where my more colour-blind friends would be somewhat unable to properly access due to how similarly coloured everything is.

Of course, the most important part of this is that I actually really like the story for how complex yet fun it was to engage with it despite the confusion it presents. The average person isn't going to deep dive into the lore of a mid ass niche Japanese RPG maker game, but [b] half of the lore is hidden behind a novel [/b] and based on people who enjoy Alicemare, the novel seems to be doing a great thing for itself and fully fleshes things out. [b] But you will not find any answers to the stories and your questions in the game, [/b] and the endings will feel lacklustre as a result since it's all hidden behind the novel.

All this is to say, I still enjoyed it since this was Miwashiba's first game and I find myself reluctant to be that critical of it. And I absolutely will be reading that novel, and I will probably really like it too.

Alicemare, developed by △○□× (Miwashiba) and published by PLAYISM, is a surreal blend of fairy tale storytelling, mystery, and light horror that captures a distinct sense of atmosphere despite its relatively short length. At its heart, it is an exploration-based adventure game that relies on narrative ambiguity, unsettling imagery, and a childlike yet uncanny presentation to create a memorable experience. Rather than leaning on jump scares or traditional horror tropes, it builds unease through mood, character interactions, and an undercurrent of darkness beneath seemingly whimsical scenarios.

The story follows Allen, a quiet boy who has recently lost his parents and is placed in a group home with other children, each with their own unique quirks and hidden struggles. One evening, after hearing strange noises, Allen investigates and stumbles into an otherworldly realm where fractured fairy tale motifs intertwine with personal traumas. Familiar figures like Cheshire Cat or the White Rabbit appear in twisted forms, and as Allen progresses deeper, the lines between dream, memory, and reality blur. The narrative leans heavily on symbolism, with every character and event hinting at themes of loss, escapism, and acceptance.

Gameplay is simple but effective, focused primarily on exploration, dialogue, and puzzles. Allen moves through different dreamlike scenarios, solving logic-based riddles, uncovering items, and piecing together fragmented stories. The puzzles are intentionally varied—some straightforward, others more cryptic—and while this creates moments of genuine satisfaction when solutions click, there are times when the lack of clear hints can lead to confusion. Unlike many games with horror undertones, there is no combat system or reflex-based gameplay, which keeps the experience accessible and emphasizes atmosphere over intensity.

Visually, the game embraces a retro pixel-art style, which complements its fairy tale themes. The environments range from cozy and familiar to eerie and unsettling, with clever use of color and design to evoke mood. The art style carries a deceptive innocence, contrasting the darker undertones that surface as the story unfolds. Sound design further enhances the atmosphere, with gentle yet haunting music tracks and well-placed sound effects that contribute to the dreamlike tension. The overall presentation strikes a balance between childlike charm and underlying unease, keeping players engaged and slightly off-balance throughout the experience.

One of the game’s defining features is its branching endings. Depending on the choices players make and how much they explore, multiple outcomes are available, each providing different perspectives on the characters and their hidden truths. This encourages replayability despite the game’s relatively short runtime of just a few hours, as players are motivated to uncover every possible resolution. The multiple endings also reinforce the game’s central theme of ambiguity, leaving interpretation up to the player and sparking reflection long after the credits roll.

While Alicemare excels at creating mood and narrative intrigue, it does have limitations. The pacing can feel uneven, with moments of strong immersion occasionally interrupted by puzzles that lack clarity or narrative beats that feel rushed. Some of the characters’ backstories, while fascinating, are only partially explored, leaving players with questions that may or may not be intentionally unanswered. The game’s brevity also means that some arcs end before they fully develop, which can frustrate players looking for more depth and closure.

Despite these shortcomings, Alicemare stands out for its unique blend of storytelling, aesthetic design, and emotional undertones. It is not a game that relies on traditional horror mechanics, but rather one that unsettles through its quiet mysteries and the way it reframes familiar fairy tale tropes. For players who enjoy atmospheric indie adventures that emphasize mood over mechanics, or those drawn to symbolic storytelling with a darker edge, it offers an experience that lingers beyond its short runtime. It may not provide all the answers, but that ambiguity is part of its charm, ensuring that Alicemare is remembered more for the questions it raises than the puzzles it solves.

Alicemare is a little gem that blends classic fairytales into a bittersweet, atmospheric experience that still holds up — especially when considering it released in 2013(?) and was the first project(?) by △○□× (Miwashiba).

What really stands out in this 3-ish hour experience is how iconic tales like Hansel and Gretel, The Boy Who Cried Wolf, Little Red Riding Hood, and Snow White are reimagined into small, distorted versions that retain their core themes while offering new perspectives. They are cleverly tied together under a main Alice in Wonderland-style narrative, a unique choice that absolutely pays off.

Despite its cute, illustrated characters, the tone is unexpectedly dark. The game leans into a subtle horror atmosphere wrapped in a picture book aesthetic, and the music complements the storytelling perfectly. Now everyone say thank you to Miwashiba for all their indie games with heart and soul.

I didn't get all the games endings, but there was no "Who, What, When, Where, Why, and HOW" moments to keep me wondering. It also didn't help that some of the stories were based on little kid stories like Hansel and Gretel or Little Red Riding Hood which was a technique done by other games before; not very innovative.

I don't want to elaborate anymore why wasn't "this and that" covered in the story or why these characters were the way they were because there might have been an ending that explained that.

During game when you are not trying to find key A to door B, the puzzles were also horrible, either they ranged from being to difficult to understand to being far too easy. For example, once puzzle makes you try and figure out the correct flower, but knowing the answer to this requires real world knowledge some people may not have. Also one of the puzzles was a late game puzzle asking "How many legs does a spider have?" Even a six year old would know the answer to that. To make it worse, the puzzles do not add anything knew to the games lore or story. Most of them are math puzzles, memory puzzles, or the kind you would find in a riddle book. The sepia brown filter is a nice touch to make everything more cohesive, but other than that, the tileset is very very basic. The cutscenes where you find notes are a nice touch, but the minimalism of the environments didn't add to the dark atmosphere. 

Conclusion: This games story and pacing needs serious work. Ao Oni was not a perfect game, some puzzles needed a guide and it's environments were beyond blocky (just like this game), but an imperfect game is better than a boring game.

Space Pirates and Zombies 2, developed and published by MinMax Games Ltd., is an ambitious blend of space combat, real-time strategy, open-world exploration, and dynamic simulation. It builds upon the foundations of its cult-favorite predecessor by expanding its scope significantly, delivering a sandbox experience where the galaxy is alive, reactive, and constantly evolving. Rather than offering a tightly scripted campaign, SPAZ 2 drops players into a procedurally generated, post-apocalyptic universe populated by hundreds of AI-controlled factions and captains, each with their own agendas, alliances, and rivalries. The result is a game that emphasizes emergent gameplay, systemic depth, and strategic improvisation, while retaining the chaotic charm of space battles and the looming threat of zombie corruption.

At the heart of the game is your mothership—an upgradable, modular capital vessel that serves as both your main tool for combat and your mobile base of operations. The ship-building system is a standout feature, allowing players to customize their craft piece by piece. Every part, weapon, and subsystem can be individually equipped, giving a high degree of control over ship performance and playstyle. Whether you favor a nimble hit-and-run design or a tanky, turret-laden dreadnought, the game rewards creative ship-building and tactical foresight. As you scavenge debris, trade with factions, or defeat enemies, you’ll gradually improve your build, making each encounter feel like a stepping stone in your personal journey of survival and dominance.

The combat system is a hybrid of physics-based action and tactical maneuvering. Battles play out in real-time, with Newtonian motion giving ships weight and momentum. Positioning, facing, and loadout synergy all play crucial roles in success. Unlike many space shooters that lean heavily on fast reflexes, SPAZ 2 encourages players to think a few moves ahead, manage resources like energy and shield capacity, and exploit enemy weaknesses. AI behavior adds another layer of unpredictability—pirates might retreat mid-battle, allies can turn on you unexpectedly, and larger factions might swoop in to capitalize on your weakened state. Every skirmish feels like a piece of a larger narrative, shaped as much by diplomacy and opportunism as by firepower.

One of the most intriguing aspects of SPAZ 2 is its dynamic, living galaxy. The game features over 200 AI-controlled captains, each managing their own fleets, bases, resources, and politics. These captains interact with one another in real time, forming alliances, waging war, building infrastructure, and expanding their influence across the map. This creates a constantly shifting geopolitical landscape where the balance of power is always in flux. You’re not the center of the universe—instead, you’re a participant in an ongoing simulation, and your actions can tip the scales in unexpected ways. You might align yourself with a powerful faction for protection, only to betray them later when you’ve gained enough strength, or become a lone wolf exploiting the chaos left by larger conflicts.

Layered onto this sandbox simulation is the looming presence of the zombie threat. The titular zombies are not just another faction; they are a creeping force that gradually corrupts the galaxy. Their infection spreads over time, consuming systems and converting ships into grotesque monstrosities. This adds a sense of urgency and escalation, forcing players and AI factions alike to contend with a common existential threat. It’s not uncommon to see rival captains temporarily put aside their differences to fight off an encroaching zombie horde—only to resume their conflicts the moment the threat is contained. This ever-present danger adds weight to your decisions and creates dynamic, unscripted moments of desperation and heroism.

In terms of presentation, SPAZ 2 takes a more stylized approach compared to the gritty realism of other space sims. The visuals are colorful, with a slightly cartoonish edge that gives the game a distinctive personality. Ship designs are modular and visually reflect your customizations in real time, which makes upgrading feel tangible and satisfying. The UI, while dense, is functional and provides the necessary tools to manage your ship, diplomacy, and resources effectively. The soundtrack adds a sense of space-western flair, and the voice acting—especially in the game's cheeky, irreverent dialogue—lends a humorous tone that offsets the grim backdrop of galactic ruin.

Despite its strengths, SPAZ 2 does have its rough edges. The learning curve can be steep, particularly for new players unfamiliar with its hybrid systems. The early game can feel slow as you scramble for resources and try to understand the galaxy’s politics. Some interface elements can be overwhelming or unintuitive, especially when managing multiple systems or tracking AI interactions. Additionally, while the procedural nature of the world adds replayability, it can also result in uneven pacing or scenarios where progression stalls due to poor RNG or faction imbalance. However, these issues are generally outweighed by the game's depth, replay value, and unique identity.

In summary, Space Pirates and Zombies 2 is a sprawling, inventive space sandbox that rewards experimentation, strategic thinking, and adaptability. It’s a game that dares to let its systems run wild, giving players the freedom to forge their own path in a reactive, living galaxy. Whether you prefer tactical combat, intricate diplomacy, scavenger survival, or all-out domination, SPAZ 2 offers the tools—and the chaos—to make each run memorable. It’s not a game for everyone, especially those seeking linear structure or cinematic storytelling, but for players who enjoy emergent gameplay and deep systemic interaction, it offers a uniquely compelling and richly layered experience in the dark, quirky void of space.

I have been playing POOLIANS for almost six years, and I would like to propose some suggestions as follow: 

Suggestion #1 – Preventing One-Turn Knockouts in Tournaments

Currently, tournament matches are played as a single-game knockout: the winner advances to the next round. I do not necessarily think that playing only one game is a problem by itself. The problem occurs when one player wins the entire game immediately after the break.
For example, after the break, a player may legally pot all of their balls and then the 8-ball in the same turn, without giving the opponent a single opportunity to play. In this situation, the losing player is eliminated from the tournament without ever actually getting a chance to play.
Although this may be completely legitimate according to the current rules, I do not think it provides a particularly fair or satisfying tournament experience. A player's entire tournament can effectively end because their opponent had a perfect run from the break.
My suggestion:
If a player wins the game directly from the break with a single uninterrupted run, the match should automatically change to a "best-of-three format". In other words, the first player to win two games would advance to the next tournament round.
This would preserve the current fast-paced single-game format in normal circumstances, while providing the other player with a genuine opportunity to compete when the first game was decided without them ever getting a turn.
I believe this would make tournaments feel fairer and more competitive, without significantly increasing the duration of most tournament matches.
As a long-time POOLIANS player, I think this would be a relatively simple change that could significantly improve the tournament experience.

Suggestion #2 – Better Tournament Balance and More Team Tournament Variety

I would like to suggest a change to the balance and variety of tournaments throughout the 24-hour period.
At the moment, the daily tournament schedule is not very well balanced between the different game types. Currently, 15-ball and 8-ball tournaments are held four times per day each, while 3-ball and 9-ball tournaments are held only twice per day.
Since POOLIANS already offers team tournaments in the 15-ball format, I believe it would be interesting to expand the team format to 8-ball and 9-ball tournaments as well.
My suggestion would be to replace two of the current 15-ball tournaments and two of the current 8-ball tournaments with team-based tournaments. Additionally, I would suggest that the 3-ball tournaments be played in single-player format rather than team format.
The daily schedule would then become:
-2 × 8-ball single tournaments
-2 × 8-ball team tournaments
-2 × 3-ball single tournaments
-2 × 9-ball single tournaments
-2 × 9-ball team tournaments
-2 × 15-ball team tournaments
This would still result in exactly 12 tournaments per day, with one tournament taking place every two hours, so the overall number and frequency of tournaments would remain unchanged.
More importantly, this would create an equal balance between the two tournament formats:
- 6 × single tournaments
- 6 × team tournaments
The main benefit would be greater variety and a better balance between the different tournament formats. Players who enjoy team-based competition would have more opportunities to participate, while players who prefer individual tournaments would still have regular single-player tournaments available.
I also believe expanding team tournaments beyond 15-ball could add an even stronger social and community aspect to POOLIANS. Playing together with friends, forming teams, and competing against other teams could create additional reasons for players to stay active and return to the game regularly.
This would not require increasing the total number of daily tournaments. It would simply provide a more balanced mix of game types, an equal 6/6 split between single and team tournaments, and a greater variety of team tournament formats.

Suggestion #3 – Giving Coins More Purpose

I would like to suggest giving Coins a more meaningful role in POOLIANS.
Players can currently collect Coins in several ways: by playing regular tournaments, playing Coin Games, winning matches in the Coin Arena, participating in the monthly Bonus Pool tournament, and, more recently, by purchasing Coins.
However, there are currently relatively few ways for players to actually spend their Coins. They can be used in the Coin Arena, where players can lose Coins when they lose a match, and in the monthly Best Pool tournament.
Because of this, I believe that many players may have lost some of their motivation to collect Coins. If there are only limited opportunities to use them, accumulating large amounts of Coins does not provide much additional value or purpose.
My suggestion would be to introduce Coins as an entry fee for tournaments.
For example, players could be required to pay a certain number of Coins to enter a tournament. The entry fee could be different depending on the tournament format, with different entry fees for single-player tournaments and team tournaments.
This could create a much more meaningful in-game economy for Coins:
- Players would have an additional reason to earn and save Coins.
- Coins would have a clear and regular purpose beyond the Coin Arena.
- Tournament participation could become another way to use accumulated Coins.
- Different entry fees could be established for single and team tournaments.
- Players would have more strategic choices about when and where to spend their Coins.
I believe this could also increase the overall engagement with tournaments, because players would have a clear goal for the Coins they earn through regular gameplay.
The important point is that this would not necessarily require introducing more ways to earn Coins. Instead, it would give the existing Coin system a much stronger purpose and a more active role in the overall POOLIANS economy.

Suggestion #4 – Separate Team TM Rankings

POOLIANS already has various ranking lists on the website, but most of them are focused on individual players.

There are also in game purchases, so not everything is completely free. That may put some people off, especially if they just want a simple pool game without extra purchases.

Overall, Real Pool 3D is a pretty good free pool game with a lot of different modes and a decent online community. It is not the newest looking game, but the amount of pool games, multiplayer options and tournaments give it plenty to do.

Inspired by shmups of the past like Gradius, Turrican, and R-Type, Super Hydorah presents a fantastic, authentically old-fashioned side-scrolling shmup mixed with some wonderful modern tweaks - not to mention some of my favourite level design I've ever seen in the genre. 

The story is kept light; we are the pilot of the Delta Lance, flying into battle to defend humanity against the Meroptian empire and their mysterious deity-general, Hydorah. Lots of worldbuilding happens in the design of the stages, however, and this is an area where the game shines very brightly indeed. Hydorah's influence - and their horrifying biomech experimentation - is felt across every world and biome, from bleak deserts to waterworlds where the waves shift in unpredictable and gravity-defying ways to catch out unwary pilots flying through. 

The basic shmup gameplay (you fly, you shoot) is buoyed up by an effective upgrade system and a robust arsenal of weapons unlocked as you progress through the game. Every primary and subweapon has their own upgrade path to track, so provided you can stay alive you're rewarded for sticking with the options you think are best, though sometimes you'll find you want to swap your loadout around in part for whatever's useful for the next stage but also because Hydorah's weapons are fun and playing around with them is a sheer joy.

Many reviewers recommend this to fans of Gradius. I've never played Gradius, and I'm not a great fan of punitive oldskool STGs.

Fortunately, this game is not all that punitive, while still being an homage to those oldskool games. Upon each death, you do lose one speed level, one bomb, some weapon power, and you get sent back to the beginning of the current section. However, most sections are actually pretty short, and recovering within them is often times fairly reasonable. You can often collect quite a few upgrades within just one section. The only times I'd say it's not reasonable is if your weapon configuration is ill-suited for the stage you're in, especially while you're fighting a boss with that configuration, as you usually can not upgrade your ship in those sections.

For that reason, while I'm not qualified to recommend Super Hydorah to Gradius fans, I can recommend it to those who have not played those games before, as I myself found it very enjoyable. It contains many unique stages, each with their own gimmick and good quality assets. Almost every stage grants you a new weapon upon beating it, and there are some branching paths in the overall layout, which gives you quite a bit of agency in choosing which order to clear those stages in, as you can return to any branch you didn't complete yet at any point before clearing the game. You can also choose your weapon configuration at the start of each stage, giving you even more agency in choice, though this often also comes with the chance that you may be choosing a bad weapon configuration.

To make the game even more approachable to new players, the game has a Novice mode which makes your shield tank 3 hits instead of just 1. On my first playthrough which I'd done in Novice mode, I'd still ended up dying multiple times as I had to understand the levels, so I would say that this is a well-balanced Novice mode.

Once you know enough about each stage, it doesn't take much effort to clear the game on Pilot mode (the original difficulty) without Continues, as long as you make sensible weapon decisions and manage your bombs well by actually using them, rather than losing them upon death.

If there's one thing that I didn't like about the game much, it's the fact that speed upgrades exist and that having none makes dodging very annoying.

Tl;dr: As a non-Gradius player, I recommend this game to other non-Gradius players.

Super Hydorah is a lovingly crafted side-scrolling shoot-’em-up that wears its classic arcade inspirations openly but confidently stands on its own strengths. Developed by Locomalito with music by Gryzor87 and released by Abylight Studios, it pays tribute to genre staples like Gradius, R-Type, and Darius, but rather than simply imitating them, it refines and modernizes their ideas. From the moment your tiny starfighter launches into its first mission, the game establishes a tone of intensity and precision. Every level is designed with deliberate enemy placement, sharp pacing, and a sense of escalating danger that rewards memorization, quick reflexes, and strategic weapon choices. It is an experience built for players who appreciate disciplined design and the gratification that comes from mastering a demanding pattern-based shooter.

One of Super Hydorah’s standout qualities is its level variety. Spread across more than twenty stages, the game constantly introduces new ideas, environments, and mechanical twists. You move from claustrophobic caverns filled with biological horrors to open-space battles where swarms of enemies surround you from all directions. Many stages layer environmental hazards into the combat—rushing fluids, mechanical traps, narrow tunnels, or shifting terrain that forces you to navigate with precision while still fighting off enemy waves. The branching stage paths allow you to choose your route across the galaxy, giving the game a degree of nonlinearity rare in its genre. This design encourages replaying levels not only to improve performance but also to uncover hidden routes, optional bosses, and additional upgrades.

Combat feels crisp and responsive, thanks to tight controls and clear visual telegraphing. Your ship’s hitbox is small and fair, allowing skilled players to weave through bullet patterns that, at first glance, look impossible. Each mission provides a choice of primary, secondary, and super weapons, and although not all combinations are equally effective, part of the game’s appeal lies in experimenting to discover which loadouts suit each level’s unique patterns and bosses. These bosses are often the highlight of the game: massive screen-filling creatures, grotesque alien organisms, and mechanical monstrosities with multi-phase attacks. Every encounter feels handcrafted, requiring not only fast reactions but careful study of attack sequences and vulnerabilities.

Visually, Super Hydorah embraces a retro pixel art style, but the detail work and effects push it far beyond mere nostalgia. The color palettes shift dramatically between levels, creating moods that fit each environment—suffocating crimson caverns, icy blue voids, or neon-lit mechanical structures. The pixel animation is fluid, and explosions carry satisfying visual weight without obscuring gameplay clarity. The soundtrack, composed by Gryzor87, is a major highlight. It channels the energy of 80s and 90s arcade music with modern layering and instrumentation, giving each stage a distinct musical identity. The audio cues, from weapon fire to enemy alerts, reinforce the rhythm of combat and help the player anticipate incoming threats.

Super Hydorah’s challenge is both its defining strength and a possible barrier. The game expects commitment. Lives are precious, checkpoints are limited, and death often means replaying entire stages to try again with better understanding. While this difficulty curve will thrill genre veterans, newcomers may find it punishing. Some stages demand extreme precision, especially those with tight corridors or aggressive enemy patterns. The game is not shy about testing your limits. Despite this, the challenge feels fair more often than not—learning is always the key, and improvement is palpable. The option for local co-op also helps soften the experience, letting two players enjoy the chaos together and making the game more accessible.

Ultimately, Super Hydorah is a celebration of classic arcade shooters elevated by modern craftsmanship. It offers a long campaign, meaningful replay value through branching routes, satisfying weapon experimentation, and a steady cadence of memorable boss fights. The game respects its roots without being constrained by them, delivering a polished, intense, and thoroughly rewarding experience for anyone willing to take on its challenge. For fans of the genre, it’s a standout example of how retro design philosophies can thrive in today’s indie landscape. For newcomers, it may be demanding but remains an excellent entry point for those ready to embrace the heart-pounding rhythm of a true old-school shoot-’em-up.

Conclusion
"Super Hydorah" is an excellent addition to the shoot 'em up genre, combining classic elements with modern innovation. With its beautiful graphics, engaging soundtrack, and challenging gameplay, the game not only pays tribute to its predecessors but also sets new standards. Recommendations

Super Hydorah returns to a classic Konami shoot 'em up style of play (at least to me) and brings many elements that were left in the past back.  And often those elements were left behind for good reason.

To give credit where credit is due, Super Hydorah is far more fair and less punishing than most of the 90s era STGs I've played.  At the time of this review, I'm about 1/3 through game.  Something I certainly wasn't able to do with so little practice in old school shmups.  That said, the game is still quite challenging.  Especially as the player unlocks new weapon options.

How can more weapon options be a weakness?  To give you an example, I had just unlocked the spread shot.  Which I wanted to play with right away.  For most of the level is was fine and a boon to have.  However, by the time I reached the stage boss I had it maxed out.  The issue was the maxed out spread shot doesn't fire straight forward.  So I couldn't hit the boss (a stationary flower) unless I point-blanked it.  But that left me completely exposed from everything growing and shooting me from behind.  It wasn't until I failed and gave it a second go.  Because the game slightly reduces the player's power when using an extend.  Now that I could fire straight forward, the fight was so much easier.

[paragraph edited for clarity] While I don't prefer checkpoint based shooters, if the game is going to reduce my firepower or weaken me is some other way, I often would rather have a check point to recover at least some what before continuing.  Super Hydorah doesn't do that with it's check points all the time.  I was playing one stage with the Sandworm boss and nearly had it beat.  When I wasn't paying attention and sandstorm (these push the player's ship to the left) caught me while I was encircled.  I failed and had to retry with weaker weapons and less special weapon uses remaining.  Which made the boss fight more than twice as difficult.  

Speaking of those limited use special weapons, I don't care for them.  Super Hydorah gives the player the chance to grab special pickups maybe 3 times during a stage.  These pick ups cycle through speed up, shields or special weapon ammo.  While the game is playable (unlike many Gradius games) without a speed pick up, it certainly isn't ideal.  And I'm a defensively minded player, especially when I don't know what's coming up in the stage.  So, I like shields.  So the special weapon ammo gets skipped.  Doubly so, since it is at the end of the power up cycle and Super Hydorah isn't the kind of game to let the player loiter in place to wait for it to cycle through.  As such, I've barely tried any of the special weapons.  Because the player starts with zero and only get them via these pickups as far as I've seen.  And the few times I've used the special weapon attack I was rather underwhelmed for as stingy as the game hands them out.  

I do like the graphical design of Super Hydorah.  It's my favorite element of the game.  I will also say that the bosses I've fought so far have been fairly interesting.  But I keep finding myself frustrated with the stinginess of weapons, power ups and anything to aid the player.  Not that they are needed, but that the game doesn't seem to want me to play with the toys it gives me or quickly takes them away unless I don't actually need them.  It's this frustration as well as me just feeling completely out of sync with the game that I just can't get into it. 

This puts me in a tough spot on recommendation.  On a technical level, the game is fine and I even find something enjoyable about it.  However, at almost no point am I having any fun while playing it.  I don't like the sluggish movement.  I don't care for the return of 'git gud' or try again with weaker weapons of 20th century STCs.  The fact the game has all these weapons to play with but doesn't really let you.  There's a fair number of stage enemies I don't care for, such as there a bit too much that attacks from behind you.  And the constant feeling that I have bad routing, but can't see where I'm supposed to be otherwise.  There's also a strange case of anxiety I get every time I use a continue due to the game stating it won't keep my score.  Which is common is STGs, but the way it states it here leaves me with the feeling I'm making a mistake picking to continue.

It leaves me in a place that I can't really find anything wrong, but I also don't find anything fun about playing it either.  I forgive classic shmups because they are classic shmups.  Super Hydorah doesn't really have that beyond returning to that game design that I personally feel shouldn't return without care and good implementation.  So ultimately I wouldn't recommend this game to my friends, and as such, decided not to recommend it on Steam either.

I can't believe I'm saying this after years of mostly just mediocre packs, but I think Party Pack 12 is overall the best one they've ever released. Most other packs have at least a few stinkers in there, but this one is solid all the way around. Let's go through them weakest to strongest.

The weakest game is probably We Forgot A Card. It's not BAD, just sort of forgettable. You come up with funny things to write in cards. It works, but there's really not a whole lot to it.

Debate and Switch is probably the next one, and we're already getting into fun territory. I'm usually not a fan of games that require you to speak out loud and be put on the spot like that, but the pressure/stakes to come up with something good to say felt a lot lower than games like Joke Boat or Mad Verse City. The switch up aspect of it is also very interesting, where players not part of the debate get to change one word in the sentence that the others are debating about. One thing I did notice in our one time playing is that the person arguing *for* something seems like they'll have an easier time winning the matchup than the person that has to argue *against* it.

I'm going to put the trivia game Idol Factions in the middle of the pack (pun intended). But not because it's a mid game, it's actually great! It's a lot more involved and chaotic than just having to answer trivia questions, in a way that I think really pays off, and without jeopardizing the integrity of the trivia itself. A lot of Jackbox trivia games have mechanics that leave winning or losing up to chance, a gripe of mine, but not this one! It can seem a bit overwhelming in your first few moments, but everyone was able to grasp it within a minute or so. And it's a team-based game, which helps players that may otherwise typically get frustrated with trivia games because they feel like they never win them.

Next up is Hyperface, the game where you do things like stretch, squeeze, and draw on faces to match emotions for certain situations. I thought this was so simple of a concept that it was going to fall flat, but I *immediately* realized I was wrong. This game absolutely got the most laughs out of any game in the pack. However, I could very easily see this one getting old quickly, and for that reason, we only played it once. Another small hang up is that this game requires your browser's hardware/graphics acceleration to be turned on. It's typically on by default for most people, but for those of us that like to keep it turned off, it's slightly annoying to have to go into my settings every time I'd want to play this one.

And finally, the star of the show, Megapals. Yet another simple concept that just works. You get a prompt, you type words related to it, you get points when people type the same words as you, the pair that made the most matches win. It's like a combination of Survey Scramble (Jackbox's take on Family Feud) and Role Models. But unlike Role Models, you don't need to be super familiar with the people you are playing with -  helpful if you've got a few friends of friends or whatever that aren't usually part of your group you're playing with. This is one me and my friends are going to be coming back to frequently.

Three thumbs up, one thumb sideways, and one thumbs up with caveats.

We Forgot a Card! - The purest, "Jackbox-iest" of the pack, it's pretty much just Quiplash with a thin greeting card veneer on top.  Competently presented, easy to understand, moves quickly, has a cute art style.  Nothing special but it delivers what it promises.

Megapals - I think this is Jackbox's first successful attempt at a "get to know your group" game that's still playable with strangers or a pickup group.  Sometimes the fuzzy matching/typo compensation is overly generous and grants a lot of false matches, but I think that just adds to the atmosphere of the game and I think it's preferable to being too strict.

Debate and Switch - A more structured version of Talking Points, which is a double-edged sword.  The extra structure is welcomed and helpful, but it lives or dies on whether your group can come up with prompts and twists funny or intriguing enough to argue about.  This one has my favorite art in the pack, especially the debate loss animations.

Idol Factions - I like this a lot but I think it suffers from being stuffed into the Jackbox game template.  Juggling the main game display and the player device controls is a hassle, and it's too fast-paced for anyone expecting the slower tempo and downtime of a typical Jackbox game.  I'd love to see this as a standalone game with its own client, though; the presentation is immaculate, the cooperative gameplay is just the right amount of hectic, and the categories are esoteric but varied enough that nobody in my group was completely at a loss for all the potential categories during a round.

Hyperface - It's all right, but it feels more like a tech demo than a full-fledged game.  The different rounds are all pretty same-y since the first and third are always the same and the random second round doesn't really throw any significant curveballs into the formula, the library of stock photos is small and you can only choose from two at a time, and at least one player's lost a submission or had their game client crash or stop responding in about a third of the matches I've played.  I'd like to see another attempt at this formula in a future pack because I can see the vision but the execution's too anemic.

[i]The Jackbox Party Pack 12[/i] is, in simplest terms, just okay. I was initially skeptic when the games were revealed, and thought to myself that this pack may not hold up. Now despite my negative review of this pack, there's nothing WRONG with the pack per say, it just doesn't really DO anything. And if I'm being asked to spend $30 on a Party Pack going forward, I want to say more about it than "just okay". 

[i]We Forgot a Card[/i] was the game I was the most skeptic about before release, due to Jackbox's heavy emphasis on buying the cards after the game rather than the game itself. It is not as bad as I initially thought, it is a nice simple Quip-like that does what it sets out to do. My only issue with this one is its fast-pacing. I understand that the premise, being last-minute gift shopping, fits faster-pacing quite nicely, but I just don't feel the connection when I play the game. One example is how players are encouraged and rewarded for writing their cards faster so they can fill out custom prompts for other players to use, thus giving them more potential for higher points. Also, why can any player now skip the tutorial? This is an issue with the entire pack, as it only takes one person to click a button for the others to get lost in the dark. 

[i]MegaPals[/i] is the pack's standout game, but not by a wide margin. I can see myself coming back to this pack EXCLUSIVELY for this game... infrequently, that is. While this game is certainly enjoyable, it features a problem that every game in this pack has; it doesn't warrant coming back to playing. It is fun for the first few times, but then the charm wears off rather quickly. Also, words that are completely different but are one letter apart are counted as the same. Which is annoying, because this happens incredibly frequently and can throw players off. 

[i]Debate & Switch[/i] is essentially [i]Let Me Finish[/i] merged with [i]Talking Points[/i]. It's nothing special, but it also does not really hook me enough to keep me coming back for more like mentioned previously. There isn't enough sustenance with the game to warrant playing this game over a different presentation game. Being only one round as well is kind of a bummer, but I really don't have much to say about this game.

[i]Hyperface[/i] is the biggest miss for me in this pack. Morphing the faces on the devices is fun itself, but the game absolutely does not benefit from the head-to-head voting style. I'm not too fond of this game being counted as the drawing game of the pack, as every time I play this one I regret not loading up a different game. And the game feels way too fast-paced, but unlike [i]We Forgot a Card[/i], I cannot see a valid reason for this. This is most obvious with how the host works in this game, he comes in and says about five things all game. Who is he? Why is he hosting [i]Hyperface[/i]? Why is he important? What does he do? These questions are answered by EVERY host in [i]The Jackbox Party Pack 11[/i], and two of the other hosts in this Party Pack. Another thing with the game's fast-pacing, why can't players pick the next prompt category? Why does it have to be random? The whole pack feels fast-paced when it really shouldn't be.

[i]Idol Factions[/i] is another big miss for me in this pack. The concept is amazing, but the execution is far from. The biggest issue is players cannot vote on what categories they want to play with. This is a giant hinderance, as a team can essentially lose the game on the spot if the other team knows more information about all three categories. And a personal issue I have is how the bombs are handled in this game. Why do they cover the player's screens as well as their side on the main screen? I see absolutely no reason for this, as it allows the other team to continuously send MORE bombs, rendering an entire team useless for a wide margin. 

In short, I do not believe that [i]The Jackbox Party Pack 12[/i] is worth the $30 price tag. None of these five games stand out by any means. I hope Party Packs do not continue costing $30+, since after both this and [i]Trivia Murder Party 3[/i], these price tags are seemingly getting more and more impactful with every underbaked release. I also am confused as to why this pack has no sequels, because I can completely understand the decision for [i]The Jackbox Party Pack 11[/i], but I cannot see a valid reason to do so here. I truly do not hope sequels are standalone or small pack exclusives going forward.

If you are looking for a Party Pack for $30, check out [i]The Jackbox Party Pack 8[/i]. Maybe wait until [i]The Jackbox Party Pack 12[/i] goes on sale by a good margin before considering picking it up.

A slightly weaker, but still a very successful continuation of Jackbox's return to form that began with last year's pack. For my full 2700 word long thoughts that couldn't fit in here, [url=https://medium.com/@lukehthomas/13567441350b?source=friends_link&sk=b9d0dc6326e3a381217920b14b049d54] check out my full review here[/url]. Otherwise, here's a briefer summarization of my thoughts on each game.

We Forgot a Card: A smart, simple reskin of the Quiplash formula that leverages all the slight differences the mail-theming makes for a very worthy aside of Jackbox's biggest genre. The mixture of set-ups provided giving some written by the game and some written by your friends was a great idea. It should support 10 players, but whatever.

Megapals: A strange but engrossing experiment of scrambling to type as many words and phrases that fit the prompt, while also figuring out the specific phrases your friends may write too. A great intersection between genres, though a bit too competitive for playing with less tech-savvy family. But it's only major blunder is that the final round frequently just has really bad prompts for some reason.

Debate and Switch: A intrinsically flawed improvisation game that fails to give its players any good guidance or comedic support for their debate arguments. There's nothing here that you can't do without the game and its switch mechanic is useless because it doesn't mitigate the core problem. Too difficult to make good improv and too frequently unfunny, it's the only real failure of the pack.

Hyperface: Turns out making botched, silly faces is actually inherently very funny, and the excellent and simple morphing and drawing tools let this game shine even brighter. It almost sits with the greatest of Jackbox's titles, but there's not enough twists on the core gameplay loop round-by-round to fully make it up there. Still very, very good though.

Idol Factions: A really fun and really chaotic team-based mixture of sorting trivia answers, portaling bombs, and swapping to empty locations. While the trivia itself is a bit simple, the real appeal here is the hectic nature of juggling all its mechanics, and its categories here are frequently very good to great. It's also just nice to have another [i]good[/i] team-based trivia game in the catalog.

Four very good games and one that's very bad. Overall, a pretty solid ratio for this year's release, I can easily say this is one of the best Party Packs so far. It currently slots fifth out of thirteen for me, but I could make an argument for raising it all the way to third. A pack that's very well worth it, so hopefully Party Pack 13 will keep this quality going.

I overall give this a recommend, BUT...we need to talk about a few things.
(This is from the perspective of someone who livestreams these games.)

- I appreciate the attempts at encouraging more in-person gameplay. HOWEVER, especially for live-streamers, I feel that if certain games rely too much on requiring pre-planned voice-chat (owning a Discord, etc.) & the games don't handle well without that pre-planning then they don't stand well on their own. This being the case for Debate and Switch & Idol Factions. I felt that these two games were CLOSE at getting this right & aren't necessarily bad, but they missed the mark in several places. I'll get to that in a bit. The short summary is: a good Jackbox game, or any group game for that matter, should be able to function regardless of if you use voice-chat or not. Some games manage w/both. Some don't. More of the former would be nice, please.

- I personally really don't like that everyone in the lobby has the ability to SKIP TUTORIALS while playing. That's not great for first-timers who might be playing with very impatient people. In my honest opinion, skipping should only be an option for the VIP host of the lobby. (Sorry. Call me a control freak.) If there were an option to toggle that so that it could be either way, then I wouldn't have even brought this up at all.

- The music's good, even with games I didn't particularly love. Hyperface's lobby is a bop.

Anyway, GENERAL THOUGHTS:

We Forgot a Card: It's solid. I've heard folks say they don't like this game because it's too much like Quiplash or other games that involve this type of head-to-head style. I'm sorry. That's a bad thing? For me, as long as the game functions, doesn't insult the integrity of past games & is still charming, I think it's fine(?).

MegaPals: My favorite from this pack. I don't have much to say. It's good. My people loved it. This is what Word Spud should've been. If I only had one complaint? Maybe a bit too lenient with some matches?

Debate and Switch: WHY IS THE TEXT FOR THE PRESENTERS SO SMALL!? I was actually thinking to myself having the option to turn that on for presenters was going to be great & something that could SAVE this game from being only good for voice-chat, but no. It didn't help at all. That needs to be WAY bigger if you're going to give us that option. Other than that...I don't know. I think fundamentally this game already struggles. You're going to have topics that people will absolutely not budge on no matter how well a person debates & some presenters are left in the cold. I understand. "Improv" and all that. Proceed with caution.

Hyperface: I was very worried that this was going to be like Cookie Haus with needing Graphic Acceleration on. I'm extremely happy to say that this wasn't the case & Hyperface worked gangbusters, regardless of if I had put Graphic Acceleration on or not. A funny picture-morphing game & fits Jackbox perfectly.

Idol Factions: I WANT to like this game, but I honestly think that this would've worked better if each team took turns sorting things rather than at the same time, akin to Quixort. As it is, it's WAY too chaotic & while people have suggested things like using two separate voice-chats for this I feel that that shouldn't be a requirement. I personally did not like The Devils and the Details for this reason & it's why I sadly didn't enjoy this.

On the whole:
Some good stuff, some baffling changes/choices, a mixed bag leaning on a pass.

[h1]Jackbox Party Pack 12 is a nice new pack.[/h1]
[i]Jackbox Party Pack 12[/i] is the next new pack for the party game franchise that gave us lots of fun memories. It is the game series that founded our friendly server and gave us a lot of fun memories. I admit after [i]Trivia Murder Party 3[/i], I was very nervous for how this would turn out. Thankfully I can leave a thumbs up for the mini-games. Which games this time around were fun with me and my group of friends, though? Let's find out.

[h1]Games and their rankings[/h1]
[list]
[*] We Forgot A Card is a game where you make special occasion cards on the fly, and you create your own text within them as well as plushies to add later. I personally was not the biggest fan, but all my friends loved it even putting it at their number one for [i]Jackbox Party Pack 12[/i]. One of my friends told me it works best with more people so if you have only four, then I would say skip it. I love the idea of creating your own cards, though, and it adds more replayability to see all the images.
[*] MegaPals is sort of like Wordspud in that you need to create all the words you can imagine, except this time you need to get synergy with your friends over the most wacky of topics. I will admit I was a MegaPals hater at first, but it grew on my VERY quickly once I realised what it was capable of becoming later in the game. It does start slow, but give it time to really settle in. 
[*] Debate and Switch is a game that tries to alter the premise of Talking Points, but does it not well. Remember the old adage that every Jackbox game has a dud? Well, my friends, it is this one. The idea is you create your own debate topics and then others debate your topics, which is cool until you realise that you cannot actually choose what side you want to debate. Later, you get to change up A SINGLE WORD in that debate (e.g. WE HAVE TOO MANY BUTTONS could become WE HAVE TOO FEW BUTTONS). The issue is we need to be able to edit MORE than that. It feels too restricted and open-ended at once. 
[*] Hyperface is a game that reminds me of the startup screen from [i]Super Mario 64[/i] where you just morph the fuck out of Mario's face. This game was the HIT game for all of us. You morph faces based on prompts, and then you let the laughs roll in. You get quite a few options from morphing to even drawing on it, which I think helps a lot. It also has a UI that reminds me of when websites used to have personality.
[*] Idol Factions is team-based trivia where you have to think on the fly in order to get points. You send answers to various topics, hope you are correct, and avoid bombs that enter your midst by sending bombs to your friends instead. I love the idea, but I think it works better if you are PHYSICALLY in the room with your friends so you can easily talk it out better. I do love the designs, though.
[/list]

I find that [i]Jackbox Party Pack 12[/i] does not really live up to the expectations from [i]Jackbox Party Pack 11[/i], but it is certainly leaps and bounds better than [i]Jackbox Party Pack 10[/i]. Seriously, what the fuck even was FixyText? Still, it has some nice games and I think it could be a fun time for you and your friends especially Hyperface and MegaPals.

MegaPals: This one got mixed reviews. Our first playthrough was rough, cause if you're not sure what you're putting down, it's hard to match with anybody.  We agreed that this game would be better for the end of the night when the energy between friends is strongest.

Debate and Switch: Generally positive reviews. Another prompt based game, and has a fun twist on the debate mechanic. It feels almost like a Talking Points successor, but not as well thought out.

Hyperface: We didn't even get to play this. We tried to start the game several times and it would break on the first round every time.

Idol Factions: Nobody really enjoyed this one outside of myself. People complained about having to keep track of two screens, not understanding the categories, the tutorial being confusing, and all around issues with coordination. 

Generally, I'd say this is a skip unless you can get it on some form of decent discount. If I had known what my experience was gonna be like beforehand, I would have waited for at least a 50% off myself.
