This is the first pack where i genuinely enjoy EVERY game they included. I dont think its ever happened in the previous 11 packs (and naughty pack, but that one was not good). Usually (for most people) you like 2 games a lot, 2 are only fine, and 1 just is not your cup of tea. But in this pack, its genuinely one where i enjoyed all of them.

Keep in mind, i have currently played for 2 hours with 2 friends. (so 3 people total) this means that I am looking at this from the minimum amount of people required. 
Here is my list from least to best:

MegaPals - A simple matching game where you type as much as comes up in your mind and hope that your friends type the same. The depth is surface level, but its fun to see the words people come up with that somehow match anyway. The visuals are good and the sounds help with the overall feel of this game. The fact that it is kinda surface level means that its the lowest, but its still a great experience with 3 people. (I typed Jackbox and the announcer went 'JAAAACKBOOOOX' and I thought that was funny)

Idol Factions - A solid trivia game that has you do trivia, manage timers and quickly swap between places to get as many correct trivia as you can. While both trying to screw over the enemy team. Since we played this with 3, I was on my own, which meant that it was a lot of focus. The questions are fun, it has some sneaky options too. It does seem easier if you are on your own, as you have full control of the board. But Idol Factions is a great spin on the (in my opinion) kinda stale trivia genre. Allowing team work, quick thinking and fast reaction times to really shine too!

We forgot a card! - A good game about making cards, write your funny prompt and get people to laugh type of game. I had a lot of fun with this, but I do think it needs some retooling. Either let you pick the picture on the card yourself, or add in a dedicated round where people can type their card prompts, as sometimes people were done too fast to allow for someone to write the prompts. With 3 players, you get Gene back again, who with his dry humor is still a good opponent. I do think this one was a solid game that will be enjoyed by almost anyone getting this pack.

Debate and switch - A fun game about debating talking points, fast, quick and putting you on the spot! A simple game where the fun comes from what you can make of it. Talk, discuss and try to convince the audience that your side is totally the good side and the opposition is stupid and stinky! Most of the fun from this one comes from the player interaction. 3 players works well, but its obviously a game more tooled around having more people to play with. Also tried it with 2 players, it does not work. Dont trust the jackbox announcer when they say it will work. it doesnt! youre not really earning points.

And the top one, Hyperface! - A really robust tool of morphing, stretching, shrinking and enlarging faces! Its really fun to make a good face that fits the prompt. Making you put in the effort and going to make you laugh. Minor complaints (please fix jackbox) drawing onto the painting doesnt morph with the tools, AND doesnt have an eraser. And I wish zooming in allowed the face to only show what the user has on their screen. (so if I only show an eye by zooming in, only show the eye). 

Overall, its a genuinely good pack where you can obviously see the effort they put into it. Great visuals and music (as usual), but in my opinion the best of it all, is that they made completely new games. No repeats, not even any that remotely look alike. And I can respect that. 

This game is a massive recommend from me! And the first time I think most people will love the content they added!

We Forgot A Card: As someone who loves joke-writing games, I have to admit that I do feel Quiplash and Joke Boat do joke writing a bit better. Having said that, I do think WFAC does hold up just fine and I do appreciate the variety of themes because even though this is a parody of greeting cards, adding twists like Valentine's Day (1800s) and Christmas (Dickensian) helps even if people keep picking similar themes. While the joke ran thin for other games like FixyText with me, I do think this will hold up better.

MegaPals: My favorite in the pack because of how you to have match with others and the best people that match will end up being double winners. Which is a nice change in course for the games for sure. Very fun and replayable.

Hyperface: Initially, this was the game I was concerned about because if it was just contorting and morphing images, I would be less inclined to replay it. However, Jackbox adding drawing is a huge positive and helps keep the game very funny and replayable.

Idol Factions: A team-based game where talking out loud is not just encouraged, but necessary. Ideally, it is best in the same room but is viable for Discord streaming. Since stream delay isn't as bad as it would be on Twitch. As someone who doesn't mind chaotic games and is a trivia fan, this is right up my alley. However, if you fold under pressure too easily and can't handle stress well, then this game isn't for you. This is not a dig btw for clarification. As it is perfectly valid to feel that way. As there are other games I love I wouldn't recommend for everyone depending on context.

Debate and Switch: I have to admit this is the only game in the pack that isn't clicking for me. I remember some saying this is just Talking Points 2, but tbh, I honestly prefer Talking Points a lot more. The big issue I have with this game is if the topic in question is too logical and makes too much sense, then it's harder to be contrarian to it for the sake of it. No matter how persistent or funny you are, you're not likely to sway anyone who already will inherently agree with it and that does affect the voting. If it was all ridiculous topics, I would be more open to it. However, as it is, it's not really resonating with me.

Overall, this is a pretty solid pack to me with only one game I'm not big on, but there's still fun to be had here!

[b][h1]Hellbreach: Vegas[/h1][/b]As a huge fan of Cod Zombies I really wanted to like this game, I went into this with an open mind but this is just pretty lacklustre, it's only gonna take you a couple games to experience all this game has to offer, that is unless you enjoy going for high rounds on different maps with the exact same gameplay every game. It's not like there's an obvious story or an overarching Easter egg on the maps, it's simply an average hoard survival game.

I'm also not a fan of the visual style, everything is shiny and reflective and feels like they just upped everything to the max because it's made in Unreal engine, same goes for the lighting, every enemy glows in some way that makes them feel out of place and the enemy animations feel like silly placeholders, they'll jump up and kick with both legs or do flips and shit while still moving and it just looks like their animations are floating towards you. The maps themselves look fine but everything else is so jarring that it's hard to focus on it.

[b][h2]Gameplay[/h2][/b]Looking at the game generally, it has a lot of systems very similar to Cod Zombies, just switching out the theming to Vegas and the zombies to demons, there are weapons, special weapons, perks, powerups etc. If you are familiar with Cod Zombies then you'll know how to play this game. Upgrading weapons opts for a global % damage bonus across all your weapons which I liked, and ammo boxes are abundant on all maps so you can never easily run out but at the same time that makes it so that there's never really much of a challenge.

From the moment I started playing I hated the movement, it feels like default game engine character controls if that makes any sense, you can jump and move around rapidly in mid-air, it feels awkward. And despite the slide having an animation that can be viewed by your co-op partners, in first-person it looks like you can mega dash across rooms.

Different enemy types are a game of "how annoying can we make the next one", one explodes into damaging gas, another shoots at you from a distance, there's these tiny crow enemy that are so small that they're frustrating to even hit, and those goofy backflip and jumping animations I mentioned earlier? they make it impossible to hit enemies with single shot weapons.

If you happen to like this game then at least there's content to back it up, with 10 maps, 5 gamemodes, 3 difficulty modes there's enough available for different types of players, but when the gameplay is as repetitive as it is I wouldn't see myself coming back to play it for fun. Hellbreach: Vegas is a high-energy, arcade-focused first-person shooter that leans heavily into the thrill of survival combat and old-school horde design. Developed by Infinity Ape Studios and published by Iceberg Interactive, the game transports players to a demon-infested version of Las Vegas where neon lights still glow amid chaos and destruction. Rather than building a complex narrative framework, Hellbreach: Vegas places its emphasis squarely on moment-to-moment action, challenging players to survive escalating waves of enemies while mastering weapons, perks, and positioning. It is a game that understands its roots and proudly embraces its arcade sensibilities, offering fast gratification and replay-focused design.

The core gameplay loop is immediately familiar to fans of wave-based shooters. Enemies spawn in increasingly aggressive numbers, and each successful kill rewards players with currency used to unlock better gear and upgrades. Weapons range from basic sidearms to high-powered firearms that dramatically shift the pace of combat, encouraging experimentation and adaptability. The casino-inspired economy is one of the game’s most distinctive features, with slot machine-style systems that allow players to gamble their earnings for randomized rewards. This introduces a risk-versus-reward dynamic that fits the Vegas theme perfectly, creating tense moments where players must decide whether to play it safe or chase a potentially game-changing payoff.

Combat is fast, chaotic, and intentionally unforgiving. Enemy waves grow not only in size but also in complexity, introducing tougher foes that demand focused fire and movement rather than static defense. Positioning and awareness become increasingly important as arenas fill with threats, forcing players to constantly relocate and manage space. While the gunplay does not attempt to rival the weight and realism of military shooters, it succeeds in delivering responsive, arcade-style feedback that prioritizes speed and spectacle. Some weapons feel more impactful than others, and balance can shift noticeably as difficulty increases, but the overall flow remains engaging and energetic.

Variety plays a crucial role in maintaining replay value. Hellbreach: Vegas offers multiple game modes that reinterpret the core survival concept in different ways, ranging from traditional endurance-focused play to modes that restrict movement, rotate weapons, or increase challenge thresholds. These variations help keep sessions from blending together and give players reasons to return even after mastering a particular map. The environments themselves, though limited in number, are visually distinct and designed to support different tactical approaches, with a mix of open spaces and tighter corridors that change how waves must be handled.

Visually, the game leans into a stylized, neon-soaked aesthetic that blends demonic imagery with the excess of Las Vegas iconography. Bright lights cut through darkened environments, making enemy silhouettes readable even during intense encounters. This strong color contrast enhances both atmosphere and gameplay clarity, though occasional visual clutter can emerge when effects, enemies, and environmental details overlap. Character and weapon customization options add a layer of personal expression, even if cosmetic depth remains modest compared to larger live-service shooters.

Multiplayer is where Hellbreach: Vegas truly comes alive. Cooperative play with up to four players transforms the experience from a test of endurance into a shared survival effort, where teamwork, resource sharing, and coordinated movement can make the difference between a successful run and a quick collapse. Solo play remains viable thanks to scaling systems, but the game’s design clearly favors cooperative chaos, where the unpredictability of teammates and shared gambles at upgrade machines create memorable moments. Match availability can depend on player population and region, but when everything aligns, co-op sessions highlight the game’s strengths.

In the long term, Hellbreach: Vegas is best enjoyed in focused sessions rather than marathon play. Its mechanics are built around repetition with variation, and while the loop is satisfying, extended play can expose its limited enemy variety and progression depth. That said, the game succeeds in what it sets out to do: deliver an accessible, adrenaline-driven horde shooter that values fun over complexity. It may not redefine the genre or compete with high-budget contemporaries, but it offers a polished and enthusiastic take on wave survival that feels honest and energetic.

Overall, Hellbreach: Vegas stands as a confident indie shooter that thrives on intensity, replayability, and style. Its casino-themed progression, multiple modes, and cooperative focus make it a compelling option for players who enjoy arcade-inspired FPS experiences. For fans of wave-based survival games who appreciate fast combat, thematic flair, and the thrill of pushing “one more round,” Hellbreach: Vegas delivers a chaotic and entertaining descent into neon-lit demon slaying.

What "Hellbreach: Vegas" offers is a simple round based demon (zombies) shooter akin to the likes of older CoD Zombies, and I think it does a really good job in doing so especially with one developer.

Gameplay is exactly as you think, it feels like zombies. You run around shooting demons, buying weapons and perks, just trying to survive, but there are a couple of twists that do make the game feel unique;

- No perk limits which is both a pro and a con as it can make you feel really powerful right from the get-go, but you'll soon realize that feeling will eventually fade as you get up higher in rounds. 

- Barricades are here, but they aren't used to slow zombies down from spawn, but instead when you buy a gate you can place them here as a way to slow them down temporarily and I didn't know this until today, but you can actually shoot the portals the demons come from to temporarily disable those, both of these make an interesting, but also a welcome change.

- You do get 2 separate points systems, the first being cash in which you can buy the normal perks, weapons, whatever, but then you get skull tokens which are mostly used for buying gates ingame, but can also be used to customize your loadout, buy gun skins, outfits, stuff like that and are also used to level yourself up. I get having to skull tokens to buy cosmetics and everything, but can be a little weird getting used to them buying up rooms ingame.

- The one problem with 'Hellbreach: Vegas' I find is that it can be quite repetitive, the game does offer 9 different maps to play through which is really nice, but without any main quests to do and with how easy it can be right away, you will have seen everything a map has to offer in less than 10 rounds which is a shame as the game is fun to play. However it does also give you 4 other modes to play through that can keep it kind of fresh; Royale, which is exactly as it sounds. Gun Pro, you're playing gun game, but with demons. Nightmare, normal game, but in the dark. Trapped, you are stuck in the starting room of a map unable to go anywhere else, which might present a challenge to some people. These modes are here that can alleviate some of the repetitiveness, but again once you've played them for a while, it can get stale.

- Some people have reported some bugs going on with the game, but I haven't experienced anything other than sometimes the demons getting stuck in portal spawns, but that's it. Game runs pretty flawless for me.

Overall I would recommend Hellbreach especially since I got it for a buck on Fanatical and the game is really fun to sit and play a game or 2 here and there. And for a one developer game, this is really good for what it is.

Hellbreach: Vegas is basically an indie alternate to CoD Zombies made by like 1 dude, and it is a bit flawed, but very fun.

Gameplay-wise it's akin to the classic CoD Zombies experiences where you run around, buy weapons with points, open doors, and build barricades while surviving hordes of zombies (or in this case, demons) until you either die or hit the wave limit (which can be set in the pre-game settings between 10, 15, and Endless). However, there are new mechanics that change up the formula a bit such as the barricades function differently in Hellbreach than they do in CoD. in Hellbreach, enemies spawn from portals which you can shoot to temporarily disable, and the wooden barricades can instead be placed in the places where you open doors as a form of area denial once the enemies have already spawned in. It sounds weird, but I actually like this changed and it actually saved a few of my runs when utilized intelligently. You don't open doors with the points you earn from combat, but instead open doors using these skull tokens, which also double as the game's permanent currency you use to buy cosmetics and permanent upgrades. There's new enemy variety too with exploding zombies, screaming ice banshees, ninja demons, which isn't exactly super special but it does add some variety to the formula. Now this is just the core mode, there are other variants of this horde mode you can play like one that randomly swaps your weapon every time you get a kill or one with a shrinking zone, but I haven't tried these yet as of writing this.

As i mentioned briefly before, there is an XP and progression system in this game that allows you to not only get cosmetics, but new starting weapons and starting perks. Yeah, perma-perks are a thing and you can't lose em like in BO2. The Skull Tokens you use to buy these unlocks (and open doors while playing) basically drop randomly from enemies and you can also spend the normal in-game points on a slot machine that can drop 0-6 Skull Tokens per spin. There is also a Canyon Challenge map that doesn't have any doors so you can use it to farm skull tokens pretty easily (tho since people complain about repetitiveness and all non-cosmetic unlocks are also level-locked i don't recommend this). Also, if you're worried about spending all your hard-earned reserve tokens you've saved between matches on doors in future matches, do not worry. You can only buy doors using Skull Chips you've acquired in the current match you are in, what you save back can only be spent on unlocks. It's kinda dope.

Now the flaws in this game largely come in the form of this game kinda feeling repetitive, and that's largely because there's no unique per-map enemy variants and about half the map roster is similar in both layout and aesthetics. Like, I know the game takes place in Vegas, but if there's a way to at least get some more map variety I want it. 

The rest of the negatives mostly boils down to bugs like screen tearing, getting stuck in barricades if I build them at the wrong time, and melee weapons sometimes not registering hits. These issues are annoying, but haven't been enough to hamper my experience. Some people are also reporting issues with multiplayer, but I haven't had the opportunity to play multiplayer yet so i cannot confirm.

As someone who's been itching for some CoD Zombies experiences that aren't CoD, this scratched the itch very nicely, along with Sker Ritual which pulls off the CoD Zombies formula in a more easter-egg-oriented direction in its own flawed but fun way, and you can get both in a bundle for a decent price during a sale.

Unfortunately there's a lot left to be desired.

[hr][/hr]
[h2] There's a lot to like here. [/h2]

The gameplay loop is solid but could use some refinement; as the game is right now, I can't recommend it.

It feels very arcadey; movement is light, enemies die quick, and gun recoil is barely more than visual, but the challenge is near nonexistent, even at it’s hardest. It's good (and can even be pretty fun) if you just want to load in, shut your brain off; not so much if you want a challenge.
[hr][/hr]

[h3]Enemies are too weak, both in damage and health.[/h3]
With common demons this is understandable, but often times I found that I could take out the stronger enemies before they were able to pose a threat. When they did manage hit me, the damage they did was negligible to the point that I could walk past them and eat it, never feeling as if I was in any actual danger.

The crows can be [b]outright ignored[/b] as long as you keep walking and, unless there’s more than 6, can’t outdamage your health regen. Speaking of ...

[h3]It is far too forgiving.[/h3]
Taking damage should [i]feel[/i] threatening, but that feeling ends up lost when I already have half that health back by the time the demons swing animation is finished.

The lack of delay on health regen, the fast speed of it, and the relatively weak damage from the demons lead to me treating them as a joke. Most times I got close to death / [i]did[/i] die were because I was messing around and didn’t care whether I did.

[h2]The UX problems and design.[/h2]
[b]Aside from the of the Skull Token Icon and the Ammo[/b] the rest of the HUD feels lifeless. It does it’s job, but is bland, and can be difficult to see elements, [b]especially against the skybox.[/b]

Perk icons are hard to distinguish; very similar and seeming to suffer from a scaling issue; most of the names borderline unreadable. Either give the perks color / forgo the shared icon shape and lean more into the perk icons themselves. This would make them stand out and have a little more life to them.

The pause menu is a cluttered mess that could use some separation / consolidation of options.

The Main Menu has some serious frame rate issues and feels very generic, like that every F2P Live Service game out there.

The red screen should have it's intensity tied to the percentage of health remaining, as opposed to when hit. Often it would fade while I still had low health or activate while I had most of my health still and it didn't feel right.

[h2]Game Feel[/h2]

Player movement itself should be made a little tighter and given more weight, but I wouldn't change much. The lighter movement works in the games favor, though things like jumping feel off. The animation is too linear and lacks the natural flow you would expect. It's rarely useful with very few things you can jump on / over.

Demons [i]feel[/i] slower than they should. The attack and movement animations are good, but their movement speed itself is slow, leading to a mismatch. I’m able to out walk demons that are [i]clearly[/i] running and it doesn’t feel right.

[hr][/hr]
[h3]The Stamina System[/h3] has me conflicted.
Melee weapons shouldn’t consume stamina. There's a perk that negates that, but it’s still a punishment for using them. I have to put myself in danger to fight, and if I [b]fight too much[/b] I run out of stamina and escaping is made harder.

The melee weapons themselves aren’t very powerful, especially when compared to the rest of the weapon roster.

In truth, I would rework the entire system around

[h2] The Crouch Slide [/h2]
Hitting crouch while in sprint you forward for a small stamina cost. We've seen it before, but in this game it sends you [b]far[/b]. It feels great, and I found that you can change the direction left or right mid slide, transferring the momentum. It seems jank and unintentional, [b]but [i]feels[/i] incredible.[/b] The only limitation that bothered me was having to slide forward for before changing directions.

I would rework stamina around this and treat it as a movement ability.[olist]
[1] I would remove the stamina cost of sprint.
[2] Increase the demon speed to offset this.
[3] Make sliding [i]multi-directional[/i], keeping the sprint requirement.
[4] Increase the stamina cost of slide.
[5] [i]Replace[/i] crouch with a dodge. This would be a speed boost like the slide but only a third of the distance for a lesser stamina cost, but could be done in any direction without needing to sprint first.
[/olist]

[hr][/hr]
[h2]Game Modes[/h2]

[h3]Gun Pro[/h3]
This mode has you get 10 kills with each weapon until you’ve gone through them all. I was having a lot of fun with it until I got to the melee weapons and things were dragged down to a crawl. They’re not nearly as quick or powerful as the other weapons you get, leading to them taking a lot longer to get through.

I also think it would be interesting if different modifiers came into play. Something like a Gun Pro Infinite where you keep cycling through the weapons rerolling with a damage boost and the end of each set..

[h2]Royale[/h2]
[h3]Interesting concept; poor execution.[/h3]
The safe zone is too large to meaningfully effect game play and doesn’t shrink enough to change that. It does too much damage, being more dangerous than the demons, and I died in goofy runs through it than [i]anything else[/i]. It’s [i]good[/i] for the storm to be threatening, but it was overpowered to the point that going through it for almost any reason was almost always not worth the risk.

If the storm was weaker, but the zone shrunk more and moved to different points of interest throughout the map every once in a while it would be more interesting; however I would overhaul the mode entirely.
[hr][/hr]
I would rename it to stormfall and change it so you would have multiple small safe zones on the map instead of one large one. The zones can move / change between rounds, and to get around the map you have to brave the storm.

I think of it like the [b]Dark Aether[/b] in [b]Metroid Prime 2: Echoes[/b] and imagine the zones focused around the different ammo caches / a few other spots on the map instead of how it currently is.
[hr][/hr]

This mode also highlighted the issue of demons getting lost on the map and taking [b]forever[/b] to get to me. If demons are too far from me, ideally they would just respawn closer.

[h2]Trapped[/h2]

I like how it reworks the map have everything accessible within the first room but there was some maps that I felt had more interesting areas to turn into a one room challenge.

[h2]Misc Elements[/h2]
The sprint animation should be slightly faster. It’s smooth but slow, making it feel unnatural.

Skull Tokens and Cash being separate felt unnecessary and seemed to dampened the other. Combining the two into better system would be ideal.

Damage boosts should be weapon specific, making it so that you have to consider which weapons to upgrade.

I love the dancing demons mode, and the modifiers give strong cheat code vibes that I would love to see more of (super speed and moon gravity perhaps?).

If you’re not paying attention it’s easy to mistake perk machines for other perks or – what happened to me – the grenade spinner for the weapon spinner, as they don’t have much differentiating them.

When power-ups are picked up in quick succession they overlap each other, making it impossible to see which ones you got using the HUD.

Perks don’t very impactful. They’re useful but weak overall, and some perk effects seem like they should be combined into a singular perk.

Enemy animations are great and I appreciate the attacks being properly telegraphed, they a bit long however; still, better that than too unreadably fast. You did an excellent job in this regard.

Drops just vanish without any sort of indication. An animation that shows when they’re about to disappear would go a long way into making that feel better.

It does have some glaring issues that will need to be solved like weapon balance (looking at you storm bolter), a half-baked follower system and some minor bugs, but that is to be expected of a new release and I'm sure most of these issues will be addressed in the near future. 

It is almost identical to vampire survivors in terms of gameplay and progression with some unique mechanics thrown in here and there, but I imagine the difference between the games will only grow as time goes on. It is also noticeably harder than it's predecessor but I think that only works in its favour, both in differentiating it from the original and improving the flow of progression.

Another thing a lot of people have complained about is the end-of-round bosses, but in the original the red death would come and kill you between the 15-30 minute mark regardless and this boss system makes it a bit more organic and strategic than just get the 2 items that make you basically invincible to kill it. I don't know how I feel about having to get certain weapon evolutions for each though, having to delay your progress to ensure you get the right drops and then having enough time to upgrade and evolve it can be tedious and I would certainly prefer the weapon and passive to be stage items on their respective levels, but this is very low on my list of things to change.

In terms of the weapons, most are fine, several are almost exact copies from vampire survivors but that's a given considering there are only so many ways you can shoot a gun and those baseline weapons need to be covered to establish different playstyles. The weapon balancing is a bit all over the place, some feel next to useless or too situational (looking at you again storm bolter) and some are clearly a bit too strong even unevolved but I feel for the most part it's okay, and the ones that stand out REALLY stand out.

With characters you will find a lot of the same, since again there's only so many ways to increment stats and the baseline has to be covered, inevitably crossing over with vampire survivors a lot. So far there has only been 1 character that stood out to me as very unique, besides name drops for characters I know about in lore.

The last thing I wanted to talk about is the disparity of content between AoS and 40K, I know of course more will be added, but it's still a bit sad to see how little AoS got even if it's not my preferred universe, I mean 7 non-secret characters? Really?

Overall, it's a pretty good game I'd say, worth the price with the knowledge that content will only be added from here on out and for the people who are saying it should have just been a dlc for the first game, I disagree. I don't think I could take it seriously if a red amogus was out there beating up the 'nids. Solid 7/10 for me right now but I imagine that will go up as more content comes out.

I feel very mixed on the game. On one hand, I think the game has some great ideas I haven't seen before. The primary weapon, the Gun, is really fun to use and I like the way the game uses it for exploration. The game also has Zelda style items that you can find, each item their own unique utility. The Mod systems a cool idea, letting you apply Modifiers to your gun in a grid-based slot system. I also like the sound design, very crunchy stuff. And I do like that the game is challenging and there were some fun fights in the game. The items you got were always surprising, there were some unqiue mechanics in the game so discovery wasn't too bad.

Regardless of that, I still found some of the passive upgrades just... kinda boring? You find them very quickly and you don't really get much else, I suppose the items make up for that, but passive upgrades just stopped quickly, so the pacing feels weird there. Exploration started to feel very dull after a while. There isn't much going on in the world except for some enemy combats and the occassional puzzles and platforming. The rooms don't feel so interesting and the NPCs kinda go by very fast and I forget them quickly. 

The game also suffers from QOL issues. The platforming in some areas feel very difficult. some of the hitboxes are crazy big and throws me off a lot, especially the spikes in certain platforming areas. You do get a wall jump quite early, but you need to be hugging the wall to actually propel yourself. If you face the other way while trying to jump, you'll immediately stop wall jumping, so wall jumping to the other side feels kinda awkward [spoiler] The Flamethrower was such a fun ability to use, but actually maneuvering it was very difficult. You build momentum way too slowly for an item with a limited usage. [/spoiler] Marking on the map feels kind of awkward too. Early in the game you will find some Flitterflies, but you can't grab them until later, so you have to mark those on the map, but the map marks are limited to less than 20 marks, which feels too little. I understand why we could a map mark limit: it encourages me to go back to the older areas before things get overwhelming, but not being able to grab the Flitterflies early feels strange, so I had lots of map markers for just Flitterflies.

Some of the enemies are also downright cruel. I will say I'm kinda at fault, since I was fighting a lot of bosses without using the dodge roll, I honestly forget it was a thing. I don't think the game really comminucated the dodge roll well enough because I was trying to dodge using the items and the gun. The normal enemies don't really force you to use the dodge roll, so by the time I fight the boss I kinda forget it's there. Enemies can also sometimes teleport out of bounds which makes it impossible to hit. Some bosses attack so quickly you don't have enough time to really react. [spoiler] The UFO boss especially was a really annoying. The star ads weren't a big issue, but the sudden teleporting around was really unpredicatable. Sometimes the boss might finish an animation and immediately animate to some other direction super fast so I get hit very sudden. [/spoiler]

I also noticed some smaller UX issues. Menu buttons can sometimes lose focus on a controller, so while trying to navigate the pause menu, you might get stuck and have to use your mouse instead. Swapping items in the inventory requires the bumpers instead of triggers, which is inconsistent since you use the triggers to actually use the items, and as far as I know, there is no way to remap controller inputs (only keyboard imputs are there). I also noticed some sprite flickering above certain enemy sprites, but it's nothing game breaking. 

I didn't put all the issues I faced but the ones that bothered me the most. I didn't 100% the game, but I beat the boss and got most of the Mods and Items. I didn't really want to explore anymore. I feel really on the fence on the game. On one hand, it has super cool idea, but on the other hand, it feels very unpolished and incomplete.

I believe the price is the biggest factor here. For $12 I really expected a bit more polish-wise. My issue isn't that the game is short, I like short games with a clear vision and Dewdrop does *have* that, but the rooms feel very dull, the items except like two of them are meh, and the game is really missing a lot of basic polish. I really hope the devs come back for some more updates, or maybe even a sequel, because there are some good ideas here with the mechanics implemented in the game, and also an underground dynasty setting, but for $12, it feels too basic.

There's a lot here that feels pretty competently done for an action-platforming game, but as a metroidvania, this game falls short in so many ways. I have to address the camera first and foremost because it simply tracks the player and doesn't assist you with any kind of look-ahead. That means when you're falling down or platforming upwards, you can only see a short distance above or below you which makes for some very frustrating blind jumps at points. Most of the platforming in this game feels good except for this problem. 
The second big issue is the map design. It's very large, maybe too big for its own good. Traversing it takes time, and while normally a larger map in a metroidvania translates to more shortcuts and secrets, here that is not the case. There are simply too many rooms connecting other rooms that offer very little in the way of secrets or enemies. They may as well be corridors. There is a fast travel system available later which helps, however even then you'll find yourself walking quite a bit between the available travel points. There are some secrets to be found in the larger rooms, but I didn't find them to be very satisfying. You will mostly find tickets that can be redeemed for currency (which can be farmed relatively easily), and every few tickets you redeem will earn you a larger upgrade to health or ammo. There is the occasional health upgrade you can find, but I suspect veterans of the genre will hardly notice if they have extra health or not. The difficulty of the game is not very demanding, and even as someone who is only okay at video games, I don't think I would have noticed if I only got a quarter of the possible upgrades.

The enemy and boss design is okay, nothing bad, but nothing to write home about either. They are mostly frustrating because you'll encounter many enemies that take 5 or 6 extra hits to die than you might expect. This leaves you feeling like your weapon is under-powered, but you won't find any direct weapon upgrades outside of the mod system. The system is a tetris-like grid that lets you change your weapon slightly, but nothing dramatic. You can slightly increase your range, bullet speed, add a small critical hit chance, burning effect, etc. They're helpful upgrades, and I do like the puzzle element they introduce to weapon customization. However, because you have to pick and choose, you won't be able to have some of the very basic upgrades that make shooting feel much better alongside some of the other upgrades, like ammo count or the single damage upgrade (the range upgrade never left my grid, for instance). 

As for the other abilities and upgrades you will find, some of them are pretty neat ideas, but not all of them will see much use beyond functioning as keys. You unlock a crawling ability eventually, but it really only allows you to access new areas. It isn't used for any puzzle elements a la Samus' morphball, and it also doesn't shrink your hitbox as far as I can tell. Similarly, there's a pocket watch that lets you stop time briefly, which could make for some interesting platforming sections, but it's really just used as a key to allow you access to new areas. As far as I know, the time stop doesn't affect any enemies either, so you won't use it to dodge attacks or get free hits. I did find myself using the dash item and flamethrower item consistently. The dash is a very generous directional dodge that gives you i-frames, which is an additional dodge on top of your basic dodge-roll. The flamethrower allows you to hover, and you can use it outright ignore a few boss attacks, including during the final boss. There's also the dynamite, which is mostly used for opening up new areas, but it can (technically) be used as a weapon. It's awkward to throw and make sure it lands near an enemy, then you have to shoot it to detonate it or hope the enemy doesn't walk away before the fuse finishes, and even then it doesn't do that much damage (it can hurt you though). I used it a few times and then mostly forgot about it. 

All in all, someone has clearly put a lot of time and passion into crafting a world with a certain aesthetic, but when it comes to getting lost and playing in that world, the emptiness of it becomes too apparent to ignore. I'll be very interested to see what this developer creates next, but unfortunately I can't recommend this game to fans of metroidvanias. For players looking for an action platformer with some very light metroidvania elements, this isn't a bad choice at a discount, maybe.

At the moment this game does only two things well and the rest of it is so irritatingly bad and misrepresentative of the metroidvania title.

Before I begin I would also like to note this complaint at the top here to hopefully help people in their purchasing decision. The dev last said on August 6th, 2026 that more updates were on the way. I don't know if something happened in their personal life, but I have yet to see them respond to ANY community engagement since then, which was over 2 months ago at the time of this review. If the dev doesn't have plans to return to updating the game this game VERY MUCH should have been listed as an early access title. It feels very incomplete - it STILL doesn't have controller rebinding 3 months after launch - and it feels like a very misleading quick cash grab.

Anyway the two good:
The pixel art is great.

The movement is very fluid and the physics based interactions are very well done.

The bad:
Wall cling/jump still absolutely sucks. I lose track of the wall and fall into spikes still very often. I often have little control mid air off a wall jump because of the stick movement required to directional wall jump.

Looking down and up is not instant. You will sit on a platform and hold the directional stick for a brief moment before you can see what's below you to move on. So unnecessary. 

The world is so incredibly empty. There are numerous NPCs mucking around that serve absolutely no purpose. There are a handful of interesting looking POIs that yet again serve absolutely zero purpose. The bulk of the world is useless other than for running from point A to B.

There are quite a lot of breakable and false walls with no indication that they are such. If you want to uncover all the secrets currently in game you need to smash your character or throw TNT at every surface in the game. This issue combined with the issues with the map make this such a chore.

I'm not sure why this genre still struggles with the map despite the community yelling to the high heavens at every game for years of what the minimum expectations for a map should have. One of the core features in a metroidvania (if you consider this game one) is backtracking and exploration right? Well when you enter a new room the entire map section for it is completely populated, leaving no display of where you've actually been and not been. There also aren't enough map markers to mark all the items you eventually need to backtrack to. The game also lacks any sort of tracking mechanics to help you know how many tickets or flitterflies you've turned in or how many are even left to find. This makes finding secrets an extreme exercise in tedium. 

The Webulix fight in Pipe World is so aggravating for reasons outside of 'git gud'. There are several no telegraph attacks in this fight where the boss moves into them in a specific position that you will often be in from dodging the previous attacks.

This game is very much an early access title that was misleadingly dropped as 1.0. The dev hasn't provided any updates in months.

Really cute and fun Metroidvania with cozy graphics, smooth control and interesting mechanics. Reminds me a lot of Haiku the Robot and Lone Fungus - two brilliant indie classics in the genre.

I enjoyed my time with it but there are a few things that absolutely need addressing ASAP in order for it to truly reach its potential. Right now, I'd say it was a mostly positive experience for me but not a phenomenal one.

1) Dying means you lose drops (the main currency in the game). And there's absolutely nothing you can do about it. Of all the possible death mechanics that are available, this is 100% my most despised one. Both Hollow Knight games catch some slack for their corpse runs mechanics but at least they allow you to pick your currency back; Haiku has these banks that can store unlimited coins; Dewdrop Dynasty goes the "fuck you, you better not die" route which is really, REALLY not fitting for a Metroidvania IMHO. It reminds me (negatively) of Kingdom Shell that has the same issue. This is especially frustrating against bosses where you are forced to just watch your drops slowly bleed away as you keep dying over and over again. Awful feeling.

2) The custom map pins are not nearly enough for the size of the game. And I don't mean the "types" of custom map pins, I mean the quantity of different pins that you can place on the map. I ran through the maximum allowed number of pins in just the first 2-3 zones. So I had to keep removing old pins and remembering where they were. Until at a certain point I didn't even have any pins left that could be removed. Beyond frustrating having to backtrack and wander around for 30-60 mins trying to figure out where your point of interest was because you had to remove the pin about two hours ago for something more important.

3) The firefly quest feels genuinely pointless. First of all, there is no indicator how far along you are into the quest - you can be one firefly away from completion, you can be 30 away. The shop NPC doesn't tell you shit, just collects your current fireflies and that's it. And for such a massive quest (I assume it's massive since I found and returned over 20 and I still didn't finish it), the reward being some stupid hat.... really?!? C'mon now, is the game trying to troll you? Not only are you not receiving continuous rewards at certain points while returning these fireflies (like you normally would in such long collecting quests) but the grand reward at the end being some useless cosmetic... No. Just no. You need to do better here, Goodgis.

4) The teleport system is just barely usable. All the zones having only a single teleport that connects to a giant hub makes it so that it takes a massive amount of time to go from point A to point B when you're backtracking. There should really be a late game ability that allows you to freely teleport between the flower save points, the current system is just needlessly tedious.

5) Finally, and this isn't necessarily a must but rather a suggestion that I feel very, VERY strongly about - introduce something late game that allows you to see the collectables you've missed. Similar to how Ori 2 does it: long delivery quest with an awesome reward that lets you view everything you've missed on the map without having to consult with an outside guide (which doesn't exist as of writing this review btw). I can see in the ingame menus that I have some missed collectables and the map percentage clearly indicates I have more stuff to find... But I have no clue where!!

So anyway, these minor (and not so minor) flaws aside, I think there's a really solid game underneath. The world and level design was great, all areas felt unique and interesting, enemies and NPCs were entertaining and boss fights were awesome. The shoot-ground-to-jump gimmick actually works great and it only gets better once you unlock more and more abilities that play into it.

I believe the price is more than fair for the quality that Dewdrop Dynasty presents and I would give it a narrow recommendation. But I would really like to see some of the aforementioned flaws being addressed in future updates.

I have spent a long time waiting for this title. I gave it a single full playthrough and beat the final boss, but can't be bothered to 100% it. The abilities are pretty uninspired (at worst you gain the abilities to crawl and push crates, both of which are unapologetic keys-for-locks that lack meaningful interaction with the world or in combat).

The map design is among the absolute worst I have seen in a Metroidvania - there are countless instances of the developer clearly hoping for you to take one path, when you spend upwards of 10 to 20 minutes navigating down the other path and come across a dead end having accomplished nothing with that time. I hate to use the word "backtracking" as it has lost all meaning (some would call climbing Red Tower after the Ice Beam "backtracking" in Super Metroid) but this game so very easily earns the use of the word that it will be my new example to use for it. It does not help that the game is incredibly sparse in how it deals in items - there is not much to actually obtain, and yet the scale of the map would suggest that there is more. So many rooms are just downright worthless - they don't serve any artistic purpose, don't contain any items, and are just some arrangement of platforms and enemies that you dash through because you have to go through 5 more rooms like it to get where you want to be. Then it turns out that you don't have the item to proceed in this area and the place that you [i]really[/i] wanted to be was 10 rooms back. Which rooms? Figure it out. The stimulating portion of this game lasted for maybe an hour out of my 4.6 hour playthrough. I quit my session twice in situations where I realized I went the "wrong way" and saved the backtracking for when I had more patience to spare. If you would like for your integrity to be tested on why you like Metroidvanias, you may learn something new about yourself playing this game.

The flitter flies are an interesting way to add re-exploring, but feel tedious and they are mostly in hard-to-reach spots. Graphics - Pixel art is really good, it feel like retro platformer and I love it. there is 1 small thing, I use 1080p monitor and it was showing a white border in game all time. It was very thin like 1 pixel line covering the screen so it didnt distracted me but I hope Developer look into that.

Performance - Game runs very smoothly, there were time menuscreen  got stuck or my player was walking forward and not responding to any button for a sec and sometime after respawn it freeze for 2 sec. nothing was game breaking it usually happend in very rare scenerio, So I'm OK with it.

Music and SFX - Sound effects are good but i feel a lot of enemy use distorted sfx when they die and im not fan of it. Music blend in pretty well, some place it very good and some place its very forgetable but not bad.

The problem is you cannot map your ability in Gamepad(it has only 2 option LT and RT), some ability like crouchwalk is locked to RB, you can't change it and you dont need that ability in like 99.9% of the game, so its big waste. In my gamepad Y, R3 and L3 were completely empty, i could have used that in other small mechanics.

03. Need upgrades that makes character strong and accessible from start so hard boss fight does not stop the Pace.(its fine If i have to grind it)

The game has some good ability for some areas like flamethrower and I like it. Need more of that. Dewdrop Dynasty fundamentally misunderstands what makes a metroidvania (or any game) fun - it's not just running around a huge empty map. It's very linear, takes an eternity to traverse, and there are barely any secrets, most of which are just money you can farm from enemies anyway. Enemies and bosses are little more complex than "run at the player in a straight line" or "shoot a projectile every 3 seconds". The game's runtime is massively padded by everything you fight being a damage sponge. Even small critters can take a good minute of continuous shooting to kill, and bosses can be like 10 minutes of dodging the same five attacks.

Some small details are good. Basic movement feels nice, animations are cute, cutscenes have tons of clever and fun effects. Unfortunately, these aren't enough to compensate for the major problems with enemy and level design.

I am a massive fan of platformers and metroidvanias like Celeste, Silksong, Terraria, and Ultrakill. I've been watching Goodgis's devlogs for years and have been very excited for the game to come out.
However, I wasn't expecting much from this game. I was wrong. This game surprised me with how much charm was put into it. The platforming is great, the enemies are all fun to fight, and the artwork is beautiful. I love how unique and well worked the mod system and the items system worked with the game. Both of these were very unique ideas. Being able to choose what abilities you want for any area is a very fun concept (eg: choosing the dash item for a section). However this game does have its flaws and imperfections that I would like to address.

First of all, the bosses just aren't great. Each boss has little to no wind up time for any attacks, making it feel like a pure game of chance. The hitboxes for some attacks are pretty janky, and of course almost every boss has the ability to teleport. Having the boss randomly teleport on top of you is extremely common and unfair as there's nothing you can do. Some of the bosses like Webulix and Bonsai feel extremely stretched out which leads to the fights feeling too long repetitive and boring.

The other major problem I felt was the camera. There is so much going down and the camera never shows you what's beneath your feet leading to guessing and random enemies showing up. Even with the new looking down feature recently added you cant do this mid air. The biggest problem with this was one of the long rooms in the snow head that keeps going down where you don't know what to do next.

Despite these I was pleasantly surprised at how unique and fun each area was, making the whole world feel fun and exciting.

I am excited to see what comes next for this game, and for what Goodgis has in store. I will definitely keep playing.

[b]TL;DR:[/b]

[b]I recommend this game, with a bit of an asterisk.[/b] The game has a lot of issues. Some of them are minor bugs and unpolished edges, while others are more fundamental. Exploration isn't consistently satisfying, obtainable abilities leave much to be desired, and the short runtime (6 hours in my case) can leave you wanting more, even with the decreased price from launch. However, there are strong points. The game looks gorgeous, the game feel is solid, the characters and dialogue are charming, and combat is (mostly) fun, and the music is a vibe. For all of my complaints, I enjoyed my time with the game. I'm not fully sure if it's worth its asking price or not, but it'd feel wrong to say I flat out don't recommend the game.

[b]Traversal & Exploration:[/b]

Moving around as Poe feels great. Jumping and running feel good, and the midair gunhop Poe has access to makes even early-game traversal a lot of fun. This only gets better as you acquire more traversal abilities. My only complaint is that the dodge roll you start with feels quite slow, so it can get overshadowed even as a precision dodging tool once you get other abilities (namely the [spoiler]dash[/spoiler]). I would love if it traveled the same distance but covered that distance faster.

While micro-level platforming feels satisfying, macro-level exploration feels lacking. Many of the nooks and crannies in each room lead to dead ends, and the ones that aren't only offer chests with low-reward tickets. I would've liked to see more weapon mods—which you can equip in a grid to modify your weapon—appear in chests rather than in shops. Another big issue is that rooms fill entirely on the map when you enter them. This not only gives away the structure and exits of a room the moment you get in, but it also makes it hard to tell what parts of a room you haven't been to yet.

Some of the worlds, particularly the ones containing dewdrops, follow a very similar formula: go down the main path, run into a gate, go down the secondary path to acquire a key (or keys), unlock the gate, continue down the main path, get the dewdrop, and backtrack to the nearest fast travel point. There were a couple of worthwhile side paths that stood out to me (e.g., [spoiler]Longford's house[/spoiler]), but most felt underbaked.

Lastly, this game is [i]short[/i]. It took me 6 hours to beat the game, and that's with fumbling around at the beginning because I couldn't find the first ability. There [i]is[/i] more to do for 100% completion, but I honestly didn't feel compelled to go for it (it's just grinding currency for shop items and finding collectible, often unhidden "fitterflies" strewn around the map).

But I will note that despite these complaints, I did mostly enjoy my time wandering through Underland. Even if the world layout and composition was a bit boring, traversing that world as Poe was enjoyable enough that I still had fun.

[b]Visuals & Audio:[/b]

Aesthetics are easily one of Dewdrop Dynasty's biggest strengths. The pixel art is super charming, the animations are great, and much of the UI looks super clean. I especially appreciate the different hats Poe can wear and the effort that must've gone into animating them for all of Poe's different movements. The mixels—different pixel sizes—can be a bit much at times (e.g., explosions having massive pixels), but the game looks amazing in spite of that.

The different regions of Underland look particularly gorgeous. While the concepts of most biomes are pretty basic (your typical [spoiler]jungle[/spoiler] area, [spoiler]lava[/spoiler] area, [spoiler]snow[/spoiler] area, etc.) the bright, saturated colors give each one a lot of character and distinguish them a lot.

On audio, the music slaps and the sound effects are juicy. Not much more to say here.

[b]Abilities:[/b]

Being a metroidvania, Dewdrop Dynasty of course has obtainable abilities. Some of them are passive upgrades that you can use all the time. Others are items that must be equipped to be used. You can only equip two such items at a time, so you'll often have to go into your inventory to swap stuff out if you want to use certain abilities.

The abilities are one of the game's major weakpoints imo. Some of them, particularly the traversal ones, are super satisfying to use and have plenty of utility. Others, however, only serve as keys used in a small few areas—sometimes even just one region (looking at you [spoiler]time-stopping clock[/spoiler])—throughout the world. There's also a lot of overlap between most of the traversal abilities, so each new one you get sometimes means using the ones you got before a lot less. Many abilities felt like they could've been more useful with some tweaks (e.g., [spoiler]dynamite being easier to aim with less fuse time, flamethrower dealing a more powerful burn effect[/spoiler]), but they're left underbaked.

I also didn't care for the equipping system. Since many of the equipables are just keys, I'd just keep the same two in my inventory and briefly swap one out whenever I came across a "YOU MUST HAVE THIS ABILITY TO PASS" gate.

[b]Story & Dialogue:[/b]

The story is pretty simple, but that's not a bad thing. I do think there was space to flesh out the lore a bit more, and I found the writing at the end uncompelling ([spoiler]loved the concept behind the twist for the final boss, but found the dialogue iffy and would've liked a bit more beyond "mwahaha we want our power back and we're the truuuuuue eeeeeeeevillllllllll 'NOW DIE'"[/spoiler]), but for the most part it serves its purpose well in giving some context to the world and making us care about Poe.

The characters you meet throughout the game are lovely, both in design and in dialogue. It's all very silly and lighthearted, and I love it for that. I also love Poe's little animations that he uses to talk (his "no" head shakes are always so well timed).

[b]Combat & Bosses:[/b]

Combat is a bit mixed, but overall my opinions lean positive. Poe's gun feels great to use. You can shoot it in four directions, which means that while you can't shoot diagonally, you [i]can[/i] move horizontally while shooting up or down. It's a very satisfying system that works especially well with the gun's platforming uses.

My main complaint with combat is that enemies have a lot of health, and you never really that much more damage. I spent the whole game waiting for some new gun to replace the B33 revolver, but it never came. In lieu of better guns, the game has mods you can use to upgrade your gun. These mods are fun and really let you make your gun your own, but in my playthrough enemies still felt like tanks through to the final boss. Some enemies have even more health on top of the high amount of health every enemy gets and ALSO are a pain to fight, so I just tended to ignore those. The [spoiler]legally distinct kameks[/spoiler] did not need that much health.

Bosses are generally pretty good! The concepts are all nice, and they're mostly fun to learn. There was only one I thought genuinely negatively of: [spoiler]the legally distinct thwomp I forgot the name of, which (A) makes you wait ages to attack it and (B) can be cheesed by just sitting at the edge of the room[/spoiler]. There are also a few attacks on individual bosses that I feel need tweaks, particularly on the final boss.

[b]Conclusion:[/b]

As mentioned in the TL;DR, the game's a mixed bag. Enjoyed playing it enough for me to not [i]not[/i] recommend the game, but too many complaints for me to recommend it confidently. If you have reservations, consider grabbing this later (once more bugs have been fixed, QoL features added, etc.) and/or at a discount.

Pros:

- Some solid worldbuilding, with the Underland (setting) being a beautiful place to traverse as each biome sets itself apart from the rest through unique environmental themes, hazards and enemies, all of which come to life in glorious 8-bit visuals boasting vibrant color palettes.

- I appreciated each area’s structural layout, with every room featuring a design that favors uneven edges which give your surroundings the organic quality expected from a natural setting, thus increasing immersion.

- Beauty aside, said biomes also ignite the embers of nostalgia for those of us who grew up during the retro-gaming era, since the vast majority of them draw clear inspiration from the Super Mario games, both for their themes as well as the enemies that populate them. I mean, I dare someone to look at the game's flower enemies, or the armadillos that look and move like turtles, or some flying mages, or to travel through the ice and lava biomes and not get instant flashbacks from when they were holding an SNES controller in their hands while staring excitedly at the red-clothed plumber in their CRT TV screen. Even the fast travel system is inspired by Nintendo’s juggernaut series, though more on that later.

- Awesome music, with each biome featuring its own fantastic melody, all of which have the uncanny effect of making you wistful as if you’ve heard them before, even though they’re completely original.

- Exploration leaves a lot to be desired. On the upside, the game has several collectibles for you to gather, including upgrades for your health pool and ammo cylinder, various items, gear and weapon mods that influence combat and exploration, as well as a bunch of Flitterbugs you must find and return to an NPC for a reward. For the downside, see cons.

- The map overview is kind of a mixed bag. Starting with the good, the overview is logistically accurate in terms of design and matches each area perfectly. It also displays merchants, save and fast travel points, as well as your own location on it. In addition, it offers a limited number of manual markers to place wherever you wish, which you should start doing immediately because I never found a way for collectibles to be marked automatically. For the downsides, see cons.

- Platforming is fun, for the most part. You have a solid traversal arsenal at your disposal, including a dash, wall jump and gun hop, the latter of which allows you to stay airborne for a few seconds while shooting down and is incredibly fun to utilize. Most of your traversal abilities are tied to items you find or purchase, of which you can have a total of two equipped at any given moment, which may sound restrictive but I can’t say it caused me any trouble. Now see cons for the bad stuff.

- Combat is a highlight of the game due to the simple yet entertaining nature of just shooting things in the face. Ranged is the name of the game here, with Poe mainly relying on his gun in order to dispose of his enemies, which is incredibly satisfying to use. You eventually gain a skill that enables you to unleash a more powerful shot by holding down the attack button and charging your weapon, which is nice and also allows for very high jumps if aimed downward. Your battle arsenal is further complemented by equipable gear items such as a dynamite stick as well as the aforementioned flamethrower, though, to be honest, I never really bothered with them since the gun is just way more efficient. In addition, there are weapon mods you can buy and equip in Tetris fashion, that offer benefits to your pistol such as occasional double damage and faster shots, among others, which are incredibly useful. Now go to the cons for some bad stuff.

- Cool bosses. With one somewhat dull exception, the rest of the big bads were very fun to duke it out with, featuring unique attack patterns that made each fight an engaging little puzzle for you to solve and overcome, effectively providing a healthy challenge without ever feeling unfair.

- The game offers three different difficulty options for you to choose from, so there’s something here for everyone.

Cons:

- On the downsides of exploration, most of the aforementioned collectibles are not found but purchased from the various merchants populating the world, which is truly a missed opportunity since there are several places you’ll come across when exploring the kingdom of Underland that will feel like they could be holding a secret, only for you to realize that a suspicious wall is just a wall or a pretty section is simply ornamental.

- When it comes to gear items, which correspond to headgear that changes the way you look, there’s no clear explanation whether that change is simply cosmetic, or if it has some added benefits.

- I’m fairly certain that when it comes to the health upgrades, which refer to half pieces of four leaf clovers that increase your health when gathered in groups of two, the game failed to raise my health at one point even though I had collected the required number.

- On the downsides of the map overview, there are some rooms where the player icon and map layout do not align, which can lead to confusion when navigating those parts. Furthermore, there’s no fog of war and every room you enter is immediately marked as fully visible, which is never helpful when trying to remember which parts you need to revisit after getting a new traversal ability.

- While I loved the theme of the fast travel system, which has you descending into large flowers like Mario sliding down a pipe and then leads you to a hub area from which you can choose where to fast travel next, each area only had one such flower, which often led to some tedious backtracking in order to return to that flower and fast travel to the hub area so that I could use the flower of a different biome. In my humble opinion, adding one more flower to each area would make things infinitely better without simplifying the process too much, so here’s to hoping.

TL:DR:

In conclusion, I had a lot of fun playing Dewdrop Dynasty despite its flaws. I loved its whimsical world and the interesting characters populating it, I adored its musical score, I had a lot of fun with most of the platforming challenges, I thoroughly enjoyed combat and had a blast with the bosses. On the downside, the wall-jump and flamethrower issues did sour parts of the platforming experience for me, exploration left a lot to be desired by making a good chuck of collectibles merchant products, the map overview could use some quality-of-life improvements, some of the items need better explanations on their utility, the flying enemies need to stop being able to go into walls and it would be nice to have a way to retrieve currency you lost upon death.

Despite a rocky start, Dewdrop Dynasty is a clear labor of love that improves with every patch released. It wasn’t as good as I expected it to be but, for a solo developer project, it is quite impressive and will definitely function as a stepping stone for Goodgis to create something exceptional in the future.

Final Grade: 6.8/10

Ahh Dewdrop Dynasty. I had never heard of this while it was a kickstarter project. I was simply checking out the new steam calendar feature and decided to buy this on a whim, and so I got to enjoy an okay game. 

Starting out the strongest aspect is the control and feeling of playing. Your jump and movement feels responsive and your gun feels good to fire. This enjoyable game feel proves to be true for all the different powers you gain through the game, my personal favorites being the ground pound and dash. The core gameplay feels satisfying to play. However I some of the button choices I find questionable, mainly I don't like how they choose to map the right bumper to crouch. This game handles powers like Zelda where you need to go into a menu and assign them to buttons. An unavoidable downside of this method is having to make trips to the menu often to equip the powers you want / need. Currently the game only feature two slots for powers, having left bumper be a quick map is a nice feature, but having the right bumper permanently locked to just crouching when a third slot would greatly help ease the inventory problems is a sting to me.

Level design is kinda mixed to me. My main problem is how far apart everything is. The areas barely loop back around and between each other instead. Even with the fast travel hub you unlock it it can often take a while to get to where you want to go. It was an often scenario where I wanted to go to a different area only to realize that the shortest route was over eight large screens away, and that's just to get to the general area. I really think this game needs more pathways to the other areas and shortcuts, there were many times I completed an area to get the important item I needed only to have to back track down the same chunks of level I just did to get out. This problem is enhanced by the health of a lot of baddies. Until  you find the damage upgrade a lot of enemies take a lot of punishment, about 4 or five charged shots, so if you are like me and just kill any baddie you see for the money your often going to be traveling at a crawl like pace. Another annoyance is that fireflies, one of the main collectables, can only be caught with a net you need to get from a late game area, the Dino zone. Even if you rush to this place  you will need to explore three areas to get to it. I passed a lot of fireflies at the first half, but because I didn't know they were a collectable I forgot about where they were. This all combined to kill my desire to go hunting for goodies and lead me to focus on beating the game.

The price drop is nice, but I would still recommend Silksong or other staples to play first. This is a 7/10 passion project you choose to buy because you appreciate and desire to support the love and effort that went into making a small charming indie game even when the might not be perfect. Whether that describes you is your judgment to make

Dewdrop Dynasty random thoughts after completing the game (12 hours playtime total)

PROS:
- Loved the artstyle. Very cute aesthetic, especially the NPC's
- absolutely loved the soundtrack. Probably my favourite single aspect of the game.
- The platforming mechanics with the gun felt fluid and natural
- Boss fights were challenging and varied which I liked
- Each individual zone had a unique feel and playstyle
- Short and sweet. Didn't drag on forever and every time I picked it up I was keen to pick up where I left off
- I loved how you could collect cosmetic hats and wear them in game

CONS:
- The backtracking became tedious at times. Maybe I'm just not into Metroidvanias
- Some of the items/abilities that are mandatory to collect felt useless other than being used as a "progression" checkpoint
- Some enemies felt very unfair due to the lack of telegraphing with their attacks
- Some enemies felt like a bullet sponge. Way too much health.
- Lack of being able to move the camera down when traversing meant that you would jump downwards as a leap of faith, often landing on spikes or an enemy you couldn't see previously.
- If you die in a boss fight and go to retry the boss, you have to sit through their entire cutscene again without the ability to skip ( I think the dev is fixing this soon)
- Narrative felt a bit meh to me. I didn't really connect with any of the characters or care for their story. Some of the characters dialogue was humorous or witty or whimsical but otherwise felt a little flat.
- You unlock the fairy bug net item that allows you to catch the fairy collectables way too late in the game.

Overall 7/10, I enjoyed my time and for the price I think it's worth it. Will I play it again any time soon? Probably not but I think i got a fun experience regardless.

The aim mechanics feel odd until you have some play time with them. We played a 5 hour session and had a great time. 
Some tips:

 Play a round or two of zombies before you play to get ammo and med kits. The game tells you you will lose ammo and med kits but we were able to essentially farm this to get equipment. I think this is a good feature for now at least until the game is further in development.

Adjust the creature hearing in the menu down or up. Every microphone is different if you're whispering and your mic is picking up more than 2-3 bars you need to adjust it down otherwise the creatures will know your location all the time. 4-6 bars seems to be where the creature can hear you very well.

Play on easy if it's your first time doing a mission this prevents the creature from hearing your voice and allows you to freely communicate while you are learning.
