Moo Who? is a multiplayer party game that takes a simple social-stealth concept and gives it an unusually funny identity through voice imitation. Instead of relying entirely on disguises, special abilities, or complicated deduction systems, the game asks animal players to hide among NPC herds and convince hunters that they are ordinary creatures. The defining twist is that hiding visually is not enough. Players must actually use their microphones to imitate the animal they have been assigned, turning something as ridiculous as mooing like a cow or clucking like a chicken into a legitimate survival mechanic. It is developed and published by SAT Productions, with the same studio handling both sides of production.

Matches support 2 to 8 players and are designed around relatively short bursts of chaos. Animal players attempt to move and behave naturally among NPCs while hunters carefully observe the herd for anything suspicious. The concept works because human-controlled characters can betray themselves in several ways. Strange movement, unusual positioning, hesitation, or an especially terrible animal impression can attract attention. Successful play therefore requires more than simply finding a crowded group and standing inside it. You need to understand how the NPCs behave and imitate them convincingly enough to avoid becoming the obvious target.

The microphone mechanic is where the game develops its strongest personality. Depending on the assigned species, players may have to moo, cluck, oink, or baa. These sounds are not merely optional role-playing opportunities. The game actively pressures players into making them. Remaining quiet for too long during designated sound-pressure moments causes buzzing flies to gather around the offending animal, creating a visual giveaway for attentive hunters. It is a clever solution to a potential problem with the concept because players cannot simply refuse to participate in the voice mechanic and remain hidden indefinitely.

Playing as a hunter creates a different kind of tension. Hunters are armed, but their ammunition is valuable enough that firing randomly is a poor strategy. Shooting an innocent NPC wastes an opportunity, whereas correctly identifying a disguised player moves the hunting side closer to victory. This turns observation into the hunter's most important weapon. Listening for suspicious noises, watching movement patterns, and waiting for someone to behave unnaturally can be more valuable than immediately pulling the trigger. The uncertainty surrounding each shot gives the otherwise comedic experience a surprisingly effective layer of suspense.

The relationship between these two roles generates most of the entertainment. Animal players know they are being watched and consequently become increasingly self-conscious about every movement and sound. Hunters know that an obvious-looking target might still be an innocent NPC. A nervous player can accidentally reveal themselves by overcorrecting their behavior, while a confident player might survive simply because the hunter doubts what appears to be an obvious clue. The game benefits greatly from this mixture of bluffing, observation, hesitation, and improvisation.

Its strongest moments are likely to emerge from the people playing rather than from scripted events. Hearing friends desperately attempt convincing farm-animal noises while knowing that another player is actively searching for them creates the kind of spontaneous comedy that suits party games extremely well. Wrong accusations, embarrassing vocal performances, missed opportunities, and disastrous shotgun decisions can all become memorable moments. Online PvP and online cooperative functionality complement this social focus, while Steam Achievements provide some additional goals beyond simply winning matches.

Visually, the colorful and stylized presentation suits the intentionally silly premise. The game is not attempting to create a realistic hunting simulation. Instead, its environments and animals serve as readable components of a social deception playground. The combination of first-person and third-person perspectives associated with the different sides also helps distinguish the experience of hunting from hiding. The basic rules are easy to understand, making the game suitable for groups that want something they can start playing without studying an elaborate collection of mechanics beforehand.

There are nevertheless some limitations inherent to the design. A working microphone is essential to experiencing the game as intended, and players who dislike voice interaction will miss the feature around which practically everything else is constructed. The quality of a session will also depend heavily on the participating group. Enthusiastic friends willing to embrace the absurdity can transform a straightforward match into something hilarious, whereas quieter players may make the same mechanics feel less energetic. The relatively focused gameplay loop also means that long-term variety depends considerably on unpredictable human behavior rather than an enormous amount of mechanical complexity.

The developers also disclose the use of generative AI assistance for localization, certain in-game GUI icons, and sound effects. Players who consider the use of such technology when evaluating games should therefore be aware of its presence. Beyond that, the game includes multiple interface languages, English subtitles, Steam Achievements, multiplayer functionality, and Family Sharing support.

Steam Deck compatibility deserves particular caution. The Steam store currently does not provide Moo Who? with an official Valve Steam Deck Verified or Playable classification. The listed operating-system support is Windows, and the experience fundamentally requires online multiplayer and microphone input. While the Steam Deck has microphone and communication capabilities and Windows games can sometimes function through Proton, there is not enough official information to describe this title as fully Steam Deck compatible. Anyone specifically purchasing it for Deck play should therefore consider its compatibility unverified and expect that manual configuration or compatibility issues may be possible.

Moo Who? ultimately succeeds most as a compact social experience rather than a mechanically dense competitive game. Its smartest decision is making the player's real voice part of the stealth system instead of treating voice chat as an optional extra. Limited hunter ammunition prevents the opposing side from solving every problem by shooting randomly, while forced animal noises prevent hiding players from winning through silence. Those two systems complement each other remarkably well and create a constant cycle of suspicion and comedy.

For groups that enjoy social deduction, party games, voice chat, stealth, and deliberately ridiculous situations, there is a genuinely entertaining idea here. It may not provide the depth expected from a large competitive multiplayer title, and its reliance on microphones and willing friends narrows its audience, but it knows exactly what kind of experience it wants to deliver. When everyone participates enthusiastically, pretending to be an innocent cow while desperately producing the perfect moo can become far more entertaining than the premise has any right to be.

I enjoy the game overall, there are some elements that I find ever so slightly annoying that might take away enjoyment for a few moments, but its nothing that would make me not want to recommend the game to people who might enjoy this genre. 
There aren't any bugs or major glitches I have come across so far, I love the little quests you can do and how you're able to own more than just houses. I love the full range of creative liberty you have with the spaces and how many items you can buy to use in the store. I wish you were able to change the colors of the items or even scale some items like candles and pictures. The game seems to be optimized pretty well, I haven't encountered the game slowing down because of how many items I put into the spaces, but I also have decent hardware. 
I'm going to mention what I personally find slightly annoying or would love to see changed because I know this is early access and still being worked on. I'm getting a degree in game development so my "issues", because they're not really issues, are more nit picky than anything. 
For starters, a lot of the assets used for decorating the spaces are very repetitive, with no real variation other than color changes or a slight change in shape. A good chunk of the assets have weird boundary boxes to them, and it wont let you place other objects near it even if the actual mesh itself wouldn't be obstructed. I think they used a square boundary box on all the items, which for the most part is fine. But some of the items would greatly benefit from changing the boundary box to fit the actual shape, so you can place objects around it better. Again though, this is just me being nitpicky. I love to be super detailed about my decorating, if I wasn't a very detailed oriented person this wouldn't even be noticeable to me. Maybe if there was an option to turn off clipping, so you could place objects technically inside of each other. 
The scaling of the assets also feels off sometimes, some items feel way too small and others feel way too large, specifically the armchairs. I have yet to use a single armchair because of how large they feel compared to the couches and other items. Maybe if we could scale the furniture (I can't remember if I already said this)
The shapes of the first handful of spaces you get access too feel really weird, its slightly difficult to decorate them and there isn't too much noticeable variation for them to be noticeably unique. There's a lot of strange hard to decorate corners. 
The snapping is kind of rough and I don't use it much. Navigating also feels kind of slow, meaning when you're trying to move around the map the camera just feels a little too sluggish. 
The textures on the walls feels off, I think its just the way the UVS were unwrapped, and the textile density, in some rooms if you don't have a plain colored wallpaper the patterns will be upside down for some wall panels or enlarged for others. Again, it is barely noticeable, especially when you're decorating the walls. 
And lastly, I wish there was an option to speed up the time even more, only because I'm inpatient and want more money faster so I can buy more furniture to decorate more spaces. 

Overall I am really enjoying the game and its a great game to turn my brain off too and listen to some podcasts while I decorate. I haven't gotten too far into the game because I spend so long decorating the spaces because of how fun it is, but I need more money to do it.

Dearbnb offers a relaxing blend of property management, interior decoration, and business expansion, creating an experience that emphasizes creativity and steady financial progression. Developed by Gameshaft Studio and published by GrabTheGames and Gamersky Games, this simulation places players in the role of an aspiring property entrepreneur who begins with limited resources and gradually builds a successful real estate business. Rather than overwhelming players with complicated construction mechanics or demanding economic systems, the game focuses on furnishing properties, attracting occupants, maintaining facilities, and generating income. Its approachable design makes it particularly appealing to players who enjoy cozy management experiences with clear objectives and plenty of opportunities for customization.

The gameplay begins with relatively modest properties, encouraging players to transform ordinary living spaces into attractive accommodations. Interior decoration is one of its strongest features, allowing players to experiment with furniture arrangements, flooring, wall colors, and decorative objects. Every room becomes an opportunity to express creativity while improving the overall quality and appeal of a property. Unlike traditional building simulators that require extensive structural planning, Dearbnb concentrates on individual interiors, making the decorating process more manageable and immediately rewarding. The connection between aesthetics and profitability provides an additional incentive to create comfortable environments rather than simply filling rooms with random furnishings.

Property management adds another dimension to the experience by introducing responsibilities beyond decoration. Players must consider rental prices, maintenance expenses, cleanliness, repairs, and customer satisfaction while working toward greater profitability. These systems establish a straightforward but engaging economic cycle in which earnings can be reinvested into improvements and additional properties. The satisfaction comes from watching a modest investment gradually develop into a valuable asset. However, the simplicity that makes the game accessible could also limit its appeal for players seeking intricate financial simulations. Its management mechanics appear designed to complement the decorating experience rather than dominate it.

Progression plays an important role in maintaining motivation. As players accumulate money, experience, and achievements, additional districts and investment opportunities become available. Moving from economically disadvantaged neighborhoods into more prestigious locations creates a tangible sense of accomplishment. The inclusion of skills, unlockable rewards, and progression milestones encourages continued development beyond simply accumulating wealth. This structure gives players meaningful goals while preserving the freedom to expand at their preferred pace. Nevertheless, the long-term appeal depends on whether later properties and districts introduce enough variety to prevent the gameplay from becoming repetitive.

One of Dearbnb's more ambitious features is the opportunity to expand beyond residential rentals. Players can pursue commercial ventures involving cafes, shops, supermarkets, cinemas, theme parks, and other entertainment facilities. This variety gives the business simulation a broader identity and introduces the possibility of developing several sources of income. The prospect of managing different types of establishments adds excitement to the progression system, especially for players who enjoy watching small operations evolve into substantial enterprises. However, the effectiveness of this feature depends on how differently these businesses function. Distinct management requirements would provide greater strategic depth, while similar operational routines could eventually make expansion feel more cosmetic than mechanical.

Visually, the game embraces a colorful and welcoming presentation that suits its relaxed atmosphere. Its room-focused environments emphasize decorative details and the everyday activities of occupants, helping properties feel like inhabited spaces rather than static displays. Watching characters interact with furniture and perform ordinary activities contributes personality to the experience. I thought Super Meat Boy Forever was just another endless runner that took a character I already knew and put him in a different kind of game.

I was wrong.

The graphics are simple. The gameplay looks simple. Meat Boy runs.

That's it.

And somehow, it is absolutely brutal.

At first, you think you can handle it. Then you hit a wall. Then another. Then another. Suddenly, you're repeating the same section for the tenth time, wondering why you haven't given up yet.

But you don't.

You keep going.

There's something strangely satisfying about finally getting through a section that has been destroying you for the last twenty minutes. The levels move fast, the obstacles are unforgiving, and every mistake feels like your own fault.

Which somehow makes winning even better.

What I love most is that Super Meat Boy Forever doesn't make things easy just because it looks simple.

It expects you to learn.

It expects you to fail.

And then it expects you to try again.

I've played games with massive worlds, incredible stories, and hundreds of hours of content.

I don't remember most of them.

I'll remember the levels that made me want to throw my controller.

I'll remember finally beating them.

And I'll remember saying, "Okay, one more try," approximately fifty times.

Some games are fun while you're playing them.

Super Meat Boy Forever makes you suffer while somehow convincing you that the suffering is worth it.

100% recommended.

Or phasing through the clinic boss when it's your turn so many times that you assume he's invincible and you're supposed to wait longer only to waste 50 more deaths and realize that the hitboxes are just screwy. 

Then there's the matter of the pacifiers. When I see them, I collect them just like bandages, and it's usually pretty fun to go for them, but the problem is that there's only 30 in the game and you have to get 90 for all the unlocks. I had a great time 100%ing Cotton Alley's light and dark world from the first game, but imagine having to do all of that three times. The game tries to keep it interesting by raising the difficulty of the chunk generation with each NG+, and generating a new seed for every NG+ run, but this is the wrong approach to replay value IMO. The fact that you can accumulate pacifiers through NG+ runs endlessly is a blessing and a curse. It's a curse because it means you're replaying levels over and over just for completion's sake, but it's also a blessing because I can't seem to find all the pacifiers. I'm fine with replaying the level if I happened to see the pacifier and accidentally skipped it, but hunting for them after the fact is really annoying and replaying levels over and over trying to find the missing pacifier is not fun at all. The game will not so much as tell you whether a level has a pacifier, and I know from reading forums that each world has 6, so imagine my frustration when I've scrubbed 6 light world and 2 dark world levels and only find 2 pacifiers, and am told that the chance of the four unexplored dw levels having the missing pacifiers is virtually 0%. I'm finding it so annoying that I have considered doing 4 or 5 NG+ runs just to amass pacifiers by sheer volume.

The menu UI is the most undercooked of them all.

- On a level-end replay there is a button to restart the level, but no restart level button in the pause menu. This means if you need to restart, like when you're going for the no-death half of an S rank (thankfully you can get the time and death requirements in separate runs), you have to back out to the menu and then go back into the level. Which is just, why do I have to do that?

- On the level select you have to select a level to switch characters, but there is no dedicated character switcher UI.

- Some warp zones require you to beat them with a specific character to unlock something, yet you can't switch characters when selecting the warp zone, which means you have to select a regular level just to switch and then go back to the warp zone. To make matters worse, sometimes warp zones will just switch your character after you finish them. On Break Lil Slugger, I had this happen to me where after I beat it with bandage girl, I went for a run with meat boy, and then it switched me to Bandage Ripper for no reason.

- There's a lot of menuing in circles that could have been avoided by adding one extra button or menu in general. Very inefficient.

- The level end screen tells you how many deaths you had but does not show it in the HUD during the actual run nor in the level select despite all three telling you the time.

- It does not save past replays to give you the opportunity to view them again. This is a personal nitpick, but it just seems weird to have a replay feature and not offer a way to save and watch them later.

- There is no copy file button.

- The pause menu is often sluggish to come up and sometimes just refuses, seemingly when you're airborn and right after respawning, which only makes it take longer to back allllll the way out to the level select to restart a level, which I wouldn't have to do in the first place if there was a restart level button in the pause menu.

- When you die having not reached a checkpoint, the death still counts towards your death counter, which is stupid and causes even more menuing in circles to restart, more wasted time, more tedium.

The list goes on and on.

Again, I don't think SMBF is a bad game, and I'll even recommend it to that point, but it's baffling to me that they thought it was ready to release, and even more baffling that these basic QoL issues haven't been patched by now. If you're gonna make a game and have people hate it, at least stand by it. Even the infamous No Man's Sky eventually got an overhaul update.

If your timing is off by even a little, you do what you expect to do: fly to the left at mach 5. You then land on the other side of the belt and have to wait forever for it to drag you to the right. This is the newest entry on the axis football franchise, and it is the best one yet!  

If you're looking for a game that gives you the deepest franchise mode on the market, team customization options that put Madden to shame, improved graphics, and serviceable gameplay, then axis football 27 is for you!

Pros:

-a new graphics engine
  -lighting was overhauled and looks good.
  -over the course of the game, lighting changes.  If a game starts in the late afternoon & ends in the evening, you'll see the game start out in bright sunny weather before transitioning to night time by the end if the game
  -weather effects were overhauled, which was desperately needed
    -snow effects look way better
    -rain not only looks way better, but the amount of rain that comes down differs from game to game (and can be adjusted in play now)
  -player models are the same as last year, but they look better because of the new lighting and graphics engine
  -while not as good as other games, the graphics in Axis Football 2026 are easily the best in the series

-new presentation
  -the UI of the menu was changed for the first time since 2020, and it looks great
  -player chatter was added to the game, mostly with pre-snap QB cadence and players screaming as they get tackled.
    -combined with the overhauled crowd noise & color commentary from axis football 26, this creates the most immersive axis football yet

-new gameplay features
  -defensive AI was overhauled so that AI pass defense is not as helpless as it was in Axis Football 26
  -gameplay sliders were introduced this year so that if the default AI skill and difficulty is not to your liking, you can adjust 
  -a new tackling system was implemented into the game, one based on physics and momentum.  New tackling animations were added as well.
  -new animations were added for ball carriers and receivers for diving over and rolling over defenders in the goal-line area.
  -when playing inside a dome stadium, all weather effects are disabled, which was not the case in previous games.
 
-new team customization features
  -thanks to the new graphics engine, the field editor received an upgrade where you can change different parts of the field that you couldn't before
    -you can change the goal posts, the font and position of the yard-line numbers, the turf types, the colors of specific parts of the field, the sidelines, etc
  -the create-a-team, create-a-playbook, and create-a-play features return, giving axis football 27 a level of team customization that crushes madden 27's team customization options

-new additions to franchise mode
  -a mock draft during the season that projects which players in the draft pool will go to which team in which round.
  -when scouting players, you can now view their college stats.
  -they added AI-generated team newspaper articles and league newspaper articles that cover team and league news.  We're talking full-length paragraphs highlighting players, game previews, etc.  Not even PS2 Madden games ever did that.

CONS:

-default player speed is slower than madden
  -setting the game speed to maximum in game settings makes the game speed more tolerable

-the animations and physics need to be smoothed out more on tackles.

-fair catches need to be added to the game

-in-game instant replays are not present
  -adding these in future games will make the game's presentation feel more like a tv broadcast

-no online play

-no practice mode

-still more work to do on adding more user control

-the ability to create our own formations needs to be added to create-a-play

-while graphically improved, the game's player models are still behind industry standards.  That could change when new player models are rolled out in next year's game.

Based on the standards I hold AAA games to, I give this game a 7.4 out of 10.  Please support this small indie developer by purchasing this game and spreading the word about axis football to everyone you know.

Not to be dramatic or anything, but I think this is the football game I've been hoping for my entire life.

To provide some context:

- I'm 62 years old. I had a Pong console and an Atari 2600. When I say "my entire life," it's been a minute.
- I once worked as a programmer for a company that made sports games, including football.

What I want in a football game is to be able to coach and develop the team. If I'm playing an FPS or something like Assassin's Creed, sure, give me a controller. For football, however, I don't want to skew the results with my twitch skills. I want the full-on strategic experience. So while Axis Football 2027 allows you to grab a controller and get involved, nothing about my review touches on that part. I jumped into franchise mode and I've been making trades, upgrading my infrastructure, and calling the plays.

If you know anything about this game, you probably already know that the graphics aren't trying to compete with the bigger titles. The graphics are, however, in my opinion, sufficient to give one the feel of seeing the game they're coaching play out on the field. I watch it and I get excited (almost!) like I'm watching the Vols on a Saturday afternoon.

I want a football game to be full of under-the-hood stats about players and probabilities. I want heavy rain to affect play styles. I want to make the best choices that I can for my team - on the field and off - and, realizing that there's some chance involved, know that the software gave me a fair shot based on my choices.

Axis Football 2027 really seems to be a game that takes football seriously and focuses on making the numbers work.

I bought this game because I started diving into sports games from smaller studios, such as GOALS, UFL, etc. I did a full Franchise simulation for one year and a little bit of on field gameplay as well.

PROS:
- Menus are feature rich, with things like league news, team morale, trade requests, and scouting adding immersion
- In depth stats, including team rankings, team leaders, league leaders, and hall of records all available at a glance
- Simulation time in franchise is very fast (RTX 4070 Ti GPU, I9 CPU, 32 GB RAM)
- Tier system option in franchise is unique and adds tons of playability to mode. It acts similar to the European soccer leagues where the bottom team gets relegated and the top team in the lower tiers move up a division
- Player attributes are simple and easy to follow
- Game visually looks very solid
- Momentum tackling system looks good and realistic
- Scouting simple, yet manual. One of my biggest gripes with Madden over the last couple of years is that you just set what positions your scouts look for and basically leave it alone until the offseason
- "Real" player faces add immersion
- Bevy of coaching positions, such as position coaches and coordinators, add depth to franchise
- Facilities that carry impacts to certain attributes (good trainers room will positively impact injury chance and injury recovery time) is great
- Season stats for player align with attributes. When I looked through who the top five players were in passing yards, rushing yards, receiving yards, tackles, sacks, and interceptions after the season, most of the players were in the B+ to A overall range
- Draft screen is very cool, with sound made when pick is in, ticker on bottom, and option to choose speed of draft. Reminds me of watching the NFL Draft

CONS: 
- Game having issues detecting PS5 controller (wired and overclocked to 4,000 hz using BattleBeaver), works with Xbox Elite Series 2 controller wired
- No option to see full roster in franchise, only can see it through the depth chart
- Same trades offered multiple times, even after rejecting
- No option to sort in draft player pool for just players you have added to your watch list

VISUAL GLITCHES:
- When browsing players, if you highlight second string or player not at top of list, game automatically highlights top player, making it a tad annoying to try and see stats of other players
- Shows multiple tabs highlighted, even though only one should be. Example would be when in menu of franchise, it would highlight the actions tab as well as play next game, even though you are only hovering over the actions tab
- Both left and right stick toggle options on franchise menus, making it tough to scroll through items on screen such as awards for offensive and defensive player of week and team rankings
- Player movement can feel sluggish at times
- Blue line indicating box score being selected in game stats page will also be below LB/RB button guides

I have not dove into the team customization aspect of the game yet, but I have heard that previous title have a lot of options.

OVERALL:
This game is very solid, especially from a smaller studio. It has a very good amount of depth and is well worth the $20 price tag. Definitely recommend giving it a shot.

This is my first Axis Football. I wasn't going into this thing expecting the polish and graphics of Madden. I wanted to get away from EA, and now being a Linux user, can't even play their games now, anyway. When I saw the visual improvements between this and last year's version, I decided to give it a go. As launch neared I was actually pretty excited about it, and purchased it as soon as I got home from work on launch day (today).

I know this is a 20 dollar game, but ... man this just feels cheap. I'm using a computer that can easily emulate games, and I'll be honest with you, the 2K series on the Dreamcast plays better than this (not talking about looks); a series that's a quarter of a century old. The controls feel floaty and off-putting. I never really feel like I genuinely have full control over my player. Pass deflection feels good, and throwing feels good. I'd say the passing game is the game's strength, and offers everything you'd expect. However, running and ESPECIALLY defense, I feel like it's on rails. I don't have the ability to control the player in a way that ever feels like the success or failure was earned. Breaking tackles feels random, making tackles feels random, and everything feels hollow. Nothing FEELS like a hit, it feels like people in the backyard with no pads on, playing football without trying to hurt anyone. I swear running vs not-running feels like the exact same speed to me. It feels very slow and clunky.

Play selection works well. The menu system works just fine. However, there are bugs and I've only played for about an hour. I called a timeout, and when I came back from the pause menu I couldn't hike the ball. It forced me to wait the 30-odd seconds until I got a delay of game. Controls worked after that play, but screwed up my drive. I've had players circle around doing laps near receivers, like he couldn't figure out where he was supposed to be (also, making it clear how little control I have over my player...). Players run through each other like they don't exist nearly every play; even players that should be interacting with each other like receivers and defenders, or defensive players vs a QB who they're trying to sack. I literally had dozens of plays go in completely different ways than they should have simply because players ran through the other team's player. Again, reinforcing everything feeling scripted and out of my control, as if the game was basically saying "well, the play SHOULD look like this... unexpected player in the way of the play be damned". 

I won't get into graphics much; you've seen the trailer, you get what you get. It only plays at 1440p, it's sharp, but in an "I'm emulating an old game on really high end hardware" sort of sharp, as if the graphics don't really match the resolution you're playing at. Crowds are cardboard cut outs, the statium looks simple and blocky, lighting is VERY bright, but shadows are exceptionally weak. They need some contrast on the field, it looks like the players are floating. But again, I'd be ok with all of this, and frankly, EXPECTED all of this... if only it played well.

If it looked primitive but played great, I'd have kept the game and left a glowing review. We don't need fancy graphics, advanced animations, and flashy crowd reaction shots to make a good football game. You can have knock off teams, a lack of deep modes, and for 20 bucks will be more than good enough to get people to switch from Madden. But it has to FEEL GOOD. And this really does not. 

I wish the team the best. I saw somewhere they're working on animations for Axis Football 2028. Maybe it'll be better then? But even with better animations, they need to get the weight of players right, and offer controls that make the gamer feel they have full control over the player on the field. At this point, in defense and running plays, it nearly feels like the computer gets to just interpret whatever I'm doing in whatever way it seems fit. And if I'm not really in full control, I'm not really playing a game; I'm watching it.

I hope this helps anyone on the fence. If you're ok with my complaints, by all means give it a go. Worst you do is refund. It does work on Steam Machine beautifully with ZERO tweaks; so it has that in its corner, and I thank the devs for that. I really hope I can come back to the franchise when it doesn't feel like a mobile game or something as I feel they have the ingredients for something more. But it's just not with this release.

PS1 graphics, pixel art, retro visuals to invoke a feeling of nostalgia. Unconventional game design. It's something conventional that's twisted around into an abstract idea of a video game. It doesn't feel like something that exists, but because it doesn't exist, means that it does exist. These games do not have a specific type or genre, they just have a style that encapsulates the entire collection. For lack of a better name, I've opted to call them "trans games".

Firstly, if I could, I would give this game a thumbs sideways. But since I can't, and since the specific phrasing of the question is "Do I recommend this game". I must give it a thumbs up. This game is experimental, weird, and flawed. But it is doing things I've never seen out of any game before it, and its $7 at the time of writing, so really whats the harm.

The core mechanic, exploring an infinitely descending fractal world of cubes, with limitless detail to be found within, is incredibly solid and interesting. Its the design and mechanics that surround that core that become increasingly questionable in their implementation.

The game takes after the boomer shooters of yore for its combat system. Health and Armor with a variety of weapons with obvious differences in utility, the majority of which being projectile based and not hitscan. Enemies however have "projectile" attacks with such high velocity they may as well be hitscan. So you have a recharging shield and regenerating health... meaning things eventually devolve into cover shooter style play. 

the SFX design, as it currently stands, is actively detrimental to the experience. The game, as far as I can tell, does not support stereo, and enemies do not make any noise except when taking damage or dying. So you only know you are under attack when you take damage. Real damage to be clear, your regenerating shield also makes no sound when hit. But there is this pink sphere that appears that tries to map the full 360 degree field of view around you into an indicator of damage direction. Also there is no falloff to the volume of any sfx based on its distance, nor are enemies that are from a scale level above your current one given a lower pitch. This lack of audio feedback makes the game feel very unresponsive.

In addition, all enemy sound effects that I've encountered so far are just weird mouth noises, some of which are *incredibly* uncomfortable. The mouse enemies in particular, who's sfxs I would describe as wet lip smacking and gargling. I don't know what these noises are supposed to convey. They definitely don't give me any insight into what these weirdly names creatures that are all just strange textured mapped to a UV sphere are supposed to be.

The lack of any music or ambient sound at all also detracts from the experience. It would do so much to add to the atmosphere and help differentiate your current location, if different chunks had different background sounds to represent them based on what generation algorithm was being used within that chunk. (mossy air vs stoney air, etc.)

Overall, flawed but compelling game. sound design is the only aspect that *needs* a change, as there is a dire need for better feedback to be provided to the player, and audio is definitely the place for that feedback to come from. Everything else is quirky but does not stand out as actively detrimental. Please:

- passive enemy sounds, or sounds when enemies fire off attacks to alert you to their presence
- directional audio with distance falloff to assist with locating enemies by the previously mentioned passive sounds
- more sounds for taking damage, at least one for when shields are being hit, so I can react before my shields are already depleted
- environmental ambient audio, to further distinguish each region that you are in, and give them even more unique character

If you've got $7 you can burn, this game is worth giving a shot to see if you like it or not.

Definitely a weird little game, but I enjoyed it. The game told me my save took 10 hours, but Steam tells me I played 16 hours in the past 2 weeks, and that's how long it took me to beat the game (although I have 22.5 hrs total from previous attempts, so I knew a little bit going into this attempt.)

The game has a very surreal feel. It almost feels like something out of a 12 year old's idea/dream/nightmare of a game, made into reality by someone who clearly has the chops to code up this wacky science experiment of a game. This is both a good thing and a bad thing. For one, obviously not focusing on visuals or sound design let Dan Hathaway focus entirely on the core of the game, that being the fractal exploration. And the weird vibes certainly have a unique feel worth experiencing. On the other end, I can't exactly call this game "avant-garde", it's moreso just weird and working within constraints. I think the game suffers from a lack of music that could have established an atmosphere, and the sound design is just flat out bizarre. Again, it's kind of a strength in that it creates a unique experience, but I hesitate to compliment the game for these decisions.

Where the game really shines is the exploration. The shrinking and growing mechanic that turns the world into a couple of blocks on a whim, or turns a flower into an entire dimension worth exploring is mind-boggling. Frankly, there was an overwhelming amount of stuff to explore in this game, so I decided not to. I stuck to the main path of the game, which thankfully the game does tell you about through text boxes you can find throughout the world. The generous amount of waypoints you can freely teleport between also made sure I never felt truly in an unescapable situation, or that I would lose a ton of progress by choosing to venture in one way or another. I could always teleport to backtrack, get upgrades, then come back exactly to where I was on the main route. This game also shows a lot of the potential of creating unique procedurally generated block environments, and it makes me think that games like Minecraft haven't actually fully tapped into the potential that block proc-gened worlds actually have.

If I had to list a negative, it's that the gameplay doesn't really feel as up to par as the core of the game, the exploration. Don't get me wrong, I enjoyed piloting my ship around and killing enemies, and the game does have the unique feature of making enemies more or less dangerous if you shrink or grow near them. However, given just how long you can explore in this game, which is many more hours than I actually put into it, I feel like the combat and piloting wears thin much quicker than the exploration does. I was starting to feel a little bored/frustrated in the last couple of hours because of this. Of note, I disabled "True Up", meaning any direction could be up when piloting the ship. This did make the ship more involved and fun to pilot around in my opinion, but this doesn't fully save it if you ask me.

Overall, I really enjoyed this game, and I really don't want anyone to miss such a unique gaming experience. And it's cheap too and runs on crappy hardware, so you might as well try it. I ended up exploring only a tiny fraction of what the game has to offer, but considering that tiny fraction still turned into 16 hours of gameplay, you can see how I felt overwhelmed and was content just beating the game.

To Dan Hathaway (if you see this), one recommendation I have for the game is to implement some sort of note taking system into the game. Maybe just the ability to save screenshots or the text boxes in an accessible place in the menu. I'm imagining something kinda similar to Morrowind's journal system, if you're at all familiar with that. I had to save screenshots in folders open on my second monitor, and I think the game would be that much better if it did the information saving and sorting for you as you find it in the world.

We Gotta Go is a cooperative horror-comedy experience developed by FuzzyBot and published by Mad Mushroom that transforms a deliberately absurd premise into a surprisingly entertaining multiplayer adventure. Combining exploration, survival mechanics, procedural level generation, environmental interaction, and chaotic teamwork, the game places players inside a haunted mansion where a supernatural nightmare collides with an increasingly urgent personal problem. The result is a unique blend of comedy and horror that relies on player cooperation, improvisation, and constant panic to create memorable moments.

At first glance, the concept appears intentionally ridiculous. Players find themselves trapped inside a mysterious mansion while desperately searching for a bathroom before disaster strikes. However, what could have been a one-dimensional joke quickly develops into a fully realized gameplay system. The urgent need to reach relief becomes a constant source of pressure that influences exploration, decision-making, and teamwork. Every minute spent wandering through dangerous corridors increases the tension, creating an unusual form of survival gameplay that feels both stressful and hilarious.

The game's greatest strength lies in its ability to balance horror and comedy without undermining either. The mansion contains genuine threats that require caution and cooperation, but the circumstances surrounding those threats are often absurd enough to generate constant laughter. This combination creates a unique atmosphere where players can be frightened by an unexpected encounter one moment and laughing uncontrollably the next. Few games manage to maintain this balance successfully, but We Gotta Go consistently embraces both sides of its identity.

Cooperative multiplayer serves as the foundation of the entire experience. Working together is essential for survival because the mansion is filled with hazards, puzzles, and hostile creatures that are difficult to overcome alone. Communication becomes increasingly important as situations become more chaotic. Friends must coordinate exploration, share resources, assist one another during dangerous encounters, and make quick decisions when plans inevitably begin to fall apart. These interactions generate many of the game's most memorable moments.

The mansion itself is designed to encourage replayability. Procedurally generated layouts ensure that each run feels different, preventing players from relying entirely on memorization. Corridors, rooms, objectives, and routes shift between sessions, forcing teams to adapt to new situations every time they enter the building. This unpredictability helps maintain suspense and ensures that even experienced players remain uncertain about what lies around the next corner.

Exploration is surprisingly rewarding thanks to the large number of items and interactive objects scattered throughout the environment. Players can discover useful tools, equipment, weapons, and various resources that assist with survival. Many objects serve multiple purposes, encouraging experimentation and creative problem-solving. The ability to interact with the environment gives players additional options during moments of crisis and helps prevent gameplay from becoming repetitive.

Enemy encounters provide a significant source of tension. The mansion is inhabited by strange supernatural creatures that range from unsettling to outright bizarre. Rather than relying exclusively on conventional horror monsters, the game embraces unusual and often comedic enemy designs that perfectly match its tone. These threats create pressure during exploration while contributing to the game's distinctive personality. Players never quite know whether their next encounter will be terrifying, ridiculous, or a combination of both.

The environmental puzzles help diversify the gameplay loop. Progress frequently requires players to manipulate objects, unlock pathways, and solve cooperative challenges while under constant pressure. Because the game rarely allows players to relax completely, even relatively straightforward objectives become exciting when completed under stressful conditions. This pacing helps maintain engagement and prevents exploration from feeling aimless.

One of the most entertaining aspects of the game is how it handles failure. Rather than removing eliminated players entirely from the experience, the game introduces unconventional methods that allow them to remain involved. This approach keeps everyone engaged throughout a session and reinforces the lighthearted nature of the overall experience. It also helps reduce frustration, ensuring that mistakes contribute to the fun rather than interrupting it.

Character customization adds another layer of charm. Players can unlock and equip various cosmetic items that personalize their appearance. While these additions do not significantly affect gameplay, they help create a stronger sense of identity and provide extra incentives for continued exploration. Discovering new cosmetic rewards contributes to long-term progression and encourages repeated play sessions.

Visually, We Gotta Go adopts a colorful and exaggerated style that perfectly complements its unusual concept. The mansion is spooky enough to support the horror elements, but the presentation never becomes so dark or realistic that it overshadows the comedic aspects. Character models, environmental details, and enemy designs all contribute to a world that feels simultaneously eerie and playful.

Audio design deserves recognition for how effectively it supports both halves of the experience. The game uses environmental sounds, sudden noises, and unsettling effects to build tension during exploration. At the same time, humorous audio cues reinforce the absurdity of many situations. This careful balance helps maintain the game's identity and ensures that neither the horror nor the comedy dominates the experience completely.

What truly makes We Gotta Go stand out is its commitment to its premise. Many comedy-focused games struggle because their central joke wears thin after a short period of time. Here, the developers continuously introduce new mechanics, situations, and challenges that build upon the original concept. The humor remains effective because it emerges naturally from gameplay rather than relying solely on scripted jokes.

The game also excels at creating emergent stories. The most memorable moments are rarely planned. Failed rescue attempts, unexpected monster encounters, accidental mistakes, and desperate last-second escapes combine to generate unique experiences that differ from one session to the next. These unscripted moments are often far funnier and more exciting than anything intentionally written, giving the game significant replay value.

We Gotta Go ultimately succeeds as a creative multiplayer experience that combines cooperative survival, procedural exploration, horror elements, and outrageous comedy into a surprisingly cohesive package. Its unusual premise may attract initial curiosity, but it is the strong teamwork mechanics, replayable structure, and constant stream of unpredictable situations that keep players engaged. For groups seeking a multiplayer game capable of delivering equal amounts of tension, laughter, and chaos, We Gotta Go offers a distinctive adventure that stands out from more conventional cooperative titles.

This game had so much momentum going into release and I preordered it. It has been a disappointment from day 1. It launched almost a week late in a massively buggy and unfinished state. I understand that it is early access but basic gameplay was completely broken and unplayable. From there the dev quickly "fixed" a couple of issues and has since vanished into the aether. He doesn't update the discord almost at all (last update was October 7th as of posting this review) and allows crypto scams to be pumped into the server pretty much every single day without any moderation. He hasn't updated the game in well over 2 weeks now which places his promised date almost a week past where it should be, and all the "fixed" bugs mentioned earlier have come back. 

The procedural generation makes only 4 "biomes" which are yellow, pale yellow, green, and red with literally no differences besides color. The generation also has many flaws that make the "infinite" world end up with closed loops that make it so that continued exploration is physically impossible. I mapped out an entire seed with a friend in a little over an hour and there was nothing more to do and we ran out of research points to continue completing objectives. 

There are 2 monsters and both of them are also extremely buggy. You are supposed to be able to punch the monsters to momentarily stun them, but this doesn't work. They noclip through walls somewhat frequently and ignore collision with most objects except chairs for some reason, and they are extremely inconsistent about the way they hit. Sometimes a small entity will literally instantly down your character because it hits 3 times in under a second and other times they will just run into you for like 10 seconds without hitting at all. The big entity is just worse in every way. It has all the same bugs, but it grabs you and locks you into a 15 second long animation where it carries you away randomly and then instakills you. There is no way to escape this without another player, so single player is pretty much doomed. There is also no natural regen so far as I can tell. If you mess up and get hit by an entity, you permanently have 1 less HP out of your 3 HP maximum.

There are 5 missions that play on repeat throughout the entire game. Collect 100 research points, take pictures of entities, take pictures of strange structures, take videos of entities, and find the lost employee. Every single one of these has game breaking bugs attached. The 100 research point one has the afformentioned procedural generation bug where you can just run out of objects on the map fairly easily if you get a bad seed. The camera is meant to store pictures that you take, but it will randomly just delete everything you've done which makes you restart from scratch, this includes all pictures on the poster board. The camcorder missions are practically impossible to complete solo because they require 10 seconds of uninterrupted footage of an entity, however because of their pathing you can't get that without them being aggroed onto you and they move faster than you when you have the camcorder out and will always reach and kill you before the 10 seconds have been captured or they will lose aggro and exit the range of the camcorder. The lost employee has the most annoying bugs of all. There is an item dedicated to finding him and about 90% of the time it points to him either being in the starting area spawn wall or a random wall in the backrooms. I have found through trial that this isn't just a bug with his spawning but also with the item. It will get caught on the previous spawn and never move to the new one which makes finding the guy almost impossible without the help of other bugs.

TL;DR: Game is unplayably buggy, dev doesn't update community almost at all, there is also almost nothing to do assuming you somehow don't encounter bugs, entities are horrendous, and is unbearably empty.

Pros:
-The procedural generated layouts (though limited in diversity) is very promising for a backrooms game. You never really know what is going to be around the next corner.
-Lab home base systems are really cool and helpful when booking it away from an entity.
-Lab shop system is good, though I see room for expansion of gadgets.

Cons (room for improvement):
-Diversity of entity type would be nice, in my limited time I've experienced the large and normal sized still lives. Though they do have different appearance variations among them, and perhaps its already in but in later days you could maybe start experiencing the more horrific ones from the various backrooms iterations.
-The cart, at this moment I only used it as a way to prevent entities from hitting me which I know is essentially bug abuse. I'd recommend removing it entirely due to the speed, lack of navigable space, and the abuse mentioned above. There also doesn't seem to be collision with the randomly placed furniture. 
-Doors, IDK if I'm crazy but I swear I've run from entities shutting a door behind me only to continue hearing them chase me. Are they opening the doors or running through them? I've been too scared to turn back and check lol.
-Entity speed, the path finding and prediction of the players path is quite good, the entities can often cut you off when you want to juke them out. I'd recommend turning down the speed just a bit more to allow the player to gain some ground ahead of them in the often event you run into a dead end room. This could then introduce a stamina mechanic to prevent the player from full sprinting all the time and just long enough to break contact.
-Equipment, it would be helpful to have the cardboard cutouts hold them up just a bit longer, maybe have entities grab them for a couple seconds and then smash them. A pressure gauge or some similar reading for the anesthetic gas charge would also be very helpful.
-Occasional bug where you can no longer equip items after being downed.

Overall I got what I came for, some uneasy feelings as I solo explored the backrooms and tried to fulfill my contractual goals. Backrooms: Code Yellow approaches the familiar Backrooms concept as a cooperative workplace nightmare rather than a straightforward walking simulator or chase-focused horror game. Developed and published by GameMechanic, it places one to six players in the role of employees entering an enormous, unpredictable network of rooms and corridors to perform assignments, gather data, and hopefully make it back alive. The premise gives exploration an actual purpose, which helps distinguish the experience from Backrooms games that rely almost entirely on wandering through liminal environments.

The strongest part of the design is its expedition-based gameplay loop. Players enter the Backrooms with objectives to complete, explore procedural environments, search for useful resources, and deal with whatever dangers appear along the way. Surviving and successfully returning provides funding that can be spent in the shop on equipment for future excursions. This creates a satisfying sense of preparation and progression. Entering deeper areas becomes more meaningful when there is something tangible at stake, and deciding whether to continue exploring or return safely can create some of the game's better moments of tension.

Procedural generation is particularly appropriate for this setting. The Backrooms are supposed to feel impossibly large and difficult to understand, so unpredictable layouts reinforce the idea that players are exploring a place that refuses to follow normal architectural logic. Endless-looking corridors, strangely connected rooms, repetitive spaces, and distorted architecture establish the unsettling atmosphere. Randomization also gives repeated missions more value because memorizing one route does not necessarily eliminate the uncertainty of later expeditions.

Multiplayer is where the concept has the greatest potential. Up to six people can explore together, creating an interesting mixture of horror and cooperative chaos. Communication becomes important when searching large environments, completing missions, keeping track of teammates, or responding to threats. A group can feel reasonably confident while everyone remains together, only for that confidence to disappear once players become separated. The resulting unscripted situations are often exactly what cooperative horror needs, since fear can emerge naturally from confusion and uncertainty rather than relying entirely on predetermined scares.

There is also single-player support, although the design naturally feels suited to groups. Playing alone changes the atmosphere considerably because there is nobody else to provide reassurance or assistance. Empty corridors become more oppressive, and encountering something dangerous carries greater consequences when another player cannot immediately help. It therefore offers two noticeably different styles of experience: multiplayer emphasizes coordination and unpredictable social situations, while solo play places greater weight on isolation.

The mission and progression systems are important because procedural horror can become repetitive when exploration has no meaningful objective. Collecting data, completing assignments, earning funding, purchasing equipment, and preparing for another working day establish a recognizable cycle. The challenge for long-term replayability will be ensuring that missions, entities, environments, and equipment remain sufficiently varied. Random generation alone cannot create endless variety if the underlying objectives repeatedly ask players to perform similar actions.

The game is currently in Early Access, which should strongly influence expectations. Its foundation already includes a large procedurally generated environment, dangerous enemies, multiple mission types, multiplayer for up to six participants, equipment, tools, funding, and a shop. The development plan is intended to expand the existing systems with additional tasks, enemies, architecture, and other content. As a result, the current experience feels more like the framework for an ambitious cooperative horror game than a finished final product. Some systems may evolve considerably as development continues.

Atmospherically, the game understands why the Backrooms concept works. Fear comes from uncertainty, strange architecture, isolation, and the possibility that something hostile occupies the same seemingly endless space. It does not need constant combat or jumpscares to create tension. Simply moving farther from safety while carrying valuable progress can make an otherwise ordinary corridor feel threatening. The procedural nature of the environment complements this because players cannot always rely on perfect knowledge gained during previous sessions.

Steam Deck compatibility is currently rated Playable. The game can run on SteamOS, and its interface text is considered legible, but the handheld experience comes with compromises. Some functionality may require the touchscreen, virtual keyboard, or an alternative community controller configuration, while controller prompts may not always match the Steam Deck. Graphics settings may also require manual adjustment for suitable performance. Another important limitation is that single-player requires an active internet connection. It is therefore usable on Steam Deck, but it is not as seamless as a fully Verified release.

Visually and technically, its relatively modest PC requirements make it approachable compared with more demanding modern horror releases. The real attraction is less about graphical spectacle and more about environmental scale, unpredictability, and atmosphere. The distorted architecture and deliberately repetitive spaces suit the source concept, although the effectiveness of these environments over dozens of hours will depend on how much architectural and gameplay diversity is eventually introduced.

Backrooms: Code Yellow is ultimately a promising cooperative interpretation of liminal horror. Its combination of procedural exploration, missions, data collection, dangerous entities, equipment management, funding, and persistent progression gives players reasons to repeatedly return to the Backrooms. The ability to play alone or with as many as six people broadens its appeal, while its Early Access status leaves substantial room for expansion. It still needs continued development and greater content depth to demonstrate lasting replayability, but the core loop already provides an engaging foundation for players who enjoy cooperative horror built around exploration, uncertainty, and extraction-style risk.

Rating: 7/10

I had 3 crashes in 41 hours of gameplay.

The combat is pretty cool, but I finally got my team with some really good gear, and they can jump on a group of bandits and win, but I have now finished the early access location, unless I'm missing something. 
After the tutorial area, the first quest didn't work for me.  The quest says to enter a cave and has a location marked on my map, but I get there and it's a small town and no cave, but I may have just missed it.
I spent most of my time building up my crafting and making money, which went surprisingly well considering how hardcore the other parts of the game can be.
I walked up to a group of people on the road, and didn't realize they were bandits, and they wrecked my team.  I fought a troll with 3 characters, whole team wiped out, tried again with better gear and 4 member team, and it took longer, but eventually whole team wiped out.
The combat, especially with the trolls, is pretty awesome to watch.  Yes there are some glitchy looking moves happening, and items falling through the map, and re-appearing later in the game, but the combat is actually a really cool activity.  Trolls have special moves that occasionally happen, and humanoids also have rare special attacks happen.
The mechanics for combat are really cool as well, but no archery yet or shields, unless I missed a location for bows, but all of the stats for combat are impressive.  Dodge, block, block reduction, physical resist, defense resist, armor penetration, physical damage, crit chance, crit damage bonus, skill bonuses.  These might seem like normal stats to use in a crpg or rpg game, but its complicated to make them all work as well as they are doing it in this game.
I do believe its like early access Kenshi and Wartales combo, and it has amazing potential. 
This is more like Divinity 2 early access beta 1, or Wartales early access beta 2 than a fully completed game.  All of the basic mechanics are established, and decently polished, but its definitely got some more work to do, before it's ready, which is why its in early access.
Many people are saying its missing a lot to be early access, but I believe its in early access to provide additional funding, and let people get a taste of something that they have been waiting for.  This game by definition is early access, it has a large playable area, you can speed up, and stop time, otherwise I would have over 100 hours to get to the same place I got to in 40 hours.  Exploration is rewarding and fun, events happen in the world with or without your characters being present.

To close this review, there are a lot of improvements still needed, but it is having a great start for me.  I'm rating the below on a 1-5 star rating
-Crafting currently 5 stars, it is really cool, and seems really polished.
-Combat currently 3 stars, it is great, but needs some more polishing to how characters move in the combat, because they can move into locations you can't get to and can fall through walls etc.
-Building currently a 1 star, but looks like it will be awesome, but you can currently only build storage, bedding. decorations, crafting stations, lighting, and I look forward to being able to build a house, castle, etc in the future.
-Optimization currently 3 stars for me.  I don't have a super powerful PC and my RAM is lacking horribly for most games, but this game played really well, and to be early access in unreal engine and only crash 3 times on me is impressive.  It needs some improvement, because the longer you are in the game it seems like more data is being cached and I don't have the RAM to process everything, then it crashes and it only happens when I'm running at 3X speed for game speed, but I didn't read the crash report or investigate to see what was wrong, FYI Valheim and Conan Exiles does this on occasion to me as well.

Overall I'm impressed, but it needs some work, and I recommend this game only to people who don't mind supporting an early access game, which still needs some work done.  I look forward to them making more improvements and releasing additional features, and hopefully they will keep making progress on this.

As someone who spent a big part of my youth playing custom tower defense maps in Warcraft 3, Element TD 2 feels like finally coming home.

I’ve been searching for years for a standalone TD that captures that classic feeling: one run = one full game, all the tools available from the start, no annoying grind, no artificial “campaign with tiny upgrades and resets every 10 minutes”. Just you, the waves, the build choices and the experiments with different element paths.

Element TD 2 is the first game i played that really respects that legacy. It feels like a careful, loving continuation of the old Warcraft 3 Element TD rather than a “modernized” version that throws away what made it fun in the first place. The pacing, the focus on builds, the freedom to try combinations in a single session - it’s exactly what I wanted from a proper PC tower defense game.

To the developers: thank you for treating the original design with so much respect. After trying a lot of other TD games that went in completely different directions, I’m genuinely happy this one exists. This is the one I was looking for.

The Good: Visually, the two-person developer team actually nailed the atmosphere. On max settings, the forest environment looks incredible, and the audio design pulls you right into that eerie, isolated wilderness.

The Bad: But the moment you actually try to play it, the experience face-plants. You hit the opening watchtower sequence only to find dead-end interactions that go absolutely nowhere. You trudge down the road to scavenge, fighting a pixel-hunting chore just to find invisible sticks and stones blended into background textures, only to reach a vendor system that locks basic survival tools behind a wall of frustration. Between the clunky, unnatural movement mechanics, stuttering interior spaces, and half-baked loops, it fights you at every single turn.

The Verdict:
There's a neat visual concept here, but charging $13.99 for an unoptimized, mechanically broken prototype misses the mark entirely. In a market packed with fully realized survival titles that cost the same or less and actually work, releasing a game in this state feels premature. Hopefully, the developers take the criticism to heart, because right now, even the forest isn't the only thing that's completely lost.

I've found all the other animals and have gotten their crafting materials, but I could not find a single bear in my playthrough. Luckily the devs scattered everything you'll need all over the map, so just do some exploring and you'll eventually find everything you need without the need to buy anything from the vendors.  I did not buy a single armor or weapon upgrades from any vendors.  I simply played the game and found them.  The graphics in this game is almost photo-realistic and the atmosphere feels like you're actually trapped in a forest.  This game is not the typical grind-it-out-resource-gathering to build a base so it's a nice change of direction. Resource gathering is focused on traveling long distances, rather than staying in one place and gathering resources within close proximity to your base.  There's nothing wrong with this game design-wise.  It's just a different type of survival game.  It grew on me over time and now I like it.  There are some parts of the game that feels exactly like The Forest and Sons of the Forest.  You'll have to play it to find out.

Pro Tips:
As soon as you've gathered enough resources, build the Trail Flag and Warehouse before you build anything else.  Not even the Repair Station because throughout the game you'll find better weapons or duplicates of the same weapon to replace your broken one, so save your resources early in the game to build the two mentioned structures first.  Build the Repair Station as the third priority, after the Trail Flag and Warehouse.  The Trail Flag will help you find your way back to your base camp no matter where you are on the map.  I like to set the icon on the Trail Flag as a camp icon so I know it's my base camp.  Leave that as the only camp icon for your base camp so it's unique, that way you don't get confused with other camp icons.  I'd also recommend building your base camp at the first Tower you come across because you'll be coming back here a lot throughout the campaign, so might as well make this place your permanent base camp.  It's also the closest camp to all the vendors in the game, and it has a river you can fish and gather water.  You don't really need to build the rain water collector because it works exactly the same way as getting water from the river.  In both cases, you'll still need to boil the water to make it safe to drink so there's really no point in building one, although I've built two because of my past survival gaming instinct kicking in.  Turns out I can just get the river water instead.  As for the Warehouse, it's crucial you set this structure up ASAP because you'll be constantly running out of inventory space in your backpack, so I make it a habit every time I go on a resource run, that I always return to my base camp to drop off supplies and materials in my Warehouse.  It's a permanent storage chest.

[h1]Huge NO[/h1]

I [i]really[/i] wanted to like this game, but The Forest just doesn’t care about the player. There is no character creation, no proper tutorials, no onboarding of any kind. You’re dropped in and basically told: “Figure it out. Or don’t.” And the problem is, figuring it out isn’t satisfying, it’s just confusing.

Most mechanics aren’t intuitive at all, and the game never explains what’s important and what isn’t. Half the time you’re guessing whether something is a feature, a bug, or just bad design.

The physics are also… weird. Grass waves like it’s underwater, objects behave inconsistently, and immersion constantly breaks because things don’t react the way you’d expect in a survival game. And yes, it’s often broken. Sometimes I literally couldn’t pick up mushrooms — a basic survival resource — because the game just refused to register it. Stuff like this happens way too often to ignore.

The UI doesn’t help either. It’s clunky, awkward to navigate, and feels like it’s actively fighting you when you’re already struggling to understand the systems. The game itself is somewhat atmospheric, but nothing like promised. It plays like an Early Access game, which would be fine, if I hadn’t paid for a finished product.

If you enjoy games that explain nothing, break immersion regularly, and make basic actions frustrating, you might have fun. Otherwise, be prepared for a lot of unnecessary friction.

[b]Not recommended — unless your idea of survival includes fighting the game itself.[/b]

It is helpful to think of this as a space-based Souls-Like game, where avoiding damage is the optimal solution, and it is entirely possible by getting through the learning curve or just taking some good advice.

There is a simple trick to dodging everything, but it requires learning the way the system punishes attempting to move in straight lines. In full transparency, I can find a lot of things that you *could* choose to consider as lacking. The story is shallow, the rogue-alike nature means you don't really feel like you're exploring regions of space so much as traversing on rails, and much of the fun comes simply from unlocking and crafting to enhance your combat effect.

But that said, it does what it does very well, putting you right into fun-time arcade-style action with a pacing that's just slow enough to let you appreciate the view before you have to fight for and possibly end your life... again.

I'm not even the biggest fan of rogue-alike death systems as I like to feel like I'm making progress when I play a game, but the variety of ships to upgrade and refit keeps it from feeling like wasted effort when you die, and the unlocks are meaningful ones that can shift the entire play style. 

If you see this on a big sale, and you like spaceflight shoot-em-ups with a slow-but-steady pace, this is honestly probably more worth buying than the legendary Elite: Dangerous, which we all know turned a bit stale in the end.

The game gives you different weapons, equipment, resources, crafting, upgrades, perks and ships, and there is a system that lets you compare weapons through their stats and descriptions. My issue was never that the information was missing. The problem was the way all of this was presented. The menus themselves are incredibly basic and, for me, completely boring. They do their job, but they have no personality and nothing about them makes finding a new weapon or piece of equipment feel interesting. If the intention was to keep these systems simple, I think they could have been presented in a much better way. There are games with simpler systems that still make you want to look at what you have found, understand it and try something different. Here, I never had that curiosity.

That became a bigger problem because the gameplay itself was not giving me much reason to keep pushing forward either. The whole loop is built around progressing as far as you can, gathering resources, unlocking upgrades and perks, eventually moving on to other ships, dying and starting again. There is nothing wrong with that structure by itself, but it only works when the time spent inside each run is enjoyable. For me, it wasn't.

I found the ships and the overall pace of the game boring, and the combat never became interesting enough to change that. One of my biggest problems was the way the game handles enemy indicators. When an enemy is outside your field of view, the game uses arrows to indicate their position, whether they are behind, above or below you. The problem is that, during combat, those indicators can easily get lost between the ship's effects, the environment and the debris around you. The arrows are there, but with everything happening on screen, I often lost track of them and had to keep turning around just to find where the enemy actually was. The HUD also does not give you the option to adjust the size of these indicators, which made the problem even worse for me. On a 1440p monitor, many of these symbols felt too small, and allowing players to increase or decrease the size of HUD elements could have made them much easier to see. 

The problem, was not the genre or the type of experience EVERSPACE was trying to create. It was the way the game put everything together. There are other games that use similar ideas and manage to keep things simple while still making the player want to continue, experiment and see what comes next. EVERSPACE never did that for me. I found the overall experience boring, the gameplay loop tedious, and many parts of the game unintuitive.
