Love this genre, but at present can't recommend this game for a multitude of reasons that hopefully the devs will address (and to their credit they have already implemented fixes for certain issues the community has raised). The premise of this one is that you start in a mall with only the first store opened. You earn money through sorting items, picking up trash (more on that later) and the odd dollar found on the floor. You can then open up the other stores once you have enough cash. As to why I can't recommend it:

[list]
[*]There are labelled shelves, but only as a general category of item. For example 'White Wine' for the wine shop, leaving it up to you to arrange them as you please. Nothing inherently wrong with that, the problem is that most of the shelving cannot hold the entire stock of a particular item, so you end up having to split them amongst different shelves. Folk play these games to organise and tidy, so not being able to do that in the vast majority of the game is very dissatisfying. I've spent hours in the wine shop trying to make them look neat but the devs simply haven't optimised the shelf space, which is confusing because if you've made the game surely you know how many spaces there are and create items that fit properly within those spaces?
[*]The interface initially was absolute sensory hell for me, way too much going on. Certain abilities and text on the interface block/hinder what you're looking at. Thankfully, there's options to turn a lot of this visual noise off in the settings but it feels very overwhelming at first play when it's like TIPS, TIPS, HAVE SOME TIPS, HERE'S WHAT GOES ON THIS SHELF NOOOO WRONG SHELF- etc. Bit extreme on the handholding imo. It's a sorting game we're not training to be surgeons here lmao
[*]Very little visual variety in items means that what should take a moderate amount of time to complete turns into an absolute pain of a slog. The wine shop (my nemesis clearly at this point) is a lesson in pain. You have rose wine with a pink cap then cherry wine with a slightly different shade of pink cap, then white wine has a slightly lighter green cap than the apple wine which also has a green cap... you can see where I'm going with this. The bottles themselves largely have very little variation which means you spend a lot of time stood skirting your aim over each individual bottle because you can't simply tell them apart at a glance. Oh, and if you pick the wrong bottle up don't drop it because then it smashes and you have to buy a new one. You also can't run whilst holding bottles.
[*]Trash spawns randomly throughout playtime and you can pick it up (one at a time only though because apparently I only have one hand despite having 14 inventory slots by this point) and dump it in the trash for a couple dollars. Unfortunately they have collision which means while you're going from shelf to shelf you may suddenly find yourself stuck on the trash bag. I just find this irrationally annoying and a totally unecessary feature given how much money you earn from just doing the tidying.
[*]Every couple of minutes I get horrendous lag spikes and I've attached my specs to this review - no idea why it happens. I've tried changing different settings to no avail and even playing it on the lowest of settings it still happens. I feel like the environments are so small that this really shouldn't be an issue.
[*]The 'gather' skill only gathers things within a seemingly 2cm radius around you, no indicator of the radius either. Again, the stores aren't exactly huge so why it doesn't just gather all the items up to what will fit in your hand is ridiculous.
[/list]

Overall I feel like the devs have tried reinventing the wheel a bit and instead of creating something novel and new it's just another weight round your ankle. I do think it has potential and I'll carry on playing for the achievements but I wouldn't recommend folk buy it at present. Megastore Chaos turns the strangely satisfying act of organizing clutter into the foundation of an entire simulation game. Developed and published by Dynamic Dice, it places you inside a shopping mall where stores have descended into disorder and thousands of products need to be returned to their proper places. Instead of emphasizing sales figures, demanding customers, or stressful time limits, the experience concentrates on restoring order one item at a time. It is deliberately repetitive, but that repetition is also where much of its relaxing appeal comes from.

The basic gameplay loop is immediately understandable. You enter a messy store, locate misplaced merchandise, pick items up, determine where they belong, and gradually transform chaotic shelves into organized displays. There are six different stores to tackle, including a supermarket, bookstore, game shop, electronics store, wine shop, and toy store. Each location changes the types of merchandise you handle, giving the same organizing concept a different atmosphere. With more than 30,000 objects involved across the experience, some locations can initially look genuinely overwhelming.

What makes the game satisfying is the visible progress created by every small action. A shelf covered in random objects eventually becomes neatly arranged, an entire section becomes recognizable, and a store that initially appeared hopeless slowly starts looking functional again. There is no constant timer forcing you to rush through this process, so organizing can be approached at a comfortable pace. This makes it particularly suitable for players who enjoy cleaning, sorting, unpacking, and other task-oriented simulation games where completing routine jobs is the main reward.

There is also progression beyond simply placing objects correctly. Completing tasks provides money that can be used to advance through the mall and gain access to additional areas. Experience contributes to a skill system that improves your ability to handle increasingly large workloads. Upgrades affecting factors such as carrying capacity and organizing efficiency become valuable once the number of items starts increasing. Quests provide additional objectives and help give direction to what could otherwise have been an entirely freeform cleanup simulator.

The biggest question is whether the central activity remains enjoyable after several hours. Organizing tens of thousands of objects inevitably involves repetition, and the game does not completely escape that limitation. Players looking for deep business management, complex economic systems, action, or rapidly changing objectives may find the routine too narrow. On the other hand, anyone who enjoys methodical jobs may see this as the entire point. There is an almost meditative quality to concentrating on a single section, steadily clearing the mess, and then stepping back to see how dramatically the environment has changed.

The first-person presentation complements this concept because every object feels like something you personally handle rather than an abstract resource. Different stores provide visual variety, while the quantity of merchandise helps sell the idea that these are substantial cleanup projects rather than tiny puzzle stages. Controller support is another useful addition for players who prefer a more relaxed control setup. Achievements, cloud saving, Family Sharing, multiple language options, and accessibility features further round out the package.

Because Megastore Chaos is an Early Access title, its current content should not be treated as the final form of the game. The existing foundation already demonstrates the intended experience through its stores, quests, skills, progression, and enormous number of sortable objects, but additional content and refinement could significantly improve its longevity. More locations and item types would be especially valuable because environmental variety is one of the best ways to keep such a repetitive core mechanic interesting over a longer period.

Steam Deck compatibility is currently best considered Unknown/Unverified rather than officially Steam Deck Verified or Playable. The game's controller support and relatively approachable hardware requirements are encouraging for handheld use, but an official compatibility badge should be the standard for claiming full Deck support. Players intending to use a Steam Deck should therefore expect that some settings adjustments or interface considerations may be necessary until an official compatibility status is established.

Megastore Chaos ultimately knows its audience. It is not trying to turn retail organization into an elaborate management empire or a frantic race against the clock. Its attraction comes from taking an intimidating pile of disorder and steadily converting it into something neat and understandable. The massive object count provides scale, while upgrades, quests, multiple stores, and progression provide enough structure to make the cleanup feel purposeful. Repetition prevents it from having universal appeal, and Early Access means there is still considerable room for expansion, but for players who genuinely enjoy organizing virtual spaces, its straightforward approach can be surprisingly absorbing.

Despite a lot of polish, rich customization features, and 6 separate stores (with more to come) this game is fundamentally not good at its core.

Let's look at the Wine Shop. 1956 bottles there. ALL bottles have the same shape and size (very minor deviation). There are only 15 types of bottles, and they each come in series of 186 or 72 identical items. That is an absurd amount of copy-paste. Worse yet, each shelf holds either 18 or 36 bottles, so 186-series cannot fit nicely - they MUST bleed into other shelves.

Let's look at the Book Store. A whopping total of 6070 slim books in a small space piling together. ALL books have the exact same shape, same size, and feature colorful covers, with fronts and backs often being completely different (e.g. dark green & purple back, white & red front). So you can't sort by size, can't sort by shape, and sorting by color is exceedingly difficult. Especially when they are in piles of rainbow vomit.

I managed to sort 960 / 6070 books and it is not getting any easier nor exciting. Worse yet, each shelf is a 3x7 (so 21 sections, each section then holding 12 books). But many books come in series of 8 or 10. I.e. you have a shelf with 21 sections, you fill it up with two types of books for 10 + 10, and there's a hole left. Oh, and yes, this does mean each book can have 96 to 120 identical copies in the store... Which is insane.

It just sucks to sort AND even if you do it, the end result is dissatisfying.

If it wants to be any good, this game needs at least several of its current stores completely thrown out, AT LEAST 5x to 10x more TYPES of items to be introduced, a large variety of sizes and shapes used, and shelves completely redesigned to account for it closely.

Dear dev, please pick virtually any random 3 Tidy Up games, play them, and see what makes them good. You've put a lot of effort into polishing and enriching an experience that fundamentally just does not live up to the quality and excitement of the majority of other Tidy Ups.

[b]A 3D collectathon that [i]feels[/i] like none other![/b]

I tell you, the programming behind this sleepy, slippery snake is masterful -- unlike [i]anything[/i] I've seen before or since this game came out.  Whatever movements you imagine a sentient cartoon snake pulling off, you can do it here, and you'll [i]have[/i] to do it, [b]all of it[/b], to have a prayer of collecting the shiny [b]whatsits[/b].  If you're reading this, you've probably long-since internalized the running, jumping, and momentum of a standard platformer -- so much so that you can immediately start playing any game that uses such mechanics -- but you'll have to change neural gears [i]entirely[/i] to master this new set.  [b]Right Trigger[/b] starts driving forward, [b]Left[/b] grips (you can see him shake with the effort), [b]A[/b] lifts his ophidian noggin, [b]Y[/b] gets the hummingbird friend to grab his tail to reduce rear weight, and the sticks are, well, pretty obvious.  The way it all comes together feels alien at first, like learning to ride a bike when you're a kid, or playing your [i]very[/i] first NES game some Christmas morning.  Once you've got it down, though, it's just another part of you, a brand-new way to play. 

[i]Twining[/i] is the movement you'll have to practice the most of all, because there are [b]tons[/b] of trellises and poles in this game, and you cannot jump.  There's no context-sensitive button, either, that you can press to play a mini-cutscene in which it's done for you; you'll have to [i]manually[/i] wrap the snake up and around -- using [b]A[/b] to lift up the head and upper body, releasing it to droop 'em, [b]A[/b] to lift again, while steering your metaphoric needle with the stick.  Going up vertically, you can rest on horizontal spars; going [i]horizontally[/i] on long bridge-poles, you will have to occasionally [b]grip[/b] to keep the gravity from tugging you to your doom, and then wrap your fore-section tighter, before taking off again with a burst of good traction.  Grip is good for long upward climbs too, but especially important for crossing chasms.  [i]Thread it!  Grip it!  Wrap it tighter!  Weave it![/i]  Don't let out too much forward or rear slack, because this [i]is[/i] still a physics-based game, and Noodle has weight!  Support the length of that big, slinky [b]bad boy[/b] and always seek a stronger hold, and you can do it all.  Remember:  where poles and stones intersect, your grip is stronger!   

I originally tried this about five years ago.  I liked it, was even enamored with the idea, but I just didn't . . . [i]get it[/i].  I couldn't handle the twining movement, and after a few levels of brute forcing and flopping around, I stopped playing.  But recently, I just started it up, began a new game . . . and instantly [i]got it[/i].  I don't know why.  But when you know how to play this, and you just start to intuitively [i]feel[/i] it, this non-human character controls so wonderfully and smoothly that it's unlike anything else.  I had to go find all the [b]whatsits[/b] and put my snaky skills to the test.

Keep in mind this is a sluggish snake, not a fast snake.  He's in no hurry.  For that reason, [i]Snake Pass[/i] is kind of chill, but it's a challenge, too -- you will die a goodly number of times slipping to your doom, and mastery is necessary to get a lot of the [b]whatsits[/b].  Is the story anything to write home about?  Nah, it's just basic collectathon stuff:  the magical thingies are scattered, and you must get 'em.  Are any of the levels really [i]startling[/i] in their design or uniquely memorable?  Not really, but they're crazy-fun to navigate and the world is generally very pretty to look at.  

Really, it's the [b]snake[/b], man, it's all about that [b]snake[/b]!

I love controlling him, I enjoy chillin' with him, I like fighting wind and gravity with him.  The [b]snake[/b] is the game and no other article of vidya on earth has one like him.  If you [i]think[/i] you know of one, tell me.

[h1] Long and short – but both head toward paradise's salvation [/h1]

Snake Pass is a really unusual physics-based platformer. You won’t be jumping or running in the way you’re used to. You control a duo: a snake (either a cobra or a python) and a tiny hummingbird. The story mostly takes a backseat, since all the attention is on the gameplay.

The game has 15 levels, and in each one your goal is to collect three crystals (yellow, pink, and green) to unlock the portal to the next level. For those who love to scavenge every nook and cranny, there are extra challenges: over 20 blue bubbles and 5 golden coins. The coins are hidden in the trickiest, hardest-to-reach spots, acting as mini-secrets for the most dedicated players. And the blue bubbles make the snake bigger, but that doesn’t make it any easier to control.

Physics and controls are both the game's main highlight and its biggest pain point. The developers say the snake’s physics is “unrealistic but believable.” And that’s totally true: you can really feel the weight of the animal, how it flows, and how it grips surfaces. The snake doesn’t feel like some plushy sausage — it has inertia and personality.

But here’s the catch: keyboard controls. Holding down the left mouse button, space, and maneuvering with WASD to keep the snake from tumbling off a ledge isn’t easy. The game clearly seems built for sticks. Luckily, the developers recently confirmed Steam Deck support, and honestly, I think this project shines best on consoles or with a gamepad.

Over time, the levels throw increasingly tricky obstacles at you: from simply wrapping around bamboo poles and underwater sections to levers and wind-based puzzles. The hummingbird isn’t just there for looks — it helps lift the snake’s tail or toss you between little islands, which becomes crucial in the later stages.

The game runs on Unreal Engine 4. No bugs, everything runs smoothly, but subjectively, the graphics feel a bit too glossy and sometimes a little cheap. It’s not entirely clear why this style was chosen, but that’s a matter of taste.

So, Snake Pass is great for developing spatial thinking. It’s a game that makes you think differently, not like in standard platformers. Despite the slightly tricky controls on PC, I can recommend it to anyone looking for a fresh gaming experience and who doesn’t shy away from a challenge.

2D/3D platformers offer some of the most straight forward and entertaining challenges that most can jump in with no issue. There's plenty to collect, improve, and master as the player to keep yourself hooked for many hours. But here comes what is probably the most unique "platformer" to exist, Snake Pass.

Contrary to every other game in the genre, you can't jump, attack, or move normally. And there's also no bosses, lives, or power-ups the more you progress, mainly because your just a limbless snake. 

As a result, you REALLY have to learn and master these controls, as you'll mainly be shuffling on the ground to move, wrap yourself around poles and such to traverse the landscape, and use your body in varying lengths to acquire whatever collectable on your way. You even have a cute little bird companion who offers support by grabbing your tail, which can be a lifesaver in certain situations!

It's somewhat similar to other games that have a frustrating way to "play" like QWOP or Getting Over It, but while those games are designed on purpose against the player, this game is a lot more compact and the difficulty ramps up just enough where it feels fair.

This game will not be for everyone, and I can see how this will turn off players who can't gel with the controls, especially since it can be very easy to get agitated with failure the more you progress. Snake Pass is a simple concept with remarkable execution, and it really deserves a lot of praise for what it's achieved. If you're interested in games with unique controls - things like Getting Over It or QWOP - but feel like those are a bit too focused on being hard rather than enjoyable, Snake Pass is the perfect middle ground. 

Snake Pass is, overall, very simple. It has a simple story that just gives you a goal to follow while snaking around, and light touches with music and atmosphere support the meat and potatoes of this game - the controls. (If you don't enjoy learning new control schemes, this probably isn't for you.) The adaptation of a snake's movement is the core of the platforming challenge; figuring out how snake locomotion works is exactly what makes this game so fascinating. Noodling around with Noodle and finding new ways to overcome obstacles is a refreshing variant on the platformer genre which can sometimes be extremely formulaic. 

I think it was a good call to make Snake Pass light on story and heavy on gameplay. If it had been any more complicated, or if they had spent less time getting the controls to work like a well-oiled machine, it wouldn't have achieved what it did. More story or more presentation would only have distracted from the experience. 

Overall - this is a wonderful gem of a game, especially if, like me, you enjoy novel twists on platformers using unique control schemes. Snake Pass is such an obvious labour of love that I find myself coming back to it again and again.

Hokko Life is a relaxed community and life simulation game developed by Wonderscope Games and published by Team17. Built around creativity, exploration, crafting, and village development, it invites players to leave behind ordinary city life and settle in the peaceful town of Hokko. The basic premise is deliberately uncomplicated, allowing the experience to focus on establishing a new home, becoming acquainted with the local animal residents, and gradually transforming a modest settlement into a personalized community. Its gentle atmosphere makes it particularly suitable for players who prefer games where progress can be made at their own pace without constant pressure or demanding objectives.

Customization is one of Hokko Life's defining qualities. The village is not simply a static location where players complete tasks, because buildings, houses, interiors, and outdoor spaces can gradually be changed to reflect individual preferences. New homes can be constructed for residents, while existing structures can be positioned around the settlement to create a preferred layout. This gives village expansion a personal quality, since two players can approach the same available spaces in noticeably different ways. Instead of merely watching Hokko develop automatically, players have a meaningful role in determining what their version of the community eventually becomes.

The workshop provides even greater creative control. Materials gathered throughout the world can be taken back and turned into furniture and decorative objects, while the design system provides opportunities to create items rather than relying entirely on a fixed collection of predetermined furniture. Different shapes and materials can be manipulated to produce customized creations, allowing enthusiastic designers to spend considerable time experimenting. Furniture can also be painted, further increasing the number of possible appearances. The system can take some patience to master, but it is arguably the feature that gives Hokko Life its clearest personality within the crowded cozy simulation genre.

Creative options extend beyond furniture. Players can produce their own wallpaper and flooring, customize clothing, and use flowers gathered during exploration to create paints. These systems complement one another nicely because gathering resources has a visible purpose. A flower discovered outside the village might eventually contribute to the appearance of a room, while materials collected elsewhere can become part of a newly designed piece of furniture. The Community Store adds another dimension by allowing designs to be shared through creator codes and downloaded for use, while themed creator challenges provide additional motivation for players who particularly enjoy the artistic side of the game.

Life outside the workshop consists of several familiar but appropriate activities. Trees provide wood, mining produces useful materials, and exploration supplies resources needed for construction and crafting. Farming offers another peaceful occupation and fits comfortably into the rural setting. These mechanics are generally straightforward rather than highly technical, which suits the game's accessible design but can leave players seeking a complicated agricultural or economic simulation wanting greater depth. Hokko Life is much more interested in providing a collection of pleasant activities than making any individual system extremely demanding.

Fishing gives players another reason to explore different parts of the environment. Fish have varying behaviors, and craftable bait can help when attempting to catch particular varieties. Insect catching similarly encourages exploration, with a net allowing creatures to be collected and added to the player's discoveries. Neither activity radically changes the game, but together they create useful alternatives whenever decorating, crafting, or farming starts to feel repetitive. Hokko Life works best when these activities are regularly alternated rather than pursued individually for long stretches.

The residents provide the social foundation of the village. Players can get to know the different personalities living around Hokko and gradually build friendships with them. Constructing homes for new inhabitants makes village expansion feel connected to the community rather than functioning purely as a building exercise. Decorating those homes also gives the customization mechanics a practical role beyond designing the player's own residence. Seasonal activities and other events help provide variety, although players expecting an especially deep relationship simulator or an elaborate narrative should keep their expectations measured. The social component supports the cozy atmosphere more than it drives a complicated storyline.

Visually, Hokko Life adopts a colorful and friendly style that immediately communicates its intentions. Its anthropomorphic characters, pleasant countryside, small houses, gardens, and decorative possibilities create an inviting environment. The graphics prioritize charm and readability rather than technical realism, which is a sensible choice for a game where players may spend hours arranging furniture or modifying their village. As the settlement becomes more developed, the player's customization choices become increasingly noticeable, giving the visual progression a satisfying personal element.

The game's relaxed structure is both an advantage and a weakness. Players who enjoy setting personal objectives can easily become absorbed in designing furniture, reorganizing homes, gathering materials, expanding the village, collecting creatures, or perfecting individual rooms. Those who depend on strong narrative momentum or constant rewards may find the experience noticeably slower. Repeated trips for resources and routine activities can eventually become monotonous, particularly when a player is more interested in reaching a specific construction goal than enjoying the process of gathering everything required for it.

This means Hokko Life is at its strongest when approached as a creative sandbox with life-simulation elements rather than as a deeply structured role-playing or management game. Its design tools provide considerably more freedom than its simple appearance initially suggests, while farming, fishing, insect collecting, crafting, exploration, social interaction, and village building create a broad assortment of supporting activities. Not every mechanic has enough complexity to stand alone, but together they establish a comfortable routine that rewards patience and experimentation.

Overall, Hokko Life is a charming and ambitious cozy simulator whose greatest strength is allowing players to leave a personal mark on their surroundings. Wonderscope Games places customization at the heart of the experience, and Team17's published release offers a substantial mixture of furniture creation, house decoration, community development, gathering, farming, fishing, collecting, and social interaction. Some repetition and relatively shallow supporting systems prevent it from reaching the highest level of the genre, especially for players seeking extensive storytelling or sophisticated simulation mechanics. For creative players who enjoy slowly constructing and decorating a community without being rushed, however, Hokko Life provides an appealing and pleasantly flexible escape.

Developer asked us to put in our input so here is my honest take.

As a 100% completetionist, I strive to get everything done, which is incredibly difficult for this game. Positives: 
Good to pair with a second activity like a movie
Fun on Steam deck
Insane customization in terms of building objects.
Very plausible 100%
Mayor Merits make the game more fun

Negatives:
Very limited customization in terms of what the games gives you - only a few furniture items, floors, etc. - its all very random
End game content is extremely grindy, and the Island activities hunting for artifacts it near soul-level difficulty to get an object, and some aren't even guarenteed. I played 10 hours straight and couldn't get this one artifact I wanted, and I do NOT consider myself a Bad player.
A lesser version of animal-crossing

(I put my TL/DR Near the bottom so don't forget to click "Read More")
It's a gender-neutral content creation game...First thing you'll notice when creating a character, there's hairstyles and colors for what are traditionally considered "Boy" and "Girl" Styles, no matter which you pick your character is referenced using non-gender child-like pronouns (e.g. "Tyke"."Dear",etc). There is no female/male selection, only hairstyle and colors(hair/skin/eyes/accents)...

That's the player character, once your in game, the game plays a lot like animal crossing only without the multiplayer features. The Core Gameplay Loop revolves around designing objects and crafting them from materials, but it would be an error to consider this "Open World Survival Craft" since the designs are made from "Parts" that you can assemble into dedicated objects; this system works for any of: Furniture, Wall Patterns, Floor Patterns, and Clothes. With the latter being gated behind certain story events (don't worry this is laid back, it's not a challenge, just time consuming). 

There is dyeing of the parts eventually and you will unlock dyes quite early on. If your like me and love pink the good news is you don't have to suffer my pain now because I'm telling you those white rocks on the beach are chalk, i spent ages looking for that in all the wrong places...

There's also a nice array of brush types for clothing dyes and painting. Normal Furniture is painted "per piece" but clothes and actual paintings or coverings (wall/floor) are free-hand drawings using brushes (with an optional "Fill All" Option)

Basically? The Game is targeted at children between 6 - 16 leaning on simplicity and creativity rather than violence or sex appeal. There are no tasks required of the player that I am not 100% confident a six year old could manage with enough reading skill, as the directions are often simple and to the point. That is not to say it is strictly a "Kid's Game"...but it lends itself well to this facet.

Best Played with a Controller for younger children, but teens and young adults may find the mouse and keyboard more responsive.

My Only Complaint is there is a "Undo" button, but no "Redo" button...

TL/DR: The Game is fit for children interested in arts and crafts, and has enough content of its own to allow even teenagers and young adults to enjoy the experience.

I will start my review off with a reminder that at the time of my poasting this the game is in Early Release. Glitches and some frustrations are par for the course. 

I was so excited when the release date was announced as this game had been on my wishlist for a very long time (multiple years). When the demo became available I jumped on it and was very happy with what I was seeing so far, and of course purchased the game when it came out. 

I'm having an absolute blast playing this. I've only done a few hours but it's been great. Pretty early on in game you get quite a number of blueprints for farm equipment, building items, and furniture, and you don't need to pay for them, so it's more a matter of how much material you can gather. You also get a car pretty early as well, and I'm glad I didn't have to pay to repair it upfront because the amount I'm paying for repairs just from driving is more than enough. I'm happy with quests you can generally skip the driving part as I end up driving like it's grand theft auto then crashing. There are lots of choices for cars once we get some extra cash to burn which is exciting and it looks like you can paint them too.

My only real gripe at the moment is the building mechanics for your house. As I said, you don't need to purchase anything, so as long as you can get the material you can go as big as you want, so I went big. I built out a nice roomy Georgian two-storey style house (aka a big box). Unfortunately, when it came time to put the roof on it hasn't really worked out well. I need a 3rd tier for the middle, so right now I have a hole in the middle of my roof. The verandah roof also cannot be layerd, so you cannot have a nice deep porch at this time if you want it covered. Also, I've been having some issues with decorating the interior as the game gets confused on which level to put the items (first or second storey), so that's been quite finicky.  

I'm really happy with the ability to design my own house instead of having something prefabbed and just updating it, and I'm hoping these little quirks I've been struggling with will be smoothed out overtime. In the meantime I would suggest going small and taking design examples from the houses already existing on the other farm lots. 

Otherwise I haven't run into too many glitches, and it is still in Early Access so I would assume more will be added and/or changed overtime. I'm really excited to see how things progress. At this time I haven't tried romancing anyone, as I've been more focused on organizing the farm plot and building.

Not sure why so many people are having issues with this game. I am having a great time playing it and I think is a fresh look at a farming sim and not some re-skin cookie cutter BS that has been done since Harvest Moon & Stardew Valley. Looking at you Fields of Mistria.

-the driving is fun and not wonky imo. Have had no camera issues with it. The car drifts if you go too fast around a turn....like you do in real life....if people are expecting a GTA or beam.ng type of complex driving experience from this your expectations are WAY too high. Also if you don't like the driving, you can take a bike or THE FCKING SUBWAY??? No one is mentioning the in-game subway system. There is also a "skip driving" option if you want to not drive.

-Love the cop antics. It isn't something I've seen in a farm sim before. Love stealing from my neighbor and then outrunning the cop drones & cars. You can also purchase your own firearm and use it.

-I am so excited to see what other things are going to be added to the game. Hunting is going to be added, as well as a full blown functioning CASINO. Which you can already explore in the game, fully built and fleshed out (just w/o any gambling type games). I can't wait to gambling away all my farming money. I am excited to see where this Monsanto-inspired (iykyk) seed company thing goes, too. Feels like...there is a "good guy" way to run your ranch & make money and a "bad guy" way.

-The map is pretty big, but a large chunk of it is still in development. Excited to see how it fills out.

-About the multiplayer: If you actually read the description AND their website, it does explicitly state the multiplayer functions as so. So it is working as advertised. Those who are complaining about its functionality clearly did not read the game description. Also, I did try this multiplayer, and it is fun. Your friends can do the same things you can. Just build onto your house so yall can live together instead of in different homes a la Stardew Valley. 

-About the online connection: I understand how needing to be connected to the internet 100% of the time while playing even single player can be cumbersome. But I did not have the connectivity issues others were experiencing. Not single player or multiplayer. 

-the game obviously needs some polish; but also remember it is early access and they are very explicit in it being so. The player avatars look a little strange, the dialog has some grammatical errors & typos, and there are some very minor quality of life issues (when using a tool & not hitting anything, it consumes energy). But the devs are super open to feedback. It states in the game description here they really want the community to be involved with its development, and there is even an in-game function to send the devs a message. Have not seen that with any early access games I have played previously (maybe others know of some?)

TL:DR: I see the vision the developers are going for and am excited to see where this goes, as it feels like a fresh unique new look on the ever increasing shovelware-flooded farming sim genre. The Positives:Let's start with the positive:
 The graphics are amazing. The subway and bike ideas are incredibly smart alternatives for players who don't like driving. Personally, I have nothing against the driving mechanics. The car is fully controllable. Of course, if you take a corner at 100 km/h, it will not respond immediately—but that is how it works in real life too.The world is big and beautifully designed. I can clearly see that the developers put their heart and soul into this game, which is why it is really hard for me to criticize it. However, as a paying customer, I believe it is my right, and as a gamer, it is my duty to try to help improve the game by pointing out its issues. I cannot fully recommend the game in its current state at this price point, but I would definitely change my mind if development continues in the right direction.
The Negatives:
Lack of Crop Options & Descriptions: Having only 2 to 3 types of crops per season is not enough. Additionally, there is a lack of information when buying items. When I purchase a multi-harvest crop, I expect it to last the whole season unless specified otherwise. The same goes for blueprints—a few are intuitive, but most are not.
Plot Demolishing Delays: Waiting for a tilled plot to disappear is highly frustrating. If you invest over 16k credits in Zerkonite to make a sprinkler, you shouldn't have to wait 3 extra days for old plots to vanish. To make matters worse, if it rains or if you accidentally water that field, the waiting timer resets. Please implement a shovel tool that players can buy to manually revert fields back to normal grass and clear out dry patches instantly.
Wonky Building System: The building mechanics feel a bit unpolished. Many times, construction pieces and furniture do not snap together as they should, especially if a roof is already in place. Speaking of roofs, the roof above the garage does not hide properly. It seems that if the character is standing at ground level, the hiding visual mechanics fail to trigger.
Tedious Looting (Clicking Fatigue): Having to click on every single piece of stone or log is incredibly time-consuming. Combined with the camera angles, it becomes frustrating. Please bind a key for bulk picking (for example, holding Ctrl+Click should pick up everything within a certain radius of the character). For players who work and have limited time to relax and enjoy the game, this click-heavy mechanic is a major drawback.
Minor Bugs: I found a couple of bugs. They aren't game-breaking, but they need fixing. Once, my car got stuck in the terrain with the wheels half-sunken, preventing me from driving away. Another time, I couldn't pick up my chickens after purchasing them. Fortunately, both issues resolved themselves the next morning after sleeping
Lack of Mid-to-Late Game Content: There simply isn't enough content yet for a €25 game. By the end of Summer, I found myself with nothing to do besides watering plants and feeding chickens. There is no cooking, no jam/juice making, and no pickling. I don't know if these features unlock much later or if they just aren't in the game yet, but the gameplay loop stalls out quickly.
There are a few more minor issues, but these are the main ones for now.
 Best regards, and best of luck with future development!

ServiceIT: You can do IT, developed by picture4u and published by PlayWay S.A. together with FreeMind S.A., sets out with an appealing and somewhat unconventional premise: transforming the everyday work of an IT technician into an interactive simulation. Rather than focusing on spectacle or fast-paced gameplay, it builds its identity around problem-solving, technical tasks, and the gradual growth of a small service business. It’s the kind of concept that immediately stands out, especially for players curious about the inner workings of computers and networks, but it also carries the risk of feeling overly niche if not executed with enough depth and polish.

The gameplay centers on running your own IT service company, starting from modest beginnings and slowly expanding your capabilities through contracts and upgrades. Early tasks are relatively straightforward, involving basic repairs like replacing hardware components, cleaning PCs, or diagnosing simple software issues. As you progress, the game introduces more advanced responsibilities, including configuring networks, managing servers, and even engaging in light cybersecurity activities. This layered progression is one of the game’s more compelling aspects, as it mirrors a learning curve that feels grounded in real-world concepts. There’s a clear sense of growth as tasks become more complex, pushing players to understand not just what to do, but why they are doing it.

A notable strength lies in how the game attempts to simulate the breadth of IT work rather than focusing on a single aspect. It blends physical interaction—such as assembling and repairing hardware—with more abstract processes like navigating command-line interfaces or setting up network systems. This variety helps keep the experience from becoming too repetitive early on, and it gives the impression of a living, evolving profession. The inclusion of a loose narrative involving a hacker interfering with your operations adds a bit of intrigue, breaking up the routine of contract-based gameplay and giving players a reason to stay invested beyond pure simulation.

However, the game struggles significantly with execution, particularly on the technical side. Bugs and instability are persistent issues, often interfering with basic tasks or halting progress altogether. Problems such as missing items, malfunctioning objectives, or sudden crashes can disrupt the flow of gameplay and diminish the satisfaction of completing jobs. In a simulation that depends heavily on precision and consistency, these technical shortcomings are especially noticeable and can quickly turn what should be a rewarding experience into a frustrating one.

There are also design concerns that become more apparent over time. While the early hours feel fresh and engaging, the game’s depth begins to plateau as players become familiar with its systems. Many tasks start to feel similar, and the lack of more advanced or varied challenges can limit long-term appeal. Additionally, while the game introduces complex ideas like networking and server management, these systems are often simplified to the point where they may not fully satisfy players looking for a deeper or more realistic simulation. The interface and controls don’t always help in this regard, as they can feel unintuitive and occasionally cumbersome when juggling multiple responsibilities.

Visually, the game adopts a straightforward, functional approach. The environments and tools are designed with clarity in mind, ensuring that players can easily identify components and complete tasks. While this practicality suits the simulation aspect, it also means the presentation lacks visual flair or memorable design. The progression of your workspace—from a basic setup to a more equipped operation—does provide a sense of advancement, even if the overall aesthetic remains relatively plain.

Despite its issues, ServiceIT: You can do IT still manages to carve out a unique space for itself. Its educational undertones and focus on real-world skills make it stand out among simulation games, offering an experience that can be both informative and engaging when it works as intended. It has the foundation of something genuinely interesting, especially for players with an interest in technology or problem-solving, but it falls short of its full potential due to its lack of refinement.

In the end, ServiceIT: You can do IT feels like a project with strong ideas that hasn’t yet reached the level of polish needed to fully support them. It offers moments of satisfaction and a compelling core concept, but these are often overshadowed by technical problems and limited depth in the later stages. For those willing to overlook its rough edges, it can still provide an enjoyable and occasionally insightful experience, but it remains a title that would benefit greatly from further development and improvement.

Fun simulation game; the graphics is nice and the physics is not that bad overall. 
It is playable and enjoyable, but there are bugs; and other issues in terms of polish that should be easy to address at this point:

1) There are some nasty bugs where you go to pick up an item from the solder station, and try to put it on the shelves, which cause the item to freak out the physics engine until it disappear through the floor. Had to cancel few contracts because of this bug. If it is not possible to add items to the shelves close to the solder station, you should disable the action there, and just allow to use the rack for storing items.

2) interacting with the computer or packages is all over the place; you hold the LMB to open the box, then the item is in your hands, but when you are interacting with other items, like laptops, you need to use Shift+LMB. The whole game has these little inconsistencies in how interactions are done, and would be great if you could just align everything to the same control scheme. On a computer for example pressing ESC quit the computer interaction, so you are forced to use the X to close the window to move between applications. 

3) Tutorials messages require you to hold E to dismiss; and sometimes they get stuck so the game has to be restarted/reloaded.

4) Juggle between the phone to read instructions to perform and work on a computer is OK, except when you need to read also the commands for terminal. Would be great to have a "scratchpad" on the computer so you can pin the instructions on the screen, while you use the phone to read the commands syntax. Or allow the terminal to print out the commands list (man command would be great); so we can just use the keyboard in the terminal directly to get the commands syntax help. Eventually you remember the commands; except for things you don't do that often, so it would help newcomers.

5) Some instructions on the jobs/contracts are not clearly explained. For example took me 10 minutes trying to log in on a FTP for a job, before realize that you have to go to the customer location for that activity. It could have been easily solved if a tutorial message would explain that some jobs are done from your computer, while others are done at the customer location or on the customer hardware shipped to you.

6) Terminal is fun to use but barebone. PWD for example is not implemented; SSH is not implemented and instead you connect via FTP (which is incorrect, you cannot use a remote terminal via FTP if you are working with a company ). DF is also not implemented so it is quite hard to figure out how many partitions a drive has (and there is a job that ask you to restore a partition). Would be great to see the terminal become more and more similar to its real counterpart

7) The soldering station has nice items, although you can turn off the multimeter but can't turn off the DC power supply? It is fun to swap SMD components but I hope there is more gameplay than just swap resistors, as would be nice to connect to these SBC via serial port to test if they actually work, instead of just power them up and see if the light is red or green

I give it a 6 out of 10, for what it is offering now; worth the money but hopefully the game will be more realistic, adding more repairs for the boards and more realistic terminal.

Here is an update to my previous review – to be continued.

Basically, would  a great IT simulation game . For people who are already familiar with the stuff (like me), it's not so difficult and easy to understand. For people who are new to the subject or interested in it, it is very educational. It comes close to reality in many ways.

The attention to detail is really good, and you can tell that the developers know their stuff and have added some great features.

I like the concept and would love to play it with a good feeling, but unfortunately that's not possible at the moment – see below.

I'm surprised that the game is relatively resource-intensive at the highest quality setting, even though not that much happens. It's not a visual masterpiece, nor is a content  monster. You mainly move around in three of your rooms or your office or in  one room at the customer's location.  But ok,  you can play it. 

Now unfortunately the huge list of bad points:

- Only one save game. There is no option to load a previous save game if errors occur which are too often.
- The game sometimes freezes, for example when copying and pasting from a smartphone to the terminal.
- Sometimes the game crashed random and completely .
- Copy and paste does not always work immediately and often has to be repeated.
- The controls and key assignments are very poorly designed and frustrating. ESC here but not there, Tab, Shift+Key, Alt+Key,  CTRL+Key, right-click in all variations. Hey, it's not ARMA3. Even after hours of playing, you still don't know your way around. How on earth could they make it so complicated?
- The editing mode is not well designed at all. It's a real pain to use.
- If you repair marketplace devices and don't finish them right away and want to continue the next day because you have to order parts, the electronic components hover above the motherboard.
- Spare parts often disappear, especially if you press the wrong keys.
- If you remove defective server parts from the customer's servers and take them with you, they are no longer defective in the office...good for youi but...weired.  Sometimes orders cannot be completed because something is glitching again...and again.
- Sometimes tasks cannot be completed because something is glitching again.
- Tasks within assignments are often marked as incomplete. - Luckily, when you finish the assignment, it is mostly considered complete—but this is not always the case.
- If you don't do the tasks in order, you may not be able to perform or complete the previous steps. So you have to proceed in order, even though this shouldn't really be necessary.
- It also often happens that even if you do everything right, the tasks are not evaluated.
- The smartphone is quite nice, but it's a lot of unnecessary fiddling around.
- A window layout, or the ability to move or minimize windows on the desktop, would be very practical and helpful. You can only open or close the windows. 
- A simple text editor is missing and would be very helpful, or rather, it's actually a must-have. - The automatically generated notes on the smartphone are insufficient and somewhat annoying because you always have to go back to the home screen.
- An inventory overview of all your spare parts stock would be very helpful.
- Why do I always have to buy new server keys? Because if I put it on my desk, it's gone the next day. That's why you should always keep it in your inventory.
- The terminal, or input console, is more than minimalistic. No autocomplete, which means you either have to learn the commands (As Linux user it's not dramatic but not handy) or use the smartphone app, which then becomes a back-and-forth process (see missing text editor).
- In a server tutorial (Network Master) where you have to install cables, you'll have a hard time. - I had to start over again and again because either the patch cable disappeared or something else happened. I haven't been able to finish it yet. Frustration Overflow...

These are definitely not all the points, but enough. 
There are a few minor things that I can't think of right now that I haven't even mentioned. It's just too much. Or maybe I've just come to peace with it. I don't know. 

So, if you can ignore the negative points, you should go ahead and buy the game. Because it actually has huge potential. But only if it's on sale.

I really don't feel good about giving a negative review, especially because I like to support small development teams.  And the idea is great.
But I can't recommend it with a good feeling. Because a lot of the points I mentioned shouldn't be there. Like I said in my previous review. Small mistakes here and there aren't a problem. But all together, it's just too much.

I hope they make improvements and that the development team doesn't get discouraged by the criticism. I wish them all the best. Really. The overall concept is great. 

But we have to be realistic, and if we're supposed to buy and support it, then improvements definitely need to be made. 

I might update my review later, eventually once I've finished the game... if I don't lose interest.

If you're looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if you're looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.

Ingredients:

1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie

Directions:

1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Tempest, developed by HeroCraft and published by HeroCraft PC, is a pirate-themed action RPG that invites players to live out the age-old fantasy of commanding a ship on the high seas. The game blends open-world exploration, naval combat, and light role-playing elements into a single seafaring adventure. From the moment you set sail, the sense of freedom is striking—you can chart your own course across the ocean, take on quests, engage in trade, hunt sea monsters, or simply plunder other ships for profit. Unlike many pirate games that focus on scripted storytelling, Tempest leans heavily into player choice and open-ended discovery. Its strength lies in the feeling of captaining your own vessel through dangerous waters and watching your modest sloop gradually evolve into a fearsome warship adorned with unique upgrades and mythical enhancements.

The world of Tempest is spread across multiple regions, each dotted with ports, factions, and opportunities for wealth or trouble. The player can take contracts for various factions, engage in smuggling, or form temporary alliances—all while keeping an eye on the wind and the weather that affect how their ship handles. Trading is straightforward but rewarding: goods fluctuate in price between islands, encouraging long-distance commerce for profit. Combat, meanwhile, offers the kind of cinematic tension that makes piracy so thrilling. Ship-to-ship battles rely on positioning, timing, and cannon management, with the choice of ammunition types adding a layer of tactical decision-making. Watching cannonballs tear through enemy hulls while waves crash around your vessel is deeply satisfying, and the addition of boarding mechanics allows for close-quarters chaos when you close in for the kill.

As the journey unfolds, Tempest introduces fantastical elements that set it apart from traditional pirate simulations. Mythical creatures like the Kraken and Leviathan lurk in the deep, and players can acquire enchanted crystals that imbue their ships with supernatural powers—reflecting projectiles, boosting speed, or summoning monstrous allies. These touches of fantasy add spice to the experience, though they may not appeal to purists seeking a historically grounded pirate adventure. Still, they help keep the gameplay loop fresh by mixing seafaring realism with magical spectacle. The balance between these two tones—the historical and the mystical—is one of Tempest’s more distinctive qualities, even if it doesn’t always mesh perfectly. It’s clear that HeroCraft wanted to create a world that felt larger than life, where folklore and adventure coexist just beyond the horizon.

Visually, Tempest performs admirably for an indie project. The ocean is dynamic and beautiful, with changing lighting and weather patterns that make each voyage feel unique. Ship models are well detailed, and there’s a gratifying sense of weight to how they move across the waves. While not pushing the limits of graphical fidelity, the art direction captures the romanticism of high-seas adventure. The user interface, however, can sometimes feel dated and clunky. Navigating menus, equipping upgrades, or managing trade goods lacks the fluidity of more polished RPGs, occasionally breaking immersion. The audio design fares better, with a rousing orchestral score and the distant boom of cannons enhancing the mood. The overall presentation succeeds in drawing the player into a world that feels alive, even if it’s occasionally rough around the edges.

In terms of pacing, Tempest’s open structure can be both a blessing and a curse. The freedom to explore means you can spend hours trading and upgrading your ship before diving into combat-heavy missions. However, that same freedom can lead to repetition, as many of the game’s activities—raiding merchant convoys, collecting bounties, or escorting allies—follow similar patterns. The quest variety isn’t deep, and over time, the repetition of naval battles may diminish the sense of novelty. Yet for those who enjoy the meditative rhythm of exploration and ship management, this repetition becomes part of the charm. There’s something undeniably relaxing about sailing from port to port, selling rum and silk, then fending off a sudden pirate ambush before returning to calm seas. It captures the ebb and flow of a pirate’s life, alternating between moments of chaos and tranquility.

Tempest’s RPG systems, while not overly complex, give a sense of progression that keeps you invested. Earning gold and reputation allows you to purchase better ships, weapons, and crew members, while upgrading your vessel with mystical crystals adds strategic variety. Crew morale plays a subtle role in determining how efficiently your ship performs, reminding you that your success depends on the people who keep the cannons loaded and the sails trimmed. The game’s difficulty is forgiving enough to welcome newcomers but offers enough challenge to satisfy those who seek tactical naval combat. Despite occasional technical hiccups and a few bugs, the overall experience is stable and smooth, especially after post-launch updates that refined many of its earlier issues.

Ultimately, Tempest captures the essence of what makes pirate adventures compelling: the thrill of freedom, the danger of the unknown, and the satisfaction of building your own legend at sea. It’s not a game that tries to overwhelm with cinematic storytelling or complex systems—it’s a game that trusts the player to create their own tales of adventure. While it suffers from limited quest diversity and occasional clumsy interface design, its charm lies in the authenticity of its ambition. Sailing across the ocean, battling foes, and discovering mysterious creatures provides a sense of escapism that few pirate games manage to sustain so effectively. For players who crave an open-world experience driven by exploration, trade, and naval combat, Tempest offers a voyage worth taking. It may not reach the heights of AAA polish, but its heart, atmosphere, and spirit of adventure make it a rewarding journey for anyone who has ever dreamed of hoisting the black flag and claiming the sea as their own.

20hr update: Game is still pretty solid after 20 hours, but I have some concerns: 

The stuttering and latency on even low quality graphics setting is a bit concerning. You'd think a game with relatively small maps and only a few dozen enemies spawned at any given time would run fairly smoothly on low graphics, but it's really quite a strenuous game to run on your PC at this stage of development. I'm hopeful that the developer continues their efforts to optimize the game, but at this point the game turns my competent gaming setup into a furnace in minutes, and before I've finished a 5-8 minute round my PC is already throttling my CPU down. Especially an issue with the cast animations, I hope the developer can offer some lower-quality options for those in the settings in the future.

The difficulty scaling is pretty wild, you can be killed in under a second by even a single low-level enemy on just normal difficulty. I get that mages are squishy, but we're kind of missing the forest for the trees here. It's not fun to be this fragile even after 20 hours of grinding upgrades. Rule of fun should prevail and allow us to have more upgrades for regeneration, shield recovery/performance, reflecting damage, freezing foes who touch us, other hexes and spells which would give users some variety on the defensive side when dealing with mobs/bosses. I don't expect to have a mage tank, but I do expect to enjoy playing the game and not have to flee from every single creep fearing that even a single hit may end my run. Maybe for the first 5-10 hours this would be fine, but not after grinding 20 hours of upgrades, I want to feel a bit more powerful in the defense department. 

Some aspects of the game are genuinely un-fun, unfair to the player, and hopefully will be addressed soon. For example ranged enemies will shoot directly at you even if they are facing the opposite direction, you can't 'juke' them until the arrow is in the air. The arrow passes through their body to target you precisely. The arrows also pass through buildings, rocks, trees, etc. Another example is enemies spawn already drawing their bow perfectly aimed at you, or sword-carrying enemies damaging you before their sword-swing animation even triggers. I'm not looking for perfect realism, it's a fantasy videogame, but come on. I have to charge every attack (via cooldowns/reloading) and they spawn midway through their charge-up, I can't even hit them with a spell before their first shot is already off. It's great to make a game like this difficult, even punishingly so, but when the difficulty comes from cheap tactics or unintended outcomes like this, it just turns me off. 

My only other concern is a tougher one to address than the others, it's the fact that after 20 hours total playing time over the course of a couple of weeks, I'm getting bored of the game. It is incredibly repetitive, with little difference between runs unlike every other popular roguelite game where your choices make big differences to the run, which makes every run feel distinct.  Every run feels the same right now, maybe because you get to pick too many cards on a run and end up basically getting to pick ALL the cards by the time you finish. Or maybe the root cause is related to the lack of variety of enemies/behaviours, or the lack of variety in the pool of spells you get to pick from. If this is a 'pick it up once in a while, play a couple hours a month' kind of game for you, you probably won't feel this way. I like to play an hour or two of the same game every night until I complete it, then move on to a new game, and I'm finding this one is just a bit boring in this format, which means I probably won't complete it.  Right now upgrades aren't very interesting (and descriptions lack important details), new cards and craftable gear both unlock at a painfully slow pace. If everything was explained perfectly in the upgrades, I'd have more motivation to grind towards specific upgrades, but with vague descriptions and limited impact, they're just not tantalizing enough to make me want to 'squeeze in just one more run' which really is how a good game from this genre should make you feel. Sometimes I'm honestly looking forward to the end of a run because it's been nothing but kiting and shooting 2 spells. 

I've given a few concerns here, but if I ended the review there it would be unfair to the developer. I recognize they are putting a considerable effort into the game, especially right now in preparation for version 1.0. The game is already quite fun for an hour or two at a time, and it has tremendous potential. It has a consistent and thoughtful developer who is communicating a lot, and the game is priced very competitively. These positive factors outweigh all of my concerns mentioned above, so even if I don't complete the game and unlock every little thing, I will definitely get more than my money's worth just from enjoying the game occasionally. Thanks to the developer for bringing this game to the market, I hope you sell a lot of copies and can fund future updates because this game deserves more attention and has the potential to become a big deal in the roguelite and bullet hell genres if you keep building on what you've already made so far.

This game for me right now is worth a mixed review, but I am giving it the thumbs up because it is really fun to play and it is cheap.

Now, why is it mixed if it is so much fun to play? Because it is a lot of fun as an fps, feeling as if they would have mixed Wizard of Legend with Vampire Hunters (said in a different way, as if they have turned Wizard of Legend into an arena FPS roguelike). However, the roguelite/like elements are underwhelming and incredibly grindy. 

Let's talk about how a run works. It is pretty similar to games like Risk of Rain 2; you get into the level, where you get to kill as many enemies as you want, while getting currency that will help you level up to get upgrades, but, be careful, because the longer you play, the harder the enemies get. After killing a specific number of enemies you will be able to activate the boss fight, and you will have to kill it to proceed (again, you don't really HAVE to, but game will get harder). That doesn't sound too bad, does it? The main problem here is that enemies escalate way too fast, while, on the other hand, the upgrades you are getting are similar to "5% more critical chance", "8% more shield", "2% more critical damage", "10% more max hp", so you better rush it, because, after 20 minutes, you will die in 2 hits... and here I am talking about medium difficulty (in hard difficulty after 10 minutes all enemies feel like a boss and it takes over a minute to kill one, while they can instakill you, turning the game into an insanely tedious experience).

The previous paragraph might make you wonder "but is there any kind of permanent progession to help?". And the answer is YES, THERE IS, but it is even worse than the upgrades during a run. After a good run, you can get around 2k gold, which sounds like a lot, but it will help you get 10% more max HP, 1% AOE, 0.2 more critical damage and maybe one more minimal thing... And that is considering if you extracted, because, yeah, this is a extraction roguelike (I forgot to mention); if you don't, you barely get anything. 

Also, sad problems, at least during my last runs I faced a few bugs that made my game crashed or just forced me to restart the game, losing the run... but at least I see the developer working on updates.

So, if it doesn't bother you to be grinding dozens of hours for slight upgrades, as long as gameplay is fun, this might be for you.

Oh, right, there are also some extra characters and a lot of spells to try, but they use the same currency that you use for the other upgrades (and they are EXPENSIVE), so it didn't really feel worth it... I honestly feel like characters should be unlocked in different ways, same with spells (Risk of Rain 2 style, by completing challenges or just beating levels).

Still, I mentioned so many problems that could make you think this is a bad review... But the action is just so good that I had a lot of fun playing it, and I feel like they can turn this into an awesome game with the proper balance, so I will just keep the good review in the meantime, hoping to see some nice updates.

If you were to play only briefly every day, just enough to advance each bear's story as much as you could; this game has you playing over 120 days to experience all of its content. There's a fine line between creating a chill no-pressure type of game and creating one that milks its content in a way that is utterly disdainful of its players.

If you want to play a game that deals with anthropomorphic animals at the end of their lives with emotionally powerful narratives, then I recommend skipping this entirely and go play Spiritfarer instead. If you want to play a game like Animal Crossing, then go play Animal Crossing instead. If you want to play a game that doles out minuscule slices of content and narrative that will have you grinding at every step to unlock, then by all means suffer at the hands of this game.

First time playing a cozy game tied to real-world timer, and I must say, it is not to my liking, ultimately. 
TL;DR I do not recommend it to anyone who wants to progress at their own pace, who wants to shape the environment around themselves, who look for a bit more variety in missions than simple fetch quests, who look for interesting characters or a story that even has the slightest bit of stakes in it. (Yes, cozy game, got that, but a cozy game can still have an entertaining story. This one doesn't)

Sure it is nice to have an hour-two hours of stuff to do every day, however, that also persists when you would have more time to actually progress the goddamn story, e.g. on the weekend. Once you get like 8-9 residents on your island, the progression slowls down insanely, made worse by the fact that at this point 8 times out of 10 most of the bears will just give you pointless fetchquests to run around the island and try to find the same needles in a haystack over and over and over again. (Even the story-progressing missions are fetch quests, let's not get things mixed up)
The island also constantly changes around you, so you are guarantee to get stuck on obstacles while you are running around for Worthless Letter #9456 to hopefully somehow spot in the middle of the biggest chaos imaginable. Also the hints on where to find certain fetch quest objects are super unhelpfully vague, especially when the whole damn island is constantly changing.
I've also read that you never get the option to clear out trees, bushes and rocks, so you are never be able to create a clearing for example for your garden and/or animals.
The Interact action ("E") is buggy as all hell - you may stand next to the very thing you want to interact with, hit E, and instead your character decides to literally walk dozens of meters away and interact with a random thing you did not want to. (Happens to me at least 5 times during a daily session)
Overall, the game feels restrictive, mind-numbingly repetitive, cluttered, the characters reveal so little about themselves for so long that they become irrelevant, the story is ultimately boring because there are no stakes even though the letters from your Scoutmaster is constantly joking about how you might die (cozy game, duh), and the Interact button is often bugged out.

If you play every other day, the story moves much more smoothly. 

Another negative about this game's real time / limited playtime aspect is that it's easy to lose track of each bear's storyline. I was interested at first, but as the game stretched on I started forgetting where we left off, and the emotional impact was lessened.

I think it would take most people around 6 months of diligent playing to complete this game. It took 66 days for the credits to roll (I hadn't even unlocked all the bears), 80 days to unlock the final bear, and 96 days to complete all the bears' memories. remember, playing every day DOES NOT finish the game faster.

One of the most annoying parts of this game was that you sometimes need to wait for one bear to give you a tasks, so you can complete another bear's quest, so there would be days where I'm waiting and waiting on one bear to move forward with the game. The worst was when I had the peak number of bears unlocked (a few days before day 66) and I had a complete back up of quests because each bear is waiting on the next, so I only ended up doing one quest per day, untill I finally got the quest reward I needed to complete all the other bears' quests.

I think this game is good for the super casual gamer, who doesn't play many games, and doesn't have a lot of time to play either.

Weed Shop 4: Highland – A LOT of potential, but still needs work!

As of October 19th, the game is honestly three times better than it was when I first played it in July. It's finally playable, and you can actually make progress. However, there's still a LOT of room for improvement.
As someone who played Weed Shop 3, I had pretty high expectations for this game. While it's definitely improving, there are still several things that need to be addressed.

THE GOOD:
- Better graphics: The graphics are definitely an improvement over Weed Shop 3, but they're EXTREMELY buggy. I wouldn't recommend playing on high settings because of the constant stuttering and freezing.
- New map: The new map is more interesting and has a lot of potential, but it still feels unfinished.
- Still fun: Despite all its problems, the game is still enjoyable. It's definitely not the same experience as Weed Shop 3, but there's still fun to be had.
- Constant improvements: The game has improved A LOT since I first played it. The developers are clearly working on it, and the difference between July and October is noticeable. I really appreciate that, and it gives me hope for the future of the game.

THE BAD:
- NO BACKGROUND MUSIC!! Seriously, how does a game like this have absolutely no background music? It's ridiculous, although I believe this will eventually be fixed. Music was a big part of the atmosphere in Weed Shop 3, and its absence here is really noticeable.
- Unfinished menus: The menus feel extremely unpolished, with some really weird background images. They just don't look finished, and the overall presentation lacks personality.
- Confusing beginning: The game barely explains anything when you start playing. Most of the mechanics have to be figured out on your own, which makes the early experience unnecessarily confusing.
- ANNOYING WATER SYSTEM: The whole water mechanic is incredibly frustrating. It gets better later on, especially once you reach the city, but having to constantly buy water bottles and refill them over and over again is absolutely unbearable. Even with the recent improvements, it still feels like unnecessary busywork rather than an enjoyable mechanic.
- NO EMPLOYEES!! I'm currently level 27, and there's STILL no option to hire someone to work at the shop and sell products for you. Having to manage everything yourself gets frustrating, especially as you progress. At this point, I really expected to have some sort of automation.
- BIG BUT EMPTY MAP: The map is huge, but there's barely anything going on. So many areas feel empty, and the whole world lacks life. It has potential, but right now, everything just feels unfinished.
- Tedious inventory management: Managing items can feel unnecessarily complicated. Too many basic actions require repetitive work, making certain parts of the game more frustrating than they should be.
- Lack of meaningful progression: Leveling up unlocks new things, but the game still lacks meaningful improvements to how you run your business. At level 27, I expected more management options, automation, and a greater sense of progression. Sometimes it feels like you're just doing the same things over and over again.
- Missing the charm of Weed Shop 3: This is probably one of my biggest complaints. Weed Shop 3 had a certain atmosphere and personality that made it special. Weed Shop 4 has better graphics and a bigger world, but somehow feels less alive. The lack of music, empty areas, and unfinished mechanics make it feel like something is missing. Bigger doesn't always mean better.

FINAL THOUGHTS:
Despite all these complaints, I'm still giving Weed Shop 4 a positive review.
The game has improved MASSIVELY over the past few months, and I genuinely enjoy playing it. There's definitely a good game here, and I can see the potential.
However, compared to Weed Shop 3, it still feels like a step backward in several areas. The previous game had more personality, a better atmosphere, and an overall more complete feeling.
The biggest problem with Weed Shop 4 isn't that it's a bad game. It's that so much of it still feels unfinished.
There's a LOT of potential here. Hopefully, with more updates, Weed Shop 4 can eventually become even better than Weed Shop 3.

Weed Shop 4: Highland has the same fun core loop I loved in Weed Shop 3, but now with multiplayer, something I've wanted since Weed Shop 3. Building a weed shop from nothing, growing, selling, and expanding with a friend finally being a thing has me genuinely hyped. It's early, but the start is already really fun.

It's Early Access. That's the label on the box, not an excuse. You're buying something unfinished, rough edges included, with a roadmap to fix it.

On the AI-assisted art and music: this is a small team, maybe even one person, not a studio with a full art department on payroll. Leaning on AI for early concepts and rougher passes, then having a human finish and integrate them, is a reasonable budget call for an outfit this size, not laziness. Honestly, even if they hadn't touched it up by hand at all, I don't think it would've mattered much.

That said, they didn't disclose any of this when the game launched, and I'm not going to defend that part. Whether that was because they genuinely didn't realize it needed disclosing or they just didn't think about it, it doesn't matter. It should've been on the store page from day one, and it wasn't. That's a legitimate miss on their part, full stop.

The "Disable AI" toggle now reads: "Disable AI-generated content and continue pretending you're morally superior while consuming algorithm slop everywhere else." I think that's funny, and honestly kind of accurate. Half the people yelling about this in a $20 indie game are scrolling AI-generated garbage on their phones for hours a day without a second thought. Maybe not everyone, but if you spent time trying to strip all the AI out of your feeds and news, you're probably just trying to look more sophisticated about it, and honestly, I (and a lot of people I know) think that's a bit of a weird hill to die on.
