The problem with Planet Centauri is that it is a sandbox, and only a sandbox. Competing products such as Terraria and Starbound are simply so much better. Terraria has tons of odd random loot to keep you going. Starbound has a complex story you'll want to complete. Both of these games have interesting NPCs. Terraria exploration finds you new NPCs and new loot. Starbound exploration finds you new planets, new cities, and more stories.

Planet Centauri drops you on a planet and says "yeah, now do whatever or something". That's it. Same tedium, similar mechanics, but there's none of the driving passion that made those great. However, there are some positives that deserve mention. The combat combo system with special moves is way more robust and complex than either of its competitors. Sadly, that's just not a substitute for a meaningful world to explore.

So, at face value, Planet Centauri is a wonderful game.

I spent a few days on this, going in blind to something that looked promising and hopefully refreshing, only to realize I was waiting to for the fun to begin that whole time. This felt underbaked; the skeleton of something awesome is here, but omfg it is torture in it's current state.

-Crafting:
UI for literally every menu is clunky and fighting your inventory for screen real-estate. I truly believe there needed to be a tutorial to demo how I should even engage with all the menus to play as intended, the design felt that hostile. Infinite character inventory space feels surprisingly cumbersome and labyrinthine given the sheer quantity of unique, yet unutilized, items that are acquired in the due course of all your activities. I found that the pervasive menu-jank made me avoid entering crafting menus as much as possible.

-Farming and cooking:
every meal you can make requires like a million different ingredients. It takes eons to get a farm set up / discover useful ingredients -> these are usually fun adventures in any other game, but both prepping the literal dirt and finding foods is/feels completely random and irrespective of the effort you put in. The benefits of meals you manage to craft are extremely underwhelming and lackluster. Harvesting and replanting never becomes less of a chore (I really wish I stopped engaging with this loop sooner)

-mining:
it's so, so painfully slow + the first armor set increases mining speed to a "tolerable" degree -> further ruining the activity as you try to progress through armor sets and realize you NEED the speed boost to make this agony last as little as possible. This activity is eventually, suddenly, completely obviated by magic (I did not have the patience to get to that point)

-Combat?
you start with essentially your full move set for melee: the animations feel super cool, but rarely do the attacks perform as demonstrated. The character skills barely offer actual utility and are absolutely overshadowed by your basic attack. Armor specific skills actually offer great utility and are fun to use! It's just too bad you need to swap armor constantly -> very tedious to do as well. 

++++++++++++  This was the straw the broke the camel's back  ++++++++++++
The magic spells initially looked awesome; I was most excited to learn how spell creation actually worked in this game and mess around with making crazy stuff. That appeared like a solid part of the combat for this game (maybe not a main focus of this sort of game, but like something that was going to make the experience very interesting and spice things up)

> Quickly found the crafting UI to be inscrutable more so than anything else I encountered; online resources barely aided this, but it's more the fault of how complex + unintuitive the system  is
> On top of that there's basically no progression as far as what spells you have access to working with. Save for a few types that are locked behind bosses, you can immediately work with all options, and there is very little variety
> The real progression is simply making spells that launch an additional / beefier projectile. I think that is what endgame content for basically any other similar game boils down to, but that's the entry point for magic here
> at least from what all I could tolerate playing through, damage type match ups with monsters were rarely important at best; therefore, there are very clear studs and duds among those options
>>> ON TOP OF THAT, at least early on, it is prohibitively resource intensive. The game already does not respect your time gathering other resources, and the resources for crafting spells are purely RNG based drops

If I could have started off the game being able to play with spells and warm up to this system, I think it would have been tolerable. But up to the point where spells could even have begun to be crafted and utilized, it feels like a waste of time to even consider transitioning away from melee or mixing spells into combat for their utility, i.e. range (and nothing else)
Abandoned.

And you'll wish everything required half as many resources as it does. 

Also, as others have pointed out, there's a partial absence of Quality of Life features and partial absence of information and a definite presence of glitches. (You can't split a stack of items in half, so feeding my chickens requires a hundred clicks to distribute their food! Mana regeneration is unbelievably slow, despite magic being a big focus, so that's more disincentive to experiment! What on Earth is going on with weapon upgrades and item scarcities!) Those all add friction, but are forgivable on their own. It's a wiki game, but there's not enough of a community for an adequate wiki to exist. 

It might be more fun for you if you have a huge appetite for this kind of game. It has bad ideas, but only a few. It has good ideas, but only a few. Maybe I missed something, or failed to find the intended entry point to engage with the systems just right, but 15 hours of Waiting For The Good Part To Begin is my limit.

Planet Centauri blends sandbox survival, RPG progression, and exploration into a colorful pixel-art world. Craft gear, fight monsters, build your base, and shape your character however you like. With plenty of freedom and a cozy-but-dangerous atmosphere, it’s a great pick for fans of open-ended 2D adventures. 🌍🛠️⚔️

Planet Centauri is an ambitious and densely packed sandbox experience that reflects both the creative freedom and the growing pains of a long-term indie project. Developed and published by Permadeath, it sets out to be more than just another 2D survival game by layering exploration, combat, crafting, automation, magic, farming, and engineering into a single, sprawling framework. While its pixel-art presentation and side-scrolling format inevitably draw comparisons to genre staples, Planet Centauri distinguishes itself through sheer mechanical scope, offering a world where curiosity and experimentation are just as important as combat prowess or resource gathering.

From the moment players enter its procedurally generated world, Planet Centauri establishes a sense of openness and possibility. Mining and crafting form the foundation, but progression quickly branches outward into numerous interconnected systems. You explore underground caverns, ancient ruins, and hostile biomes filled with enemies that possess unique traits and modifiers, making combat more varied than simple damage trading. Gear, spells, and consumables meaningfully alter how encounters play out, and permanent stat boosts gained through food and progression systems provide a tangible sense of growth tied directly to how you choose to play.

One of the game’s defining features is its breadth of player expression. Building is not limited to basic structures; instead, Planet Centauri offers hundreds of block shapes and materials that allow for detailed architectural designs and extensive terraforming. Players can shape the world around them in practical or artistic ways, whether constructing fortified bases, intricate towns, or elaborate contraptions embedded into the terrain. This creative flexibility is reinforced by systems that support farming, cooking, alchemy, and enchanting, all of which feed back into survival and combat in meaningful ways rather than existing as isolated mechanics.

Perhaps the most distinctive and ambitious aspect of Planet Centauri is its circuitry and logic system. Using soul-powered components, players can create logic gates, counters, sensors, and arithmetic systems that enable everything from automated farms to complex machines and puzzles. This “magitech” layer transforms the game into a playground for engineering-minded players, blurring the line between survival sandbox and creative simulation. While entirely optional, it adds enormous depth for those willing to learn it, offering possibilities rarely seen in 2D sandbox games.

The game also encourages interaction with its ecosystem through monster taming and breeding. Creatures encountered in the world can be captured, trained, and housed, each bringing different abilities and traits. Breeding mechanics allow inherited attributes, adding long-term planning and personalization to companion management. These systems lend personality to the world and create additional goals beyond simple progression, making the journey feel less linear and more player-driven.

That said, Planet Centauri’s greatest strength—its abundance of systems—is also its biggest weakness. Many mechanics feel promising but unevenly realized, with limited depth or unclear feedback that can make them feel incomplete. New players are often confronted with a steep learning curve, compounded by sparse tutorials and interfaces that struggle to clearly communicate the purpose and interaction of so many features. Quality-of-life limitations, occasional balance issues, and inconsistent polish across systems can make the experience feel overwhelming or unfocused, particularly for players expecting a more streamlined sandbox.

Combat and exploration, while generally enjoyable, can also feel inconsistent. Enemy difficulty spikes, underexplained modifiers, and occasional clunky interactions sometimes disrupt the flow of progression. Yet these issues coexist with moments of genuine discovery—finding rare items, uncovering hidden structures, or devising a clever mechanical solution—that remind players why the sandbox genre remains so compelling. Planet Centauri frequently rewards patience and experimentation, even if it doesn’t always guide players clearly toward those rewards.

The game’s long development history and eventual full release add further context to its identity. Years in early access shaped a project that grew organically, sometimes faster in ideas than refinement. As a result, Planet Centauri feels less like a tightly curated experience and more like a vast toolbox shaped by experimentation and community feedback. This makes it especially appealing to players who enjoy setting their own goals and tolerating rough edges in exchange for creative freedom.

Ultimately, Planet Centauri is a game defined by ambition rather than polish. It does not aim to compete with genre giants through refinement alone, but through variety, flexibility, and the joy of discovery. For players who value sandbox depth, experimentation, and systems-driven gameplay—and who are willing to accept imperfections as part of that journey—it offers a rich and often rewarding experience. While it may not fully realize every idea it introduces, Planet Centauri stands as a bold, eclectic sandbox that invites players to explore, build, and invent in a world that rewards imagination as much as survival.

I haven't been playing for very long, but unfortunately I think I've already hit the limit of what this game has to offer. I was originally interested because of the selling points: immersion, vehicle maintenance, realistic driving, and supposedly one of the most realistic traffic simulations around. On paper, that sounded exactly like what I wanted. In practice, it isn't even close. The AI is probably the biggest problem. I've driven around the city obeying the rules of the road, only to watch traffic completely collapse because one AI car has stopped awkwardly in the middle of the street. Suddenly you've got multiple lanes blocked, roads gridlocked, and absolutely nothing happens to resolve it. I've also seen pedestrians walk into a tiny gap between a lamppost and a wall, get stuck, and then have another ten pedestrians pile up behind them like some bizarre conga line. That kind of thing completely destroys the immersion.

The driving itself has some nice touches, like the way an automatic car creeps forward in Drive, but other parts feel rough. Some of the vehicle sounds are genuinely awful. When you accelerate, you'd expect the engine note to rise, hear a gear change, then hear the revs drop and build again. Instead, some cars just produce one long, loud revving noise while the speed increases and the gear indicator quietly moves up. There's barely any audible change between gears, and after a while it becomes incredibly irritating. There are also smaller bugs everywhere. The game repeatedly tells me to turn my headlights on in broad daylight for seemingly no reason, and little issues like that keep chipping away at the experience.

The map is another disappointment. If you're going to release this as a proper sequel to City Car Driving and sell it heavily on immersion and free driving, the world needs to feel substantial. It doesn't. The map feels quite small, and the UI doesn't help matters either. I'm coming from Euro Truck Simulator, which admittedly sets a high bar, but the GPS in the bottom-left corner here is horrific. Parts of it are cut off, it fades into the background, and half the time I can barely see the roads I'm supposed to be following. As a navigation tool, it's practically useless.

That's the frustrating part, because I really wanted to love this. The idea of just getting into a car, cruising around a believable city, dealing with traffic and enjoying the driving experience is exactly what appealed to me. But immersion only works if the world around you behaves believably. When you're driving down a road and the entire city has gridlocked because one AI car has stopped in the middle of an intersection, the illusion disappears immediately. Combine that with poor vehicle sounds, bugs, a small map and a frustrating UI, and it all adds up very quickly. If you're going to make a proper successor to City Car Driving, then go all in. Make the traffic AI genuinely impressive, make the cars sound convincing, and give us a world worth exploring. At the moment, this feels far too unfinished and limited for what it's trying to be.

Mixed bag — useful for the wrong reasons, rough for the right ones

I'm a US driver, and that matters here. The original City Car Driving let you pick which country's traffic rules you wanted to play by — US, Canada, EU, Russia, Australia, whichever. I came into 2.0 assuming that carried over, since the devs had already done the research to model all those rulesets once. Turns out it's gone. There's no regional selector anymore, and the store page never says which country's laws you're actually being graded against. That's a bigger deal than it sounds like, because if you're using this to practice for real US driving like I am, you genuinely can't tell whether the violations you're racking up reflect US law or not. Updating rules you've already built to current-year standards should be a lot less work than starting from scratch, so I'm hoping this comes back.

Picked this up after the original wouldn't let me shift gears or move in and out of park without dropping to the keyboard, even with the controller scheme set to Xbox. 2.0 fixes that part, but it's clearly early access. Only three vehicles right now — a diesel hatchback, a petrol automatic sedan, and a pickup — and the cockpit camera in the sedan sits low enough that the hood blocks your view of the road unless you mess with FOV or switch to the hood cam. And the FOV slider doesn't actually raise your seat, it just pushes you back, so it doesn't fix the problem.

I should explain why I'm even playing this. I'm a disabled driver working toward a restricted license with hand controls, and I'm trying to get reps in on the road-specific stuff — scanning, reacting to traffic, navigating while under load — before my actual evaluation. There's no real way to simulate hand controls on a PC without building a custom rig, so a gamepad is the closest rough stand-in I've got. It tests the mental side of driving fine. It does nothing for the physical side of the equipment I'll actually be using.

Traffic and hazard variety are decent, and there's a GPS-style destination system on the minimap that works well enough. But the controls need real work. Steer the stick a fraction of a millimeter and the car does a turn and a half, and it doesn't matter how you set the non-linearity, dead zone, or threshold sliders, it still happens. It needs actual weighted steering that mimics real turning radii instead of just scaling raw input. Throttle has the same problem in reverse, it jumps from barely touched to full send instead of ramping up smoothly, so holding a partial throttle just isn't really possible right now.

Then there's the violation system, which is strict in ways that don't line up with how driving actually works. Headlights have to be on at all times no matter the weather or time of day, which doesn't track, especially since the game already models weather and lighting changes and could just adjust for that. Turn signals get required in places where no real driver would ever use one, like pulling out of a space with signage that already tells you which way to go, or pulling into your own driveway during story mode. And a few times when I signaled, changed lanes, then swerved back for a second just to straighten out, it flagged me for not signaling the lane change at all. That one might be tied to the same stick sensitivity issue, but either way it needs tuning.

If you've got a wheel and pedals, I'd bet this plays a lot better, and credit where it's due, the traffic simulation itself is genuinely good and the density feels close to right.

I get that it's early access and a lot of this is probably already on the radar somewhere. But as it stands I wouldn't recommend it, and I've put it down myself so I don't accidentally build bad habits before I get behind the wheel for real. If you're trying to use this for actual practice the way I was, give it more time to bake.

City Car Driving 2.0 (Early Access) — 12-Hour Review
Tested On: Direct-Drive / Force Feedback Wheel

Prior Experience: ~6 hours in City Car Driving 1.0

Status: Early Access

The Verdict Up Front
After 12 hours behind the wheel, City Car Driving 2.0 feels less like a complete, polished leap into the next generation and more like a rough early-access foundation with high potential. Switching to Unreal Engine modernizes the visual presentation, but step-backs in content structure, optimization, and wheel integration hold it back from replacing the modded original. Having played 6 hours of the first game, the contrast in mechanical freedom makes these issues even more glaring.

What Works (The Good)
Visual & Audio Upgrade: Unreal Engine delivers a noticeable leap in interior details, lighting, ambient sound design, and wiper animations. Turn signals and cabin acoustics sound realistic and grounded.

Low-Speed Cruise Atmosphere: When cruising smoothly below 60 km/h, basic street navigation and city traffic offer a relaxing commuting experience.

Core Issues & Feedback for Developers:

1. God-Tier Automated Fines (Immersion Breaking)
Zero Speed Tolerance: Dropping from a 50 km/h zone to a 40 km/h zone instantly triggers a fine if you are even 1 km/h over. The original game had a forgiving ~5 km/h buffer—removing it makes driving feel extremely restrictive.

Terrain Fines: Going down a slope where momentum naturally increases your speed, or revving up to climb a steep parking garage ramp instantly slaps you with a speed fine.

Feedback: Fines should be tied to visible speed cameras, CCTV, or patrolling police cars rather than an omniscient, god-mode detection system.

2. Lack of Road Feel & Force Feedback Detail
Smooth as Glass: The road surfaces feel artificially smooth. There is a distinct lack of road texture/grain vibration and no physical thump over speed bumps, leaving Direct-Drive wheels feeling underutilized.

3. Brain-Dead AI & Pedestrian Behavior
Gridlock Entrapment: If your car obstructs an AI driver or pedestrian, they will stop dead in front of you instead of routing around.

Double Penalties: Trying to maneuver out of these AI standoffs almost always results in a collision fine, and bumping a pedestrian who refuses to move sends you straight to the police station.

4. Repetitive Content & Map Limitations
The current Early Access build offers very few main missions with little variety, making gameplay repetitive quickly. The map desperately needs more recognizable landmarks, scenic routes, and a wider selection of vehicles.

Key Breakdown & Score
Graphics & Audio: 7.5 / 10 — Solid engine upgrade; realistic cabin detail and ambient sounds.

Physics & FFB: 5.0 / 10 — Low-speed turns are fine, but lacks road texture and speed bump detail.

AI & Traffic Rules: 4.0 / 10 — The biggest flaw. AI lacks basic decision-making, and instantaneous fines ruin the fun.

Content & Variety: 4.5 / 10 — High mission repetition with limited map areas and landmarks.

Final Score: 5.5 / 10 (Early Access — Wait for Updates)

Bottom Line: Players come to this simulator to enjoy the relaxing experience of safe urban driving—not to run a "bankruptcy simulator" from relentless automated fines. With AI fixes, road surface FFB tweaks, and a fairer penalty system, this could become a great title.

The trailer and gameplay are kind of deceptive - yes, they showcase the whole city in its current state, but they carefully avoid displaying the map boundaries until it's too late to request a refund. The city currently is about (guesstimation) a mile by a half mile (~2km by ~1km). If you include the one road that goes to the NE edge, sure, maybe maybe *maybe* 3 miles of road from SE edge to NE edge. But that's one road, and a dirt path. This 'city' needs to be at an absolute minimum, 4x it's current size. Comparing it to Midtown Madness 1 (1999, Chicago), it's about the same size. It's got more depth, but by less than you'd think. Midtown Madness 2's (2000) two cities (San Francisco, London) absolutely crush the city in CCD2. Midtown Madness 3 (2003; Washington, DC and Paris) are very detailed environments, even by modern standards, and take several minutes to go from one end to the other with comparable cars vs CCD2, while CCD2 takes about a minutes of aggressive driving to cross the city.

The environment needs expansion, badly. I haven't done a proper test but I'm pretty sure CCD1 has slightly bigger maps (note the plural). Lower the price, at least until a proper release ($10 is what I would call good, $15 not on sale is pushing it, in this state). Expand the environment, by quite a lot. And ease up on the rule enforcement; I shouldn't feel that the Gestapo is in my backseat.

Stuttering, bugs, and fundamental design flaws.

First off, the dev's claim that this is "a driving simulator designed to help novice drivers master driving" stinks of the same false, deceptive advertisement as Disney's "Baby Einstein" crap. Make no mistake: This is a GAME. It will not teach you to drive any more than playing Red Dead Redemption will teach you to ride a horse.

I knew it was a game going in. I expected nothing more, but sadly got a whole lot less.

But let's start with the positives. The graphics are pretty. The rain effects are nice. Having proper pedestrians walking across the roads adds a lot to the immersion compared to other driving games like Motortown, SnowRunner, or SCS's Truck Simulators.

Yet, as much as I knew and accepted that this was not an actual teaching tool, I certainly didn't expect it to be yet another "grandpa's old" game, where you start by inheriting something from a relative that you neither earned nor deserve. Grandpa's old farm, grandpa's old rifle, grandpa's old fishing boat, grandpa's old fill-in-the-stupid blank... In this case, it's your ugly, peppy, super-talkative uncle giving you his crappy old car, but the concept is the same. (Seriously, "grandpa's old" really should be its own game genre by now!) Having a "story" in a game like this always reduces the enjoyment factor, but it's even worse when the story is this trite and unimaginative. All we needed were proper objectives like in Motortown, but the sandbox mode doesn't allow you to do delivery missions and such, so if you want objectives and progression, you're stuck with Uncle Whatever-his-name-was.

But the annoying uncle is just the start of this game's problems.

Compared to other driving games, the steering feels awkward on a standard gamepad. Making precision turns in a car was harder here than driving a truck in ETS2. The dev seems to assume all players have a proper wheel and pedals set up. Many of us don't.

Meanwhile, the gamepad's right stick can be configured to move the camera, but your character doesn't freely turn his head. Instead, the camera near-instantly snaps 45 degrees to the left or 90 degrees to the right. There's no in-between, so you can't turn your head properly to the left to check for on-coming traffic, or look over your shoulder when backing up. You can't even tilt the camera up to check the traffic light above you. There's no way to look around the car's blind spots without switching to 3rd-person view, and even then, the camera movement is strangely limited.

What was the dev thinking here?! How do you mess up something as insanely simple as a 1st-person-view free-look camera? Did it not occur to the dev that a player might want to look over their shoulder, or look 45 degrees to the right instead of 90 degrees, or look 90 degrees to the left instead of 45? This might have been acceptable in an arcade racer, but not being able to freely turn your head in what the dev claims is a "driving simulator" is beyond incompetent.

This alone would have easily warranted my refund request, but sadly, there were performance issues as well. The game frequently stutters with noticeable frame rate drops. The UI is clunky and can freeze up for several seconds at a time. The phone GPS is tiny and generally useless. Why isn't there a proper GPS in the actual car?! What is this, 1984?

Yes, I'm well aware that it's Early Access. But many of the problems here are not of the "early access" variety. They are fundamental design flaws at the conceptual level. It is not "by accident" or "a bug" that the uncle exists or that the cockpit view is useless. It is by design. And that says enough about this game and its dev that I shall have nothing more to do with either.

(It's also very telling that the dev is replying to nearly every negative review on Steam: it shows that the dev is wasting time doing PR damage control when they could be actually working on improving their game.)

Hellpoint

What's the Point? The Point Is Hell.

🛑 Confession
I beat the entire game at Difficulty 1. Now, don't get me wrong. Just because it's called "Level 1" doesn't mean I picked Easy Mode like some casual. Difficulty in this game is managed through Breaches, but here's the catch: adjusting it in either direction requires rare consumables. Why did I stick to Difficulty 1? Because, well, it's an indie game. Let's be real: indie devs have a pretty bad track record when it comes to balancing difficulty and pacing. Combined with this consumable-based system, that left me paranoid about cranking up the difficulty, worried that doing so might make the game brutally unplayable—not just difficult, but straight-up broken. Worse, I was genuinely afraid I might end up permanently softlocked simply because I'd run out of Fearful Effigy, the items needed to lower the difficulty again. So, to all the "Git Gud" sweatlords who think my review is worthless because I didn't max out the difficulty: by all means, see yourselves out.

For everyone else who's still here for a raw, unfiltered review written immediately after beating the game, one more thing I should come clean about: I dropped the DLC halfway through, because of a character-freezing bug. It's exhausting just trying to review this thing. What a mess.

🌀 Massive (PogChamp), Disconnected (KEKWait), Labyrinth (NotLikeThis)
With its unique sci-fi aesthetic, the sheer scale of the areas could have made exploration rewarding. Except, predictably, there's no map, the layouts are a complete labyrinth, and worst of all, the world connectivity is absolute garbage. Take Dark Souls 1, strip away its brilliant, organically interconnected world design, and you're left with this exact mess. The level design will burn you out long before any mob or boss gets the chance.

And yet, if fast travel between Breaches were unrestricted, the game might still be salvageable. Naturally, the devs made sure to snuff out even that last glimmer of hope. Fast travel is locked behind really rare consumables. You have to burn a rare Breach Synchronizer just to unlock fast travel at a single Breach. And, of course, you'll be lucky to find even one per zone—and only after scouring every last corner of the maze. Look, I could almost forgive a messy, fragmented world. Maybe the devs just didn't have the chops to make the areas connect in a meaningful way. But why go out of your way to cripple fast travel, too? The result is a world nobody in their right mind would ever want to revisit, especially when just getting through it once was already a miserable ordeal. What was the point of making these massive levels? To have players slog through them once and never look back? Or to drive them away entirely? If that was the goal, mission accomplished at 200%. The devs deserve a bonus. 

I hate consulting external wikis on a first playthrough. Once the magic of a blind, unspoiled adventure is gone, you can never get it back. But this game managed to shatter that principle for me. The lack of a map, relentless asset reuse, tortuously convoluted level design, and infuriatingly vague navigation cues all combine to make exploring and finding your way around on your own feel damn near impossible on a first playthrough. "Impossible, you say? Then how the hell did the people who made the walkthroughs find their way around in the first place?" Beats me. I'd genuinely love to know. Honestly, those folks should've spent their luck buying lottery tickets instead of burning through a divine gift just to navigate Hellpoint.

🔥 Base Game: Barely Passable. DLC: Not Even Close.
Remember when I mentioned how shockingly bad indie studios can be at balancing difficulty and pacing? Well, this DLC puts their complete lack of competence on full display. How they managed to hide it throughout the main campaign is beyond me, but let's call it what it is: a shameless cash grab that amplifies everything wrong with the base game while introducing a whole new set of problems.

1. Pathfinding Somehow Got Even Worse
Honestly, you almost have to admire it. The base game was a walk in the park compared to this absolute nightmare. The devs went out of their way to make navigation so miserable it practically drains your soul. The world's connectivity is still a mess, and shortcuts are just as poorly implemented as ever. The worst offender has to be the Dominion Baths. From the start of the base game all the way through to this point, hitting walls to break them open was never a mechanic. Then, out of nowhere, the game throws a progression roadblock at you that can only be cleared by punching a wall. How the hell is anyone supposed to figure that out without looking up a walkthrough? What were they thinking? Simple: artificially inflating playtime.
2. Exposing the Devs' Incompetence
And let's not forget the enemy encounters in these DLC areas: absurd mob density and Brutes spawning in pairs. Classic. It's DLC, so naturally, they had to crank up the difficulty, right? Except their idea of making things harder is about as creatively bankrupt as it gets. You're constantly forced to deal with two DLC-buffed Brutes at once—or, on the rare occasion there's only one, the devs throw in a whole swarm of trash mobs to make up for it. Figures.
3. Game-Breaking Bug
Playing DLC has been pure torture rather than anything resembling fun. But the real dealbreaker? A character freeze bug. Honestly, my blood boils just writing this. During the Philomycus Queen fight in the Dominion Baths, my character froze in place without any warning. Naturally, I got pummeled to death. How many attempts did it take for this to happen? Two. Exactly two attempts, and both times, my character froze. The first freeze happened when the boss was at 25% HP. The second came when she was down to just 10%. And with no shortcuts on the runback—because why would the devs give us one?—this game-breaking disaster completely killed any motivation I had to try again. All that was left was pure, unadulterated rage.

Two attempts, two freezes—a 100% crash rate. That's when I knew right away that this game was technically unplayable. So, yes, I beat the base game. But I dropped the DLC right then and there. Do I regret it? Do I have the nerve to review DLC I didn't even finish? Not in the slightest. If anything, I feel an overwhelming sense of relief. Quitting might genuinely be one of the best decisions I've made in recent memory. I'm just glad I didn't sacrifice any more of my remaining lifespan to this scam-ridden piece of garbage.

⚖️ The Verdict
The DLC is a shameless cash grab, and the main campaign is a massive letdown. Whatever strengths this game has are utterly forgettable, but its design flaws will haunt you at every turn. Combat is aggressively mediocre—not outright broken, but entirely devoid of personality. The controls are serviceable in combat, but platforming during exploration is an absolute nightmare. The visuals and atmosphere are good. Unfortunately, when a game leaves you perpetually lost in a labyrinth, you stop appreciating the scenery and start losing your mind.

So, here's my recommendation: if you have no idea what a destination is supposed to be and enjoy wandering around like a headless chicken, by all means, buy it. Just wander through dark hallways, smack some enemies around, and never bother asking yourself where the hell you're supposed to go. If you're a sane human being, stay far, far away from this game. And just to be clear: even if you're one of those weirdos who'd enjoy that kind of experience, the DLC is still a hard pass. You might enjoy wandering pointlessly, but I doubt you enjoy the game freezing bug.

To list some:

If you want to change the difficulty, whether it is up or down, you'll have to find a specific item for each of those actions.
Problem is, it's a random drop, and it never fucking drops.
So if you wanted to experiment with already cleared sections, but on a higher difficulty, to either have some "fun" or farm some resources, once you want to progress further back, you're fucked.
The gameplay experience then becomes a devastating entropy to your psyche, unless the gods (RNG) mercifully give you the chance to escape this torment.
And also, I haven't found a way to replay bosses on a higher difficulty, "fun" right?

The checkpoints are well placed, and there's plenty, with enough spacing to hit the green spot of efficiency.
But whenever you're done with the environment and just want to go straight to the boss, there's always that 1 missing checkpoint that could be conveniently placed near the boss or a gameplay mechanic letting you just replay the fight.
By the time I make my way to the boss area, half of my HP is down from trying to ignore and evade the mobs and having to fight them every time, and tracing the route there every time is just too time-consuming and frustrating.
The checkpoints also offer quick travel between them, but not always? 
I haven't figured out why. 
Maybe it's another RNG item? 
The point is, I haven't been able to come back to a location to upgrade my loot for quite some time, which again I find as a very stupid gameplay mechanic, pointlessly limiting the player and making the experience harsher than it has to be.
Fictional difficulty or whatever it's called.

This is technically not a gameplay mechanic, but it's very much present through and through the whole game, and since it's not fixed, I might as well call it this game's mechanic.
Bugs, glitches, and the game being overall quite unpolished.
The game is already hard enough in difficulty.
This just makes it so much more unpleasant to plow through, an unnecessary obstacle.

I always have these long rants when criticizing games, because the amount of effort put into making these games pleasant is going into polishing my writing as well.
I see this game being great. 
If only it would be worked on for a little bit more, with less but better content, quality over quantity.

I really like the setting.

This is a tough recommendation, but I think there's still enough good here to make it worth it.

What I like:
- The vibes in this game are great. The setting of a giant space station that's been invaded by outer gods is unique and allows for some really cool aesthetics.
- The map design doesn't quite reach Fromsoft's genius, but this is still pretty good.
- Weapons gain bonuses as you use them, and your upgrades are applied to a swappable attachment so you never get a new weapon and have to build it up from scratch.
- It's small, but I appreciated the minimalistic UI. It does exactly what it needs to without requiring any extraneous button clicking.
- You can jump at any time, which means you get jump attacks and platforming, and it's actually pretty good platforming at parts.
- Your main healing item can be refilled by landing attacks, so even when you are out you have a chance to get more. This allowed for some cool comeback moments.
- You can't automatically warp between checkpoints, but you can use an item that adds one to your 'network', which adds an interesting logistical element; do you save your warp items for checkpoints later, or do you use one later so you can easily travel to this spot? I like how they made it an impactful choice.

What I disliked:
- The game has a fair bit of jank. Combat feels very stiff, and there's some sort of counter/parry thing with shields but it felt very inconsistent. There isn't a dedicated backstab animation, but you do more damage hitting enemies in the back, so you are heavily incentivized to just get behind enemies and spam attacks. There's some sort of block-to-parry thing, but it felt extremely inconsistent, to the point that I didn't feel like I could ever depend on it.
- The platforming is generally good, but there are some jumps that require a bit of precision, and your jump sometimes doesn't allow enough control, meaning you'll overshoot things. Plus, it felt like sometimes i would want to run for a jump and the run wouldn't kick in so I'd go nowhere near far enough and fall to my death.
- Enemy variety is fairly low, and for the most part weren't that interesting.
- There is a story in here, but I never found myself interested in it. As you progress you'll get 'data' from actions and encounters and you are supposed to gather a bunch and return to a particular place. At some point I had like 50% of data, and then after one event it just jumped to 100% without warning.
- There's a whole mechanic around a clock representing the space station orbiting a black hole and passing through storms, and depending on the time on the clock, different places are open, different events are available, and enemy placements might change. This is awesome in theory, but in practice it felt frustrating; you'd find places you are locked out of and it's unclear if this is due to the clock state, some other condition, or if that's just somewhere they didn't implement. There's no method I know to change the clock other than to wait, so if you had a suspicion that something would change if the time was right, you had to just...stand around.
- When you die, there's a relatively high chance that a 'ghost' spawns that is basically a version of you (same equipment), that hangs around the area where you died. Killing it nets you a nice reward of 'axions' (this game's currency). But sometimes it's near other enemies that might have killed you, and now you have an extra enemy to contend with.
- There's only a few boss fights in the game, and I found them to be fairly unimpressive.

There's a lot more I could say but those are the main things. I think some of the stuff I disliked weirdly elevates the game; it would be less interesting if it was more polished maybe? Anyway, I think the experience is worth at least one playthrough, but I would consider this lower on the list of souls-likes over many others.

So you've decided to play Hellpoint, it is certainly a little bit of a mixed bag, but way more positive than negative.

[h3]Positives:[/h3]

The atmosphere is great, it's one of the few souls-likes, alongside Bleak Faith: Forsaken, where the devs actually played and understood Dark Souls. No over reliance on background music, mostly just ambients sounds and your own footsteps, making the world and exploration the focus and storytelling which is more like a puzzle than a complete story.

The art style is very 2010 games meet 80s and 90s scifi inspired, and usually I'd complain about a game looking outdated, but the more I play Hellpoint, the more I start believing it's deliberate and a stylistic choice, which I absolutely respect.

Overall, Hellpoint is heavily carried by its world and exploration, the actual combat and bosses feels quite weak and under developed. But kind of like Bleak Faith: Forsaken, the world itself goes very far, far enough to gain a positive rating from me even if I'm not really feeling the combat too much.

[h3]Negatives:[/h3]

Many animations look and feel slow, janky and clumsy.

Enemy design isn't super varied, you will primarily spend your time fighting the same 5-6 different enemies through the entire game. But I've seen games that did this in way worse ways, so it's not the end of the world.

I'm not a huge fan of the inventory screen, it's not super clear what everything does at first glance, there could have been more time spent on giving each item a backstory (it is true that some items do have it, but the majority does not), sticking with the understanding Dark Souls theme that is.

[h3]Conclusion:[/h3]

What you will get out of it depends on what expectations you go into it with. If your expectations are great combat, flashy animations and cinematic boss battles, you will be disappointed. However, if you go into it expecting a well crafted world, good atmosphere and exploration, the yes, Hellpoint is absolutely for you.

Before I dig into the details, I need to complain about the performance. I have a pretty decent rig; even so, this game has some jank. Specifically, jank with the Steam version. I eventually had to switch over to the GOG version to finish the game. Steam's version crashed when quitting to the main menu and, at one point, kept thinking I was hitting the inventory key. I unplugged everything, uninstalled and reinstalled, and all that. Despite my best efforts, the second I tried to confirm camping or movement, the game insisted I was riding that ‘I’ key. Installing my version from GOG resolved all of these quirks. I did get to over 40 hours on Steam before the great "I" event of 2026, so it does work. 

It was a subtle reminder that maybe having two gaming libraries across platforms isn’t so bad. Dirty_Jared is my username on Galaxy. Friend me, and we can play ancient strategy games together!

With my complaining about technical issues settled, I will touch upon the other aspects of the game and then wrap this ish up.

First things first, there are women in combat roles. I know some of the young ‘uns out there don’t like “woke” games or whatever. If that’s you, you’ll hate this. Personally, I am a geezer, and I have seen ladies in prominent roles in my RPGs since the dawn of time. I know some people care a lot, though, so this is your heads-up.

This game has branching decisions, but there are a couple of spots where you may be forced to do things that you don’t want to. Welcome to trying to be altruistic in the New World. 

Speaking of altruism, that is just one of several personality traits that your followers can have. You get to pick your company before you start, and picking followers that fit your playstyle makes everything smoother. Want to slaughter all the indigenous peoples? Pick the ‘racist’ trait. Want to spread the good word? ‘Altruistic’ and ‘pious’ might be good options. The racists will grumble if you are nice, so leave them in Spain for this playthrough.

As for units, you have ‘soldiers’ who excel at sword and board, ‘scouts’ who are badass melee units that can’t use guns, and hunters who dominate ranged combat. As for support units, there are ‘doctors’ and ‘scholars’. Doctors are pretty self-explanatory and necessary. Seriously, have one in the field and level them up so they can cure poison. Scholars are basically professional buffing units. You can get some powerful results by leveling a scholar, and they can change everything in battle. Also, even if they miss while shooting, they will expose a weakness on the unit they shot at, leading to increased damage when others attack it.

Levelling is quite flexible as there is an experience pool. You can level up units however you please, provided you have the experience to cover it. There is also a resource simply known as “equipment.” Providing this resource to your units will level up their weapons and armor. Not to belabor the point, but flexibility is on full display in this game.

The combat itself is awesome, but it can be ball-bustingly hard and relies heavily on RNG. Personally, I love RNG, but I totally get why others do not. You will miss despite high accuracy percentages, and it will happen at the absolute worst time.

To break it down briefly, you fight on a battlefield of flat-top hexes, the superior hex. There is a cover system and a bunch of fancy skills you can use. Soldiers can buff adjacent units' defense, hunters can shoot twice with reduced accuracy, etc. 

There is also a cover system, penalties to accuracy when fighting in the dark (which change depending on how close a target is to a fire or torch), and various traps, barriers, and gadgets you can deploy. It cannot be overstated how fast a battle can go sideways. Sometimes that one hex of caltrops can make all the difference. Also, fire spreads.

If you want a complete strategy experience and don’t mind dated graphics and a little jankiness, then I recommend this game, along with Expeditions: Viking and Expeditions: Rome. As for Expeditions: Samurai? I’m all set. This company released three amazing and complete games with a distinct art direction and a brilliant combat system. Samurai just looks like every other indie tactics game. Buy this instead!

That's my first game in the expeditions series and I jumped in knowing next to nothing about the game.

I liked the setting (not enough RPGs are set in this era), I liked that it tries to be realistic (no magic), I liked the stories you encounter and the characters you meat. I think the role-playing aspect of the game is actually pretty good.
However, some aspects of the gameplay are not great.
- Limited movement on the map and camping become tedious very fast. I guess the idea was to trigger random events while camping and the need to manage your rations to avoid mutiny. But the way it's implemented it feels more like a nuisance, than part of the story. The good thing is you have good enough difficulty adjustments, so you can pretty much chose to ignore this mechanic if you chose.
- Difficulty spikes - some battles are considerably more difficult. I'm fine with losing battles and trying again, but overall it felt very uneven sometimes
- Battles themselves in the mid to late game become repetitive (apart from spike in difficulty for some battles).
- Abilities are per class, not a character. So 2 different characters of the same class would be more or less the same in the battlefield. IMHO missed opportunity for character development.

Overall, I enjoyed the game for the story and role-playing. Battles are good enough to keep it interesting, but don't expect anything spectacular.

After reading and hearing mixed opinions I've been pleasently surprised. 
First I really like unique/less exploited settings and that is exactly what we get here, La conquista de América is rather rarely used in games, probably even less in RPGish genre. Worth noting is that, it's not just based on facts, as there are some changes and even a little bit of paranormal activites, which only makes it even more interesting.

I'd say plot is good, so is writing, dialogues might not offer many branchings but are solid, and so are options we are presented with. The best thing is that choices actually matter, sometimes a lot, so the game can be replayed not only in order to try new builds but also for different plot choices.

Combat can be fun, it doesn't allow much variety per class, as almost all perks are shared, there are clear winners in terms of certain weapon types usability, like arquebus is much better than bow, to the point a hunter using a bow might make you think the class is just weak but the second you try EXACT same build but with the gun it's magically starts to deliver. RPG enthusiasts might be disappointed by how equipment is implemented - we put 'equipment' points into slots making armor, melee or ranged weapon better by some percent - which is quite boring and uninspiring. Along our troops we can use some craftable items like spike traps, barricades, torches etc. which can affect the fight dramitcally (especially on higher dificulties levels it might be crucial).

I have mixed feelings if it comes to survival elements, in general it isn't bad but after some time becomes bit tedious, as we have to camp every 15 seconds while trying to travel between two far away locations. The good thing is we might get lots of random encounters, most of them is nice but one in particular seems way too brutal but fortunately it's rare. What I also like is that we are not forced to win all battles/camps, we still can retreat it just will affect the outcome in sometimes surprising way - in my opinion that's really cool.

TLDR: If you like more tactical approach to 'survival rpgs' and are bored with yet another high fantasy, cyberpunk or sci-fi setting, give it a try. If you are not sure sometimes there are big sales that might save you 'wasting' money in case you won't like it.

Expeditions: Conquistador surprised me with how much it made me feel the weight of my own choices — I went in expecting a straightforward tactics game and ended up genuinely unsettled watching my expedition descend into brutality, all of my own volition. The party morale system is clever: your pious companions bristle when you side with the natives, your greedy soldiers cheer when you loot a temple, and that tension gives every decision a cost beyond just resources. The hex-based combat is challenging and satisfying, though the camera being glued to your character on the overworld gets genuinely frustrating when you're trying to navigate dense jungle. The camping loop — hunting, healing, assigning tasks — starts as an interesting survival puzzle but does get repetitive by the midgame. Still, for an indie game this ambitious, the writing and moral complexity punch well above its weight, and I walked away thinking about it long after the credits rolled. Recommended, especially on sale.

Expeditions: Conquistador is a hybrid tactical role-playing and strategy game developed by Logic Artists and later published by THQ Nordic that places players in command of a 16th-century Spanish expedition to the New World. Rather than romanticizing conquest as a simple tale of victory and expansion, the game frames exploration as a tense balancing act between ambition, survival, diplomacy, and internal cohesion. From the beginning, it is clear that success is not measured solely by winning battles, but by how well you manage people, resources, and difficult moral choices in an unfamiliar and often hostile land.

The game is structured around an overland campaign map where movement, planning, and logistics are just as important as combat. Each journey across jungles, coastlines, and mountains consumes time and supplies, forcing players to think carefully about routes and priorities. Camps must be established at the end of each day, where you assign party members to tasks such as hunting, guarding, scouting, or healing. Random events frequently occur during these moments of rest, presenting narrative decisions that can improve morale, cost valuable resources, or spark conflict within the expedition. This system gives the campaign layer a constant sense of tension, as even periods of apparent calm can have long-term consequences.

Character creation and party management form a core pillar of the experience. Players create their expedition leader with a range of skills that directly influence dialogue options, exploration outcomes, and camp events. Attributes such as diplomacy, leadership, medicine, survival, and tactics are not abstract numbers but meaningful tools that open or close paths throughout the game. The wider expedition is made up of companions drawn from different classes, including soldiers, scouts, hunters, doctors, and scholars. Each brings unique combat roles and non-combat benefits, making recruitment and squad composition a strategic decision rather than a cosmetic one. Personalities and morale matter, reinforcing the idea that the expedition is a fragile social unit rather than a disposable army.

Tactical combat takes place on hex-based maps that emphasize positioning, terrain, and coordinated actions over brute force. Encounters are deliberate and methodical, encouraging careful use of cover, flanking, and class abilities. Soldiers anchor the front lines, scouts maneuver for mobility and disruption, hunters apply ranged pressure, doctors keep the party alive, and scholars manipulate the battlefield through support abilities. Combat is tightly linked to the campaign layer, as injuries persist beyond individual fights and require time and medical resources to heal. Reckless victories can leave the expedition weakened and vulnerable in the long run, reinforcing the game’s emphasis on sustainability over aggression.

Narrative and choice play a significant role throughout the journey. Dialogue is heavily skill-based, with options appearing or disappearing depending on the leader’s abilities and the composition of the party. Diplomacy can resolve conflicts without bloodshed, establish alliances with native factions, or reshape how future encounters unfold. While the game draws inspiration from historical themes, it allows players agency in how events play out, offering opportunities to pursue more cautious, cooperative approaches rather than defaulting to domination. These choices often have delayed consequences, lending weight to decisions that might initially seem minor.

Visually, Expeditions: Conquistador is functional rather than extravagant. The art style prioritizes clarity, ensuring that maps, units, and interfaces are readable and easy to navigate during both exploration and combat. While the graphics may feel modest by modern standards, they support the game’s systems without distraction. Sound design and music are similarly restrained, reinforcing atmosphere without overpowering the experience, and allowing the narrative and mechanics to remain front and center.

The game’s learning curve is steep, particularly in the early hours. Systems overlap and interact in ways that can overwhelm new players, and early mistakes can have lasting repercussions. However, this complexity is also one of the game’s greatest strengths. Once the systems click, the experience becomes deeply rewarding, offering a sense of authorship over the expedition’s fate that few strategy RPGs achieve. Each campaign feels shaped by the player’s priorities, skill choices, and moral stance, encouraging replayability through experimentation with different leadership styles.

Overall, Expeditions: Conquistador stands as a thoughtful and ambitious blend of tactical combat, resource management, and narrative choice. It is not a power fantasy, nor a simple strategy game, but a measured exploration of leadership under pressure. Players willing to invest time into understanding its interconnected systems will find a rich and immersive experience that values planning, empathy, and foresight as much as battlefield success. For fans of historical RPGs and strategy hybrids that challenge both tactical skill and ethical judgment, it remains a distinctive and rewarding title.

Expeditions: Conquistador is the first entry in the Expeditions series of games, which could be accurately described as historical turn-based RPGs with heavy emphasis on players choices. I actually played Expeditions: Vikings first, without knowing it was a sequel to this game. I was pleasantly surprised by it, so I decided to have a go at the other Expeditions games as well.
The year is 1518. and the American continent was only recently discovered. You are the son of a wealthy noble who's been given commission by the king of Spain to organize an expedition into the New World. As you're already experienced with managing soldiers, you are given free hands to choose your companions and take command of the expedition. Inspired by the adventures of Christopher Columbus and encouraged by the prospect of finding fame and fortune, you and your men set sail across the Atlantic ocean.
The story of Expeditions: Conquistador is divided into two parts. The first part takes place on an island of Hispaniola (today's Dominican Republic), where Columbus erected the Spanish settlement of Santa Domingo. After completing the events on Hispaniola, you'll continue your journey to mainland, where the second part of the story unfolds. I have to say that the story of Conquistador is quite good and I was pleased with the amount of impact the player has on the storyline through choices. You will encounter various individuals and native tribes and it's entirely up to you how you'll handle them. The game also possesses a strong atmosphere, created by a mix of random world events, camp management mechanics and fitting background music.
Combat in this game is surprisingly good, considering it's a historically accurate game without magic or other such nonsense. Your companions are divided into classes and you can equip them, promote them and pick their abilities . They also have their uses outside of combat, in random events or daily tasks. You'll need to collect food, make medicine and construct various equipment used in combat. Each night, your expedition stops to camp. During this period, you can assign your expedition members different roles, which can range from guarding or patrolling the camps perimeter to hunting for food or stitching wounds. These "camping mechanics" are what the Expeditions series is famous for, and they were first introduced here.
The presentation aspect of the game is not as good. The camera outside of combat is absolutely terrible and most of the time it's impossible to tell where you're going without consulting the map. Picking up items or interacting with objects is buggy as hell. The graphics are passable at best, with no scaling options for higher resolutions. The game has lengthy dialogues and no voice acting, which can be tedious. But you eventually get used to all that.

Expeditions: Conquistador is an unpolished game, but definitely one worth of playing. If you regularly play story-oriented RPGs, you'll be refreshed by the different approach Expeditions: Conquistador takes.

At the time of writing this review, I picked up the game again more than ten years after its release date in 2013, in an attempt to unlock some more difficult achievements. Graphics and most mechanics feel outdated on this point. The oldskool simplicity of the more established mechanics, however, felt very refreshing. Being able to go back to the essence of tactical combat without getting too overflowed with different leveling options and skill trees, was a clarifying experience.

Expeditions: Conquistador focusses heavily on tactical combat, exploring and map travelling with a repetitive, optimized survival group minigame. Most of the time spend is traversing and exploring on one of the two maps, Hispaniola and Mexico, completing quests, occasionally getting into combat. The party needs to rest, camp to survive and gain movement points, which can be used to travel. During camping and resting, a setup screen becomes active, where the player can assign each expedition member to different tasks. This involves guarding, hunting, tinkering, etc… A thin line between prosperity and deterioration has to be walked. In time, when expedition members start to gain levels and skill points, this minigame becomes somewhat easier and more flexible to set up. At first, the camping is very fun and appealing, but becomes very repetitive during the course of the game, since you will do a ton of resting in a single playthrough.

The simplicity of the combat game is what Expeditions: Conquistador excels in. There is quite a lot of similarly feeling combat in the game, with the battlefield map and scenery accordingly being the only different aspect. There are some different objectives in combat, however, such as escape battles or battles where you have to hold on and survive for a given number of turns. From the very efficient abilities to rewarding sound effects, the simplicity and integrity of combat play, all gives a satisfying refreshing feel. Not a lot of planning ahead what your next turn will look like is needed, this makes for a relaxed, progressing flow of combat.

A mere five classes are available in the game: doctor, scout, hunter, scholar & soldier. Given, each character can only level up five times, with most abilities acquired upon leveling, are the same among each of the classes, not much difference in gameplay will be noticed. Most tweaking comes from the variety in features that can be chosen, which are quite a few, but have minimal impact on gameplay, though.

Background music is very well composed, with very catchy tunes, quickly immersing the player. There are too few different music loops, which is a shame, and rapidly get repetitive and slightly annoying over time. Some rather special audio tracks are used during more unique battles, too bad the developers did not spread all tracks somewhat more equally over the course of the game.

There is a lot of unspoken dialogue in the game’s storyline, so do expect of lot of reading and interpreting. Only dialogue that is spoken, is played during the three cut-scenes which run during the intro, outro and between the two different scenario, map locations.

Sixty achievements are to be unlocked in order to reach the “perfect game” status. Given the fact most players will need multiple playthroughs make this a more challenging, time consuming task. For instance, the “Masochist” achievement requires you to “Complete the game in Iron Man mode on any difficulty”, and the “Aguirre” achievement needs to be unlocked by “Completing the game on Insane difficulty”. These two achievements alone already, are not quite complementary for obvious reasons. There are also opposing ones for choosing sides with one of two factions in-game.Exept for Iron Man mode, savescumming is a viable option, make sure to save regularly and before each important oncoming event.

Achievement hunters and completionists can opt to perfect Expeditions: Conquistador, since all achievements are manageable to unlock, given to spend some 30 hours per playthrough. Do take into account, however, at least 2 full playthroughs are required, whilst most achievements can be cheesed by reading guides or using common sense.

To conclude: Despite the fact the game has been released over 10 years ago, do not expect fancy new mechanics, tons of tweaking options, but a game that has held up really well in its core basic turn-based tactical combat. The game is not too long to play through, so it lends itself to get back to once in a while. A fun, unique tactical game in a mysterious real-life setting.

Recommended for: fans of, more basic, turn-based tactical combat games with a small focus on roleplaying elements, where choices do impact storyline

n 2014, I embarked on a journey to conquer the New World in Expeditions: Conquistador, only to get shipwrecked on the first island. Fast forward to this year, having played the Viking-themed sequel, Expeditions: Vikings, I decided to revisit this oldie.  Let me tell you, Conquistador holds up surprisingly well.

Sure, you might need to dim the graphics a bit for a smoother experience, and the overworld map benefits greatly from a decluttering. But beneath the slightly dated visuals lies a gem of a strategy RPG.

For those unfamiliar with the Expeditions series, you take the helm as leader of a band. Unlike sprawling armies, you manage a concise group of warriors, clerics, and doctors. You navigate an overland map brimming with RPG elements, with exploration leading to turn-based combat encounters on a grid.

Conquistador flirts with historical realism. While the core gameplay feels grounded, there are creative liberties taken: a higher number of female warriors than historical records might suggest, dialogue with a more modern tone, and even some contemporary viewpoints sprinkled in.

Despite these deviations, the game offers a gripping storyline. The small-scale skirmishes, typically 6v6 or when you are unlucky v12, feel perfectly suited to the setting. There's a constant tension as you navigate the harsh realities of exploration and conquest.

However, the setting itself is a point of contention. The game takes place during a dark period in the Americas, a time of societal collapse, genocide, and slavery. The developers deserve credit for allowing players to approach this sensitive historical period with a degree of honourable conduct. But be warned, if this subject matter deeply troubles you, this, and the other Expeditions titles (Vikings and Rome), might not be for you.

Ultimately, Expeditions: Conquistador is an enjoyable experience that has aged surprisingly well. It offers a captivating story, strategic depth, and a unique exploration-combat blend. Just be prepared to adjust the visuals and accept the sometimes fictionalised, yet thought-provoking, take on this historical period.

I enjoyed this game more than I thought I would. Graphics aren't appealing, but gameplay and story are pretty good. 

There are some RPG elements: you can create your character (you may even play as a woman, as I did, although historically it doesn't make sense; curiously she/he won't engage in combat); your party can have different character classes (like doctor, soldier, explorer, ranger, erudite), which differ if the character is Spanish ou Native American; and, as you gather XP by fulfilling quests, you level them up and they gain new abilities and points for upgrading their stats. 

Map exploration is very similar to the "Heroes of Might & Magic" series: you have a fixed number of movement points for each day. When you reach zero, you have to camp, and then the management bit begins: you need to ensure that the members of your expedition are well-fed, equipped, safe, healthy and in highs spirits (for that you need to hunt, find herbs in the wild or trade with the natives); you can also research improvements and craft items such as traps or cannon balls, for use in battles. 

Combat is turn-based and happens in maps with hexagonal grids, with a party of up to 6 characters. It works similarly to the XCOM games: you can take a turn to move and another to attack (if you don't act, you gain a small defense boost). There are melee and ranged units, besides healers and support classes. The positioning of troops is important: you need to prevent being flanked by enemies and also flank them, because there's a significant boost to attacks. Units can also be poisoned or stunned. Enemy AI is pretty good: they will go for the easiest kill (probably your healer), so you need to be careful. The interesting bit is that you don't get a "game over" screen if you lose; you just carry on in a worse state, because you lose money and items. 

This is not a casual game, but it's also not difficult if you learn how to play it and do it well. Even if things go sour in your playthrough, there will be chances to correct the course and come out on top. But you may have to make some pretty tough and ruthless decisions; the choice-and-consequences factor of this title is pretty good, too!

I already own "Vikings", the next installment of this series, and eventually I might get "Rome", too. I hope these developers keep doing their thing!

Normally I'm not really into tactical RPGs, but I've heard good things about the Expeditions series and I've always felt the Spanish conquest of the Americas is a criminally underutilized setting in games so naturally this game caught my interest. 

While it drew me in pretty quickly, this game isn't for everyone. It has a pretty steep learning curve and really makes you feel like you're just barely surviving, at least initially. This game pretty much front loads most of its difficulty and the whole Hispaniola section of the game is quite difficult despite being the tutorial area. I felt like the game got considerably easier after arriving in Mexico. Whether that is a result of me just learning how to play the game better or my party members being leveled up more in addition to the resources I had amassed at that point is up for debate. 

If you can get past that initial learning curve there is a lot of fun to be had here though. The game utilizes its setting well and is well written. The combat, while not great, is serviceable and if you're playing correctly you should be able to avoid a lot of combat scenarios or at the very least go into them in such a way that you are at an advantage. The exception to this are some rather brutal random events that will occasionally pop up as you camp at night that can lead to combat encounters that are more difficult than anything you face in the story missions and no-win dialogue options that will lead to the death of one of your expedition members. It's for that reason I recommend saving often so if you get one of these bullshit events you can load a save prior to that random event.

Chariot is a whimsical physics-based platformer from Frima Studio that builds its entire identity around one unusual and endearing concept: dragging a royal funeral chariot through a sprawling network of underground caverns while the ghost of the late king hovers nearby, endlessly critiquing your efforts. What initially sounds like a quirky premise quickly reveals itself as the core of a thoughtful and surprisingly intricate puzzle-platforming experience. As the princess and her loyal fiancé attempt to deliver the king to his final resting place, you journey through beautifully crafted environments full of hidden passages, collectible loot, and environmental hazards that constantly test your creativity and coordination.

The foundation of Chariot’s gameplay lies in its physics system. The chariot itself is heavy, unwieldy, and constantly affected by momentum, slopes, and gravity. Every platform, ledge, and slope becomes a small puzzle as you figure out how to drag, push, or hoist the cart using ropes and clever positioning. The challenge is never just about moving your characters—it’s about understanding how terrain interacts with the chariot’s weight and how to manipulate both the environment and the cart to progress. As levels become more complex, you encounter rail systems, collapsing bridges, icy pathways, and timed mechanisms that require careful planning. This physicality gives the game a distinctive rhythm: thoughtful, deliberate, and occasionally chaotic when the chariot picks up speed where you don’t want it to.

Visually, Chariot is full of charm. Its art style leans into vibrant colors and expressive animation, giving each underground biome its own distinct personality. The lighting glows warmly in some areas and ominously in others, and the caverns feel lively despite their subterranean setting. The characters’ animations are fluid and full of personality, and the king’s ghost adds humor with constant commentary that ranges from playful to grumpy. The game never takes its premise too seriously, allowing the whimsical world-building to complement the clever gameplay design without overshadowing it.

Co-op play is where Chariot truly shines. While the game is perfectly playable alone, dragging the chariot through intricate obstacles is clearly designed with teamwork in mind. With two players, the mechanics open up in satisfying ways—one can anchor the chariot while the other climbs ahead, or both can swing it like a pendulum to gain momentum and clear larger gaps. Communication becomes essential, especially in areas requiring synchronized movement or rope-based tricks. Many of the game’s most memorable moments emerge from collaborative problem-solving and the small triumphs of successfully navigating a tricky slope or retrieving a difficult collectible through well-timed cooperation. It’s a local co-op experience reminiscent of classic couch multiplayer, offering moments of both hilarity and frustration in the best possible sense.

Chariot does have a few rough edges. The deliberate pace, especially in solo play, can feel slow compared to traditional platformers, and lengthy stages sometimes contribute to a sense of repetition. Certain environments introduce slippery or fast-moving mechanics that, while inventive, can tip into frustration if the chariot gains too much momentum or the camera lags behind. The lack of online co-op is another missed opportunity, as the gameplay’s cooperative nature would translate naturally into online play. These limitations don’t undermine the core experience but may temper enjoyment for players who crave a faster or more fluid platformer.

Despite these caveats, the game offers a wealth of content. Each level features multiple routes, secret chambers, hidden treasure, and blueprints that unlock new upgrades for the chariot. Completionists will find a satisfying amount of replayability, with time trials and collectibles encouraging mastery of each area. The structure rewards patience and careful exploration, making the sense of progress feel earned rather than handed out.

Chariot ultimately succeeds because of its personality and inventiveness. It merges puzzle mechanics, platforming, and physics-based problem-solving into a cohesive experience anchored by charm and humor. While it can be slow-paced and occasionally demanding, it offers a rare kind of cooperative gameplay that values communication, timing, and shared triumphs. For players looking for a cooperative adventure that stands apart from typical action platformers, Chariot is a heartfelt and clever gem worth experiencing—especially with a partner, where its design truly comes to life.

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.
