[h1]About the game.[/h1]

Before going into the game itself; [b] I will strongly recommend you to play this game with someone else and not by yourself. [/b] Otherwise the game will be boring really quick and you are not able to get certain goodies or very hard to get on your own.

You are either playing as princess or the fiancé that needs to carry the coffin on the dead king. The king demands gems and other treasures that is laying around on each level. The coffin is the only one that is able to pick up the treasure and other goodies on the way. You will be holding a rope to pull and drag the coffin around like a true slave and you will be jumping over platforms to platforms until you have reached the exit of the level. You are able to get an upgrade if you have found the blueprint, allowing you to carry one item with you on your level.

There are Co-op area's which means you can't complete them on single player or a certain item may be unlocked in order to reach it(if that is possible). If you do have an item that is able to help you, you will still struggle a ton in order to get it, if you are able to get it that is. Completing co-op area's will grant you a rewarding gem or other treasures, like skulls.

The game looks interesting, unique, polished and you may think "It's a nice game". These thoughts will change really quickly and even quicker when you are solo. The levels are filled with platformers, straight out lines/hills, somewhat "emptiness" levels and struggling with the coffin from time to time. Checkpoint gaps can be quite big at times and if you are not able to reach your coffin or one of you is stuck and can't help out. You will have to reset yourself, losing the progress you have made so far and you will be playing on your last save (so like save and load game)

The gems or treasure itself are either inside of the walls or above the ground and some of them are on ridiculous places and it may be very difficult to reach with the coffin.. which can be quite struggling and demotivating to obtain at times. There is no such thing as 100% gem collecting but there is 100% map finding. Skulls will be kept forever and saved upon hitting on a checkpoint. same goes for resetting your character. But sometimes you are or you can't reach this without an upgrade or a co-op partner.  ALL GEMS will be reset on the moment you are playing the same level over again.. all SKULLS will be saved. So you could technically grind money that way but it's some slow progress.

[h1]Good things:[/h1] 

At start this game is really good and you can see that positive reviews are mostly from people who played only for a few hours so world 1 and maybe start of world 2 only. This game has an original gameplay and nice art style and music. The game is challenging but fair at the start. The good thing is also that there are upgrades for your chariot and some gadgets for you that you can also find and upgrade. The game does not hide from you that by playing it in coop it will be easier and you will get more loot and that you really really really should play it using a controller not the keyboard.

[h1]Bad things:[/h1] 

Level design is bad. Some sections are just tedious and long and many times you don’t know if you should explore the level or not. Some levels you can move in circles and get back to the start while in others you can’t ever go back and you have to play each level 3-4 times to see everything in it. First world is fine and looks like the game will be simple fun platformer with some straight-forward nice mechanics. But world 2 and I guess rest of the worlds just change everything as difficulty curve climbs up fast. I felt that many times the game was unfair and it was more important to have luck than to have skills as you can try to do something 50 times and each time fail at a different moment just because of the game physics and mechanics and how precise you have to be.

Other things that also frustrated me were: slippery slopes, timed switches, needless enemies, and bounce pads. When you start you don’t know the map and because of slippery slopes you have to replay most maps 3-4 times to get all the skulls and chariot upgrades and gadgets as you can’t go back up to the place you were seconds ago. Timed switches open doors but at start these doors were close by but later on you don’t even know what or where got opened and the game does not tell you in any way so you don’t know if you should run up or down or left or right and you have to do everything by trial and error way. Needless enemies because they don’t really attack you they only go for the chariot and try to steal gold from it and they show up only when chariot bumps into thing loudly near their nests or when you collect treasure near their nests. Why are they needless? Because all you have to do is stand on the chariot and spam one button to chase them away and lose nothing. They are in the game only to make you stop for a while to spam one button before you can continue on your way. Bounce pads are stupid as the rest of the game require you to be precise but bounce pads are all about luck and luck only. If you are away for more than 5 seconds from your chariot you get teleported back to check point and it is pure luck for your character and the chariot to make it to the ledge at the same time when using bounce pads. That means lots of trial and error before you will get lucky.

Physics in this game felt strange many times and too precise for me as it was very important to mix the speed of the moving chariot with the length of the rope and the right moment to jump and use the rope to pull chariot to myself before it falls down. I played it on gamepad and was mashing buttons like crazy and I can’t imagine anyone to try to play it on keyboard as sometimes you need to press 3-5 buttons at the exact same time in order to succeed. For me the game changes from enjoyable to unbearable and frustrating very quickly.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1] 

Buy this game only if you are going to play it in coop mode and only if both of you can’t get angry fast when you fail the same thing over and over again.

Overall score 3.5/10

Chariot is a very fun, yet very difficult platforming game where you must constantly babysit a chariot carrying the remains of your king and find the appropriate burial place for your king.  Each world leads to a possible place to bury him, but obviously, not until the last world does he find the correct place.

During your travels you, and possibly a friend, must use a rope to pull and hold onto the chariot.  You need to work to get through all of the obstacles with your chariot always with you.  This is quite a challenge especially as you reach the lava levels, the ice levels, and the quicksand levels.  This is definitely not an easy game and by yourself may or may not be easier depending on the skills of your partner, but playing co-op is definitely recommended as it is a lot of fun.

During your travels you will collect blueprints that allow for your chariot to be upgraded so that it can survive in lava or have wheels that can handle icy terrain.  Also, some blueprints will give your character special items such as a peg so you can place a peg in the ground tying a rope to your chariot to ensure it remains still while you go do something else.  Others are time slow down, magnet, and much more.  Not one item is necessarily more useful than others or absolutely necessary, but in certain levels specific items do offer more help than others.

This is a difficult game and the difficulty curve ramps up pretty quickly once your reach world 3.  I am still attempting to obtain all achievements, but the last level, the bonus level, is quite painful and the speed run asks you to get it done in less than 50 minutes.  Still I do enjoy a challenge in a game versus something so simple that I will easily forget it.  The challenge is here and the fun is here, so this game will definitely remain in my memory for a while.

As for the animation and controls, they are very fluid.  It takes a getting used to pulling or controlling the chariot with a rope while you jump around, but eventually it will become second hand and you will understand the physics of it and they make sense, it just takes practice to get used to.  The graphics are very cartoony and cute and fit perfectly for the type of game that it is.  At it's heart it is a platforming game and it does a really good job of offering a variety of levels with a variety of terrain and added difficulty as you travel from world to world.

If you have a friend you enjoy playing games with this is a great co-op game, but if not and you still enjoy a difficult but fun platformer, then pick this up.  I doubt you'd be disappointed.

# Amazing Potential, But Not Enough Long-Term Gameplay 🐔

As someone who absolutely loves chickens, ducks, geese, turkeys, and pretty much every farm animal imaginable, I genuinely enjoyed playing this game. Unfortunately, after around **12 hours of gameplay, I had essentially reached the end of what the game had to offer.** For the price I paid, that was disappointing.

I played for hours across two days because I was genuinely hooked. I wanted to keep expanding, raising more animals, improving my farm, and seeing how far I could take everything. Instead, I reached a point where there was very little left to work towards. I had plenty of money, but no meaningful progression, further expansion, or additional achievements to chase.

The ongoing expenses, such as food, vaccines, and trays, are there, but they don't provide enough meaningful gameplay on their own to keep things interesting.

**Here is where I think the game could really shine:**

More animals and bigger farms:
I want thousands of chickens, ducks, geese, and turkeys! I would love to see the ability to expand enclosures, add more coops and animal houses, and increase the number of animals I can raise. Having such large spaces with a relatively limited capacity feels like wasted potential.

More building, decorating, and customisation:
I like the existing coop skins, but I would love to do much more with them. Let us place additional buildings, move structures around, redesign layouts, decorate the farm, and upgrade our facilities. Give us the freedom to make the farm our own rather than being restricted to a relatively fixed setup.

A more useful shed and storage system:
The shed has a lot of potential, but much of its functionality feels underutilised once you progress. I would love to upgrade the shelving, increase storage capacity, and organise food, vaccines, trays, and other supplies more efficiently.

Personally, I found it more practical to keep supplies near the relevant coops and enclosures rather than constantly relying on the shed. Being able to place storage wherever it makes sense would make farm management feel much more natural.

Hire workers and automate the farm:
The automatic feeders are a great idea, but why stop there? I would love to hire employees who could help feed animals, organise supplies, restock enclosures, and handle everyday farm tasks. As the farm grows, managing everything should become a different kind of challenge rather than simply reaching a point where there is nothing left to do.

Having employees, management upgrades, and additional responsibilities would give players a reason to keep expanding and investing in their farms.

Meaningful long-term progression:
This is my biggest issue. I wanted a game I could return to for dozens or even hundreds of hours, continuously expanding and improving my farm. Instead, I completed practically everything within 12 hours.

More unlockables, achievements, animal varieties, larger facilities, upgrades, and ongoing progression would give players a reason to continue playing after reaching the current endgame.

My overall thoughts:
I genuinely like this game. I love the animals, I love the concept, and I think the developers have a really good foundation to build on. This isn't a case of me disliking the game; it's a case of me wanting so much more from it.

I played so much because I was enjoying myself. That's exactly why reaching the end so quickly was disappointing. I wanted to keep going, but there wasn't enough left to do.

However, considering the price and the fact that I reached the end of meaningful progression in approximately 12 hours, I personally cannot recommend purchasing it in its current state. I don't feel I received the long-term experience I was hoping for, and there isn't much incentive to continue playing once you've reached that point.

I would love to change this review to a positive recommendation in the future. With expanded farms, more animals, additional buildings, proper customisation, employee management, storage upgrades, and meaningful long-term progression, this could become an incredibly enjoyable farming game.

Please don't take this review as me saying the game is bad. I'm saying that it has so much potential, and I would love to see that potential realised. I want to spend 100+ hours building my dream farm, not run out of things to do after 12.

For now, I would recommend waiting for further updates before purchasing. I genuinely hope the developers continue expanding the game, because I would happily come back for more content.

I have raised chickens, ducks, geese, and turkeys in this game and let me tell you: the geese are absolutely running a protection racket and I respect it.

Eggstreme Farming is what happens when a Stardew Valley knockoff gets audited by the IRS. You're not just collecting eggs into a tray and slapping them in a vending machine (a business model that, I cannot stress enough, works flawlessly) — you're also juggling feed quality, vaccines, pen upgrades, and a water/electricity/internet bill that arrives with the emotional timing of a horror movie jump scare. Nothing humbles you like going bankrupt because your turkeys wanted the good water.

The loop is stupidly addictive: collect eggs, sell eggs, level up, unlock a slightly fancier license to own slightly more birds, repeat until 2 a.m. wondering why you care this much about poultry logistics. The day-night cycle means there is always "one more coop to check" standing between you and sleep, which is either a design triumph or a personal problem, TBD.

Is it realistic? The birds are rendered in glorious 3D and still look like they're plotting something. Is it deep? No. Is it exactly the right amount of dumb fun for turning your brain off after a long day of adulting? Absolutely, 10/10, would go bankrupt over duck feed again.

If you've ever wanted to know the exact psychological toll of an electric bill on a goose economy, this is your game.

Verdict: Eggcellent. Sorry. Not sorry.

This game is not... bad per say, I enjoyed dealing with the eggs and unlocking automation, I think it's a fun game when you need a little bit of calm, no thoughts game, but it definitely needs improving. The leveling system is way too quick, making the game way too short. I mean, I unlocked the turkeys before I'd even gotten one goose because I was trying to automate the chickens first, so I think the leveling system would benefit from putting the breaks way more.

But if you slow it down too much, you get to the second problem, which is that there is really not enough to unlock and progress. The automation goes to eggs and water and that's where it stops. Which means that for the food, the selling, the cleaning and the pre-emptive medication, it's your job to do it even if you're 100 levels above the last unlock. I had to stop adding more birds to the cages because the cleaning alone would take me multiple hours in game, and the medication was so incredibly tedious, between checking the animals, buying the medication, manually carry it to each of the cages one by one, administer it, and then redo it every 2-3 days. I don't mind the use of medication, but it should be reserved to if an animal gets actually sick, not having to pre-emptively give it all the time, and the cleaning should definitely get an update, whether it be better equipment or employees to do it for you.

Since the price of the game is actually cheap, I will give it some slack, but I still don't believe it's really worth the price considering it took me 8 hours to fully automate everything and have everything unlocked and purchased, and it mostly took me that time because of how much I was running around trying to catch up with the cleaning, feeding, medicating and even more, carrying everything everywhere, one by one. It feels weird to me that the most fun part, the eggs, is the first to get automated but everything that's the most boring and repetitive to do doesn't.

I still recommend the game because have hopes that they will add more stuff to automate the process, and I do believe that simply rebalancing the different tasks, like lowering the medication need and the cleaning spots, or slowing down the leveling up by half, would make it instantly much better, but until then, if you want to play this game, honestly, just play the demo, it's got the most fun parts of the game without the tediousness of the endgame, and it's free.

Eggstreme Farming is a first-person farming and business simulation that takes one small part of agriculture and turns it into the foundation of an expanding commercial operation. Developed and published by Sagitta Studios, the game revolves around raising poultry, collecting eggs, selling products, managing expenses, and gradually increasing the size and efficiency of the farm. Instead of spreading itself across dozens of unrelated farming activities, it concentrates on a straightforward production cycle and attempts to make that cycle increasingly demanding as the player's operation grows.

The basic routine begins with purchasing animals and preparing suitable spaces for them. Chickens are naturally central to the experience, but ducks, geese, and turkeys can also become part of the farm. Animals arrive in boxes and must be placed in appropriate pens, giving expansion a physical, hands-on feeling rather than reducing everything to menus. As the number of birds increases, organizing pens and maintaining an efficient layout becomes increasingly important. This makes the farm itself feel like an evolving workplace rather than a static backdrop.

Producing eggs is only useful if the animals remain healthy and productive. Players need to provide sufficient food and water while paying attention to the quality of their feed. Medicine and vaccination mechanics introduce additional responsibilities, making animal health another consideration alongside profit. These systems add welcome depth because successful farming is not simply about purchasing as many birds as possible. A larger population also creates more work, consumes more resources, and increases the consequences of poor management.

Egg collection is deliberately interactive. Players collect the products with trays before selling them through a vending machine, creating a repeated sequence of gathering, transporting, selling, and reinvesting. Selling eggs generates money while regular farm activities also contribute experience toward progression. It is an uncomplicated loop, but it fits players who enjoy games where small repetitive tasks gradually produce visible improvements. Watching a tiny operation develop into a busy poultry business can provide the satisfying sense of advancement that management simulators depend upon.

Expansion brings a more interesting economic challenge. Additional pens can be rented as production requirements increase, while shelves, furniture, decorative plants, and other items allow the working environment to be reorganized and customized. More space and equipment can improve the farm, but growth also introduces additional expenses. Water, electricity, internet, animal supplies, and other costs prevent earnings from functioning as pure profit. The player therefore needs to balance ambition against affordability rather than expanding without consequences.

An experience and licensing system provides another reason to continue completing everyday jobs. Collecting eggs, selling trays, and caring for animals contribute toward XP, while higher progression levels provide access to additional licenses and opportunities. This structure helps turn repetitive chores into longer-term objectives. Instead of completing tasks solely because the animals require them, players are simultaneously working toward the next stage of the business. For anyone who enjoys watching numbers increase and unlocking increasingly productive options, this should be one of the more rewarding aspects of the game.

The day-and-night cycle adds some atmosphere to the routine, while the first-person presentation keeps players physically involved in activities that could easily have been handled through interfaces. Inventory management and organization also become more significant as the farm grows. There are 34 Steam achievements for players interested in additional milestones, alongside single-player functionality and Family Sharing support. The overall design is clearly aimed at people who enjoy methodical progression, organization, resource management, and performing practical jobs themselves.

Its narrow focus is also the main factor that could limit its audience. Feeding birds, maintaining water supplies, collecting eggs, carrying trays, and selling products naturally involve repetition. Players who need frequent changes in objectives or a large selection of unrelated activities may eventually find the routine restrictive. There is considerably more appeal here for someone who enjoys optimizing a familiar process and improving efficiency over time. The various animal species, expenses, licenses, health mechanics, and expansion opportunities help provide variation, but the fundamental activity remains centered on poultry and egg production.

The Steam listing also discloses AI-assisted material in certain promotional or cover artwork, achievement icons, marketing assets, and parts of the translation process. This does not define the actual management mechanics, but it may be relevant to players who pay attention to how visual and localization assets are produced.

Steam Deck compatibility is currently not officially categorized by Valve with a Verified, Playable, or Unsupported rating on the game's Steam listing. As a result, it is best regarded as having an unverified Steam Deck status rather than assuming full compatibility. The game may still be capable of running through SteamOS and Proton, but controller behavior, text readability, performance, and other handheld-specific details should not be treated as officially guaranteed until testing or a formal compatibility classification becomes available.

Overall, Eggstreme Farming takes an amusingly specific idea and develops it into a structured farming-management experience. The combination of animal care, egg production, selling, operating expenses, licenses, facility expansion, and organization gives the player several systems to manage without making the concept unnecessarily complicated. Its repetitive nature will not suit everyone, but that same predictable rhythm could make it relaxing and satisfying for fans of task-oriented simulators. Building a small poultry setup into a profitable operation provides a clear motivation to keep improving efficiency and expanding production.

It offers a focused and approachable management loop with enough economic and animal-care considerations to give its simple premise substance. Greater gameplay variety would strengthen its long-term appeal, but players who enjoy gradual progression and hands-on business simulation should find plenty to appreciate.

Really Enjoying It! Lately, I’ve been in a bit of a gaming slump and have been looking for a game that could actually catch my interest. When I came across Eggstreme Farming, I thought it looked pretty interesting, so I decided to give it a try.

And honestly? It’s actually really good! 😂 I’ve been enjoying it more than I expected, especially the whole farming and taking-care-of-animals aspect. That said, I do have a few suggestions that I hope the developers might consider adding in the future:

Extra Farm Hand – Cleaner

Cleaning the animal pens every day is totally fine when you only have a few pens. But once you start unlocking and opening more pens, cleaning them one by one can become pretty time-consuming. Having an extra farm hand specifically for cleaning would be such a huge help!

 Extra Farm Hand – Egg Collector

This is probably the one I want the most. 😂 When the automatic egg collector is full, you have to go collect the egg trays, while also keeping up with cleaning the pens. Sometimes it feels like I’m constantly running back and forth between everything. Having a farm hand who could collect the egg trays would make things so much smoother.

Extra Farm Hand – Order Unpacker & Organizer

I’d also love to have a farm hand who could unpack the orders and arrange the items for me. Sometimes you have so many boxes coming in, and having to unpack and organize everything yourself can take quite a bit of time. It would be great if we could hire someone specifically for this job.

Automatic Feeder

I’d also love to see an automatic feeder added. Having to constantly go back and forth to refill the animals’ food can get tiring, especially when you have several pens. It would be really nice to have an upgrade that could automatically feed them.

Bigger Egg Crates

I hope we can also get bigger crates for storing eggs. The current ones feel a little too small, especially once you start producing a lot of eggs.

Animals Not Eating or Drinking?

I’ve also noticed that some of my animals sometimes won’t eat or drink even though they’re healthy and there’s plenty of food and water available. I’m not sure if this is a bug or if there’s something I’m missing, but hopefully it can be looked into.

Overall, I’m really enjoying Eggstreme Farming! These are just some quality-of-life improvements I’d love to see in the future. I’ll definitely keep playing, and if I think of anything else that could make the game even better, I might add another review/update later.

Keep up the great work, developers! 🐔❤️

First off, I want to say that this game has a really cool, unique, and very interesting premise with the nomadic style movement and walker combat. 

I don't think this game should be "season" based. - My take is that this can only be done with a larger player base. The "end of seasons" have a huge player drop-off and this can make it look like there are no players. Imagine the loss of new players coming in towards the end of season thinking the game is dead, or having to start over after just getting situated. I think they should just introduce "walker maintenance" - most of the gameplay mechanics are geared towards oasis cleanup and "starting over" anyways. There is no need for seasons.

The other issue I see is the new player tutorial. It goes over some of the basics, but it doesn't set up new players or solo players off correctly. New players and solo players need to be set up for success to defend against small scale attacks. Anti-personnel should be something that can be done in cradle; it should be a highlighted aspect! Telling new players and solo players that they should use their walkers as a "nomadic" base and using the trade station as a home-base is another thing - most new players and solo players setup a small base only to be raided shortly after.

Set up your player-base for success and the rest will emerge naturally. Most PVP games fail to do this correctly. I know I would personally love to engage in PVP if I was allowed to grind enough in a safer way, but these games seem to always create systems that punish small and solo player bases -  Which is a large chunk that is consistently lost. Losing gear is not the problem, losing everything is.

I’ve put a lot of hours into Last Oasis, going all the way back to its earlier seasonal content, and I’ve always really loved the core concept behind the game. The idea of a nomadic survival MMO with massive walkers, clan warfare, and a constantly shifting world is honestly one of the most unique concepts I’ve seen in the genre. When it works, it really works—and that’s what has kept me coming back.

That said, one of the biggest issues I’ve experienced over time is the lack of consistency. The game has gone through so many changes that it’s been hard to stay grounded in what the “core experience” is supposed to be. Systems, mechanics, and direction seem to shift frequently, and while change isn’t always bad, it often feels like there isn’t a clear long-term vision tying everything together. As a returning player, it can be confusing trying to relearn systems that have been reworked multiple times.

Since coming back recently, I’ve noticed that some things have definitely improved. The skill tree, for example, feels much better than it used to. The addition of the perk system adds more depth and gives players meaningful ways to customize their playstyle, which is a big step in the right direction. It feels more rewarding to progress and build your character now than it did before.

However, not everything has seen that same level of improvement. The NPC AI is still pretty rough and can break immersion at times. Encounters don’t always feel engaging or challenging in a good way—they often feel predictable or poorly executed. Visually, the game still looks about the same as it did before, which isn’t necessarily a bad thing, but it also doesn’t feel like it has evolved much in that department either.

Overall, Last Oasis feels like a game with an incredible foundation that hasn’t quite reached its full potential yet. It’s still enjoyable in many ways, especially if you appreciate the core concept, but it clearly has a long road ahead before it can fully deliver on what it promises.

I still have hope for the developers, because I genuinely want this game to succeed. There’s something special here—you can see it. If the team can find a consistent direction, improve core systems like AI, and continue building on the better changes like the skill and perk trees, this could easily become a standout title in the survival MMO space.

The walkers, the desert survival, the nomadic PvP... it’s one of the most unique survival games I’ve ever played. Unfortunately, the same issue that drove me away years ago still seems to be alive and well in Season 6.

The biggest problem for me has always been griefing with glide suits and grapple hooks. A single player can endlessly harass a group or walker with almost zero risk. They fly in, swing around like Spider-Man, take shots, break something, then grapple away before anyone can realistically catch them. Even if you repel them, they can just come back five minutes later and repeat the same thing.

This isn’t about losing a fair fight... PvP is part of the game and I’m completely fine with that. The frustration comes from the fact that this style of gameplay feels more like harassment than combat. One player can waste hours of your time without any meaningful risk or consequence.

What’s disappointing is that this was a common complaint back in Season 1, and it doesn’t feel like it was ever effectively addressed. I came back in Season 6 hoping the balance around mobility and griefing had been improved, but it still feels like the same problem.

The game still has an amazing foundation and some of the coolest mechanics in the survival genre. I genuinely want to love it. But when one person with a glide suit and grapple hook can disrupt an entire group indefinitely, it makes it hard to stay invested and entertained

TL;DR: Good bones but too many bugs to be enjoyable finishing and no prospects of fixes in the near future.

When the game first came out, I was really excited to follow its development and purchasing it when it was complete. However, due to issues in the developer's personal life, the game was released in an unfinished state and there hasn't been a lot of communication with the developer since 2019. The game has been stuck in the relatively same state that it was when it was taken out of early access. That is why I wouldn't recommend this game. This doesn't mean that I didn't like the game.

The unique premise of the game that hadn't really been seen before or since the release is rather well handled with the player being able to take a bunch of different paths. Both factions get access to various pieces of equipment and are able to use them in various ways to achieve level goals. In Global mode, the manner in which the player achieved the previous level's goals will have an effect on both your faction and the enemy faction. If you were peaceful in the previous level, the enemy will be less willing to be violent. If you were violent in the previous level, the enemy will be more willing to be violent. These repercussions on gameplay and how it affects your playthrough made me love the game. But there are many bugs within the game that makes these mechanics fall flat.

In one of the early levels of the game, there is a bug where your units can get stuck in the back of the map if you perform an action which you are incentivized to perform by the level's hints. These units are then useless, leaving you to either fail or restart the level. In another level, the level interaction between you, the actual level terrain and your enemy can get you or the enemy stuck in a part of the level where you cannot beat the level. As I mentioned earlier in this review, there most likely is going to be no fix for this in the near future.

If this doesn't dissuade you and you're willing to push through the bugs, this game provides an interesting experience that really no other game has.

RIOT: Civil Unrest, developed by Leonard Menchiari, IV Productions, and Ivan Venturi Productions, and published by Silver Lining Interactive, is a real-time strategy game that explores the tension and dynamics of public demonstrations from both sides of the conflict. Set against the backdrop of historical and contemporary protests, the game gives players the opportunity to experience the challenges faced by both law enforcement and protesters. By allowing players to control either faction, the game offers a nuanced perspective on the delicate balance between authority, civil rights, and public safety, making it a unique entry in the strategy genre.

The game is inspired by real-life events, including the Arab Spring in Egypt, Spain’s Indignados movement, and the NoTAV protests in Italy. Leonard Menchiari, who personally participated in the NoTAV demonstrations, brought firsthand insight into the design, aiming to convey the chaotic, unpredictable, and emotionally charged nature of civil unrest. Players encounter scenarios that reflect the frustration, tension, and decision-making pressures that both protesters and police face during such events. This approach imbues the game with a sense of authenticity and urgency rarely found in strategy games.

Gameplay in RIOT: Civil Unrest is presented from a top-down perspective with pixel-art visuals that are both functional and atmospheric. The pixelated environments capture urban streets, barricades, and the throngs of participants with clarity, allowing players to focus on strategic planning rather than intricate graphical detail. Players must manage unit placement, movement, and timing carefully, whether controlling the police to maintain order or the protesters to achieve their objectives. Despite its thoughtful design, the game’s controls and AI behavior can sometimes feel inconsistent, creating moments of chaos that mirror real-life unpredictability but may frustrate players seeking precise tactical control.

One of the game’s strongest features is its emotional impact. Playing as a protester often evokes empathy and tension, as players must navigate threats from law enforcement while attempting to meet objectives. Conversely, controlling the police highlights the pressures of crowd management and maintaining order, often requiring players to make quick, morally complex decisions. This duality encourages reflection on the human element of civil unrest, making the gameplay feel more meaningful than mere tactical maneuvering.

The audio design complements the game’s visual and emotional tone. A mix of electronic and industrial-inspired music sets a tense atmosphere, while sound cues signal crowd movement, clashes, or escalating situations. These auditory elements heighten immersion and reinforce the chaotic energy of street-level confrontations. Combined with the pixel-art visuals, the soundscape creates a convincing sense of being present in a volatile urban environment.

While the game has been praised for its ambition and the depth of its thematic exploration, it is not without criticisms. Some players find the controls unintuitive and the AI behavior unpredictable, which can detract from the strategic aspect. Additionally, the juxtaposition of serious, real-world events with arcade-style gameplay mechanics has sparked discussion about whether the game fully honors the gravity of its subject matter. Despite these challenges, RIOT: Civil Unrest succeeds in presenting a provocative and thought-provoking experience that few other games attempt.

In conclusion, RIOT: Civil Unrest is a distinctive strategy game that places players at the heart of socio-political conflicts, offering perspectives on both protest movements and law enforcement. Its combination of historical inspiration, emotional resonance, and strategic gameplay creates a compelling, if sometimes imperfect, experience. While it may not appeal to traditional strategy gamers seeking precise mechanics, its bold approach and willingness to engage with complex, real-world issues make it a noteworthy and memorable title in the realm of interactive media.

----------
Overview
----------

An interesting concept, with intriguing visuals.
Unfortunately, the game mechanics are sloppy, non-responsive garbage, and seem heavily dependant on RNG factors.
This game would be better off as either a protesters vs. police themed UEBS (Ultimate Epic Battle Simulator) or a screensaver/desktop background for something like Wallpaper Engine.

--------
Details
--------

For some reason, protesters are far more motivated and capable of charging a wall of shields, batons and aggression than they are trying to get past a few scattered cops with single-shot teargas launchers and little else.

There might be massive gaps between the ballistics police that any person with half and brain and a pair of legs could WALK through, or around, yet the protesters will instead flee and completely ignore anything you tell them to do. If you play like 4 missions, you'll quickly get to this point, and be unable to proceed any further. You can go full defensive, you can go full offensive, you can go full passivity, or full violence, it doesn't matter.

The devs explain that when the game "becomes too difficult" that you just need to go back and replay the previous missions over and over "with different strategies" to boost your "publicity advantage".

Despite being unable to unlock any of these "different strategies" (because you can't complete that one awful mission), you roll your eyes and replay the previous missions a few more times as recommended.

But then, irrespective of completing the previous missions repeatedly with "perfect victory" being the result for each instance, the aforementioned "publicity advantage" will instead DECREASE, making it even LESS likely for you to complete that one mission.

I'm assuming you just need to keep replaying that same terrible mission over and over until the RNG is in your favor, but why bother? If you're relying so much on RNG in a game to determine the outcome of action, instead of conscious decisions or strategy, it may as well be a simulation, not a game.

You can keep spamming hotkeys and repeatedly ordering your groups to move or act, and they'll just ignore you or any actual opportunities to be of any use, simply because there is some arbitrary or vaporous instruction in the background keeping you from proceeding unless you're boosting play time statistics.

On top of the nonsensical instructions and game mechanics, the UI is also poorly executed. The lack of responsiveness both in-game and in-menu is frustrating. Having to wait 5 minutes for the game to tally my score at the end of every match, without being able to skip or speed up the process, is just stupid.

This game has become my new obsession, and I would 100% recommend this game to anyone who enjoys beautiful/artsy casual survival/exploration games. What's funny is at the 1 hour mark I was close to quitting and refunding it as I wasn't very engaged and had read countless reviews warning of bugs. However, I played on in the story and by hour 2 I was fully emersed. I hope you will give this game a chance as it has real potential and has already improved bug wise drastically since launch. I'll break my review down into three sections: the first, being my favorite parts of the game, the second, things that took time to grow on me, and third, where the game still needs work. 

Why I love the game. The main I had to the game was the premise, but also the look. Even 25 hours in I still take a few moments here and there to admire the landscape, or look on to my ever growing village. The natural progression that the story mode seamlessly teaches you, allows you to take your own pace and learn the mechanics on your own. I also enjoyed the subtle complexities in the mechanics that push you to experiment and accomplish growth without holding your hand too much. While the story is great with teaching you the basics, the sandbox is where the game shines. You can explore a infinitely generating world (I believe, I haven't found the world edge yet and I've rowed multiple days in each direction) with multiple biomes making exploration necessary and enjoyable.

Where the game took time to win me over. While I raved on about my favorite aspects of the game, it's important to note that I didn't always feel this way about the game mechanics. For instance, some areas of progression were unexplained and while it forced me to learn on my own, I struggled for a while and wasted a lot of resources. There doesn't seem to be many online guides yet so it can be challenging to answer specific questions. That said, it did also create a lot of fun learning experiences so I still enjoy this aspect of the game a lot. Another area that held me back at first was the lack of a narrative or story, other than survival and progression. I think that the lack of a story pushes you add your own narrative, or to let other areas of the game drive your interest which it did for me. While I did talk highly of the exploration, I will say that at this time it can feel a bit dull as there isn't much diversity to the regions other than which base resources spawn more and possibly animals. There isn't any unique fauna or resources in these regions, so they can feel decorative at times. All this made early game sandbox (after I completed story) mode exploration feel repetitive as I scoured the clunky generate landscapes looking for a good settlement location. That said, with time the exploration became more fun especially as I got companions and would fight other tribes and loot stone formations. 

Limitations and areas for improvement. While I absolutely love this game, there are a few things that need improvement, as well as lot of additions that could further improve this game. There are still a few bugs in the games current state, that while not game breaking can be frustrating. To name a few, animals captured in pits often despawn before you get them, or just have trouble falling in, arrows disappear/fly around, as well as the occasional (average once a session) crashing. I will say that I haven't noticed the amount that are mentioned in other reviews, but it is something to note before playing. Outside of bugs, the game has a lot of room to add depth as once you get to camp level 8 in era 2 there isn't anything else to progress to. I hope the developers can add another era(s) that maybe transitions into the copper (maybe even early bronze age). I also think that more random spawns could be added, like random traders/recruitable villagers with high skills or special abilities, in addition it would be nice to be able to be friendly or trade with other tribes instead of them always attacking you on sight. Missions or events in sandbox could add more variety, or a religion/spiritual system where you are compelled to go to certain locations and sacrifice an animal or something could be interesting too. 

In conclusion, I love this game and see so much potential for it and give my biggest thanks to the developers for making such a great game! I hope they continue their work on this game (I've spent some time in Czech and would love to give any feedback to help with the game). I would 100% recommend this game in it's current form at this price as it will at the very least give you countless hours of paleolithic fun! I'm sure the price will go up as the developers improve the game and add more content, so get in now!

[h1] Great Concept, Mediocre Execution [/h1]
[h3] Riddled with bugs [/h3]
I was initially excited after watching the trailer and reading the concept. Survival Crafting game with colony sim style management. That's pretty much what it is but the game is like a shallow pool. The survival/crafting/combat is functionable, but not particularly interesting. The Colony management is just assign one task to a tribe member and as far as I could tell that was pretty much it. Make sure they have food and a bed and your good. 

[b] Positives [/b]
+ Visually pleasing artstyle: I usually stray away from games that look like they just use a synty low-poly asset pack, but I was actually pleased with how the game looked. 
+ Core Gameplay loop isn't terrible: I don't mind wandering around picking up sticks, hunting smaller game, manually crafting basic supplies, at least at first. 
+ Timing mini-game: Lots of little QTEs for fishing, cooking, harvesting. It's a small detail that makes the game more engaging than just pressing E to pickup loot. 
+ Craft from storage: Such a necessity for modern survival games. Happy to see this wasn't overlooked

[b] Negatives [/b]
- [b] buggy [/b] [i] it's an ugly planet, a bug planet [/i]: This is what ultimately stopped me from wanting to continue my campaign. NPCs getting stuck, housing not detecting correctly, items falling to ground and vanishing, lock on getting stuck on something invisible.. I can handle some jank (I love you Kenshi) but this was just plain frustrating especially in a 1.0 build. 
- Ai: Companions, Animals, NPCs, they just all seem so sporadic. You can easily cheese the pathfinding to get away from things, the pets run circles around my feet while I'm trying to dodge roll (just like my dog while I'm trying to cook) commands that do something but nothing noticeable.
- Combat: Lackluster. Aiming ranged weapons is never where I want it to be, lock on just feels floaty and off. It's not the worst combat ever, but it's just nowhere near what it should be if hunting is going to be a huge part of the game. I would prefer something simpler akin to runescape or kenshi to something floaty and offputting. 
- Colony: You can assign tribe members a task to gather, hunt, craft or cook. That's about it. They get a single task they can do. No stock limits to stop them from turning all your wood into arrows so you have to micro-manage their one task, they're like worker ant drones powered by a single core ai. Happiness seems pretty linear and just boosts or debuffs the productivity of their single task, but it's extremely easy to keep them happy. 
- Unexplained Mechanics: I'm all for the figure it out as you go style of learning. You can play the campaign which has a sort of tutorial, or jump right into a sandbox. I went the campaign route and still didn't really understand much. [b] I.E. [/b] not sure how the tech tree works at all, do I need to craft all the types of items to unlock the next? do I need a certain number of building/tribe members? If that is the case, why would I need to go back and craft a wooden hammer/axe to get the checkmark if I just skipped it and went straight to stone? Does my character level up and get better at skills like the tribe members do? Is that why my aiming with the bow was so off? No idea. 

[h3] TLDR [/h3]

[h1]Great atmosphere and potential, but needs quality-of-life polish[/h1]

After nearly 15 hours of playtime, [i]Polylithic[/i] has proven to have incredible potential and a deeply engaging core loop. You can truly feel the prehistoric atmosphere—traveling alone through the dense forest while watching out for predators or hiding in the bushes at night gave me actual goosebumps. I also really enjoy the tech progression (though it could be even slower and deeper) and the clever mechanic where you have to manually complete an action multiple times before delegating it to your tribe members.

However, despite being out of Early Access, several technical issues and QoL oversights need urgent attention from the developers:

[list]
[*] [b]Performance:[/b] Severe FPS drops and stuttering occur frequently, even on lower graphic settings.
[*] [b]Pathfinding & AI:[/b] Villagers regularly get stuck on decorations around the campfire when heading to sleep. Animals also teleport across riverbanks instead of swimming or routing properly.
[*] [b]Automation & Tasks:[/b] The campfire management task is unreliable—fires often burn out overnight despite having active assignments and sufficient resources in storage. Expanding the task queue or priority system for tribe members would be a huge improvement.
[*] [b]Cooking Automation:[/b] The cooking UI/logic feels completely unintuitive when assigning tasks to AI. It constantly displays a "missing ingredients" icon even when the required resources are available in storage or the cook's inventory.
[*] [b]Inventory Management:[/b] A basic sorting feature for inventory and storage containers is desperately needed.
[/list]

Overall, it’s a very promising title with a fantastic vibe that I recommend checking out, but it definitely needs a few more patches to reach its full potential.

I cannot recommend this game to anyone who doesn’t have a lot of patience and an almost unhealthy level of optimism.

I’ve spent a few hours playing it, and the biggest positive for me is definitely the prehistoric setting. That concept alone kept me playing for quite a while. The idea of building your own village and managing NPC workers isn’t exactly new, but it is presented in a fairly simple and enjoyable way.

Unfortunately, that’s about where the positives end.

The game is simply broken. NPCs either don’t do what they are supposed to do or wander around the map for no apparent reason. Quests regularly bug out, and progression can get stuck. Sometimes restarting the game fixes it, but not always.

One example is moving your village to a new location as part of the story. After that, new features are supposed to become available, such as the underground storage. The storage gets unlocked, but the shovel required to build it doesn’t.

Another example is the hunter. When hunting rabbits, he would regularly walk straight into the river and get stuck there.

The game even openly admits at the beginning that it is being made by an inexperienced team. That’s honestly fine. But admitting that doesn’t make the constant bugs that block progression any less frustrating.

And the worst part is the lack of technical support. I’ve reported bugs, but nobody responds. There is no real communication, and it feels like you are left on your own when something breaks.

At this point, I feel the game needs at least another year of development to figure out how everything is actually supposed to work. Without functional technical support and communication with the players, progress is likely to be painfully slow.

The core idea is interesting, and the prehistoric setting has potential. Unfortunately, right now the bugs and broken progression make the game very difficult to recommend.

A few things I’d personally love to see:

1. Automatically disable slow-walking during combat.
This is was one of my earliest frustrations while still learning the game, but I’ll be sneaking up on prey, get spotted and become the prey, and suddenly I’m trying to fight while my character is still slow-walking. Once combat starts,  that slow-walk should automatically turn off so I can actually RUN when things get chaotic.

2. More storage + an easier resource overview.
More storage options would be great. It would also be incredibly helpful to have a resource count somewhere on the HUD or in a menu, so I don’t have to open my chest every time just to figure out how much of something I have.

3. Let us abandon and reacquire quests.
This would be a huge quality-of-life feature during Early Access. With some quest bugs still around, having the ability to drop a quest and pick it back up could potentially prevent players from getting stuck or having their story progression disrupted.

PlinkIdle is an entertaining incremental idle game that takes the simple pleasure of dropping balls and transforms it into a steadily expanding experience filled with upgrades, multipliers, automation, and colorful environments. Developed by Black Heart Games LLC and published by Gamersky Games and brokenworm, the game combines nostalgic arcade mechanics with modern idle progression systems. Its approachable design, relaxing atmosphere, and satisfying visual feedback make it particularly appealing to players who enjoy watching modest beginnings evolve into increasingly elaborate systems.

The gameplay begins with a straightforward ball-dropping mechanic that generates resources used to purchase improvements. As players accumulate earnings, they unlock upgrades that increase productivity and introduce additional mechanics. What starts as a relatively quiet experience gradually becomes a lively display of falling balls, coins, bonuses, and multiplying rewards. This continuous escalation creates an enjoyable sense of accomplishment, although the fundamental gameplay remains deliberately simple throughout.

One of the game's strongest features is its incremental progression system. Every upgrade contributes to greater efficiency, encouraging players to optimize their resource generation and pursue increasingly ambitious milestones. The satisfaction comes from observing how previous investments accelerate future earnings. This progression loop is easy to understand but potentially addictive, especially for enthusiasts who appreciate watching numerical values grow and production systems become increasingly powerful.

Environmental variety adds another appealing dimension to the experience. By filling ball-o-meters, players unlock additional stages featuring distinctive pixel-art backgrounds and atmospheric themes. These environments provide visual rewards for continued progression while preventing the presentation from feeling completely static. The colorful scenery complements the game's retro aesthetic, creating a pleasant combination of nostalgic visuals and relaxing gameplay.

PlinkIdle also incorporates lucky buffs, special drops, and occasional bonus spawns that introduce unpredictability into its otherwise repetitive mechanics. These features create opportunities for temporary boosts and enhanced resource generation, adding excitement to the progression cycle. Although randomness does not fundamentally transform the gameplay, it provides satisfying moments when production increases dramatically and previously distant objectives become easier to achieve.

The distinction between active and passive gameplay is another noteworthy strength. Players who prefer minimal interaction can utilize Rombo the Autobot to automate certain activities, allowing progression without constant attention. Meanwhile, those seeking greater involvement can invest in combinations, GoldCoins, and Disco balls to improve multipliers and maximize their earnings. This flexibility accommodates different playing styles, making the experience suitable for both attentive players and those who enjoy keeping an idle game running alongside other activities.

The prestige system further extends the game's longevity by rewarding players for reaching major progression milestones. Advancing through prestige ranks provides additional power and encourages repeated runs with improved efficiency. Each successful cycle makes earlier stages easier to overcome, creating opportunities to reach increasingly impressive levels of production. While this system offers meaningful long-term objectives, repeatedly restarting familiar progression sequences may become tiresome for players who prefer constant mechanical variety.

Visually, PlinkIdle embraces charming pixel graphics and a retro-inspired presentation. The increasingly chaotic movement of falling balls creates an engaging spectacle, while colorful environments provide a welcome sense of atmosphere. Its visual identity emphasizes simplicity rather than technical sophistication, allowing the gameplay mechanics to remain the primary attraction. The presentation is particularly effective when numerous effects and bonuses appear simultaneously, reinforcing the satisfying nature of incremental growth.

Audio design contributes significantly to the game's relaxing personality. The repetitive sounds of falling balls create an ASMR-like experience, supported by atmospheric chiptune music. Customizable volume settings allow players to adjust the soundscape according to their preferences. This combination makes the game suitable for casual relaxation, although the continuous repetition of sound effects may eventually become distracting during extended sessions.

Several accessibility and convenience features improve the overall experience. Players can save their progress, adjust audio settings, and enjoy gameplay without demanding reflex-based challenges. Steam achievements provide additional objectives, while Steam Cloud support offers convenient synchronization. The inclusion of offline earnings also complements the incremental structure, allowing players to benefit from periods spent away from the game.

Despite its appealing presentation, PlinkIdle has noticeable limitations. The gameplay relies heavily on repetitive resource accumulation, and its strategic decisions primarily involve selecting upgrades and improving efficiency. Players seeking substantial challenges, complex mechanics, or diverse activities may find the experience lacking depth. The prestige system provides longevity, but it does not entirely eliminate the repetitive nature of the underlying progression loop.

Steam Deck compatibility is a notable advantage. The game is officially Steam Deck Verified, with its core functionality working through the handheld's controls and its interface remaining usable on the smaller display. Controller prompts and general navigation are appropriately supported, while the game can run using settings suitable for the device. Its viewpoint and methodical pacing also translate naturally to portable play, although demanding visual settings can still make sensible performance adjustments worthwhile for players prioritizing battery life or consistent performance.

Overall, PlinkIdle delivers a pleasant combination of incremental progression, relaxing audiovisual design, and satisfying automation mechanics. Its greatest achievement is transforming a basic ball-dropping concept into an engaging cycle of upgrades, bonuses, and increasingly impressive production. Although repetitive gameplay and limited strategic complexity prevent it from offering universal appeal, its cozy presentation and accessible mechanics make it an attractive choice for enthusiasts of idle games and casual progression experiences.

A charming and relaxing incremental game with satisfying upgrades, enjoyable automation, and appealing pixel-art environments. Its repetitive foundation limits its depth, but its accessible mechanics provide an entertaining experience for fans of the genre.

Pixel Puzzles Ultimate is a good simple game. The developer (I assume) uploaded jigsaws based on public domain art and photography. They can vary in size and detail. - Pieces snap into place on the board, instead of connecting with each other. You can't notice that 3 pieces go together and then move them around as one chunk, which I'd much prefer.
- There's the option to enable rotation, but the shaded edges of the pieces reveal which way round the piece should go anyway. (The sides that should be top and left are lit, instead of the sides that are *currently* top and left.) So it's not worth playing with that enabled as it just adds extra squinting.

But yeah, trying it out is basically without risk so you might as well.

==SUMMARY==

I don't recommend this game. While the base game is free (dlc is not), there are other free jigsaw puzzles online that IMHO are much better.

The basic puzzle completion is pretty much as you would expect but there are several design decisions that can affect gameplay and definitely make the experience different from completing a physical jigsaw puzzle or ones on free sites like jigidi which I will get into below.

Tho since base game is free, no harm in trying it either.

==GAMEPLAY==

I'm assuming you know what a jigsaw puzzle is. So I will cover how this game differs from a real-world jigsaw beyond the obvious.

This basically defines a fixed "board" area and the goal is to place the scattered pieces into their fixed positions on that board. When you start a new puzzle, the pieces are scattered in an area adjacent to the board, which is in water, and is refered to as the "pool" in the game. Depending on the puzzle / number of pieces, the pool can appear on either 1 side (usually the bottom), 2 sides (left and right), or 3 sides. I have completed several pieces with 810 pieces and never saw any where the pool was along all 4 sides of the board. There are settings (and hotkeys) for cycling through several preset colors on both the board and the pool, independently of each other.

Still, I personally dislike the entire "pool" concept and just found it annoying to have to drag all my pieces around even more. By default, the pieces in the pool drift around on the water (tho thankfully you can turn this off in the settings) - which makes it harder to manually sort things inside the pool - and there are fish swimming in there which if you accidentally click on them, the fish wiggle around for a few seconds, obstructing part of your view. Any pieces that you have on the board area that are NOT in their final, fixed position are returned to the pool any time you hit escape (which takes you back to the main menu rather than pause), the F key, or when your game/system crash.

Their solution to this is that they also have a "tray" area that has multiple tabs where you can store pieces. This storage persists even when you exit the puzzle / game. But this quickly grows annoying as you now have to pick thru pieces in the pool and put them into different tabs, then take them back out and try to fit them on the board. When you compare to physical jigsaws or jigidi, where you just dump everything on a flat surface and move things around, I could almost believe that this was specifically designed to inflame RSIs.

But then main way that this differs from both physical jigsaws and sites like jigidi are that in Pixel Puzzle, you can ONLY snap pieces into their exact position on the fixed board. You can NOT snap pieces together unless at least one of the pieces is already on the correct position on the board. So, no unattached partial pieces that you can move into position.

The game also had some kind of hint system but I never used that because IMHO it kind of defeats the point of a game like this.

I also feel like there were a lot of arbitrary UI decisions that make the game less fun than it could have been and that it is lacking features that could have made it a lot better.

==PROS==

- lots of puzzles

- base game and some puzzles are available for no cost

- Has hotkeys (buy they are not customizable).

==CONS==

- I had a few system freezes while playing. Not tons but they were there. My system is older but definitely not a "potato" - I can run multiple virtual machines on this system without issue. I have run games like Ark, Satisfactory, Saints Row 4, and many others. Those games had the occasional crash or freeze too. But you wouldn't think a simple jigsaw game would have issues like that.

- During one such freeze, the game screwed up its internal saves bc the next time I loaded the game my progress for EVERY SINGLE PUZZLE IN THAT PACK had gotten wiped out. Which tells me that the devs have a very poorly designed save system that does not keep progress for individual puzzles but instead lumps everything into 1 save per puzzle pack. It also tells me that they don't do the common practice of making a backup of the current save, then performing the save, then having the game try to load the main save and fall back to the backup if the main save gets corrupted.

- Zooming in feels like an after thought. It exists. But there is a limit to how far in you can zoom. On easier puzzles without as many pieces, it might not even be that big of a deal. But when you are playing puzzles with 400, 600, or 800 pieces, the zoom level feels increasingly insufficient. I actually measured it with a tape measure and compared to jigidi to make sure I wasn't imagining it. Max zoom in Pixel Puzzle ended up being about 1/2 of what jigidi's was (with ~400 pieces on each). It also doesn't work with their "tray" at all. If you are fully zoomed in and open the tray, it will reset the zoom level which is quite annoying.

- I really really hated the whole fixed board concept and definitely considered it a CON. If it was a single mode that I could change in the settings, I probably wouldn't have cared but I strongly prefer being able to play with ALL of the table surface and to be able to lock random pieces together without them being in the proper place relative to the edge pieces. The CON here is that that you are forced to play in a way that differs from real jigsaw puzzles.

- Feels like there is a LOT more dragging of pieces than there needs to be due to the arbitrary decision to use a fixed position board, a "pool" for unattached pieces, and "tray" with multiple tabs. I would advise anyone that has an RSI to stay away or limit yourself and have an icepack ready.


==LACK OF FEATURES==

- If you look at the jigsaw piece shapes that you see in the store page screen shots, they have non-standard (often more complex) cut-outs than your typical physical jigsaw. That's not a bad thing but it appears that the shapes are tied to specific puzzles and each puzzle has its own unique cuts. I think it would have been a lot cooler if could have had a variety of cut patterns which would get applied to a picture and then let the user choose the cut complexity and possibly even the exact cut style.

- There is no timer in the game. I mean that both in terms of a counter showing how long you have taken on a given puzzle and in terms of simply display the system clock (which you can't see in fullscreen mode - though TBF, I could probably play in windowed mode if they didn't restrict the zoom level so much). When I complete jigsaws on jigidi, I get a timer and can even pause it (which blurs the pieces but stops the timer until I start again) - which is great if I get a phone call, want a snack, or have to use the bathroom. This game simply has no timer feature at all.

- Since they are all about making you put things into tray tabs and there is a hint system already, would have been nice if they went full-on cheater and just gave you a way to just filter things... like maybe add a drop-down on the tray tabs that would add e,g, all unattached red pieces to that tab... or all unattached pieces with an "innie" on the right side. I know this is probably overkill for a jigsaw game, but still would probably save a ton of dragging (and hence RSI problems), could be ignored by those who don't want it (similar to me ignoring the hint system), and since it doesn't actually solve anything, would probably make it much more enjoyable for some.

Pixel Puzzles Ultimate Jigsaw Puzzles is a digital interpretation of one of the simplest and most enduring forms of casual entertainment. Developed and published by Pixel Puzzles, it avoids unnecessary complications and concentrates on the familiar pleasure of sorting pieces, recognizing patterns, and gradually transforming a scattered collection of shapes into a completed image. Its appeal is straightforward: traditional jigsaw puzzling without requiring a large table, physical storage space, or concern about losing pieces.

The most significant strength is its flexibility. Puzzle sizes range from very small 21-piece challenges to enormous creations containing as many as 1,410 pieces. Smaller puzzles work well for brief sessions or newcomers, while the largest can become lengthy projects requiring considerable patience and visual concentration. This broad range means players can choose something appropriate for the amount of time available rather than committing to the same level of difficulty every session.

The fundamental mechanics remain faithful to physical jigsaws. Players examine colors, shapes, textures, recognizable objects, and edge pieces before determining where everything belongs. The digital format allows unusual piece cuts that would be less practical with traditional cardboard puzzles, giving some sets additional personality. Successfully connecting difficult sections remains satisfying, especially when a seemingly confusing mass of similar pieces finally begins forming a recognizable picture.

Convenience is where the digital approach demonstrates its greatest advantage. An unfinished 1,000-piece physical puzzle can occupy furniture for days, whereas progress here can simply be saved and continued later. Automatic saving makes lengthy projects particularly comfortable because players can complete a few sections, leave the game, and return whenever convenient. There is also no possibility of a missing piece ruining hours of work.

Several themed and interactive environments surround the puzzling area. These provide visual variety without distracting excessively from the actual task. Customization options allow players to adjust aspects of the experience according to personal preference, which is useful because different people have very different habits when organizing and solving jigsaws. The interface generally prioritizes accessibility rather than trying to turn puzzle manipulation into an unnecessarily elaborate system.

Hints and power-ups provide additional assistance when a puzzle becomes frustrating. Experienced enthusiasts can ignore these features and rely entirely on observation, while casual players can use them to maintain a more relaxing pace. Assistance becomes particularly valuable during larger puzzles where dozens of nearly identical pieces can make finding one specific connection unexpectedly difficult.

Content variety is potentially enormous. The game supports a vast collection of puzzle packs covering subjects such as wildlife, scenery, architecture, fantasy, historical imagery, holidays, nature, countries, dinosaurs, seasonal themes, and many other categories. This makes it possible to concentrate on imagery that genuinely appeals to individual tastes instead of repeatedly solving subjects of little interest.

However, the extensive DLC structure is also one of the game's more controversial characteristics. The base experience is free, providing a convenient opportunity to test the mechanics, but much of the broader puzzle library is distributed through numerous additional packs. Players interested in only a few themes can selectively purchase what appeals to them, making the system reasonably flexible. Completionists who feel compelled to own everything will face a substantially larger investment.

Achievement hunters receive an unusually substantial attraction. The game contains thousands of Steam achievements, many associated with completing individual puzzles and collections. This provides additional motivation for players who enjoy seeing measurable progress accumulate alongside their finished images. Steam Cloud functionality is similarly useful for preserving progress, particularly when working through large puzzles over multiple sessions.

Presentation remains deliberately understated. The puzzle images themselves provide most of the visual appeal, while the interface avoids overwhelming the player with unnecessary spectacle. This creates a peaceful atmosphere suited to quiet evening sessions or relaxed background entertainment. It is a game that can comfortably occupy attention without constantly demanding fast reactions, complicated strategic decisions, or narrative engagement.

Naturally, this narrow focus also limits its broader appeal. Someone who finds traditional jigsaw puzzles tedious will probably not suddenly become fascinated simply because they are presented digitally. There is no elaborate storyline, character progression, exploration, or major mechanical transformation hiding underneath the puzzle format. The activity remains fundamentally about finding matching pieces and completing pictures.

Digital puzzling also lacks the tactile sensation of handling real cardboard. Physically moving piles of pieces and feeling them connect has an appeal that a screen cannot fully reproduce. In exchange, Pixel Puzzles Ultimate provides unlimited workspace convenience, instant saving, unusual piece shapes, very large puzzles without physical clutter, and access to a library that would require considerable storage space if purchased physically.

Steam Deck compatibility carry an official Valve Playable classification. Its modest graphical requirements mean raw performance should not be the primary concern, but the game was designed around mouse-style interaction rather than specifically around Valve's handheld. The Deck's trackpads and touchscreen can potentially provide suitable cursor control, although the overall experience remains unofficial and may require custom controller configurations or Proton adjustments. It should therefore be considered unverified rather than guaranteed to work perfectly.

Pixel Puzzles Ultimate ultimately delivers exactly what its title promises: an expandable digital home for jigsaw enthusiasts. Its huge range of puzzle sizes, automatic saving, unusual cuts, assistance options, themed environments, thousands of achievements, and extensive additional library give dedicated players substantial longevity. The DLC-heavy structure and specialized gameplay will not appeal to everyone, but people who genuinely enjoy jigsaws can find a convenient and relaxing alternative to covering an entire table with physical pieces.

Rating: 8/10
