Sudden Signs of Life!

Signs of Life is a science-fiction survival sandbox developed and published by Sweet Dog Studios that blends 2D platforming, open-ended exploration, and deep crafting systems into a slow-burn adventure defined by isolation and discovery. Set on a distant alien world following the catastrophic failure of a human expedition, the game drops you into an unforgiving environment with little guidance and few comforts, asking you to learn its rules through observation, experimentation, and persistence. Rather than pushing a tightly scripted experience, it leans heavily into player-driven progression, where survival itself becomes the narrative thread that binds everything together.

The premise is simple but effective: after escaping a doomed mission via emergency pod, you awaken alone on an unknown planet with minimal equipment and a damaged AI companion. From the very beginning, the game establishes a sense of vulnerability and scale. The world stretches far beyond the initial landing zone, layered vertically with surface biomes, underground caverns, abandoned facilities, and hostile ecosystems that gradually reveal themselves as you push deeper. Storytelling is largely environmental, conveyed through derelict structures, scattered logs, strange alien technology, and the gradual realization that this planet is far more complex—and dangerous—than it first appears.

Gameplay revolves around a tightly interwoven loop of exploration, resource gathering, crafting, and combat. Mining ores, harvesting plants, and scavenging remnants of past expeditions provide the raw materials needed to craft tools, weapons, armor, and survival equipment. Progression is not gated by traditional experience levels but by knowledge and preparation; reaching new areas often requires crafting the right gear to withstand environmental hazards such as extreme temperatures, toxic zones, or heavily fortified alien structures. This creates a strong sense of purpose behind crafting, as every new item directly expands your ability to explore further and survive longer.

Combat in Signs of Life is deliberate and sometimes punishing, emphasizing preparation over reflexes. Alien creatures range from passive wildlife to aggressive predators and mechanical threats, each demanding different approaches. Early encounters can feel harsh, especially for new players still learning movement and weapon behavior, but success gradually comes from understanding enemy patterns, using terrain intelligently, and ensuring you are properly equipped before venturing into more dangerous zones. While the physics and movement can occasionally feel imprecise, especially in tight underground spaces, the tension this creates often reinforces the survival theme rather than undermining it.

One of the game’s most compelling strengths is the depth and flexibility of its crafting systems. The crafting interface supports a wide range of recipes that unlock progressively as you discover new materials and technologies. From basic tools and melee weapons to advanced firearms, drones, scanners, and utility devices, the game encourages experimentation and long-term planning. Base-building elements further deepen this sandbox appeal, allowing players to establish safe zones, storage hubs, and crafting stations that serve as anchors in an otherwise hostile world. Over time, the satisfaction of turning a fragile survivor into a well-equipped explorer becomes one of the game’s most rewarding arcs.

Visually, Signs of Life balances functional pixel-art characters with more detailed, atmospheric backgrounds that give the planet a sense of scale and mystery. Environments feel distinct and purposefully designed, whether you are navigating dense surface terrain or descending into dimly lit caverns filled with unfamiliar technology. The art direction prioritizes mood over spectacle, and while animations and effects may lack the polish of higher-budget titles, they effectively convey danger, isolation, and discovery. Sound design reinforces this atmosphere, using ambient audio and subtle musical cues to heighten the feeling of being alone on a distant world.

The game’s Early Access roots are still apparent in its pacing and onboarding. Direction can be sparse, and progression is sometimes opaque, with players expected to learn through trial, error, and community knowledge rather than explicit tutorials. For some, this lack of hand-holding is a defining strength, enhancing immersion and reinforcing the survival fantasy. For others, it can lead to moments of frustration, particularly when essential mechanics or progression paths are not clearly communicated. Patience is very much a requirement, and those willing to invest time into understanding the systems tend to find the experience far more rewarding.

Community reception reflects this duality. Players who enjoy slow, system-driven survival games often praise Signs of Life for its depth, freedom, and sense of discovery, highlighting the satisfaction of mastering its mechanics and gradually uncovering the planet’s secrets. Criticism most often targets uneven difficulty spikes, unclear objectives, and occasional technical roughness, but even detractors frequently acknowledge the ambition behind the design. The game’s continued updates and expansions over time have steadily broadened its content and refined its systems, reinforcing its identity as a long-term sandbox experience rather than a tightly paced campaign.

In the end, Signs of Life is a game defined by curiosity, patience, and self-directed problem-solving. It does not chase instant gratification or cinematic storytelling, instead offering a dense survival sandbox where progress is earned through understanding the world and adapting to its dangers. For players drawn to sci-fi survival games that reward exploration, crafting depth, and emergent storytelling, it stands as a compelling and often absorbing journey into an alien wilderness that feels genuinely hostile, mysterious, and alive.

Rating: 7/10

Overall Signs of Life is a fun and relaxing exploration/surviving game with crafting/mining elements.

[h1]The Good[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Combat is great, almost every feature I'd want is here. Weapon combos, charged/lunging/aerial attacks, dashing, dodge rolling, shield bashing, stamina/energy management. The only thing I'm really missing are perfect guards and/or parries.
    [*]The skeuomorphic UI manages to reinvent the wheel without being awful. Also provides a standard grid alternative for the inventory.
    [*]A new world provides multiple ways to progress through it. You can dig down, collect ores, and craft gear in a sandbox fashion, or progress through the story, recycle stuff, and skip about half of the gear progression.
    [*]The alien technology provides very little hand holding, but it's designed in a way that it can be figured out in a reasonably quick manner. There are some instances which might seem like grade A moon logic at first, like the offensive use of the white tablet, but considering its proximity it makes sense as an unmarked tutorial.
    [*]There's a plethora of weapons, gadgets, and cybernetics to play around with.
    [*]There aren't too many creatures in the game, but they're fairly distinct from each other.
    [*]Recipes have a progression that makes sense. First you just cook your ores as it is (copper, iron, tin, etc...), then you start combining multiple ores (copper and tin makes bronze, iron plus carbon makes steel), and finally you start adding stuff like acids (platinum, titanium). You don't mine steel ore and other nonsense. Recipes also accept alternatives, you can use both ores and cooked bars for making alloys.
    [*]The graphics are lovely and there are a lot of detail going into the animations. My favourite is probably the "reloading" of the acute energy weapons, it slides open, the character pulls out a heat exchanger and holds it out to make it cool down faster.
    [*]Can be a bit hit or miss, but the game does have a sense of humor.
    [*]Native mod support with LUA scripting. Sadly, it doesn't have an active Workshop community.
    [*]The current version seems to be DRM-Free, runs fine without Steam, sans the multiplayer. Good, otherwise I would have to complain about the outdated Humble version.
[/list]

[h1]The Bad[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Interaction is hard bound to right click and so are secondary attacks. I end up throwing and shooting stuff whenever I try to press a button. Could really use a dedicated activation key.
    [*]Damage mitigation is a bit aggressive. Mid tier armors will almost completely block all damage not just from bugs, but also from droids with 9mm turrets. And then you add in cybernetics. Most shields just block 100% of all damage. Could really use a balancing pass with some of the flat reduction replaced with percentage based. I don't mind he lowliest of enemies becoming nothing more than stagger hazards, but the rest probably should still have some bite to them.
    [*]While pathfinding is alright, most feral creatures could use some additional ranged and/or targeted attacks, like pounces and diagonal strikes. Even without exploiting the terrain, getting a spear kinda trivializes them. Which sure sounds quite realistic, but still.
    [*]Toolbar's a bit weak. The automatic one is serviceable, but the manual one is too small to be truly useful.
    [*]The lack of in-game map notes/drawings is quite painful for a game where you essentially have to triangulate the position of underground structures.
    [*]Realtime crafting can be a bit tedious when you don't have anything else to do.
    [*]Newly unlocked recipes are not tracked between play sessions and there's no indicator whether you've already acquired in item previously. This makes unlocking the last few missing recipes quite a chore.
    [*]The crafting window is an inconsistent mess. Sometimes you can right click an ingredient to navigate to it, sometimes you have to use the target feature, sometimes neither works, sometimes it takes you to a completely different recipe and unlocks something else. Required crafting stations are listed with a navigable sprite in the requirements panel, or with a non-navigable sprite in the preview panel, or with text only, or in an entirely separate menu. There are items that are only produced as byproducts, like tallow, which you can't even search for.
    [*]Cooking is bogged down by trial and error, food won't show their effects until you try them, some not even after you do.
    [*]Ladders are textbook awful. Hard to avoid, slow to get on, slow to get off. I remove them all as soon as I can.
    [*]While the tools provided for building elevators are great, they don't seem to respond when they're too far away from you. I assume it has to with how the world is chunked.
    [*]The variance in block crafting costs is weird. For a stick and some plant fiber, you get 5 tiles or 5 platforms. For a whole bar of steel, you get 5 tiles or a single platform. I probably won't make platforms out of steel.
    [*]Having to mess with crafting station batteries in a facility with a running generator is kinda silly. Really wouldn't mind an item that provides infinite power, but only works in the generator's vicinity.
    [*]The combat update messed with the pickaxes and removed the secondary precision strike, so now half the time I tear up the ground under the deposits I try to mine. [b]Rage![/b]
    [*]The only thing I don't like about the inventory is that equipment swapping puts the old gear in some random spot instead of the new gear's place. A bit annoying if you carry around some secondary gear in a container.
    [*]Dyeing is just a flat tint that removes most of the details from your gear and doesn't properly work on shields. Could really use some partial palette swapping here.
    [*]I find the placement grid a bit too granular for decorating, would much prefer if I could switch to a block based grid.
[/list]

[h1]The Ugly[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Development is still ongoing, but it's glacial. Unfortunately, it seems the game didn't do particularly well. Hopefully the eventual 1.0 release will bring some attention to it.
    [*]Multiplayer is as basic as it gets, entirely based off of Steam friends. No game browser, direct IP, or dedicated servers. Not too helpful for building a multiplayer community.
[/list]

Maybe I've just been spoiled by the quality of some of the other, superb World of Darkness-based interactive fiction from Choice of Games, but [b]Out for Blood[/b] is hard to recommend. The initial hook is interesting enough: as the protagonist, you're compelled to return to a small town to take over your late grandfather's store and in the process discover there's something supernatural preying on the town. As you might expect you can approach that threat with a militant commitment to destroying it or curiosity and a desire to learn more. Approaching Vampire: the Masquerade from a human—but not a Hunter's—perspective seems ripe for storytelling opportunities. There are multiple characters, mysteries to investigate, a store to run, different factions to consider, but all that ends up feeling like far too much ambition for a surprisingly short narrative.

Take the store management aspect as one example: if you've played [b]Night Road[/b] or [b]The Book of Hungry Names[/b], you might expect a similar, cyclical format where your store is your home base from which you balance managing your finances with following leads and developing relationships with the narrative's characters. In [b]Out for Blood[/b], the story is too short for any of it to feel coherent or fleshed out. It's entirely possible to only spend a few paragraphs 'working' in the store, despite the game having vestigial systems for managing inventory and marketing. Before you even know what's happening, the game warns that you're out of further chances to spend your experience points and you're heading into the final act.

I have other qualms about the quality of the writing and the at times cliché characterisations, but for the most part it'd be serviceable enough. And while it utilises World of Darkness-inspired systems and concepts, it's also an extremely loose adaptation, with some key plot points that seem to contradict my (admittedly casual) understanding of the setting's lore. In the end, though, I keep coming back to the combination of the short length of the game and the decision to fill it with multiple plot hooks that really needed more time to unfold. If it was just a breadth of choices that might work for replayability, but the game is always going to end at the same point, with almost every potential plot feeling rushed and undercooked, and entire features and systems practically unexplored.

When there are other games of this type that offer stronger writing and a more recognisable World of Darkness, I'd suggest skipping [b]Out for Blood[/b] unless you're really desperate for another Choice of Games title.
I don't understand why this is labelled Vampire the Masquerade when it's clearly a Hunter the Reckoning game?

Overall, I'd certainly put [i]Out for Blood[/i] in my top five of Choice of Games' [i]World of Darkness[/i] gamebooks, though not without caveats. The caveats aren't "for me," though, so much as they are "for other folks, maybe."

It's very much a slow-burn sort of story; slow enough that the ending seems rather abrupt, as if there should be more buildup for it, but that's less a function of the story being terse (I'd hardly call 450k+ words a short CoG story) and more a function of everything else being as detailed as it is.

And goodness, there's a lot to cram in there! Sure, there's an antagonist, and sure, having to deal with them is ultimately the story's main thread, but there's so much to do in the interim that it's easy to get lost in the "everything else." Jericho Heights lives and breathes, with plenty of cast members to talk to (many of whom have quite significant roles in the story) and plenty of things to do outside of worry about the whole "vampires" business. In particular, being a store-owner is quite a fun little thing that crops up just often enough for me to wish there was more (and low-key hoping for more Store Management stories from CoG in general.) 

So what's not to like? Well, it goes hand-in-hand with what i just mentioned: if you're looking for a story about vampire hunting, it's...only technically that kind of story. There's a lot more of investigating what's going on with the Antagonist, and talking to the people that they've influenced throughout their storied career in the town, than there is of actually fighting them. [i]Out for Blood[/i] isn't about being a hunter; it's about being a mortal, in out of their depth, with a few other folks similarly out of their depth against supernatural forces they don't entirely understand. If you like the thought of getting in that headspace, you'll probably like this. And if you were looking for more straightforward Stake-n'-Baking of humanoid leeches, you should probably find something else, because [i]Out for Blood[/i] isn't that kind of story.

Definitely worth a Thumbs Up from me, but not the sort of CoG title I'd unequivocally praise, like [i]Night Road.[/i] Read a few other reviews if you're on the fence and not quite sure. I wouldn't call it a bad story by any means, though - just not everyone's cup of tea.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 626:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆☆☆ (7/10)

In [i]Vampire: The Masquerade — Out for Blood[/i] (“OfB”), the protagonist returns home expecting to settle their grandfather’s affairs, only to slowly uncover his connection to the local supernatural scene. It’s much smaller-scaled and more grounded than Night Road, but it gives the story a more grounded horror vibe that works well for the setting.

I’m really glad OfB has 173 Steam reviews at this time of writing. I’ve quickly glanced through all of them, and each review dismantles the game pretty well, so you should do your research and know what you’re getting into. I broadly agree with all the reviews, good and bad, making me settle on giving the game a 7/10. Dattilo’s strengths clearly lie in mechanical flexibility, atmosphere, and immersive detail, especially when depicting vampirism, violence, and the more intimate horror elements of the setting. At the same time, many of the criticisms are completely fair. The tone can feel uneven and unintentionally goofy, the cast often lacks strong personalities, several mechanics feel underutilized, and the ending feels noticeably rushed. [b]As always, thank you to the staff for a free copy![/b]

[b][h2]Pros:[/h2][/b]
✅ [b]Broad choices.[/b] Dattilo’s biggest strength is probably mechanical design and player freedom. OfB gives you a surprising amount of flexibility in how you approach situations and relationships. You can agree, disagree, betray people, delay important decisions, or commit fully to a course of action without the game constantly forcing you into a binary morality system. Conversations often feel more natural because your character can hesitate, deflect, or partially cooperate instead of instantly picking a “good” or “evil” route. You also have to pick choices carefully; you have a wide variety of leads to investigate, but you can’t choose all of them. It’s neat!

✅ [b]Long, thorough descriptions.[/b] Not a lot of writers put this much detail into the setting, with paragraphs being devoted to the actual place you are in. There’s also a lot of description about getting bit by a vampire, some nasty scenes of violence, and the allure of being a vampire’s plaything.

✅ [b]Depiction of faith.[/b] It’s a small choice, mostly flavor text, but I really like how choosing to play as a Christian affected my playthrough. Quite often, Dattilo mentions completing morning or afternoon prayers. When encountering a dead body, you pray that they will find peace in the afterlife. Faith touches on romance briefly: an RO jumps your bones pretty quickly, and there’s a line about how your faith doesn’t allow premarital sex. I liked these thoughtful touches!

✅ [b]“Big bad.”[/b] Listen, all vampire writers will write the same archetype[spoiler]—evil villain MILF ooga booga[/spoiler]—and I will eat it up every single time <3

[b][h2]Mixed:[/h2][/b]
🟨 [b]Tone. [/b]This is my biggest “hey, wait a minute!” moment. The tone is much more lighthearted, almost camp, and it’s quite a stark difference from V:tM works. At some points, the relaxed tone works, creating a more intimate, focused horror vibe. But some comedic moments fall really flat for me. For example, [spoiler]your adult friend group is being led by a child into believing in and killing vampires. And the MC is also quite stupid! A vampire trying to use their power on you? Huh, must be tired. Multiple people saying spooky things? Eh. A vampire going through a glass door? Must be your imagination. Someone BREAKING into your home?[/spoiler] Must be the wind.  

[b][h2]Cons:[/h2][/b]
🟥[b] Underutilized “store management” aspect. [/b]I was bummed that there wasn’t a bigger focus on running your grandfather’s shop. In the initial chapter, you’re promised an opportunity to stock the shelves, market the place, advertise, remodel, etc. However, I only chose a couple options, so my store was under-stocked and poorly-advertised throughout the rest of the game. I felt like I didn’t interact with the store until at the very end.

🟥 [b]Flat prose and characters.[/b] Might just be a me issue, as I haven’t vibed with Dattilo’s writing in the past. The game introduces a fairly large cast and clearly wants you to feel attached to this little vampire-hunting community, yet I never really got the “found family” vibe the narrative seemed to be aiming for. Most of the cast simply exists around you rather than feeling like fully realized people with distinct voices, motivations, or dynamics. They show up when the plot needs them, contribute information or support, and then fade back into the background without leaving much of an impression. Honestly, outside of the two female romance options and a couple of central figures like Lam and Chastain, I struggled to remember much about anyone by the end.

🟥 [b]Rushed ending. [/b]For a beautiful eleven out of twelve chapters, the build up is delicious. Each chapter adds a new mystery, a new lead, and the pacing was a slow and steady march toward your inevitable death. But the critics were right, I discovered, after playing through Chapter 12. All this exhilarating buildup just … ends in a really deflating way with a couple deus ex machinas. I don’t want to get into too much detail, but the reveal of [spoiler] Damien and Uncle Allen was incredibly rushed to me. That part came out of nowhere and felt like “okay, we need to give the player a good ending if they fail.” And I didn’t love the villain’s sudden emotional softening near the end.[/spoiler] The emotional transition happens so quickly that it never really landed for me.

➡️ What really hurt the finale, though, was how little room the story gives itself to breathe. Huge confrontations, character resolutions, deaths, revelations, and epilogue material are all compressed into one chapter. The villain can die in an almost bizarrely unceremonious way, considering how much buildup surrounds her. Then the game jumps into ending slides so quickly that I was left wondering what emotionally happened between half the cast. There’s barely any time for fallout, awkward conversations, grief, reflection, or even processing what the protagonist just survived. After such a slow-burn buildup, the finale needed more space to emotionally land.

Out for Blood is a pretty great story straddling the line between Vampire the Masquerade and Hunter the Reckoning. Playing as a normal person coming to a small town after your grandfather passed away to put his affairs in order is a pretty good setup (which incidentally  made me think of the opening to Stardew Valley) and it is difficult to get the "small town with more going on beneath the cozy exterior" wrong, as it's an excellent trope for a story like this. And it very quickly becomes apparent that there is a lot more going on than meets the eye.

Compared to Night Road, Out for Blood has a slower pace, which I think works well for it. The character progression is slower and feels more deliberate, since this time you're just a human and not a vampire, meaning you have to think more carefully about how you spend your XP. The choices also felt a lot more meaningful than they did in Night Road, which I think is due to a smaller, more personal scale to the story.

Having said that, the one major gripe I have with it is the ending. As with Night Road, there are multiple endings, though it's much less obvious which one you're on track for, and the ending I ended up getting [spoiler]being kidnapped by the FBI and put in "witness protection"[/spoiler] felt unsatisfying and like a complete Deus Ex Machina. I hope the other endings are better than this, though I'll admit, to me personally, that bar is not set very high.

In conclusion, if you enjoyed Night Road, and don't mind seeing the world of Vampire from the other side of the Masquerade, you'll probably enjoy Out for Blood too.

[b]TLDR:[/b] I am absolutely recommending this to anyone who might like a Choice of Games game featuring a more slow burn mystery, just be aware of the uneven pacing and inobvious gameplay mechanics.

Out of the three first VtM Choice of Games I think this one has connected with me the most. It has some strange pacing, and some kinda obscure game logic, and maybe I would have wanted a bit more depth to the characters, but the star of the is very much the amazing setting. There's a charm to the town and the story that to me entirely outweighs the parts that have frustrated me, and I've found myself caring about what's happening to the game world and its inhabitants more strongly than I did in Night Road or Parliament of Knives (that on the other hand have stronger narratives).

Central to the gameplay or story flow in this game is discussion hubs where you're either talking with someone or researching something and you're given a set of actions and given the opportunity to explore most of them. This results in a slower pace than other games in the genre where it feels like you're making progress in chunks, and I've found it really helped make the world feel like a thing that exists that you get to explore, more than the backdrop to a story that is happening. I really enjoyed this!

The downside to this, apart from if one dislikes the slower pacing, is that you as a player has very little insight into what's happening behind the hood. If you read along with the code you'll see that there is actually a whole lot of game logic happening as you're chugging through the investigation -- it reminds me a lot about Disco Elysium (it's the only game I've played D: ) on a much smaller scale with how there is a bunch of different small logic flags keeping track of seemingly minute game actions that impact the story in various ways. Even with save management and viewing the code (its available in plain text in the game folder, you can just read it in notepad++ or use a third party tool designed specifically for CoG games) it can be frustrating to figure out which game actions you want to take for a given outcome, much more so if you're just playing vanilla. If you're just along for the ride, excellent! If you want informed agency behind your choices this might be a struggle.

The story being told behind these mechanics I really did like! The world feels alive, there are many appealing characters and even with the pacing being a bit uneven I really think that for the ending I got it was a really coherently told story all throughout. If you thought it was a bit alienating to dip into a bunch of disconnected locales in Night Road or disappointed you didn't get to see how Kindred society actually integrates into Ottawa in the Parliament of Knives, this game really delivers on the game world. And the perspective of playing normal human beings (gasp) that are the victims of vampires is handled really well in my opinion, even though if you're somewhat savvy you're probably going to figure out what's happening some 40 hours before the dense protagonists do. Oh! Let's not forget that there are many small details that just makes it [i]nice[/i], from the super cute graphics used for town signs and stuff in the start (wish they had budget for more of those) to the fact that the PC will change tone of dialogue depending on the disposition scores you get from the choices you pick.

Where the story is lacking is pacing and character depth. When it comes to pacing, I agree with anyone saying that the mid point up to the climax feels a bit rushed. But I'm also missing some connective tissue between scenes and events within scenes that can make the reading feel jagged and uneven at times. It's not too ugly when you shrug off teleporting to Next Location (tm) but when you teleport into being a leader of a vampire hunting squad of five dudes and you have no idea why two of them are there it gets a bit unsatisfying!

And while the main characters in this book are all quite appealing, I do feel like I'm missing some substance to them, stuff that sets them apart from each other. Salem is a very cute love interest! But emotionally speaking, I don't feel there is much setting her apart from your other childhood friend Adam who's also a curious and supportive love interest (guy flavour this time). Lacey does make a big impression from an exceptional introduction scene, but then there's Marcus who... has a gun? I think the story would have benefited if all major characters got more space to breathe (or there was more conflict in the group) or if everyone got more unique and present connections to the fictional world they inhabit. Oh, I should point out that there are a lot of interesting and memorable minor characters! The world very much feels human, it's just that there is an opportunity to develop the main cast further.

Oh, if you enjoyed this one and haven't checked out Werewolf: The Apocalypse - The Book of Hungry Names that one is very similar in its exceptionally appealing medium size town setting but with consistently exceptional storytelling and characters. And Hunter: The Reckoning - The Beast of Glenkildove will give you more fantastic monster hunting, that goes even harder on making the threat of the supernatural feel personal to the player character and their coterie, and the characterization of the coterie is excellent.
The only thing I can honestly say is just pass on this. It's meh at best.

Vampire: The Masquerade — Out for Blood is an text-based urban dark fantasy thriller adventure based on the popular World of Darkness franchise of tabletop role-playing games. in Out for Blood, you create and portray the grandchild of an ill-fated Hunter. Your character inherits their grandparent's small-town business in Chicago, Illinois and is tasked with resolving an ongoing turf war between local vampires hiding in town whilst, at the same time, staying out of trouble and out of debt.

With this premise in mind, this game honestly plays more like a Hunter: The Reckoning chronicle than a Vampire: The Masquerade game, especially since your character starts out as a mortal. Furthermore, depending on how well you develop and navigate your character, you can spare them from being embraced into vampirism.

As an example, during my initial playthrough of this game, I developed and portrayed a kind-hearted and down-to-earth thrift store owner with high Composure, Intelligence and Resolve. Though my character started out as a soft-hearted outsider, I ultimately developed them into a compassionate and sharp-witted Buddhist whose courage and True Faith led them to vanquish the Camarilla ancilla and her vampiric influence.

This game is well-structured in a twelve-chapter narrative, fleshed out with a diverse cast of characters as well as various scenes which pay homage to numerous pre-existing horror media, from classic vampire novels to 1980s horror cinema: Bram Stoker, Stephen King, John Carpenter, Stanley Kubrick, you-name-it! This is what makes Out for Blood a charming supernatural rollercoaster to remember.

If I had one thing to complain about this game, it's that I wish this game probably incorporated Hunter Edges and Perks. Then again, this game was published before Hunter: The Reckoning had its long-awaited 5th edition released. Therefore, if this game were to receive a sequel or a re-release, I would love to see additions from Hunter's 5th edition made.

This isn't the worst VtM game, but it's forgettable in every aspect once done and its major flaws can't be ignored while playing.

Characters in your vamp hunter team are superficially diverse, but lack real personalities and their "flaws" get completely glossed over when it's too inconvenient for the plot to deal with. For example, I can appreciate what they wanted to do with Adam as a disabled dude who pushes against his limitations; but he's not on a cane, he's full on paraplegic from the waist down and in a wheelchair. Yet in most endings they've got him rolling up on a vamp fight with a rifle in his lap, through a park/forested area, and your target (who is said to have precognition abilities and was waiting for you to show up with her hostile childe) is conveniently too fixated on her phone to notice. And no, he's not a mage; there's no glamour helping him out. Just super lucky plot armor. For all that people trashed Blade Trinity, at least THAT movie handled having a disabled vamp hunter realistically in that the blind scientist stayed at base to develop tech for field hunters, and her attempt to defend herself when attacked by the OG vampire ended realistically in her death. Other forms of media have done similar things for the character to be helpful, have badass moments, but not stretch credulity. If the writer REALLY wanted Adam to be in the field, a far more reasonable scenario of location and/or creative solutions for how he's getting around needed to be constructed. But wheeling on up outside the way he did, along with the rest of the amateurs, and it going down just peachy for a stealth opening attack against CELERITY *and* AUSPEX buffed vampires/ghouls, and then surviving the ensuing brawl after that?? Even when an enemy was sneaking up behind him and I decided to put the mission first by concentrating on taking out the head vamp for the good of the whole town? Not buying it. He's tragically dead and we all know it.

And if, like me, you select the option to make your character bi/pan for sexuality, but then never flirt with anyone in a run because you don't find them interesting enough to bother, they'll still attempt to make passes at you if you're simply nice to them. Even if you pass on them and have low charisma, some keep flirting. You apparently inherited a rizz aura from your homewrecking, vamp-attracting grandpa that makes people spill their dirtiest secrets and toss themselves at you.

As other reviewers have noted- the pacing is all over the place, with a ponderous start and then a baffling breakneck middle and end. I'm not sure what happened for this game's development cycle, but it feels like this was severely rushed. 

There's also a ham fisted reliance on horror genre tropes. Spooky disembodied voices. Missing teen vamp girl popping up your first night back with preternatural movements and being obvious about what she is. A cop being supernaturally attacked on the highway in front of you. Impossible moving shadows at multiple points. Windows open that you had closed, etc. HOWEVER, despite growing up with the rizzler grandpa who tried to prep you with survivalist and magicky lessons, and potentially taking background options that give high occult and intellect skills- your character will still initially shrug off all the blatant signs something is wrong on the supernatural front and make painfully stupid decisions just so the plot happens. Even if you pick all the options at the beginning to get a semi-naive, ignorant character despite your childhood, there's still no way they'd remain so oblivious as long as they did. And options to try remaining in denial even once you know you've been a vamp's midnight snack and outside people are saying vamps are real? That's just silly to include unless your character has an unnamed source of brain damage. If the game wants you to be the ignorant human who slowly wakes up to the possibility of vampires, it needs to only give background options that support that and not be hitting your over the head with the supernatural clue-by-four every other paragraph from the very beginning. 

The coding, even a few years and patches later, is janky. Example- despite not talking to Marcus at the party in my first run because I went into the game blind and didn't know he was a recruitable character, and him only showing up at my place later because of pre-teen shenanigans better fit for a Nickelodeon tv show, somehow I later end up scoping out the vamp manor with him... Without any plans to that effect having been made previously. Just suddenly being told while I'm running other errands that it's getting to be time to meet with him and then jump cut there.

Tone is an issue. This game bounces between cliche horror beats, to aforementioned teenage shenanigans, to serious talk on a friend's mental health, to BDSM scene being stumbled upon, to getting a video message from someone AS THEY SUCCESSFULLY COMMIT SUICIDE- and the shift can happen in the space of a paragraph. Much of this felt like it belonged in that old episode of Scooby Doo that had the crossover with Johnny Bravo and was far more adult themed but still goofy AF. But as something that's supposed to be in the World of Darkness universe? No.

Side note, writer of this game, should you ever see this: you have a fixation with featuring women who have strong jaw lines. No hate. Just commenting how often that very specific facial feature popped up in even the first chapter alone. Might want to branch out your character ideas. Unless we're to assume this town is made up of steel jawed locals for some cultural reason that was never explained. Maybe they have a yearly jerky chewing contest and they've built up those strong chomping muscles practicing for it? I don't know. Nor can I take this story seriously,

Also, the "big bad" vamp might be a century old Toreador, but she's only a 13th gen vampire. She's not an actual Elder or the demon from IT who can simply will the entire town and surrounding world to forget about the missing people and weird bouts of "anemia" that so many inexplicably come down with and only one local doctor with sketchy practices is corroborating. Even with her "hacker" ghoul pulling some impossible shit for someone who isn't a mage, there's way too many loose ends over too many years for this to have not blown up long before you deal with it.

The stats mechanics suck. Whatever you arrange your character to be in the first chapter intro, don't expect growth because it's a short game, you're a weak WoD human, so you only get a couple upgrades. As much as I usually hate min-maxing, you're best off going custom build and concentrate on having Dex and Cha or Manip for main attributes, with your skills being Awareness, Persuasion or Intimidation, then Combat or Clandestine. 2 attributes and 3 skills decently leveled are all you legit need for interactions and gain most all the "lore" within two plays of the plot. Get a BFG with fire rounds, obviously, or your weak self will get wrecked in melee combat. Faith or Occult can be the minor stat for flavor/endings options you spend you highly limited XP on. Trying other "builds" aren't worth the XP investment and loss of skill where it matters, especially when main options are usually also available to get basically the same result.

Tl;dr: This game feels like a college student's first big project that they started making late because they forgot it was due, and they're publishing it on Itch for others to play and give feedback for quick tweaks before turning it in to their professor. If that was the case, I'd be far more forgiving and encouraging of a novice artist being a one person show and trying to juggle all their responsibilities. But that's not the case. This is on Steam as part of a bigger franchise and by a professional team, selling in average VN price range. I can't recommend it unless it's having a big 90% sale and you REALLY want a couple hours of subpar VtM media.

This game LIT up my brain! I've played many Choice of Games and Vampire: the Masquerade titles, and my brain will dwell on VtM: Out for Blood for a long time coming. As others have pointed out, Out for Blood feels like a mellow Hunter: the Reckoning game. The writing style is simple and matter of fact, giving the player a sense of their eyes opening to a clear view of the real insidious nature of vampires. There's no rush of power, no satisfaction of a new Discipline learned; no glamour to hide how much vampires can suck. The small town setting, Jericho Heights, wasn't a perfect place before her, but a certain ancilla's pervasive corruption made life way worse, like rot creeping into already scarred tree roots. The characters and narrative framing constantly encourage striking these vampires down. Any option to become non-human must be very late game, I think. Choice of Games announced that they're going to release more World of Darkness titles, and I hope Dattilo writes a HtR one.

Hunter was the general vibe, and the nitty gritty the storytelling and coding techniques impressed me too. On the coding side, I was in awe how Dattilo made it possible for the player to input pronouns. VERY cool! On the storytelling end, Out for Blood showed me a character type I've never encountered before: a wheelchair user who is also an outdoorsman. Adam navigates a forest and shoots a vampire from his chair. It was really exciting to see. I wonder if romancing Adam changes his decisions and feelings about his chair.

Though Out for Blood has a big word count and the vast machine of code does stutter under its own weight, the game felt short--something new was always drawing my attention, begging to be investigated, prodded, and flirted with. The romances are the standard light fare for a Choice of Games title and well woven into the other plotlines. Another reviewer said the sex scenes set their eyebrows on fire, but the scenes like one step above fade to black. In movie terms, maybe rated R in USA and PG-13 for Europe? My PC's love scenes were more romantic and sensual.

Overall, what an astonishing, fun game, and an unique entry in the CoG/VtM universe. I want to play Out for Blood again and again and again.

I haven't played many CYOAs as far as video games go, but I am familiar with the concept from various books tackling the very thing over the decades. Backed by Vampire: the Masquerade's license, which seems to have thrived insofar as CYOA titles go, Out for Blood has to be intentionally miscategorized. This is no Vampire game, but rather a Hunter one. Something to keep in mind if you're going into this with certain power fantasies... which may yet be realized.

Our story takes place in Jericho Heights, town with under 20 000 residents as our [INSERT NAME HERE] protagonist returns having received the news that his grandfather had died, and left you a store as inheritance. Cutting a long story short you'll rekindle old friendships, discover that something has subtly gone wrong in this quaint town, and depending on what kind of a character you build will have impact on HOW you go about it. Since this is exclusively a text-centric affair, baring some pieces of art for characters and chapter titles, it means author's imagination and responsiveness to your choices are only limited by the word count. And yes, there are certainly limits here as you're not working within a sandbox scenario aka there's a fixed mystery to unravel, but what tidbits you discover will depend on your choices/type of character. To put things into perspective - there are TWELVE endings to a game that lacks manual saving and only one autosave slot. Expect replays aplenty if you want to discover all the hidden angles or hunt for achievements. Twice was enough for me and even then some parts I didn't even get a whiff of with my second character.

Something I was extremely pleased to see was implementation of a proper tabletop character sheet you not only get to make full use of during character creation, but also add to as you accumulate experience. Needless to say you will be using said Attributes, Skills and Backgrounds while playing the game although I wish it was more transparent in how exactly they're being employed. You see what's used in a specific action, such as STR + Combat, but you have no idea what chance you actually have at succeeding as you cannot see what you're rolling against. In essence you'll want to keep an eye on your character sheet and concept you're going with in mind before committing to choices. There's also a matter of ever-fluctuating relationship points you have with characters, both allies and antagonists, which come into play at certain points. As well as Paths your character can adhere to. And no, for Vampire: the Masquerade aficionados out there these are not the Paths you're thinking about. Out for Blood is hellbent on being a foremost narrative experience so you have to enable the Storyteller Mode just to see actual numerical values shift or you'd have no way to know that, for example, bringing up a certain topic increases Salem's stress. Not showing the player how it all works under the hood probably culminates in endings themselves. Some obvious factors like deaths or major choices aside, they end up being a combination of exactly those things game has decided to keep hidden from you. 

So, would I recommend this one? CYOA holds limited appeal considering games are a visual medium, but I enjoyed the writing quite a bit. I was honestly surprised how much unique content my smooth talking faith-based character had. In comparison my second run with a pugilist marksman landed me a more straightforward deal, although I also fared better in situations I had to carefully tread in diplomatically before. There's a beautiful pin drop moment when realization hits the group and protagonist goes something along the lines of "they all have to die", and I was inclined to agree. Your mileage may vary.

When I started to write a review on this game, I was on the fence about whether I should recommend it or not. It is extremely middle-of-the-road for me. After a while I just closed my laptop, and went about my business, intending to think about my review later. And then I forgot about the game & review entirely for a week.

The draw to come back for additional playthroughs wasn't there (though I still did it so my review would be more fair). The plot is engaging enough and the writing is good, but most everything of interest and relevance was revealed in a single playthrough. You as a player get to choose who to romance (if anyone), if you'll save your grandfather's store, and who you'll side with in the end. But these choices don't really affect the overall story or change much. And your personality and skills, while they affect how the MC can respond to situations, don't really affect how the world responds [i]to you.[/i]

I also feel like the game has a hard time distinguishing where time should be spent. Taking care of the store and researching in the library is fine on the first playthrough, but feels bland and tedious in additional playthroughs. Meanwhile, actions like... breaking into a vampire's underground haven or convincing a group of full grown adults that vampires exist... are very quick and easy. The gameplay elements are just super unbalanced and the pacing is odd.

I also want to echo two other valid critiques others pointed out at length: 1) It doesn't really feel like a VtM story, and; 2) It's glitchy. Or rather, there are discrepancies in the text; like the game wasn't quite edited with due diligence.

All that said, I do think the length is good and the story is interesting enough (albeit predictable) for one solid playthrough. The writing is decent, if not a bit far-fetched at times. The relationships the MC has with (most) of the characters are fleshed out and believable, and those characters are also unique and likable (this is the strongest point of the game to me). But overall... I just felt pretty blaise about the whole thing, nothing about it really *sparkled* for me.
I wish there were more of these.

While the narrative is compelling and the writing capable, the choices in "Vampire: The Masquerade — Out for Blood" come across as exceptionally hollow. Regardless of the alternatives you pick, the story will still play out the same way, and you can barely alter it at all.

One good and early example of this is that you can’t so much as decide who works in your own store and will end up hiring a very dislikable person no matter what you pick, and consecutive playthroughs will highlight many more instances like it. Apart from several romance options that were very well done, barely anything changes.

By the end of the predominantly linear story, your choices have a bit more impact, and I saw noticeable differences, but it never felt quite enough. As a whole, the game has a pretty good story it wants to tell, and for the most part, you’re only along for the ride. If that’s what you’re looking for, this may appeal to you, but if you want to be able to influence the story in a meaningful way, you may want to look elsewhere. (2/10)

Unfortunately this game proved a massive disappointment. I adored Night Road. For a very long time I thought I wouldn't be able to get into one of these text-based games, but Night Road broke me of that with it's incredible writing, important choices, fantastic key art, and amazing story. This game has the fantastic key art. 

While the story itself isn't terrible, it has no reason to be a Vampire: The Masquerade licensed game, in fact, it really feels like the license was slapped on after the bulk of the game was already planned out. This is most evident in [spoiler] the late game when a thin-blood vampire become mortal again when she kills her sire [/spoiler] such a thing has never been stated as possible in V:TM despite being common in other Vampire stories. The only thing like that in the lore is [spoiler] Golconda [/spoiler]. Such a process is made clear to be expressly impossible in numerous sources including Bloodlines and LA by Night. The lore in this game is tacked on at best. 

Don't expect a V:TM game here. Half of the game is more about learning the local area and building suspense, with the actual enjoyable part of the game shoved in the last 3-4 chapters as you meet much more interesting characters.

While their are many endings and choices, some choices are completely ignored. In the last chapter I told a character I never wanted to speak with them again. Later in that same epilogue chapter I'm forced to hang out with them at a bar and they're extremely friendly. Other examples of this are all over the game, awkward interactions to keep the player on the rails of the story. I acknowledge that's necessary at some points, but the jarring nature of it kills the experience.

Speaking of jarring, while some of the writing is quite good, the dialogue is... stiff at best. Characters talk in ways that immediately remove you from the vibe of the world, with awkward word choice. Saying people's names when you never would in the sentence as though to remind the reader of who's in the scene, or a lot of "yeah, I could see that" that feels like canned dialogue to respond when the writer doesn't actually have anything to add there. 

I will say what little key art for characters exists in this game is rather fantastic, the artist has a style and it pops. While they aren't common and I'd guess there is less than 10 in the game, they really help form an image of the character for the player.

I understand it's might not be fair to compare this to Night Road, but I feel it's unavoidable, and this game can't come close to matching it. Lastly, please add an undo button that works at least one, I've read the FAQ as to why it isn't included in the company's games, but picking the wrong choice on accident and having to replay the game because you refuse to watch a character you like die, fucking sucks.

Compared to "Parliament of Knives" and "Night Road" the writing in this game is just plain bad.

There is a lot to love in this game.  The writing is very good, the setting is great and the art is a nice but not overwhelming addition. But, the game absolutely falls apart at the end.  In the last few chapters, the coding seems to simply be broken.  Characters reference other characters that were never referenced before as if I know them, characters ignore that other characters are (or aren't) there with the protagonist, characters end up saying complete gibberish because of poor coding (such as, "You should use guns if your can and if your can do can do."  It seems obvious that there's a ton of missing text that's supposed to reference things like shooting and friends/allies based on context but ends up just not working), etc.  But the worst thing is that the final confrontation is completely broken for me.  Spoilers ahead.

In the final confrontation, two groups of vampires fight, an elder vampire and a group of young vampires.  I managed to get the retainer (Gabriel) of the elder vampire to get himself thrown in jail and was using the confrontation as an opportunity to wipe out both groups of vampires.  In the fight in the end I shot at both groups and killed one of the young vampires (Jace).  Then, immediately after Jace dies, the narrative describes how Gabriel (having appeared out of jail with no warning or acknowledgement that he was in a police cruiser a few hours earlier) gets incapacitated and then Jace is holding down the elder vampire as it gets staked and I'm allied with the young vampire group with no further choices despite having ALWAYS planned, explicitly, to kill both groups and having just killed one of the young vampires.

I ultimately ended up hating my experience playing the game because of the narrative-destroying bugs at the end.  My choices literally didn't matter and not in any way that the author intended.  It sucked.

This is my second foray into the long, well-written branching-path novels written for V:tM (the first one being Night Road, which I can also highly recommend). This game has a different tone than most of the other media set in this universe: you're uncovering and defeating the conspiracy, rather than becoming an awesome vampire (probably; there are endings for that).

This game is really what you make of it; your head cannon is what makes the game tick and makes the amazing characters meaningful. In my first game Alaine McNair was a warm and loving fortune teller, who could have made it as a personal counselor in another career; she ended up attracting two young and kind lady lovers, losing the thrift store but moving in with one of them. In my second game, Tamika King high-school athlete that turned to crime instead of college, a daredevil and cat burglar. She ended up being a better sleuth in some ways than one that was formally trained at it. Together with the footloose, disgraced cop, she left the all vampires in town on stakes and became a FBI informant. For a third playthrough, who knows - perhaps someone with true faith who can talk down all parties from the turf war? There are many options, limited only by your imagination. Personally, I'll return to this months or years down the line, and see then.

This game features many great traits - branching paths, background-specific text and options, passive checks (that modify text), active checks (with degrees of success), well-written characters, evocative description that deserve to be read out loud, erotic sex scenes about which the same could be said, diverging plot-opening paths (frequently mutually-exclusive), allies that can join you or open up to dialogue as relationships improve, and most of all NO BACK BUTTON - your choices have consequences that you can't roll back, leading to a dozen different endings (some more likely than others).

Like Night Road, the difficulty ramps up in the game, requiring fewer overall pips to succeed early (2-4) and more to succeed later (5-7). Unlike Night Road, the experience is much more tight (upwards of 50 total) with skill boosting requirements mirroring the pen-and-paper game (i.e., 3 or 5 xp per pip). As such, if you want to start with 3's and even more so 4's in anything, you really need to make a priority to do start out with them (you can manually assign pits). That said, the game still makes failure interesting and rewards low-level skills in small, sometimes tangible ways.

It's also fun to make a mental checklist of options as they appear, outside of the official achievements:
- Can you save your store, through sheer money or through other less savory options?
- Can you set up your best friends with each other?
- Do you hire a dedicated-if-annoying staffer (you should), and does he survive to the end of the game?
- Do you actually manage to kill the sociopath who has it out for you?
- Do you learn about the science of blood and blood alchemy?
- Can you eavesdrop on the conversations between the sheriff and mayor, to hear what's going on?
- Can you uncover the leverage that interested parties have over your NPC friends?
- Can you uncover the history of your grandfather's financial ruin and past love lives?
- Do you side with the plucky kids, the influential villain, neither, or both?
- Will you get a run in with an America's Most Wanted star and vampire hunter ally?
- Can you get laid by a vampire?
- Do you opt to get turned into a vampire or ghoul, and why?

All in all, highly recommend. It's fun in some ways playing out a power fantasy, but also in playing an ordinary person trying to do their best. That's something missing in nearly all the World of Darkness universe games, in person or electronic. Enjoy!

I want to balance out the mixed reviews to say that I really enjoyed this game. The big issue, which other reviews have mentioned, is that this is marketed as a Vampire: The Masquerade game, but it probably shouldn't have been. You play a human, there's little vampiric politicking, and aside from some small WoD easter eggs, you could have probably swapped this out for any other vampire lore and the game would be largely unchanged. That being said, I think if you adjust your expectations, you can still have a really good time. It might be helpful to note that the story here is much more in the vein of Twin Peaks/Stranger Things/Buffy the Vampire Slayer in that it's a "supernatural forces are threatening our small town and now we have to band together to stop them while uncovering our community's darkest secrets along the way" mystery sorta thing. 

I've played through the game three times now and had drastically different experiences each go. The writing is evocative, the story is engaging, and there's a ton of branching paths to explore. I particularly like the chart that shows the percentage breakdown of your character's behavior types, even if it's mostly just cosmetic. If I had any complaint, it was that the skill checks felt a little unbalanced (on my first playthrough, I went for science/intelligence build and struggled to pass checks in a lot of places, but 2nd time through went for a charisma build and got through practically every check successfully). There are some places where the transitions and reactivity feel a little shaky, but overall I didn't have many gripes and found myself super engrossed. 

All in all, I would recommend this game if you're looking for a spooky small town mystery. It's inevitable that it will be compared to Night Road, and I think they're both solid games, just very different. I can respect that this was an attempt to reimagine WoD from a different perspective, and even if it didn't totally hit the mark as a Vampire: The Masquerade product, I still think a really fun experience came from it independent of that.

This game is 2 in 1: [b]Hunter: the Reckoning[/b] (minus the Imbued part) + [b]Vampire: the Masquerade[/b]. There are several possible endings, and you can choose sides and to decide either [spoiler]to stay mortal or become a vampire[/spoiler]. The first half is promising and well-paced, but the ending is kind of abrupt and everything leading to it felt rushed. I also spotted a few inconsistencies in the story along the way. The whole picture is not revealed in one playthrough, so, I guess, there's some replay value in this, but I feel little incentive to do it, because I didn't really connect with any of the characters and the story in general; therefore, I don't really care what could have happened, had I taken different choices. You can pretty much guess it from the story and the achievements page anyway.

The quality of this game is much lower than in the [b]Night Road[/b], so I feel disappointed after finishing it. But I don't feel disappointed enough to give it a thumb down. And I appreciate the attempt to write a [b]VtM[/b] story from a human's perspective.

[b]My overall rating[/b]: [u]6/10[/u]

Just started this game today and I am really excited to keep exploring it. The editing is really versatile and you can customize it a lot. The two best resources are the 3D tool that allows squashing and stretching in three dimensions of all objects and the categories for basic shapes and building elements. You can put those together to make a simple item more complex looking or "create" items that you need by combining pieces together (i.e. if you want to make a nail for clutter, use a flat round shape and a thinned out cone shape).

They also included a color wheel so there is no limit to what colors you might want to use but also have simple base colors for quicker edits. Color wheel choices also appear to auto save for each build you are on, so it is easy to do things like make all your "wood" furniture the same mahogany shade or all your "metal" the same blue-toned gray. I will also hype up the ability to import custom pictures as well as custom patterns for walls and flooring (with the guide on how to do so right in game). I have long wished for the ability to add custom repeating patterns on House Flipper to make my own wall paper, and this game also lets you do it for floors so you can make a unique tiled floor or multicolored wood parquet look. 

That said, the reason I am so hyped about the editing tools is that the build options are otherwise pretty basic and I would love to see that built up more. This game does have an available Steam Workshop with community created items which I will absolutely be taking a look at, but I do still hope the devs themselves will keep adding more unique items to the game as there is a clear style to their items that makes it all pretty consistent.  Given that (at time of posting) their most recent update was less than a month ago, it does seem like they are going to be adding more.

One sort of simple addition I would like to see is a "finish" category; taking a part of an item or the entire item to make it metallic, frosted, glossy, wooden, etc. Because of the lower poly style I don't want it to be super realistic, but it would just add to that diorama making feel of the game. A snapping and grid tool would also be cool, or even the ability to create invisible rulers that won't show up in photo mode to align things like paintings, windows, or lighting fixtures.

Despite the limitations, this is a really cool style of a home design type game and I could easily sink a lot of time into it. And even those limitations are pretty minor in the grand scheme as you can basically place things anywhere you want, make everything whatever color you want, change the sizes, change the heights/widths/depths... It is the sort of game where a lot of the limits are restricted purely to the imagination.

I've seen a few conversations from longer term fans of this game, whose words I can not confirm, who've made statements in regards to how it initially launched as an early access title and was rushed to 1.0 without fully being developed. I think I could see that, just judging by the storytelling. Like they had a grander plan that faltered at some point while producing the rising action so it was rushed out to be something more vague.

Gameplay wise your first dropped into Wardenclyffe. A small safe area to walk around in. This is your home base. You can swap between characters here who do have their own unique stats, you can select which perks or magics or weapons you'll use. You can also make permanent upgrades. During play enemies will end up dropping things like pink crystals. You'll keep these in your pocket when failing or succeeding in each run. These crystals are the resource used for all this upgrade stuff at Wardenclyffe.

Besides this, sometimes they'll drop batteries. The batteries do a couple different things depending on which character or loadout you are using. Sometimes you can use them as situational currency, sometimes you can use them in place of charges for magic attacks and so on. Sometimes the combat maps will have a location within it, that you can spend the points. Like a well or laboratory thing.

Besides the magical offhand attack, you'll also get up to two guns. The guns themselves, are much like the characters, and will have their own quirks. The guns will even have levels determining stats. There's a pretty standard set, you do start with a pistol and move into shotguns and tommy guns before the more scifi stuff like rayguns. It starts getting really fun when it is mixed together as then you end up with things like gauss shotguns or plasma shooting machine guns.

What takes the cake for me is the mech. It spawns in with limited time and has a gatling gun in each hand. Once its timer is up it'll explode into several pieces across the map. You go pick them back up and the machine is yours to drive... until it blows up again. Also if you play as Lovecraft you get a monster instead of a mech and if you're Shelley the mech has a dolphin brain in the pilot seat so you can run around in tandem with it.

And speaking of running around in tandem, Wardenclyffe does seem to have an interactable box which clones. I believe this is for setting up multiplayer coop mode. I didn't play this at all so I can't be sure but it seems to go up to four players and I assume is played split screen.

Okay so main gameplay loop. You select which part of the map you want to go into. The city, the farms, or the caves. From here you'll be shown a map, with different areas on it. This overall map is called the chapter, and the specific stage you're on is listed as a numbered cycle. Each cycle area is a slightly different objective, biome, or reward. Sometimes in tiers. And all these areas path out in different ways. Main goal is to make it to the final boss fight area. On the way you get objectives like survey the hive, where you wait out a timer, or close the rifts, where you defend an area and so on. Sometimes just pick up certain items, other times kill certain things. Statues or minibosses. After you complete this you get a reward, which is usually a perk, that is some sort of stat boost upgrade in some way, until an overall game win or lose.

A big catch is that the whole thing is set to a difficulty TIMER. So if you're planning on sitting in the entry levels farming kills for currency and perks you'll slowly be ramping up the entire difficulty of the entire run. This forces you to attempt to make your way through the levels as quick as possible.

Did I explain that okay? I hope so. I feel like I'm having an off day. Regardless, my overall opinion of the gameplay is that its okay. It doesn't feel BAD but is kinda repetitive which can lead to it becoming boring. I feel like this one lacks a bit of a drive to keep playing. The overarching level-up system that follows you across all the runs feels like it runs out of steam pretty quick which didn't really make me want to continue playing this one after I'd unlocked... pretty much everything I felt was important enough to unlock. Which only took a few hours.

I think my biggest criticism of this one as a product with a price tag on it is just how short it is. I wouldn't say I play at an expert level when it comes to action roguelikes but it took me a little over 3 hours to complete all the maps, unlock all the characters and get nearly all of the steam achievements. On one hand this did unlock a new game plus mode afterward with increasing difficulty however there really just isn't enough of game there for me to want to continue playing it. A huge part of the appeal of these neverending, randomized games comes from the feeling of mystery and a "whats the next thing for me to discover that is going to be a gamechanger" but I experienced none of that during my play.

Initially I thought this would be in the perks, the weapons, the characters... but at a certain point everything began feeling very same-y. Or at the very least very lacking in the "gamechanging" factor. An example of this with weapons being, shotgun. We all know what a shotgun is, it shoots a multi-spread of bullets at short range. The variations of this come in things like, repeating shotgun, which is the same but shoots faster or gauss shotgun which is the same but shoots bullets further. I do like these as additions and they were admittedly fun to play with but they weren't SO different enough that you'd want to change up your build setup to cater to them as a playstyle as much as you would use them if it was better than whatever else you had on hand.

Final thoughts? This one is pretty middle of the road. It has these brief moments of where the gameplay feels like it really picks up because you've picked up a cool set of temporary bonus items that make the screen fill with flaming bullets but the majority of the gameplay is really just meh. I don't think its a BAD game in that it is fundamentally broken or unfair or necessarily unfun, but at the same time it was just kinda boring. Which is a shame, because the setting is pretty cool. I thought this would be a great Halloween game, its got enough spooky monsters, has a great colorway, the visual side of this one is pretty good but overall there just isn't much there as a whole experience. Or at least not anything that isn't done better by a long list of other games.

Tesla Force is a roguelite top-down shooter game.

First of all, the game isn't meant to be rushed, but I did manage to get past through the entire game in 3 hours. For a game this expensive I would've expected a lot more content, Tesla vs Lovecraft (the game I would suggest to play over this one) lasting me more than double the amount of time! There are cycles and upgrades to grind the game further, but knowing it will be the same re-used content it just makes it somewhat meh.

Now in general I wouldn't have given it a negative review because I hold 10tons games close to heart, but this one was a deception to me. I really thought there would be far more content and a lot less bugs (no, not the monsters). First of all, the game is extremely RNG dependant. In one run I got a BFG and annihilated any monsters on screen all the way to the boss, in my final run I was stuck with an underpowered close-range shotgun against the final boss of the game, which I got in the level right before the boss (I was stuck with an Ion pistol before that.)

As for the bugs, well maybe an oversight but half the time I don't know what stuff does. Hovering your mouse over icons should give you some explanation and having to go through 'Character menu' every time is annoying. The most OBNOXIOUS bug is the teleport that randomly starts working! Perhaps this wouldn't be an issue with good RNG, but I lost an entire run right before the boss because my teleport ability randomly stopped working for an ENTIRE MINUTE. This is unforgivable in a game that ends your 20 minutes long run when you die, especially since some monsters almost 2-3 shots you with 120 HP!

Ranting done, the graphics are on par with all other similar games, so nothing to say about that. The music was alright, it's definitely not on Neon Chrome's level, but it's not bad. The sound effects were OK. The gameplay in itself is fun, but the game is too short, too repetitive, feels unpolished, is buggy, unbalanced and too RNG dependant.

Overall, worth playing if you get it really cheap, or just purchase Tesla vs Lovecraft instead.

Upfront, I really love 10tons for their minimalistic, crisp, short-leveled action twin-stick-shooter-games with high variability and extremely addictive flavor (if you’re German, I’d call them “kurz und knackig”). Actually 100%ed nearly every title from them until now. But Tesla Force, oh man, it really pains me to say this, but this is a step back. Don’t get me wrong, I don’t want to say that the game is bad, but it’s just kind of a roguelite spin-off to Tesla vs. Lovecraft. It’s got exactly the same mechanisms and gameplay, the only differences are 4 characters (2 of them are pretty useless), and instead of lots of designed levels, this time we only get 3 ‘segments’ with procedurally generated sub-levels with varying objectives (only 4 or 5). Therefore all in all the game is much, much shorter. There’s even no reason to master several cycles of these segments, because it actually doesn’t change anything, not even giving you additional cutscenes. And you can get all achievements in the first cycle as well.

Final verdict, if you like 10tons and like Tesla vs. Lovecraft, go for it, because it’s at least 5 hours of additional fun, especially in coop mode. But only on a really heavy discount, because, as I said, the game is much shorter than the original. Nevertheless I’ll still give this a thumbs up, just because I love 10tons so much, but please, guys, put some more effort into your future games.

As a result, one playthrough and you'll have seen everything the game has to offer multiple times over.

There are upgrades both within each chapter, that you buy with batteries, and overall, that you buy with crystals. The drop rate for these batteries and crystals is not great at the start, until you upgrade the passive bonus that increases drop rate. Thus the starting grind is very slow, and you'll need ever increasing numbers of crystals to get the upgrades you want.

All of that said - the game is still really fun. Once the drop rate is maxed, monsters will constantly be dropping bonuses ranging from frost bullets to multiple barrels to increased fire rate. It's entirely possible to saturate the entire screen with your bullets. With extra teleports you'll be zooming around the screen dodging monsters while completing your objectives. This is really fun gameplay and it's just a pity the rest of it is slightly substandard.

I really really love games like this because it shows a fine example of someone really trying hard to make something they're passionate about, but it doesn't really come together well in execution. I love seeing these great ideas put into scale and into production, and I've always had a passion for bad or *bad-ish* games. I wouldn't call this game *bad*, it's definitely bad *ish* though. 

It's basically a WWII RPG kinda deal, no stats or anything but you get to equip yourself with all sorts of guns and gear from the time, different sights and scopes that seem era accurate and quests you can do for different people. There is a lot of passion put on display here and I commend the developer for making their passion, HOWEVER. This game has a LOT of problems that need to be ironed out. One example is the inventory, it's incredibly limiting with only 25kg before you are over burdened, and that is NOT a lot of room for all the guns you want to play with. I usually like holding three guns, a long range rifle, a mid range battle rifle, and a short range machinegun/smg. That puts me pretty much at the limit of the inventory, putting me at about 21ish kg's, and THEN you have to hold all the consumables that will keep you alive which puts you at the complete limit of 25kg to hold those life-saving bandages and medicines and foods that you need to manage. Yes, there is a food system, so you need to hold food to keep you filled up. This is an RPG where you're supposed to be getting and using all the different weapons and items you can find, and yet you are incredibly limited in what you can pick up. When you're overburdened, you walk at a snails pace, so trying to transport weapons to SELL, you know, like in an RPG where you're trying to save money to get better weapons and scopes and such is a living hell of slow paced walking. It's jank and not very well thought out.
