It is REALLY hard to control your guns and especially when aiming down your sights. You will always have issues of taking your shot, and it misses by one pixel because your mouse just refuses to sit in the right spot because the sensitivity is too high. You move it, and it moves too far to the side and you're a pixel off on THAT side now too. It's really frustrating to play, I'm not going to lie because of the really exact and small hit-boxes the enemies have. It makes the gunfights feel finicky and annoying as you're just trying to shoot your targets and you're literally fighting with your mouse the whole time. 

The vehicles are all drive-able, however they are all REALLY awkward on the ground. You will literally be bouncing all over the place if you even go an INCH off the main roads, which are constantly patrolled by Germans. You are encouraged to go off-road, however doing so will make you bounce so bad you flip over. You CAN flip the vehicles back over, but it brings about another issue. The way you get off your vehicle, is you basically just spawn outside of it and if you're on your side, or upside-down (which happens a LOT), you will spawn under the map and fall infinitely until you load your save. Speaking of; 

The save system. You cannot save mid mission, and the missions/quests are usually long and annoying to get to. Each mission you have to walk or drive to and they are usually a thousand and more meters away. They are long treks across the countryside, and if you die during the mission, you go back to your last save in camp. This *wouldn't be that bad* if it weren't for the constant glitches and pointless deaths that happen because of how jank the game is. When I started, I had spent at least two hours replaying the first two missions over and over again because I wasn't used to the jank and didn't know how to avoid the game-breaking glitches. The game doesn't let you save at first until you complete the two missions, and that is a solid hour or so of having to run without getting glitched or killed, which again, is really hard to have happen. 

Combat is also always jank as heck. On top of the sights being very precise and your aim having to be really perfect, you're fighting with the mouse as I said earlier. Enemies spawn in strangely when at a distance. They aren't always in the world until you get around 100-150 meters in proximity, and from far away they can be visible through terrain and obstacles, which you will shoot at and find that they are actually *behind* something that they're glitched through. Either that or you'll be accidentally shooting the crazy huge hitboxes that cover has. I was trying to shoot around a rock, and I had to step TWO METERS out of cover before my shots actually started hitting enemies. I was just shooting a hard spot in the air because the rock I was behind had such a huge hitbox, all the while the enemies have really small and exact hitboxes. Again, it becomes very frustrating to play, and I only recommend this game to people who have an affinity for jank and bad games like I do. I can play this game just fine because I have the patience to get past the glitches and the jank and the broken BS, but I know a lot of others WONT have that patience and I suggest they give this a miss until it gets a lot of work and polishing. Especially that mouse sensitivity issue, there needs to be an option to lower it because it is *incredibly* frustrating to play without it. 
People have brought up this issue and the dev hasn't done anything about it which doesn't bode well for the future of the game. I have no idea if they plan on updating the game, but since it came out there has been NO UPDATES at all. No clue if the dev just put the game up and left it, thinking it's all finished, or if they've just released an unfinished mess, but I'm hoping they come back and actually put in the work to polish this game. I like it, it's got charm and it's fun when it works. It's fun to play with all the weapons and scopes and manage the different ammo types, but the limited inventory and the rest of the issues really make it difficult to recommend, as it's overall more negative than positive; more frustrating than enjoyable.

A Front Too Far: Normandy is a story and narrative driven first person shooter set in WW2, as the title implies, you take on the role of an American special forces paratrooper in the invasion of Normandy, meet up with the French Resistance and do some missions and adventuring as well as liberating France. 

I've played more video games than anyone else on the planet, at least 10,000 games on Steam (of which I've reviewed over 9,500).  As I wade through the lower end of the Steam marketplace, I come to expect each game as it comes up as probably being garbage.  I thought the same thing would be true for A Front Too Far: Normandy.  Well, A Front Too Far: Normandy is [i]not[/i] garbage.  This is a sincerely made game and there's some real elements of professionalism and understanding from the developer about what goes into making a real solid game that gamers would enjoy.  So for that reason, at least, I certainly hope the developer departs the indie/amateur scene and goes onto a professional engagement with a serious development company who can make good use of their obvious talent.

See, I can't recommend A Front Too Far: Normandy, despite the effort that went into it and the areas where the game does show great promise.  And those include good map design, attention to detail, fairly okay voice acting (proper accents and everything)... this is certainly head and shoulders above most amateur games on Steam, and with over 9,500 product reviews on Steam, I can say that with great confidence. 

But a few good ideas don't make a complete game, and the amateur nature of this game does shine through... games have to be a complete package, the best of the best, for me to recommend them, and there's some issues with A Front Too Far: Normandy.  Usually when writing a game review I'll pick out the obvious defects, and for most games that really do fall into the 95% of games that barely make any money at all for the developers or for Valve, those defects stick out like a sore thumb. 

Here, the only obvious defect is the poor quality graphics.  The game features lazy low-polygon "retro" assets, making this look like a barely functional 3D game from the mid 2000s.  It's unclear why the developers weren't able to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets for the game, and also irrelevant... what matters is that this looks bad as a result of their decisions, a compromise PC gamers shouldn't have to put up with.

That's not much that's wrong with this, but overall, the game also lacks polish, many areas of it are clunky.  The FPS combat is lacklustre... the decent storytelling unfortunately can't counter those defects.  It's not really pleasant to play, and that's a shame because the story is engaging.   This really comes across as Arma 2 from Wish, and that's unfortunate.  But at the same time, it's a pretty big achievement for an amateur project like this to do well enough to even merit that comparison. 

A Front Too Far: Normandy has an over ambitious price of around $6 USD, it's not worth it.  Games don't exist in a vacuum.  There's hundreds of better, professionally developed FPS games, many cheaper or at similar price points (like Arma games when they are on sale).  But I do hope the developer does go on to get a professional role in the industry so they can get better opportunities to contribute with their talent (and get paid properly for it).

There aren't many top-down extraction shooters. I'm not really an extraction shooter guy to begin with, but I've been craving a top-down loot-focused game for a while. If you're looking for a more complete experience, you're probably better off playing Zero Sievert (or waiting for its sequel), or Neo Scavenger if you enjoy text-based survival. That said, none of them are direct competitors to No Such Place.

So there is an incredible potential. The gunplay is crisp, the sound design and the overall aesthetic are mostly on point for what would you expect from an SCP-adjacent world. However, it still has a long road ahead.

There are a few missing localizations, although none of them are particularly critical. The game also desperately needs more voiced dialogue. I was caught off guard when I finally heard spoken dialogue near what seems to be the final area. More narration throughout the game would also go a long way toward making the world feel more alive.

One of the biggest issues is player guidance, in a way. Yes, the game warns you to adequately prepare before major boss fights. It marks quest locations and, to some extent, tells you where to find certain items. However, many main missions boil down to traveling from point A to point B only to discover there's little or nothing of value there. You'll often spend entire expeditions simply moving between objectives, barely bothering to loot because your stashes is already full by the time you arrive. 

Speaking of loot, the amount of it is simply overwhelming. From the beginning of the game until roughly 15 hours into my playthrough, I constantly felt buried under mountains of items. I'm currently sitting on around 1.5 million in-game currency with almost nothing worthwhile to spend it on. The only consistent expense is buying hundreds of rounds of ammunition and that's nothing compared to valuables you can recycle. Ammunition is somewhat of an issue during the early game, at least until you progress far enough to unlock the neutral Bazaar zone, where the traders replenish their stock.

That said, I would agree that ammunition shouldn't be a concern in the late game. The real problem is that the economy is fundamentally broken, so there's hardly any reason for a secondary shop to exist in the first place. The Bazaar only has four merchants, and most of them sell fairly uninteresting items. Hell, one of them was selling just three consumables.

And, if you buy hundreds of rounds of ammunition at once, of course you're going to become encumbered. Purchased items don't even get sent directly to your stash. I really wish this game had mod support.

Insurance is also extremely cheap, but even if you lose your gear, recovering isn't particularly difficult. You can redo certain activities like killing bosses or unlocking stashes because many important rewards are fixed and the layout (or the spots of the key items/codes/bosses) are not procgen.

On one hand, that's reassuring because I wasn't looking for a sweaty extraction shooter. On the other, it significantly reduces the excitement and tension. This ain't a dungeon crawler.

The first ten hours of my playthrough took place almost entirely in Origin00 (The Forest). As far as I can tell, it currently has three versions. The default version is set in 1961, an infected variation populated by corrupted soldiers, zombies, fungal creatures, and such. The second variation is 1963, where raging fires and extreme heat dominate the landscape. A third variation exists but remains locked. Unless I missed something, I assume it's WIP.

Most regular enemies are easily dispatched with a single shot, especially once you obtain a decent shotgun or a scoped rifle chambered in 7.62. Your first real skill check will probably be Highlander, the Wendigo boss. My first death belonged to him. Be careful not to enrage him, although, iirc, one quest later requires you to kill him while enraged. The second major boss, the arsonist, was also enjoyable to fight. Both are noticeably tankier than anything you've encountered beforehand, but they still felt fair.

Then I got sliced by a samurai. He killed me in two hits. I spent roughly an hour and a half finally defeating him, only to discover he drops absolutely nothing. I won't pretend he isn't one of the biggest reasons I'm leaving a negative review.

Origin08 (The Edifice) takes place inside a 12-floor office building set in 1999. It features a hand-drawn map, shorter extraction timers, and a progression system centered around mapping the connected floors. Elevators serve specific levels, while inaccessible floors require using the stairs. It's nothing overly complicated, but it's easily the strongest map in the game. Enemy movements are incredibly predictable in that level but they at least look cool, and the 15-minute extraction timer creates genuine urgency compared to the 40+ minute expeditions in The Forest.

The final area, Origin12 (Grey Birch Mountain), is a snowy region inhabited by skeleton enemies that must be killed twice to stay dead. Here, the game rapidly siphons your ammunition as large enemy groups can overwhelm you while deep snow slows your movement.

Unfortunately, neither of these later regions feels nearly as content-rich as The Forest. Grey Birch Mountain doesn't even display the names of POIs on the map, which ultimately burned me out and made me stop searching for The Remnant. That's probably for the best, considering I hadn't even managed to defeat the fly boss on the executive floor of The Edefice, meaning I was already behind the eight ball.

Overall, No Such Place sits in a strange position.

The stamina and inventory management are really frustrating. Eventually, you train yourself to recognize what is and isn't worth picking up, but the sheer volume of loot constantly taxes your attention. Many materials feel too valuable to leave behind because future quests might require them (and they do), yet most remain useless until much later. Crafting and construction resources occupy plenty inventory space but you only need few of them at a time so I didn't worry. 

There's also a corruption system where you recover corrupted items and cleanse them. Personally, I never found anything worthwhile from this mechanic and eventually ignored it altogether. You can eventually build a forge but cannot craft equipments or anything like that, it does let you to craft ingots and such but the associated questline was marked as WIP as well. 

Unless you're prepared to thoroughly map everything yourself and wait patiently for future updates, I'd recommend leaving No Such Place on your wishlist for now. It has tremendous potential, but it desperately needs additional balancing, more playtesting, and a stronger sense of progression.

By the end, I found myself spending hundreds of rounds of ammunition on one or two bosses while rushing throughout the maps and skipping everything else. Since it's just PvE there's nothing else that could potentially punish you. 

I don't usually rate Early Access games, but if I had to, I'd give No Such Place v0.7:
★★★☆☆ - Needs a massive overhaul before the launch to realize its potential.

Most of the negative reviews are either plain stupid or glaringly false.

The game is in EA, it's new, and it has only a few dedicated devs; it's gonna have bugs but I have yet to come across anything game-breaking or run-ending. Expecting a completely polished game from an actively developing game where the devs DO take their time to respond to you if you talk to them can only be read as spoiled. The enemies in the beginner area of the first map have little awareness because it's literally the beginner area. It's canonically the most stable area and there isn't much to fear in the possible spawns. Even in the first map there are areas that are locked that have enemies capable of one-shotting a fully armored character if you don't read their attack patterns and areas with teams of ACTUAL soldiers with the ability to snipe you if you go in unaware.

If you don't have inventory space, build more crates. Each one can be upgrade to be as big as your starter supply box, which is a LOT of space on its own. Also, you can store furniture for FREE and place it back down to complete missions you already did in the demo. The localization isn't perfect, but it's a WIP, and I appreciate the effort.

Anyway, I personally find the game's systems to be extremely fun and they scratch an itch most extraction shooters don't. The quest structure really does make you comb every nook and cranny of the given maps for your goals but it never feels like a grind (especially with the amended drop rates for things like the dreaded nuke egg).I also appreciate the extremely forgiving insurance system. I'm not the kind of person who enjoys random stat mechanics with permanent gear loss so the choice to include the option to insure my guns with 5 specialized parts mish-mashed from several runs if I mess up affirms the philosophy of fun first. If you don't like that system, you could always just not use it, it's cheaper if you don't.

Super fun PvE extraction shooter. cheaper than I was anticipating from what I played with the demo. I was budgeting for 20-$25 not $16.

I like the weapon platform system the game has. You can press G on any weapon to open the modding screen and from there you can mix and match compatible parts. Early on your choices for parts is pretty sparse but as you progress you gain access to more weapon types, manufacturers, and even special effects on parts (called corruptions). These special effects can really change up your gun like Polyshot allowing a gun to accept any type of ammo, or another corruption allowing it to accept any weapon part (IE I can put a 7.62 drum mag for an assault rifle on a 7.62 pistol if the pistol has that corruption and so on). Theres even other corruptions that invert stat changes on a gun allowing you to make use of otherwise terrible parts or making parts like Drum Mags even stronger.

Gameplay is as you expect, you are dropped into a very large map and are expected to fight against zombies and other nasty creatures like spore monsters and zombies and other factions trying to control these twisted lands. You have 1 hour in each run to do your business and find an exit. Otherwise you die.

Thankfully death is a lot more forgiving here than some other extraction shooters thanks to the game's insurance system where you can insure your gear before each run. Its a relatively cheap process and the more times you beat a particular map the more "safe" the insurance company labels it giving you a discount on future insurance policies. 

The game does have its flaws though. 

The main menu music is way to loud by default.

Classes need some serious rebalancing. Support is by far and away the strongest class currently leaving R&D in the dust. Support can highlight loot, increase search speed, has a chance to teleport loot back to base via special dropoff points. And their final perk removes the weight from equipped gear. While R&D gets 25% cheaper crafting costs, 25% stronger crafted tacticals, upgrades their crafting grid from a 2x2 to a 3x3 (sounds nice until you realize that pretty much anything worth making can be made in a 2x2 and the other stuff you could make in an emergency still requires you to find a workbench because its bigger than a 3x3.

Combat class feels relatively balanced for what its trying to do. it doesn't need touching but R&D certainly does, or it needs a lot more crafting recipes available to it early on or at least a lot earlier.

There is translations missing in two spots that I have seen. One in the construction menu in a single line at the bottom of the tooltip for the toilet. And the other being scoped in with a 3.8x scope at max range probably saying max range or something.

The AI isn't really an issue, the only AI I can say I've noticed is the video at the beginning and that was done to replicate an old 70s-80s employee orientation/onboarding video. Which was disclosed in the ai section of the store and has been for a while with the demo.

Other people are complaining about quests being reset for some reason. Guess they didn't read the notes saying that quest progression was reset and that it was recommended to start a new character anyway. Don't see why that's surprising to anyone, demos usually are like that. But there is a reason they disallow comments on their reviews because they know they're spouting off shit and they'd get ratio'd otherwise xD

Overall, current state of the game is quite fun. If pve extraction shooters are you thing it'll definitely scratch that itch. Game does support multiplayer in a P2P format so try to get your friend with the gigabyte speed to host.

Edit: They reduced the volume of the main menu but its still very loud, reducing the music volume in the options by half its the perfect volume but that means losing out on the ingame music sadly.

[h1]Good, but Could Be Better[/h1]

I got Hellslave (1) on a big sale, finished it, and immediately bought Hellslave 2 because I wanted more. I just burned a week of my life away playing them, and I had a good time. But, in all fairness, I must say that Hellslave 2 gets somewhat repetitive after a while.

Upon starting the game, you quickly notice major improvements over the first one: a clearer way to select your character's class, an overhauled UI, a fully-drawn open world map, multi-screen dungeons that you get to actually walk through (instead of just right-clicking on a mini-map), enemies moving around that you can avoid (instead of being randomly attacked out of the blue), side quests, better item drops from enemies, you get to see your weapons during combat (a nice touch), etc. Much has been improved upon. But not everything.

As I'm about to lay down a series of constructive criticisms, [b]let me get something out of the way first:[/b] 

The game is good. If you think you'll like it by checking the screenshots, you probably will. Steam's 2-hour refund window is more than enough for you to know if you are happy with your purchase or not. In the worst case scenario (if you don't like the game [i]and[/i] blow that window), your money will still be going to an extraordinarily competent guy who totally deserves it, because this game was wholly made by a single man (art, coding and writing). And Hellslave 2 is also not too expensive. So definitely give it a shot.


With that being said, here are some things I believe "Ars Goetia" could improve in a potential third installment in the series:  

There's one change in particular that made Hellslave 2 more repetitive than the first one. In Hellslave 1, each dungeon had its own drop pool. When entering a new one, you knew you'd drop new items, so you had something to look forward to. In this one, you keep getting the exact same items throughout the entire game. As you move on, you just keep dropping the same stuff with slightly better numbers. (I did get a few items I had never seen before at the very end of the game, when being level 50, but the exceptions were few.)

As it was in Hellslave 1, the skill trees (active and passive) remain pretty much the same: there are still about the same number of skills available, and each tree contains skills for multiple different classes at once (skills that you'll find repeated if you create a new character with a different class). This is a way to fool the player (or potential buyers) into believing the game actually contains a lot more character-building-depth than it does. I'd usually frown [i]hard[/i] upon this, but since this is a solo-dev project and still a good game anyway, I'll just let it slide for once. 

As the game progresses, you get to unlock some new ways to make yourself stronger. This was clearly implemented precisely to shake things up a bit, to make the game less repetitive and more rewarding. But it fails in doing so, because the "different" stuff you unlock actually do the same thing your passive skills, items or something else already did. They don't really [i]change[/i] anything. It might be a good idea to add things that meaningfully change [i]how[/i] you play, such as unique items, gems or whatever that, for instance, "Make Active skill X hit 3 enemies instead of one," or "Make active skill Y attack thrice, adding its effects 3 times to enemies." 

This time around we have "gems" (I forget how the game actually calls them) to insert on items, to buff them up a bit. But the buffs granted by gems are so crappy that I beat the whole game without ever inserting a single item with them. Also, if you find a better item or upgrade a unique one, whatever was socketed into it is lost, so there's no point in socketing gems into items below max-level. 

Exploration is better now than it was in the first game, but there isn't really anything particularly interesting to be found. There should be some secrets scattered around, and particularly interesting and hard-to-get rewards to be discovered.

In Hellslave (1), bosses dropped some exclusive items, so you had reason to farm them. You needed to get stronger before moving on, so you had to grind a bit. You did some dungeon runs, hoping to drop what you wanted, and that was fun. In Hellslave 2, it's all linear. You clear one place up, once, and move straight to the next area. 

Finally, going through the trouble of making different items visible on the player's avatar is kind of a wasted effort in a game in which you don't see your character in combat, and in which the items do not show up on the avatar that moves around either. I like seeing different items on my guy, but given how much work this takes and how particularly little it pays off in the present case, the effort of implementing that is not worth it.

 
As [b]a final aside[/b]: 

An "anti-AI" logo shows up amid the game's splash-screens. I get why someone who manually drew a whole game would feel like that about AI-made images, but come on... that's like a whaler protesting against electricity because no one will use oil-fuelled lamps anymore. Or a professor protesting against internet-streamed classes because now a single person can teach the entire world instead of everyone needing to physically go to a school to learn something from a lesser teacher. Progress always wins, and it does so because it makes everyone's lives easier -- including the lives of those who try to hinder it.

Also, just to throw it out there, since what anti-AI folks are worried about is mainly losing their jobs (a strictly selfish reason, I should note): there's no such thing as "unemployment" -- the problem we have is "excess people." When people can't find jobs, it's not because the market doesn't work and all of humanity is wrong. It's because those people simply aren't needed. We've never managed to solve this problem because, as societies, we refuse to acknowledge what the true problem is.

[h1][b]HellSlave II: Judgement of the Archon Review[/b][/h1]

[h2][b]Overall Rating:[/b] 7/10[/h2]

[h2][b]Playtime at Review: 10 hours[/b][/h2]

[h2][b]Price/value:[/b] Wait for Sale[/h2]

[h1][b]Summary/TL;DR[/b][/h1]
A solid dark fantasy dungeon crawler with stunning visuals and great music. However, the mechanics rapidly shifts from brutally hard to trivially easy. My biggest complaint is the length: it only took 10 hours to complete. Despite developer posts estimating ~14 hours (and developer quoting his playtesters took 20), it feels quite short for the price point.
[hr][/hr]
[h2][b]The Good[/b][/h2]
The hand-drawn artwork and dark grimfake vibe are phenomenal. Equipping new gear updates your character's visual appearance on the inventory screen (though unfortunately not on the overworld).

The music fits the mood brilliantly, though a few sound effects are a bit loud out of the box.

While a single play-through is short at 10 hours, there are multiple classes to try. Rotating through different builds could easily net you 40–50 hours overall.

The game lets you fully reset your skills and stats whenever you want, making build experimentation a highlight.

[hr][/hr]
[h2][b]The Mix[/b][/h2]
The difficulty curve is bizarre. You either get instantly overwhelmed by stacked debuffs and chain attacks, or you dump all your points into a hyper-focused build and one-shot every enemy in sight. There is rarely a middle ground.

Skill critical hits and enemy death animations feel heavy and satisfying, but fighting hordes of basic fodder enemies eventually bogs the pacing down.

[hr][/hr]
[h2][b]The Bad[/b][/h2]
Stats felt like they didn't really matter at all. Items outweigh the stats almost completely. I re-rolled my stats a few times and it felt like they had no impact no matter what i put them into.  The later mastery stats you can put into seem irrelevant since their bonus is so small.

Itemization is also pretty poor. There is only a few items in the game. Once you pick a strategy and skill to focus on you can ignore 99% of items and just filter for one or two stat lines. Not to mention lower tier rarity drops have no value at all in the game. After the first two dungeons, you will have all gear slots equipped. Then grey -> blue items have no value at all. 

Lore was cool even if a bit long winded. However, most characters were extremely one dimensional. You never really seem to care for their motivation in doing the things they do. You also never really interact with them long enough to care [spoiler] except for one character =( RIP Hraban. Baal was pretty forgettable. I felt nothing for his storyline. The main character's motivation to help him also seemed to come out of nowhere. [/spoiler] Most NPCs just seem there to give you a fetch quest here and there. I actually wanted to care a bit more about people's stories since their designs were cool. I wish the side quests chained into longer quests or affected the outcomes or shops in a city.

[hr][/hr]
[h1][b]Breakdown[/b][/h1]

[h2]Gameplay & Mechanics:[/h2] 8/10
[h2]Story & Writing:[/h2] 5/10
[h2]Visuals & Art Style:[/h2] [b]12[/b]/10
[h2]Sound & Music:[/h2] 9/10

[hr][/hr]
[h1][b]Closing[/b][/h1]
I think overall HellSlave II: Judgement of the Archon is a good game. The lore and characters were  shallow. The game itself is really short. However, I am not playing a dungeon crawler for its story and lore. This isn't a visual novel so the lore doesn't matter as much. It is still really fun to feel like a demon god and murder waves and waves of fodder. I would still wait for a sale. I think the length of the game stops me from recommending it at full price.

I loved the first Hellslave. [b] A LOT[/b]. It was one of those games that completely clicked with me, so when Hellslave 2 came out, I bought it both for myself and as a gift for someone else. I had been waiting for this game for a long time.

There are things here that I genuinely love, and I want to start with those, because I don't think this game is bad because the developer didn't care. Quite the opposite - I can see an enormous amount of work, research and experimentation behind it.

[h3] The good stuff [/h3]

[list]
    [*]Music is fantastic. Seriously, I loved it. It is atmospheric, memorable and feels very high quality.
    [*]Art style is also great. It is consistent with first game, which I really appreciate. Visual identity of Hellslave is still very strong.
    [*]I also really liked the variety of mechanics. You can clearly see that the developer has studied and experimented with a lot of different ideas. There is a lot of knowledge and creativity packed into this game, and I absolutely respect that.
[/list]

[h3] Neutral points [/h3]

[list]
    [*]Quest journal only keeps one active quest visible at a time, so there is no convenient way to see the full list of things currently going on. You can switch between quests on the map, so it isn't difficult - just unnecessarily inconvenient.
    [*]There are also still quite a few bugs despite the game being released. I reported several of them in Discord: disappearing UI elements, the map breaking or shifting, and situations where picking up loot requires you to basically spin around in one spot for an absurd amount of time.
    [*]The sound settings were also a surprisingly big problem for me. The music and sound effects are extremely loud, but there is no proper way to balance them individually. Even when I turned the master volume almost all the way down, the sound effects were still ridiculously loud. Eventually I just lowered the entire game's volume on my laptop so I could play without getting annoyed by the audio. That's not really how this should work.
[/list]

[h3] And reasons why this review is negative in the end [/h3]

[list]
    [*][b] Excessive fighting[/b]: enemies can summon totems, swords or other objects onto the battlefield. You can kill the enemy (all the enemies even) and still have to fight all those objects with tiny amounts of HP till the end. This doesn't make the encounter more challenging. It makes it take longer. So instead of having one interesting, difficult fight, I repeatedly got lots of smaller fights where the same enemies were shuffled around.

    [*]That feeling gets even worse in the [b] Purgatory levels[/b]. Clearing them was easily the most tedious part of the entire game. You fight the same enemies over and over again. They don't meaningfully evolve, their skills don't change, their compositions don't really change, and the main thing the game seems to add is a tiny amount of extra HP. Level 1 and level 15 of Purgatory felt exactly the same to me. Maybe I had to hit something a few more times. That's not meaningful difficulty progression.

    [*][b] Achievements[/b]: 15 Purgatory levels, 3 classes and 3 demons require multiple playthroughs. I normally don't mind grinding achievements, but I'm absolutely not doing it here. In this specific game it is not feels like "can you create a powerful enough build to overcome this challenge?" and more like "can you tolerate the game doing the same thing to you for long enough?" The game doesn't offer enough variation to make another playthrough worth player's time. 

    [*][b] Items[/b]. How are the level 11 gloves I picked up in the Forbidden Shrine still better than basically everything I received later while checking every chest till 15 purgatory? Item progression should not work like that and we are not in Path of Exile, c’mon.  And why can a level 12 item and a level 48 item differ by only 1%? And why can an older, lower-level item of the same rarity be better than a newer one? Eventually, finding new loot stopped being exciting because it was not actually an upgrade.

    [*][b] Gold & loot[/b]. There is way too much money and loot everywhere. Because item stats are so randomized, most of what you pick up ends up being sold or destroyed. If you sell it, you quickly accumulate hundreds of thousands of gold - but there is basically nothing to spend it on. I genuinely don't understand why gold is even in the game.

    [*][b] Merchants[/b]. Random blacksmiths and merchants standing in completely empty places immediately after massive battles with demon lords in destroyed settlements are incredibly immersion-breaking. Walking through a devastated settlement after a huge demonic battle and finding a random guy casually waiting there to sell me a sword is just absurd. But maybe it felt like that because the world was so empty.

    [*]Storytelling
[/list]

[spoiler] Story was probably the biggest disappointment for me, especially compared to the first game. Up until Mammon, I was still following what was happening and was reasonably interested. After that, I completely lost the thread. There is technically a story, but it stopped feeling meaningful. I genuinely think the developer knows the material extremely well, and you can see how much research went into it. But knowing the material and writing an engaging story are different skills. I think the game could have really benefited from some consultation with a narrative designer.

Hellslave 1 had a much stronger sense of progression. We were trying to reach Hell, the situation on Earth was getting worse, demons were becoming more prominent, and the whole thing gradually felt more dangerous and grand. Here, I mostly felt like I was walking around killing everyone and everything for no reason. 
The idea of demons pretending to be rulers and manipulating people is interesting, but I don't think the game communicates it very well. Having people immediately call the player a spy and try to kill them every time they pass through a gate (IT HAPPENED THREE TIMES) doesn't make the population feel manipulated - it just makes them feel stupid.

For a large part of the game, we are simply carrying out the requests of random strangers. We never really think about how our allies' actions affect our plans. In almost every side quest, the protagonist demands gold. When people he barely knows give him orders - we simply follows them. There is no analysis, no strategy, no real decision-making. We don't have any options and just go around bonking whoever happens to be in our way, whenever the game tells us to: demons, their subordinates or ordinary people simply following their orders or just existing near demons by chance. It is really hard to actually have at least a little bit of agency in here. [/spoiler]
 
[list]
    [*]Most side quests are basically "go there, kill X things, bring me X things." There isn't enough variety or storytelling to make them interesting, so eventually I was doing them because they were on the map rather than because I actually cared about them.

    [*]Ending… [spoiler] I was told that I could stay or leave, but I wasn't actually given the choice. The credits started immediately. I really wish the game had let me decide whether to stay or go through the portal first and then started the credits. It's a small thing, but if you tell the player they have a choice, let them actually make it. Let it feel immersive even for a second, at least at a grand final.  [/spoiler]
[/list]

Despite this negative review, I really hope the developer keeps making games. His projects clearly make me feel a lot of emotions, and I think that's exactly because I can see so much potential in them. I genuinely believe his future projects could benefit from consulting with specialists in areas outside his own expertise, and I would be very happy to see what Ars Goetia creates beyond Hellslave. I may not have enjoyed Hellslave 2, but I still want to see what comes next.

But I really would have liked to see some missions that dealt with the aftermath of the main story.  There are a handful of minor characters that play a particular role in the main story but just drop off once you progress far enough and I would like to know what happened to them.

A unique blend of Slay the Spire and Diablo. This game is promising and I crushed it in about 14 straight hours. I played full mage glass cannon and loved it, but there are some major problems with this game that they will hopefully fix with patching.

Pros:
- Unique game design with high levels of customization for your character
- The gameplay is fluid and I like how you can actually heal your life/mana by fighting
- Items and spells are fun and easy to understand. Not too much clutter. 
- Can be very hard at times, bosses taking several attempts or more
- Respec is free and unlimited!
- Rewarded for clearing and exploring
- Interesting story from the pov of demons
- Artwork is charming and they don't use AI

Cons:
- The cut scenes. You can't skip them. When you encounter a boss, there's a huge cut scene. If you die, you have to run back and go through the whole cut scene again. You can't skip it, only fast forward it by clicking your mouse fast, but its still slow. Needs a button to skip.
- I couldn't see the bottom part of the screen. Tried windowed mode and fullscreen, didn't help. It wasn't an issue until the end game when I couldn't go to purgatory level 9 because it was off the screen.
- There is a broken quest where you are taken prisoner and lose all your gear (level 43 area). You have to defeat 1 monster to get your items back and it feels IMPOSSIBLE. Almost quit the game over it. Only way I won was extremely lucky RNG.
- Speaking of the RNG, its extremely brutal. You'll put all your power into a single attack and the monster will just parry or dodge it. In this sense, sometimes you get bad RNG and just lose. Sometimes you get great RNG with crits and such, and delete a boss. 
- If you get a bad parry, you pretty much just lost the fight and have to wait to die to try again. There should be an easy way to reset to your last point pre-fight to save time rather than wait out dying.

It's worth buying but should probably cost a little less until they fix some issues.

If Steam allowed neutral ratings, that's where I'd land.  The concept is an A+; the execution is a very mixed bag.

Pros:
Music is befitting
Concept is great

Things I really don't like:
1) Autosave is too infrequent and/or 'exit game' should prompt a save option. I lost a bunch of progress exiting without actively saving. This approach of having a tiny text warning about exiting without saving is 20 years out of date.
2) Compared to other games in the genre, the controls feel clunky. While you can adjust keybinds, the default design is bad. Some of it stems from needing a 'rotation' command, certainly, but not all of it. Why is 'drop' G?
  2a) Also, the reference book is a good idea, but navigating the reference book absolutely sucks.
3) The 'puzzle' aspect of this just doesn't carry enough weight to land. Some of the paintings have 4 pieces, some have 12+. 
4) The game gets too much of its "difficulty" from pieces being upside-down. Randomly flipping pieces over is....something to do, I guess. But it's not compelling gameplay, again even by the standards of the genre.
5) Conversely, the game seems to deposit half or more of many puzzle's pieces right around the place where they go. From a roleplaying perspective, sure, that fits the 'there was an earthquake!' premise, but it's a place where a little more randomness might have been worthwhile.

It's not a bad game, and the vibe is nice if you just want a vibe.  Unless you've either exhausted other options in the genre though, or really like tiny depictions of art, I'd recommend other options.

Note: if the reviews were mostly negative I probably would have rated it mildly positive to balance. I'm rating it negative because the current "Overwhelmingly positive" vastly overstates the situation here and people are going to be lured to buy this assuming it's great.  It's a 5.5/10, maaaaaybe a 6/10.

The artstyle is consistent and clean, some of the character designs are really clever and fit the role of that character perfectly.
Overall, I'd say it's a cute TD that does a stellar job at being what it tries to be, and it comes together in a nice way, especially with the amount of content you get for the price. (and an update coming too!)

​At first glance, Antivirus Girl might look like a game that relies entirely on its suggestive, fan service-heavy character designs to make a quick impression. However, don't let the provocative art style misguide you into thinking this is just a low-effort cash grab. Look past the eye-catching aesthetic, and you’ll find a surprisingly fun, well-crafted, and genuinely good tower defense game underneath.

You take control of Reta, a recently activated admin for a freshly installed copy of the Sentinel antivirus software. The core loop is classic tower defense: you place towers to analyze incoming data packages and eliminate viruses before they breach the firewall.

However, Antivirus Girl injects enough unique mechanics to keep it from feeling like a generic TD. First, Reta isn't just a passive observer; she can move freely around the map and attack enemies directly, adding a great layer of active participation. Second, the game features multiple mob spawn points that combine and rotate with each wave, keeping the battlefield dynamic. 

Another mechanic is the pathing system. Packages and most viruses follow specific routes, you can alter these paths with your tower placements. This allows you to control the flow of the mobs, making their movements more predictable or steering them away from conflictive areas. It adds a layer of strategic maze-building to the standard formula.

In terms of challenge, Antivirus Girl leans heavily toward the easier side, making it a perfect pick-up-and-play experience. Most levels can be completed with a perfect rating on your very first try. Only a handful of stages required me to repeat them a couple of times to secure that perfect score. Success usually comes down to your tower placement and type, Reta's loadout, and a fair bit of RNG, which can occasionally dictate the flow of a run. It's highly accessible, though veterans of the genre might find it a bit too forgiving.

For a game that could easily have treated its narrative as an afterthought, the story in Antivirus Girl is actually quite engaging. While it's true that almost all the characters are one-dimensional stereotypes, the plot moves at a good pace and delivers a genuinely fun conclusion. It's a nice bonus that elevates the experience beyond just the mechanics.

The soundtrack, on the other hand, doesn't leave much of an impression. It isn't bad by any means, it successfully provides the right atmosphere for the digital, cyber-themed setting, but the tracks aren't particularly memorable and easily fade into the background.

Antivirus Girl is a highly recommended title for anyone looking for a fun, casual tower defense experience. Chowbie has managed to wrap a solid, strategic game in a highly suggestive package. If you can look past the fan service, you'll find a genuinely entertaining game with active combat mechanics, smart pathing systems, and a surprisingly engaging story.

Antivirus Girl turns the normally invisible process of computer security into a colorful defense-shooter built around inspection, preparation, and quick reactions. Developed and published by Chowbie, the game places you in the role of a new inspector working for Sentinel, an advanced antivirus organization tasked with protecting computer systems from outside threats. Instead of using cybersecurity merely as decoration, the game incorporates scanning, malware identification, network traffic, and defensive modules directly into its core mechanics, resulting in an unusual blend of tower defense, top-down shooting, strategy, simulation, and real-time tactics.

The basic gameplay structure begins with preparation. You directly control the protagonist and deploy modules at important positions before incoming files begin moving through the system. These modules help establish the routes that traffic will follow, making placement an important tactical decision rather than a simple matter of increasing firepower. Once an inspection starts, the game shifts toward active defense. Files arrive from an external network and must be scanned so that you can determine whether they are legitimate data or malware. Safe files should be allowed to continue, while malicious ones need to be destroyed before they can compromise the protected system.

This distinction between harmless and dangerous files gives Antivirus Girl considerably more personality than a conventional arena shooter. Firing at everything is not the solution because successful defense requires judgment as well as reflexes. You must observe incoming traffic, identify threats, manage positioning, and react quickly enough to stop malware without interfering with legitimate files. Different malware types possess their own characteristics, encouraging the player to adapt rather than depend upon a single defensive arrangement. The resulting loop combines the satisfaction of constructing an effective defense with the immediacy of personally entering the fight.

The tower-defense influence is particularly important because the modules and routes create a strategic layer underneath the shooting. Planning a useful path can make enemies easier to manage, while poor preparation can leave the player scrambling once the inspection becomes busy. Because the protagonist remains directly controllable, however, mistakes are not necessarily decided during the setup phase. You can reposition and respond personally when the automated portion of the defense proves insufficient. This relationship between preparation and improvisation is arguably the game's strongest mechanical idea, preventing it from becoming either completely passive or purely dependent on twitch shooting.

Sentinel itself provides narrative context for these mechanics. The antivirus organization is divided into departments such as Scan, Clean, and Analysis, with different agents associated with the organization and its operations. This effectively personifies familiar antivirus processes, turning what would normally be background computer functions into locations, responsibilities, and characters. It is a playful interpretation of cybersecurity that fits naturally with the game's anime-inspired presentation and female protagonist. The story component also gives players something to follow between defensive encounters instead of reducing the experience to an isolated succession of battles.

Visually, Antivirus Girl embraces a cute and deliberately stylized anime direction. Its character designs are also openly fan-service oriented. The Steam description specifically notes revealing high-leg leotards and tights, including partial exposure around the chest and upper legs. That aesthetic is therefore an intentional component of the presentation rather than an incidental detail. Players interested primarily in the tactical mechanics should be aware of this emphasis, while those already comfortable with anime games featuring suggestive character designs will probably find that it complements the game's playful tone.

The overall genre mixture is both an advantage and a possible source of friction. Traditional tower-defense players may initially expect more emphasis on automated defenses, while shooter fans may need to become accustomed to scanning, route construction, and threat identification. Antivirus Girl is most successful when these elements are viewed as interconnected parts of one system. Building defenses prepares the battlefield, scanning determines what actually constitutes a threat, and direct combat provides the means of responding when malware appears. The individual systems are relatively straightforward, but combining them creates enough simultaneous responsibilities to keep encounters engaging.

There are useful supporting features as well, including Steam achievements and Steam Cloud functionality. The single-player focus suits the concept because the player is essentially managing a complete inspection operation while simultaneously serving as its active defender. The relatively unusual premise also works in the game's favor. Many independent defense games rely on familiar fantasy, military, or science-fiction scenarios, whereas representing network security as a physical battlefield gives Antivirus Girl an immediately recognizable identity.

Steam Deck compatibility is worth considering for anyone planning to play primarily on Valve's handheld. The game's underlying top-down action and relatively compact interface concept make it suitable in principle for portable sessions, and Steam provides filtering for reviews from players who played mostly on Steam Deck. However, prospective Deck users should treat the experience as something that may benefit from checking current compatibility information and community reports, particularly regarding text readability, interface presentation, controls, and any minor display issues. Its gameplay structure itself is well suited to handheld play, especially for shorter defensive stages, but it should not automatically be assumed to provide a completely flawless console-like experience in every respect.

Antivirus Girl ultimately stands out because it commits to its cybersecurity idea rather than simply applying computer terminology to an unrelated shooter. Scanning incoming files, distinguishing legitimate data from malware, designing routes with modules, reacting to different malicious threats, and interacting with Sentinel's specialized departments all contribute to the same central concept. The combination can occasionally feel busier than a dedicated tower-defense game or straightforward shooter, but that hybrid nature is precisely what gives it character. Chowbie has created a compact but imaginative interpretation of antivirus work that balances tactical preparation with hands-on action and wraps the whole concept in a distinctive anime presentation.

Antivirus Girl is an inventive defense-shooter whose unusual subject matter is supported by mechanics that actually reflect its theme. Its mixture of file inspection, module deployment, route planning, threat recognition, and direct combat creates an engaging gameplay identity, while Sentinel and its agents give the concept additional personality. The fan-service-heavy presentation and hybrid design will not appeal to everyone, and Steam Deck players should remain mindful of interface and compatibility considerations, but for players attracted to unconventional tower defense and top-down action, it offers a creative and memorable variation on both genres.

On entering the simulation and strategy genre, Subway Builder does so with a bold vision, presenting itself as a focused and specialized game devoted to management of public transportation. Unlike conventional city-builders, Subway Builder takes away the aspect of building your own city and is more so a simulation to create the most efficient subway system possible. Subway Builder makes underground logistics the main emphasis of the whole experience. The game achieves this by giving priority to structural geometry, financial realism, and dynamic commuter pathfinding rather than to the superficial design of the city, thus creating a highly technical and engaging sandbox. It manages to convey the scale of urban transport planning and offers an exceptional level of depth for enthusiasts like me who enjoy this type of management.

The main way the game works comes down to striking a careful balance between building physical tunnels through complicated underground areas, handling a large number of passengers, and making sure profits dont go under. To build tracks, you must carefully select were you want to put them and avoid going through buildings unless you are digging lower than 10m. Demand stats are well shown and it is easy to plan out a path. Although it is cheaper to lay tracks close to the surface, I soon found out that doing so creates opportunities for eminent domain that increases costs. On the other hand, digging deep tunnels through bedrock doesn't disrupt the surface, but it increases both the construction costs exponentially. 

In addition to simple excavation, the track-laying engine provides a high degree of precision when it comes to the layout of the infrastructure and the tracks. I experienced great satisfaction in building quad-tracked main lines, since this enabled my express trains to skip the local outer stations and take the large number of passengers directly into the dense districts. This level of mechanical detail is complemented by a surprisingly advanced commuter artificial intelligence; the simulated citizens do not move at random but instead adhere to specific schedules, starting points, and destinations drawn from actual census and demographic data, and you can manage fares by creating fare zones or simply making a flat fare across the entire system. If you stack multiple lines on one track, it quickly leads to a chain reaction of delays throughout entire sections of the line, which will affect the efficiency of your system if delays is not properly attended to.

In appearance, Subway Builder has a neat, schematic style similar to that of professional computer-aided design programmes and architectural plans, and at the same time the user interface and controls are surprisingly easy to use for a simulator of this kind. The experience, however, is greatly worsened by one major defect: hardware optimisation. As soon as the transit network grows beyond a small number of active lines and starts calculating thousands of real commuters, the performance of the system collapses. Frame rates drop regularly to a painful 10 FPS, so that what ought to be a smooth exercise in planning becomes a slow, jerky and frustrating experience.

In my opinion, Subway Builder is a great achievement in terms of concept and design for fans of transit simulation games, but it is almost completely limited by its serious technical problems. Rather than including casual, superficial features, the game opts for a strict and highly satisfying management system, and the core simulation logic is something that is incredible. On the other hand, unless the developers deal with the severe drops in performance which continually bring the frame rate down to 10 FPS when mid-to-late game operations are taking place, only the most patient people will be able to tolerate its remarkable depth.

DISCLAIMER: I received a steam key for free and the game's main dev has donated to my youtube channel. I will be keeping this review as unbiased as possible.

Background: I probably have over two hundred hours across the steam and website version. I got the game in October after seeing City Planner Plays try it out. I was instantly hooked, I was entertained by the game's simple progression build line -> get ridership -> build more lines. I started making videos based with gameplay in Boston which caused me to research the city I had just moved to so it was a win-win-win. I have played a lot of different maps either during a video, stream, or just offline (I just finished a Baltimore save that kept me busy during my last two flights). Each map has its own challenges and it's fun to find out the best solution for each. I would play this game just as much if I wasn’t making videos on it. With that being said I will try to be as fair and honest in my pros and cons.

Pros: 
-Insanely addicting
-Easy to learn depending on your willingness to search out for help when needed
-Simple gameplay loop but rewarding
-Accurate data which leads to interesting discoveries (like I didn't know 5,000 people worked at that car factory or wow 20,000 people live over there in that suburb lets connect it)
-Recent updates have improved the vanilla gameplay greatly (such as offline mode being added)
-Easy to mod using the app Railyard
-Super fun to try out different transit plans for your city or many different places (40+ cities now in vanilla and I think now 200+ cities are available through mods)
-Major Issues like pathfinding, performance, and statistics have all be improved recently 

Cons:
-High Price Point for Indie Game (this is based on general consensus with my background and love for these types of games the price point was fine for me)
-Performance still needs work on lower end computer systems
-Weird bugs (I seem to be very lucky cause I’ve only had the game crash when using mods never with just vanilla)
-More train types need to be added (they're working on streetcars)
-Devs poor response to general community during steam release and recent modding drama 

To finish this review I think the game is headed in the right direction. Depending on the main dev's willingness to proceed with focus the sky is the limit. What this game is doing exactly what an idle game is supposed to do. It does the work FOR you. Without forcing you to spend much time on actually progressing. [h3] What makes this game great? [/h3]
Tiny Terraces has an unique style and more importantly, unique personality. This game is really, REALLY cozy. Thanks to the atmosphere, lightning and the pixel art style. The little guys are also something likeable, they walk silly and feel like they have a personality.

As I mentioned, the progression in this game is easy and not time wasting. It tells you the goal and you just plant and wait for it to grow and let your little guys pick stuff up for you.

[h3] Summary [/h3]
Tiny Terraces is one of the best idle games on steam at the moment. It delivers you easy progression without wasting your time and beautiful art style with atmosphere.

Okay, now for my issues with the game. I still very much enjoyed it, but developer has work to do for some big frustrations I had.


The little guys system sucks. Little guys do your tasks. You make more by investing a resource, but it costs exponentially more every time (starting with small increments). Each type of guy shared the same exponential pool.

So if you want to upgrade to a different type of guy, you have to remove your previous ones and lose all of their levels if you don't want to suffer EXTREME costs. The game seems to really want to cap you out in the 100ish area, so if you reach later "guys", you'll have to destroy all of your guys to switch to them. That... feels bad. I wanted to make some kale and cabbage guys, but it was super expensive, so I destroyed almost my entire assemblage of birch and oak... only to discover that birch and oak are better??? My kale and cabbage guys move incredibly slowly, even at level 30! Why are they WORSE than the birch and oak I kept? I used an exploit to get 190 little guys, and they STILL aren't enough for me to use 1/3 of the total area of the game and keep up with production in lategame, with slow to grow crops. I'm restricting my area so much because kale and cabbage guys just... can't carry anything fast enough, while the 20 birch and oak I kept fly around. The kale and cabbage ones have BETTER numbers!

Just let us spend a resource to change the type of existing guys, or better yet make each little guy type exist on it's own exponential curve to remove decision regret and encourage diversification of little guys, so people don't end up with a crappy monotype like me.

Can the guys recognize that they are standing BESIDE a storage bank and drop their stuff off a little more often? I see my guys carry 10 items across the world to grab an 11th too often. Make task assignment prioritize proximity more, I kept seeing guys get assigned to buildings across the map when there were things to do right beside them still.

The autoleveling is bad. It's inconsistent between types, and you have to set it manually per guy which... is so laborious and I have no idea what will be worth it for a guy until they are already level 30 and it will cost millions and hours to redo my guys.

Same with the priorities, I can't keep up with production so I end up totally neglecting the bottom two on the list, maybe some randomness could be added so SOME buildings get handled and SOME weeds get pulled.

Eggs lock up a guy unless you grab the egg? That requires active play, not really idley. Plus, you have to FIND them and that can be tough, especially if they are in your tree farm.

Fishing... why? I played two fishing minigames total, I think I only ever saw trash, and I bought autofishing before I even really understood how it worked. I barely engaged with it at all, which is a shame. Could have been more interesting. But really, there's no reason to use it. I haven't seen a single use for fishing resources.

Which, why not? Why are the progress goals only crops, juices, jams, and jellies? You have more stuff in the game. Engage with it! I have been collecting honey, sap, fish, vinegar, eggs, flour, etc. in massive quantities, and if I've used any of it I haven't noticed at all. I picked up Tiny Terraces during the Steam Summer Sale for around €3.34, and honestly, I’ve been more than happy with my purchase.

I originally went into this expecting something I could have running in the background as a little idle game while doing other things. And for the most part, it absolutely works for that. The funny part is that, every now and then, it somehow stopped being an idle game and turned into “okay, I’m just going to spend another two hours making this one little corner of my terrace look nice.” Hahaha.

There’s something really charming about the whole game. The little guys, the art style, the atmosphere, and watching your terrace slowly turn into something that actually feels like your space all work really well together. My biggest recommendation would honestly be: Take it slow. Enjoy the characters, enjoy the art, and make something pretty.

Which brings me to the one thing I think the game accidentally made me do wrong.

I saw all the goalposts for unlocking new items, and immediately my brain went into completionist mode. I wanted to unlock EVERYTHING before I properly committed to designing my terrace. That ended up making the game feel a little more rushed than I think it needed to be. The achievement grind is probably my biggest complaint. There’s an achievement for harvesting 1 million plants, and, well... That's a lot of plants! Especially if, like me, you’ve spent most of the late game focusing on making a beautiful terrace rather than building the most efficient plant-harvesting machine known to mankind.

You can apparently get much more efficient by fencing in the little fellas and setting things up specifically for faster harvesting, but I didn't really want to do that. I wanted my terrace to look nice. So eventually I found myself staring at that 1,000,000 plant number thinking, “Oh. This is going to take a while...”

There are also a few things I’d love to see changed or added.

For one, I think it would be nice if either cosmetics or seeds were unlocked through currency, rather than both being tied to objectives. Having one progression system based around objectives and another based around currency could make the pacing feel a lot better. As it stands, I found myself constantly thinking about what I needed to unlock next instead of just designing my terrace.

I also wish there was a way to see everything that could eventually be unlocked. Not knowing what equipment and cosmetics were coming later made it difficult to commit to a particular layout, because I was always wondering whether I was about to unlock something that would completely change how I wanted the terrace to look.

And then there are some quality-of-life improvements that I would love to see.

Being able to place multiple tiles, decorations, or structures at once would be fantastic. Even better would be some kind of copy/paste system for layouts, or the ability to pick up and move an existing section of your terrace as a whole. Because let me tell you: discovering that your grid is slightly off after you've already built half your dream terrace is a special kind of pain. Having to completely destroy and rebuild everything just to move something over by one tile hurt a little more than it probably should have.

These are all fairly minor complaints, though, especially considering what I paid for the game.

TL;DR: Great little game that I’d absolutely recommend. Take things slow, enjoy the little guys and the art style, and don't let the unlocks trick you into rushing through the game. There are some areas where the progression and building system could use a bit of polish, but for €3.34, I’ve gotten more than my money’s worth.

And honestly, there’s something strangely satisfying about leaving Tiny Terraces running in the background, coming back later, and realizing your little terrace has quietly become a place you actually care about. 8/10

Honestly I'm torn on whether to recommend or not recommend this game. 

It certainly has promise, and it's not asking a ridiculous up-front cost. It has a very nice art-style and a very addictive gameplay loop.

However, this game has been in development for just over 2 years, with it being in a demo state from early August 2024, releasing into Early Access in July 2025, with the Dev saying on this very store page "It will be in EA for roughly a few months", and here I am writing a review for it another year later in August 2026, with it still being in EA.

I do get it's a solo-dev or very small dev team, but don't say it'll be a few months if it's going to take several years, or you just don't know.

It does kind of makes sense that it's still in EA though, because although there have been updates to it over the last year, there are still a lot of core issues that need to be worked on, especially that the early-game is very micro-management heavy, and the UI when the game is stuck to the bottom of your Desktop, is clunky at best. 

That's not even talking about bugs, such as clicking on a "building" with an AoE, and the white AoE circle just sticks on the screen no matter what you do, needing a reload. Upon unlocking the fishing mini-game, which I still have no idea on how it works, the "guys" will all randomly run down to the river and stand there doing nothing, then run back to do actual farming. 

Then there's the lack of any kind of meaningful tutorial. Now no, this game isn't exactly hard to pick up, but it'd be nice to have something there at least.

My big complaint though goes back to how slow and tedious the early-game is, and arguably how weird the progression track is. The "orders" you need to fill out to progress and unlock new things, which you're not told about and have to know/find for yourself in the UI, will still randomly want extremely early-game crops, even if you're several hours in. It's also a bit strange how you'll unlock, say, Radishes, but they aren't even wanted until several orders later. It just comes across as very strangely paced. That isn't even bringing up how some of the prices and balancing on certain items also just don't really seem to make a lot of sense, with a good example being:
- Lettuce costs 3, takes 45s to grow, sells for 6
- Garlic costs 10, takes 3m to grow (x2), sells for 16 (x2)
So, in the time it would take for a Garlic to be "used up" (6 min), which would net you 22 profit (32-10), you could grow 8 Lettuce, costing 24, but netting 24 profit (48-24). 
Now yes, Garlic would take up less slots, but it also "locks" a slot down for 6 mins, only to get less profit than just spamming out Lettuce, which is the second plant you unlock.

It's kind of a jarring juxtaposition that there's a progression track, but the early-game stuff is worth the same, or sometimes more than the later unlocks, which ends up making it not really feel like progression at all. Are you meant to just grow everything, or is it so you can grow what you want and still make similar money? I don't really get it.

As it is right now, I think I'm settling on not recommended. For a supposedly chill game that you leave at the bottom of your desktop while doing other things, it requires a lot of actual input and focus to get to a point where it is the game you can just let play itself.

Definitely nails the Backrooms aesthetic.  BUT...  Roughly 2 hours was spent on the hotel level alone, and I ultimately had watch a YT video to figure out how to get to the bottom and back up.  The Playrooms level is a similar exercise in cartography, requiring either an incredible memory or a map to figure out.  The contextual clues are almost non-existent, if there are any at all, and the same-ness of every turn and twist ensures you will get lost repeatedly.  Combine that with expansive dead ends and you may find the experience tedious at best, boring at worst.

Yes, part of the Backrooms dread is that constant feeling of being lost - I get that.  But when compared to another BR game WITHOUT entities, POOLS immediately comes to mind.  Every turn in POOLS results in progress or a return to a familiar, noteworthy area.  As a result, it's easy to remember which paths you have or haven't taken and keep the progress going.  Dreamcore, on the other hand, goes out of its way to create navigational pain, offering no hints, no clear path, no level design pattern, and few memorable areas.

Imagine an empty room with 4 doors.  You pick a door and go through it, entering an empty room with 4 more doors.  Repeat this over and over again for hours and that's the Hotel level.  You might just keep going in one direction, or try to find the edge of the map and work your way around, but add in a few dead ends, hallways, and no directional reference points and you're lost.  The elevators only go 2-3 floors at time, forcing you to navigate across the floors  - that doesn't sound too bad, right?  It was when I took an elevator down to what was obviously a dead end that I realized the hotel was filled with multi-floor dead ends.  You might need to go down 2 floors, then up 1, then down 3, then up 2, then up 1, then down 2, and on an on.  Did I mention some of the rooms are multi-floor, breaking the topography of the floor above?  Did I mention that a critical doorway is at the end of dark hallway and is almost impossible to see?  Miss it and you won't finish the level.  Can you tell this game can be extremely frustrating?  I noted the first time I took an elevator to a different floor that I received an achievement only 13% of players had completed, telling me that most people simply don't have the time, patience, or graph paper to map out these gigantic level-mazes.  Try searching the internet for a map of the Playrooms level - the sheer complexity of those maps (yes, plural) will immediately clue you in to the time-killing nightmare in front of you.

The game has good atmosphere, is polished, and was clearly designed to inspire a sense of aimless wandering with little hope of finding an exit.  Great job, developers!  Because of that, I DO recommend the game as a solid entry in the BR gaming universe.  But the game is real work to complete (without a guide or a map), and isn't "fun" in the traditional sense.  And the cold, impersonal, sanitary nature of the Backrooms results in completions that feel anticlimactic.  The "journey" feels a lot more like random luck and less like skill.  If you want an experience that's more casual and entertaining, you may want to look elsewhere.

The graphics are pretty good; it's the standard 'vintage' first person camera footage POV. Not a lot to interact with, so exploration/finding the exit is the main goal. The various themed liminal spaces don't feel completely empty or overly repetitive. It's an actual challenge to complete the levels and some of them drive you mad- you feel like you're looping about endlessly with little to no sense of direction but that's the whole point! You really do have to keep an eye on your surroundings and keep track of exactly where you're going in order to find the hidden spots/exits.

You are lost in these vast empty places and it can sometimes can feel claustrophobic and hopeless, contributing to the psychological aspect of playing a liminal ''horror'' game. However, there are no monsters, so the ''creepiness'' you feel is a result of your own imagination which can make you feel like your seeing and hearing things that aren't 'quite' there. Lots of hidden secrets, minor jump-scares and genuine liminal space exploration!

My only critique would be that I wish there were more unique sounds and audio tracks. Like a bit more musical ambiance or special audio ques rather than empty silence and static buzzing. For those that actually want mostly silence, maybe you could put an option for it in the settings.

That aside- over all, it's a pretty well rounded game and I look forward to any updates and future games from the devs! :D
