Will To Live Online is a free-to-play online survival MMORPG developed and published by AlphaSoft LLC that blends first-person shooting, role-playing progression, exploration, and survival mechanics into a harsh post-apocalyptic setting. Instead of focusing solely on action, the game places players in a devastated world where every journey outside secure settlements becomes a struggle against hostile mutants, environmental hazards, and other survivors. The game's premise revolves around staying alive while uncovering the secrets of a ruined civilization, encouraging players to explore dangerous territories, complete missions, improve their characters, and gradually establish themselves in an unforgiving online world. Its emphasis on freedom allows each player to choose whether to concentrate on combat, exploration, crafting, or social interaction, creating a flexible experience that accommodates multiple playstyles.

The world itself is one of the game's strongest features. Large open environments filled with abandoned villages, industrial facilities, contaminated forests, underground laboratories, and hazardous anomaly zones provide a constant incentive to venture beyond safe areas. Exploration feels rewarding because valuable resources, hidden equipment, quest objectives, and dangerous enemies are scattered throughout the map. Rather than presenting a series of disconnected levels, the game creates a believable wasteland where every location contributes to the atmosphere of isolation and survival. The environmental storytelling also helps establish the setting without relying heavily on lengthy narrative sequences, allowing players to piece together the world's history through observation and exploration.

Combat successfully combines traditional shooter mechanics with survival-oriented decision-making. Firefights require more than quick reflexes, as players must carefully manage ammunition, healing supplies, weapon condition, and protective equipment. Mutants come in various forms that require different tactics, while encounters with other players introduce an additional level of unpredictability. The possibility of losing valuable equipment during dangerous expeditions creates meaningful tension that keeps every encounter exciting. Whether hunting hostile creatures, defending against ambushes, or participating in competitive PvP battles, combat remains one of the primary driving forces behind the overall gameplay loop.

Character progression offers long-term motivation through experience gains, equipment upgrades, improved weapons, and access to increasingly difficult regions. Quests provide structure while allowing players to steadily strengthen their survivors over time. Crafting also plays a major role, enabling players to transform gathered materials into ammunition, medical supplies, consumables, and better gear. Resource collection, trading, and inventory management encourage careful planning instead of reckless action, making survival feel genuinely earned rather than automatically granted. These interconnected systems create a satisfying cycle of exploration, scavenging, upgrading, and returning to increasingly dangerous locations.

The multiplayer component gives Will To Live Online much of its lasting appeal. Cooperative play allows friends and strangers alike to tackle difficult missions, hunt powerful enemies, and explore hazardous zones together, while competitive elements such as faction conflicts and PvP encounters provide additional excitement for players seeking greater challenges. Clan participation introduces another layer of progression through coordinated activities and large-scale engagements that reward teamwork and strategic planning. Because the game world is persistent, player interactions help shape the overall experience, making social cooperation and rivalry equally important aspects of survival.

Visually, the game favors atmosphere over cutting-edge graphics. Weather effects, lighting, environmental details, and ambient sound combine to create an oppressive mood that constantly reminds players of the dangers surrounding them. The soundtrack remains understated, allowing environmental audio, distant gunfire, mutant cries, and unsettling silence to strengthen immersion. Although some character models and animations reveal the game's modest production budget, the overall presentation succeeds in delivering the bleak tone expected from a post-apocalyptic survival title.

Like many ambitious online games that have continued evolving over time, Will To Live Online is not without shortcomings. New players may find the learning curve demanding due to its numerous interconnected mechanics, while occasional technical issues, interface limitations, balancing concerns, and performance inconsistencies can interrupt the experience. Nevertheless, the developers have built a game with considerable depth that rewards persistence, exploration, and long-term investment. Players willing to learn its systems will discover an engaging blend of MMORPG progression and survival gameplay that distinguishes itself from many traditional online shooters.

Overall, Will To Live Online delivers a compelling survival experience that successfully merges exploration, crafting, character development, cooperative gameplay, and competitive combat within a persistent online world. Its oppressive atmosphere, rewarding progression systems, and emphasis on meaningful survival create an experience that feels both challenging and immersive. While technical imperfections and a steep learning curve may discourage some newcomers, those who appreciate open-world survival games with strong multiplayer elements will find plenty of content to enjoy over many hours.

[b]An Absolute Masterpiece of Raw, Unforgiving Post-Apocalyptic Logistics and Survival Engineering[/b]
If you are exhausted by modern, hand-holding survival shooters that cater strictly to casual playstyles, Will To Live Online is the definitive, intellectually stimulating tactical oasis you have been searching for. It is an incredibly robust fusion of old-school MMORPG mechanics, hardcore survival systems, and precise first-person ballistic modeling. For players who appreciate rigid structural loops, complex resource allocation, and absolute operational discipline, this game delivers a deeply satisfying, scientifically gritty atmosphere that rewards calculated strategy over mindless rushing.

[b]Sophisticated Progression Matrices and Hardcore Economic Anchors[/b]
The mechanical depth under the hood of this post-apocalyptic simulation is an absolute triumph for optimization purists.
[list]
[*]The distinct class architecture introduces an incredibly well-balanced, multi-tiered combat and utility framework where every role—from the frontline Soldier to the high-tech Engineer—possesses unique metabolic and tactical parameters.

[*]The weapon customization and ballistic feedback loops require surgical precision. You aren't just spraying bullets; you are forced to account for realistic bullet drop, armor penetration indices, and tight recoil patterns that demand true muscle memory and spatial awareness.

[*]The economy and crafting pipelines are beautifully engineered. Every piece of scrap, chemical compound, and mineral you extract from the hazardous anomalies serves a strict logistical purpose, forcing you to constantly audit your inventory and optimize your processing workflows to maintain peak operational efficiency.
[/list]
[b]An Authentically Bleak, Dynamic Anomalous Ecosystem[/b]
From an atmospheric standpoint, the game is a masterclass in establishing a cold, unyielding, and fiercely individualistic world.
[list]
[*]The environmental design captures a brilliant, hauntingly realistic post-Soviet wasteland, juxtaposing decaying industrial infrastructure with unpredictable, highly volatile physical anomalies.

[*]The PvE and PvP faction dynamics create a beautifully tense social ecosystem. Stepping out of safe zones requires absolute situational vigilance, as the open-world looting mechanics introduce genuine, high-stakes consequences for operational failure.

[*]The mutant and anomaly AI routines are brilliantly unforgiving, converting simple hunting expeditions into high-pressure tactical gauntlets where one wrong step into a radiation pocket or a gravitational anomaly means instant death.
[/list]
[b]The Verdict[/b]
Will To Live Online is a rare, uncompromising gem in the modern multiplayer landscape. It masterfully bridges the gap between gritty atmospheric storytelling and complex, data-driven survival mechanics. It doesn't insult your intelligence with easy victories; instead, it demands that you study its rules, respect its harsh biological and chemical hazards, and engineer your way to the top of the food chain. For any hardcore simulation and sci-fi enthusiast seeking elite mechanical depth, brutal combat tension, and a living, breathing world of raw post-apocalyptic survival, this game is a breathtaking, 10/10 essential masterwork.

You'd think this is one of those "the developers killed the game by doing X" type of scenarios, but it isn't. Yes they made a number of questionable changes that certainly did impact player sentiment, (hello RPGs and Testing Grounds), but it's really a matter of developer competence. For one, the game doesn't really know what it is trying to be. It advertises itself to be a survival STALKER type game with harsh PvE, artifacts and factions, but the PvE is just a brief EXP treadmill serving to gatekeep new gear, the artifacts are entirely irrelevant and your faction choice comes down to whether you want to always win or always lose in every PvP engagement. And don't think that you can avoid joining a faction. You can, but you're cutting yourself off from the entirety of the mid-to-late level content. 

Not only is there uncertainty to the direction of the game, but the developers themselves seem incapable of actually making anything themselves. The bulk of the game assets come from epic store asset packs [url=https://www.fab.com/listings/13143978-3009-4fb1-893c-689e28b2e122]1.[/url] [url=https://www.fab.com/listings/4126bd7b-53a2-4adc-8d67-8b5ef82352b7]2.[/url] [url=https://www.fab.com/listings/248c759c-95c3-4614-99cf-6d79dd7c9814]3.[/url], [url=https://www.fab.com/listings/515af6b5-6ec9-4efb-8d79-76b8d98b564b]4.[/url] including an entire prefab portion of one of the main player hubs. This is true not only for old content but new as well. Overall game polish is in the absolute dumpster, with large swathes of the world map being entirely devoid of anything (literally just bushes and trees), and other parts just having no reason to ever go to beyond a single quest. Localization as a whole is abysmal. Cats are Liquid – A Better Place is a deceptively simple-looking platformer that reveals depth, emotion, and mechanical creativity as you progress. At first glance it presents itself as a minimalist 2D adventure where you guide Lumi, a liquid-like cat, through abstract environments built from clean shapes and soft colors. But beneath this unassuming surface lies a carefully constructed world that evolves across dozens of levels, gradually reshaping both how you move and how you interpret the story. The game wastes no time establishing its tone: it feels gentle, quiet, and strangely comforting, yet with an undercurrent of melancholy that becomes more pronounced the deeper you venture into its surreal landscapes.

Movement is the heart of the experience, and A Better Place builds on the foundation established by its predecessor with a much stronger sense of flow and responsiveness. Lumi can shift between states—solid, liquid, and in later stages even more unusual forms—which transforms the platforming into a playful mix of sliding, squeezing, bouncing, and maneuvering through tight spaces. New abilities are introduced at a steady pace, each one expanding how you interact with the world. Tail hooks let you swing across gaps, bursts of light break through barriers, and character swapping adds puzzle-like layers to traversal. The game’s 120 rooms are designed around these evolving mechanics, often challenging you to think creatively about momentum, angles, and spatial awareness. While the platforming is accessible enough for casual players, mastering its subtleties delivers a deeply satisfying rhythm.

The visual style supports this sense of dream-like motion. Environments are composed of soft gradients, warm lighting, and clean geometric layouts that give each room a calm, almost meditative atmosphere. These soothing visuals contrast with the emotional weight hidden within the narrative. Although much of the story is told through implication rather than dialogue, the themes become clear as Lumi’s journey continues. The world feels constructed—artificial in a way that suggests someone built it for her, both as a refuge and a cage. The presence of friends, memories, and subtle environmental shifts hint at struggles with loss, separation, and the desire to hold onto moments that inevitably slip away. The game never becomes heavy-handed, instead trusting the player to connect dots and interpret the metaphors at their own pace.

One of the most impressive features is the built-in level editor and Steam Workshop support. Once you complete the main campaign, you can create your own worlds or explore others made by the community. This extends the game's lifespan significantly and gives players a creative outlet that mirrors the game's own themes of construction and discovery. The editor is intuitive, allowing both simple puzzle layouts and elaborate multi-room creations. It’s a natural fit for a game that already feels like a digital terrarium—modular, expressive, and endlessly reconfigurable.

Despite its strengths, the game isn’t without gentle limitations. The physics can sometimes feel slightly floaty, which may not appeal to players expecting tight precision platforming. The pacing of the story is intentionally subtle, which some may interpret as vague or underdeveloped, and certain emotional beats may not land equally for all players. The minimalist presentation means environments can occasionally feel similar if you move quickly through them. Yet even these aspects feel more like stylistic choices than shortcomings, forming part of the quiet, introspective identity the game aims to cultivate.

Cats are Liquid – A Better Place ultimately succeeds by offering an experience that blends mechanical creativity with emotional resonance. It isn’t a loud or demanding game; it invites you to glide, experiment, and reflect as Lumi grows through the challenges placed before her. For players who appreciate atmospheric platformers, gentle storytelling, and fluid movement systems, it delivers a memorable and heartfelt journey. It may look small on the surface, but it leaves an impression that lingers long after the last level fades away.

Coloring Game 4 is a relaxing casual game focused entirely on colouring pictures and creating simple artwork. Like the previous games in the series, it is not designed around complex gameplay or challenges, but instead offers a calm experience where players can fill in images, experiment with colours, and enjoy a stress-free activity.

The biggest strength of Coloring Game 4 is how easy it is to use. The controls are simple, and there is no pressure to complete tasks quickly or achieve high scores. It is the type of game you can open for a few minutes when you want something relaxing without needing to think too much.

The colouring system works well for what it is trying to do. Choosing colours and filling sections of pictures gives a small sense of satisfaction, especially when finishing a detailed image. It can be enjoyable for players who like creative activities or relaxing games.

The game also benefits from being accessible. You do not need gaming experience to understand it, and it can appeal to people who simply enjoy digital colouring books. The simple design makes it easy for anyone to start creating something.

However, the biggest issue is that there is not much depth. Once you understand the basic idea, the experience stays mostly the same. There are no major challenges, progression systems, or gameplay mechanics that add variety over time.

The presentation is also fairly basic. While the artwork provides the main appeal, the game does not offer many advanced creative tools or features. Compared to dedicated art programs or more detailed colouring games, it can feel limited.

Replay value depends entirely on how much you enjoy colouring. Players who find the activity relaxing may return often to complete more pictures, while others may finish the available content and have little reason to come back.

Overall, Coloring Game 4 is a simple and relaxing colouring experience that does exactly what it promises. It is not trying to be a traditional game, and for the right audience that simplicity is part of the appeal. However, the lack of features and limited creativity options keep it from being more than a basic casual title.

For those unfamiliar with what actually makes something a game, a "game loop" describes the interaction and feedback a gamer has when playing a game.

Tetris, for example, has a game loop where a random block appears, the gamer interacts with the block to position it, and then the game decides if that finishes a row or not, increases the players score if any rows were completed, then gives the gamer another block to position.  Counter-Strike has a game loop where a player seeks another player, tests their skill against that player by shooting them or being shot, the computer rewards the player if they win, and then if the player survives, they repeat that loop.

There's no loop here, no true interactive feedback.  It simply is not a game, it cannot be "played".

A short and sweet review for a short and sweet game: Fatum Betula feels wide and daunting at first but quickly coalesces into a manageable indie experience that doesn't overstay its welcome. I had actually visited the spot and had simply not gotten the right RNG [/spoiler]. So that being said, the game is fully within the scope of a single user poking at the seams, and feels adequately rewarding to do so. Try it for yourself. 

That being said, [spoiler] I actually had collected the liquid bone, the oil, the recursive fish and the fruit (knowing what to do with it) before ever even pouring a sample into the birch water, and had originally assumed the game was much wider and deeper than it is, but after getting my first ending I realized it was a bit of a simpler experience than I assumed. Truly one of the more unique experiences I've had playing a video game. 

Fatum Betula has a very unique visual style with it's retro ps1 era graphics that compliments it's atmospheric style extremely well. It feels like you're playing one of those ARG video games that don't exist and the feeling it gives me scratches an itch that I don't think any other game has scratched yet for me. 

The game deals with extistentialism, death, abuse and nihilism and with each dialogue and ending gives you so much to think about, it's such an aesthetically pleasing think-piece of a video game. Aesthitically everything blends in so well, from the weird textures, the dialogue, hell even the font that's used feels so perfect for it.

The gameplay is more or less a walking simulator where you interact with npcs, find objects and solve puzzles, which are quite obtuse to get different endings. The puzzles really had me confused and walking around aimlessly but figuring it out myself in the end felt quite rewarding. Even the obtuse and nonsensical requirements for the endings played pretty well into how the game is meant to feel. The soundtrack is also quite wonderful. 

Every single aspect of this game fits into each other like pieces to make a unique and sensory stimulating game.

If you're into things like LSD: Dream Emulator or even just find the visual aesthetic of the game pleasing, I assure you a couple of hours on Fatum Betula will make you love this game

[h2]Fatum Betula, a game you've played before[/h2]

A lot of games try to do retro, not just for the sake of being retro, but to adhere to a certain aesthetic. This is where Fatum Betula shines. It doesn't just look like an old game. It feels like one you've played before.

It feels like a game you played as a kid but never quite got around to finishing or fully exploring. Something you vaguely remember but never got to fully understand. It fills you with nostalgia and melancholy without you ever having touched it before.

The visual style plays a huge part in this. There's something about the primitive 3D environments that reminds me especially of games like The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Not necessarily because Fatum Betula is similar to it as a game, but because it captures that same feeling of exploring a strange world from that era.

But that melancholy doesn't just come from the retro style. Fatum Betula presents a dying world that slowly tells its own story as both it and its inhabitants fade into nothingness. Exploring it feels like walking through the remains of something that is slowly disappearing around you, with its inhabitants being just as much a part of that dying world as the environments themselves.

fatum betula is a game tense with potential energy. existing forever (or only for a moment?) without the player (would it exist without them?), in a limbo, in apathy, waiting however long or brief for some semblance of change. the world is immutable, immortal, quiet. a held breath that has not exhaled, can not exhale, will not exhale without a gasp and the player punching it in the gut.

in fatum betula, change is violent, but the act of change is temporary and fleeting, and the world settles back into a new steady-state. a ball rolls down a hill and rests at the bottom. a dam bursts, water rushes, carves a path. the new riverbed is deep.

the way that bryce bucher tackles storytelling in fatum betula reminds me a lot of marco polo in [i]invisible cities[/i]. to describe a city, polo uses a few scattered objects (a pebble for a grave, a page for a library, a can for a neighborhood) and in their placement, position—their gesture, really—a different city is described. perhaps this city existed forever. perhaps just for a moment. these cities often long. perhaps for immortality, or for industry, or for something else entirely. the player points: break this, grind that. the story slants, is changed. often for the worse.

fatum betula's atmosphere is thick. beginning the game, the world feels immense. anything could be hidden in the fog. but as you become accustomed to the world, its size compresses. the game changes from mood piece to mechanical. unearthing all the endings, you essentially follow a flow chart, program logic. the game begins by feeling like exchanging ghost stories at a campfire; later, it feels like a conversation with bucher, potential ideas and ways for the story to unfold. what can flex? how can we recontextualize these chessmen, this board? the final secrets feel like bucher inviting you to his heavy writing desk, showing you his pens, his notepads, his thoughts.

fatum betula is a mood piece with a lot of surface area. bucher knows this too. this game is his invitation to sit, see his world, poke it, prod it, to see what happens.

Fantasy Idle Dungeon, developed by Leaves Games and published by Leaves Games alongside Gamersky Games, is a relaxed yet systems-heavy idle RPG that leans strongly into the pleasures of long-term growth, creature collection, and passive progression. It presents itself as a game designed for players who enjoy watching numbers climb, teams evolve, and systems slowly unfold over time, rather than demanding constant manual input or mechanical precision. From its first moments, it establishes a rhythm that prioritizes steady accumulation and incremental improvement, making it well suited to casual play sessions or background progression.

The central focus of Fantasy Idle Dungeon is the collection and development of creatures known as Jenin. These creatures form the backbone of your combat teams, each coming with their own stats, skills, and growth paths. Acquiring new Jenin through hatching and summoning is an ongoing process, and much of the early game revolves around experimenting with different lineups to see how they perform in automated dungeon runs. While individual Jenin initially feel simple, the depth emerges through evolution, fusion, and talent unlocking, which gradually transform basic creatures into specialized and powerful units.

Combat operates almost entirely on an auto-battle basis, embracing the core philosophy of idle game design. Once a team is assembled, battles play out without direct intervention, allowing players to focus their attention on preparation rather than execution. Victory depends less on reflexes and more on thoughtful team composition, stat optimization, and gear synergy. As dungeons scale in difficulty, progress becomes less about raw levels and more about whether your Jenin are properly evolved and equipped to handle increasingly demanding encounters.

Equipment and gear systems provide one of the game’s more engaging layers of complexity. Weapons, armor, and accessories can be crafted, enhanced, refined, and socketed with gems, offering numerous ways to tailor each Jenin to a specific role. This creates a satisfying feedback loop where dungeon runs feed materials into crafting, crafting strengthens your team, and a stronger team pushes further into new content. While the gear progression is largely incremental, the cumulative impact of upgrades becomes very noticeable over time, reinforcing the idle genre’s emphasis on long-term investment.

Progression in Fantasy Idle Dungeon is deliberately paced. Early advancement comes quickly, introducing systems and features at a steady clip, but later stages slow considerably as resource requirements increase. This shift is intentional, encouraging players to rely on idle gains rather than rapid active grinding. For some, this slower pace is part of the appeal, allowing progress to happen organically in the background. For others, it can feel repetitive, especially when optimal progression involves revisiting earlier dungeons to accumulate currency or materials more efficiently.

The game’s presentation supports its casual nature. Pixel art visuals are colorful and readable, emphasizing clarity over spectacle. Dungeon environments vary enough to convey a sense of progression, even if they are not deeply interactive or narrative-driven. Animations are functional rather than flashy, keeping the focus on systems and progression rather than visual flair. Sound design and music are understated, providing atmosphere without demanding attention, which aligns well with the game’s idle-focused identity.

Narrative elements exist largely as flavor rather than a driving force. Fantasy Idle Dungeon offers a fantasy setting with a loose sense of exploration and discovery, but story beats are minimal and secondary to mechanical advancement. This design choice keeps the experience streamlined, though it may leave players who crave lore or character-driven storytelling wanting more. Instead, the sense of purpose comes from strengthening your roster and overcoming increasingly difficult dungeon thresholds.

Community reception reflects this balance of strengths and limitations. Many players appreciate the accessibility, low-pressure design, and satisfaction of watching steady progress unfold with minimal effort. At the same time, recurring feedback points to repetition and resource bottlenecks in later stages, where progress can feel more like waiting than strategizing. The game’s reliance on auto-battles also means that moments of direct engagement are limited, which may reduce long-term appeal for players who prefer more active control.

Ultimately, Fantasy Idle Dungeon succeeds most when approached with the right expectations. It is not an action-heavy dungeon crawler or a deeply narrative RPG, but a systems-driven idle experience built around collection, optimization, and patience. For players who enjoy idle RPGs, creature progression, and the slow satisfaction of incremental growth, it offers a comfortable and engaging loop. While it may not reinvent the genre or provide endless variety, it delivers a consistent and approachable idle experience that rewards persistence and long-term planning.

Cleaning Simulator is a deliberately grounded simulation that attempts to turn everyday household chores into a playable, low-stakes experience. Developed by Damaged Games and published by RockGame SA, the game positions itself within the growing niche of job and “cozy” simulators, where satisfaction comes not from challenge or narrative twists, but from steady progress and visible transformation. Rather than exaggerating its premise for humor or spectacle, Cleaning Simulator plays its concept straight, inviting players to methodically restore messy environments to order through hands-on interaction with a variety of cleaning tools.

The core gameplay loop revolves around entering cluttered interiors and systematically eliminating dirt, grime, trash, and disorder. Each level presents a different location with its own mess profile, requiring players to mop floors, scrub surfaces, vacuum carpets, wash dishes, dispose of garbage, and manage pests such as flies. Every action is tied to a specific tool, and progress is immediately visible as surfaces brighten and rooms slowly regain a sense of cleanliness. This visual feedback is the game’s primary reward system, and when it works well, it taps into the same satisfaction found in other transformation-based simulators.

Early stages do a solid job of establishing this rhythm. The tasks feel clear, the spaces manageable, and the transformation from filthy to clean is noticeable and rewarding. There’s a meditative quality to the process, particularly when cleaning large surfaces or watching grime gradually disappear under a mop or pressure washer. For players who enjoy repetitive, tactile gameplay loops, these opening levels successfully sell the fantasy of being a professional cleaner tackling neglected spaces.

As the game progresses, however, the experience begins to reveal its limitations. Later levels introduce more back-and-forth movement and object placement tasks, shifting the focus away from cleaning itself and toward inventory-style interactions. This change can dilute the original appeal, as progress becomes less about careful cleaning and more about repeatedly carrying items from one location to another. While these mechanics add variety on paper, in practice they can feel like busywork, slowing the pace and interrupting the satisfying flow established earlier.

Progression is supported by a light upgrade system that allows players to improve their tools. Upgrades generally increase efficiency, reduce tool wear, or slightly expand cleaning coverage. These improvements help streamline later tasks and reduce friction, but they remain modest in impact. There’s no deep customization or strategic decision-making involved, which keeps the game accessible but also limits long-term depth. The lack of meaningful progression beyond incremental efficiency gains may leave some players feeling that their growth as a cleaner isn’t particularly transformative.

Visually, Cleaning Simulator adopts a clean, functional aesthetic that prioritizes clarity over artistic flair. Environments are readable and react convincingly to cleaning actions, with lighting and surface reflections helping emphasize progress. Optional graphical features such as enhanced lighting effects add some visual polish, especially when rooms transition from dull and dirty to bright and orderly. While the presentation isn’t especially distinctive, it serves the gameplay well and reinforces the core appeal of visible improvement.

The game’s pacing is one of its most divisive aspects. For some players, the slow, methodical tempo is exactly the point, offering a calming experience that can be enjoyed without pressure or time limits. For others, the same pacing feels sluggish, particularly when combined with repetitive objectives and limited movement speed. The absence of shortcuts, automation, or more dynamic task variation makes longer sessions feel increasingly monotonous, especially once the novelty of cleaning wears off.

Narrative elements are minimal and largely inconsequential. While there are hints of environmental storytelling or collectible fragments scattered throughout levels, they don’t coalesce into a meaningful storyline or thematic arc. As a result, the game relies almost entirely on mechanical satisfaction rather than emotional or narrative engagement. Players looking for context, progression beyond scores, or a sense of purpose beyond “finish the job” may find the experience lacking in motivation.

Community reception reflects this mixed identity. Many players appreciate the straightforward concept and find genuine enjoyment in the act of cleaning and organizing virtual spaces. Others criticize the lack of depth, repetitive objectives, and uneven level design, noting that the game struggles to sustain interest over its full duration. These criticisms don’t stem from broken mechanics so much as from a sense that the concept wasn’t expanded far enough to support longer-term engagement.

In the end, Cleaning Simulator is a game that succeeds most when approached with the right expectations. It is not a deep simulation, nor is it a narrative-driven experience or a challenge-focused game. Instead, it offers a simple, tactile loop centered on visual transformation and routine. For players who enjoy cozy job simulators and find satisfaction in order, cleanliness, and repetition, it can provide a relaxing diversion. For those seeking complexity, creativity, or evolving systems, it may feel underdeveloped and overly constrained. As a niche title, it occupies a narrow but understandable space, delivering exactly what its name promises—no more, and no less.

With the word simulator in its name, you can already tell the game does not go the extra mile when it comes to storytelling. You play as Emily, and each job begins with a short call or message from a client. While there is some sense of progression since you start in a small house and slowly move on to larger locations, the game is ultimately just a collection of ten stages that must be completed in order.

Each location is filled with trash, stains on floors and walls, objects that need washing, and other similar tasks. Everything must be done, but you can either tackle tasks as you notice them or focus on one type of job at a time. You might start by collecting trash, which you pick up with a button or hold down to grab multiple items, then carry it to a trashcan.

The trashcan can be moved to reduce the need for constant back and forth trips, but it can still be frustrating due to the physics engine. Trash must be dropped directly into the can, and since each item has its own physics, it is easy to miss or have objects bounce back out. It is also very easy to bump into the trashcan and spill everything onto the floor again. To avoid this annoyance, you need to tie the bag once it is full enough and carry it to a dumpster or burn it.

The simplest cleaning task involves putting objects back where they belong. When you pick something up, a waypoint and a green outline show where it should be placed. Objects are meant to snap into place when moved close to the outline, but this often fails to work. To fix it, you usually need to drop the item near the outline and pick it up again, which then forces it to snap into position.

The task you will spend the most time on involves cleaning floors with a mop and walls with a sponge. This also requires a bucket that needs to be refilled frequently in the bathroom once the water gets dirty. This happens often because both the mop and sponge become dirty after only a few swipes. Since you cannot make new messes, you are free to run around with a dirty mop without consequences.

You can improve both tools by adding soap to the bucket, but you must buy a new bar of soap every time you refill it. Thankfully, the actual cleaning process is not tedious. You simply equip the correct tool and click on a stain. There is no need to hold the button, and cleaning continues automatically until the stain is gone or the tool becomes dirty.

Fortunately, you can buy better mops and sponges from a store that opens with a single button press. They are somewhat expensive, but they make the game much easier and make soap pointless. Improved tools take longer to get dirty, and their biggest advantage is that they clean a stain in a single swipe instead of several. You can also buy a better bucket, increase how much trash you can carry, and purchase a few other upgrades, though these are not essential.

Money is earned for every cleaned stain and every object placed correctly. You only earn a few dollars per task, but later stages set in more prestigious locations reward higher payouts. Money carries over between stages, and you can replay completed ones to easily earn enough for upgrades. You do not even need to finish a stage. You can jump in, complete a few quick tasks, quit to the main menu, and keep the money. This makes it easy to buy all upgrades before reaching the final stage.

One area where the game performs very well is its waypoint system. Whenever you pick up trash, a marker shows where the trashcan is, and when your tool gets dirty, a waypoint points you to the bucket. There is also a separate waypoint tied to a hint system. This is especially useful since stains and objects can be difficult to spot. 

By pressing the hint button, the location of a missing task is revealed instantly. Unfortunately, the hint does not automatically move to the next objective, so you must press the button every time. Another assistance feature works like a thermal vision mode that highlights all task related items by changing their colors. This effect is temporary and needs a few seconds to recharge.

In addition to basic cleaning, later stages introduce extra tasks to keep things varied. These include vacuuming rugs, unclogging sinks, making beds, and washing dishes and cookware. Washing dishes requires some precision because items do not snap into the dishwasher, so you just thrown them inside. The cleaning process takes around half a minute, after which you must return the dishes to their proper places.

The good news is that additional tools such as the vacuum cleaner and pressure washer never get dirty and do not require refilling. They work consistently at all times. Tools that are not needed for a specific mission also cannot be selected, which is a welcome quality of life feature. The stages themselves are decent and each one feels different. While the early levels focus on houses, later stages move on to larger settings such as hotel rooms or a warehouse where you stack boxes, which is about as dull as it sounds.

In conclusion, the game is short and easy to complete, contains no visible bugs, and earning three stars on each stage is never a challenge unless you leave the game idle or forget to pause. You may need to repeat a few stages for achievements related to dishwashers or story items, but overall the experience is very straightforward and forgiving.

Time to get our clean on and relax while scrubbing, mopping, vacuuming and organizing a wide variety of environments. 

[h3][u]Gameplay & Settings[/u][/h3]

A new cleaning sim that has us mopping, cleaning, scrubbing and arranging items back to their original spots. We can also pressure wash and collect trash. I know, I know…I make cleaning sound exciting!  

First off the game has 10 levels with each level unlocking as you progress. Once played however you can replay a level at any time. 

You really have to scrub and mop at the beginning. You are also constantly running to clean your mop and sponge until you get the upgrades. However most sims in this genre have that same mechanic so when you do upgrade it feels meaningful. There is only one upgrade per item and they more or less just make cleaning faster and it takes longer to dirty your mop and sponge. You never have to worry about filling your pressure washer or charging your vacuum (those are unlimited). However there is an upgrade for your pressure washer to have a wider area of coverage. 

The game also really has no narrative, once you complete the tutorial you just just go in and start cleaning. There are some conversation snippets here and there but nothing substantial. 

[u]Things to Note[/u]

🟡 There is a timer that will reward you stars upon completing a level in a set time. There is a corresponding achievement for finishing three levels with three stars. I managed to get the achievement without even trying so it is obtainable without too much frustration.

🟡 There are story elements to collect in each level but I have no idea what those are supposed to be. I did find story objects but if those were the elements they did not keep count so it could have been a glitch.

🟡 The items you have to place back into their proper spots will snap into place once picked up and where they go will be highlighted in green with a silhouette of their shape. 

🟡 Hints are free to use and there is no limit, just press H. Cleaner-vision is also available and free to use (you can extend its time though an upgrade). Just press Q. 

🟡 For the achievement “Dishwhisper” you’ll need to replay certain levels to achieve this one as not all levels have dishes to wash. I recommend level 1 as it is the easiest one and the dishes are right at the dishwasher. 

Settings & extras include; audio controls, brightness level, languages, invert axis and field of view options. There are also plenty of graphical tweaks such as ray tracing (on or off), display and resolution options, texture and lighting options, shadow and post processing options.
 
[h3][u]Overall Experience[/u][/h3]

Overall the game is okay, there were some elements I really enjoyed and others not so much. Each map is unique and well rendered and my system had no problem running the game. I also did not encounter any game breaking issues. The cleaning instruments all felt good to use but I do wish we could have run faster. 

In the later levels it also felt most of the effort went into the map looking good as opposed to the actual gameplay. I noticed a drop in gameplay once I hit level 7. Levels 7-9 were more fetch quests, having to put items in their place (one by one) or running to collect boxes to dump into the garbage bin (again one by one). The slow running made this tedious. The element of cleaning became a second thought as there was a lot less to actually clean (with the exception of level 10 being a bit better with more to do). 

So my stance on this one is neutral with some good and some not so good elements. It took me about 5.5 hours to complete all the levels and earn all the achievements. 🧽

Vangers is an extraordinarily unconventional blend of vehicular action, exploration, trading, role-playing mechanics, and open-ended adventure. Developed by K-D Lab and published by Association K-D Lab, it immediately separates itself from traditional driving or combat games through a bizarre science-fiction universe where almost everything, from the terminology to the landscapes, feels deliberately alien. Rather than providing a comfortable introduction, the game drops players into an unfamiliar civilization and expects them to gradually understand its rules through observation, experimentation, and persistence.

The player assumes the role of a Vanger, traveling through interconnected worlds using strange biomechanical vehicles known as mechos. These machines are much more than transportation. They determine mobility, cargo capacity, combat effectiveness, and how successfully different environments can be explored. Acquiring better vehicles and equipment becomes an important part of progression, especially as journeys grow more dangerous and valuable opportunities begin appearing farther from relatively safe settlements.

Driving forms the foundation of the experience, but Vangers is far removed from a conventional racing game. Players cross enormous, twisted landscapes while transporting goods, collecting unusual resources, searching for hidden locations, completing tasks, fighting enemies, and participating in strange competitions. Navigation itself can become a challenge because terrain significantly influences movement. Hills, depressions, water, pathways, and other environmental features require players to understand the capabilities of their current vehicle instead of simply driving directly toward a destination.

Combat adds considerable danger to these expeditions. Mechos can carry weapons and equipment, allowing encounters with hostile vehicles to develop into chaotic battles where movement and positioning are just as important as firepower. Players must consider whether a confrontation is worth the potential damage and resource expenditure. Escaping can sometimes be more sensible than fighting, particularly when transporting valuable cargo. This risk-versus-reward element gives routine journeys an unpredictable quality because a profitable expedition can quickly become a desperate struggle for survival.

Trading and inventory management provide another important dimension. Cargo space is limited, forcing players to decide which goods, weapons, resources, and equipment deserve valuable storage capacity. Buying and transporting commodities can generate useful profits, while exploration may uncover objects that are worth carrying back to civilization. These economic mechanics integrate naturally with the larger adventure instead of functioning as an isolated trading minigame. Better financial decisions eventually provide access to stronger equipment and vehicles, which in turn make dangerous areas easier to explore.

Perhaps the most memorable element is the setting itself. The game's universe is filled with strange concepts, creatures, objects, rituals, and vocabulary that initially seem almost incomprehensible. Instead of translating everything into familiar science-fiction conventions, Vangers expects players to absorb its terminology naturally. This approach creates a steep learning curve, but it also produces an unusually convincing sense of entering a genuinely foreign society. Gradually understanding what different words, locations, activities, and objects mean becomes a form of progression in its own right.

The environmental design remains equally distinctive. Although the technology behind the visuals naturally reflects the game's age, the artistic direction gives the worlds an almost biological appearance. Landscapes look warped, organic, colorful, and occasionally disturbing. Vehicles and structures follow the same surreal philosophy, resulting in a cohesive aesthetic that remains recognizable even when compared with far more technically sophisticated modern games. The unusual presentation ultimately works because it complements the equally unusual mechanics and fiction.

Accessibility is where Vangers presents its greatest challenge. Tutorials and explanations are limited compared with contemporary standards, while the interface and controls can require significant adjustment. Objectives are not always communicated with modern levels of clarity, and the strange vocabulary makes early conversations particularly confusing. Players expecting straightforward quest markers and constant guidance may become frustrated. Those willing to experiment, read carefully, make mistakes, and gradually learn the world's logic are far more likely to appreciate what the game is attempting.

There is considerable satisfaction in reaching the point where previously confusing systems begin to make sense. Knowledge becomes almost as valuable as equipment. Understanding routes, resources, trading opportunities, vehicle capabilities, dangers, and the purposes behind unusual activities dramatically changes how confidently the player approaches each expedition. This creates an effective progression curve without relying exclusively on traditional character statistics.

Steam Deck compatibility is best considered Playable rather than completely seamless. The game can run on Steam Deck, but its age and PC-oriented interface create some handheld inconveniences. Certain interactions may benefit from touchscreen input or customized controller layouts, text can occasionally be small on the Deck's display, and some configuration may be necessary for comfortable controls and resolution. Once properly configured, however, its exploration and relatively lightweight technical demands make portable play practical.

Vangers is ultimately a fascinating example of uncompromising game design. Its dated interface, difficult introduction, cryptic storytelling, and unusual controls prevent it from being universally accessible, yet removing those eccentricities would also diminish much of its identity. The combination of vehicular exploration, combat, trading, racing, resource management, and surreal world-building creates an experience that remains remarkably difficult to categorize. For patient players who enjoy discovering complicated systems without extensive guidance, it offers an imaginative adventure that still feels genuinely unusual.

Vangers is a product of an era where developers were eager to try new things instead of repeating the same formulas over and over. It's weird, and it's not for everyone, but it's one hell of an experience. And it's still more engaging that most modern games.

So there's these bug human inbred hybrids that for some reason have interwoven racing and religion. Both the aliens and the interface are dripping with 90's green-slime creepy claymation aesthetic. I'm pretty sure the programmer was an insect hybrid too because you need six to eight appendages to use the archaic control scheme this game has. You buy low from the cockroach looking guy and drive it over to the caterpillar looking guy to sell high, hopefully not getting into a high-speed weaponised car chase on the way. You collect larvae for this blue frog lady who keeps hitting on you. You enter holy races for money and luck. You have no idea what you are doing because these bug-boys talk to you in their own vocabulary the entire time and you thought you were in for a video game, not a lexicography degree. Eventually you find a protractor which lets you draw runes on the screen to unlock magic powers, and then a messiah device which makes the protractor look like a toy. The game is rendered with these lightly-connected voxels which means everything deforms when you drive on it, shoot it, jump over it etc, and there's a setting in the options to make the game track all of this damage permanently across your entire play through. 

The whole thing is so impenetrably, ambitiously, obtuse. It's incredible. It's a deeply flawed masterpiece. And like many masterpieces, engaging with it first-hand unaided isn't the greatest way for many to experience it for the first time. There's a reason museum guides exist - and this thing needs one. Go find a let's play and watch someone who is intimately familiar with this play through it and explain it along the way. For the average 'modern' gamer, that will be a much better way of engaging with this.

So it's weird - I really genuinely recommend this, I just don't recommend playing it straight away.

I enjoyed it, it's exactly what it says on the box: a short but sweet detective game where you have a bunch of evidence and you go through it in more or less any order. 

"More or less" because there are several "stages" of evidence gated behind making some number of correct deductions with the evidence you already had, but it didn't feel restricting (and may have kept me from being overwhelmed by having *all* the evidence dumped on me at once).

The evidence makes sense, the setting is amusing (a tongue-in-cheek take on startup office politics, with lots of intertwined things happening, some of which have to do with the crime). I felt smart when I figured things out. Most of the time it feels like I'm genuinely figuring out what happened, rather than guessing what the designer intended.

There were a couple of instances where I wish the UI was a bit more accommodating: I nearly had to take a piece of paper out for a puzzle (because the built-in notepad has variable width font, but I needed a grid; and I wanted to be able to associate name/job/picture without committing to which org chart position it goes in yet, but the game is short enough that I just kept that in my head.
If you loved the Roottrees are Dead and you need more, this is the game for you.

A Case of Distrust is a short (3-4 hour) document based deduction game where you connect names and photos to an organizational chart in the hopes of shedding light on the death of its CEO. Through various reports, notes and other paraphernalia, you'll use the connections between these people you're trying to identify to learn about their lives.

Lots of them have loving families, friends and furry (and not so furry) pets. One of them is also a murderer.

You'll see it compared to The Roottrees are Dead a lot. As someone who's got that one pending, please consider it a mix of Obra Dinn and Strange Antiquities (my eternal fave). Like the latter, it's pretty much pure UI. You are provided with fake documents, tabs and even a notebook to keep track of your ideas. For the most part, it can be purely played with a mouse, as you'll be allowed to scroll up and down a list of names and surnames when naming characters.

You can also type them to filter them out, but it's good to have that flexibility in accessibility and, also, I appreciate when mystery and deduction games have confidence enough in their plot to not distract me with not exactly unnecessary but sometimes actually unnecessary gameplay mechanics that add nothing.

The plot itself is simple, most of your time will be spent trying to find that one line or name you think you read five minutes ago and can't find because you forgot to take notes. I'd suppose that if you're quite the attentive reader, you'll be able to source all the data to complete the chart in 2 hours, maybe just a bit more than that.

There's a bunch of evidence to parse through too, lots of which are a bunch of red herrings and distractions to add some difficulty. I'm perfectly fine with that, it correctly emulates the experience of digging through mountains of office docs trying to find the one form someone signed for something. The resolution itself is just as mundane, though I did feel rewarded by the end.

The tone itself is sweet, accurate, nothing too mind blowing but good enough to pass as believable. You'll come to care a bit about these doofuses' lives, specially because a handful of them have such cute pets you want them to be innocent for the sake of their horse or turtle. For a first game, this was rather excellent and I'm following whatever the devs do next. Not that much replayability, but I'd rather have an afternoon of a good mystery rather than a full week of sidequest fluff.

A couple of reviews mention bugs and not being able to 100% the game. I'd say that whatever inconsistencies and issues there were are now patched, as I found no bugs and was able to get all achievements in a single run.

For more reviews of games that are cute, or creepy, or both, please check my curator page: https://store.steampowered.com/curator/44079361/

I was not sure what to expect with this game. I knew I wanted a murder mystery, an investigation to sink my teeth into for a little while. Something light, but engaging with puzzles and rewarding shots of dopamine for a keen eye and a quick logic. 

A Case of Fraud was exactly what I wanted in a charming, roughly $10 CAD package. The bulk of the game is combing through documents to find little strips of information, nuggets of data within a believable pile of emails, memos, notes, office flyers, and birthday invitations; then, having accumulated your notes, the puzzle of putting together the coporate tree and eventually solving the central murder takes centre stage. Imagine a red string corkboard. Now imagine it with funny pets. That's a Case of Fraud.

Naturally I can't go into many, if any, details; however, I do think it's safe to vaguely gesture at some highlights. First, the puzzles were simple, but fun to solve. It's the kind of thing I absolutely would pull with friends at my own job if they had the penchant for secret messages and riddles. 

Second, the art and drawings are entirely charming. Every person is distinct and memorable, which helps with the investigating, while all the pets and animals were super fun to find and paste next to their families and owners. It lends a nice, fuzzy edge to an otherwise fairly serious topic of murder, while also being a fun way to get several memorable non-human faces into the game. 

Third, though the mystery itself wasn't complicated or difficult to parse (to the point where I was definitely overthinking the problem), it was only that easy to solve thanks to the almost slice-of-life mundane office politics you dig into over the course of the game. The progression forces you to read a lot more than some people might prefer before solving the case. That reading means, however, that you're well informed and can easily pair information from earlier research into witness statements and evidence acquired later on. In short, the onboarding is smooth, maybe a bit long, but definitely worth the trouble. 

Especially considering the length and quality, A Case of Fraud is a remarkable nugget of a mystery game within a tide of the things on Steam. I highly recommend it to anyone who wants the murder mystery but with a relaxed, easy-going atmosphere. It takes an afternoon, less for the more clever, to complete, and is worth the price of admission.

Instead, all of the information is handed to you as you fill more names in, though precise details may be hidden in the backgrounds - I particularly enjoyed scouring the text chats, as they had many small details that were easy to pass over the first time. They also did a good job of making finding the names of people at least somewhat challenging - including a certain red herring where two characters had very similar names.

The murder mystery case itself is potentially the weakest part of this game, unfortunately. Though there are again a few red herrings, a careful examination will easily clear most of them away. I found myself more concerned about whether the answer could really be so easily determined, but it was - the culprit's plan left a lot to be desired, to say the least. I really liked the idea of having the pet being able to testify as well, but the evidence it provided was far from necessary to solving the case, too, which again was disappointing. I won't say it was useless, but none of the evidence provided was unique to that source, which I would have liked to see.

Despite its flaws, I really enjoyed this game and would recommend it to other mystery-lovers, with the caveat that it is quite short. The office politics on display were interestingly toxic, despite the best efforts of some of the staff, and it was fun to solve, even if it wasn't as hard as it could have been. Bravo Hesperus Games, I shall look forward to your next project!

I’m giving this a thumbs up because, despite the controversy surrounding its release mechanics, there is still a beautiful, unique experience here if you approach it with the right mindset.

If you judge Cube World solely as a traditional RPG where you endlessly stack stats linearly forever, you might get frustrated by the region-locked gear system. But if you look at it as a pure exploration and scouting game, the charm completely takes over. The voxel-based, procedurally generated worlds are vibrant, gorgeous, and incredibly fun to traverse. Scaling a massive mountain, hang-gliding across a valley, or sailing through uncharted waters feels fantastic.

The action-based combat is snappy, active, and genuinely satisfying once you master the dodging and combo loops for your class. Taming pets to fight alongside you or act as mounts adds a great layer of classic RPG flavor, and diving into ancient dungeons with a buddy in co-op is where the game truly shines.

It’s not perfect, and it requires you to shift your expectations about progression, but the sense of wonder and discovery in this infinite blocky frontier is absolutely worth experiencing.

BUTCHER, developed by Phobia Game Studio and Transhuman Design and published by Crunching Koalas and Transhuman Design, is a brutally intense 2D side-scrolling shooter that unapologetically embraces the raw, violent spirit of classic 1990s arcade action games. From the moment players dive into the game, they are thrown into a relentless bloodbath where the main character—a cyborg assassin designed to exterminate humanity—tears through hordes of enemies with unyielding ferocity. The game’s emphasis on speed, precision, and carnage offers an adrenaline-fueled challenge that tests players’ reflexes and strategic thinking in equal measure, making for a satisfying yet punishing experience.

Gameplay in BUTCHER is deceptively simple in concept but brutally demanding in execution. Players navigate linear levels filled with waves of hostile creatures and deadly traps, armed with an arsenal of weapons that range from shotguns and machine guns to explosive devices. The core loop revolves around rapid movement, quick aiming, and aggressive combat. Every encounter demands a blend of fast reflexes and tactical awareness, as enemies spawn relentlessly, and even a moment’s hesitation can lead to death. The game rewards mastery of its mechanics, encouraging players to optimize weapon usage, learn enemy patterns, and execute chain kills to survive the merciless onslaught.

Visually, BUTCHER is a striking homage to retro pixel art aesthetics, drenched in a grimy, dystopian atmosphere. The graphics feature detailed pixelated environments that feel both nostalgic and unsettling, with dark industrial backdrops stained by blood and littered with debris and corpses. The character and enemy designs are deliberately grotesque and exaggerated, amplifying the game’s horror undertones while maintaining a stylistic coherence that complements the fast-paced action. The careful use of lighting and shadow effects enhances the mood, creating claustrophobic spaces that heighten tension and emphasize the brutal nature of the gameplay.

The audio design further amplifies the game’s aggressive tone. A pounding industrial soundtrack drives the relentless pace, infusing each level with urgency and intensity. Weapon sounds are impactful and visceral, each shot feeling heavy and satisfying. Explosions, enemy screams, and environmental noises blend seamlessly to create an immersive soundscape that pulls players deeper into the chaotic world. The audio cues also play a functional role, providing feedback critical for reacting quickly during combat and navigating dangerous areas.

While BUTCHER has garnered praise for its faithful recreation of classic shooter mechanics and its uncompromising difficulty, it is not without its criticisms. The game’s high level of difficulty and fast pace may alienate players who prefer more forgiving or varied gameplay experiences. Additionally, some players have noted that the repetitive nature of enemy encounters and level designs can limit long-term engagement, as the core loop, while thrilling, offers limited diversity in objectives and environments. However, these factors are also what appeal to fans of old-school arcade shooters, where repetition and challenge are integral to the experience.

In essence, BUTCHER stands as a powerful tribute to the unforgiving shooters of the past, delivering a visceral, fast-paced, and brutally satisfying action experience. It combines precise gameplay, striking pixel art, and a pounding soundtrack to create a cohesive and immersive package that is sure to resonate with players craving a retro-inspired challenge. Though it may not cater to every taste, those who embrace its punishing mechanics and relentless combat will find a rewarding and cathartic outlet in the world of BUTCHER. This game is a blood-soaked celebration of old-school gaming violence, designed for players who want to push their skills to the limit in a dark, dystopian setting.

At the start of the game this game was fun, being a fast pace shooting game, which I don't really play a whole lot. But soon after I realised this game wasn't what it was going to be during them first 30 odd mins of playtime.

Beating this game made me feel the exact way the achievement that popped made me feel. The game can be tedious and repetitive because of the gameplay loop. It's always Kill Enemies > Go platform a little > Extermination zone of small enemies. This is one part of the game I just didn't like. It felt all the same especially as the background changes very slightly so it just feels like you are doing the same thing over and over. 

The game itself isn't difficult. The difficulty in it (at least on controller. I may have missed a button but I don't think I did) is the controls. Looping your weapons in a fast pace shooter game needing to use different weapons on some other enemies, with a total of 5-6 weapons makes it god awful to play. Hell, shooting one weapon and then running out of ammo puts you to a random other weapon automatically. For example I was shooting with a strong weapon and then it switched to a shotgun that did basically no damage. 

A side objective like killing a small boss here and there would have been nice (For example at the end of a level or even just a single level could have been putting a boss fight in). However, their is only one boss fight and it's right at the damn end. Getting to the end itself is so annoying because of the controls and because of the gameplay as mentioned above. It's hard to say I enjoyed this game. I did enjoy it for the first like 2-3 sections of the game but thats about it and 3 is a slight push. The only other thing to do during a mission is look for skulls with the risk of you dying. And if you do die. Well you have to do the whole level again. Sure they might not be very long. But doing extermination sections once is enough. Let alone doing it a 2nd or 3rd try just because you wanted to explore and collect things..

Overall I think the game suffers from repetitiveness and really bad controls (even L1 was to jump which well... most games dont do...) but as an inbetween game or whilst waiting for someone or just needing a break for 5 mins, this game might be able to do it. It's not very long and playing it in incremental steps might be the way to go. However, the things I'v listed about the game just make the game feel meh. Towards the end I wasn't enjoying it as much and wanted it over with. So, I would say it's not recommended but I don't play many of these games so maybe it's just me. Either way, its a game you could play from time to time in small amounts whilst waiting for someone etc as mentioned so if that's what you want give it a shot maybe you'll enjoy the loop more than I.

[h1]2000 years later, the New Testament has gone playable[/h1]
An approachable biblical walking simulator that presents its subject clearly, even when its interactions feel rigid.

When I reviewed the prologue a few years ago, I found I Am Jesus Christ intriguing for tackling a subject rarely explored in games. At the same time, its odd design choices and missing quality-of-life features left me uncertain about the full release. Now that the complete game has arrived, I returned to see whether it lived up to the... less anticipated reception on Steam.

The New Testament is told in form of a first-person walking simulator. After the intro told of *our lord and savior's birth and upbringing, an angel set me out to find John the baptist and the story takes off... 

From there, the game follows his journey through familiar biblical events, teachings, and encounters. Its accessible storytelling makes the material easy to follow, while optional sermon references provide additional context without forcing players through lengthy explanations.

Presentation is straightforward and keeps the journey moving at a comfortable pace. Loading interruptions are sparse, while optional fast travel makes revisiting previously explored locations considerably less tedious. The main weakness comes from character interactions, which can feel stiff and occasionally break the immersion. Even the Mary Magdalene scene (which came as an update after release) turned up as an after-thought, leaving out the stoning drama, which I found memorable since before.

While being an agnostic myself, I found the game to be a decent entry point for anyone curious about the New Testament's overview, without wanting to approach it solely through traditional religious media.

The more you expect something to jump out and then not, makes the expectation like a guitar string that keeps getting tightened until it finally snaps. And once you get hit with a good jump scare, the pay off is phenomenal. I also enjoyed that there was just enough dialogue from the protagonist to drive the story. It also left just enough room for me to be able to ad lib between myself and the character. Ultimately providing ample room to build on a lot of fun moments and comical banter, which I really appreciated. Silent Still 2, developed and published by SolitaryStudios, is a deeply atmospheric psychological horror experience that delves into one of the most terrifying human phenomena—sleep paralysis. Rather than relying on traditional horror tropes or an abundance of jump scares, the game centers its fear on vulnerability and the slow suffocation of helplessness. You awaken in the dark, unable to move, unable to scream, trapped somewhere between dreaming and waking while the world around you shifts into something unrecognizable. The premise is simple yet profoundly unsettling: to survive the night, you must endure it. SolitaryStudios captures this raw, intimate terror with a level of restraint and focus rarely seen in the genre, crafting a game that is less about what you see and more about what you feel.

From the very beginning, Silent Still 2 grips you with its claustrophobic tension. You play as a character suffering from recurring episodes of sleep paralysis, each represented as a chapter that immerses you in surreal environments shaped by fear and confusion. The first-person perspective reinforces the sense of entrapment, forcing you to experience each moment as if it were happening to you personally. Shadows flicker in the corners of your vision, distant whispers crawl closer, and your own breath seems to echo louder than it should. The game’s pacing is deliberate—slow and unnerving—allowing the tension to build gradually until every sound or movement feels threatening. It’s a masterclass in minimalism, proving that horror doesn’t need spectacle when dread can be cultivated through silence, uncertainty, and anticipation.

The audiovisual design is one of the game’s strongest achievements. Every environment is rendered with photorealistic detail, yet the lighting is sparse and carefully controlled, casting long, uneasy shadows across empty rooms. The color palette is subdued and cold, emphasizing the detachment between reality and dream. Sound, however, is the true instrument of fear. The game’s 3D audio design places the player in the middle of every creak, murmur, and shifting noise. Sometimes the silence stretches unbearably long, broken only by a faint scraping sound that feels too close for comfort. The combination of visual realism and meticulous sound design creates an immersive sensory experience that lingers long after the game ends, not through shock but through unease that slowly seeps under your skin.

Gameplay in Silent Still 2 is intentionally sparse, designed to mirror the limitations of the body during paralysis. You cannot freely explore or fight back; instead, you observe, listen, and piece together the fragments of the protagonist’s memories and fears. The interactions are subtle—looking in a certain direction, reacting to noises, recognizing patterns of movement in the dark. Each chapter introduces new variations on the same theme, representing different stages of mental and emotional deterioration. There are no weapons, no clear enemies, and no victory beyond surviving your own terror. This simplicity makes the experience more personal and introspective, transforming what might have been a straightforward horror game into a disturbing psychological journey. It is an exploration of how fear manifests when stripped of control, when the only thing separating safety from disaster is the fragile boundary between consciousness and oblivion.

While the game’s presentation is hauntingly effective, its brevity and simplicity may leave some players divided. With a runtime of under an hour and minimal interactivity, Silent Still 2 prioritizes atmosphere over depth. Those expecting a complex narrative, branching choices, or multiple endings may find its linearity underwhelming. Yet for what it sets out to accomplish—a concentrated descent into a state of waking nightmare—it succeeds with remarkable precision. Every second feels deliberate, every image crafted to evoke discomfort rather than shock. It’s the kind of experience best approached as an interactive short film rather than a traditional game, something to be absorbed rather than conquered. Its pacing demands patience, but that patience is rewarded with one of the most authentically unnerving portrayals of sleep paralysis ever depicted in interactive media.

Silent Still 2 stands as an example of how psychological horror can thrive through restraint. It forgoes monsters in favor of the mind’s own distortions, replacing chaos with the stillness of fear and noise with the sound of one’s heartbeat. It’s not a game for everyone—it’s slow, abstract, and deeply personal—but for those who appreciate horror that unsettles rather than startles, it delivers a chilling and intimate experience. SolitaryStudios has crafted something that feels both grounded in real human anxiety and elevated by artistic precision. When the credits roll and the silence returns, the echo of its tension lingers, leaving you with the eerie feeling that the nightmare hasn’t quite ended—that perhaps, somewhere in the darkness of your own room, something is still watching, waiting for you to fall asleep again.

Pure Pool Pro is honestly one of the most realistic pool games I’ve played. The physics feel great, the presentation is clean, and after the recent camera fix, the game is fully playable and enjoyable. The career mode is deep and rewarding, and I really appreciate that you can unlock everything through gameplay instead of being pushed toward microtransactions.

That said, there are a couple things holding it back from being perfect.

The AI can be frustrating. It’s supposed to mirror your play style, but instead it often blasts every shot at full power and pulls off some ridiculous, near-impossible shots. In 9-ball especially, it regularly clears the table in a single turn.

2-player is oddly limited — there’s no support for two controllers. You have to pass one controller back and forth, which feels outdated for a modern pool game.

Overall though, the foundation is strong. The physics, career mode, and unlock system are excellent. If the AI gets tuned and local co-op is improved, this could easily be the best pool game on Steam.

I really hope the developers continue updating it.

I really wanted to love Pure Pool Pro. As a long-time virtual pool fan and someone who’s spent way too many hours in games like Virtual Pool 4, I was excited to see a new, more serious take on pool. Unfortunately, while there is solid content here, some major design choices hold it back.

[h1] The Good [/h1]

There’s actually a decent amount of content:

- A full career mode

- Several different game modes

- Advanced settings for players who want a more simulation-style experience

On paper, this sounds great. It should be the kind of game pool enthusiasts sink hundreds of hours into.

[h1] The Not-So Good [/h1]

🎯 AI Is Unrealistically Strong (and Frustrating)

This is the biggest issue.

The AI opponents:

- Make an absurd number of long, low-percentage shots

- Fluke balls constantly

- Rarely miss routine shots

- Almost never make positional mistakes

What really breaks immersion is that they seem to play screw (backspin) on normal shots where no human realistically would. It feels mechanical and unnatural, less like playing a skilled opponent and more like playing a shot-making robot that ignores realistic risk.

Instead of feeling competitive, it feels unfair.

[h1] 📷 Camera Problems (Especially in Advanced Mode) [/h1]

If you turn off the cue guide to play on advanced settings, the camera sits to the right of the cue when resting on cushion, which makes lining up shots extremely awkward. You can’t properly sight down the cue ball.

On top of that:

The camera is too close to the table

Judging bank shots becomes very difficult

There aren’t enough view or zoom customization options

Compared to the flexible camera controls in VP4, this feels restrictive. A proper pool sim needs multiple camera presets and adjustable zoom levels. Right now, it just doesn’t offer enough control.

[h1] Final Verdict [/h1]

Pure Pool Pro has the foundation of a good pool simulator, career mode, multiple game types, advanced settings, but the AI balance and camera limitations seriously hurt the experience.

If you’re looking for a casual pool game, you might still find some enjoyment here. But if you’re looking for a realistic, competitive simulation experience, be prepared for frustration.

5/10 – Solid concept, but held back by AI and camera issues.
