I am someone who has played both previous 'Crew' games by Runner Duck, Bomber Crew and Space Crew. I enjoyed both of them and I believe they are good games, so when I heard Badlands Crew was coming out I was excited for it, but now having played it, I believe out of them all, Badlands Crew falls short of both Bomber and Space Crew. That's not to say that this game is bad, there are parts I enjoyed like the idea of making my entirely own vehicle, the setting is interesting, and being able to diversify crew members a lot easier than I remember being able to with Bomber or Space Crew (At least I think, I haven't played either in well over a year). But the core aspects to the game are... Lacking. I'll split up up each aspect as I believe they are each important to talk about.

[h2] 1. Building/Customization [/h2]

The building aspect of Badlands crew is the massive thing that sets it apart from the other crew games. Being able to build your vehicle from scratch and upgrade it as the game progresses in ways more than just upgrading guns, critical systems, or armor. It SHOULD be the thing this game does the best in comparison to the other crew games. But if anything, Badlands Crew's car building makes me wish I could go back to the Bomber/Space Crew way of doing things. I should not need to struggle for over a minute trying to get a plow onto the front of my car, and the main reason for that is there is no way to manually move objects up and down, you have to HOPE that it snaps exactly where you want it to go and it is beyond finnicky to the point of aggravation. 

The building aspect of Badlands Crew is additionally also hampered by the shift from just needing money and research points to build/upgrade to now a wide array of materials. Honestly, it probably wouldn't be that bad, and maybe it really isn't, but I for the life of me could never get a substantial amount of one of the basic crafting ingredients, scrap wood. Maybe that was just me getting unlucky with drops from the enemies/missions, but it was beyond frustrating having to hope that I get enough drops from enemies or find a mission that gave scrap wood as a completion reward just so I could actually build what I need when I had every other ingredient by the boatloads.

[h2] 2. Driving [/h2]

In the previous crew games, driving/flying was something I never even thought about. It was smooth, it was simple, it wasn't even something I had an opinion on because it just worked. Badlands Crew's driving makes me want to pull my hair out. By default, the game automatically steers you onto roads and away from obstacles except what it actually felt like was that you have to fight your car to go where you actually want to go and the car will still hit obstacles regardless which made for a miserable experience that made me thankful I could turn it off. But honestly, even if both weren't headache inducing, why are they on by default? I would be fine if they existed, but having them on by default feels like handholding. I, the player, should be punished for not looking where I'm driving or not avoiding obstacles.

[h2] 3. Combat AI [/h2]

I'm going to get straight to the point for this one. The AI in this game is bad. Quite bad in fact. I have seen enemies drive off of cliffs and into ravines while actively fighting them for really no reason. Allied AIs consistently got in the way of my car. Both enemy and allied AIs occasionally get stuck on objects or sometimes just straight up nothing. And it isn't limited to your allies and enemies either, trying to order your driver to do donuts or chase cars isn't much better. Sometimes your car will just take the donut circle super wide and make you have to take manual control or else you'll crash into a wall that wasn't near the donut circle. Chase is just... finnicky, no other way to describe it. Trying to fight using anything other than manual driving isn't worth it.

Also, this may be inaccurate as obviously I haven't completed the game, but where are the Aces??? Them, their personalities, and the added challenge factor was an incredibly fun part of the other Crew games but I haven't encountered a single one so far minus something called a champion? If it was like an ace in the other games it didn't even speak to me?

[h2] 4. Polish [/h2]

Bomber Crew and Space Crew are very well polished games, nothing comes to mind for me when I think of unpolished aspects of them. Badlands Crew has a whole enemy type that looks like they're from a beta version of the game. The juvenile sand worms animations just look silly and static, not to mention unpolished. A lot of the other core aspects of the game also fall under a lack of polish, but I believe I've talked enough about my problems in each of them.


In conclusion, I think Badlands Crew started off as a really promising idea, but the execution by Runner Duck leaves a lot to be desired. I hope they fix the problems this game has, as it was undergoing patches, but as the last patch as of writing this was nearly 7 months ago, I don't have high hopes. Here's hoping this was a one time occurrence, and the next 'Crew' game is great just like Bomber and Space Crew.

You can put the guns wherever you want them, not just at the static gun emplacements. I really like the premise of this game, and I really enjoyed Space Crew, but there's something about this game that misses the mark for me.

The biggest changes from the previous game: It's open world instead of being a string of random subsector encounters, You control the vehicle yourself, instead of just managing the crew, and you can customize every part of your rig.

All of that sounds great, in theory, but in practice I found them to be a huge headache. The biggest disapointment was the fact that I had to control the rig myself. It's not just that it's unwieldy, but instead of stearing you set a dirrection for the rig to go. 

In theory this would mean you wouldn't have to micro manage as much. In pratice the rig rarely goes where I want to. There are wierd delays in turning which not only makes ramming hard (a tactic the NPCS use frequently) but I fidn my driver often drives into walls when the terrain is narrow, despite the fact that the SHOULD be able to turn. 

It's because the game works on this strange hybrid system where you're supposedly telling the driver what to do, while they actually drive. It's awkward.

Second, the open world is fun... for the most part. However, because it's open world the spawns are random and sometimes my rig is completely messed up before I can get to a mission area. It's not uncommon to encounter 2 or more groups at once, drawing you into an extended fight, and because you're so slow you really can't run from most encoutners easily.

Finally, customizing the rig. Actually fun! You can blueprints for new parts hidden around the wasteland, and there are a lot of options. However, the cost of adding even the smallest, weakest points requires a LOT of resources. LIke I would go out, get into half a dozen fights, then not even get enough resources to add a single small structural part.

I think that would be fine for people that like the grind, but I was playing on the easiest version, and on harder difficulties when your rig is destroyed you loose a large percentage of your gear.I feel like that would go way beyond a grind.

You build a battle wagon and head out into the wasteland to tackle specific objectives while exploring the environment and deciding whether or not random encounters are worth your time and resources. Spying a secondary objective in the distance and looking at your fuel gauge and healthbars to decide whether or not you should veer off is an exciting moment. 

There are (not enough) big sandworms that (don't really) pose a huge threat. They're spectacular and I love seeing them. There are environmental hazards that randomly spawn and you have to decide if you should sidestep around the acid rain or just tank the damage even though you didn't kit your guys out for poison defense.

There's a rock-paper-scissors-esque damage/defense system, but I never really struggled with it. You build your battle wagon how you want; I chose a rig with huge starboard broadside firepower. The Clowns enemy type was the only one to ever cause me trouble, meaning I had to equip my guys with poison-defense gear and build turrets that dealt damage that the clowns were weak to. They're the only enemy I had to counter.

I loved Badlands Crew. There's a ton of character customization, the plot is fun and interesting, the controls are clunky enough to make you feel like you can master them. It's not as challenging or grueling as it maybe could have been, but I had a lot of fun playing through it and exploring all its nooks and crannies.

Pawnbroker Simulator approaches the business-management genre from an unusual angle, placing the player behind the counter of a pawn shop where almost every object represents both an opportunity and a financial risk. Developed by Next Sky Games and published by Ultimate Publishing, Ultimate Games S.A., and PlayWay S.A., the game focuses on building a small operation into a more successful business through careful appraisal, bargaining, loans, inventory management, security, and store improvements. Instead of simply purchasing products from suppliers and selling them at predetermined prices, the experience revolves around determining what customers bring through the door and deciding whether a deal is genuinely worth taking.

Appraisal is one of the most important parts of the experience. The game includes more than 250 different items, with prices influenced by condition and a changing market. Examining merchandise therefore becomes more meaningful than simply looking for the highest number on a price tag. Players gradually develop expertise that helps them recognize valuable objects, questionable merchandise, and potential bargains. Knowledge can be improved in categories including Fine Art, Arms, Gear, and Collectibles, while specialists can assist with unusual finds. The confidence-based appraisal system adds uncertainty to transactions, which fits the pawn-shop theme well because an inexperienced player cannot always be completely certain that an apparently valuable object is actually a great investment.

Negotiation works alongside appraisal and forms another major part of the economic gameplay. Customers have different personalities, patience levels, and characteristics that affect how transactions unfold. Some may be difficult negotiators, while others can possess traits such as Hoarder, Reseller, or Aggressor. This makes bargaining more interesting than repeatedly choosing the lowest possible offer. Pushing too hard can jeopardize a promising transaction, whereas accepting a customer's demands too quickly can destroy the potential profit margin. Regular customers can also become more valuable as relationships develop, opening opportunities for special deals and giving some continuity to the people who visit the shop.

The actual pawn system gives the game an important distinction from ordinary retail simulators. Players can accept pawned property and issue loans with interest rather than treating every object as an immediate purchase. Verification is required when customers return to reclaim their belongings, introducing additional responsibility to the process. Loans also create another layer of financial planning because money committed to one transaction cannot necessarily be used elsewhere immediately. Combined with changing market demand, this means a theoretically profitable object can still become a poor decision if too much capital is tied up at the wrong moment.

Financial management consequently plays a substantial role. Rent, utilities, maintenance, item upkeep, improvements, and other costs constantly compete for available cash. Successful management requires more than accumulating expensive merchandise because a shop filled with valuable stock can still struggle if there is insufficient money available to cover operating expenses. Reputation provides another progression system, with higher tiers granting access to rarer merchandise and more demanding customers. Skills covering appraisal, negotiation, prediction, and management can also be developed, while qualifications provide additional advantages. These mechanics establish a satisfying progression from an inexperienced shopkeeper making uncertain decisions to a much more capable business operator.

Restoration adds further value to the appraisal and inventory systems. Damaged merchandise is not automatically worthless because players can restore items through a dedicated mini-game connected to their skills and qualifications. This creates situations where an object in poor condition can actually represent an attractive investment. Buying cheaply, restoring effectively, and eventually selling at a better price produces a rewarding business cycle. It also gives condition-based pricing greater importance because damaged goods are not merely weaker versions of pristine ones but potential projects for players willing to invest time and resources.

Shop customization and expansion provide a more visual form of progression. Floors, walls, furniture, decorations, displays, signage, and other elements can be personalized, allowing the business to evolve from a basic workplace into something more distinctive. Expansion has practical consequences as well because inventory is handled through limited physical storage slots. Players cannot simply accumulate endless merchandise without considering where everything will go. Displays can be arranged to attract suitable customers, while additional space provides more freedom for storing and presenting valuable goods. This helps connect customization with actual management instead of making decoration entirely cosmetic.

Security introduces another welcome source of pressure. A pawn shop naturally contains items attractive to criminals, and the game allows players to invest in cameras, alarms, locks, reinforced doors, and secure display cases. Thieves can create problems during both daytime and nighttime situations, and players may eventually need to confront them when preventative measures fail. The interesting part is that security becomes another financial calculation. Spending heavily on protection reduces the money available for inventory and expansion, but neglecting security risks losing merchandise that may have required considerable investment to obtain or restore.

The dynamic economy helps connect these individual systems. Demand can react to economic conditions, meaning today's attractive purchase may not necessarily remain equally profitable later. Combined with condition, restoration, negotiation, expertise, customer behavior, and limited storage, this gives inventory decisions more depth than simply purchasing everything below an obvious market price. Pawnbroker Simulator is at its strongest when several of these mechanics overlap and force compromises. A rare item might offer an excellent return but consume most available cash, require restoration, occupy valuable storage space, and demand improved security before it can safely be displayed.

The first-person presentation is also appropriate for the concept because much of the appeal comes from physically operating the store rather than managing it entirely through spreadsheets and menus. Examining objects, interacting with customers, organizing merchandise, modifying the premises, and protecting the business all contribute to the feeling of personally running the shop. The game supports single-player play and includes Steam achievements, Steam Trading Cards, Steam Cloud, and Family Sharing. The developer also discloses that AI tools assisted with specific store asset components before human artists edited, refined, and finalized those assets.

Overall, Pawnbroker Simulator offers a distinctive variation on the increasingly crowded business-simulator genre. Appraisal uncertainty, personality-driven bargaining, loans, interest, restoration, fluctuating demand, reputation, limited storage, customization, security, and operating expenses combine into a surprisingly involved representation of running a pawn shop. Its repetitive structure and uneven depth prevent it from becoming an exceptional management simulation, but the interconnected mechanics provide enough decision-making to keep the central business loop engaging. For players who enjoy slowly building wealth through calculated purchases, careful negotiations, and constant reinvestment, it provides a solid and appropriately specialized simulation experience.

This is a very fun game. Is it perfect? No, not at all. It has some balancing issues. But the bones are good and the gameplay can be immersive if you let it. 

As every simulation game, you start off with a shop from your late father. A family member is guiding you through the first steps, which is the typical tutorial. After that, it is up to you how to manage your business. 

The game is a shop simulator disguised as a pawnshop. Instead of ordering your stock from a supplier, your customers are your suppliers, and the trash if you run out to search the trash bins around the block for some low tier items. If you're lucky, you'll get a mid tier item which is worth a couple hundred dollars. 

To get the most out of your shop, you need to upgrade your shop appeal, your shop and item attraction or synergy and your character. Shop appeal goes up by decorating and having better items in your showcases. The synergy or attraction of your items are a bit more difficult to manage. It will give a boost in shop appeal too. The difficulty lies in having the correct items showcased together, which is mostly tied to the categories of the respective items. If you mismatch your showcases, the attraction goes down and with that your appeal too. Cleanliness is also part of the game, you start off with a simple manual cleaning mechanic but this part can luckily be replaced by automated vacuum bots. 

your character can be upgraded by unlocking upgrade stars, which can be spend in four skills that each give you bonusses for running your shop. The best skills help you with appraisal and pricing your items. 
You'll get skill points by levelling up. My current level is 50 or 51 and I have one more thing to unlock, which costs 5 skill points. 
Each item has categories, for which you need to get better knowledge. Increasing your knowledge is automatically done when you investigate items that cross your counter or that you find in the trash. Better knowledge seem to add to better appraisals.
The shop can be upgraded two times, which will enlarge your shop area and storage area. There is not much customizing in the area. You can't build walls or change the shopfront. You'll end up with three identical shop fronts with each a door, and three doors to your storage area. Basically, each expansion is a copy of the first shop area. 

The last upgrade section is based on unlocking licenses. With these licenses you are able to get better items or get other perks that can help you with running your business. 

Shop interior is important too, the game has a theft mechanic. Thieves will get in our store and take stuff, usually the expensive items. The fun part is to attack the thieves with a slipper to get your item back. This mechanic can be disabled in the options, it can also be countered with blocking off your items from the customers. My shop is divided in half with counters and showcases. Customers can't reach any item but will "look" around and buy items from every showcase. 

To optimize the pawning mechanic, I have my counter in front of one of the storage doors. I run in and out to store or get pawned items easily. Because items aren't accessible to customers, I also run around getting each item they buy or put each bought item away to keep the attraction high. 

The unbalanced part of the game lies mostly in the end game. Each customer has traits, and each customer negotiates in the same way. I usually automatically reject certain customers because I know they don't come below the top price of the item(s) if they want to sell them. With buying there seems to be a bit more randomness to how far they want to stretch what they are willing to pay. 

High ticket items usually loose money when negotiating. I found that at least 50$ with single items is not counted while haggling. In bundles it is more random but it can go up to a 100$. 
I.e. an item is listed for 24587 dollars, while haggling the max price you can ask the customer could be 24550. It automatically makes you loose money. But to be honest, in my current game this doesn't matter if the daily profit is about 100k. 

The pawning system is not balanced well. I receive a storage rack full of pawned items for each Monday. The amount of items lies between 50 and 80 packages. Tuesdays usually get about 30 pawned items and Wednesdays to Fridays usually less than 20. 
This makes the Monday a very busy day. This is where my setup is useful because I can organise the Monday packages on Sunday, making it easy pickings when Monday business hours start. 

Customers always start haggling around the top price of the item. Most customers will accept offers well below the market prices, at least in my game. I started a couple new games to see how RNG works. In one game I got every customer with bad traits, that lead to them not willing to haggle and making me unable to get new items at reasonable prices. Another game, customers came in with items that are well worth over the amount of money that I had. I am talking about items well above the 20k price tag. I think the RNG could be handled better, to balance the game out more. 
The RNG for offered items needs work too. In my current game, what the customers offer me consist mostly of items like swords, shields, jewels, ancient knives, masks and statues. Less frequent are treasure maps and pendants. Very rarely I get other items. There are supposed to be firearms too, in my 40+ hours, I've seen 5 rifles past the ones that you get to unlock a license, but all as pawned items. I just don't get many items that exist in the game. 

In some other games I found that there are many items that I didn't see in my main game. Like tools, pillows, guitars and more. 

I would like to see more customers. Sometimes the same customer is twice or three times in the shop. 

The game is great already and it can be even better, especially with some balancing. A bigger store, or even a way to customize your store with walls, would be amazing too. 

If you love simulation games, this could be for you. 

I've seen many of the negative reviews too and I understand that the pacing can be a struggle. All I can say is that, for me, it all came down to shop interior and easy access to the storage area. 
I play without stamina, because I dislike that in a simulation game, so I can run around 24 hours per day. With stamina, it is surely more demanding. The hard part is to get through the first couple phases of the game. Unlocking the correct skills early give you a boost in appraising and pricing your items.

The game is enjoyable, but it doesn't offer much long-term replay value. After around 6–7 hours, you've pretty much seen everything it has to offer. While the gameplay is fun at first, it eventually becomes repetitive, with the same activities and objectives repeating over and over. It's worth playing if you're looking for a short experience, but don't expect it to keep you engaged for the long run.

Summary: A game where you just can’t please anyone.

Long version:
I hesitated for a long time about what rating to give, but I’ve ultimately concluded that I cannot give a positive review in its current state. The game has a solid concept, but it’s poorly balanced. Your rating is based on several factors, one of which is customer satisfaction—meaning whether you buy/sell an item at all and whether the price is to their liking.

Unfortunately, more than two-thirds of the customers I got during the day only wanted to pawn items, so I usually spent most of my cash on that (and if you don’t accept an item, your rating drops again). Then there was no money left to buy items outright, leading to another rating drop. Situations where I had 2,000 in the bank and four customers in a row wanted to sell items for 20,000 each were more than common. On top of that, you’re forced to close on Sundays, yet people want to pick up their pawned items that day. If you don't close = penalty; if you don't return an item on time = penalty.

Even when you do everything right—pawn items at their price, return items on time, have a million security cameras, and act polite—you still get a lower rating. Last but not least, you get billed for nonsensical items in the hundreds or thousands. I tried playing on the lowest difficulty, but it was essentially the same.

I don’t need to make millions, but I also don’t need to be under this much pressure from all sides. I expected a relaxing game; instead, I was just glad to finally uninstall it after getting all the achievements.

If you go into Pawnbroker Simulator expecting a slow, repetitive shop sim, you’ll be pleasantly surprised—it’s far more engaging, strategic, and addictive than it first appears.

Right from the start, the game hooks you with its simple but satisfying core loop: assess items, negotiate prices, and build your own thriving pawn empire. But what really makes it shine is the depth behind those interactions. Every customer feels like a mini story—some are desperate, some are savvy, and some are clearly trying to pull a fast one. Deciding whether to trust them or challenge their claims adds a constant layer of tension and excitement.

Visually, the game keeps things clean and immersive. The shop evolves as you progress, transforming from a modest setup into a bustling business filled with rare and valuable items. There’s a real sense of growth and accomplishment as you upgrade your space, unlock new features, and expand your reputation.

Where Pawnbroker Simulator truly stands out is in its attention to detail. Item inspection is surprisingly nuanced—you’re not just clicking “buy” or “sell,” you’re checking authenticity, spotting flaws, and making judgement calls that directly impact your profits. It makes every transaction feel earned.

The progression system is equally rewarding. As your skills improve, so does your ability to negotiate better deals and identify high-value items. It creates that perfect “just one more customer” feeling that keeps you playing far longer than you planned.

Sound design and atmosphere also deserve praise. The subtle background noise, customer chatter, and shop ambience all come together to create a believable and relaxing environment—one that you’ll genuinely enjoy spending time in.

Overall, Pawnbroker Simulator is a hidden gem in the simulation genre. It blends business strategy, psychology, and progression into a highly satisfying experience that’s easy to pick up but hard to put down. Whether you’re a fan of simulation games or just looking for something different, this is absolutely worth your time.

Verdict: A deeply engaging and rewarding simulator that turns everyday transactions into compelling gameplay.

Pawnbroker Simulator is a surprisingly deep and rewarding simulation game.

Running a pawn shop involves negotiating prices, evaluating items, and trying to make the best deals possible. The systems feel detailed and rewarding once you start understanding how everything works.

The game also keeps you on your toes with mechanics like thieves trying to steal items from your shop.

One of the fun touches is being able to find items in the trash outside and sell them in your store — truly one man’s trash is another man’s treasure.

If you enjoy store simulators but want something with more depth and interaction, this is an easy recommendation.

I really love this game, its a ton of fun to play and a lot of the stuff you see in pawn stars. 
My only complaints are these. 1. lack of decorations only like 6 or so. 2. Lack of item variety (lots of same items). 3. The inspect feature is rather boring you don't actually look for any damage such as scratches dents or cracks to help determine value and condition. 4. The repair feature some items you repair actually decrease the value which is highly confusing.  Other than those the game is really good for a simulation game and one of the better ones out there.

The game is fun and definitely has potential, but it’s missing variety in several areas.

First, there isn’t much décor or customization for the store. It would be nice to have more options to make your shop feel unique

Customers and items also start to feel repetitive. After a while you keep seeing the same types of people bringing in the same items. This becomes very noticeable in the endgame. I currently have over **600k and everything maxed out**, and at that point progression basically stops.

The **certificate progression** was enjoyable, but once you complete them all there’s not much left to work toward. I also ran into a bug where the **Media certificate never completed** because I never had a customer come in with a media item.

Another issue is the offers you get in the late game. Even with a fully upgraded shop, customers still come in trying to sell **low-value items like shovels, bracelets, and toys**. At this stage of the game, those deals feel pointless. I end up denying almost everyone unless they bring in **treasure maps**, which are the only items that really make good money.

The game would really benefit from:

* **Workers or employees** to help run the shop
* **More customer variety**
* **More interesting and valuable items** appearing in late game
* **Better scaling offers** as your shop becomes more successful

Right now, running the shop solo gets repetitive. You make a deal, put the item on the shelf, and a minute later it sells. That part feels satisfying, but you can’t really fill your shop with items just for decoration because if you price them normally they sell almost immediately. The only way to keep things on display is to **overprice them**, which feels a bit awkward.

Overall, I’d say the game is **very enjoyable for about 10 hours**, but after that it starts to feel repetitive once you reach the endgame. That said, the core gameplay is solid and the game has **a lot of potential** if more content, variety, and systems are added.

I managed to max out the quest books in about 10 hours. It would be great to have daily quests; for example, customers coming in looking for specific items that I’d need to source—perhaps even through "shady" means like weapons deals, etc.

The 24/7 shop opening hours aren't ideal. It makes it difficult to go out to source and repair items found on the street or fix purchased goods. If I close the shop, I might miss a customer coming back for a pawned item, which results in a penalty. Because of this, the "skip time" feature feels pointless; I practically never close, which also makes the shutters redundant. It would be better if time stopped at say, 22:00, allowing me to close up, repair items, restock, and go to sleep. This would actually give the door bolt a purpose. A daily summary screen would also be a great addition.

Regarding pawned items: it would be fair if customers tried to come back at least once more for their items instead of me failing the deal immediately. Also, despite having cameras and alarms, items sometimes just disappear or get stolen without warning. I only realize they're gone when the police returns for them. I don't understand how they can take them without the cameras alerting me. Furthermore, if I spot a thief and hit them before they manage to steal anything, all the other customers get scared and leave, which feels unrealistic. Adding a security guard who stands at the door to catch thieves would be a huge help. Also, if I close the shop, it would be better if the customers already inside stayed so I could finish serving them.

The shop itself should be upgradeable and expandable. Currently, certain items like sofas or center-floor displays feel like a waste of space because the shop is too small.

A fast paced roguelike platformer successfully translates the chaotic energy of bullet filled combat into a side scrolling format. Constant movement, quick reactions, and unpredictable weapon rotations create an engaging gameplay loop that keeps every run feeling active. The pace rarely slows down, encouraging adaptation to changing situations and making each climb feel distinct.

Combat stands out through a large variety of weapons and power ups. Frequent equipment changes introduce an element of improvisation, turning every encounter into an opportunity to discover new combinations and strategies. Rather than relying on a single build, success often comes from making effective use of whatever tools become available during a run.

Level design supports the action with compact arenas, vertical progression, and enemy layouts that constantly challenge positioning and awareness. Platforming and combat work together naturally, creating encounters where movement is just as important as firepower. The result is a satisfying balance between precision and controlled chaos.

Progression systems provide meaningful incentives for repeated attempts. Unlockables, character improvements, and additional gameplay options create a strong sense of long-term advancement. Even unsuccessful runs contribute toward future progress, making continued play feel rewarding and productive.

Presentation complements the gameplay through expressive animation, energetic sound design, and a distinctive visual style. Humor, creativity, and fast paced action are woven throughout the experience, helping maintain momentum from start to finish. The overall result is a polished roguelike adventure that offers strong replay value, satisfying combat, and an enjoyable twist on familiar mechanics.

JUMP INSTEAD OF ROLLING. The game doesn't exactly tell you this, but it becomes way, way easier if you just jump instead of rolling most of the time. Exit the Gungeon takes the chaotic insanity of Enter the Gungeon and turns it into a much faster and more arcade-style experience.
Instead of exploring rooms and slowly clearing floors, the game focuses on nonstop vertical action while the Gungeon literally collapses around you. It feels more like a frantic bullet-hell platformer than a traditional roguelike dungeon crawler.

At first the changes can feel strange if you loved Enter the Gungeon, but once you adjust to the faster pacing, the game becomes pretty fun in its own way. The constantly changing weapons keep runs unpredictable, and the smaller room-based encounters make the action feel nonstop.

The humor, weapon designs, and overall style are still great, and the game keeps the same goofy charm as its predecessor. It’s just a much more simplified and streamlined experience overall.

The good:
- Fast-paced and chaotic gameplay
- Great pixel art and animations
- Same fun humor and charm as Enter the Gungeon
- Weapon variety is still ridiculous and entertaining
- Easy to pick up for short sessions
- Boss fights are fun and visually impressive
- Strong soundtrack and sound design
- Runs move quickly with very little downtime
- Bullet hell gameplay feels satisfying

The bad:
- Not nearly as deep as Enter the Gungeon
- Constantly changing weapons can feel frustrating
- Less replayability compared to the original
- Platforming sections can become annoying
- Runs start feeling repetitive faster
- RNG sometimes feels too influential
- Some encounters become visually overwhelming
- Feels more like a spin-off than a true sequel

Overall, Exit the Gungeon is a fun and chaotic side game that keeps the style and humor of the original while going for a much faster arcade-style experience. It’s not as addictive or deep as Enter the Gungeon, but it’s still an enjoyable bullet-hell roguelike on its own.

It's an arcade-style variant of Enter the Gungeon. If you're looking for more rogue-likes, this is probably not what you want. There's no sprawling maps with hidden secrets. Its a straightforward elevator ride with each level having its own gimmick.
I do like arcade games, but they generally can't keep me for longer play sessions. Whenever you're bored, play a few minutes and move on - it's that kind of feeling.

Unfortunately, this doesn’t come close to what its predecessor did right. In 2D, the EtG formula just doesn’t translate well. The controls feel stiff, room layouts are cramped and the movement speed is very oddly tuned, everything feels a bit off. At times the camera perspective is genuinely disorienting and instead of skillful dodging it can feel like you’re just trying to keep up with the fking chaos.

Mechanically, a lot of the systems feel more frustrating than fun. Blanks don’t feel balanced for how often you need them and weapon variety is heavily dictated by randomness. Your starting weapon gets replaced constantly, and you rarely feel like you’re building toward anything consistent. Later stages even introduce hazards like moving platforms that shoot at you, which just piles on unnecessary difficulty. The whole flow often feels like you’re fighting the game’s structure rather than the enemies themselves.

There’s also a lot of repetition and loss of depth compared to Enter the Gungeon. Most weapons and enemies are carried over rather than reimagined, which makes the experience feel more like a stripped-down version than an upgrade. A lot of mechanics from the original, like synergies, alternate paths and other side content, are either missing or heavily reduced, which really hurts replayability. Even some lore and item descriptions feel inconsistent with what the items actually do in game.

That said, it’s not all that bad. Some bosses are genuinely creative and well-designed and the overall aesthetic still holds up. Runs are also much shorter, which makes it easier to jump in and out without committing a full hour like in the original. It might feel a bit anticlimactic at first, but the constant weapon swapping in the “Blessed Run” system are more enjoyable here then the Normal Runs once you get used to it. since it keeps things unpredictable and fast paced. It definitely has moments where it feels like a arcade shooter, even if it doesn’t always land.

Overall though, it feels like a downgraded and more chaotic version of what came before, without enough new systems to justify the trade offs. The main ideas are somewhat interesting, but the execution just doesn’t fully work. So yeah, I wouldn’t recommend it, 3.4/10.

Exit the Gungeon is a 2d sidescroller action roguelike spin-off sequel to Enter the Gungeon, where gun that can change the past has been used, but now they need to get out of that place. To do so player rides elevators that are heading up, while enemies spawn around. This changes a playthrough's structure a lot from the Enter the Gungeon, since there are no more branching paths and one act's structure typical is:
1. Going up (fight waves of spawning enemies)
2. Stop at a shop (or you can visit one to three small tunnels that are either friendly or full of hostiles).
3. Going up again (more waves of enemies)
4. Fight act's boss
5. Shop and head to next act. 

This means that gone are those two guaranteed chests that contained one item and one gun. To adjust the lack of guaranteed weapon spawn Dodge Roll changed the main weapon functionality completely. Where previously you had infinite ammo pistol and one main weapon, now you only start with infinite ammo pistol. However after 30 seconds (?) your pistol changes to another random weapon, based on your combo-value; that being 0-20 depending how many enemies you have killed without taking a hit. After you sunken hundreds of hours into Enter the Gungeon this play structure feels first like a Sorceress or Bowler's extra game mode, so it's no surprise players criticized it on Exit the Gungeon game's launch. Thankfully in the game's final and only content update Hello to Arms they added Arsenal Mode, where you can also pick up weapons to inventory alongside the changing weapon. This way you still have lot of variations between runs but if also have some level of own choose if current random weapon wasn't to your liking with current perks or if not at all and I felt like this is definitely better game mode than the regular Blessed Only mode.

[h1]Verdict:[/h1]
Despite Exit the Gungeon content is 90% of same content from Enter the Gungeon, Exit the Gungeon is a spin-off sequel that I can recommend for those that liked the Enter the Gungeon and/ or whom like roguelikes with shorter length (a complete runs take around 30 minutes, or up to one hour if you get the clone perk). Exited to see what they are cooking up for at Enter the Gungeon 2.

Because it isn't, it's a spin-off title originally released on mobile.

Got a few thousand hours in on Enter The Gungeon. Still play it and love it. Tried to play Exit some years ago on Switch, immediately quit out of disgust. Came back recently on Steam and chewed through every character's route, and am thoroughly convinced that this was a well-dressed creative failure issued forth to appease fans clamoring for more EnTG.

Apologists for the game strawman nay-sayers via the argument "It's not EnTG" being refuted with "It's not supposed to be, they're different games, etc". I am fully on board with Exit's gameplay model and in no way expected it to be an EnTG clone. Well, guess what? They cloned EnTG anyway. No new guns, no new characters, no new music, no new enemies. They did add a couple of npcs to hawk cosmetics that no fan of gameplay would care about...and took away a LOT.

You see, there were a few things that they forgot to clone over- like synergies. Whoops! Guns have no companion items. Particularly sad about the loss of synergies is that you can't make a crap gun semi-decent anymore through hunting the other set items. That won't be a problem though, since the gun shifts every few seconds between something you don't want and something you don't need. Fighting The Last Dragun? Here's Casey. 20 enemies on screen? Have an RC Rocket. I don't know whose idea it was to force "blessed" runs on players, and hope they were hoisted by their own petard right into profound depression at the realization that gun roulette as a mechanic sucks ass and no-one in the history of gaming has been delighted to have their choices restricted, EVEN WHEN they enjoy the mechanic. "You don't have to swap guns," say the apologists. Fair point, Guy LeDouche. You can instead have "gun drops" that take up the space of other usable items, have restrictive ammo availability, and will cause you to press r when you realize you have once again been gifted the gungeoneer's best friend, Klobbe. Gun drops are a bigger waste of time than gun swaps for that reason unless you enjoy challenge runs with terrible weapons, of which there are MANY.

Of course, that doesn't matter much either, because even the great weapons strangely seem to take the same amount of time to defeat an enemy. Standing in front of a Gun Nut with an AK-47 vs. an RPG, firing constantly, results in the same time of explosion for Mr. Nut. Thunderclap vs. Rube-A-Dyne? Same difference. Nothing matters gunwise except explosives' ability to destroy bullets and one-shot tiny or small enemies, which isn't that much help when they are spawning left and right and your rate of fire is slow. "Sure, it's a skill issue," say the apologists. Except I no-hit the Dragun and every other boss, so put that in your pipe and huff, Prof. Puffnstuf. Skill is not the issue. Bad design is the issue. Bad can be "The game is held together by duct tape, walls are a suggestion", or it can be "balance doesn't exist (possibly because nothing matters)", or it can be something worse, which is "This isn't fun for avoidable reasons having nothing to do with the individual taste of the player". In this case it's a bit of all three.

...But let's talk about bullets for a second. First of all, there's too many. Yes, it's a bullet hell game. Don't care. Other games have done far, far better in managing the patterns and mechanics used to avoid them. Boss firing pattern design ranges from "this is trivial" in the early stages to "this is stupid" in later ones.

Players are expected to dodge roll and have been given a jump and extra mid-air dodge, which seems good until you realize that there are so many bullets on-screen that dodging just put you onto another bullet. Add to that platforms that will put you on a bad plane if you tap jump for longer than a frame. Add to that platforms that shift left to right as they drift top to bottom. Add to that platforms that shoot at you. Add to that platforms that leave the stage and return later. Add to that platforms that buckle up and down and block shots. Add to that fall damage. Add to that some other stuff. All of this probably seemed cool on paper and feels terrible in-game. Not that they're bad ideas per se; it's that this game is a clusterbuck(shot) of things, about five pounds worth, crammed in a two-pound bag, none of it explained, justified, or necessary.

Also, the enemy bullets will randomly:
A: Hit you from nowhere 
B: Not hit you even though you walked right through a cloud of them 
C: Hit you even though you dodge rolled through it 
D: Hit you even though you blanked before it arrived 

And, since the hit will cost you a master round, these things are annoying. EnTG's Dragun felt awesome, climactic, epic, and FAIR. ExTG's Dragun feels like I want to become my money back because it is truly a shit of piece...don't get me started on Glocktopus.

Aside from the bullet issues, the controls just don't feel particularly good. This game moves at a much faster rate of speed than EnTG, while simultaneously having slower bullet firing from enemies. Consequently, clouds of bullets are floating around while you have to frantically leap around and find time to shoot, since dodge rolling cancels all other player action.

Minigames were added and unanimously suck. Angry Birds with bad set-ups, Pachinko, and Golf with bad set-ups. None of them belong here.

Forced cutscenes were added. Who thought that was a good idea? Dialogue is also frequently slow and unskippable.

Shops. They'll sell you stuff. That stuff will likely suck. What doesn't suck?
A: Homing Bullets
B: Bouncy Bullets
C: Angry Bullets
D: Then you win

It's really that simple. Flak Bullets, Fat Bullets, and Heavy Bullets don't  do much. +1 Bullets are 100% ineffectual. Ammolets = pointless & expensive. Heart containers are cost-prohibitive given master rounds. Boots of any type are literal trash. Magnet & Dog are useless. The Hot Lead family doesn't mean much since you already killed the target. Ditto the Gungeon Pepper, which won't even KO a micro-blob after four seconds. Blanks meant something in EnTG and were useful situationally. Blanks in ExTG don't get legs since there is either no reason to use them or a never-ending stream of crap sprayed across the screen, sure, save a handful for Dragun and Glocktopus, whatever. Good companions will cost you 3 floors worth of shells even with Disarming Personality, so get used to waving goodbye to those. Can't steal anything even though it makes perfect sense here, more so than EnTG- you're leaving and never coming back while the place falls in on itself, why again is the convict not going to rip off Bello and everyone else in the Underbreach? Great opportunity to make Bello a boss fight but nah.

No Rat fight anymore either, nor meaningful interactions with the R.R., who as I recall was fed to a snake that was then fed to a High Dragun...how is R.R. around again? They said the game isn't a sequel, then included all of the elements of a sequel, then didn't use those elements to create any cohesive narrative; everything just exists but don't ask too many questions or look behind the curtain. No-one's losing their minds in the hub room even though its never once explained how they expect to leave. They just carry on happily (or not) selling you stuff, which is one hell of an unintentional analogy.

There are just a series of rooms and a hand-held slot machine, which some might say is the distilled essence of a roguelike. For me, the original Rogue had more character than this game. ExTG gives an uncanny sense of looking at the Hollywood facade of a old western town: The building faces are there, actors and extras mill around, and behind it all is nothing but dust and a tired-ass heartless script meant to make somebody a buck or two. BARF.

⚔️ Hero Siege – A Loot-Filled Hack & Slash Adventure!

If you're a fan of action RPGs, dungeon crawling, endless loot, and smashing through hordes of enemies, Hero Siege is definitely worth checking out!

Hero Siege delivers an addictive blend of hack-and-slash combat, roguelike elements, and classic RPG progression. The gameplay is fast-paced, chaotic, and incredibly satisfying, with tons of enemies to fight, powerful bosses to defeat, and mountains of loot to collect.

One of the best things about the game is its character variety. There are multiple classes to experiment with, each offering different abilities, playstyles, and builds. Whether you prefer getting up close and personal with melee attacks or destroying enemies from a distance with powerful skills, there's plenty of room to find your own playstyle.

The loot system is another huge highlight. Finding better equipment, discovering powerful combinations, upgrading your character, and constantly improving your build makes every run feel rewarding. There's always something new to chase, and that classic "just one more run" feeling is dangerously addictive!

The pixel-art graphics give the game a charming retro atmosphere, while the combat effects, enemy designs, and environments keep things entertaining. It's especially fun when the screen fills with enemies, abilities, explosions, and ridiculous amounts of damage!

Of course, the game can get pretty challenging, and grinding for better equipment is part of the experience. But that's also what makes progression so satisfying. Playing solo is enjoyable, and teaming up with friends makes the adventure even more chaotic and entertaining.

Pros:

Fun and addictive hack-and-slash gameplay.

Lots of character classes and different builds.

Plenty of loot, equipment, and upgrades to discover.

Challenging bosses and huge enemy hordes.

Cool retro pixel-art style.

Great replayability and progression.

Multiplayer adds even more fun.

Final Verdict:

Hero Siege is a seriously entertaining action RPG for anyone who loves dungeon crawling, grinding for loot, experimenting with builds, and destroying endless waves of enemies. It has that classic RPG addiction where you keep telling yourself you'll stop after one more run… and somehow end up playing for another hour!

If you enjoy games like Diablo, roguelikes, and old-school pixel-art adventures, Hero Siege deserves a place in your library.

Hero Siege is a good (not perfect) ARPG soured by a landslide of (largely frivolous) negative reviews.
I've been deeply invested in ARPGs for around 25 years now, from Diablo II onwards. I'm not a "tourist" or whatever you want to call people that bounce off this genre after 30 hours.
I played the original Hero Siege 1, and I think the current iteration of the game is a massive improvement.
If you're considering playing this game but have doubts due to the negative reviews, I have some thoughts on that and I'll list them below.

Some reviews complain about how the game changed and it's no longer what they paid for back in 1984.
What those reviews are referring to is Hero Siege 1. That version of the game is still available, under Game Versions & Betas.
If the last version of Hero Siege 1 (5.9.6) isn't what you're looking for, you can also install literally any version of Hero Siege via the download_depot command, see: https://www.reddit.com/r/HeroSiege/comments/1lo7vbr/comment/ni6g8de/

Some reviews complain about paid classes.
There are currently 5 paid classes remaining (Illusionist, Exo, Butcher, Bard, and Prophet). Paid classes are gradually being phased out (as in: made free, with the old DLC being converted to skins). Marauder, Plague Doctor, Shield Lancer, and Jötunn became free with season 10.

Some reviews complain about Hero Siege Plus, specifically calling it "pay to win."
This is just false. It offers no gameplay advantage and is frankly a waste of money.
The only feature that arguably might have been called pay to win was the ability to see stat ranges, but literally nobody ever paid for that as it was simply made a part of the base game prior to launch.

Some reviews complain about bad performance.
These complaints are completely valid, the game has historically run like hot garbage. Thankfully this is not a permanent state the game is stuck in. Season 10 (and the upcoming season 11) have improved this substantially.

Some reviews complain about cheaters, anti-cheat, or getting banned.
These complaints are a mix of valid and total nonsense. It is true that the game has had issues with cheaters. It's also true that people have been banned incorrectly. It's false to suggest that the developers aren't doing anything about either of those issues, or that the game is in an unplayable state because of this.
I have literally watched people get falsely banned, open a ticket, and have their automated ban lifted by support in under an hour. Everything you do is logged, if your ban was a mistake you'll be fine.

Some reviews complain about paying for literally anything after buying the game.
I don't really know what to say to those people. The game costs like $3 on sale. Servers for a live service game cost upwards of $30,000 per month. The developers aren't going to work for free. They have to charge money for something to put food on the table. It's not a pay to win game, someone that spends $500 has effectively zero advantage over someone that spends $3. If you're looking for a pay to win ARPG, I can recommend Torchlight Infinite. In general Hero Siege is moving away from paid content.

Some reviews complain about Elias (the CEO) himself, which I mean.. fair, I guess.
He does have schizophrenic outbursts from time to time, and edgy opinions on a lot of different topics.
If you find that off-putting and don't believe him when he apologizes this might not be the game for you.

Hero Siege is overall an enjoyable game, but it has some major issues that are hard to overlook.

First, the game is full of bugs, especially once you reach mid-to-endgame content. A lot of the deeper character-building mechanics involve special items, passives, and interactions that depend on specific “skill tags.” Unfortunately, many of these interactions either don’t work properly or are poorly documented. This makes it extremely difficult to tell which passives and items are actually benefiting your character. You can spend a lot of time building around something only to discover that it barely does anything. This just covers the itemization bugs but there are a lot other annoying ones.

Second, I’ve had a very negative experience with the developers and the community management. False bans, no explanations. The official Discord can also be difficult to deal with instead of being a place where players can ask for help or discuss problems.

Third, It has "crossplay" among pc and mobile but it require re-purchasing everything again if you want to use both, including all dlcs, mtx, skins etc.

The game itself has a lot of potential and can be fun, but not in its current state.

I understand this is early access, and I’m not trying to be overly harsh just pointing out the issues that really stand out and should be noted. The game definitely has potential it just needs tighter execution and more polish.

Jeff The Killer: Horror Game is a first-person survival horror experience developed and published by SU Company Games that draws heavily from internet creepypasta culture while reshaping it into a slow-burning, stealth-focused nightmare. Rather than relying on excessive gore or constant jump scares, the game builds its horror through atmosphere, vulnerability, and the constant sense of being hunted. Players awaken inside an unfamiliar, abandoned house with no clear explanation, immediately placing them in a state of confusion and dread. From the outset, the game makes it clear that survival depends not on strength, but on caution, awareness, and the ability to stay one step ahead of an unpredictable threat.

The narrative is deliberately fragmented, unfolding through environmental details, scattered notes, and unsettling flashback sequences that hint at how the protagonist ended up trapped and why Jeff is stalking them. This indirect storytelling invites players to piece together the story themselves, encouraging careful exploration despite the ever-present danger. As more information comes to light, the story gradually shifts from simple survival to a more personal and psychological ordeal, adding emotional weight to the fear. The mystery surrounding Jeff’s motivations and the player’s role in the situation keeps tension high, making each discovery feel meaningful rather than merely decorative.

Gameplay places a strong emphasis on stealth and sound awareness. Jeff is not a passive enemy; he reacts dynamically to player movement and noise, turning even simple actions into calculated risks. Running carelessly, opening doors too loudly, or knocking over objects can draw fatal attention. Because direct confrontation is rarely a viable option, players must rely on hiding spots, smart positioning, and patience. This design reinforces a sense of helplessness that is central to the horror, as progress often means creeping through familiar rooms that feel increasingly unsafe the longer the game goes on.

Exploration is tightly interwoven with puzzle-solving, requiring players to search for keys, tools, and clues that unlock new areas of the house. These puzzles are generally grounded and intuitive, avoiding abstraction in favor of logic that fits the environment. Backtracking through previously explored spaces becomes increasingly tense as Jeff’s presence grows more aggressive, transforming once-quiet rooms into psychological minefields. Flashbacks occasionally interrupt the present timeline, offering disturbing glimpses into past events while also providing crucial context for the unfolding story.

Visually, the game adopts a restrained but effective aesthetic. The house is dimly lit, claustrophobic, and intentionally repetitive, reinforcing disorientation and the fear of being trapped. Shadows and narrow hallways are used to excellent effect, often obscuring threats just enough to make players question whether danger is real or imagined. Sound design plays an equally important role, with distant footsteps, sudden silences, and subtle audio cues signaling Jeff’s proximity. The lack of constant music allows ambient noise to dominate, making every creak and whisper feel significant.

One of the game’s more compelling features is its multiple-ending structure. Player choices, exploration thoroughness, and actions during key moments influence how the story concludes. This adds replay value and encourages players to engage more deeply with the environment rather than rushing toward escape. The branching outcomes also reinforce the idea that survival alone is not the only goal; understanding the truth behind the nightmare can be just as important as escaping it.

Despite its strengths, the game does show the rough edges typical of small indie productions. Animations and interactions can feel stiff at times, and the pacing may feel slow for players accustomed to constant action. However, these limitations rarely undermine the core experience, as the deliberate pace aligns well with the game’s focus on tension and suspense. In many ways, the minimalism enhances immersion, allowing atmosphere and fear to take center stage.

Overall, Jeff The Killer: Horror Game succeeds as a focused and unsettling horror experience that prioritizes dread, storytelling, and player vulnerability over spectacle. By transforming a well-known internet horror figure into a persistent, intelligent threat, SU Company Games delivers a game that feels tense from start to finish. For players who appreciate psychological horror, stealth-based survival, and atmospheric storytelling, this title offers a chilling journey that lingers long after the final ending is reached.

[url=https://youtube.com/live/70bDvqOlL6Q] You can find it here! [/url] I actually did end up beating the game unlike some others, so I am trying to give you the full rundown.

[h2] The Good [/h2]
[list]
    [*]There aren't any notable bugs, which is better than a lot of other games.
    [*]The game-play is genuinely engaging, albeit needing work (will address this later).
    [*]There is a decent level of replay-ability, albeit needing work (will address later).
    [*]The puzzle aspect is fairly linear, and of a reasonable difficulty.
    [*]I like the idea of the animated intro, especially with it being hand drawn. It adds something special that sets this game apart.
[/list]
[h2] The Bad [/h2]
[list]
    [*]I'm gonna be real, Jeff looks a little cheesy. I see the idea, but the current model gives mascot horror vibes vs the creepypasta many of us know and love. Maybe that's intentional, but not my thing. Mostly a personal gripe.
    [*]Jeff LOVES to camp. The lack of wandering can make certain areas extremely difficult to manage, although I do recognize some of this can be avoided by baiting him with sounds, then running past once he investigates. 
    [*]There are too many interactive drawers/points that are unnecessary. In all my runs, not once did something spawn in the top pull out drawers of the cabinets found around the house. Instead, they just acted as points I would accidentally click while trying to open the bottom cabinets, which got tiring at times. I also expected something to eventually spawn, but nothing ever did? I honestly hate "fluff" that exists to waste time, and there are already so many spots to check. Unless items start spawning there, I'd like to see the points of interest reduced a bit.
    [*]Honestly I'd like to see ALL points of interest reduced. Half of my play time was spent opening dozens of cabinets and drawers just to find absolutely nothing. You have to open everything regardless though, because key items can spawn anywhere. This also leads to some runs that feel completely useless. For example: [spoiler] In one run I had the hammer spawn under the stairs, then when I entered the wall next to it, I immediately was given a fuse and piano paper. Other runs there is no hammer there, nor anything in the wall. I also had one run where I collected all three fuses to unlock the powered door, and spoiler alert: There was nothing inside the LOCKED area. That whole run was honestly a bummer. [/spoiler] By reducing the POI, the player fatigue would dramatically decrease. Sometimes there can be TOO MUCH variation. There was also one absolutely ridiculous POI that I would have never found by myself. [spoiler] In the left corner of the purple room, there is a hidden alcove that I only noticed because Jeff walked out of it while I was standing there. I only had an item spawn there once, and nothing else exists in that tiny alcove. It feels a little purposeless. [/spoiler]
    [*] My escape just felt.. empty? Idk I didn't feel super rewarded outside of the relief from not having to continue playing. [spoiler] To be fair though, I did escape by car. I still had a few items such as a mysterious key i never found use for, so maybe an alternate ending would feel nicer. [/spoiler]
[/list]
[h2] The UGLY [/h2]
[list]
    [*]I gotta be real, Jeff's AI SUCKS. I was only able to complete the game on ghost mode after tons of failed attempts-- even on the easy difficulty. Not only does he heavily camp certain areas, but sometimes he is literally just standing there behind a closed door or around a corner. There is 0 indicator he is even nearby at times, so many runs are wasted by just casually opening a door to greet him face to face. 
    [*]Jeff has no blind spots. I swear. Trying to sneak past him or peek around corners felt futile. Most of the game I felt helpless, regardless of difficulty mode. I am not the most advanced gamer so I don't expect it to be a breeze, but easy mode should at least be beatable for the average gamer... And it didn't feel that way. This game is similar to granny, and although I have never played it I had a viewer in my stream who considers himself a pro. He actually bought this game to see if it was actually hard, or I just sucked. Even he felt like it was ridiculously difficult, leading him to throw in the towel. I'd love to see better difficulty balancing.
    [*]Some of these puzzles have... strange solutions to say the least. [spoiler] When confronted with freezer ice, I was confused as to why I couldn't break it with the hammer, but ultimately moved on. When I found the lighter, I assumed that was the answer to melt it, but nope! The actual answer is finding a bucket, filling it with sink water, then dumping it on the ice. Sure, it logically makes sense, but as a player it was confusing. Also, blasting the key at the stairs down with the shotgun? I almost gave up on the game before realizing that was the solution. Again, it logically makes sense once you know the answer, but as a player it is frustrating and confusing when you find a reasonable solution but are told it doesn't work. [/spoiler]
    [*]Not sure if this was a bug or intentional but [spoiler] When I found gasoline, a glowing yellow square appeared in one of the first floor rooms where you crawl out of the vent. This prompted me to pour it on the ground, meaning I later couldn't fill the car to escape. Here is the kicker though: I couldn't even do anything with the gas puddle. I tried the lighter, but nothing. Lure Jeff, nothing. I assume there is a reason to pour gas, but I couldn't find it, which left me only feeling frustrated. Ultimately I had to restart my run to add the gas to the car instead. [/spoiler]
    [*]Hiding spots are incredibly limited, as only safe rooms or lockers really seem to work. Even then, there are so many enclosed spaces that if Jeff enters the same as you you are cooked. You can't run past (I've tried), and hiding in a locker in front of him doesn't save you.
    [*]There are not enough audio clues to know where Jeff is at. If you hear him, it is too late.
    [*]To be honest, 99% of the problem is JUST Jeff and his AI. Fix this and it's golden.

Ended up refunding this game. It's not the worst thing I've played, and it does have things going for it, but I ultimately found it more frustrating than fun or scary. I didn't beat the game, and my gameplay was limited, but I could tell it wasn't going to be something I'd want to keep playing, and I know it'll be the same for others, so I do want to give it a detailed, fair review, based on my own thoughts. (Also, note, that I only played before the first patch came out, so maybe some of this got changed/fixed.)

First, the Pros:
- The opening cutscene is pretty cool. I wasn't expecting the hand drawn animation-style, and found it to be surprisingly atmospheric and expressive. Only critique I really have is that it does look a little unfinished, like it's the storyboard or rough draft. Still, I think it works. There's some other instances of hand drawn artwork that's also rather nice.

- The art direction overall is cohesive and atmospheric.

- The different death animations you get after running out of days/lives is neat, although some felt kind of goofy, like the buried alive one.

- Movement and interactions felt smooth. Key items were easy to find thanks to them being highlighted. 

The Cons:
- The gameplay is just Granny. This can be a pro or con depending on how much you like this style of gameplay, and unfortunately, it's not one for me. But I know it's not inherently bad, but it doesn't seem to try anything different with the genre. I understand that this is only a $5 game, though, and so one can't expect too much from it. It definitely reflects the price. However, I'm someone who never really liked the defenseless run and hide/pure stealth style of horror games, as I quickly find them more frustrating than scary or fun.

- Trying to hide or outrun Jeff is a major gamble. On lower difficulties he's either the same speed or slower than you, so generally you can outrun and LOS him if he sees you in the hallways. The problem is the rooms. You need to go into rooms to search for key items, but hiding spots feel *really* limited. You can really only hide in these yellow lockers, and some rooms don't have them. Crouching under desks don't seem to work, as he sees you anyway. Can't hide under beds or in cabinets/closets. Plus, he has no footsteps or any proper directional audio. This means that he could open the door to the room you're searching at any moment, without you hearing him coming, and get fucked. You have no time to get into a locker because he'll see you, and if it's a room without a locker at all, then you're just shit out of luck.

- Following that, you can't juke him. His reach is *long*. Getting cornered in a room that doesn't have any other exits or lockers means trying to juke him is your best bet, but I could never pull it off, as it felt like he could grab you from halfway across the room. I found this especially frustrating, as getting caught is an instant life loss and a restart from the basement.

- As previously mentioned, the audio design is basically nonexistant for Jeff. In a game like this, you kind of need to be able to hear where he's coming from and how far he is. All you get are his voicelines (his voice acting is...fine. You can tell his VA isn't experienced.) and the sounds of him opening and closing doors, which lacks clear directional queues. And as far as I could tell, he had *no* footsteps. Nothing to really help you gauge where he's coming from. More than once I got caught by him opening the door right in my face when I was trying to leave a room because I couldn't even hear him coming, causing me to lose a life/day.

- You can only hold one key item at a time. This is a little annoying but I wouldn't actually call it a con. As it does force you to plan your item management, making it one of the ways to express planning and problem-solving in this game. Which is cool! But the *real* issue is that dropping items seem to make sound no matter what. And making sound attracts Jeff's attention. There doesn't seem to be any way to quietly drop an item so that you can pick up another---you're *forced* to drop it and hope to god that he's far enough away to not hear it. And considering the previously mentioned under-baked sound design, it's really hard to gauge his actual range. And, no, for some reason you can't throw items far away. Which is weird, because you'd really think that kind of mechanic would be a no-brainer, right? Being able to throw items as a distraction would be a really nice way to introduce more skill-expression, problem-solving capabilities, and interactivity in general to the game.

- There's no lean function. Not a dealbreaker, but it's hard peeking around corners without risk of getting seen.

- Jeff's model is kinda goofy looking. Something about his face/head shape. It's kind of hard to take him seriously. Maybe it's just me, though.

- I don't find the game scary at all. It has a jumpscare when you're caught, but that's the only thing that ever kinda got me. And unearned jumpscares are almost always cheap as hell. But, to be fair, I'm pretty desensitized to horror games now so this opinion might differ for other people.

- Not much of a story, but I didn't finish the game so I can't fully speak on its actual quality. But based on what I played, it felt very...I don't know, like an excuse-plot? It doesn't feel like a very 'Jeff the killer' story to me. But, then again, he's a character that has always allowed anyone to do their own thing with, so I can't speak too much on this as a criticism, especially as I hadn't finished the game. So while my first impression of the story wasn't very, well, *impressed*, I don't think I could properly rate it due to not finishing it.

Overall:
I can't see much reason to play this game over others that do a much better, much more extensive job of expanding upon the Granny formula. This game really offers nothing to make it stand out, and clearly is relying mostly on the Jeff the Killer iconography to be the main draw. Still, it's only five bucks, and if you like this style of gameplay, you might be able to find something out of it, so I say it can be worth a shot. I do hope future updates improves and adds upon the game---if they do, maybe I'll give it another try sometime. I can tell the devs are skilled, and I think they could really go somewhere if they just continued to work at it. There's some potential here!

IdleOn — From a great game to a frustrating mess

I’m a long-time player and a heavy P2W spender. I’ve purchased practically every paid offer and upgrade the developer has released. I have no problem supporting a game I enjoy. Unfortunately, IdleOn has become increasingly frustrating.

1. Bugs and performance

The game is riddled with bugs, some of which directly block progression. Certain mechanics stop working on mobile, while others can destroy weeks of preparation.

Imagine waiting a week for a mechanic to recharge, only to encounter a bug that wastes your attempt. Now wait another week.

Meanwhile, the developer keeps releasing new content instead of prioritizing critical fixes.

Performance is another major issue. FPS drops, freezing and stuttering make certain activities practically unplayable. Sometimes FPS literally drops to zero.

What’s the point of adding content if the game struggles to run what already exists?

2. Forcing players to stay online 24/7

Keeping your PC online 24/7 is practically mandatory for reasonable progression. Without it, your progress can be hundreds of times slower.

This is supposed to be an idle game. Having a life outside it shouldn’t be a disadvantage.

3. Broken balance and P2W

The developer introduces overpowered P2W upgrades, then balances new content around increasingly ridiculous requirements. It’s an endless power creep cycle.

Endgame content is effectively balanced around heavy spenders.

Here’s another absurdity: you can purchase every upgrade, stack enormous bonuses and discover that the game itself cannot handle the numbers.

Your drop rate can become so high that you actually lose loot because of overflow. You’re paying to increase your drop rate, only to reach a point where the game cannot properly reward you.

4. Disrespect towards paying players

Tourney and raids(pure p2w activity) often feel like a lottery. Spending more money doesn’t necessarily improve your chances of winning.

But raids are even worse.

The hardest raid offers an exclusive pet with an original drop rate of 1 in 50. Even after purchasing everything available, you might win roughly once in ten attempts. That’s an expected 500 attempts per pet.

Apparently, that wasn’t difficult enough. The developer reduced the drop rate to 1 in 80 AND made the raid harder.

Don’t worry, though! You can always buy that exclusive pet for approximately $300.

You can spend hundreds supporting the game and still be unable to reliably obtain a reward. Then you’re offered the privilege of spending another $300.

This isn’t rewarding loyal customers. It’s exploiting their investment.

5. Playing the game has become a second job

There is so much content that keeping up with everything feels like actual work.

Every update adds more daily activities, progression systems and things you supposedly shouldn’t miss.

The developer seems focused on how much money players can spend, forgetting that paying players also have jobs and lives outside the game.

What’s the point of spending money to save time if I still need to dedicate an unreasonable amount of my free time to keeping up?

A game should compete for your free time, not demand that you sacrifice it.

6. FOMO and monetization

Limited-time offers, rotating shop items and exclusive bonuses create artificial urgency.

Some upgrades are so impactful that missing an offer can put you at a significant disadvantage.

You’re not buying something because you need it, but because you’re afraid you’ll regret not buying it later.

I don’t mind paying for a game, but I don’t want to be pressured by artificial scarcity.

7. Your previous progress can become worthless

You can spend months or years optimizing a system, only for a new update to change the balance or make your previous investments significantly less relevant.

Players should feel that their progress is accumulating, not that they’re running on a treadmill that keeps getting longer.

8. Enjoyable until World 7

To be fair, most of my complaints concern the endgame.

IdleOn is still a pretty enjoyable game up to and including World 6.

F2P progression is perfectly reasonable, and spending a little money makes things more convenient without being essential.

However, things change dramatically from World 7 onwards.

If you’re F2P and approaching World 7, I’d honestly recommend looking for another game.

Spending just $10 can potentially save months or even YEARS of grinding. Something is fundamentally wrong with that progression design.

P2W players don’t fare much better. Even after spending heavily, you still have to tolerate bugs, ridiculous RNG and content balanced around people who have purchased practically everything.

Final thoughts

I actually WANT to enjoy this game. I’ve invested considerable time and money into IdleOn and supported practically every P2W offer.

Instead, I feel that my time, money and loyalty are being taken for granted.

I understand that game development is difficult, but there is a difference between running a business and continuously pushing monetization while neglecting the product.

Fix the game. Optimize it. Respect players’ time. Stop making progression miserable just to introduce another monetization opportunity.

IdleOn increasingly feels like a game where the developer’s business model has become more important than the game itself.

And honestly, I wouldn’t be surprised if the developer gets offended and bans me for this review. That would be quite an ironic way to prove my point.
