A strange follow up to Dark Descent. Very little interaction with the world, creatures far less scary than those of the first game, limited puzzle solving, very linear progression and a convoluted story that leaves you confused rather than satisfied by the time the game wraps up. Has great voice acting and sound design, especially in the last moments, but beyond that very disappointing. Maybe a 3 out of 10.

I understand why fans of Amnesia the Dark Descent would be disappointed in this, but honestly on its own I thought that this was a really good walking sim. The atmosphere was really well done, I liked the story, and I liked the general setting of the game. And it was also very easy to get all the acheivments.

In terms of gameplay, you can tell that it's an Amnesia game but the things that made TDD great aren't present here. There's not that much in terms of horror OR atmosphere, so it's not actually that scary minus a few unexpected moments here and there. There's no resource management, and puzzles are extremely easy. If you're a simpleton then you'll be satisfied with the puzzling which boils down to finding a switch or carrying an item from one location to another. 

Technically speaking, the game either runs really well or like ass, with no in between. I think that there might be memory leaks, as it crashed during a loading section after I played for a while. If a new section gets opened up, it'll start to chug but I managed to get around that by going to graphics options, toggling any setting on/off, and then exiting out. 

Story-wise, the concept I think is actually really good. The setting is set in London in 1899, it starts in a manor house (like TDD), where you find hidden passageways and other dodgy stuff, and you start to put the pieces together about what's going on. As you progress through, the underground machine-world starts to open up, which is pretty cool but has quite a lot of repetition and because it's super linear, there isn't really any exploration. 

The execution of the story, however, is pretty poor in my opinion. You get inundated with "My Journal" entries which are designed to keep you on track but are not needed because of the simplicity of the puzzles and how linear the game is. The core of the story regarding Magnus becomes very apparent relatively early on, so there's not much in terms of mystery, environmental storytelling, or enemy variety that would give you anything else to think about.

The vast majority of sections can be sprinted through and ,despite me stopping to read every note I found (in an attempt to find a glimmer of something interesting), it only took me seven hours to complete.

Might be worth playing if you can get it really cheap, otherwise you'd be better off playing TDD or the Bunker.

Following up on a masterpiece like The Dark Descent takes immense courage, and while I truly appreciate the effort that went into this sequel, the execution ultimately falls flat. When I heard that Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs was being developed by The Chinese Room, the minds behind Dear Esther, published by Frictional Games, and serving as a sequel to a game I absolutely adored, I thought to myself: how could this possibly go wrong? 

As it turns out, it absolutely could, and it did. 

I actually have a major soft spot for walking simulators and deeply enjoyed atmospheric, narrative-driven titles like Dear Esther, Firewatch, and What Remains of Edith Finch. However, that specific gameplay philosophy completely clashes with the core identity of what makes an Amnesia game work.

The Dark Descent always prioritized active, mechanical gameplay. When that game wanted to show you a flashback, it would briefly flash the screen a blinding, ridiculous white, which is a pretty silly design choice in hindsight, but it kept you moving and viewing events in real time. In Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs, the entire experience slows to an absolute crawl just so you can stand around and listen to floating dialogue. The mechanical engagement is entirely stripped away. Gone is the inventory system, gone is the strict resource management, and gone is the signature character sanity meter. Because of this, you feel vastly less engaged as a player. Worst of all, the horror design relies far too heavily on cheap jump scares, completely abandoning the creeping, psychological dread that made the first game so brilliantly terrifying.

The story drops you into the life of Oswald Mandus, a wealthy industrialist in 1899 London who awakens from a feverish nightmare with severe amnesia. Spurred by the distant, echoing voices of his missing twin sons and guided by a mysterious figure on the telephone, you are forced to plunge into the underbelly of his estate to repair a colossal, incomprehensible machine. The plot naturally devolves into a repetitive loop where you are trying to solve an immediate industrial crisis while simultaneously trying to make sense of your own fractured past. The ultimate downfall is that I never truly understood the inciting incident. Why did the main character have these nightmares and suddenly embarked on this specific path right at the beginning? A second playthrough might help make sense of the narrative gaps, but honestly, I am not keen on replaying this anytime soon. Having just beaten the original game the other day undoubtedly skews my perspective, making the sudden lack of mechanical depth feel even more jarring.

This narrative repetition isn't saved by the environment or the enemies, either. The initial setting is completely fine when you are exploring the surface-level mansion. I honestly couldn't get enough of that grand, eerie upper estate. However, once the game forces you underground into the industrial meat-packing facilities, the environment becomes incredibly bland, monotonous, and uninspired. The musical score is just okay, but the industrial setting itself feels entirely underused. The enemies you encounter are profoundly dumb and simply aren't all that frightening. Despite a deeply unsettling premise on paper: deformed, mutant pig-hybrids patrolling the dark, the actual sound design and audio editing applied to them fail to deliver any real terror. They simply sound ridiculous rather than terrifying.

Ultimately, I don't regret playing Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs. It is a fascinating historical artifact, but The Chinese Room's minimalist gameplay philosophy is fundamentally a terrible match for the Amnesia franchise. I’ve heard rumors that Frictional Games struggled with their own direct follow-ups to their breakout hit, but I’ll have to judge those later installments for myself when I eventually get to them. It won't be anytime soon, though. For my own mental sake, I need to take a long, well-deserved break from this universe. As for The Chinese Room, this experience hasn't totally put me off their work. I still really want to play their recent horror title, Still Wakes the Deep. It looks like a maritime psychological nightmare right up my alley, especially since it isn't chained down by an already established IP. I just wish my current PC rig was powerful enough to actually run it...

As much as I love the Amnesia games, this one is a step back in many ways from The Dark Descent. The very convoluted storytelling, filled with highly sophisticated terms, also makes it hard to understand. There is also at least one corridor that simply vanishes after you go through it, and I don't know what to think about that. Notwithstanding these radical design choices, I still love A Machine for Pigs. It is immersive, extremely dark, and ends satisfactorily with some of the best monologues and music I have ever heard in a game.

It's undoubtedly an Amnesia game in spirit, and it's actually rather good; the issue is that The Chinese Room switched to a walking sim with low stakes away from a tense resource management game. For a walking sim it's not bad, but for Amnesia it's not ideal.

A Machine for Pigs is without a doubt one of the best stories I have ever encountered in a game. It is a testament to The Chinese Room's mastery at storytelling, and I urge anyone who loves a good story to pick this game up when it goes on sale. It is a remarkable experience.

But for some reason, The Chinese Room have been given two franchises, World of Darkness and Amnesia, games that both have depth in gameplay. And Oh Boy, The Chinese Room is NOT that good at gameplay.

A Machine for Pigs is a walking atmospheric sim, where you very, VERY frequently have to stop to read your characters mental thoughts, and notes on the ground. I like it, it's fun. As a survival horror game, it sucks, absolutely. Almost all (And my almost I mean genuinely like 90%, not exaggerating) mechanics that make dark descent a great game and classic have been removed. Sanity management, item management, roaming enemies, fuel management, non-linear level design, all of it is gone. There isn't even an inventory or sanity system at all. The only reason you know it is an amnesia game is because it looks like amnesia, and has mentions of Vitae, though even that is scarce.

If you are coming here after playing the Dark Descent, or The Bunker, and are expecting a similar experience, don't, It's not worth it.

If you are coming here after Soma, Still Wakes the Deep, or maybe Rebirth, and you want a game with a great story, absolutely buy this game. The Chinese Room are in my opinion the single best storytellers in the horror gaming genre. This game will not disappoint.

[b]Bottom line[/b]: If you are looking to play this because you liked ATDD and don't want to miss any lore... You don't need to bother. The story doesn't seem to add any relevant lore from what I can tell.

🐷 Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs — мрачная атмосфера, странная история и слишком мало настоящего ужаса. 6.5/10 🕯️

Есть игры, которые пугают тебя настолько, что после выключения хочется проверить, точно ли в коридоре никого нет.

A Machine for Pigs немного другая.

Она скорее заставляет чувствовать себя неуютно, чем действительно пугает.

Я запускал её с ожиданием получить ещё одну безумную хоррор-историю во вселенной Amnesia. И в плане атмосферы игра действительно смогла меня зацепить.

Но чем дальше я проходил, тем сильнее появлялось ощущение, что разработчики сделали ставку на атмосферу, а всё остальное отправили куда-то в подвал. 💀

🔥 Атмосфера и визуал

✅ Вот здесь игра действительно хороша. Лондон конца XIX века, мрачные помещения, фабрики, коридоры и постоянное ощущение чего-то неправильного.

✅ Звуковое сопровождение отлично работает на атмосферу. Скрипы, шум механизмов и странные звуки за стенами создают постоянное напряжение.

✅ Само окружение выглядит достаточно детализированным и запоминающимся. Некоторые локации действительно хочется рассматривать.

❌ Но атмосфера постепенно перестаёт удивлять.

Ты идёшь по очередному тёмному коридору и уже примерно понимаешь, что тебя ждёт впереди.

👹 Хоррор

И вот тут начинаются проблемы.

Если вы ждёте от игры напряжения уровня первой Amnesia, можно слегка разочароваться.

❌ Исследования стало меньше.

❌ Механик стало меньше.

❌ Ощущение беспомощности уже не такое сильное.

❌ Многие моменты больше рассказывают историю, чем заставляют тебя бояться.

И самое главное — игра слишком часто ведёт тебя за руку.

Вместо ощущения:

«Чёрт, куда мне идти и что здесь происходит?»

получаешь:

«Ладно, очевидно, мне нужно идти дальше по этому коридору».

📖 Сюжет

Зато история здесь намного интереснее, чем может показаться в начале.

Постепенно раскрывается довольно мрачная и странная история, связанная с семьёй, индустриализацией, войной и последствиями человеческой одержимости собственными идеями.

Некоторые сюжетные моменты действительно заставляют задуматься.

Но подача местами слишком запутанная, а темп повествования может сильно проседать.

Ты вроде понимаешь, что происходящее важно...

Но эмоционально не всегда получается зацепиться за происходящее.

⚙️ Главная проблема

Мне кажется, A Machine for Pigs слишком сильно пожертвовала игровыми механиками ради повествования.

Это уже не совсем тот хоррор, где ты постоянно исследуешь окружение, решаешь загадки и пытаешься выжить.

Скорее это атмосферное путешествие по довольно неприятному миру, которое периодически напоминает:

«Не забывай, что вообще-то это хоррор». 💀

И именно поэтому я не могу поставить ей высокий балл.

I didn't mind the lack of interaction or the anemic puzzles or even the overwritten dialogue, I simply cannot recommend it because it could barely run.  It crashed between every level transition and half the time while saving or loading.  There is a NoSteam.exe in the game folder that works better, but the fact that you have to dig to find it to make the game work should say enough.

Technical Issues. People complain about the game being too dark. The reality is that this game uses a "per level" shader for gamma. The result is that after setting gamma, you need to reset it each level. Since the gamma is actually a shader, this then causes stutters and swinging frame rates.

Gameplay. People have called this a "walking simulator" - sadly this is true. I have not played the previous Amnesia game, but have plenty of experience of other titles. There is hardly any gameplay here - it is more of a (barely) interactive movie. There is almost no exploration or choice here, you are "funneled" to the next encouter - a door will be mysteriously locked until you do something, then you will be channeled to the next area. There are no puzzles, and with no invetory, you pick up thing and put thing in slot. The "thing" is often just in the next room. Gameplay also includes "hunt the pixel" - find the place to click to get event to happen.

Plot. Unlike a game like say "The Medium" which some have also critized as a walking sim - the plot is very basic. You wake up with Amnesia and try to find the missing children. The plot is mostly expoused through a few audtio logs and some notes which you are channeld towards.

Pretentious. The devs are trying to put metaphores in via the artworks, music and amiguity as to your mental state. It just comes accross as an overwrought mess, as if someone just clicked a  bucket list of things a horror game should do.

One good thing is the art direction. Some of the areas could look good, but this is ruined by their messed up "home brew" gamma and color settings - so in the end getting to a new areas is often met with the frustation of messed up visuals.

Conclusion. Don't waste your time, there are so many better offerings. I spent 5-6 hours on this and felt done dirty and that I'd wasted my time.

So it is a spiderweb software game. You know what that is if you are here, if not it is a game made by a dude, his wife, and a handful of people who get contracted on occasion, it will be a very classical style of computer RPG, and the writing will have a particular flavor to it, a love more of talking about the world itself and the relationship those individuals have to the world/political situation at large. This game hits all of those notes but tragically experimented in a way that was not the best received. 

This game is not pretty, even by Spiderweb standards because the design is meant to quickly and accurately communicate the state of the battlefield, it is a wonderfully set up map, if you are judging it as more of a tabletop RPG encounter, this is built for you to look at the field, know everything and make sure you can learn what all the pieces on the board do so that you can have a handful of short but vicious fights on that map, achieve what you went there to do, and move on to the next thing you need to do, the next decision you need to make. 

Because that is what this game is, political and moral choices that can come with consequences down the road  broken up by some pretty clean fights and good pacing (as long as you don't drag your feet too much). It is damned good in my book, I enjoyed all the time I put in to my playthrough, grew to enjoy the primary movers and shakers in the plot, and appreciate the twists some of the factions themselves have. It is a great game, but unfortunately it may be the last time Spiderweb software really gets to try making something new. 

Give it a buy at a price that you'd feel fine with 40+ hours of neatly paced indie CRPG fun if you are being a bit of a completionist , or better yet play the demo that covers about 1/6th-ish of the game and decide that price yourself and since every spiderweb software game has a similarly generous demo, give them a try too if you like this one, maybe Avernum or Geneforge is more your speed than this and that's A-Okay, but give Jeff Vogel your money for his and his wife's tireless efforts for over 30 years to make fun budget CRPGs.

Developed and published by Spiderweb Software, Queen's Wish: The Conqueror is a role-playing game that proudly embraces the traditions of classic computer RPGs while delivering a surprisingly fresh take on empire-building and personal choice. Instead of placing players in the role of a destined hero saving the world, the game casts you as the child of the Queen of Haven, sent to a distant and rebellious frontier colony with the task of restoring the empire's influence. What initially appears to be a straightforward mission quickly becomes a complex political journey where loyalty, ambition, and morality constantly collide. Rather than dictating a single path, the narrative encourages players to decide what kind of leader they want to become. You can faithfully expand your mother's rule, sympathize with local factions, pursue diplomacy, or carve out an entirely independent future, making every major decision feel like it carries genuine political and personal weight.

One of the game's strongest qualities is the remarkable amount of freedom it gives players throughout the campaign. Exploration is never treated as a simple checklist but instead serves as the foundation of the experience. The world is filled with ancient ruins, isolated villages, fortified enemy strongholds, dangerous wilderness, and hidden secrets that reward those willing to venture off the main path. Side quests are plentiful and often provide meaningful stories rather than simple errands, introducing memorable characters and difficult choices that further enrich the setting. The branching structure ensures that many situations can unfold differently depending on your actions, encouraging multiple playthroughs to discover alternate alliances, story developments, and endings. This emphasis on player agency gives the adventure lasting replay value and creates the satisfying feeling that your version of the story truly belongs to you.

Combat follows a turn-based tactical format that rewards thoughtful planning instead of quick reflexes. Battles require careful positioning, proper use of character abilities, and efficient management of resources, making every encounter feel like a strategic puzzle. Character progression offers a high degree of flexibility, allowing players to customize skills, experiment with different party builds, and even reshape their strategies as the campaign evolves. Another standout feature is the fortress management system, which ties directly into the central theme of reclaiming territory. As you conquer and rebuild settlements, you unlock valuable improvements that strengthen your forces, expand available resources, and provide lasting advantages throughout the campaign. These mechanics give conquest meaningful purpose beyond simply advancing the story, creating a rewarding balance between exploration, combat, and long-term planning.

Although the visuals are modest by modern standards, they serve the game's design well by emphasizing clarity over spectacle. The isometric environments are easy to navigate, while the straightforward presentation allows players to focus on tactical decisions and exploration instead of flashy visual effects. The soundtrack supports the fantasy atmosphere with understated compositions that complement the world without overwhelming it. More importantly, Spiderweb Software's writing and world-building carry the experience. The setting is populated with distinctive cultures, political conflicts, and believable personalities that avoid relying entirely on familiar fantasy clichés. Conversations frequently reveal new layers of history, diplomacy, and family tension, making the game's world feel alive despite its minimalist presentation.

Queen's Wish: The Conqueror does demand patience from its audience. Its old-school interface, slower pacing, and extensive dialogue may feel intimidating to players expecting a streamlined modern RPG, while the visual presentation lacks the polish found in higher-budget productions. Some sections involve revisiting previously explored locations, and the sheer amount of reading may not appeal to everyone. However, for players who appreciate deep role-playing systems, meaningful choices, and strategic gameplay, these minor shortcomings are easily outweighed by the game's exceptional depth. It delivers a rewarding adventure that values player freedom above all else, proving that strong writing, intelligent design, and meaningful decision-making remain just as compelling as technical spectacle. It stands as one of Spiderweb Software's finest examples of classic role-playing craftsmanship and a memorable experience for fans of thoughtful fantasy RPGs.

Queen's Wish is a tactical turn-based RPG about conquering a country. It is fine, but I was disappointed with it.

Like all Spiderweb games, this one is a solid if non-ambitious RPG. I think when people look at screenshots, they expect those games to be an overcomplicated verbose mess like so many indie RPGs. They are not - they're cohesive and laconic (but not small!) and well put together. There are no walls of text or endless lists of modifiers, they're straight to the point. Maybe they're too simple to justify a second playthrough, but not every RPG should be an infinitely replayable colossus.

Queen's Wish is even simpler than some other games from the studio: the character progression system is very forgiving, almost all characters have access to all options, and you can freely respec them. The real progression and customization come from the equipment you find, and in this regard the game feels much more like a tactics game with RPG elements. Still, it has a somewhat non-linear story. Like many modern "big" RPGs, this one casts you as an authority figure who mostly doesn't use this authority. Unlike those other games, this one justifies this situation well. The game may feel a little bit formulaic, as every quest involves you completing a dungeon, and every dungeon has to be completed in one go - enemies respawn if you come back. It's a sensible gameplay concession even if it often makes little sense in terms of story, but it does make you feel like you're playing tactics game instead of roleplaying adventure.

So in general, it's fine. Like most Spiderweb games, it feels like a comfortable 6/10 game, and I think people should play those - you won't get a lot of high notes here, but also nothing feels bad. Except here, some things did feel bad. This game is somewhat novel for the company, and so it has UI issues and bugs, making it significantly less polished than their other games. Runes are the main way to customize your character, and the way you buy, insert, and replace those runes is extremely annoying. I had some side quests that couldn't be completed for some reason, and I endured that - but then one of the main quests bugged out on me. So I haven't finished the game, even though I came quite close. This put the game into 4/10 territory for me. Sad!

Overall, it still isn't that bad as a whole, but if you have to skip one Spiderweb game - skip this one.

I'm somewhat obsessed with all the Spiderweb Software game series, and of late, Queen's Wish has been on the top of my list of their games. 

There's everything here I've been looking for in a good RPG for years now. It has excellent writing and a compelling story with amazing world building, which is my personal biggest driver (and is true for all of their other franchises), and the game loop is just right. Tactical combat is turn based and fast paced with reasonable depth and no extraneous elements. Exploration is satisfying and the world is large and feels very lived in (and the fast travel option becomes more and more useful as the game progresses). There is a lot of content, yet none of it feels like it's there just as filler (there is some repetition in mine-cleansing quests, but it's not too problematic).

What I also like is that character progression and equipment procurement is meaningful. Each level brings much needed ability increases, and 1 added level might make a difference between a quest being possible to complete or not just yet. Equipment is rare and relatively expensive, so there's no meaningless looting here - every find is useful.

Base and kingdom building adds one more layer, and is well integrated with the questing and exploration aspects of the game. There's an interdependence between personal quests and the state of your colonies that feels natural and adds to the overall experience in a way which makes it larger than the sum of its parts. Evolving familial and personal connections are a cherry on top.

There's also an elephant in the room with these games. For what it is, I find the graphics quite compelling though. Queen's Wish doesn't try to be flashy (on the contrary, it embraces its scrappiness), but I find the graphics appealing nevertheless, and they are very readable and quite varied. No sprite or character portrait here will win an art contest, but there's many little details scattered throughout the world, and each tells a story, which to me is, again, the most important thing in a game like this.

Finally, I'll add that I'm playing this mostly on the Steam Deck, and it's great! Almost all game text is presented in dialog boxes that take a relatively small central portion of the screen, which works great with Steam Deck's ability to toggle zoom in and out on a mappable key press. I set the display zoom to 220% is settings which allows me to instantly zoom into the text portion for dialogs and for reading tool tips on the small screen. I mapped the left trackpad to an on-screen menu with numbers 1 through 6 which I also positioned centrally, so it appears overlayed on top of text popups for choosing dialog options. Loaded up with all Spiderweb games, my Steam Deck is almost like a specialized ebook reader for choose-your-own-adventure books filled with tight tactical combat. I love it!

To me, these games are like cozy adventure books with surprisingly compelling, deep and multifaceted stories, and Queen's Wish is unique among them.

I recommend this game for its writing, story, fort building mechanics, and the many choices it presents to the player.  Queen's Wish:  The Conqueror has a relatively unique premise and story line and the writing is of excellent quality.

You take on the role of the youngest member of Haven's royal house and are tasked with restoring Haven's rule over the three countries continent of Sacramentum.  Ultimately, this requires convincing a faction within each country to sign a treaties of vassalage within Haven.  This process involves finding out what the faction wants and completing a quest or quests to give it to them.  There is also the question of what caused a great calamity that drove the vast majority of Haven's forces and institutions off of the continent.  Solving this mystery is another key element of the game.  Political and economic decisions and considerations thus constitute a major part of the story, alongside the traditional fantasy elements of the game.

The fort building is a satisfying element that adds yet more uniqueness to Queen's Wish: The Conqueror.  Much of the best equipment in the game is obtained through stores built in your very own forts.  As you explore Sacramentum, you find the ruins of Haven's old forts and are tasked with restoring them.  Within each fort you can build various stores, along with other things, including barracks, bakeries, and distilleries.  The more stores that you have built across all of your forts, the better the items that the merchants can sell to you.  There is plenty of loot in dungeons and other locations and vendors exist outside of the forts, but much of the best equipment is only available if you build up Haven's forts.  Building up the forts and watching them turn into bustling a mini-towns is entertaining and provides a visible indication of progress for the main quest line.

The graphics and sound effects are basic, but adequate enough for the game.  The combat mechanics and character progression, while not extremely deep, are also sufficient.  If you are looking for an RPG with deep gameplay and combat mechanics and detailed character progression then this game is unlikely to fulfill those desires.  However, if you want to play a CRPG with an interesting story that presents that player with a large number of decisions and choices then this game is a good option.  The Queen's Wish series is more niche than the Geneforge series, but still good.

The true draw of Queen's Wish:  The Conqueror comes in the form of the world building, the writing, the story line itself, the fort building mechanics, and the fact that the player is presented with numerous choices throughout the game on a variety of topics and issues.

QW:tC is a party-based RPG in which you play the role of a young prince attempting to restore diplomatic relations with three countries located on a island continent. You will explore the over-world, build bases, interact with NPCs and experience all of the other standard stuff. 

"Dungeons" typically take the form of mines, which produce resources every set number of turns. You may usually enter and exit dungeons at your discretion, though any common foes you beat will re-spawn until the boss in defeated. Since no experience is earned by defeating individual monsters, it is of interest to beat the dungeon in one go.

At level-up you may allocate (and reallocate) skill points into each of your four characters' skill trees. The skill trees largely represent attack, magic, and healing/support, with a passive bonus provided at each tier up the tree within each school. While this system initially looks interesting, you will quickly realize that the best way to build all characters is nearly identically, so all characters get these passive bonuses. 

Upon entering any of your forts, your health and energy will be filled. Of particular note, is that only 1 energy is replenished after each battle, so the optimal strategy outside of boss fights is to only use 1 or 2 energy to heal or to summon a few pieces of fodder; otherwise you will be out of energy when you get to the boss. In combination with the design of the skill trees, you will therefore quickly realize that the best build is four nearly identical archers. Why go melee when you can snipe everything? Why use magic when ranged is almost as good and doesn't cost energy? 

The battles themselves also leave much to be desired tactically. Ranged can shoot a distant target when engaged with enemy melee for some reason. You can almost always just kite and shoot, staying out of harms way indefinitely. There is no flanking. You can even disengage and shoot that target the same turn. All of this combines to make fights extremely repetitive and boring. The lack of enemy diversity (plus their propensity to poison you) makes things tedious.

There is some level of base-building and this mechanic serves as the primary method through which you get better gear. Unique rings and necklaces may be found in the over-world, but all other gear is obtained by building duplicate structures across your various forts. Unfortunately, these buildings also cost resources to maintain, so your income may actually go negative. I personally hated this mechanic. This isn't a 4x game where these sorts of balances are needed. On the whole however, I enjoyed leveling up my forts and getting access to better gear. Of course all of the buildings looked identical for some reason, so you had to constantly walk around your forts into multiple buildings if you forgot which was which (seriously how hard would it have been to tag these somehow).

Summary: The storytelling, backstories, and world environment are above-average, as may be expected from Spiderweb. Unfortunately everything else here is lacking and I decided to quit about 65% (I think) of the way through. I think with some rework a lot of these somewhat novel systems could work, but as it stands I sadly cannot recommend.

Overall: 4.5/10

Queen's Wish follows a trend that I have observed from Spiderweb Software in that it simplifies from previous games.  In some cases this simplification has been a good thing, but Queen's Wish just takes it too far.  Character building and customization is drastically scaled back.  A single skill point awarded at each level up can go into skills that hold a maximum of two points, one skill point to unlock, and perhaps one more for a modest boost to the effectiveness of the skill.  That's literally all the character building you get to do.  Loot does not drop from enemies, nor do you earn experience from killing them.  Experience only comes from completing quests, and loot only from pre-defined loot boxes and events.  The number of NPCs you can actually interact with is drastically scaled back from previous games, with most being just props for the setting (guards and townspeople that give you one line if you click on them).
In exchange, we get a simple system for conquering territory and rebuilding forts.  When you regain a territory, the few people in a city you can actually interact with will acknowledge this and usually one will provide resources as a reward.  You can use these resources to rebuild any forts you have reclaimed and add shops to them, which increases your access to items or provides bonuses in combat depending on what you build.  This isn't a bad idea, but like the rest of the game the implementation is very basic.
Overall?  Simpler can be better, but Queen's Wish takes this concept much too far.  We've arrived at a point where simple equals boring.  Avoid this one, look to the Avernum series instead.

As this will be Jeff's last mainline series before he retires, he really wanted to make changes to the classic rpg formula he's done since 1994. It is rather hit and miss on these choices but overall I think it is for the better. Things are far more streamlined, party members can respec anytime within a friendly fort. The concept of having to clear a dungeon in one go is one I have mixed feelings about. While it does make some sense that a dungeon would replenish until the boss is defeated, conserving resources and having that balance so you're not too weak to defeat the boss is a very fine one between exciting resource management or frustration.

The main feature that I think does work are the fort building. Claiming mines and regions to have the resources pouring in is very satisfying and you really feel the progression of your expanding empire. Choosing between different factions was well done too and I found all the vassal states interesting. It's also neat that you can recruit party members of those respective cultures once you have a fort built in their lands. I highly recommend having one of each in your party, as their cultural abilities are all quite useful and can fulfill different roles.

As fort building is the main feature, you'll often be upgrading your forts to gain access to the best gear instead of dungeon crawling, though there are some neat item rewards too. In some ways it feels off, where by the time I gained some unique and cool gear, they were completely irrelevant compared to the stuff I could build in a fort with crafting upgrades. Some tweaking on that would be good for the sequels.

Combat wise it tends to be mixed as it is for all Spiderweb Software games. I found the amount of status effects was a bit much as there were many encounters where you were constantly stunned or debuffed, and it's never fun to sit there helplessly unable to do anything. You never would have enough items or energy to constantly remove them all so it could be annoying. In the last area I actually switched to casual as I found the HP bloat and constant status effects killing my enjoyment.

So I wholeheartedly think this game is worth it and I am interested to see Queen's Wish 2 and 3. Two last tips. Your prince/princess character has some cultural abilities, invest in them as they are very powerful and can make the game work easier for you. Second tip,  you can quick travel to any location once you've discovered it on the world map. Saves you a lot of time later on, and your resource income will keep flowing in anyway!

Excellent Spiderweb Studios game.  Isometric turn based low graphics indie type game.   Like all of their releases it is very well designed but people who want snazzy graphics, an easy game, or real time combat will be disappointed.  

This game differs from a lot of other releases in that almost all experience is tied to completing quests.  Quests are not open world but rather require taking out a boss or completing a key event in an instanced dungeon in one go (otherwise the boss calls in reinforcements and the earlier encounters respawn).  This makes a lot of the challenges one of resource management and attrition rather than just being able to take a powerful fight at full resources.

Other Key differences include the building and upgrading of a system of forts and the diplomacy required in obtaining vassals.  There are almost no random items just laying around, most items are construction materials used to upgrade forts and shops that you then buy from, there are a few key chests in most dungeons and a few contain powerful or useful items.

The game is very sandboxy you have a lot of freedom in what you do, what order you do it, ect even though there is a bit of structure to it.  You have a lot of leeway in what you do and just have to deal with the consequences.  Likewise you have a rich world to interact with but not a lot of scripted storylines to ride along.

If you have played other spiderweb games and enjoyed them I would definitely recommend them, if you like isometric rpgs in general and the turn based nature of the game isn't a problem for you I would definitely recommend giving it a try as well.

I am really starting to fear that these games are slowly going the way of other games these days: streamlining and stripping themselves down in order to appeal to a wider audience, while slowly changing from what the core fan base likes. As demonstrated with nearly every game that has attempted this, it doesn't usually end well. The old fans become more and more jaded as each change is made, and it is never quite what the new players really want in a game.

Don't get me wrong, I had fun playing this game, enough fun to accumulate 38 hours and complete it and all the side quests I could find. However, it was not nearly as much fun as I had playing Avernum, Geneforge, or even Avadon. The Avadon series is what first started to worry me, the changes it made to mana/energy usage, the introduction of classes with skill trees, etc. But this isn't about those games. Those games were still a lot of fun, but an early warning.

In Queen's Wish, I never really felt like I was playing my own character. 20 skill points over the entire game to put into either Combat, Support, or Magic, and they aren't even really skill trees. I was actually super confused when I first started playing, looking for where I could change the class of my main character. My stomach sank when I realized that there were only 9 skills/spells in each category, and that adding in an extra skill point only slightly improved it in terms of % to hit, % damage, etc. Also, around 3 of those in each category is a single point passive buff.

I feel like this choice of character creation took away a lot from the game. With Avadon it was right at the edge, but with Queen's Wish I think it has gone a little bit too far. But then to remove finding items in anything other than chests, to remove XP from kills but not remove overland enemies that you normally farmed, to make dungeons constantly refill with enemies unless you defeat the boss. I dunno, it all felt annoying to deal with.

It seems like a lot of this was done to help simplify and streamline combat. Yet some truly odd choices were made regarding combat. Arrows will at times fly super slow, you need to wait for your character to make an attack animation and for the enemy to make an 'I was hit' animation, for you to move onto the next turn. While the upgraded models and animations are nice, it slowed down what was seemingly supposed to be a sped up combat. Seems a bit odd, and again, I found it a bit annoying. There is also no way of knowing who is going when in combat, and no way to improve your odds of going first other than by wearing lighter armor.

Well anyways, I finished the game and got most of the achievement when I realized you could save right at the end of each nation and just do what either side there asked you to do, getting both achievements super easy. It seemed like in the older games you made your sort of 'final choice' a lot earlier into the game, and had to live with it for several hours as you progressed. This created replay value to see what the other sides and endings had to offer. With this game nothing really changes until you reach the last main quest for each area. This was especially noticeable with the Arhiel area, where there isn't even really a faction with quests opposite the Trench Towns until you get to the final city. I know it is scummy to save and get the achievements like that, but I honestly have absolutely no inclination to replay this game over at all.

And there's a reason the trailer mostly features you walking through the Titanic without much gameplay - because there isn't much. The game description is VERY misleading. There's no puzzles, there's no strategy, there's no thinking required. It's very buggy - I had to lower all my settings to stop the lagging despite having a good gaming laptop that meets all requirements. 

Even the game mechanics feels like AI went "hey these features are in a lot of good games" without understanding how they work. There is map menu with no actual map. There is a notebook with a notes and facts section that is very underused. There's an inventory that is ignored until the last 10 minutes of the game. The flashlight you're given at the start is given a limitation on its use (of something like 999,999,999 seconds) even though you really don't need the flashlight in game at all. Even the storyline doesn't make sense for a Titanic story. Why are we the going Egyptian curse route?

But the biggest red flag for me is that there are no credits listed in this game whatsoever. I had a quick google of the publisher when I finished the game and even their website is mostly broken (all tabs and links takes you to a 404 not found page) and looks not real.

Just to end on a semi-positive note, I did appreciate the little facts and biographies of some of the real people on the Titanic popping up as you (briefly) meet their characters. This is not the Titanic escape simulator you may be looking for—at least not in its current state.

I want to make it clear from the start that I do not think this is a bad project. In fact, I think there is a lot of potential here, and it is a project worth supporting. However, in its current state, I would personally recommend waiting for further updates and refinement before buying it if you are specifically looking for an immersive Titanic escape simulator.

At the moment, the game feels unfinished. It is quite glitchy, many of the puzzles feel substandard, and the story needs significant refinement. The central plot is actually interesting, but everything develops so quickly that it never has enough time to gain the emotional weight it could have.

One of the biggest problems for me is the atmosphere aboard the ship. Throughout much of the game, Titanic feels more like a ghost ship than an ocean liner carrying passengers on her maiden voyage. The NPCs generally stand around without much purpose, and very few of them make the ship feel genuinely inhabited.

Considering that more than 2,200 people were aboard Titanic, the ship feels strangely empty and lifeless. I obviously would not expect thousands of individually simulated NPCs, but there needs to be a much stronger illusion of a crowded passenger liner. More background activity, movement, conversations, crew members performing tasks and passengers going about their routines would make an enormous difference.

Because of this, I never really experienced the sense of immersion or urgency I expected. The game is built around experiencing and escaping the Titanic disaster, but at present it feels much more like a Titanic-themed adventure game than an actual simulator.

My biggest recommendation to the developers would be to slow everything down considerably.

The real Titanic took approximately two hours and forty minutes to sink after striking the iceberg. That provides an enormous opportunity for storytelling, exploration, changing environments, NPC interactions, developing panic, difficult decisions and gradually increasing tension.

The sinking does not necessarily have to occur in real time, but allowing the disaster to unfold much more gradually would make the experience far more powerful. There should be time for the player to notice that something is wrong before the full seriousness of the situation becomes apparent. Corridors could gradually become inaccessible, passengers could begin reacting differently, crew members could receive conflicting instructions, lifeboats could slowly begin launching, and the atmosphere could transition naturally from confusion to concern and eventually panic.

There is also tremendous potential before the iceberg collision.

Titanic had already been on her maiden voyage for several days before the collision, which gives the developers plenty of room to expand the story before the disaster begins. Even if only part of that voyage were represented, the player could spend considerably more time exploring the ship, meeting characters and becoming familiar with the environment.

That would also give the main story more weight. If the player has spent time speaking to certain passengers, seeing crew members repeatedly, visiting particular areas and becoming familiar with life aboard the ship, then seeing those same places and people during the sinking would have far greater emotional impact.

The dialogue also needs refinement. Many conversations do not sound natural and sometimes feel noticeably AI-generated, while several of the voices sound synthetic.

I have no problem with developers using AI-generated content, particularly for an ambitious project where resources may be limited, but generated material still needs careful editing and refinement. AI can be a useful development tool, but the final dialogue should feel as though actual people are speaking rather than characters simply delivering information to the player.

I would also suggest being more restrained when using real historical people as major characters.

Titanic was a genuine human tragedy involving real people and families. I think fictional characters could carry most of the game's story while real historical figures remain part of the background or appear where historically appropriate. This would give the writers far more creative freedom while avoiding the need to invent too much dialogue, personality or behaviour for people who actually existed.

Despite all of these criticisms, I do see something worthwhile here.

The developers have chosen an incredibly ambitious setting. Titanic itself offers enormous possibilities for exploration, environmental storytelling, survival mechanics and historical immersion. The foundation is there, but I think the game needs considerably more development before it fully delivers on that potential.

More active NPCs, stronger dialogue, improved puzzles, additional pre-sinking story content, a slower and more detailed sinking sequence, better atmosphere and further technical refinement could transform the experience.

So my recommendation is somewhat complicated:

At its current stage, I would wait for further updates if you are looking for a polished Titanic simulator.

However, I would not dismiss the game or the developers behind it. This is a project I would like to see continue developing, and I would absolutely reconsider my recommendation as the game improves.

There is something here worth supporting. It simply needs more time and refinement before it becomes the experience it has the potential to be.

Titanic: Escape Simulator is a historically fascinating experience, even if it comes with some serious baggage. First and foremost, the optimization is truly horrendous. If I didn't have a god-tier rig, I honestly don't believe that I would have been able to load let alone enjoy it. Fortunately, I do—and once I was able to push past the performance issues, there was quite a bit here to appreciate...although not quite enough to recommend. 

The narrative is relatively well executed, while the voice acting ranges from mediocre to decent, with noticeable AI usage and constantly shifting dialects with certain characters (i loved when all of a sudden, english characters took on subtly African American dialects). The first-person mechanics are fairly typical, which is honestly a good thing; they stay out of the way and allow the game's setting to do most of the heavy lifting (not enough to lift this game from the mire of bugs). The objectives are also relatively simple, giving players plenty of opportunities to slow down and truly take in the architectural majesty of the ship—although the strictly linear gameplay prevents any real freedom to explore it in its entirety at will.  Nevertheless, i was pretty stoked to see and interact with it at all. 

The Titanic itself looks fantastic, but the lighting can often be crippling, with strange flickering effects, oddly darkened areas, and other visual inconsistencies which take their toll on the otherwise magnificently crafted setting. Character models are similarly uneven. Many background NPCs look dated and stiff, with clothing that sometimes appears unsynchronized with their character models and hands permanently clipped into their laps while seated. Meanwhile, the protagonist and main female character can be surprisingly lifelike and expressive—at least when their eyebrows actually load.  The character's lips will often move while we are hearing his thoughts.  Conversely, the NPCs make tons of noise but their lips never move and their expressions never change.  Nearly all of the women share the an identical character model which is why it was so easy to spot the main-female-character from half a ship's length away before I even interacted with her - She was the only lifelike character among a sea of mannequins....but (as always), I digress. 

Ultimately, the primary reason that I purchased Titanic: Escape Simulator was simple: I wanted to interact with and observe a living, breathing Titanic during its maiden voyage. On that front, I think the experience succeeds—for the most part, at least to my satisfaction (i had a really low bar for this one). Walking through the ship, observing its passengers (but not too closely - or all immersion is broken), and simply experiencing its enormous spaces before disaster strikes is the real attraction here. I don't regret my purchase, but I can absolutely understand why most others would. 

Purchase this game at your own risk. Maybe you will enjoy the experience like i did, but its more likely that you will not.  I suppose i had vastly lower expectations for this project than most which is how i have been able to enjoy it.

Dawn Break.

My first game of SYN-STUDIO was Eternal Dreamland which was rough, choppy and glitchy but I found it enjoyable at times regardless especially for it's price as mentioned in my review for it. Complete tasks and assignments to collect more uniforms, costumes and outfits for your character to wear and look attractive. With the new updated graphics of Dawn Break your character at times is quite stunning to see, especially when dressed up as you like. 

Dawn Break visually is much more ambitious, with more direction in the game in terms of a plot which at first makes sense in that tsunamis of varying degrees have hit the world and you must survive. However more plots and science-fiction elements enter the frame at times not making sense. Something about an powered arm that scientists were experimenting on with powerful abilities which can be used against enemies.

Like Eternal Dreamland, there is no cohesion in terms of enemies and when and how many spawn attacking you. It's one of the same faults with the developer's first game repeating here, but not as excessive. The same enemy types of Eternal Dreamland return in some form, with some different designs but the same concept in general. Empty your gun into the bigger enemies, then shoot the weaker slow ones. 

Again you explore, complete tasks and assignments to collect outfits, costumes and cosmetics for your character to wear but there is also skills with points to unlock which is found via exploration. Simple concepts that yes could have been implemented better, but it is still better implemented in Dawn Break than Eternal Dreamland. 

Worth buying if on sale, but for full price £10.99 I have no regrets.

Dawn Break is a pretty solid 3rd Person shooter in the vein of Killing Antidote. Tons of content to unlock, you can customize your character to some degree, and the story mode is pretty good with some clever surprises here and there. Overall I'm really enjoying the game. I can easily recommend it for the $13 price tag. If you like these types of games, you'll probably like this one.

The cons: First things first, the game is misleading you because of the Steam tags “Nudity” and “Sexual Content.” There is none of that other than the fact that you can wear bikinis, and the clothes in fights can get damaged and maybe become more revealing, but there is no full nudity. And about the “sexual content” if you think... taking a normal shower, doing normal yoga, etc. is sexual content, then I don’t know under what rock you are living.

I don’t know what the dev intended when he decided to make the clothes become revealing. Was it meant in a sexual way, or was it more for realism? But then again, why would he put bikinis and stuff? I mean, I don’t complain about it, I just want to know what his target audience was? 

Update: After asking the developer directly, apparently the reason the game stops at revealing clothes instead of full nudity is because of legal restrictions and content regulations. So at least now I understand why the game stays in a more “suggestive” direction rather than going further.

The pros: There is a demo to see if you like the game and if it performs well on your hardware. Oh, and don’t worry, in the finished game the gauntlets work, so yeah. Only in the demo I saw the issue where they didn’t work, but after I bought the game, the gauntlets worked properly.

So remember when I mentioned the gauntlets? Well, they are the most unique thing about the game, and the dev clearly got some inspiration from Thanos in the way that you have those crystals on the gauntlet, and each crystal does something special. For example, the telekinesis crystal allows you to grab an enemy, hold them in mid-air, and then explode their head using the same crystal. It is such a satisfying thing to see in action.

And congrats to the dev, he made this game by HIMSELF!!!

I’ve honestly been surprised by how good Dawn Break actually is. You can clearly tell a lot of time and effort went into this game, especially considering it’s made by basically one indie developer. I think so anyway. For a solo project, the quality is seriously impressive and it deserves way more credit than its getting.
The gameplay is fun, the atmosphere is solid, and the overall performance is actually better than a lot of big AAA games coming out lately. The game runs on UE5. Some big AAA titles using UE5 are just a stuttery mess! So, I was expecting loads of stuttering and optimisation issues, but the game runs surprisingly smooth for the most part. Yeah, it will have tiny wee stutters here and there, but I think that's just traversal stutter to be honest. There are a few wee bugs here and there now and again, but nothing major. I wasn't able to equip my guns for example, but I simply reloaded the save. Easy as that.
One of the best parts of the game is the protagonist and the amount of customisation available. The female character design is great, and there’s a massive selection of outfits, hair styles and gear to mess around with. It gives you loads of options and keeps the game feeling fresh. There are challenge modes too. You unlock stuff when you complete them.
What I genuinely don’t understand is why the overall reviews for this game are only sitting at “Mostly Positive.” on the Steam store. For what this game is, and for what one guy has managed to create on his own, it’s surprisingly good and deserves a lot more recognition than it gets. If this was made by a bigger studio people would probably be praising it a lot more. You can check out all the previous patch notes that the dev has brought out. Clearly listening to people's feedback and ironing out the kinks.
Definitely worth trying if you enjoy Resi Evil 2 remake styled-like indie action games and want to support a developer who’s clearly passionate about what he’s making. I can tell he poured his heart and soul in to making this! One thing I do have to say bad about the game is... I’m currently playing on the hardest difficulty, “Nightmare Mode,” and even that still feels fairly easy at times. It seems it's one bullet to the head for all enemies regardless the difficulty mode. I know a lot of people probably like this, but I would rather it took a few shots to the head, on the hardest mode at least. To give me some sort of a challenge. Anyway... £10.99. Can't go wrong!

Dawn Break is a hodgepodge passion project with a few brilliant strokes left on the digital canvas. Once you learn to pull the strings around the gameplay it is a riot switching between an assortment of guns and mystic super powers while serving up gory executions!

Narrative wise there's a science cult trying to shrink then replace the moon to lessen the severity of natural disasters. There's also research that turns certain people into "mutant zombies" yet that doesn't explain the occasional troll, mecha furry, or the weird little mushroom guys that pop up from time to time as well!

Oh yeah, you survive crashing plane on car violence during a black hole anomaly. Amidst your brush with death you acquire an experimental magic-tech gauntlet powered by moon gems. While you were knocked unconscious your best friend or close sister got kidnapped by an evil masked chairman and his armed mercenaries. They whisk her away to a huge condominium that is being submerged under water by countless tsunamis.

It's as if someone wanted to go epic tier with their fever dream SCP mega-verse extravaganza but then realized it's not the easiest of tasks to perfectly translate a written story into a functioning video game.

Could I do better though? Not really. I will not delude myself into believing I can hurl criticisms from my soapbox without first acknowledging that making an enjoyable piece of interactive entertainment is an admirable feat regardless of whether or not the story is up to snuff.

Obviously if you are a literature snob and a cinema snob whom insists that a game has satisfactory character growth and coherent world building let's not sugar coat it. Dawn Break is hot garbage in that department! 

My personal take? Dawn Break's plot is best described as a beautiful train wreck or a discordant yet catchy garage band song. With a few edits, revisions, translations, and additions it would be fine! The sincerity and drive is there minus the fine tuning. 


Moving onto what actually matters..... 

1. Guns "feel good" to shoot

2. There are not many 3rd person shooters where I can multi punch zombies and mercs at super speeds into exploding meat chunks! (Saint Kenshiro, bless these fists!)

3. Attaining the moon gems then using their powers will give you the same nostalgic glee as being a child playing with bottle rockets! It's not balanced in the slightest bit yet the  "boundless chaos" is dopamine dynamite!

4. You can find and buy sexy outfits and accessories. (As well as miscellaneous items for your crib!)

5. Character movement is very smooth.

6. Want to break the game even more? Farm skill points with your equipped executions then gradually turn yourself into a Thanos She Hulk hybrid with jiggling assets!

7. The flooded condo in particular gave me Bioshock and F.E.A.R. vibes.

8. Additional challenge maps for when you beat the main campaign. (There are 4 now and hopefully more in the future.)

9. Unlockable rooms in your apartment with their own functions.

10. I appreciate the touching heartfelt bond the dev tries to establish between the main protagonist and the woman she is trying to save. However, the hackneyed childhood flash back segment setting up the atypical heroine/villain rivalry tries way too hard to be Alice Madness Returns Temu edition! I am glad it is there to establish connections and motivations but it needed a gradual escalation of metaphorical bread crumbs before giving us the whole loaf!

11. Environmental interactivity consists of finding number combinations for locks as well as keycard readers, flipping switches, and adding or removing fuses from fuse boxes. If you love brain teaser puzzles this could be a downer. For yours truly it is more of a godsend! (I will also give props to the mission that required finding an oxygen tank and a diver's suit. Giving an outfit a useful in-game purpose was a welcomed touch!)

12. The overall campaign is lean yet serviceable. The complexity of the level lay outs and enemy encounters improved as things went along. Wouldn't have objected to one or two more chapters but I understand how it is working within the restraints of time and budget. I became very invested in the "moon replacement arc" though it didn't explain absolutely everything going on. It is as if we're suppose to know about these characters, their roles relating to their own metaverse, and their relationships already yet are given only snippets of that through diaries, notes, and phone messages. 


For just over 12 dollars Dawn Break is akin to a B movie with fleeting glimpses of something greater. It is not going to be the sleeper hit that dethrones your favorite block busters. But it is totally worth the front row seat admission, milk duds, extra large cherry slurpee, and the buttered popcorn! 

We need to remember George Lucas did not start making Star Wars movies out of the gate. J.R.R. Tolkien wrote The Hobbit before he wrote The Lord Of The Rings trilogy. If you have a favorite mangaka chances are their first illustrated series was not their peak work. It is a long difficult journey for a creative person to reach his or her magnum opus. Considering Dawn Break is SYN's  second game? Impressive. Most impressive! But you are not at your full potential "yet"..... (Darth Vader voice)

Yes, Dawn Break is a bit rough around the edges, and the translation is lacking in places. This makes it difficult to fully grasp the story right from the start, but if you invest some time, you can understand what this single-person developer is aiming for or what his vision might be.

The developer is definitely dedicated and has already released several updates in the short time since the game's release. Unfortunately, he is working alone, and as a Chinese developer, he faces some challenges with English translation. Because of this, the storytelling feels a bit rough and awkward at times.

It is definitely not some kind of asset flip. The game has okay gunplay mechanics, and while the world is not perfectly smooth-looking, it absolutely has its own charm and design. The sound effects are the minimum you need and what a single person can successfully create or obtain from free sources. The same goes for the little music you can hear.

The developer definitely has talent in multiple areas, but since he is working alone, it is only natural that many things are not fully fleshed out. However, if you give it a chance, you will see that for one person, he has achieved much more than just the bare minimum. I have played it for roughly six hours now, and it’s a fun little game with potential.

If the developer reads this: I like what you have achieved so far, but you need some helping hands. Maybe check out other small Chinese studios with similar worlds, for example, the team behind The Killing Antidot, which has been in my top 3 favorite games list since I started with the demo.

I'm not gonna talk about the positives of this game because the art style is the only good thing about it. What can I say? It's cute, yeah.
So let's talk about the negatives:
[list]
[*][b]Repetitiveness.[/b] They try to spice up the gameplay with different mechanics, ingredients, and mini-games, but it simply doesn't work. Fun fact: only 25% of players made it to the midgame, according to the achievements. Check out all those reviews praising the game, the majority of reviewers only have 1–2 hours of playtime and never came back to it. Yeah, 'cause the entire gameplay loop feels like a chore.

[*][b]It's overwhelming.[/b] It starts off as an easy game — "Classic ramen for me, please!" But then they introduce so many mechanics that it just drives you nuts. You'll have to keep in mind the recipe + specific flavors the customers want ("Slightly Sweet but Not Spicy!") + their restrictions ("Don't add meat to the meatball soup") + temperature + additional ingredients they require. They almost never order a dish straight from the menu, it's always a customized one. So you're not really playing a cozy game, you're just trying to get the stats right, otherwise customers ask for a refund. Because of this, every recipe or ingredient you unlock feels like a punishment because now it'll be included in your puzzle orders too. The devs don't make it any easier for you either — you can't choose the menu for the day, you're forced to cook everything you've unlocked.

[*][b]Customizable orders aren't divided into sections.[/b] What I mean by this is that you get an order that requires you to use ingredients from three different stations — the cutting table (for vegetables), the seasoning table (for sauces and spices), and the boiling station (where you boil the ramen itself). So instead of listing the ingredients in order according to each station, they just mix everything together, forcing you to spend some time figuring out what kind of actions you need to perform at each station. Here's a typical order: onion, dumpling, chili sauce, garlic, salt, chili, and meatball. I was like, "Okay, dumpling and meatball at the boiling station; onion, garlic, and chili at the cutting table; and chili sauce and salt at the seasoning table". I was wasting my time trying to figure out how to optimize my cooking so I wouldn't have to jump from one table to another. It doesn't add any challenge, it's not hard. It's just overwhelming, as I said.

[*][b]Remember how I mentioned that you're watching stats, not actually cooking?[/b] "Meatball Brawls" (a competition for local chefs) is proof of that. There are several judges, and they all have their own preferences. So in order to win and beat your rival, you just follow their preferences and mostly end up with some shxt instead of actual food. Once, I didn't even make a dish. I just used sweet soy sauce and salt for all three rounds and won. All the judges gave it a 10/10. Because the judges wanted something sweet and salty, does it really matter that my "masterpiece" had nothing but sauce in it?

[*][b]The characters are dull and boring, and the plot isn't entertaining.[/b] When you first meet these characters, they seem pretty stereotypical, and... they actually are. They'll stay that way until the end. They have no real depth to them, and each of them can be described with a single word — shy, tsundere, serious, etc. So the storyline and little hangouts don't save the day or make the game any less repetitive. In fact, the story annoyed me the most, it feels like a game made for children. There are plot twists you'd only see in a kids' show — for example, [spoiler]the MC used to be a spy and worked for a top-secret organization, something like the FBI. And now they want to be a chef because good food puts smiles on people's faces.[/spoiler] Cool.

[*][b]It's very slow.[/b] I'm not talking about the story's pacing or the speed at which you unlock upgrades. I'm talking about the way you serve your customers. You fulfill their order, they take about 3 seconds to react, then they praise you, and after that they give you money. Then you have to watch your reputation bar go up, which takes another 3 seconds. The last part is unskippable, btw. You just wait until the game stops showing you something you've already seen 458093 times before and introduces the next customer. It just drags out the gameplay and becomes extremely annoying when you're grinding to boost your relationship levels with the characters.
[/list]

I bought this game on sale for just over $7, after playing the demo. It has absolutely captured my attention span and I have been playing it pretty much nonstop when I am not at work. It is not a perfect game, but for anyone who has that cozy cooking game itch, this will surely scratch it. It helps my case that I have been a fan of the Papa's games, (specifically the pie one, that was my favorite), Good Pizza Great Pizza, Good Coffee Great Coffee, and Galaxy Burger; which at least some of those titles served as inspiration for KuloNiko: Bowl Up.

The gameplay is pretty straightforward. Play the demo and if you like that, the full game will not disappoint. You run a meatball restaurant in a quant town called KuloNiku filled with eccentric locals who remember the reputation that your shop once had. Every day, customers will come in and either order something off of the menu, they may make requests to modify the recipe you serve, or they will give you a list of ingredients they want as their meal. While some of the requests can get a little complicated, you can review the recipe book and their order at any time during the cooking process. And the customers are fairly understanding if you make a mistake, they even tell you exactly what you got wrong. Mess up too much of their order and they will request a refund. 

Every couple days, you have the option to participate in a Meatball Brawl where you serve a dish to a panel of judges at the same time as a competitor. There are rules for this competition that encourage you to strategize your dish. There are also quick time events during the brawl (as well as during recipe unlocking). During the brawl, every step of the cooking process has its own kind of event, and during recipe progression it's just a click the button at the right time. I do not find the QTE to bring any kind of challenge. I like them in the brawl because they just make the cooking a lot more involve, but I don't care for them outside of that. 

So far, the graphics, characters, and story have all been charming. Everybody is nice, even when they challenge you, and wants to see you succeed for the most part. I say this having not completed the story yet, but it's cute. Not award winning but very cute.  The graphics are cute and simple, it really feels like it could be a mobile game or even a Switch game. It could probably run just fine on a potato PC. 

What this game does well: A cozy mode that you can enable or disable at any time that removes the timer and patience mechanic for your customers, plenty of ingredients to make unique dishes with and achieve any flavor profile (an important mechanic: almost every ingredient will affect how sweet, salty, sour, or spicy the dish is, customers often request the final result to be a specific level of a specific flavor), clear and reviewable orders. 

What I wish this game did better: I feel like the QTEs leave a lot to be desired outside of the brawls. You also cannot rebind the controls in the game which is kind of a bummer - I wanted to play without my keyboard so I rebound my mouse and got around it that way. I lack any other big gripes.

Like most reviews on this page, I really wanted to like The Spirit of the Samurai, and in some respects, I do - I like the look of the game, it's enemies and some of the environments are pretty cool - but there are just too many frustrations that are hard to ignore. 
Putting aside the marketing frustration where the game is constantly cited as being "stop-motion" (it isn't, it just has some interesting animation technique plastered on CGI models), top amongst my legitimate complaints is the platforming. I'm not entirely sure what brings it down, but it feels super clunky. Like either there is a delay or it doesn't register the button prompt, the character's hit boxes (especially when playing as Chisai) are weirdly proportioned and sometimes the true edge of the platform feels ambiguous (like knowing exactly where it ends or, when climbing, hitting my head on all the overhangs). If you're going to make a platformer and expect precision jumping the controls need to be a lot tighter. 
Another issue is the combat, it's far too easy to get stun-locked and the enemy variety is lacking – towards the mid game things get highly repetitive. The penultimate level with the seemingly never-ending exploding servant enemies can also go straight to hell. 
Finally, the story feels phoned in, especially towards the end. Without any growth or character arc the narrative feels highly forgettable. It's a shame because you can see glimmers of the developers' ambition and how much they actually wanted to incorporate, I encourage them to keep up the great work!
If you do decide to get this game (and I’d recommend only picking it up on sale), prepare yourself for the frustrations. Looking at the Steam achievements – as of writing – only 10% of all players have actually finished the game, that should tell you everything you need to know!

[h1]The Spirit of the Samurai is emblematic of why Steam needs a "Maybe" Recommend option. [/h1] [h3]I loved certain sequences and elements of The Spirit of the Samurai (namely the atmosphere and story/cutscenes) while others were simply dreadful (woeful precision platforming, repetitive combat, and a padded 2nd act) [/h3]

The Spirit of the Samurai's most appealing selling point is its distinct artstyle and setting. At times reminiscent of Little Nightmares (in gameplay, artstyle, and macabre content) while suffering from repetitive combat and a few crappy platforming sequences. 

Put more plainly, if you like Asian / Samurai / Ninja shit, you will probably like this game's overall storyline and presentation. The characters all have a distinct, stylish look to them and the voiceacting is well-done. The cutscenes are where The Spirit of the Samurai truly shines. They look amazing and craft an intriguing tale. You almost start to wonder if this would have functioned better just as a short CG film than bothering to have a videogame interspersed inbetween one captivating scene and the next. The music and sound effects (though some of those are strangely amplified to be super LOUD) are also handled deftly and add to the overall immersion. 

Where The Spirit of the Samurai stumbles and at times outright fails is its gameplay. The game starts off well as you slink through a town recently ravaged by zombies and the undead. The gameplay consists of simple mechanics navigating the 2D environments, entering doorways to find keys and the like, hitting savepoints to upgrade your base stats and unlock other moves and buy items such as healing potions, arrows for your bow, and thrown kunai. The moves you unlock, although you can get several many of them don't seem very useful or feel very intuitive to use. I mostly just stuck with the same combo throughout the entire game. 

One mistaken impression people have is that The Spirit of the Samurai is a metroidvania, however it is not, you largely progress in a linear fashion throughout the game, don't gather inventory items or other gear outside of the few consumables you can use, don't unlock new traversal or platforming skills, and the exploration is fairly limited. (For example beyond returning to an area to use a key within that same level, you're not going to be unlocking a double-jump and exploring an area from long ago.)

The bosses on The Spirit of the Samurai are simplistic battles, oftentimes falling to your blade if you just roll behind them, slash a few times, then repeat the process. The combat started to become stale by the end and they make the unfortunate choice of throwing a ton of mandatory battles at you during the game's final act. These don't do anything new and just feel like padding and quickly became obnoxious. 

The game's other major misstep is with its platforming. I ran into a glitch near the end of the game where if I held a direction for too long the character would just clip through a platform he should have easily grabbed over and over. The solution was to jump then just let go of all the controls. I also had the game crash on me a handful of times during my playthrough. 

Altogether this game is an enjoyable enough experience if youre interested in its theme but don't expect to be super engaged with its gameplay. I would only recommend this on sale as the overall package isn't polished enough to warrant its retail price.
