TL;DR: Beautiful and creative game with huge potential, but still plagued by game-breaking bugs, clunky controls, and technical issues a year after release. Not recommended.

I was excited for this game ever since I saw the trailer. A stop-motion samurai game with a cat is an incredible concept, and visually the game is genuinely stunning.

Unfortunately, despite how much I wanted to love it, I can’t recommend it.

A year after release, there are still multiple game-breaking bugs. Some progression mechanics, like using spirit power to break walls, randomly stop working and completely block progress. I nearly refunded the game because of this.

Later levels can soft-lock you entirely. If enemies fall into a chasm, their deaths don’t count, meaning you’re stuck and forced to restart the level. This happens easily since enemies frequently jump toward you.

Boss fights can also lack proper checkpoints. If you die after beating a boss due to a broken save point, you’re forced to redo the entire fight.

On top of that, there are random frame drops that only fix themselves after restarting the game.

This game had massive potential, but clunky controls (both as Chisai and Kodama) and long-standing bugs make it feel rushed and unfinished. I understand Digital Mind is a small studio, but it’s hard to excuse these issues when they’ve been known for so long.

It honestly makes me sad. I’m glad I finished the game, but in its current state, I can’t recommend it.

I stumbled upon this game during a sale for less than $3. The beautiful visuals caught my eye, so I watched the trailer. The plot seemed promising too, which left me curious about all the hate this game was getting.

And so I tried it out. NGL, there ARE several issues. 

Combat System: There’s definitely a learning curve. While I'm glad more than mindless button-mashing is required, even when you do get the hang of it, execution feels slow and clunky. Performance Issues: The game ran smoothly for about three-quarters of the journey. But once Takeshi makes his comeback, lag starts creeping in every hour or so. Restarting the game fixes it, and with decent specs on my rig, I’m confident it’s not a hardware issue.

Buggies: Items that refuse to disappear from inventory, and possibly the worst: bugged save points that refuse to save 😱

HOWEVER... despite these shortcomings, I am still heartily recommending this game. WHY?

I have always loved stop-motion animation, and the richly detailed environments create a world steeped in Japanese mysticism that I enjoyed exploring. It's a treat for the eyes.

Storytelling is compelling, but the true charm of the game lies with its cast of characters: the stalwart Takeshi, the enigmatic Kitsune, the adorable kodamas who always want to help, and most of all, the brave, little showstopper-Chisai, the ever-lovable and loyal furry potato! I stumbled across this game on Steam completely by chance. I vaguely remembered seeing the trailer a long time ago and being really intrigued, but as time passed, I forgot about it. Then recently, I noticed it was on sale, and to my surprise, it had actually been out for almost a year. I hesitated because of the forty percent negative reviews complaining about clunky controls, unresponsive combat, and unfair mechanics. But I thought, it is five bucks, if I do not like it, no big loss. So I bought it, and I am so glad I did.


Graphics and Art Direction


My first impressions were stunning. The art style and direction are absolutely beautiful. The blend of 3D environments in a sidescroller format, with stylized perspectives and some prerendered elements, gives it a unique visual identity. The dark yet saturated color palette adds mood and atmosphere. The cinematics are incredible. I know most games use in game cutscenes nowadays, but I still love a good prerendered cinematic, and this game delivers.

The character design is fantastic, a perfect blend of realism and stylization. The lighting, the rain droplets, the sweat on their faces, everything feels tactile and almost touchable. It has real personality.

I also love the HUD. I am honestly tired of the same white, semi transparent minimalist UI that most games use now. Seeing a HUD with identity and style feels refreshing.


Gameplay


After a short prologue with some simple walking, talking, and a delivery task, things escalate as demons and zombies invade your village, and you are thrown straight into combat.

The combat system is deeper than I expected. You have offensive and defensive stances, and managing stamina is crucial. You can block, parry, and dodge, but if you run out of stamina and get hit, you lose one of your three lives. Offensively, you can attack with the X or Square button, or use the right joystick, which performs different directional combos.

The best part is that you can customize your combos. You can swap out your attack moves to adjust speed, power, and style, creating your own moveset and playstyle. For example, I use quick combos for my forward attacks, and heavier, slower combos for my upper attacks when I want to deal big damage or finish enemies.

There are a few enemy types, like foot soldiers, archers, shield bearers, and smaller minions. You can level up your character, and I mostly upgraded stamina and attack. You can also collect resources and trade them for items.

You also have a bow for ranged combat. Most enemies will block arrows, but when you land a hit, it feels very satisfying, and you can sometimes bully them into submission. Potions and throwable items like kunais are plentiful and useful.

The bosses are fun. They are like stronger versions of regular enemies, but they hit harder, so you have to be more careful with dodging and parrying. They are challenging enough to be engaging without feeling unfair.

The game overall is not very difficult, but that is okay, because it feels good to play and looks great doing it.

As for complaints about hit detection and short attack range, I have not experienced any of those issues. Everything feels responsive, every parry lands, and staggering enemies is extremely satisfying. Aggressive play is encouraged, and it feels fantastic.


Level Design


Some reviews described the level design as confusing, but I honestly do not see that. It is quite linear. You climb ladders, jump obstacles, and occasionally explore a bit, but it is straightforward. It is probably the weakest part of the game, but still fine. Not bad, not great, just okay. I did enjoy the traps with unique death animations. I even triggered them on purpose sometimes just to see the animations. There are also plenty of checkpoints, so dying is never a big deal.


Story and Atmosphere


The story is solid. It is not groundbreaking, but it is interesting enough to keep you invested. The atmosphere is excellent. It genuinely feels like everything is at stake, and your enemies are a serious threat. The main character is cool, and the world feels alive and intense.


Final Thoughts


Overall, I am genuinely loving this game. I picked it up for five bucks, which is an absolute steal, and honestly, I would have happily paid full price. It deserves it.

The Spirit of the Samurai, developed by Digital Mind Games and published by Kwalee, is an ambitious side-scrolling action-adventure that combines Japanese mythology, spiritual folklore, and a cinematic visual style inspired by stop-motion animation. Released in December 2024, the game invites players into a supernatural retelling of feudal Japan, where an ancient Oni has awakened, unleashing its army of the undead to destroy a peaceful village. You play as Takeshi, a fallen samurai whose spirit becomes bound to a small Kodama guardian, joined by an unlikely feline warrior named Chisai. Together, they embark on a journey of redemption and resistance against demonic corruption. The premise feels like a blend of myth and legend, and from the opening moments, it establishes a world steeped in atmosphere—one that is both sorrowful and otherworldly.

From a gameplay perspective, The Spirit of the Samurai positions itself between a Metroidvania and an action-adventure brawler. Combat serves as the foundation of the experience, offering a mixture of light and heavy attacks, dodges, and parries. The player can switch between the main characters, each bringing distinct abilities that alter how the game unfolds. Takeshi’s sword-based combat emphasizes timing and strength, while the Kodama offers ethereal powers that interact with the environment or influence spirits, and Chisai introduces agility-based sequences suited for stealth and quick traversal. This variety adds a welcome layer of diversity to the gameplay, preventing it from feeling monotonous as the adventure unfolds. Exploration encourages backtracking through interconnected environments, where new abilities unlock access to previously unreachable areas. The design borrows familiar cues from Metroidvania titles but applies them to a mythological Japanese setting that feels distinct in tone and pacing.

The game’s presentation is undeniably its most captivating quality. The Spirit of the Samurai looks like it was crafted from living sculpture, blending motion capture and stop-motion animation techniques to create a uniquely tactile world. Characters move with deliberate weight and subtle texture, giving the impression of handmade puppets in a dark folklore tale. Each environment—from mist-covered forests and haunted shrines to decaying villages—is carefully framed with atmospheric lighting and cinematic depth. The attention to visual detail gives the game a painterly, almost theatrical quality that distinguishes it from other indie action titles. Accompanied by an evocative soundtrack featuring traditional Japanese instrumentation fused with haunting ambient tones, the aesthetic presentation fully immerses players in its mythic setting. Even the smallest details, such as wind rustling through bamboo or the faint whisper of spirits, contribute to the sense of being part of a living legend.

However, despite its artistic excellence, the gameplay sometimes struggles to meet the same level of refinement. Combat can feel uneven, with moments of brilliance—when attacks flow smoothly and parries land precisely—contrasted by instances of stiffness and delay that break immersion. Platforming, while visually engaging, occasionally suffers from imprecise controls, making certain jumps or dodges frustrating during tense encounters. The difficulty balance can also be inconsistent, with sudden spikes that feel more punishing than rewarding. These issues don’t ruin the experience but can be noticeable, especially when the visual and audio presentation set expectations for a smoother mechanical performance. It’s clear that Digital Mind Games poured immense passion into the art and storytelling, but the technical polish and responsiveness sometimes lag behind that ambition.

Narratively, the game strikes a delicate balance between tragedy and mysticism. Takeshi’s journey is not just about vengeance but about restoring balance between the worlds of the living and the dead. The story unfolds with minimal dialogue, relying instead on environmental storytelling, visual symbolism, and spiritual encounters. The dynamic between Takeshi, the Kodama, and Chisai provides both levity and emotional grounding, with their differing personalities reflecting the game’s central themes of redemption, duty, and companionship. The tone fluctuates between eerie and heroic, often evoking the moral ambiguity of old Japanese ghost stories. The way folklore creatures—such as tengu, jorōgumo, and undead warriors—are integrated into the world feels organic, giving the impression of a land haunted by its own myths. This narrative approach, while understated, adds emotional resonance and makes the journey feel deeply rooted in cultural authenticity.

In terms of pacing and structure, The Spirit of the Samurai offers a moderately compact experience. The campaign can be completed in roughly four to six hours, depending on exploration and skill, making it a focused adventure rather than a sprawling epic. While some players may find its length modest, the game benefits from a tight progression loop that avoids unnecessary filler. Each new area introduces fresh challenges or visual set-pieces, ensuring that the experience remains varied. However, because of the limited scope and occasional repetition in enemy encounters, the sense of growth can taper off toward the end. The multiple playable characters and unlockable skills help mitigate this, but the overall structure leans toward linear progression punctuated by brief backtracking segments rather than full non-linear exploration.

Reception from both critics and players has been divided but largely respectful of its ambition. Many praise its stunning visuals, rich atmosphere, and dedication to Japanese mythology, calling it one of the most visually unique indie titles of its year. Others point to the lack of gameplay polish and the uneven responsiveness as areas where the experience falls short of greatness. Still, few can deny the artistry behind its design—the stop-motion aesthetic alone makes it stand out in a crowded genre. The Spirit of the Samurai feels like the work of a studio passionate about blending art and interactivity, even if that ambition occasionally exceeds the scope of its technical execution.

Ultimately, The Spirit of the Samurai is a work of vision more than perfection. It delivers an unforgettable aesthetic experience, immersing players in a hauntingly beautiful world that feels both ancient and alive. Its blend of folklore, emotional storytelling, and creative animation techniques make it a rare and admirable entry in the action-adventure genre. Though its controls and pacing can falter, the sincerity of its craftsmanship and its atmospheric depth make it a journey worth taking for those who value artistry and cultural storytelling in games. It may not achieve flawless balance between beauty and playability, but it embodies the spirit of independent creativity—a game that dares to be different, and in doing so, captures something timeless in its mythic tale of samurai and spirit.

[h1]This Would Be Better As Horror Than Action[/h1]

Funny thing is, playing poorly designed games actually helps me learn more about myself. I used to have a rule for myself that no matter how bad the game is, I will at least play it through before declaring my opinion. Yet, that is no longer the case here. I simply do not have the patience to endure through the counter-intuitive combat, confusing designs, and the general lack of direction. The Spirit of The Samurai is such game, and sadly, I am not masochistic enough to play through the whole game. Even though the art style and the cutscenes are honestly gorgeous, they are all null and void if the core gameplay loop can't even stand on its own.

[h2]Things I Like About The Spirit of The Samurai:[/h2]

[b]Some Compliments[/b]
[list]
[*]I quite like the dark atmosphere and the developers' rendition of Japanese Folklore.
[*]Cutscenes are really smooth and well-animated.
[*]I love all the monster designs.
[*]Short as it may be, the part where you sneak pass Jorogumo is genuinely the best of this game. The creepy design and the simple but effective stealth section make me wonder if the game would be better as a full-blown horror game.
[/list]

[h2]Things I Dislike About The Spirit of The Samurai:[/h2]

[b]1. Poorly Designed Combat[/b]
If the feet can't even stand, how do you expect it to walk?
[list]
[*]The control feels clunky. The protagonist moves like tons of molasses gluing to his feet.
[*]The combat is just a mess. At first glance, all the unlockable move sets and directional input attacks might suggest the game leaning towards a more grounded Devil May Cry style. That is until you try to land an attack.
[*]The insane input delay just makes all the combo hard to connect. You can't change to a different directional attack mid-combo. The game will force the protagonist to standstill for at least a second before the new attack actually begins. You are commit to the current the combo.
[*]Every single attack is long-reaching and knocks enemies back far. Under normal circumstances, these features are great for you survival, but in this game they are the worst. Knocking enemies back makes it hard for you to connect any follow-ups. Unless you are face-to-face with the enemies, the best and most efficient way to defeat them is to just attack once and move forward a little, rinse and repeat.
[*]You know something is wrong when the most effective way to fight a boss(or anything really) is not taking it head on, but pushing both it and yourself to the corner. Then you can spam your attack, ignoring the knockback, and force a stun loop on the boss.
[*]Enemies recover from and react to your attacks faster than you think. I will even say the knockback actually benefits them more than it does for you. It helps them get out of your combo so they can assume defense faster. Their attacks are deceptively long and can easily poise through your attack.
[*]Stamina and health sharing the same bar is interesting on paper. In practice, however, it's way more frustrating to deal with. Every single enemy can take out the full bar and one of three spirits with ease. You can get stunlock to death if there are over two enemies on the field.
[/list]

[b]2. Confusing And Over-designed Levels[/b]
Despite the art style being the only redeeming factor, it sadly impedes the level clarity.
[list]
[*]The "platforming" doesn't fare well either. The ledges blend too perfectly well with the environment, and the elevated platforms are constantly obscured by background props. The worst contender goes to pit falls. Aside from instantly killing you, they are often covered by blurry foliage in the foreground, to the point you can't even tell if it's a pit fall or walkable path.
[*]The level design also does a bad job at guiding you to the next location. The environment is too dark to navigate. The stairs and ladders lack the subtle highlight to separate them from being parts of the background. There are several time which I cannot tell where the stairs are until the button-prompts appear.
[/list]

[b]3. Other Complaints[/b]
[list]
[*]Enemies with teleportation can teleport outside the locked arena, rendering the fight impossible to complete.
[*]You can't regenerate stamina in Kodama form.
[*]I really dislike the UI and the whole inventory system. Healing item being a consumable is such a product of the past.
[/list]

Overall: 6.75/10

Story:

Spirit of the Samurai wastes little time throwing you into the action as a Kitsune narrator recounts the tale of Takeshi, a legendary samurai whose village is suddenly attacked by Oni. The stakes are clear from the start; these demons destroy everything in their path, and Takeshi must rise to protect his home and neighbors. While the narrative isn’t groundbreaking, I found it to be a tight and straightforward story that serves its purpose well as a foundation, which effectively supports the gameplay and overall presentation.
Additionally, the game’s mythological elements feel naturally integrated rather than forced, with notable entities like the Kitsune, Yama-Uba, Shuten-Doji, etc. having believable roles in the world. I appreciated how the story doesn’t overexplain its supernatural aspects, instead letting them unfold through the journey. That said, the opening requires some patience, as the game introduces mechanics like side quests and item gathering that never fully resurface later in the adventure. This can make the early hours feel slightly uneven, but once the story finds its footing, it settles into a focused and engaging rhythm.
You'll quickly realize the core of the narrative revolves around Takeshi and his cat, Chisai, who plays a notable role in the story. The only other notable character past the introduction sequence is Anako, and her role is very minimal.  While it may not be the most original tale, I still found myself invested in their journey; the game’s art style and action-heavy pacing kept me engaged throughout.

Gameplay:

First things first: USE A CONTROLLER. You will 100% have a much more enjoyable and fluid experience using a controller instead of KB+M.
Nevertheless, SotS definitely has some flaws and noticeable jank, but if you accept it for what it is and meet it where it’s at, it can really be a LOT of fun.
Now, the gameplay is undoubtedly one of the main focuses here, but as for the combat itself, it’s both fun and punishing. If you've heard that this game is a Metroidvania, you can curb that immediately; this is an almost completely linear and straightforward experience with minimal exploration. Regardless, enemies are VERY aggressive and can easily overwhelm you if you’re not careful about inching through levels, but there were not many instances where the TTK of enemies felt too high, so you can get through any section with enough finesse. However, rushing in almost always resulted in death even if I was spamming dodge/roll, since crowd control options are rather limited. Boss battles, while visually striking, lack depth. In these instances, button mashing sometimes works better than actual strategy, which can lead to repetition while seemingly discouraging a generally defensive playstyle. That said, boss fights aren’t overly abundant or long, so they never overstayed their welcome, in my opinion.
Additionally, combat customization is a mixed bag. The ability to piece together your custom sword combos and unlock more attacks as you progress is one of the best parts of the game. I really enjoyed this system since it adds depth and variety to combat encounters. Yet on the other hand, upgrading stats at shrines feels unintuitive. Aside from a 10-point increase in the chosen category, the impact on combat isn't clearly shown, except for dexterity, which unlocks more attacks. I found myself mainly dumping rune upgrades into either Strength or Resistance for most of the game. On top of that, there’s no way to reset your stats other than dying, which often feels tedious since the game only saves when passing by a checkpoint or stopping at a shrine.
Speaking of checkpoints, the system needs work. If you fail a part of a level that follows a cutscene, it will play again. While you can thankfully skip the cutscenes when this happens, the repetition still makes already challenging sections even more frustrating.
Moreover, some of the basic systems feel clunky and outdated. For example, item gathering doesn’t feel as smooth as it should, and some items are easy to miss, forcing you to repeatedly sweep through rooms you’ve already cleared. This could very well be user error, but given that it happened multiple times, I figured it was worth noting, as it greatly slowed the game's pace and detracted from the action.
The additional playable characters, Kodama the spirit and Chisai the cat, help add variety, but I personally enjoyed Takeshi, Kodama, and Chisai in that order. Kodama's sections were almost as fun as Takeshi’s, but Chisai’s felt undercooked and jarring. The stealth sections interrupted the pacing too much, pulling you away from the samurai gameplay for a little too long. The game’s best moments are when you're in control of Takeshi, but even then, rough edges like frustrating enemy placements, clunky mechanics (e.g., having to pull out your bow for a full second to change arrows, otherwise you just jump upwards since they're the same button), and enemy attack speed/frequency leaving little to no time for using potions, all really detract from the experience.

World:

While this game doesn’t have the widest color palette, I still found its world and level design to be incredibly immersive. SotS's stop-motion animation and dark, moody aesthetic create a visually striking atmosphere that really pulls you into its feudal Japanese setting. Each level had a unique and interesting backdrop, even if that was mainly thanks to the art style rather than intricate level layouts.
Despite this, as previously mentioned, the game is fairly linear which limits exploration. Some areas felt a bit restrictive, and at times, the verticality and platforming were a little unclear. However, I was still impressed with how well the game’s world design complemented its eerie, supernatural themes. Even though the levels themselves weren’t always complex, the way they were presented made each section feel distinct and memorable.

Visuals:

The visuals and art style are undoubtedly among this game's biggest selling points, and for a good reason. For the most part, I loved the art direction. The stop-motion-inspired style is incredibly unique, but it felt like it sometimes impacts the fluidity of platforming and combat, leading to moments of frustration. Basically, the animations feel dynamic and look very cool, but the functionality struggles over art direction at times.
Regardless, the cutscenes are nothing short of breathtaking. All of the cinematic moments (yes, even the death scenes) were immersive and masterfully crafted, and pulled me deeper into the game's world. I didn’t have many expectations going in, but one of the best surprises was just how beautifully cinematic these cutscenes are. If there were a short film based on this game's whole narrative, I’d genuinely watch it.

Music/Sound Design:

Another thing SotS absolutely nails is the incredible soundscape that elevates the entire experience. From the moment I started playing, the music transported me straight into Feudal Japan, blending traditional Japanese instrumentation with haunting, atmospheric melodies. The OST perfectly balances moments of intensity during combat with serene, almost meditative pieces when exploring. It’s clear that a lot of care went into crafting a score that not only fits the setting but enhances the emotional weight of the journey.
The sound design is just as impressive. Every clash of swords, the rustling of leaves in the wind, and the eerie whispers of supernatural foes add a deep layer of immersion. 
Lastly, the voice acting is another highlight. The performances feel authentic and add a lot of personality to the characters. Whether it’s the narration of the Kitsune, the chilling menace of Shuten-Doji, or Takeshi's general dialogue, every line feels natural and well-delivered. There’s a strong sense of respect for the cultural and historical elements, which makes the experience even more immersive.

I honestly have mixed feelings...

The first 4–5 missions were a solid 7/10 experience for me. After that, the game starts going downhill. What makes this frustrating is that the core game is not the problem, the map design is. 

Pros
A proper Majesty-style game that adds and improves mechanics:
-Heroes can have positive and negative traits when recruited, which adds personality.
-Heroes can loot items from chests and sell them at the market, generating gold for both themselves and the player.
-Large variety of items available through the market.
-Fewer random and unavoidable hero deaths compared to Majesty or Lessaria.
-The music fits the atmosphere well.
-Tech tree to upgrade heroes and mechanics
Overall, the core gameplay loop is enjoyable and shows real potential.

Cons
The map design becomes increasingly frustrating as the campaign progresses.
They copy pasted the campaign missions from Majesty.  But they missed one detail. In Majesty at the end of each mission you could save 3 heroes(level and items) and then recruit them in future maps using a special building. You could recruit a saved hero, level him up more and save him again. Without this building this is how some missions feel: 

Burning Grove
You must defend a building that gets attacked every few minutes. Simple enough, except the building is located on the other side of the map with numerous monster and dens between you and the objective. It's frustrating but still manageable. I tried several times but could not complete it on the hardest difficulty.

Cult of Shadows
This is where my patience started running out. The mission is timed. You need to destroy specific dens, but you start with limited building options and must complete side objectives to claim buildings(clain, you still cannot build them). The Blacksmith, Inn, and Mausoleum are locked behind this objectives. Because of that  you can only recruit 3 types of heroes and learn only t1 skills and you cannot resurrect them if they die. And they will die because they have no items and sinergy(class diversity). If you recruit a new hero, he is lvl 1. And they die again. You get the point. 
But that is not all! The locations of these side objectives are not shown on the map. Good luck! 
And remember, it is a timed map. You you do not complete the main objective in x days hordes of monster spawn constantlly and you cannot win the map unless you had it almost finished. Oh, and I did not find one of the side objectives on the map after clearing about 90% of it. Terrible design without the building I mentioned above. 

Lord of Greed
Who thought an invincible monster that periodically wipes out your kingdom was a good idea?
The creature appears very early, around day three. By that point you've barely managed to construct a handful of buildings and recruit a few heroes. Then this monster arrives, destroys most of your infrastructure, kills your heroes, and leaves. A few minutes later, it comes back and does it again.
That isn't difficulty. It's frustration.

Several other maps suffered from the same problem. The most frustrating missions were almost always either timed missions or missions built around constant harassment from unstoppable enemies.
There are other issues with the game, but they are minor compared to the map design. That's what makes this so frustrating. The core gameplay is solid. The main game loop works. The foundation is there. Yes, it needs polish and balancing, but underneath it all there is a genuinely good game.

I completed about half of the campaign on the hardest difficulty and the rest on hard. I eventually rage-quit the final mission the moment I understood its mechanics. 
It's hard for me to decide whether to recommend this game or not.
The game is there. The foundation is there. Beneath some baffling mission and map design choices lies a genuinely enjoyable game. I'll give it a positive recommendation. Not because I think it's flawless, but because I think it deserves the attention needed to improve.

It's closer to Majesty than Lessaria is, and I think it's better for that.
A lot of people would consider the art style a bit bland, but it did grow on me after a while, particularly the monsters. It reminds me of the transition from Diablo 2 to Diablo Resurrected, a change which I initially hated, but after playing through it I really liked it. It can be pretty unclear, especially since monsters and heroes don't collide, so they'll just stand in messy blobs and fight, but it doesn't end up mattering that much. I really liked the monsters and lairs, they're a real highlight.
I didn't like Lessaria's economy, so I'm glad Crown of Greed stuck closer to Majesty in that regard. You can build multiple marketplaces and there's trading post and gold mine locations around the map, though I don't really know the difference between the two, aside from value.
The campaign missions are quite varied, and though you might take a similar strategy in all of them, they at the very least require you to think about what you need to do in each one. The mission map is fun, like a modern version of the original Majesty's map. I played it through on nightmare with only a couple of missions giving me trouble, but otherwise it's not a terribly difficult playthrough, though I have just finished playing through all of Majesty and Lessaria, so I might be an outlier.
The classes are cool, mostly your standards, but there's a couple of interesting ones in there, like the shooter or the dryad. I like that the heroes are mostly self sufficient and don't need extreme babysitting like they do in Lessaria, and will run away before they die. You also aren't railroaded into needing healers like you were in Majesty 2.
I really like that the heroes have randomised traits, which can make a big difference. Turning into a bird to run away, or being totally immune to poisons, or being randomly stunned by any attack. They also can be randomly bigger or smaller, so you can have a gigantic ranger, or a tiny barbarian, which is fun.

However, I do have to mention that at the time of my playthrough I ran into a number of bugs. There's issues with quest tracking (try to do all objectives in intended order, and don't do them too quickly after each other). A couple of times enemies would spawn inside the trees and my heroes would stare at them instead of doing anything else until a ranged unit came along to kill it. The quest dialogues are a bit of a mess on some missions, with the wrong character being displayed or the wrong line being played. I think a couple of them included multiple takes of the same line by accident, instead of just the one.
I should point out that I never ran into anything game breaking. No crashes, the only performance problems I had was when my kingdom was gigantic and I was playing at triple speed, and my PC is 10 years old. It may have been kind of buggy at times, but it didn't stop me playing and enjoying it.

Overall, I think this is a great spiritual successor to Majesty and well worth your time and money.

I went into this game genuinely excited. I absolutely loved The Painscreek Killings so I had high hopes for another investigative experience from the same dev team.

I love games that make me think, examine evidence, connect clues, and reach my own conclusions. I don't mind difficult cases. I don't need hand-holding, and I don't expect every answer to be obvious.

Unfortunately my experience with this game was incredibly frustrating. The investigation felt less like solving a mystery and more like guessing which obscure details the game wanted me to find. Some questions required leaps in logic that I couldn't reasonably follow and I often couldn't understand how I was supposed to arrive at the answers from the evidence provided.

What makes this particularly disappointing is that The Painscreek Killings gave me exactly what I wanted- an investigative experience that made me curious, encouraged me to explore, and made uncovering the truth satisfying.

I didn't find that same satisfaction here. Instead, I spent more time confused and frustrated than actually investigating and ultimately requested a refund.

I know this dev is capable of making an engaging investigative game, which makes this experience all the more disappointing. This just wasn't the experience I was looking for.

When I found out that this game was the spiritual successor to The Painscreek Killings I was so excited to try it! I love detective/mystery games that ask you to solve a case using only your own logic and its a genre that is seriously underdeveloped.

That said, I found this game pretty disappointing. You are not able to freely roam each scene and instead are limited to specific rooms (you cannot unlock anything with keys or codes), only the items that are visible within each room, and only the visible items that you can left click to inspect. You cannot open any drawers, doors, computers, phones etc. beyond that. There are no "if you notice this in the background it may help you, even if it's not necessary for solving" clues and the clues you are given often come in the form of journals, sticky notes, phone messages, or other written sources (aka you only have a few opportunities to notice details like the caliber of a bullet or residue in a glass). On it's own I may not have minded that lack of full exploration, but solving the scenarios with the clues you are given involves a LOT of assuming and jumping to conclusions about what happened, which defeats the purpose of the genre. There were many times where I found myself wondering if there was something that I had missed because the complete set of clues did not feel like they provided enough information to answer the questions definitively. This was especially disappointing because there absolutely WERE a few answers that give you a sense of accomplishment when you figured them out because the clues were there if you made note of them (trying to be as spoiler free as possible, but the question about the tattoo comes to mind).

Compare that with TPK where you are given all the information you need in both written documents and visual clues (including plenty of misdirects and red herrings) so long as you pay attention and decide what's important to make the proper connections between all of the details.

While I can't say that I had a horrible time playing, I don't know if I would recommend this game over any others in the detective category or even over others by the same creators.

Great game overall.

The majority of the game is exactly what I was looking for: deduction-driven investigations with minimal hand-holding, strong environmental storytelling, excellent world-building, and several genuinely emotionally effective moments. The game trusts the player to think, observe, and connect evidence rather than constantly pointing at the solution, which is increasingly rare.

Unfortunately, I spent nearly half of my total playtime on the final case, and not for the reasons I was expecting.
The problem is not that the finale is difficult. Difficult is good, welcome, and expected.
The problem is that the type of reasoning required suddenly changes.

Throughout most of the game, the player is rewarded for forensic thinking: establishing timelines, tracking evidence chains, identifying contradictions, reconstructing movements, and assigning identities through concrete clues. 

The finale often feels less like a process of deduction and more like a process of character archetyping. Several crucial conclusions appear to follow from assumptions about who the characters are and how they would behave, rather than from the available evidence itself. At times, the reasoning feels closer to "TV detective logic" and vibes than evidence-based deduction.



If you enjoy mystery games as an experience, this may not bother you at all. If you've grown tired of heavily guided Agatha Christie or Sherlock Holmes titles (which are otherwise great) and simply want to feel like a detective, you'll probably still enjoy the ending.

But if your goal is to actually perform deduction and see conclusions emerge from evidence rather than narrative intuition, the finale feels like an insult.
Which is a shame, because up until that point, the game had earned a tremendous amount of credibility.

I still recommend it. The vast majority of the experience is excellent. But the final case is less a test of deduction and more a test of whether you can think like the writer.

Cons: There are several categories here. For a game that takes place in American locations, by a team located in the US, they use a surprising number of non-American things. For instance, notes measuring [spoiler] baby formula [/spoiler] in milliliters and a receipt in NYC having an entry for VAT (value added tax), which isn't used in the US.

Some of the clues give me the feeling of cosplay. For example, not realizing that brass from a firearm ejects in one direction or the tone of a police chief. In fact, the whole Bloodbath case seems to be written by someone whose only exposure was Hollywood. And for a narrative game, it has a number of basic typos and grammar errors that shouldn't exist a few years after release.

For their next game, I hope they keep doing well in the art department, and deliberately spend more effort on the writing and editing. There should be a consistent tone across the game and even if typos make it through, glaring clue errors should not. And if they incorporate someplace with a lot of procedure, like a police station, maybe they need someone with experience taking a second look.

Scene Investigators, developed and published by EQ Studios, is a first-person detective experience that strips away cinematic dramatization and instead places full responsibility for solving crimes directly in the player’s hands. Rather than guiding you through a scripted narrative filled with dramatic twists and voiced interrogations, the game emphasizes careful observation, logical reasoning, and independent deduction. It presents itself less as a traditional story-driven adventure and more as a simulation of forensic analysis, inviting players to step into detailed crime scenes and draw their own conclusions from the evidence scattered throughout each environment.

The core gameplay loop revolves around exploring meticulously crafted locations where crimes have taken place. Each case drops you into a contained scene—an apartment, a backyard, a warehouse, or another everyday setting—transformed into a puzzle box of subtle clues. There are no glowing markers pointing toward important objects and no dialogue companions explaining what to look for. Instead, you must manually inspect the surroundings, examine items up close, and mentally piece together timelines and motives. Blood spatters, displaced furniture, documents, personal belongings, and environmental details all serve as fragments of a larger narrative waiting to be reconstructed.

What sets Scene Investigators apart from many other detective titles is its refusal to over-explain. The game embraces ambiguity and expects players to think critically. Not all clues are explicitly presented as interactable evidence; sometimes the most important insight comes from recognizing patterns or inconsistencies within the scene. This design philosophy demands patience and attention to detail. It can be deeply rewarding when deductions align with the correct solution, but it also means that progress can stall if key details are overlooked or misinterpreted. The absence of hand-holding reinforces immersion, making each solved case feel earned rather than handed over.

Structurally, the game is divided into separate investigations rather than a single overarching narrative. Each case stands on its own, functioning almost like an interactive logic exercise. This approach keeps the focus on analytical gameplay rather than emotional storytelling. While some players may miss a continuous character arc or evolving plotline, others will appreciate the purity of the format. The episodic structure allows each investigation to explore different crime scenarios and environments without being constrained by a central narrative thread.

Atmosphere plays an important role despite the game’s grounded presentation. Lighting and sound design subtly enhance the tension of exploring silent crime scenes. The environments feel lived-in, with everyday objects arranged in ways that hint at the events that transpired. There are no jump scares or overt horror elements, but the quiet stillness of each scene can create a lingering sense of unease. This subdued atmosphere complements the investigative tone, encouraging thoughtful exploration rather than rushed interaction.

Technically, the game favors functionality over spectacle. Visuals are realistic enough to convey important environmental details without striving for high-end graphical fidelity. The interface is minimalistic, designed to support note-taking and reflection rather than clutter the screen with guidance systems. This streamlined design keeps the player’s focus on deduction and analysis. While it may lack flashy presentation elements, it succeeds in delivering the tools necessary for its intended experience.

Scene Investigators will likely resonate most with players who enjoy escape rooms, true crime documentaries, and puzzle games that prioritize logic over narrative spectacle. It requires a willingness to slow down, observe carefully, and accept that mistakes are part of the investigative process. For those who thrive on piecing together fragmented stories through environmental clues, it offers a uniquely immersive and intellectually stimulating challenge. However, players seeking cinematic storytelling, character-driven drama, or action-oriented gameplay may find its deliberate pacing and minimal guidance demanding.

Ultimately, Scene Investigators stands as a focused exercise in deduction. By removing overt direction and allowing players to rely solely on observation and reasoning, it captures the essence of investigative work in a way few games attempt. Its commitment to realism and intellectual engagement makes it a distinctive entry in the detective genre, rewarding those who approach each case with patience, curiosity, and a keen eye for detail.

I enjoyed detective fiction a lot as a kid, along with one of my sisters. I ended up doing professional accident investigation at one point among other things and my other sister pursued criminal forensics. We enjoyed the Nancy Drew point and click games as kids, and we also enjoyed LA Noire. I have also enjoyed Shadows of Doubt, and other detective/puzzle games. I decided to get this game on sale to play in the company of my spouse. 

It is simultaneously a realistic and unrealistic investigative simulator. It's realistic in the sense that a lot of the subtle indicators of a death are there. It is unrealistic in the way that it handles the procedure and process. 

One of the common criticisms I have seen is that a lot of the information you are required to present should already be known to an investigator. The tutorial is a great example of this. I have already have an individual in custody, why do I not know their name? 

The indie game dev in me also sees the reasoning behind this. As it forces the player to understand the gravity of the entire situation and story. 

I believe that this is an excellent proof of concept for a larger game. It is my understanding that this hasn't been touched by the developer in some years. 

My personal favorite case in here was blood bath. There were a lot of very subtle clues as to what was going on in the office. The body placement and object placement was extremely telling to the story, and after examining it for a few minutes I was able to somewhat act out the entire sequence of events accurately. The longer part was dissecting the tale of why it happened. 

This game does extremely well with using the motive and opportunity to allow you to piece the story together. The dinner party apartment level did well at this. 

For as many complaints I have seen about red herrings I didn't struggle at all with this. For the most part all of the red herrings added to the world building or helped build other clues out. 

The only case though that seemed to be weak was the graduation party case. I was able to figure out the motive fairly quickly, but the handling of the information was awkward, even with the notebook. 

There are a handful of bugs. I had two instances where something I put in should have been accepted, and it was spelled correctly, only to back track the level thinking I missed something when I hadn't. The notepad is also poorly formatted, and after filling up a page the scroll wheel would keep resetting, and it wouldn't follow your text. 

I think that this game struggles to understand what it really is at times and can't make up its mind if it is a puzzle game or a investigative simulator. At the end of the day though I would give this game a solid 7/10.

Dice Legends takes the familiar foundations of a roguelike deckbuilder and gives them a clever identity by making dice just as important as the cards themselves. Rather than simply drawing a hand and spending a conventional energy resource, every turn requires rolling dice and deciding how their values should be assigned to available cards. This creates a satisfying mixture of planning, probability, and adaptation. Big Bite Games and Ad Luna are credited as the developers, with Ad Luna and Big Bite Games handling publishing duties. The concept sounds heavily dependent on luck at first, but the deeper mechanics are built around controlling randomness rather than merely accepting whatever the dice provide.

Each turn begins with a pool of dice alongside cards drawn from the player's deck. Dice are then allocated to activate attacks, defensive abilities, debuffs, and more elaborate combinations. A poor roll can complicate an otherwise promising turn, yet equipment, power-ups, and card interactions provide ways to manipulate outcomes. This makes effective deck construction about more than collecting individually powerful cards. A strong build needs cards that cooperate with the hero's dice and equipment, allowing undesirable results to remain useful while making favorable rolls considerably more powerful. Finding a combination that turns several modest actions into an overwhelming sequence is easily one of the most rewarding aspects of the combat.

The three playable heroes offer genuinely different approaches instead of functioning as minor variations of the same character. Arie is a Lion Paladin associated with d6 dice, specializing in powerful attacks and protective shields. Kuro is a Crow Demon Summoner using d12 dice and can bring familiars into battle, resulting in a more unusual style built around summoned assistance. Xin is a Toad Assassin who relies on d8 dice, shadow abilities, damage over time, and potentially enormous critical strikes. Because each hero uses a different type of die and has distinct deck-building mechanics, switching characters requires reconsidering which values, cards, and equipment combinations are desirable.

Progression reinforces the experimental nature of the combat. Defeated monsters provide new cards that can reshape the direction of a run, while successfully completing locations rewards equipment such as weapons, armor, and accessories. With 160 hand-drawn cards and more than 75 items advertised, there is substantial room to search for unusual synergies. The best moments come when equipment and cards stop feeling like separate upgrades and instead become interconnected pieces of a larger strategy. Random acquisition naturally means that not every run develops equally well, but improvising around what is available is fundamental to the roguelike structure.

Enemy encounters provide enough variety to encourage more than relentless offensive play. More than 50 enemies are spread throughout four visually distinct worlds, with different abilities requiring players to reconsider their priorities. Sometimes immediate damage is the sensible choice, while other situations encourage shielding, weakening an opponent, establishing damage-over-time effects, or preparing a stronger future turn. Since combat is turn-based, there is ample opportunity to examine the hand and available dice before committing to a sequence. This deliberate pacing suits the mechanics particularly well and rewards players who enjoy solving tactical problems.

Exploration is presented through a world shaped by a magical catastrophe that transformed humans into frightening beasts. Players choose destinations while searching for clues surrounding the Last Human, a mysterious mage connected to the world's transformation. The premise gives purpose to the repeated encounters and progression without overwhelming the mechanical focus. The narrative concept from Rafał Jaki brings additional character to the setting, while the hand-drawn presentation helps the heroes, cards, creatures, and environments maintain a distinct fantasy personality. LouisF's original musical score is another notable part of the presentation and complements the methodical rhythm of the adventure.

The main limitation is inseparable from the game's greatest strength. Dice introduce unpredictability, and even a carefully assembled strategy can occasionally be disrupted by inconvenient results. Players who dislike significant random elements in tactical games may find this frustrating. However, treating dice manipulation as part of deck building substantially reduces the feeling that victory is determined purely by chance. Learning to construct a flexible setup that can survive imperfect rolls becomes an important skill, and that progression in player knowledge provides much of the long-term satisfaction.

Steam Deck compatibility is encouraging for portable play. The game is rated Playable rather than fully Verified. Its default graphics configuration performs well on the handheld, it runs successfully through SteamOS, and all functionality is accessible with the default controller configuration. The compromises are relatively minor but worth knowing: some text may appear small on the Deck's display, and the game can occasionally show mouse, keyboard, or non-Steam-Deck controller icons. Given its turn-based structure, it remains a particularly suitable style of game for shorter handheld sessions despite those interface imperfections.

Overall, this is a thoughtful variation on the increasingly crowded roguelike deckbuilding genre. The interaction between cards, equipment, character mechanics, and different dice types gives battles a distinctive tactical flavor, while the three heroes provide enough mechanical contrast to make experimentation worthwhile. Randomness can occasionally produce frustrating situations, but the ability to manipulate and plan around probability prevents luck from completely dominating the experience. Its strongest achievement is making every die roll into a tactical problem rather than simply a random number. For players who enjoy deck construction, turn-based decision-making, discovering powerful synergies, and adapting strategies when plans go wrong, it offers an engaging and intelligently designed challenge.

I recommend this game, but with some pretty hefty caveats. They're big enough that I waffled a bit on the recommendation, but everything that makes me hesitant are things that could be fixed with time, and hopefully they do so. Also the bugs did not prevent me from getting ~10 hours of gameplay and that's already a decent deal for the current sale price ($14).

+Positives
+Art and theming are very strong, especially the art for the cards and the pixel art for the characters.
+I like the difference in the way the characters feel due to the dice and base abilities, it does help to give a different feel for each.
+The half card design is smart, essentially you draw 5 cards, but if you draw a half card another half card will be drawn to make a whole card slot. It's like adding card draw to cards but not as consistent, which is a good and interesting design.
+Decent spread of designs for what roll each card needs based on the die type of the character, and each card can upgrade in two different ways, which is a design more deck builders are using and I really like personally. Most of the choices aren't game changing, but are significant choices. Do you choose two uses of the card as is or get a stronger single effect?  Or you have to choose between more uses or the card becomes half size with the same effect. Lots of good things to think about.
?Mixed
?You can get alternative base powers for each character, which is cool, but the requirements to unlock them seem a bit too novel, IMO. Like 3 will be easy and one you'll have to purposely go for (for example, have 2k gold in a run at some point). So I'll beat a run, have 3/4 of the requirements to unlock the card, but the 4th requirement will be a much more niche situation that just doesn't come up as often or is harder to trigger multiple times per match. 
?The characters aren't as unique as you might expect in their card base, and all of the equipment you can get (essentially relics) are the same across all of the characters. For example, the Lion paladin has a lot of the designs you'd expect, but he has has stuff like sacrificing health for doing damage or big defenses. Not only does that feel a bit out of place for what I expect from what appears to be a holy paladin, all 3 classes have this same mechanic. In other deck builders I've played it might vary by what resource you sacrifice to get the benefit, but here they all sacrifice health, and that is what I'd expect for the warlock, but even for the rogue it feels out of character.
?While I've definitely lost runs, the game overall is fairly easy to get into a broken build very quickly, and some of the buffs are two strong. For instance, there is a buff that just subtracts from all damage you take and it is permanent per battle. I had a paladin run where I was ignoring 25 damage from every damage source in the first 2-3 turns, and combined with armor not falling off in this game, it mostly trivialized it, especially because the cards where you sacrifice life to do more damage/armor actually do damage to you so are also mitigated by this buff. It's fun to be OP, but there doesn't seem to be ascension levels, so the game doesn't seem to have the ramp up that a lot of other games do.
?It uses the Slay the Spire standard of maps with nodes on different paths, but every map pathing is the same. It's reused for a reason, but it can add to the sense of staleness, because it's clear the map is an afterthought.
-Negative
-Consistent, wide ranging bugs, to such a degree it's kind of shocking they made it in to a shipping product. I haven't encountered any gamebreaking bugs that I'm aware of, but it's things like when you're selecting a card reward and pull up your deck to view it, one of the cards will float on top, blocking some of the cards. From what I can tell it's not a specific card or card slot, but there is always 1 that floats in this way. Also, there is like a shadow highlight on cards when you mouse over them, but some cards it just doesn't highlight. While that may seem just like a polish thing at first, I realized I wasn't sure if it meant the card couldn't be chosen, and it made me less sure that I did have the card highlighted. Also an annoyance is that eventually each regular and elite encounter becomes a choice of three options after you beat the first few bosses, and the two options besides the normal play are a tougher version with some bonus (upgraded cards, a second pack of cards, etc), and a non-fight option that varies from stat manipulation to paying to go to one of the shops. While you are picking the encounter, you are not able to look at the map, which can be very frustrating at points if you can't remember how soon the next shop is.
-Enemies are arranged to the right of you, but when you hit one, they will rearrange their own order. However, this isn't a mechanic that I'm aware of and can lead to you hitting the wrong enemy if you're playing quickly, and they also seem to attack in the original left to right order that they start the turn in, which is just very confusing.
-There simply isn't enough information displayed to the user in basically every situation. For instance, there is very rarely an indication of if a buff/debuff ticks down or is just permanent for the fight, so you have way more memory overhead remembering what everything does when making choices. Compounding this, when selecting card choices there is no way to look at the upgrades. This is especially bad since every card in this game upgrades in two separate ways! There's also a lack of consistency in the language of the buffs and debuffs. For instance, you can get a stack of Ignore Attack at the same time as you have a stack of Retaliate, the only difference between the two being that Retaliate reflects the damage back. The obvious question is what happens when you take damage while you have both? The answer is I think the least common sense one of you lose a stack of both buffs and the attack takes damage. These games already tend towards a lot of cognitive load of all of the effects interacting, but this game has some (to me) baffling choices of how those interactions resolve that amplifies the lack of clarity for a lot of the effects. There's even some issues with the consistency of how effects are worded, which have been very frustrating to me at times. Especially in weird cases like what happens if we both have stacks of Retaliate and one of us attacks. 
-There are some things that the game just straight up never explains. That sounds similar to the last point, but the last one is more like there's not enough information given. There are other examples of you just never being told about mechanics. Longer review:
Dice Legends is a roguelike deckbuilder game that centers around 3 playable characters trudging through a quest to defeat the last human. The game being a roguelike has a lot of variance run to run and I initially found myself quite pulled into the game as the gameplay was satisfying and quite different every time. The art style and music are both brilliant and very fitting for the game too.
It really gave me Slay the Spire vibes, but with the addition of dice, which conceptually sounds interesting and like something that could definitely work in this type of game.

Having said that, while I enjoyed the game at the start, the cracks really started to show the longer I played. While the game was quite varied in terms of builds that you could run, realistically only some of them were really viable if you wanted to win, which severely limits player choice. The longer I played the more I understood how busted some items were and the overall balancing of the game just feels completely out of tune and wack.
This I could perhaps forgive, however what really put the nail in the coffin for me was the amount of bugs I ran into. From minor ones where certain items do not provide the effect they're supposed to (or at the level they are at) to completely game breaking ones where a battle just hangs and you have to close and reopen the game or ones where a killed enemy is still capable of attacking you...
While in modern day gaming bugs have kind of become the norm and I can forgive some jank, I think Dice Legends steps too far beyond what I find acceptable in a non early release title.

Overall, while I find the idea and some of the execution of Dice Legends great, I just think it needs a lot more polish before I could recommend it.

Let it be said, I do recommend this game. The game has very solid core mechanics, and loads of potential. Definitely play it. The free demo is a great way to test if you don't want to drop 20 bucks. I really enjoy it. Solidly. I make many critiques in the rest of this review, but I'm making them because I like the game a lot and I want it to succeed. I genuinely believe that addresses to these points how devs see fit can make this game into one of the top deckbuilder roguelikes.
So here's a rundown of Pros and Cons.

Pros:
- It has phenomenal artwork and animation. Some of the best I've seen in video games, period. The quality of the UI, enemies, characters, and map are very cool.
- The core mechanics, including the dice energy system, actions available, and card mechanics, work very well, and are fun to use. It's a combination of the best parts of the systems from Die in the Dungeon, Diceomancer, and of course Slay the Spire. I like it a lot. And there's enough variety within the basic properties of using the energy, and strategy of dividing your dice between the cards, that's really appealing.
- The character action system is a great extra dimension to each turn. As do the character passives.
- The stats are simple and comprehensible, and they feel substantially valuable at each new interval.
- The character design is pretty sweet, between playable characters and npcs. Both aesthetically, and in gameplay for the characters. They're distinct enough in combat, and all of them feel good to use.
- The division of what each shopkeep can respectively provide is really fun, and adds another dimension to routing.

Cons:
- The variety is lacking. Across enemies and having only 3 playable characters, there's not much you can do per run to have a unique experience. The portraits seem to be a decent system, but acquiring them takes up substantially more time than I suspect they are worth. I would currently consider this the most important point, however, the game is new, and if it continues to receive updates over time, then this will be a moot point as more content is added.
- The difficulty curve is *very* steep. The difference in average difficulty encounter between Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 is wild. This especially applies to the Chapter 2 boss. Perhaps it's a skill issue, but using Arie, I've made it to the Chapter 2 boss only 3 times, and I've gotten pretty wrecked on each attempt, with no hope of success. With Xin it's even worse, and I've only even made to Chapter 2 one time, and died 4 rooms in. I believe a hefty balance rework is in order.
- Items and upgrades are very few and far between. Potions are scarce too. The items also feel a little bland because many are meant to be additional upgrades rather than new dimensions of combat.
- It's not uncommon for it to feel like adding cards to your deck is a detriment, that stops you from drawing your best cards when you need them.
- Block is very difficult to come by. There are few cards that give you block, and the quantity of block you gain is pretty unimportant in later levels where a full turn or even 2 turns of block can be destroyed in 1 turn by enemy attacks. Effectively another difficulty spike issue.
- Boosting your stats is very difficult, and it feels pretty pointless to get stat upgrades instead of health when only every 3rd upgrade per stat matters in combat.
- Finally, there are too many enemies in the game that punish you for attacking them. I understand that it's hard to come up with unique mechanics for every enemy, but it feels like 40% of the enemies in the game inflict counter damage or poison on death or when attacked, and you are almost discouraged from playing the game on many of the encounters. Particularly in Chapter 2.

Most of these cons affect replayability more than anything. On initial runs it feels fresh and new, but as you play the game more, these problems become more and more apparent.

This is a really solid game that has a lot of potential, and I hope that at least some of what I'm saying the devs can get behind and tweak, so that the game is more friendly to new players, and maintains it's value to those who want to enjoy it more.

Insider Trading is a creative roguelike deckbuilding game that transforms stock market speculation into an entertaining experience built around calculated risks, strategic combinations, and financial manipulation. Developed and published by Naiive, the game replaces traditional combat with a volatile trading environment where players use cards to influence stock prices and generate profits. Its unusual premise gives the familiar deckbuilding formula a refreshing identity, combining accessible mechanics with enough strategic complexity to reward experimentation. Rather than functioning as a realistic investment simulator, it presents an exaggerated financial playground where clever decisions can produce extraordinary returns or devastating losses.

The gameplay revolves around manipulating market prices through a carefully constructed deck of cards while attempting to achieve financial targets. Each trading session challenges players to evaluate their available actions, anticipate potential consequences, and determine when to pursue additional profits or secure their earnings. Cards can influence stock values in different ways, creating opportunities to exploit price increases, market crashes, and favorable trading conditions. This system makes every decision meaningful, particularly when aggressive strategies threaten to undermine previously accumulated wealth. The constant tension between ambition and caution gives the experience an engaging rhythm that encourages thoughtful planning.

Deckbuilding represents one of the game's strongest features. Players can expand their strategies through the Aftermarket, where additional cards become available between trading sessions. With more than 120 cards to discover, the possibilities for constructing specialized combinations are considerable. Some cards provide immediate advantages, while others introduce disadvantages that must be balanced against their potential benefits. Selecting effective additions requires understanding how individual effects complement existing strategies. This encourages experimentation rather than simply collecting the strongest available cards, making successful deck construction particularly satisfying.

The inclusion of more than 60 stackable pills and perks adds another layer of strategic depth. These modifiers can enhance particular actions, alter gameplay interactions, and create powerful combinations when paired with suitable cards. The resulting synergies are central to the game's appeal, allowing players to develop increasingly elaborate approaches to market manipulation. Its combo mechanics further reward careful card positioning and sequencing, transforming ordinary actions into potentially lucrative chains of effects. Discovering combinations that dramatically improve profitability creates memorable moments and reinforces the satisfaction of mastering the underlying systems.

Character variety contributes significantly to replayability. Unlockable traders feature distinctive starting decks and specialized mechanics that encourage different approaches to financial success. Certain strategies may emphasize aggressive manipulation, while others reward more controlled decision-making or unusual combinations. This diversity prevents the experience from becoming entirely dependent on one successful formula. Combined with multiple difficulty settings, character progression provides opportunities for both newcomers and experienced deckbuilding enthusiasts to explore the game's mechanics at their preferred challenge level.

The roguelike structure introduces unpredictability through changing circumstances, randomized opportunities, and disruptive economic events. Recessions and unfavorable market developments can force players to reconsider previously effective strategies, creating situations where adaptability becomes just as important as preparation. These complications strengthen the game's replay value, although they can occasionally make unsuccessful runs feel frustrating when unfavorable circumstances undermine otherwise reasonable decisions. Nevertheless, learning to recover from setbacks remains an important part of the experience.

Visually, Insider Trading favors a straightforward retro-inspired presentation that emphasizes readability and functionality. Its pixel-art aesthetic complements the financial theme without distracting from the strategic gameplay. The interface prioritizes cards, market information, and financial outcomes over elaborate animations. Although players seeking impressive graphical effects may find the presentation modest, its simplicity suits the game's emphasis on decision-making. The playful interpretation of stock trading also helps establish an identity distinct from fantasy-oriented deckbuilders.

Accessibility features further improve the overall experience. Adjustable difficulty, text-size options, color alternatives, configurable audio settings, and the ability to save progress provide useful flexibility. Controller support, Steam Cloud functionality, and achievements contribute additional convenience and incentives for continued play. These features make the game approachable while preserving the strategic complexity that defines its appeal.

Steam Deck compatibility is officially classified as Playable. The game can operate on Valve's handheld device, and its relatively modest graphical demands make portable sessions appealing. However, some interactions may require touchscreen input, the virtual keyboard, or customized controller configurations. Certain interface elements may also appear small on the handheld screen. Despite these minor inconveniences, its turn-based gameplay makes it reasonably suitable for portable enjoyment.

The main shortcomings involve potential repetition, occasional randomness, and the possibility of unbalanced combinations. Players expecting realistic financial simulation may also find its mechanics overly simplified. Additionally, those unfamiliar with roguelike deckbuilders might initially struggle with understanding how different cards and modifiers interact. However, these limitations are unlikely to significantly diminish the experience for players who enjoy strategic experimentation and repeated attempts at mastering complex systems.

Overall, Insider Trading delivers an inventive and enjoyable interpretation of the deckbuilding genre through its distinctive financial theme, extensive card combinations, and rewarding risk-management mechanics. Its strongest qualities are the freedom to experiment, the satisfaction of discovering powerful synergies, and the constant challenge of balancing profitability against uncertainty. Although its repetitive structure and occasional unpredictable outcomes may not appeal to everyone, it offers substantial entertainment for players who appreciate strategic decision-making and replayable challenges.

A clever and addictive financial-themed roguelike deckbuilder that combines accessible gameplay with impressive strategic possibilities.

I want, so badly, to recommend this game because the potential here is absolutely wild, but, as you'll see a few reviewers saying, there are significant changes that need to be made before I can amend the review.

My main reservation here is one simple thing: 

Skyrocketing the stock price is the best thing this game has to offer in terms of a pure dopamine rush, but you only need to do it once per week (and even then it's not a wise move). The rest of the week you'll just be begrudgingly tanking the stock price and skipping, biding your time before the next week. The super "high score" runs are usually done just as a fun way to end the week: the game will even warn you NOT to trade once you've hit your goal. 

You are not rewarded AT ALL for huge increases in stock price: seeing those green candles smashing to the moon usually spells disaster for your next few turns. You won't be able to buy the stock the next day because it's too expensive. You'll usually want to beat the goal by a few hundred dollars then rinse and repeat for each week. There are a lot of potential builds, but it's the same song and dance no matter what deck you're running. 

Insider trading is ABOUT BEING FILTHY RICH, but this felt more akin to being a nervous nerd who doesn't want to be caught with his hand in the cookie jar. Oh, also money means pretty much nothing and the game's econ revolves around tokens. So yeah. 

If we see money play more of a significant factor, then I would be the first to revise this review, because WOW the art, the ideas, the music, and the concept are INCREDIBLE. I'll be keeping my eye on updates - this could become my favorite deck builder roguelike; it's SO close.
