Darwinia, developed and published by Introversion Software, stands as one of the most creative and distinct independent games ever made. It merges the structure of a real-time strategy game with elements of action, puzzle solving, and digital simulation, wrapped in a visual style that feels like a living homage to the early days of computing. The story unfolds within a massive virtual theme park known as Darwinia—a digital world created to simulate the evolution of artificial life. When a viral infection spreads through this artificial ecosystem, the player is tasked with helping the Darwinians, tiny pixelated inhabitants of the world, fight for survival and rebuild their fragile society. What makes the experience special is how it blends nostalgic computer aesthetics with an emotional sense of discovery and preservation, turning what could have been an abstract idea into something surprisingly moving.

The world of Darwinia is striking from the very first moment. Everything is presented in a stylized, low-poly visual design reminiscent of classic vector graphics, but with a vibrant color palette and dynamic lighting that breathe energy into its simplicity. Each area feels like a digital diorama, filled with geometric landscapes, abstract structures, and glowing lines that represent circuits and code. Despite the minimalist presentation, the world feels alive and beautiful, constantly humming with movement and light. The visual style isn’t just for show—it reinforces the concept of entering a simulated environment, a computer world that feels both familiar and alien. It’s a rare case where the art direction defines the tone so completely that it becomes inseparable from the game’s identity. Combined with a subtle, ambient soundtrack that hums like a machine at work, the atmosphere is hypnotic and strangely serene even amid chaos.

Gameplay in Darwinia is an intricate blend of strategy and direct control. Players interact with the environment by deploying “programs” such as squads, engineers, and officers—each represented by simple but functional polygons. Squads serve as your combat units, clearing out viral infections and defending the Darwinians. Engineers recover digital souls from fallen creatures and repair key infrastructure, while officers help organize the movement of the population. The game cleverly balances high-level management with hands-on control, allowing you to switch between overseeing the battlefield and directly steering units in real-time combat. This hybrid system gives the game a unique rhythm: one moment you’re managing population logistics and production, and the next you’re personally fighting off a swarm of enemies with laser fire. It captures the thrill of action while retaining the cerebral satisfaction of strategy.

As the campaign progresses, the depth of Darwinia’s design becomes apparent. Each level introduces new challenges—whether it’s reclaiming infected territory, guiding survivors across dangerous terrain, or reconstructing the virtual world’s systems. There’s a gentle learning curve that rewards experimentation and persistence, and every victory feels earned. The sense of progress doesn’t come from unlocking flashy upgrades but from watching the digital world come back to life. The more you save the Darwinians and rebuild their environment, the more vibrant and self-sustaining the world becomes. This creates a powerful emotional loop where your actions have tangible, visible results. Despite the abstract visuals, the game manages to evoke genuine empathy for its tiny inhabitants, making their survival feel meaningful.

The story of Darwinia is minimalist yet profound. It doesn’t rely on cutscenes or heavy exposition, instead using environmental storytelling and the natural evolution of gameplay to communicate its ideas. The premise—that you are helping a creator restore a broken digital ecosystem—is simple but layered with thematic resonance. It explores ideas about artificial intelligence, creation, digital decay, and the ethics of intervention in a simulated world. The Darwinians, though made of polygons and simple animations, become symbols of resilience and adaptation. The narrative’s subtlety invites interpretation, and players often find themselves reflecting on the nature of life and technology as they guide these artificial beings toward a new future.

Darwinia’s one notable limitation lies in its brevity and learning curve. The campaign is relatively short, and while its pacing feels tight, some players may wish it lasted longer or offered more complex scenarios. The gesture-based interface for summoning units can also feel cumbersome at first, though it becomes second nature with practice. Yet these imperfections are part of what gives the game its charm—it feels handcrafted and experimental, the product of vision rather than formula. Its concise length means it never overstays its welcome, and the sense of wonder remains intact from beginning to end.

Even years after its release, Darwinia remains an exceptional achievement in independent game design. It’s both a technical experiment and an artistic statement, proving that innovation doesn’t require massive budgets or photorealistic graphics. Introversion Software succeeded in creating a world that feels alive, mysterious, and deeply personal—a digital space where strategy meets empathy. Its blend of retro aesthetics, clever mechanics, and emotional subtlety makes it a timeless experience that still feels original today. For players seeking something different, something that feels like a cross between an old-school computer dream and a modern meditation on creation, Darwinia is a journey worth taking—strange, beautiful, and unforgettable.

Darwinia is a nice little RTS which reminded me a lot of the movie TRON. It is not an overly long game, and you could probably beat it in around 10 hours, less if you try to get through as speedily as possible. The writing is decent. The gameplay is decent. The soundtrack is okay. It should be noted that the game is single-player only, unlike most well-known RTS games.

You can tell that a lot of care went into this game. It runs well, did not have any noticeable bugs, and also includes some nice extras like a map editor. I really appreciated the work that went into the game's startup screens, which are all very nice and fun to watch. Some of them even reveal background information about the game's story. The number of different startup screens really surprised me. I finished the game over many sessions, and I had already finished just over half the game before I saw a startup screen repeated. It is certainly unusual to see so much effort put into something that most people would probably consider an extremely minor part of a game these days.

I have no more to say on the graphics, writing, soundtrack, etc. They are nothing too remarkable, but they are all decent. The gameplay is where my main concern is. Darwinia's gameplay is, honestly, pretty slow-paced. There were a lot of times when I was waiting for my units to get from one place to another. This issue is exacerbated by the fact that this game has the lowest unit cap I have ever seen in an RTS, three units! This is upgradable to five. That's it. Sure, the Darwinians don't count towards that cap, but they are not very useful except for manning fortifications and objectives, which they are required for. The upshot is that building units other than Darwinians is instant and takes no resources, so if you lose a unit you can instantly reconstitute it at the nearest spawn point.

Another complaint I have is that the tutorial does not seem complete. Sure, you get walked through a few things, but some very important basic mechanics are omitted from the tutorial. In particular, the transmission dishes which serve as bridges between parts of levels were not explained to me by the game, and I ended up only finding out about them when they were mentioned by another player. This is a central mechanic that exists on every map and is essential for the later missions! I am not sure why something so critical is not in the tutorial, especially considering that there is such a bridge in the tutorial level, though using it is not required to finish that level or the other early levels. This would not be quite so bad were it not for the fact that this mechanic is non-obvious, as the transmission dishes appear to be part of the level as opposed to something you can control. There are some other, less critical omissions as well, like how to switch a squad's weapons.

The game does have a well-executed Linux port, which I very much appreciate. The game runs natively on Linux, and it runs well. It is refreshing to see a native Linux port which works just fine and has no issues that I noticed.

If you like single-player RTS and computer-themed stuff, this is a good pick.

[h1]Timeless Gem[/h1]
[hr][/hr][i]Game remains an unique gem to this day. There are very few games which tries to portray a feeling of being in a virtual world. It retains an unique aesthetic and feeling. One which was very impressive back then and still holds up to this day. It is a timeless game, but these days and in the future we are cby a mediocre slop.[/i][hr][/hr]
[h1]☠️It should be the sin to be poor☠️[/h1]
I remember seeing this game in a gaming magazine. It struck me as such an unique and good looking game. Back then, games were trying to push 3D graphics into realism, but they were still looking quite unrealistic. Especially real time strategy games. This would put them in an uncanny valley or just make them look bad. Very few games looked graphically great in that period and AAA games were ones pushing the limits. This game stood out, because it was trying to do its own thing. It is an unique, little gem which is still great today. I only regret that I couldn't play it back then when I was a child. It would had blown me away as it would immerse me in a simulated, virtual world. I do regret of not being able to play it back then when games were a lot worse, far fewer and anything remotely good was an instant cult classic. This is one game which plays just as well today as it would had back then and it would had left much greater impression on me in those simpler times. Sadly, affordability was the main issue and childish lack of attention was another reason holding me back.

[h1]💖What makes it special💖[/h1]
Game tries to sell you an idea that you are in virtual world which is alive. Over time, this idea grows on you as game is immersive. It knows what it needs to do in order to try and sell you an idea of a world. It is not trying to be convenient or responsive. It doesn't reduce people in a game into HP and units. This inherent resistance helps you to feel that this is its own world rather than just a level which you have to conquer. Units which you control are explicitly stated to be just programs. They are directly controlled by you and are perfectly obedient. While Darwinians (local sentient inhabitants) on the other hand cannot be directly controlled. This separation goes a long way of making you believe that these two things are different and it helps with immersion. 

Another aspect of an immersion is simulation. World is simulated from Darwinians to terrain or projectiles. Even entire game map tries to portray that it is something in which Darwinians live and work in and everything is connected. Over time, it grows on you through little experiences. It plays badly, but that serves to reinforce that it is not a video game. Simulation also goes a long way. Each particle has to connect with the enemy. Grenades bounce through terrain. You start thinking in terms of line of sight and high ground. You become more engaged with the map terrain and as result, you get emotionally invested with maps themselves. Sound of difficult battle going on in the distance and your Dawrinians lollygagging at the helps to sell you this world. Likewise, you can draft them and send them to die in the war. Seeing them trying to hold on positions which they are slowly losing is a missing ingredient which so many RTS fail to give to you. In those games, map and NPCs feel lifeless where here they have their own charm as they are simulated and reacting to threats which are themselves unscripted. This naturally leads into stories and far more natural situations.

[h1]📋Stories from the front📋[/h1]
I tried to establish Darwinian colony on an island, but couldn't because other 3 colonies would constantly launch raids upon me. I couldn't control my AI units fast enough to respond to two flank assault. Their main strength - perfect obedience was turned into their weakness. So, I started capturing another, starter island so to speak. I managed to establish my colony there. It was far easier cleaning spawn point after spawn point since they were separated by greater distances and were more linear to each other. So, I had time to capture souls and convert it to my population. After conquering, I then could push into that island through transfer point. With ability to rally Darwinians to my side, I managed to make them entrenched on that spawn point. Through greater initial numbers and by carrying turrets to fortify area, I could focus just clearing one spawn point after another. 

Game often turns into a siege warfare where you cannot just use your own directly controlled units. You have to rely on Darwinians who are semi-independent. This is what gives game so much of its charm. It is one thing to see your units fighting, it is another to see local inhabitants trying their best to fight. There was a spider infestation which I couldn't clear myself as they were spawning way too quickly and it would be massive chore to do it solo. So, I had called up Darwinians and established turrets at the entrance. They started to thin the never ending swarm. Each side dragging fallen entities as souls back to the base for revival unto their side. It is trench warfare to the extreme. Then I made several more formations and ordered them to engage spiders from another angle. They went through their mountain chain and occupied at that time, relatively free high ground with my soldiers. My soldiers were shock troops which cleared landing territory and kept enemies at bay until my allies arrived with their transport tanks. They established upon high ground and they started to seriously thin down the enemy horde from two sides. This was the thing which I was looking for since now I could easily use my troops/programs to go in and take their nests out. Once I had broken their numbers, rest was just the cleaning operation.

[h1]🔧Where it falls short🔧[/h1]
This game had a surprisingly long support history. It is clearly loved and is taken proper care of. However, not all is roses and rainbows. I had issues with making Steam screenshots for the game. Steam integration could be better.

More substantial issue is that this game is simply dated. It is a game made in few years by few dudes more or less. Production values as such are low. Its unique artstyle can hide lack of graphical budget to make graphics, maps or music. However, it still has very little content. Enemies are very few and you will see most of them quite soon in the campaign. You have like one troop and one Darwinian troop. Rest are support units or gear. Enemies likewise are just 3 types. Regular lines on a ground, flying worm or a spider. Then there are recoloured Darwinians who are now evil and are fighting you. 

Then you start playing game, it can get tedious very fast. As you don't have unlocks and are not invested into the world, seeing a new map with multiple islands which are teeming with enemies, get old really fast. You need to manually kill each of those enemies and gather their souls for your Darwinias. Gameplay is slow and lacks in any variety. You sure have to get immersed and like what you are playing, otherwise you will be bored to tears.

[h1]An Unique Experiment[/h1]
[hr][/hr][i]I do wish that I could had played this game when I saw it in gaming magazine. Back then it would had struck like a truck. Its aesthetics would offer relief from mud, grey graphics at that time, awkwardly pushing for photo realism. It would be its own indie game when indie games didn't existed. Its mechanics would be seen as cutting edge and lack of content and its tedious nature would had been no obstacles to me. It is one of those rare games which could come at any period in history and still be good or feasible to make. It came out in 2005, but it's one of those rare cases where a brilliant game like this could had came out in 2000 too and be just the same.[/i][hr][/hr]

What invited me to this game in particular was its more cyber fantasy graphics than the oh to typical dystopian or medieval fantasy that's been done to death. And while I've owned it for so many years but played so little of it up to later after the 10000th Anniversary Edition update, it's high time I get to experience it to the end and finally beat it!

Being introduced to a virtual universe created by one man and developed within itself by a species of flat stick-like figures, you jump in unnoticed and are already put to use by borrowing the man's programs to combat a virus and saving his people. Keeping the graphics simple and the game running at a top 60 in a 3D world when playing a real-time strategy is essential, and I like how considerate this game was made to work with that while taking advantage of it with pixelization effects here and there to let you know when a program is about to fall apart. Also, color me impressed as to how the Darwinians were able to project the maker's face in the sky.

The controls are easy to understand well enough once you've pressed 'H' enough times to know how to control each program and get used to the interface. But it was nice and fluid to try the gesture controls for a change, especially if you have a touch-screen. In either case, the learning curve is pretty fair to get you reacting fast enough to know how to push yourself to completing objectives in each of the world's zones.

The difficulty spike can be pretty unpredictable, even with the default setting (1/10). Once you read and predict what your units and enemies are weak against, the way you strategize becomes pretty clear. You will be put under pressure later on in the story as enemies continue to respawn (either from viruses hatching from eggs or the infection that keeps rushing in waves after you). Once you've put enough hours into the game where the creator has done enough research upgrades to give you and your tasks a well-enough advantage, you'll feel like you're making a comeback, and that's very satisfying.

The way that Darwinia was made to be played and explored is a beauty in itself, and I loved how much care the devs put into it to want to keep you coming back for more. Give it a try if you want an interesting new take on a strategy game, or if it's something that'll get you into strategy without the repeat offenders of the past.

Unfortunately, in practice the gameplay consists of jumping from shadow to shadow to avoid death by radiation, the occasional puzzle.... and not much else. There IS a fun survival element in the game, and if there were more instances of that I would probably recommend this game. But as it stands I had to drop this one.

(PLEASE READ THE WHOLE REVIEW)
First: This game is unfinished. Literally. They mentioned they had to split the game near the end of development because they did not have time to iron out the bugs in later sections of the game. Some people have been very upset by this, and also that the developers are (presumably?) Russian. I have nothing to add to that conversation, because in my opinion neither of those affect the outcome of the product I actually PLAYED.

Radiosol is an absolutely charming little horror. You are a small(?) remote-piloted(?) little spider drone with magnet feet. You can walk on any surface you can make physical contact with. This alone makes exploration in this game an UNBELIEVABLE JOY. Add in the sheer exhilarating scale of some of these structures, the momentum of the charged jump, launching yourself between buildings, and the traversal in this game is, simply put, Wonderful. I fucking loved exploring in RADIOSOL.
And then you have to contend with THE SUN. The ever-present eclipse, the constant coronal mass ejection, the tinnitus whine and death-rattle crackle of your radiation dosage skyrocketing by the second. You don't see your vision burning until it's either almost too late or until you recover fully-- the lens distortion and the blindness. The sun is an ever-present horror and this game is better than most at making me constantly afraid of it.

The ambient droning music of the cityscape, punctuated with moments of tranquility, all add delightful flavor to the cityscape. The pixel textures are chunky enough to qualify as "retro-looking", but SO detailed, i can distinguish individual layers between buildings. it's fantastic.

RADIOSOL is a fantastic game, and I can't wait to see what the devs have in store for Chapter 2. My one complaint is the SD-Radio system. I would appreciate a tutorial on how to use it for more than the one absolutely-mandatory radio puzzle in the game, especially since, I hope, the second chapter will have more complex riddles to solve.

The atmosphere is great, and the setting initially feels pretty amazing. And with the broadcast you receive from the leader, the stage seems set for an amazing, dark, gritty experience and mood, but this feeling goes downhill instantly when you begin communicating with the person(?) that is guiding you, who comes off as a millennial girl quirky chungus that may as well be punctuating every communique with 'lol', which completely ruins the overall feel of the game. Add to that how their guidance is poor and unclear on your tasks or how to complete them, as well as the puzzles are poorly fleshed out and often made no sense to me. You go on your way to do what seems to be Task 1, only for you guide to literally be like, 'Oops! I guess I forgot to tell you that you would need to do XYZ first. lol.' So you then start backtracking. 

The interface style is great but doesn't lend itself to logic when trying to accomplish a simple task. For instance, though I had the level 3 access, and it was 'activated' as far as I could tell, I could never get a fan to be disabled, as it kept insisting that I needed level three access. And there was no way to communicate this to your guide, for help or assistance, so you're left trying to figure out what if-then-else you must have failed to accomplish at some point earlier or before or when you were wandering around. 

Simple pings on the display to lead you to the general area for the next task could have helped a lot but as it is you're just left to wander and hope you run across something that seems related to your task. Like the guide would say, 'Go to the repair depot', as if you know where that is, and provides no map or ping in the distance telling you generally where that would be. Also, interfacing with other devices in the game is not quite a pixel-hunt, but almost so, as you must position yourself on a certain spot on a device or structure for it to give you the prompt to interact. So you could be at the spot or have found the vehicle or antenna you think might be what you were looking for, but because you're not standing in the right spot on the item, you don't get the 'E' prompt. Also, when you would open the interface console to the person guiding you, you'd have to scroll down past every previous message to get down to the bottom to again review the last message received, and this get old, fast.

I felt like at multiple points I had softlocked progress, since every task left you feeling like 'Did I do what I needed to do? I have no clue. I think I did.' So I was left unsure if anything I thought I had successfully completed was, in fact, done correctly. As I could not progress, though I seemingly had the clearance level I needed, clearly, I hadn't. Basically, I gave up and don't feel like I will return to play further. Even your guide would give you some quirky responses sometimes, like, 'Hopefully you did that right, lol' leading further toward the destruction of the atmosphere and mood I was hoping for and just adding more frustration to the whole experience.

RADIOSOL is, inside and out, one of the most interesting games I've played in a while, which is why I'm writing a more in-depth review than I usually would. It's soul is deep and beautiful, it's conceptual execution is fascinating, and it's swathed in painful communication issues. Kinda like an ex-partner. Especially since I know I'll be texting it back when the second half of it releases.

I'll start with the flaws, because this is the kinda game that can be easily bounced off of due to them. It doesn't tell you it lacks an autosave, so you have to manually save often. It's not communicated as clearly as I'd like that only half the game is out. It's tutorial popups can be oddly timed, and/or a tad confusing. It's marketing feels a bit vague. And frankly, it's complicated relationship with gravity causes me to accidentally crane my neck while playing it. Maybe that's just me.

I say all of this to lend more oomph to this statement: I absolutely recommend this game. It's aesthetic is nailed perfectly, it's world feels so real and strange, and the minimal hand-holding mixed with fundamentally simplistic but difficult-to-conceptualize puzzle design makes figuring it out feel super rewarding. The movement of your skittering little robot is lovely, and lends itself wonderfully to crawling up intricate superstructures the environment is littered with. Wandering RADIOSOL's scorched cities and decoding it's complexities is genuinely captivating. 

This is all a summary, I could go on. The graphical style and art direction, the blazing sun. The surprisingly fantastic score, the minimal but charming dialogue. It enraptures me. 
RADIOSOL Is an odd game, and that is it's strength. For the pricetag, and a free second chapter coming soon(?), I recommend it. if this game seems like your jam, it will be your JAM. It can be confusing, but there is a helpful walkthrough on the community page that can help a lot. But I'd suggest giving it a shot. Wander. Explore. Think. Breathe it in.

That'll be all. Thank you for reading, and thank you to the devs, for putting their hearts into such a wonderfully esoteric product.

Some disclaimers.

Firstly, this game was released as a finished game with no disclosure that it was in fact an unfinished early access game. It's there now, but if you go to the October 7th dev log you can see the developer decided to bait and switch. He lied on purpose to get people to beta test the game. This is not the best first point of contact with a dev. I will probably never buy a game from them again.

Secondly, this game was made in Russia and used AI translation software to get it ready for a global release. I'll avoid my personal opinion about AI- I dont feel like this significantly compromised my enjoyment (or lack of) of this game.

With that out of the way, we can finally talk about the game. It's pretty mediocre. When I entered the world for the first time and walked out into the sun I was mesmerized by how good everything manages to look from a distance. The effect is stunning and I wanted to take screenshots and really get a look at everything from a grand vista. The game says no. No. Do not look. Do not look at anything. Stop. Any time you're anywhere that you could just... get a look at the world and actually see the one part of the game I truly thought was good- you'll die within 5 seconds. Because the sun kills you. This was, literally one of the only things the game had to offer, and one of the only things I wish I could say I enjoyed without caveat. Instead you are permitted to take peaks at the world in 5 second intervals or you will instantly die.

So- with that disappointment I started playing the game, and if you read my first disclosure up there you'll know I was an unwilling beta tester. This game is filled to the bring with bugs. They start instantly and youll learn to fear things like fences for their infinite capacity to suck you in like a black hole and kill you by holding you in the sun. After you learn that flat plane objects can and will kill you if you dare to touch them, the game will progress much smoother. You have a guide that pops text up onto your screen to tell you what you're currently doing, and where you should be going. These directions are bad, the trigger flags are poorly implemented, and the guide will often pop up to tell you that you are currently looking at something while you are trying to free yourself from a fence, or under a piece of garbage and can't see anything, or on the other side of a building.  The guide will pop up over your screen, and not pause the game so I hope you weren't doing anything because now your entire screen is covered.

I think the guide is supposed to come off as mysterious and a bit scary- and maybe she is in russian. In english shes kind of pathetic and whiney. The entire game boils down essentially to you having to walk to 5 places on the map. If your director happened to pop up and tell you what buildings you were looking at while you were looking at them, this might be pretty easy for you. Mine didn't so I ended up wandering a lot. When you reach a place, the guide will tell you that you're at a place SOMETIMES. Once while I was at place where there was nothing my guide popped up and said I was at a different place, and so I spent a really long time searching the area, then found what I was supposed to find somewhere entirely different just by chance wandering.

After you gone to the 5 places youll do the thing! At the place! And then the game is over. Chapter two coming... some day!

Its satisfying to master the movement mechanics, but they are a bit jank and the camera swinging around can be disorienting. There are a (very) few collectables that give you lore tidbits and  upgrades, which you can hunt for but don't expect every little corner to have something. The map is really for you to take your time with and soak in the atmosphere and radiation.

The world itself has plenty of broken down industrial, military, and mech wreckage that is interesting to crawl around on and see the artist's interpretation of technology. The "story" isn't much, it's maybe 5 minutes of reading text files and context clues of why shit is fucked. At the very end of the current content (chapter 1) there is ~1min of cutscene similar to the trailer that teases new themes.

I count in my head 4 major puzzles, no spoilers but:
1st is simple but neat because of its scale.
2nd is genuinely great for how much it breaks your expectations of the world and provides some tension.
3rd has clues that in hindsight make sense, but if you miss anything or are out of order you'll get frustrated.
4th is more of a victory lap with some special music.

I'm giving this a cautious thumbs up because whether you like this or not depends almost completely on what kind of challenge and experience you're looking for. 
In a lot of ways this is a throwback to 90's gaming when graphics up close were ugly, gaming mechanics and controls were very often clunky and honestly terrible and there were no things such as quest markers or automaps. You get a vague description to find x and do y, often one key word or phrase being the crucial bit of info and that's it.
While i personally am nostalgic over that period, i honestly don't miss it. As often was the case  back then, with this you will get frustrated, you will feel annoyed, you will think you have done y only to go to where you want to go and then having to backtrack to x bang your head against the wall some more. 

Yet that ended up being the thing that got me coming back to this game the most. It rekindled the old satisfaction of finally figuring it all out or finding that underground entrance that i didn't even know i was looking for. Combined with depressing atmosphere and apocalyptic aesthetic, the bad controls and frustrating objectives and difficult (and honestly great) puzzles actually add to the actual experience instead of subtracting from it. 

So this isn't really a fun game but it can be very enjoyable (if that makes sense) if the aforementioned sounds like something you might be up for.

Also to keep in mind is the fact that it is a  chaptered release with no info whether the other chapters will be free or not.

KUNAI is a nimble little Metroidvania with a clear feel for momentum. Its best moments come when movement, platforming and combat stop being separate tasks and start feeding into one another. A dash or parry is not just decoration; timing matters, and the game has a satisfying snap when you get it right. The result is an action platformer that feels lively under your hands and consistently gives its movement room to shine.

The visual style does a lot with a deliberately limited palette. The chunky pixel art has that Super Game Boy quality: bold, readable shapes and a pleasingly compact range of colors. It gives the world personality without crowding the action, and the expressive little touches keep the presentation charming rather than cold. The soundtrack is a major part of that appeal. It has real energy and gives the adventure a heart that could easily have been lost in a more generic robot-apocalypse setup.

There is a pleasing mix of influences in the way KUNAI moves. The grappling and traversal have a Bionic Commando flavor, while the quick, nimble action recalls The Messenger. Those are useful touchstones, but KUNAI has enough character of its own to avoid feeling like a mere imitation. Its level design is clever, and the platforming is precise enough to make navigating the world feel like a skill you are building, rather than a chore between fights.

Combat is fast and satisfying, and the small decisions carry weight. Parrying and dashing matter, so encounters ask for attention instead of inviting you to mash through them. That gives the action a satisfying rhythm and supports the game’s emphasis on movement. I also appreciate how naturally the platforming and fighting belong together: the same responsiveness that makes it fun to move around gives the combat its spark.

KUNAI is not quite as polished as its strongest ideas deserve. I would like the controls and combat to be a little tighter. That is a meaningful reservation in a game where precision and responsiveness are so central, and it keeps the action from reaching the effortless confidence of the very best in the genre. The comparison to Hollow Knight is an ambitious one; KUNAI has enough charm and design sense to make the thought tempting, but it is not quite there yet.

Still, the caveat does not undo what works. This is a solid, well-judged Metroidvania built around fluid movement, smart platforming and combat with a satisfying pulse. Its presentation is memorable, its music gives it warmth, and its mechanics make the adventure feel like something made with affection for the form. I recommend KUNAI to anyone looking for a compact, characterful action platformer, especially if they enjoy movement that asks to be mastered. It may need a little more control and combat refinement to stand alongside the genre’s giants, but it already has the good instincts and personality to be worth playing.

KUNAI, developed by TurtleBlaze and published by The Arcade Crew and Gamirror Games, is a fast-paced 2D action platformer that fuses the acrobatics of ninja combat with the exploratory freedom of a Metroidvania. Set in a post-apocalyptic world where humanity has been nearly wiped out by an artificial intelligence uprising, the game casts the player as Tabby—a sentient tablet infused with the soul of a warrior. From this quirky premise unfolds a stylish and energetic adventure that embraces its absurdity while delivering one of the most fluid and satisfying movement systems in the genre. Rather than relying on narrative depth, KUNAI thrives on its mechanical precision and kinetic design, turning traversal into an art form and combat into a seamless extension of motion.

The heart of the experience lies in Tabby’s dual kunai, which serve as both weapons and tools for movement. These grappling hooks allow players to swing through environments with astonishing grace, chaining momentum-based leaps, wall runs, and vertical climbs in one continuous flow. The controls are tight and intuitive, making each swing feel deliberate and weighty while still allowing for creative improvisation. Few games manage to capture such a tangible sense of speed and agility without sacrificing control. Every area feels like a playground built around the kunai system, with wide chasms, vertical corridors, and hidden alcoves encouraging experimentation. The result is a traversal system that remains consistently thrilling throughout the game, striking a perfect balance between accessibility and mastery.

Combat in KUNAI is simple but sharp, emphasizing precision over complexity. Tabby wields a katana as the main weapon, complemented by ranged tools like shurikens and firearms that are gradually introduced as the game progresses. Each encounter demands awareness of positioning, with the player constantly juggling offensive momentum and evasive movement. The grappling kunai are just as useful in battle as they are in traversal—letting you swing over enemies, launch aerial attacks, or zip across the screen to avoid damage. While the basic enemy types pose little threat, boss fights stand out for their creativity, forcing players to use every ability at their disposal. They often test reflexes and adaptability rather than brute strength, rewarding those who have mastered the game’s movement language.

Visually, KUNAI strikes a distinct tone that sets it apart from other indie action games. The world is rendered in a minimalist pixel-art style that evokes nostalgia while maintaining a modern sense of polish. Each area uses limited color palettes—muted blues, bright yellows, and harsh reds—to establish its atmosphere, creating strong visual contrast and a crisp readability that makes navigation intuitive. Character animations are expressive despite their simplicity, and Tabby’s little emotive face adds a surprising amount of charm to a robotic protagonist. The soundtrack complements this visual style perfectly with its blend of futuristic synths and driving percussion, creating a rhythm that matches the fluidity of the gameplay. The sound design reinforces feedback elegantly—each sword slash, grapple swing, and explosion lands with just enough punch to feel satisfying without overwhelming the senses.

Narratively, the game keeps things light and humorous. Rather than burdening players with dense lore or long cutscenes, KUNAI sprinkles in quirky dialogue and moments of comedic absurdity that lend the world personality. The story of an AI uprising is mostly background flavor, with much of the focus placed on Tabby’s interactions with eccentric robot characters. These moments provide levity and contrast the intensity of the action. The humor lands in a way that never breaks immersion; instead, it adds to the charm of a world that feels both desolate and oddly cheerful. The storytelling approach fits the game’s pace perfectly—short, snappy, and never in the way of the core gameplay loop.

Exploration follows the familiar rhythm of a Metroidvania: new abilities unlock previously inaccessible areas, encouraging backtracking and discovery. While the map design is functional and well-structured, it doesn’t quite reach the intricate interconnectedness of genre standouts like Hollow Knight or Ori. Some players may find the backtracking slightly repetitive due to the limited environmental diversity, though the sheer enjoyment of movement helps mitigate this issue. The world is peppered with collectibles, primarily cosmetic hats that give Tabby different appearances. These serve as playful rewards rather than substantial upgrades but reinforce the game’s irreverent tone. Despite its compact scale, the adventure offers enough hidden paths and optional challenges to reward curiosity.

KUNAI’s greatest achievement is its sense of flow. It captures the feeling of constant motion—of being perfectly in sync with your character and environment. Even during intense combat or platforming sequences, the game rarely loses its rhythm. Every input feels immediate, every movement intentional, and the momentum-driven gameplay delivers a sense of exhilaration that few platformers manage to replicate. This precision ensures that frustration is rare, and when failure occurs, it’s almost always a matter of player error rather than mechanical fault. It’s a game that encourages mastery through play rather than punishment, and that philosophy permeates every design decision.

Despite its strengths, KUNAI is not without flaws. The experience is relatively short, lasting around six to ten hours depending on exploration habits, and the story ends before its world feels fully explored. Some later sections feel more linear than they should, and the difficulty curve fluctuates inconsistently—especially during boss encounters that can swing from too easy to abruptly punishing. These shortcomings, however, are minor compared to the consistent enjoyment delivered by the movement and combat systems. The game’s tight pacing ensures that it never overstays its welcome, leaving players with a sense of completion rather than exhaustion.

KUNAI stands as one of the most polished and inventive indie action games in recent memory, a showcase of how refined mechanics and personality can elevate even the simplest premise. It succeeds not through narrative ambition or complexity, but through the elegance of its design and the joy it finds in pure motion. Every swing, slash, and leap feels handcrafted to deliver satisfaction, and every moment reinforces the game’s identity as a celebration of agility and creativity. It’s a game that embraces its retro roots while feeling distinctly modern, one that rewards curiosity and precision without ever losing its sense of fun. For anyone who loves fast, fluid platforming wrapped in a layer of humor and charm, KUNAI is an experience worth savoring—a gleeful, high-flying adventure that reminds players why movement itself can be the most rewarding form of play.

Kunai is well executed aesthetically, but unfortunately it fails to deliver a good experience because of design and production flaws.

I want to start with the obvious and the crucial by pointing out that this is NOT a metroidvania game. It is a completely linear, 2D action platformer game. The fact the developers chose to tag their game as a metroidvania means that they are either amateurs that have no idea what they are talking about, or that they tried to draw extra interests from players by riding on this trendy genre, which is worse.
The game itself starts pretty straight forward with some tutorials. You unlock the Kunais which are the main unique mechanic that the entire game leans on. It is a fun mechanic, but it not intuitive to control. You can either choose to shoot in a 45 degrees angle to the right or to the left, or both, you can't aim it freely. I did get a grasp on having it feel intuitive until I reached the mid game, where I just couldn't feel like I could rely on those Kunais due to messy level design work.
As you progress you unlock new abilities (again, in a linear way), but they fail to shine because of the bad level design, The bosses at this part of the game also get more boring, it feels more like a platforming challenge than an actual fight.
The more I progressed, I just felt like the developers became lazy with their work and decided to simplify things. There was no challenge anymore, when you have all your abilities and upgrades (which are also easy to achieve) you simply become overpowered, it feels like you are playing with cheats. I wasn't engaged anymore, I simply wanted to get done with it.

It is a real shame because the pixel art and sounds are cute, the game is clear and it is easy to distinguish between enemies and other things that go on the screen, and the cutscenes are nice too. But I feel like they put all their effort on their "nice to have" rather than on what matters first.
It was so important for them to invest in so many cosmetic hats that you find in chests followed with long animations and without a skip button, or add robotic cats and add cat references here and there, or shove childish jokes to every monologue, instead of investing in the game itself by adding other interesting abilities, tweaking the levels, and fixing bugs.

I got the game because I wanted to play something that is not taken too seriously (after playing Sekiro). It looks cute and silly but it doesn't feel like it, it falls very fast and just becomes annoying.
Finally, given the low value of this game, the price is too high for what it is.

Potentially, it could be a really nice game. But the developers preferred to focus on how it looks rather than how it functions, which is a fundamental design principle.
At least they have all their assets ready, so if they really want to, they can rework the game to make it more fun.
Until then, I cannot recommend it, it is just not worth your money and time.

Kunai feels like a bunch of usually open levels put together, with occasional one-way platforming segments. While it may technically be a metroidvania, there is only a little bit of backtracking.  The game has surprises, with unexpected platforming segments littered throughout to mix up the gameplay a little bit, which gives it that adventure platformer feel.

I can't help but wonder if Haiku's visuals and style drew a little inspiration from Kunai, with the similar donut shaped currency and little robots.  Kunai reminds me occasionally of Donkey Kong Land games for the gameboy, and segments like the airship are a clear ode to those segments in the Mario games.  

The music and sound is all quite decent.

I've read the occasional review that has pretty bad information regarding the games difficulty.  It wasn't that hard of a game, but people less used to certain mechanics within the platforming genre could certainly find it trickier.  The difficulty felt balanced and fair throughout.  The grappling hooks are very easy to use, unlike something like Rusted Moss.  One reviewer cited a boss as being difficult that i killed in one try.. He obviously is unfamiliar with the concept of down-pogo (bouncing off of enemies by slashing downwards on their head), which you will get to utilise throughout the game, which I found to actually trivialise some of the early boss fights.  

For endgame cleanup, it would have been handy to have fast travel.  It isn't much of an issue during the main story however, because your character is quite fast and it never takes long to get from A to B.  Another feature I would've liked for the endgame would be some kind of item finder to help you finish uncovering the last of its secrets.

I enjoyed Kunai, and while I found it somewhat mid given some of the great games out there, the experience was worthwhile and satisfying enough.

This game is mostly average, I played through the whole thing and was ready to give it a 5/10 but the end section was so unnecessarily frustrating that I now hate the game.

Kunai is a bit of an awkward game for me to rate. It’s closer to a thumbs up than not; it has an interesting game play mechanic that other games don’t have. It falls on the easy side though (albeit with a few jarring difficulty spikes (I’m looking at you, Furious Ferro)), and for me it’s kind of just “meh”. There’s also a bit of false advertising with this game. It purports to be like a Metroid game; while there *is* backtracking in it (you can’t even fast travel AT ALL! You *will* be walking everywhere.), the game is actually *very* linear. 

The game takes a page out of Mega Man Zero’s opening to start. An ancient robot (an AI-driven tablet on a humanoid chassis, nicknamed “Tabby”.) that is somehow simultaneously more advanced than all the other robots has been hanging out in a tube for however long. Then a resistance force on the run from an oppressive government finds it and activates it just in time for it to rescue them from their attackers. Then the player fights their way through area after area at a breakneck pace, defeating a boss towards the end of each area and then moving on. Returning to previous areas is always possible, but almost always unnecessary except to go after missed health expansions or other pick-ups.

The bosses are mostly pushovers, though Furious Ferro’s final attack sequence is unreasonably difficult, and the final part of the Zensei fight being able to insta-kill the player + making it so that the player has to hug the top of the screen to prevent that from happening + getting hit making the fight reset every time it happens was a cruel and unusual set of design missteps that came out of nowhere. I digress. 

The game play consists of side-scrolling platforming and combat. Players are given an energy-absorbing katana to start with, which they can use to slice at enemies in 4 directions. Health in this game is reframed as battery power, and Tabby is fighting other robots, so destroying other robots causes them to drop particles of energy which are absorbed by the katana, recharging Tabby. TL; DR: kill enemies, get health drops. Side note: the katana can also be used to casually deflect projectiles back at enemies, which feels awesome to do.

A little later, players get a pair of kunai (thus the name of the game). This is where the game gets a little more interesting. Each kunai in the pair are mapped to a different button (On a keyboard: A for the left kunai, S for the katana, D for the right kunai), and they’re actually used as rope darts for traversing the environment, not as weapons. Each kunai is automatically thrown upwards in the direction it’s associated with when the player uses it, snapping to (presumably) preprogrammed points in the environment. The ropes are also elastic; if the player attaches both kunai to two nearby surfaces and then holds and releases the down key, they can launch themselves upwards (though the release window for the launch part is a little finicky). There are rarely any times where the launching thing is actually useful (or even possible), but it’s a fun little extra thing. Once the player gains access to the kunai, the entire game becomes “2D Spider-Man by way of kinda-sorta-but-not-really Metroid”.

Eventually players are given a few other things to augment their abilities. These include electrified shuriken (which stun enemies, or open doors and move platforms when thrown at special receptacles), an SMG (which lets players “spray-and-pray against enemies, or allows players to “hover” across large gaps by firing down), and a rocket launcher (which can be used to blast large rocks obstructing certain paths out of the way, as well as obliterating all the robots players hit with it within a rocket’s blast radius). Players also get a dash chip towards the end of the game, which allows Tabby to dash through the gaps in certain metal bars, as well as the final boss' beam attacks.

Aside from all ^^that^^, there’s also an in-game store where players can use in-game currency (also dropped by enemies) to buy performance enhancements for all of Tabby’s weapons, as well as a smithy bot that can upgrade the katana’s base damage output. Some of these upgrades are especially useful; once I got the ability that let me charge up Tabby’s katana attacks to perform an iai slice that transitions through multiple additional iai slices via flash-stepping to annihilate all the enemies on the screen as long as I kept hitting the katana button, I was using either that or rockets for most of the rest of the game. Then there’s the rocket jump upgrade, which would’ve been a no-brainer even if there wasn’t an optional time trial challenge in the game that literally can’t be beaten without it as far as I can tell.

There are also hats to collect throughout the game. Yay. 

All in all, the game is a decent amount of fun. As of me deciding to come back and write this review, this is my second time through it, and I do remember getting to the end of the game the first time and thinking, “Really? That’s it?” The game’s ending does kind of race up and smack you upside the head. It’s just like: get mech. Go to moon. Defeat boss. Roll credits. It’s all just very abruptly over.

If I step back and give the game the Metroid test as far as length goes, it’s actually twice as long as more recent Metroid games, or *four* times as long as the older ones, but it didn’t *feel* like it was longer.  It felt like the game just honestly didn’t have that much too it compared to other games in the genre, and then it was over, in spite of how long it actually seemed to take for me to beat it. 

I would call this a soft recommendation. Kunai is a fun game. If you take a look at it, and you think you’d like it because it looks like other things you’ve played, you’re right. It looks like the other things you’ve played because it is similar, and you will probably like it. 

Other side note: the soundtrack is pretty good. Especially the songs that play in areas that players spend the most time in. If nothing else, the soundtrack is worth a listen even if you don't buy the game. "Artificial Desert" is my favorite.

KUNAI is yet another of literally thousands of 2D retro pixel platformers infesting Steam and lowering the average quality of all video games everywhere.  This console ported 2D retro pixel platformer (sigh) is a metroidvania brawler/slasher with a bizarre theme where you're a computer headed person/robot/whatever.  Or a tablet headed person/robot/whatever made by computer headed robot/person/whatevers.  It doesn't really matter, it's all just lazy pixel blobs anyway.  

Gameplay itself is uninspired, controller handling and feel is a little floaty but it "works", putting this slightly above most 2D retro pixel garbage, but being close to the top of the pile of garbage doesn't change the smell. 

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

A choice was made to use obsolete, decades old retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics.  It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low as a result.  Worse, the developer couldn't work out how to use colours properly, despite the fact modern PC displays are capable of more than 16 million colours, the developer here simply didn't know how to make the game display with even as many colours as a Commodore 64 is capable of.  Ouch... talk about epic failure. 

There's no option to change the resolution and no useful graphics tweaks.  There's no way to ensure this is running at the native resolution of your display.  There's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.

Because this is designed for consoles, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the inferior console gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the console-centric developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for consoles forces upon a game.  Once more, console peasants have made gaming worse for everyone.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

KUNAI has the ridiculous price of $17 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  This costs more than Hollow Knight, and the developers there hired someone who knew how to at least do computer graphics beyond crappy lazy pixel "art".  This game, for reference, costs more than the Mass Effect Trilogy... so is the developer delusional and thinks this 2D retro pixelcrap is better than Mass Effect?  Or just setting out to insult gamers with a cash grab?  Either way, don't buy it.  This is also competing with over 9,000 free games available on Steam, many of them far better than this paid product.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.

I never saw much point in tablets. They lack the power and ease of use of computers, but also lack the portability of phones. This has nothing to do with my opinion on KUNAI, except perhaps the fact that I didn't like it as well.

What I did like about it was the music, at least early on. Also, once I got the kunai I also was surprised by how fun it is to use them to swing around! Made me feel like I'm using ninja rope in old Worms games. And then there's the detailed, bouncy look of Tabby, our protagonist; that part is pretty good at making you think this game looks nice.

Let me rephrase that: Tabby looks nice, the enemies look nice as well, the UI is crisp, but the environments... they're very samey and flat. No real landmarks or anything to help orient yourself. And this is a Metroidvania, so orienting yourself is a huge part of the game. Luckily, there's a map to help... you... with... that?

There is no map...?

Actually, there is. As an unlockable upgrade that you get roughly 45 minutes in, in a particularly confusing part of the third area of the game. And by "there is no map" I don't mean that you only get what your character has visited. No - the feature is completely absent (until you get it). Mix that with confusing, samey environments, and you'll understand why I spent some good 20 minutes of my playtime walking in circles.

To wrap things up, let me mention the titular kunai. The way they work is simple: you shoot a little rope at a 45 degree angle either to the left or to the right (separate buttons for greater control). This makes using them very quick, easy and indeed fun; that said, whenever a level of precision is needed things slow down a lot. Because you can't control the angle of your kunai shot, it's all about being in the right place so that your 45 degree shot hits what you want. And not all surfaces are suitable for you kunai to latch onto. Take it or leave it, I guess.

Okay, one last thing. The facial expressions. Tabby makes all sorts of weird faces. Normally he has a smile on his, uh, screen, but when you attack his expression changes to this hardcore fighter frown. When you slide down the wall, the expression changes to... I don't even know. Grinning teeth? And there's more, but I feel like Tabby doesn't really have a personality, it's just "make my face into an emoji" kind of thing. Is he silly or determined? Is he cool or happy? I don't know, and I don't care anymore.

So there you go. I just don't think KUNAI is that fun to play. If you're looking for a good Metroidvania involving cute robots I'd suggest checking out [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1231880/Haiku_the_Robot/?curator_clanid=42922988]Haiku the Robot[/url] instead.

A ridiculous and over the top metroidvania adventure that will take you about 5-8 hours depending on how thorough you are. The game will keep you entertained during those hours as the pacing is really good. This is on one hand due the constant progress of your movement/combat abilities as you navigate new environments and on the other hand because movement is fast and snappy. You can traverse the dozen or so zones at lightning speed, dashing and grappling whilst destroying everything in your path. This is extremely satisfying as you can tear through hordes of enemies very quickly. Combat and movement are thus solid which is one of the halmarks of a good metroidvania, the other being good level design. Here kunai also does pretty well, the environments are varied enough both in visuals and gameplay, with backtracking & multiple branching paths, shortcuts and secrets to discover. Sadly a lack of fast travel makes it too stingey to 100% the map. Visuals are fine, good pixel art but nothing spectacular/memorable. The character designs are pretty solid though, with distinct and easy to indentify characters to meet. Music is not my cup of tea, but it's a nice callback to the soundtracks of old, which works well in this game. Performance is great, and there's no bugs that i encountered so it's a well polished game. Lastly story is unremarkable (although hilarious at times) but that's fine as that's sort of like the cherry on top of a GREAT metroidvania. This one isn't one of those, but it's a good one nonetheless, especially because of the fun movement mechanics. i'd recommend it to any metroidvania/platformer fan.

KUNAI flips weapon progression systems on their head. You start with nothing but a katana, which is already the most powerful weapon in the game (and you can make it stronger), letting you heal yourself by attacking with it. Then it gives you a RIGHT kunai (grappling hook), making you go "oooh so its like Twilight Princess with the double clawshots" and then not 5 seconds later you find the LEFT kunai and you go "ooohh...?". From there on, its pretty standard, but still some surprising twists: you get throwing stars, but they don't do damage! By the time you get the BIG EXPLODY GUN, you've probably mastered every other weapon and know when its best to use the weaker guys and when to pull out the big guns. The only things I don't like about the weapons is that their charged attack upgrades are too slow to use when you'd need them most, and the best one (the one for the katana) trades off with health, so you will probably quickly stop using it. Also, the katana upgrades cost a shit ton. I think that's because they are meant to be a last resort, but even then, where do you make that much money?

Shockingly this game has absolutely no transport/teleport/quick travel mechanic. It's like a perfect case example of how sorely needed quick travel is in action platformers (idk if you can truly call this a metroidvania), because you will FEEL IT when you need to backtrack, and it almost seems like this game wants you to backtrack. Sometimes it's almost ridiculous, with one dungeon requiring you to walk across its entire length to go through a door you just flipped open, and then do the same thing but in reverse. It sucks and also demotivated me from going back to previous areas to find all the hidden chests.

Speaking of hidden chests... This game very much falls prey to the "invisible wall with a room behind it" torture that is a staple of metroidvanias now, I guess. Like collecting or finding hidden stuff? Settle in, because you are going to be rubbing against EVERY WALL to make sure you don't miss anything cool. Blegh, please no more.

The boss fights actually featured some great variety, which confirms this isn't a metroidvania. But... Zensei... Again, it's like a case study in why some bosses need checkpoints, or just like, a way to not have to redo the entire fight because the last section is inexplicably much harder than the rest. I was so fed up with Zensei by the time I beat him, it was not at all a "YES! I DID IT!" it was a "the pain is over, and now i can begin healing".

The music is sick, Quantum Forest made me just want to spend more time there. However, I was pretty surprised to find the Final Boss music was... the same as every other boss. And the credits music... was the boss music again. I think. Or maybe it was the main menu music? Anyways, the extremely sudden credits roll with the reused track made me feel like I was giving too long of a speech at the Oscars. Like, "ok ok you did it, nice job, hurry up and get outta here".

Mixed feelings across the board. Definitely a fun time, but very much having some sore spots of major frustration.

This game has a colorful world with plenty to explore. The movement feels nice and the combat works really well. The bosses are also really fun to fight. The game kinda falls off towards the end though. The level design starts to feel unfair with a lot of blind jumps and platforms off screen that you're expected to somehow jump to without taking damage, and the final boss, as well as the final world right before the boss, are really generic and underwhelming. The final boss especially was underwhelming compared to the other really creative fights throughout the game. 

Despite this criticism, Kunai is still a great metroidvania that I strongly recommend! The game has solid mechanics, and it is was fun from start to finish.

I really enjoyed playing this game. The story was ok, wasn't really fantastic. Really loved the pixelated graphics and the animations. The best thing was to play around with the kunais. The bosses were interesting, the final one was a bit hard but it's not impossible.

There are a few downsides with this game. First downside is that, there are not teleporters. Once you complete an objectiv like "investigate the power source in a city" you have to go all the way back to your base. And the base is  very far away, it gets worse if you die cause you spawn at your last checkpoint. The second downside is that in the game has a "Blacksmith" that gives you upgrades for your sword, and it is quite expensive. The point is those upgrades are pointless. They don't give you anything. And the last thing is the dash. You unlock the dash almost at the end of the game, i think you should unlock it at the beginning.

But overall i enjoyed it. Recommend it.
